10003-my-first-years-as-a-frenchwoman-18:
Mary King Waddington, an American who married into French politics, published this memoir in 1914. Its frontispiece shows her in the Exposition year of 1878. It covers her first years as a Frenchwoman, from 1876 to 1879, when Marshal MacMahon was president.

Chapters follow the Assembly at Versailles and her husband as minister of public instruction, later prime minister. They cover the social side of a minister's wife, the Exposition year, the Berlin Congress, and gaieties at the Quai d'Orsay. Readers get the Third Republic from inside a minister's household, with gossip, ceremony, and politics together.
21788-held-fast-for-england-a-tale-of-th:
The great siege of Gibraltar, from 1779 to 1783, gives G. A. Henty the ground for this boys' tale of war. In his preface, Henty says the siege stands almost alone in the annals of war. Its length and the vast efforts made against the Rock set it apart. Yet the fortress, he notes, was never truly in danger of capture. Its defense succeeded where Sebastopol and Paris later failed.

His young hero reaches Gibraltar after privateers and an unexpected journey, then lives through the siege itself. Chapters bring a welcome cargo, cruises in privateers, and the famous floating batteries. Bob even wins a commission from the governor. Henty mixes solid history with a lad's adventures, his proven recipe for teaching the past.
22387-a-tour-in-ireland-1776-1779:
Arthur Young's Tour in Ireland covers his travels of 1776 to 1779. Young was England's best-known writer on farming and rural life. His earlier tours through England had already made his name.

The Farmer's Tour through the East of England ran to four volumes. Those appeared in 1770 and 1771 to wide notice. Encouraged, Young went on with increasing vigor to Ireland. There he inquired into farming, manufactures, and population. His Irish tour applies the same sharp questions across the sea. Readers get an economist's travel record. It shows Irish land, labor, and poverty through the eyes of a reforming visitor.
30048-the-contemporary-review-volume-36-:
Volume 36 of The Contemporary Review gathers the issues from September through December 1879, printed in London by Strahan and Company. September opens with Sir Walter Medhurst on the future of China, St. George Mivart on animals and plants, and Vernon Lee on the artistic dualism of the Renaissance. Edward Caird writes on Comte, Richard Proctor on the Great Pyramid, and Karl Blind on conspiracies in Russia.

Later months add India and Afghanistan, critical idealism in France, myths of the sea, and reviews of biblical literature, essays, novels, and poetry. The volume shows a Victorian review at full range, moving from science and art to empire, faith, and foreign politics in a single run. Readers can dip into one essay or follow a whole season of debate.
36201-francis-drake-and-the-california-i:
Francis Drake and the California Indians, 1579 is a study by Robert F Heizer, issued by the University of California Press at Berkeley and Los Angeles in 1947. It forms part of the university's publications in American archaeology and ethnology, volume forty-two, number three. A plate shows Drake being crowned by the natives of New Albion in June 1579, from a Dutch print of 1673.

Heizer weighs where Drake actually landed and careened his ship. He sets the Trinidad Bay theory against the claims of Bodega Bay and Drake's Bay, then takes apart the account in The World Encompassed. Added items from the Richard Madox and John Drake accounts and supposed Indian traditions follow. His verdict leaves the choice between two bays, Drake's or Bodega, likely forever unsettled in detail.
3656-cyprus-as-i-saw-it-in-1879:
Samuel White Baker writes an account of Cyprus as he saw it in 1879, the year after Britain took over the island's administration. Baker, an explorer and former governor in Africa, traveled Cyprus to judge its land, people, and prospects under new rule. His book describes villages, farms, harbors, and the hills and plains of the island.

Baker writes with a colonial official's eye, praising Cyprus's climate and soil while noting poverty, taxes, and old Turkish administration. Modern readers will read his judgments with care, as a view from empire. The book suits those interested in Cyprus, the eastern Mediterranean, and the first years of British rule there.
39459-the-contemporary-review-volume-36-:
The Contemporary Review, volume thirty-six, is kept here in its October 1879 number. Ten articles and a survey of contemporary books fill the issue, and the contents page names each writer. India and Afghanistan opens it, by Colonel Osborn, followed by Paul Janet on critical idealism in France.

Francis Newman writes on the moral limits of beneficial commerce, and Keary on the myths of the sea and the river of death. Darmesteter takes the supreme god in Indo-European mythology, and Mivart the forms and colours of living creatures. An Eastern statesman reports contemporary life and thought in Turkey. Osborn's opening article begins with the news that Major Cavagnari and his companions had been killed by the populace at Kabul.
39517-the-contemporary-review-volume-36-:
The Contemporary Review for November 1879 is part of volume thirty six of the journal. Seven articles fill the number. Max Müller opens with an essay On Freedom. Twenty years had passed since Mill sent forth his plea for liberty, Müller notes. In that essay, he writes, Mill for once becomes passionate. Two studies of Gladstone, by a Liberal and a Conservative, face each other next.

Von Sybel treats the old regime and the revolution in France. The actual condition of Ireland is asked and answered. Lenormant gathers the traditions of the Deluge among ancient nations. Proctor writes on suspended animation. Jevons tests Mill's philosophy in a fourth instalment, on utilitarianism. Theology, politics, and science share the review's pages as usual.
40191-josh-billings-farmer-s-allminax-18:
Josh Billings old farmer almanacs of 1870 to 1879 stand gathered here. Dillingham printed the Allminax in New York in 1902 with pictures. Comic illustrations and weather hints, perhaps rain perhaps not, front it. The title page promises a decade of farm years in one.

Sighns ov the zodiac open the text in dialect spelling style. An Amerikan brave stands attacked by the twelve constellations there. A key tew the abuv performance gives mock rules for signs. Multiply the day by the sign and hunt a dividend, it bids. Horoscope tables in the almanac carry symbols the plain text shows as marks in place.
47829-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary, volume thirty three, number two, for February eighteen seventy nine, was published in New York by the American Missionary Association at fifty six Reade Street. The price was fifty cents a year in advance. The motto reads, To the poor the Gospel is preached. Editorial paragraphs and a concert of prayer head the number. Field reports from the South, the West, and overseas fill most pages.

Pieces treat missions in Central Africa and how a college directs natural forces. Puritanism and the despised races and the re dedication of the Beach Institute share the front. Reports then come from work among the freedmen in North Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, and Tennessee. Work among the Chinese, among the Indians, and the Mendi Mission in West Africa are also told. A children page, receipts, and wants close the number. Church readers got a monthly map of home and foreign missions.
53618-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary for January 1879 is a monthly number of the American Missionary Association's magazine, volume thirty-three, number one, published at New York for fifty cents a year. The contents open with the Association's outlook for 1879 and an appeal for the new year.

The reports cover the Association's fields. For the freedmen: a revival at Howard University, a destitute Virginia county, a new church at Shelby Iron Works in Alabama, and free schools in Missouri. From Africa, the Mendi mission reports a church organised and dedicated at Avery. Other pieces treat the late Indian war and Christianity, and a Congregational association of Christian Chinese. Strieby writes on the political progress of the freedmen; Hartranft proposes five tests of American civilization. Receipts and statistics close the number. It is Reconstruction's missionary movement taking stock, two years after federal troops left the South.
53966-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary, volume thirty-three, number five, for May, eighteen seventy-nine, is the monthly paper of the American Missionary Association. The rooms of the group were at 56 Reade Street, New York, and the price was fifty cents a year. The motto on the cover is that to the poor the gospel is preached. Lists of officers fill the front pages.

The contents mix short comment, field reports, and accounts of money received. Reports from the freedmen's schools tell of tours in the Southwest and of work in Atlanta, Montgomery, and Mobile. Straight University in Louisiana and a revival at Corpus Christi also report. Other parts treat native preachers in Africa and the Chinese question on the west coast. A copy of the group's charter and its wants close the number.
54119-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary for June 1879 is one monthly issue of the journal of the American Missionary Association of New York. It is volume thirty-three, number six, priced at fifty cents a year. Its motto is: to the poor the Gospel is preached. The contents mix editorial notes, field reports, and the association's receipts and statistics.

The largest section treats work among the freedmen of the South. It reports a month-long tour through the South Atlantic states, a students' day at Le Moyne in Memphis, and new churches and schools in Georgia. Charleston's Plymouth Church and Avery Institute appear, with conferences in Alabama and Louisiana. Shorter sections cover work among the Indians and a paper on the Congregational way in missions among the Chinese. The issue is a working record of home missions in the Reconstruction South.
54131-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary, volume thirty three, number twelve, is the December 1879 issue of the American Missionary Association journal. It sold for fifty cents a year from rooms at 56 Reade Street, New York. The number is given over to the annual meeting. Contents list reports, proceedings, and a general survey. A finance report sets out the outlook for the work ahead.

Sections then report on work among freedmen, in Africa, and among Native peoples. A further section covers work among Chinese people. Named talks treat schooling and church work in the South, the Mendi country, and the Indian question. The issue shows how the group framed its tasks, funds, and fields at the close of the eighteen seventies.
54234-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
American Missionary, volume thirty three number seven, is a monthly journal from July eighteen seventy nine. The American Missionary Association issued it from Reade Street in New York. Its motto reads, to the poor the gospel preached, on the cover. The price was fifty cents a year, paid in advance by readers.

Contents list church notes, signs of the times, and answered prayer. A large block covers work among freedmen in the South after slavery. Hampton, Fisk, Straight, Tougaloo, and Howard schools report their closing days. A further block treats mission work among Chinese readers in America. Receipts, a constitution, and wants and counts close the issue out.
54429-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary for September 1879 is volume thirty three, number nine, of the American Missionary Association's monthly. The Association published it at 56 Reade Street, New York, at fifty cents a year. Its motto stands on the cover: to the poor the Gospel is preached.

Eli Corwin writes the foreword. Editorials treat the literature of the Southern work and the tenth commandment, and a column explains winding up a horse. The Freedmen section reports the Swayne School at Montgomery and the Le Moyne School at Memphis. A colored girl tells her experience as a teacher, and a Tougaloo student writes from Mississippi. Reports from Georgia describe dying scenes and pressing work, and a new field at Cypress Slash. Africa follows, with the Mendi Mission at Avery, and a piece on false brethren among the Chinese mission. Receipts close the number.
54589-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
Volume thirty three, number ten of The American Missionary came out in New York in October 1879. The American Missionary Association published it at fifty cents a year from rooms at 56 Reade Street. Its motto says to the poor the gospel is preached. Editorial paragraphs open with the annual meeting.

A worker at rest and the death of Father Jocelyn get notices. A strong appeal and the language of equatorial Africa follow. The freedmen section tells of north and south, of a remarkable conversion and triumphant death at Nashville, and of first impressions at Byron, Georgia. The Chinese section reports the beginning of harvest. Receipts, statistics, and wants close a working mission paper.
54885-the-american-missionary-vol-33-no-:
The American Missionary, volume thirty-three, number three, is the March 1879 number. The American Missionary Association at 56 Reade Street, New York, made it. Its price was fifty cents a year, paid in advance. Its motto runs: to the poor the gospel is preached. Contents open with editorial matter: a generous gift and a call to go forward.

An offer by Arthington and a new recruit for the Mendi mission follow. General Fisk speaks at a Sunday-school concert in the number. Work among the freedmen fills a long section of reports. Atlanta University saw a revival among its students, one report says. Straight University at New Orleans and Fisk University at Nashville report too. Mission work among the Chinese and a Christmas in Africa take pages. A children's page and the receipts close the number.
55156-the-american-missionary-volume-33-:
The American Missionary, the monthly magazine of the American Missionary Association, volume 33, number 11, for November 1879. Its motto: to the poor the gospel is preached. Price fifty cents a year.

The contents report the association's annual meeting and the death of the Reverend William Patton. Reports from the field follow the association's three great works: freedmen in the Carolinas, Georgia, and Alabama; the Mendi and Arthington missions in Africa; and missions among the Clallam Indians. A children's page offers cabin prayer-meetings, and receipts and statistics close the number. Readers get the machinery of post-Civil War home and foreign missions at work.
56130-letters-to-a-friend-written-to-mrs:
Letters to a Friend is a book of the notes of John Muir to the wife of Ezra Carr. The notes span the years from eighteen sixty six to eighteen seventy nine. The book was put out at Boston and New York in nineteen fifteen. Its rights were held that year by a kin of the hand. This form of the book was struck in a run of three hundred.

A first note tells how the bond of the two was made. Muir was a young man at a school of the west. He was a guest oft at the house of her mate, a man of lore. Her warm care, as a plant wise maid and a friend of the wild world, won his trust. He held her as a guide of his soul.
59916-north-carolina-medical-journal-vol:
The North Carolina Medical Journal, volume three, number four, for April eighteen seventy nine, was edited at Wilmington by M J DeRosset and Thomas F Wood. Original communications head the number. A first paper, Something about Drinking Waters, comes from Albert R Ledoux of Chapel Hill. Ledoux opens with callings and duties. Every man must have his vocation and his specialty, he says.

We are all dependent on others when problems outside our own line demand a solution, Ledoux holds. Live and help live should be the motto, not live and let live alone, he adds. Medicine has joined chemistry and architecture to form sanitary science, he notes. No question in that science matters more than drinking water and health, he holds. Doctors get a state journal of practice and hygiene.
62326-a-list-of-c-kegan-paul-co-s-public:
A List of C Kegan Paul and Company's Publications, from 1 Paternoster Square, London, is the firm's own catalogue of 1879. It opens not with books but with the firm's monthly review, The Nineteenth Century, edited by James Knowles at half a crown. The names of its writers fill a page.

Gladstone leads them, with Matthew Arnold, Froude, Huxley, Ruskin, Cardinal Manning, Tennyson, and Tyndall in the ranks. Then the books begin, each with its size and price. The autobiography of Abdulla, a Malay munshi, stands at twelve shillings, and Adams's Field and Forest Rambles, by a naturalist in New Brunswick, at fourteen. The list is a shelf-map of one London house at work.
65222-migration-of-birds-1979:
Frederick C Lincoln wrote Migration of Birds for the United States Fish and Wildlife Service, and Steven R Peterson revised it for the nineteen seventy-nine edition. Peter A Anastasi helped edit the text, and Bob Hines drew the pictures. The work came out as Circular Sixteen of the service.

Pages cover how birds are watched, marked, banded, and tracked by radio and radar. Chapters deal with why birds move, what starts the move, and when flights take place. Speed, height, weather, and land shape all get full treatment. Later parts map the chief routes from North America and name the risks birds face on the way.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: John Quincy Adams, schooled in Paris and Leyden and secretary at fourteen, fills this second volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume prints his messages and papers as president, with a life sketch of the sixth president. Adams accompanied his father to France as a boy and learned Latin and Greek abroad. The compilation preserves his official words for the historical record.
al-tabari-sasanian-history-noeldeke-1879:
Al-Tabari, the great historian of Baghdad, opened his vast History of the Prophets and Kings with the ancient world and the kings of Persia. Theodor Nöldeke turned the Sasanian portion into German in 1879. His version is the chief public domain rendering of Tabari. The text recounts Persia and the Arabs in the age of the Sasanians.

The Persian kings pass in line from Ardashir to Yazdegerd, with their wars against Rome and their court tales. Beside them stand the Arab buffer kings of Hira and the tribes of the desert. Nöldeke adds deep notes on names, dates, and Persian sources. Through Tabari, the lost chronicles of Sasanian Persia still speak.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-i:
Allen's Encyclopaedia needed a key, and the general index of 1879 provides it. Ten volumes of proving symptoms are hard to search by hand, so the index cross-references symptoms and remedies across the whole set. A reader starts from a sign and lands on the drugs that produced it.

That makes the slim index the most practical volume of the eleven for daily use. It turns a vast archive into a working tool at the desk. Anyone using Allen's record today still begins here, since the index shows at a glance where each remedy and symptom can be found.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
Allen closed his Encyclopaedia with Volume X in 1879, six years after the first volume appeared. Ten volumes hold the fullest proving record homeopathy ever made, and the last one completes the alphabetical span of remedies. Timothy Field Allen could finally point to the whole archive, finished at last.

Later generations quarried the set for repertories, keynotes, and condensed guides of every kind. The raw pages remain the court behind those courts, where a claim about a drug can be checked against the provers' own words. Volume X ends the largest homeopathic materia medica ever compiled, a monument to patient gathering.
arxiv-2412-00079:
Mohammad Ali Afshar and Jafar Sadeghi study black holes under two added twists to gravity, in this 2024 paper. One twist blurs space at tiny scales, and the other adds a curvature term. They ask how the two jointly shape light paths and orbits, and whether cosmic rules still guard the black hole form.

In a plain model, the curvature term had a hard cap, past which the object could only be a bare singularity. A richer model with strings and charge behaved differently, and even an over-charged object kept its black hole form. Heat checks in both cases fit a rule that links charge and mass. The authors argue that rule protects the guard rule for hidden singularities.
arxiv-2412-00179:
Arturo de Giorgi and Maria Ramos map what happens to an axion living in extra spacetime dimensions, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Axions are candidate particles invented to settle a symmetry puzzle in the strong nuclear force. When an axion fills a higher-dimensional bulk, it splits into a tower of modes, and the lightest is usually expected to play the standard QCD axion role.

The authors chart the full parameter space for flat and warped extra dimensions. In some regions no single mode sits on the standard axion line; instead several modes share the job of solving the puzzle. Those regions, they find, collide with tight observational limits. Only the standard pattern, they conclude, plausibly survives, and they extend the mode equations to any number of extra dimensions.
arxiv-2412-00279:
Matias Carrasco and co-authors work out the best local storage rule for items asked for over time. Their paper from 2024 frames memory keeping as a point process problem, where asks arrive as random events. The goal is the causal rule that lifts the hit chance most.

For repeating ask patterns they find a clean large system limit. As the catalog grows, the best rule compares each item live ask intensity against a fixed cut from a limit spread. Sharp bounds for finite size are also given. The rule links to timer based keeping when ask rates fall in a set way. Tests show it beats standard rules by a wide margin on regular traffic.
arxiv-2412-00379:
The LHAASO Collaboration reports an enigmatic PeVatron near the HII region G35.6-0.5 in a two thousand twenty-four astrophysics paper. A PeVatron is a cosmic accelerator powerful enough to push particles to peta-electronvolt energies, among the most extreme in the Galaxy.

LHAASO, the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory, detects the gamma rays such accelerators produce. The collaboration's author list runs to hundreds of names, reflecting the scale of the instrument. The paper presents the source as puzzling: its properties around the named star-forming region do not fit a simple explanation. Identifying what powers Galactic PeVatrons is a central open question in cosmic ray physics.
arxiv-2412-00979:
Zhe Wang, Haozhu Wang, and Yanjun Qi present a 2024 paper on teaching agents new tasks from few demos. Their base method casts learning as sequence prediction, guided by prompts. Past prompt methods used fixed prompt parts, which cannot adapt to the moment. The team adds two prompt layers, one global and one that adapts at each step.

Global tokens carry the gist of sample paths for a task. Adaptive tokens are pulled from a stored set of demo parts to fit the current step. Tests ran on seven benchmark tasks in two model worlds. The method beat all rivals in those tests. The authors argue that layered prompts are a sound path to fast learning from few examples.
arxiv-2412-01079:
Tianwang Jia and co-authors present a 2024 computing paper on reading imagined movement from brain signals without pooling private data. Brain-computer interfaces decode EEG patterns, and good decoders need data from many users. Those users reasonably refuse to hand over raw brain recordings.

Federated learning trains a shared model while the data stays on each user's side. Their method, FedBS, adds two twists: batch normalization kept local to each client, which tames the mismatch between people's signals, and a sharpness-aware optimizer, which makes the shared model generalize better. On three public data sets and three network designs, FedBS beat six rival federated methods. It even beat old-style pooled training. Privacy and accuracy, the paper argues, can rise together.
arxiv-2412-01779:
Nathaniel Bottman and Katrin Wehrheim build a frame for work with adiabatic limits, the slow squeezes that show up in geometry and Floer theory. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-four. In an adiabatic step, one part of a problem shrinks and a simpler limit comes into view. To make such steps sound, one needs to know how sets of solutions act in the squeeze.

They define adiabatic Fredholm families and the kinds of smoothness such families may carry. A worked out construction then cuts problems down to finite size. These small versions fit all common schemes for regularization. They keep the continuity and smoothness of the full family. The authors also show how to build families for limits tied to the Atiyah-Floer conjecture. Strip-shrinking in quilted Floer theory gets the same care.
arxiv-2412-01879:
Tereza Constantinou, Oliver Shorttle, and Paul Rimmer read Venus's air to learn whether the planet's interior holds water, in a 2024 paper. Venus may once have had oceans and a mild climate, or it may have been born too hot for surface water ever to settle. The two stories point to very different edges for the habitable zone around stars.

Sunlight and chemistry destroy water and other gases in Venus's air at a known pace. Volcanoes must replace those gases to keep the air steady, so the air's makeup betrays what the interior holds. The math says volcanic gas there is at most six percent water, far drier than Earth's magmas. A dry inside favors the story that Venus dried out early and never had oceans.
arxiv-2412-01979:
Jinming Xing, Chang Xue, Dongwen Luo, and Ruilin Xing present FGATT, a method to fill gaps in wireless data. Their twenty twenty-four paper tackles a common flaw: sensor and network data often go missing, which breaks the models trained on them.

FGATT mixes two tools. A fuzzy graph attention network learns how places link, even when no map is given, and a graph that adapts itself keeps those links current. A transformer encoder then reads the time pattern, so both space and time guide each fill. Tests show it beats top past methods, above all when large chunks are missing. The team aims it at sensor networks and smart devices.
arxiv-2412-02379:
Magnus Goffeng, Bram Mesland, and Mehmet Haluk Sengün build a 2024 bridge between local and global views of a deep math structure. Number theory often builds global objects by joining local pieces, one for each prime. The authors ask whether the same join works for a class of operator algebra objects tied to symmetry.

They show how to join a family of local pieces into one global piece when the pieces fit well. Applied to a known local process that builds new symmetry displays, the join gives the global form of that process. The result links two fields that grew apart. It may guide later work on both sides.
arxiv-2412-02879:
Maria Cardei and co-authors propose, in a 2024 paper, a method for spotting when two people move together through space and time. Finding shared movement patterns matters for health and behavior studies. Older methods lean on sequence models that are hard to interpret and miss partial matches.

Their method turns movement tables into trajectory pictures over chosen time windows. It then localizes the paths, checks for overlap, and matches pairs with a twin neural network. Tests on a co-walking task showed the approach works. Partial matching is the key advance, since people rarely walk in perfect sync. Interpretable pictures also let researchers see why the system paired two paths.
arxiv-2412-02979:
Cámara casts quantum facts for bent spaces in a form that shuns grid picks in this twenty twenty-four paper. Chance clouds for free bits must be re-cast when space bends from flat. A fine fact grade that no grid can sway is the core need here.

Inside, a known cloud form is stretched to hold on any bent space shape. Fact grade is then run past the mid ghost states that the cloud hides. A wave toy in flat and in bent space shows the frame at work in tests. A broad fact- doubt law is drawn for bent fields from the same base. The work ties fact, shape, and quantum craft in one shared frame.
arxiv-2412-03079:
Jiahao Lu and nine co-authors estimate depth for moving video from a single camera, keeping the depth steady from frame to frame, in this 2024 paper. Still image depth tools flicker when applied to video, and video diffusion solutions are costly and give no camera path. Their method, Align3R, borrows a recent model that reconstructs scenes from image pairs.

First they fine tune that model for dynamic scenes, feeding it single image depth guesses as extra input. Then an optimization step rebuilds consistent depth maps together with the camera's poses through the scene. Tests show the approach beating baselines on both depth consistency and pose accuracy. The authors pitch it for creators and robots that need stable three dimensional readings from ordinary monocular footage.
arxiv-2412-03379:
August Leander Høeg and co-authors present, in a 2024 paper, a neural network that sharpens 3D scans. Super-resolution in volumes has lagged behind photo work because the attention trick behind transformer models eats memory in three dimensions. That cap shrinks the area each part of the model can see, so long-range links go unused. Their model, MTVNet, works from coarse to fine scales to widen that view.

Special carrier tokens ferry facts from broad, coarse regions down to finer ones, step by step. Transformer layers run at each scale, but the token count stays modest, so attention can span large areas at last. On five 3D data sets, MTVNet beat the top rival models. The edge grew on larger images, where a wide view matters most. Code is public.
arxiv-2412-03679:
Seungone Kim and nine co-authors build a shared yardstick for judging how well language models can make training data for other models. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Fake data now fills much of post-training, so making good data counts as much as solving tasks. Past studies each used their own setup, so models could not be compared fairly.

Their bench, AgoraBench, fixes the settings and scores for the test. Six models each made over a million training items, and near a hundred student models were trained on the output. Strengths split by task: one model wrote the best new problems, another improved old ones best. Skill at making data did not track skill at solving tasks. Data traits like answer quality and task hardness predicted success better. Format and cost choices also swayed the results.
arxiv-2412-03879:
Jaelyn Liang, Rehaan Mundy, and Shriya Jagwayan study how online trade is reshaping town and country economies in Africa, in work from 2024. Online trade is growing fast on the continent and brings chances for growth and wider market reach. Yet lands differ sharply in how ready they are for it.

The team scored readiness by mobile money use, income per head, internet reach, and digital plant. Case studies cover Lagos, Kano, Nairobi, and the Rift Valley. City firms gained most in output and profit. Rural areas grew more slowly, held back by weak internet and roads. Local fixes such as mobile money and farm trade platforms are closing some gaps. The authors call for aimed spending to spread the gains.
arxiv-2412-04079:
Chantal Tinner and co-authors measure how electron bombardment breaks water ice and builds up trapped oxygen. Icy moons and comets face constant radiation in space. That radiation sputters and chemically alters their surfaces.

Lab samples of porous ice mimicked real regolith surfaces. Mass tools measured gases released under electron fire. Most products leave the ice as hydrogen and oxygen gas. Some oxygen stays trapped inside the ice under set conditions. The team quantified how long it stays and when it saturates. Water release was harder to pin down exactly. Flux levels changed the water yield notably. The data aid readings of icy moon and comet surfaces.
arxiv-2412-04279:
Alan Li and Angela P. Schoellig improve robot estimates of object pose by training on hard cases, in a 2024 paper. Knowing an object's exact position and angle is vital for robot grasping. Bin picking is tough because items lack texture and hide behind each other. Even strong models fail on certain poses and levels of occlusion.

The method first maps where the model errs across pose and occlusion space. It then uses a simulator to make realistic training images aimed at those weak spots. The approach works with any pose model. Extra training on targeted hard samples lifts accuracy where it counts most. Warehouses and factories stand to gain from fewer failed picks.
arxiv-2412-04579:
Brian Rider and Benedek Valkó set out, in a 2024 paper on math, two groups of random matrices whose eigenvalue patterns can be worked out in full. Most work in this field rests on rough guesses or on broad limits that hold for many cases. A joint pattern that can be worked out in full is rare.

Their block tridiagonal matrices give patterns unlike the field's standard gas-like forms. The eigenvalues act on each other in richer ways than the classic mean-field view allows. The authors trace the edge of the spectrum in two ways: through random differential operators, and through linked wandering processes. New algebraic identities for products of determinants appear along the way. Such solvable cases anchor a field built in large part on claims that the same limits hold for all.
arxiv-2412-04679:
John Howell and co-authors report in 2024 a low-cost multispectral camera built on a Raspberry Pi for physics teaching. The pilot ran in Ecuador, South Africa, and the United States after talks with African educators. Demand for cheap hands-on skill tools proved very high in those talks.

The printed camera reads fifteen to twenty five color bands for as little as one hundred dollars. Students learn printing, coding, control, and image study while they build it. Class projects span plant health, fruit ripeness, and insect wing patterns. One wing study won a best applied research poster award at a meeting.
arxiv-2412-04779:
Kunika Agarwal and co-authors show that correlations no classical physics allows can resurrect channels that are provably mute. A channel's zero-error capacity counts messages it can send with absolute certainty; some noisy channels have none at all. Pre-shared nonlocal correlations, of the kind Bell tests certify, change the answer.

For a family of channels in the two-party, two-input scenario, extremal nonlocal correlations let one perfect bit through where zero-error capacity was zero. Quantum entanglement alone cannot open these channels fully, the team shows, though it sharply raises single-shot success odds. In a mirrored scenario the assisted channels carry a full log-scaled payload perfectly. The authors present Bell nonlocality as a practical resource for certainty-grade communication, not just a foundational curiosity.
arxiv-2412-05079:
YingXing Cheng and Benjamin Stamm simplify a method for splitting electron clouds in a 2024 paper. Chemists often divide a molecule's electron density among its atoms to understand charge and bonding. The Iterative Stockholder Analysis does this by fitting each atom with smooth basis functions. The authors build faster approximations of that scheme using exponential basis functions.

Their family splits into a linear model, LISA, and a nonlinear one, NLIS. With the right settings, the nonlinear model can reproduce both LISA and an older minimal-basis method. Four LISA variants were built from basis sets fitted on lone atoms. Tests on fifteen small molecules, neutral and charged, compared accuracy, robustness, and cost. One Gaussian-based LISA variant gave the best balance. The authors propose new score metrics to make such comparisons clearer for future work.
arxiv-2412-05179:
Thomas Walker, Octave Mariotti, Amir Vaxman, and Hakan Bilen wrote a 2024 paper on teaching computers to rebuild surfaces from data. Neural surface methods learn a scene's shape as a smooth field. A key ingredient tells the network where things sit at many levels of detail, from coarse to fine. Current methods use one fixed set of those signals for every scene. That choice bakes in a bias that may not fit all shapes.

The authors let the network choose its own signals at each place in space. Features stored at different grid resolutions can be masked up or down as needed. Smooth areas can lean on coarse signals, while detailed areas draw on fine ones. This freedom lets the model capture a wider range of detail without adding noise. On standard benchmark datasets, the method reached the best scores reported.
arxiv-2412-05279:
Susung Hong, Johanna Karras, Ricardo Martin-Brualla, and Ira Kemelmacher-Shlizerman present a flexible way to edit 3D scenes with text, in work from 2024. Text driven image models have sped up 3D building and editing. Past editors handle color, texture, and style well but fail at large shape or look changes.

Their Perturb-and-Revise method first shakes the scene's parameters with random starts. The amount of shaking is set by the local shape of the loss. Then a generative path revises the scene toward the text goal. Extra gradients guard the identity of the original scene. Tests show edits of color, look, and shape that stay consistent.
arxiv-2412-05379:
Weather itself jiggles gravity enough to trouble future atom interferometers, John Carlton and co-authors warn in a 2024 paper. Tall atom devices will hunt dark matter and gravity waves from underground halls. Shifting air pressure and temperature change local gravity in the signal band.

Seismic noise got the early attention; this work builds the air-driven half of the story. Burying the device helps, and the team weighs how much. Global high and low noise models for pressure effects are fitted from data, with a temperature range beside them. Site choice for these costly instruments now has weather math to lean on.
arxiv-2412-05479:
Zixian Ma and co-authors present, in a 2024 paper, a family of vision-language models that hand sight work to expert vision tools. Open models do well on plain image questions. Hard ones need both sharp sight and step thought, and there they lag. Their family, LATTE, lets top vision models do the seeing. The main model then thinks over that clean sight output, in place of raw pixels. That split lets it spend its force on the thought steps.

To train it, the team built and sifted 293,000 traces of such thought over sight output. Models trained on those traces gained 4 to 5 percent over base lines on six bench sets. Tests that cut one part at a time show the gain rests on the source, form, and quality of the traces. The code path is set out for reuse.
arxiv-2412-05779:
Tao Fu and co-authors dissect the thermonuclear bursts of a newly found neutron star system. Their 2024 paper analyzes observations of SRGA J144459.2-604207, a millisecond pulsar caught in outburst that year, taken with the Insight-HXMT telescope.

Sixty bursts were caught in one detector and thirty-seven in two at once. Stacking the shared bursts revealed a dip in hard X-rays during the flash. From burst spectra the team read the fuel recipe, finding hydrogen made up about a third of the fuel at ignition. Fourteen bursts expanded the star's photosphere, which set the distance near ten kiloparsecs. As feeding slowed, the wait between bursts stretched from about one and a half to eight hours.
arxiv-2412-06379:
Sunil Das works on a question about matrices and the patterns of signs in their entries, in a 2024 math paper. A matrix is called positive when every entry sits above zero. A square matrix is called algebraically positive when some polynomial applied to it yields a positive matrix. The paper links these ideas to cycle graphs, which are ring-shaped networks.

Das asks which sign patterns, tied to such rings, force every matrix with that pattern to be algebraically positive. Patterns with this forcing trait are said to require the property. The paper sorts all such patterns for cycle graphs, giving a complete list. Results of this kind help mathematicians know what a bare pattern of plus, minus, and zero entries can promise about a whole family of matrices.
arxiv-2412-06479:
Karl Kunisch and John Simon study shape optimization with missing boundary data in a 2024 mathematics paper. The shape is governed by an elliptic equation, and part of the boundary condition is unknown. Optimizing as if the data were complete could yield shapes that fail when the missing part is revealed.

They formulate the task as a no regret problem and approximate it with low regret versions. That produces deformation fields that stay robust against the missing information. The authors analyze convergence, characterize the gradient of the cost, and propose a numerical method. Examples illustrate the robustness of the approach.
arxiv-2412-06679:
Eva González-Ruiz, Johannes Bjerlin, Oliver Dall'Alba Sandberg, and Anders Sørensen study how leaks from the driving laser spoil a source of single photons. Such sources are key for quantum optics, but in practice the excitation light can stray into the detector path. The team asks how pulse length and filtering shape the damage.

They find that the length of the excitation pulse strongly affects how pure the single-photon stream stays. They compute how the leak changes the share of unwanted two-photon events and the visibility in a classic interference test. Filtering the outgoing light can shift these traits a lot. The link between photon purity and interference visibility proves more tangled than often assumed.
arxiv-2412-06879:
Tomáš Šoltinský and co-authors weigh the odds of catching a faint pattern in radio light from the dawn of the cosmos. Their 2024 paper deals with the 21-centimeter forest, thin dips carved in a bright source's spectrum by cold hydrogen gas. The signal could reveal how warm that gas was while the first stars lit the universe.

More than thirty loud radio sources are now known from that era, and new telescopes loom. The team built fake skies and fake gear to test what can be seen. With long runs on a current dish, the broad shape of the signal should show if the gas is still at least a quarter neutral and cold. A blank result would also teach something, by ruling out cold, neutral gas.
arxiv-2412-06979:
Darin Mumma, Zhonghao Sun, Alexis Mercenne, Kristina Launey, Soorya Rethinasamy, and James Sauls run first quantum simulations of the carbon-12 nucleus in two thousand twenty-four. Solving nuclei from scratch needs computing power that explodes with particle count. Their work targets the low-lying states of carbon-12 with a hybrid quantum method.

Two tricks make the task fit today's noisy machines. A near-perfect symmetry of nuclei shrinks the model space sharply when a symmetry-fit basis is used. A Gray code mapping then lays the problem onto qubits in a lean way, matched to the banded shape of the nuclear force matrix. Even with noise, the runs returned sound bound-state energies.
arxiv-2412-07779:
Biqing Qi and six colleagues present a 2024 paper on helping large AI models reason better. When a model can follow several different paths to an answer, both the quality and the variety of those paths matter. Current methods chase quality alone, which traps the model in narrow ruts and wastes effort.

Their framework, Evolution of Thought, borrows from evolution. Candidate reasoning paths are crossed and mutated, then ranked on two goals at once, quality and diversity, using a well-known sorting algorithm. A second step clusters near-duplicate paths and merges their lessons so good ideas spread. Tests on vision-language and language reasoning tasks showed stronger results and better efficiency than rival methods, offering a new template for machine reasoning.
arxiv-2412-08279:
Marta Costa-jussa and co-authors introduce a 2024 dataset that pairs English and Yoruba for reading tasks. Yoruba is a low-resource language, and model skill in it is poorly tested. The set holds 358 questions and answers over 338 English documents and 208 Yoruba ones. Models must consult a document and answer, or generate text, in an open-book setup.

Tests showed a steady gap between the two languages. Yoruba scores fell behind English on automatic measures, even though its documents were far shorter. On matched short documents, Yoruba scores dropped by a factor of about two and a half. Yoruba scores also fell fast as documents grew. The authors release the set to expose such gaps.
arxiv-2412-08479:
Sumaiya Zoha, Jeong-Gun Lee, and Young-Woong Ko propose, in twenty twenty-four, a method for models that must work in new domains while using few labeled examples. Domain generalization trains on several source sets and tests on unseen ones. Labels are costly, so they tackle a semi-supervised version with limited labels. Old methods use fixed confidence cutoffs and suffer from noisy pseudo-labels, the guesses a model makes for unlabeled data. Their method, CAT, sets class-aware adaptive thresholds instead.

CAT pairs flexible thresholds with a refinement step that cleans noisy pseudo-labels. The flexible thresholds yield pseudo-labels with higher class diversity. Cleaning raises their reliability. Extensive tests on benchmark data sets show the method beats prior approaches, the authors report. The recipe is simple yet effective.
arxiv-2412-08779:
Martín Gilabert Vio wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-four about random walks on groups of circle maps. The maps are smooth, orientation-preserving bends of a circle. A classic alternative in group theory says groups either contain a free subgroup or have a tame structure. The author proves a probabilistic form of that choice for these map groups.

Two independent random walks are driven by probability measures whose supports generate discrete groups acting in a spreading way on the circle. The theorem says that, almost surely, from some step onward the two walk positions generate a nonabelian free group. The proof follows a strategy used for linear groups and builds on work by several named researchers.
arxiv-2412-08979:
Zirun Guo, Xize Cheng, Yangyang Wu, and Tao Jin present a cheap way to adapt large models that use more than one kind of input. Their two thousand twenty-four method is called Wander. Older add-on methods were built for pairs, such as text with images, and do not stretch well to three or more kinds.

Wander joins data from each kind at the level of single tokens, so fine detail is kept. It breaks large tensors into rank-one parts, which cuts the count of values to train by a lot. Tests on sets with varied counts of input kinds show Wander beats other cheap methods, in both score and cost.
arxiv-2412-09079:
Elisa Negrini and co-authors teach neural networks to imitate the marching of fronts: melting ice edges, spreading fire lines, and other boundaries that move by threshold rules. Their 2024 paper builds two convolutional architectures inspired by a classic front-propagation algorithm and by cellular automata, learning the dynamics straight from video.

The first network learns one specific dynamic per video, kernel and threshold fitted to that footage. The second, a meta-learning version, adapts its parameters to new dynamics. Both reconstructed and extrapolated evolving boundaries well on synthetic and real videos of ice melting and fire spread, with noise corrupting the input. Front evolution sits inside materials science, wildfire response, and image processing alike. A learned simulator that reads a front's habits from a clip could forecast where the line goes next, which is the game in each of those fields.
arxiv-2412-09179:
Nikolay Kivel revisits a subtle effect in how electrons bounce off atomic nuclei, in a 2024 physics paper. When two photons are exchanged at once in the scattering, the cross section shifts slightly. At large momentum transfer, models of the nucleus are not accurate enough, so Kivel uses an effective field theory suited to the hard region.

He improves estimates of several long range pieces of the effect and works out the size of the shift for unpolarized scattering. The updated account can explain the known mismatch in form factor values in one momentum range, though the effect is small at higher values. Kivel notes that non linear effects may matter there. He also estimates the effect for scattering off neutrons.
arxiv-2412-09679:
Julianne Goddard, Isaac Shlosman, and Emilio Romano-Diaz wrote a 2024 paper running a simulated cosmos to see what jets from a mid-sized black hole do to its home galaxy. Seyfert galaxies host mid-weight black holes that shoot out jets. How that feedback shapes the galaxy was the question. The team ran the same galaxy start twice, once with jets and once with stellar explosions alone.

The black hole seed was placed when its dark matter halo was young. Only the feeding rate of the hole was varied between runs. With jets, star formation was pushed out to wide rings, and the outer disk of the galaxy grew thick. Gas shares, disk shape, and material beyond the galaxy edge all shifted. Jet cocoons swelled to vast distances. Beside real Seyfert galaxies near us, the simulations matched well, the team says. A follow-up paper takes up their long history.
arxiv-2412-09879:
Cassie Huang and Li Zhang present a 2024 study on using language models to write formal planning files. Models that draft plans in plain words often produce steps that can not run. A better route lets the model write a formal domain file, which a solver can then solve exactly. Past tests fed the model stiff, templated scene text and asked for partial files. This study raises the bar.

The team asks for full files from scene text of varied naturalness. Most large models, they find, can write sound formal files and beat direct plan drafting. Word swaps that keep the sense do not break them much. As the text grows more natural, scores fall, and the authors chart the error types. The work maps where model formalizing is ready and where it frays.
arxiv-2412-09979:
Alexander Yosifov, Aditya Iyer, and Vlatko Vedral propose a quantum reservoir built from a homogenizer. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, targets time-series tasks. Quantum reservoirs use a quantum system's own messy dynamics to process streams, with no fine tuning. Building one that is stable and noise-tough is the hard part.

Their device repeatedly swaps a stream of fresh qubits with a fixed set. The process evens out, or homogenizes, the states over time. They prove it meets the two must-have traits for reservoir work: stability and fading memory. Lab forms could use atom ensembles or light systems. The design suits tasks like signal forecasting.
arxiv-2412-10079:
George Arthur Baker, Ankush Raut, Sagi Shaier, Lawrence E Hunter, and Katharina von der Wense study a known flaw of long-context language models, in work published in 2024. Models tend to use facts near the start or end of a long input and miss facts buried in the middle. The team asks what happens when a question needs several facts spread across many documents.

In this multi-hop setting, scores fell not only when a key fact sat far from the edges, but also when the needed facts sat far apart from each other. The team then tried fixes: trimming documents to short fact triples from a knowledge graph, summarizing them, and asking the model to reason step by step. The work maps where long inputs still trip models up and which trims help most.
arxiv-2412-10179:
Campbell and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four hunting for the Casimir energy, a subtle shift in vacuum energy between close plates. The Casimir effect, described in nineteen forty-eight, arises because plates block some field modes inside a cavity. Whether the lowered ground-state energy changes physics inside the cavity is an open experimental question.

The team placed a superconductor inside such a cavity and watched its critical temperature, the point where resistance vanishes. They saw no shift larger than twelve millionths of a degree. Theory predicts a shift about a thousand times smaller than that sensitivity, so the null result fits expectations. The paper frames how far future setups must go.
arxiv-2412-10379: Ol'ga Sipacheva and Aleksandr Solonkov study free topological Mal'tsev algebras in this 2024 mathematics paper. The paper opens with a brief tour of universal algebra and of topological algebras and their varieties. A Mal'tsev algebra carries a special three place operation that generalizes the behavior of groups. The free topological version is the most general such algebra on a given set of generators. The authors study its main properties, its links with topological groups and with heaps, and how it splits as a direct limit of simpler pieces.
arxiv-2412-10779:
Palni and co-authors edit the proceedings of Hot QCD Matter 2024, a conference on the bulk traits of matter at extreme heat. The meeting, held at IIT Mandi, gathered theory and experiment work on heavy ion collisions. Such collisions brew quark-gluon plasma, a soup of freed quarks and gluons.

The volume holds 19 contributions. Topics span the dynamics of electromagnetic fields, transport traits, hadronic matter, and spin hydrodynamics. The role of conserved charges in high energy settings also gets its share. The editors frame the set as a step toward sharper theory for the plasma's thermodynamics. Hydrodynamics, spin dynamics, and fluctuation studies all feature in the mix.
arxiv-2412-10879:
Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang, and Zhouli Xu settle, in a 2024 paper, the last open case of the Kervaire invariant problem, a question in topology that stood for decades. The problem asks in which dimensions there exist smooth framed shapes carrying a particular invariant value of one. Case by case, the answer had narrowed to a short list of dimensions and one stubborn remainder: dimension 126.

The authors prove that a certain element in the Adams spectral sequence, a central computing device of the field, survives as a permanent cycle. That single fact guarantees the shapes exist in dimension 126. Combined with earlier theorems, the full answer is now exact: such shapes exist in dimensions 2, 6, 14, 30, 62, and 126, and nowhere else. The paper closes a problem that shaped algebraic topology for generations.
arxiv-2412-11979:
Oren Neumann and Claudius Gros study why the game playing system AlphaZero improves as a power law in a 2024 paper. Power law gains with scale appear across AI, with no agreed cause. In language, one theory ties them to Zipf's law, where a few items are very common and most are rare. The authors test whether board game states follow the same pattern, and whether learning order matches that theory.

Game states in training and play data do follow Zipf's law, which they trace to the tree shape of games. Agents improved first on the most frequent states, even though those are not the simplest to model. That order matches the theory. They also find a failure mode: when end game states rank among the most frequent, larger models can get worse. Bigger models shift focus to those common but minor states and lose ground on key early states.
arxiv-2412-12179:
Steven Phillips and Naotsugu Tsuchiya sketch a math level theory of consciousness, in a 2024 paper. No agreed theory of conscious experience exists, so the authors step up a level and ask what shape any such theory should take. Category theory, built to compare math structures, offers the tools.

They set it against a leading axiomatic theory that lists six properties every conscious state should have. All six, they show, follow from one category idea: a universal mapping property, a unique existence condition across a domain. Their slogan is that consciousness is a universal property. The frame is offered as a base for further formal work.
arxiv-2412-12379:
Yisheng Lei, Zongfeng Li, and Mahdi Hosseini report a more efficient crystal memory for storing light in quantum networks. Future quantum links need memories that hold many frequencies at once without losing much of the signal. Their device uses a crystal doped with thulium ions, in which laser pumping carves storage windows into the absorption spectrum. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team applies several pumping and tuning tricks and shows storage working at warmer temperatures than usual for such systems, without narrowing the memory bandwidth.

Storage efficiency passed a quarter of the incoming signal while the memory spanned a wide frequency band with many windows. The authors also propose a general recipe for wideband memories based on a broad family of rare-earth ions, promising higher efficiency and bandwidth together. The work targets practical quantum repeaters.
arxiv-2412-12679:
Yupei Li and three co-authors detect machine-written documents in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Large language models make generated text easy to produce at scale. That fuels plagiarism and misinformation risks. Detectors that read only surface features are easily fooled. Paraphrased, long generated texts fool them most.

The authors bring in discourse features, the structural traits of a whole document. Besides a public benchmark, they built two new paraphrased data sets. One extends long-form question answering, the other writing prompts. Paraphrases were made with GPT and a discourse paraphrasing tool. Their methods aim to catch machine text that mimics human style sentence by sentence. Readers get detection aimed at document structure, where paraphrase cannot hide as easily.
arxiv-2412-13079:
Sai Teja Erukude and co-authors show how to unmask hidden bias in image datasets with simple picture transforms in a 2024 paper. Image networks act as black boxes, and slanted test sets can flatter their scores. A classic tell is background leakage, where models learn scenery rather than the object itself.

When no clean background crop exists, the team applies Fourier and wavelet transforms and median filters to the full image. These views recover the background signal a network may secretly ride on. Checked across common benchmark sets, the method flags biases that plain accuracy hides. The authors urge bias hunts before any score is believed.
arxiv-2412-13179:
Shirin Qiam, Saipraneeth Devunuri, and Lewis Lehe build tools to map parking lots from satellite photos automatically, in a 2024 paper. Debates over parking rules need such maps, yet drawing them by hand is slow and open datasets are scarce for US cities. The team added a near-infrared channel, which plants reflect strongly, to ordinary color images.

Two datasets of 12,617 image-mask pairs were made, one with color only and one with the extra channel. Five deep learning models learned to paint parking pixels. The infrared channel helped, since lots often sit in grass, and cleanup steps that filled holes, smoothed edges, and erased roads and roofs helped more. The best pairing hit about 85 percent overlap with hand maps.
arxiv-2412-13279:
Mahieyin Rahmun and seven co-authors build a classifier that names which speech synthesizer produced a voice clip, in a 2024 paper. The work was the team's entry to a 2022 signal processing challenge. Synthetic voices now come from many text-to-speech systems, known and unknown, and telling them apart matters for fraud and media forensics. The team trained an attribution model on speech from various generators.

Classical methods, support vector machines and Gaussian mixture models, were compared with deep networks, including ResNet and VGG-style image models fed with sound representations, plus two shallow end-to-end networks. Deep methods on raw data performed best. As synthetic speech floods phone lines, attribution tools are a first line of defense.
arxiv-2412-13679:
Neetha Jambigi, Michael Felderer, and co-authors add smart text sums to a tool that finds why database replay tests fail, in a 2024 paper. Replaying a saved work load checks a new database build for faults. False fails from time shifts or thread quirks can swamp real ones, though.

A learned sorter sorts fails by cause but stumbles on new kinds of faults. The team adds short sums of failed queries made by a large language model. The sums give the sorter fresh clues that split causes more cleanly. Scores rose by a clear margin on their data, and users gain plain notes on each fault as well.
arxiv-2412-13779:
Yichen Li and co-authors present a 2024 method for shared learning across devices that keeps learning new tasks over time. In such setups, each device holds its own data and no raw data leaves it. The hard part is learning new classes without forgetting old ones, a task most past methods solve by replaying saved old data.

Replay costs memory and can breach privacy, so the team turns to penalty methods that guard key weights instead. A known penalty method works well when all devices hold like data but fails when their data differ a lot. Their new method adapts that penalty for mixed data across devices. Tests beat top rivals, with less compute and no saved old data at all.
arxiv-2412-13879:
Yuanhe Zhang and co-workers introduce an automated denial-of-service attack on large language models, in a 2024 paper. Such attacks aim to exhaust computing resources and block service for real users. Most past work assumed white-box access to the target model, which real attackers rarely have.

Their method builds an attack tree and expands its coverage step by step, tuning prompts by transfer across models. A hidden length trick helps the attack slip past existing defenses. In tests it raised response latency by more than two hundred fifty times and drove up GPU and memory use. The authors frame the work as a warning for defenders.
arxiv-2412-13979:
The PandaX Collaboration reports a search from two thousand twenty-four for a rare nuclear decay that may not exist. In neutrinoless double-beta decay, two neutrons in a nucleus change at once without releasing neutrinos. Seeing it would prove the neutrino is its own antiparticle and reshape particle physics.

The team used the PandaX-4T detector, which holds several tonnes of natural xenon rich in the isotope under study. They rebuilt the data and modeled background noise with care in the key energy range, then analyzed the data blind. No excess over background appeared. From that silence they set a lower limit on the decay's half-life, which bounds how rare the process must be if it occurs at all.
arxiv-2412-14079:
András Márton Gunyhó and six co-authors demonstrate heat measurement at the zeptojoule scale in this 2024 paper. A zeptojoule is an almost unimaginably small amount of energy. Thermal detectors that turn energy into heat are among the most sensitive tools for such tasks.

The team used a metallic sandwich sensor to measure microwave pulses one microsecond long. Their energy resolution came in finer than one zeptojoule, equal to about one hundred seventy photons at the test frequency. Past claims at this level rested on estimates, not direct measurement. The authors see a path, with carbon-sheet sensors, to catching single photons in real time near ten gigahertz. Such a device could weigh quantum states precisely and aid hunts for dark matter particles.
arxiv-2412-14179:
Bryce Judy builds the first shared benchmark for tariff classification software, in a 2024 paper. Every import into the United States needs a Harmonized Tariff Schedule code, and vendors sell tools that assign them, yet the industry has no standard test for who is actually good. Borrowing the benchmark habits of the language model world, the author fixes that.

The framework grades tools on speed, accuracy, reasoning quality, and code alignment against a common set of goods. Several leading products, from Zonos, Tarifflo, Avalara, and the World Customs Organization's BACUDA, were put through it. Each showed distinct strengths and limits. The results point to where classification tools must improve, and give buyers a yardstick beyond sales claims.
arxiv-2412-14379:
Phuc Nguyen builds a detector that finds tilted objects in aerial photos with less waste. This 2024 paper targets oriented object detection, where ships and planes sit at any angle. Anchor-based detectors spawn piles of preset boxes and burn compute. Anchor-free ones run fast but train on fewer samples. The hybrid design keeps one preset anchor per spot.

A special convolution that knows orientation then refines those anchors. Scores hit 75.41 on one aerial benchmark and 90.2 on a ship set, rivaling heavy anchor-based leaders. Compute fell sharply at the same time. Nguyen argues the hybrid route suits drone and satellite vision, where tilted targets and tight budgets meet.
arxiv-2412-14479:
Zihan Chang and co-authors build a serverless trainer for large language models on mixed graphics hardware, in this 2024 paper. Developers usually must hand-pick how many and which graphics cards a training job gets, a fiddly burden. Their system, Frenzy, first predicts a job's memory needs, then picks and schedules the hardware itself.

On a cluster with three card types, memory guesses landed within eight percent of true use. Scheduling overhead fell tenfold, and jobs finished twelve to eighteen percent sooner than with leading methods. Users just submit the model, the authors note.
arxiv-2412-14579:
Qianpu Sun and co-authors present a 2024 paper on teaching self-driving systems to map which space around the car is occupied, using only weak labels. Earlier methods render scenes with a costly technique that forces a trade between speed and accuracy. They also render each viewpoint once, which produces duplicated predictions where views overlap.

Their system swaps in a faster rendering method based on Gaussian splats, which simplifies sampling. A ray compensation module borrows features from neighboring frames to cut the duplicates. A redesigned loss also removes the influence of moving objects leaking in from other frames. The aim is occupancy maps that are accurate, fast, and free of double-counted obstacles.
arxiv-2412-14779:
Aditya Kapoor and co-authors address reward credit in multi-agent learning in a 2024 paper. When many agents learn together and rewards are rare or delayed, each agent struggles to tell which of its past actions helped. Long tasks make that judgment even harder, and learning can stall.

Their method, called TAR squared in plain terms, splits a sparse global reward across time steps and across agents by estimated contribution. The authors prove the split acts like a known reward shaping method, so the best policy stays the same. In tests, learning became steadier and faster. Added to single-agent learning methods, the approach matched or beat standard multi-agent methods, which broadens where it can be used.
arxiv-2412-15479:
Jiabao Qiu, Zixuan Ke, and Bing Liu introduce, in a 2024 paper, a way for a large language model to keep learning new tasks using prompts alone. Continual learning means learning task after task without forgetting the old ones. Their paradigm, CLOB, treats the model as a black box. Nothing in it is retrained, and no new trainable parts are added, which suits models reached only through an online interface.

Their technique, CIS, learns by summarizing as it goes. Each new task's lessons are folded into a growing summary that is fed back as a prompt. That trick also beats the model's input length limit, since the summary stays compact. In experiments, the method beat the baselines by a very large margin, the authors report. The work suggests that careful prompting can substitute for retraining in some lifelong learning settings, a cheaper path for closed models.
arxiv-2412-15679:
Hauke Maathuis, Roeland De Breuker, and Saullo Castro bring a global search method to aircraft design problems with many variables and many limits, in a 2024 paper. Bayesian optimization searches widely and needs no gradients, but it strains when the design space grows. Their test case is aeroelastic tailoring, where stiffness is tuned so wings flex in helpful ways. Safety rules from many fields must hold at once.

The team shrinks the design space first, using Gaussian process models in the smaller latent space. The method handled a known benchmark with hidden constraints. It then worked on the real tailoring problem, with its large stack of limits. The authors say the result shows global Bayesian search can stay practical for high-dimensional engineering design, not just small problems.
arxiv-2412-16579:
Armario, Egan, Kharaghani, and Ó Catháin generalize a special vector concept tied to a family of complex matrices used in coding and design theory. For Butson Hadamard matrices, whose entries are roots of unity, a bent vector maps under the matrix to another vector of unit-length entries. Their 2024 paper studies bent vectors that map back to themselves, or to their own conjugates, up to a factor.

Using tools from algebraic number theory, the team proves conditions on the size and order under which such self-dual vectors can or cannot exist. They also build concrete examples with product constructions and a special matrix family. The paper closes by applying the results to the covering radius of certain nonlinear codes that extend the classic Reed-Muller family.
arxiv-2412-17379:
Souhir Ben Amor and colleagues estimated the carbon cost of one extra unit of electricity demand, hour by hour, in a 2024 paper. That marginal emission factor tells climate policy which hour's savings matter most, and future grids with high renewable shares will swing it wildly through the day. Two estimation routes are compared for a decarbonized German system, past and future years alike.

A detailed energy system model computes the factor step by step as a benchmark. A faster statistical model, a Markov switching regression that flips between hidden regimes, tries to match it. Across historical and projected years, the statistical model proved more accurate than a dynamic rival named in the comparison, offering speed with fidelity.
arxiv-2412-17479: Charlotte Kristjansen, Xin Qian, and Chenliang Su compute the spectrum of quantum fluctuations in a defect version of ABJM theory. Their 2024 paper studies a half-BPS domain wall form of the model. The spectrum reflects the setup's supersymmetry, as expected. Knowing it opens perturbative study of the linked defect conformal field theory, order by order. The work is brief and technical, aimed at gauge theory and holography readers who need the fluctuation list for further defect calculations.
arxiv-2412-17979: Guang Yang, Peter Trinh, Sannan Iqbal, and Justin Zhang introduce a new cryptocurrency in a 2024 paper. Called PHICOIN, it uses proof of work, where computers compete to secure the network by solving hard puzzles. Mining has grown centered on special hardware, shutting out ordinary users. Their design aims to resist that hardware and keep entry fair. The paper sets out the coin's technical details, its mission, and its roadmap, and presents it as base infrastructure for proof-of-work coins.
arxiv-2412-18179:
Jincheng An and Ganpathy Murthy wrote a physics paper in 2024 about graphene in a strong magnetic field. Graphene is a sheet of carbon one atom thick. When its charge carriers cancel out, the sheet sits at a neutral point. In that state, the material can settle into many different ordered phases. Which phase appears depends on small forces inside the sheet and on outside fields.

Telling these phases apart in the lab is hard. Some signs can be seen with sharp scanning probes. Others, which mix the spin and valley traits of the electrons, leave no easy trace. The authors propose a test using two kinds of measurement together. One is how the energy gap for charge flow shifts as outside fields change. The other is the count of certain wave-like modes. Together, they argue, these give each possible phase a unique fingerprint.
arxiv-2412-18279:
Jiacai Liu, Chaojie Wang, and colleagues improve multi-step reasoning in language models with a new reinforcement learning method in a 2024 study. Reasoning tasks pay off only at the final answer, so rewards are sparse and training signals weak. Standard reinforcement learning is also unstable on such problems, demanding many samples to make progress.

Direct Advantage Policy Optimization attacks both issues by using advantage estimates more directly in the update. Smoother, better-fed training should reach strong reasoning with less data. Progress here matters because reasoning quality, not raw recall, is the current frontier for deployed models.
arxiv-2412-18379:
Xuan Luo and co-authors added a neural network to fluid tracking in a 2024 computing paper. Their base method follows fluid parts as they move, while also using a fixed grid. Finding each part's new spot by a step-by-step search is slow, and the cost grows fast on large runs with many machines. Long search paths force much talk between machines.

The new method first guesses each part's new spot with a pattern-reading network. The old search then starts from that guess, so paths are short and results stay exact. In large, fast flows the gain grew with scale. Tests cut path length by about ninety-six percent and run time by about ninety-seven percent against the old search alone.
arxiv-2412-18579:
Oliver Cassidy, Marta Andronic, Samuel Coward, and George Constantinides present a way to shrink lookup tables in computer hardware, in a 2024 paper. Such tables store ready-made values for hard math. In neural networks, the stored patterns are irregular, which defeats standard logic tools. Big tables waste chip space.

Their method, ReducedLUT, adds don't-care entries into the compression step. Those free entries create more repeated patterns in the table. Known splitting methods can then exploit the repeats. The result is a set of smaller tables that rebuild the original values. The authors show a machine learning use, where unseen patterns are swapped for free entries. Smaller tables mean cheaper, faster custom chips.
arxiv-2412-19879:
Robie Hennigar and co-authors compute vibration spectra on a lumpy Einstein space in a 2024 paper. The Page metric is a famous uneven solution of Einstein's equations on a joined projective space. How scalar waves ring on it was unknown. Symmetry reduces the problem to one dimension.

The wave equation becomes a singular Sturm-Liouville problem, solved by pseudospectral numerics. A nearby exactly solvable problem gives perturbative checks that back the numbers. The team also compute the spectrum for tensor waves of the Lichnerowicz type. The results give relativists concrete mode data on a classic inhomogeneous geometry, useful for stability questions.
arxiv-2501-00079:
Tommaso Matteuzzi and co-authors define when a copied unit in a network can be trusted in a paper dated 2024. Take a dynamical network and clone one of its units. If the clone shadows its original exactly, it is internally reliable; if it drifts away, it is anti-reliable.

A single number, the transversal Lyapunov exponent, measures the split. In a classic model of coupled oscillators, units at the edge of the frequency spread misbehave before sync sets in, while central ones stay faithful. Big cloned groups are always anti-reliable in that model. A recurrent neural network flipped the pattern, with single units always reliable.
arxiv-2501-00279:
Linear algebra routines called BLAS sit inside most scientific computing, and graphics processors run them fast, but moving old code onto those processors takes real effort. Junjie Li and co-authors present SCILIB-Accel, a tool that offloads the work automatically. It intercepts BLAS calls inside a running program, with no changes to the code, and sends the heavy level-three operations to the graphics processor.

The design leans on modern unified-memory chips, where processor and graphics memory stay coherent. A first-use data policy, modeled on a classic technique from multi-socket computing, keeps transfers between the two memories to a minimum. Tested on quantum physics codes running across hundreds of graphics nodes, the tool delivered promising speedups, including a threefold gain for one widely used materials method on the newest hardware.
arxiv-2501-00479:
Nicolo Valle reports on a new kind of particle detector in a 2025 paper. The device is a calorimeter, which measures the energy of particle showers, and it reads each shower two ways at once. Twin reads let physicists sort the shower's parts and sharpen the energy call.

Valle walks through the current fiber-based test units, with fibers packed in fine tubes. A new high-resolution, finely grained demonstrator, called HiDRa, gets a full account of its build and assembly. Simulation results round out the picture, along with the beam tests planned to prove the design in real particle fire.
arxiv-2501-00779:
Huyen Nguyen and co-authors pick in 2025 the best seed users to spread a message across layered social networks. Influence maximization matters because the right seeds cut the cost of spreading information. Older methods have hit their limits, and learning-based ones need good training examples and known spread patterns.

Their framework, REM, mixes several expert propagators to model how influence travels. A generative model, trained by reinforcement, proposes seed sets and learns to improve them. On real network datasets REM beat leading methods on spread, scale, and speed. The authors stress that it needs no sample seed sets of high quality to learn from.
arxiv-2501-00979:
Sanya Gupta, Navin Sridhar, and Lorenzo Sironi use computer simulations to study how particles gain their first energy boost in magnetic reconnection, in a 2025 paper. Reconnection, where magnetic field lines snap and rejoin, may power the brightest flares in space.

The team simulated a thin plasma of paired particles with no guide field. They tracked how much early energy gain happens in spots where the electric field beats the magnetic field. In strong settings, over eighty percent of that early gain took place in such spots. The share grew with field strength and particle energy. The pattern did not depend on the size of the simulated box, which aids wider use.
arxiv-2501-01079:
Yi Han bounds the spectral radius of random matrices whose entries vary in spread, in a 2025 math paper. For tidy random matrices the largest eigenvalue settles at a known limit, well inside the operator norm. Real data matrices are messier: entries are independent but not identical, each with its own variance.

Han proves upper bounds driven by the largest single entry's standard deviation. After normalization the radius stays near the tidy limit down to near-optimal sparsity. A small deviation inequality captures fluctuations past that scale, and a large deviation result covers Gaussian entries with balanced variance. Even heavy-tailed entries with barely more than two finite moments behave under an uneven variance profile. The proofs lean on the trace moment method. The results matter for non-Hermitian band matrices, a model class drawn from physics.
