arxiv-2501-01179: Quentin Posva constructs pathological singularity examples in algebraic geometry in this 2025 paper. The setting is the minimal model program in positive characteristic. Singularities there can behave worse than in characteristic zero, and sharp examples are valuable. Posva builds them as quotients by a special group action, called an alpha p action, in every positive characteristic.
arxiv-2501-01679:
Lei Tang and co-authors built an adaptive prompt method in 2025 to lift machine translation by large language models. Such models are touchy about the sample pairs shown to them, and one fixed set fits few inputs well. Their frame picks the best samples for each new sentence on its own. It hunts a stock of paired texts for the nearest kin of the input, using the model's own inner reads as the map.

The model then drafts a few versions of the translation and ranks its own drafts for sense fit. To test the frame, the team built a fine Chinese-English set of more than five thousand pairs from diplomatic texts. On that set and on a United Nations set, the frame beat fixed-prompt rivals.
arxiv-2501-01879:
Castellanos Durán and co-authors measured magnetic fields in bright bridges inside sunspots, in a 2025 paper. Light bridges are bright lanes that split a sunspot into parts with opposite magnetic poles. A few past cases found fields there twice as strong as in the dark spot core. The team asked whether such superstrong fields are rare or routine in these lanes.

They studied ninety-eight bridges in fifty-one sunspot groups, many of them scanned again and again. Every bridge held fields above a high threshold at the visible surface. The fields faded with height faster than in the spot core or its fringe. Brightness paired with strength set the bridges apart as their own class. The mix hints at a little-explored way that magnetic fields and hot gas interact on the Sun.
arxiv-2501-02279:
Seyed Shahram Yadollahi, Hamed Kebriaei, and Sadegh Soudjani study stochastic games where competing agents share chance constraints, published in 2025. Each agent lacks full knowledge of the uncertainties, which have a concentration property. In general the problem is non-convex and NP-hard, so a tractable route is needed.

The authors replace the chance constraints with tightened expected-value versions, a convex under-approximation that yields a workable game. They prove a stochastic generalized Nash equilibrium exists in the new game, and that its variational equilibrium nearly solves the original, with the gap spelled out through approximation errors and multipliers. A semi-decentralized, sampling-based algorithm with shrinking step sizes finds the equilibrium. It needs no knowledge of the uncertainty distribution and, under standard assumptions, converges almost surely.
arxiv-2501-02379:
Sebastian Loeschcke and seven co-authors introduced TensorGRaD in twenty twenty-five, a memory-saving method for training neural operators. Neural operators learn solution maps for scientific problems across resolutions, using tensor-structured layers. At industrial scale their optimizer states devour memory, blocking high-resolution training.

TensorGRaD factorizes each gradient into a low-rank tensor plus a sparse one, capturing both the bulk signal and outliers inside the optimizer. A mixed precision recipe trims memory further without losing accuracy. The authors prove advantages over matrix-based gradient compression. On Fourier neural operators across several PDE tasks — including turbulent flow at high Reynolds number — total memory fell by over half while accuracy held or improved. The method targets practical, large-scale scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2501-02479:
Xin Zhen and co-authors compute the properties of nuclear matter, the dense stuff of atomic nuclei, with a method that avoids step-by-step approximation, in a 2025 paper. Such calculations start from forces between two and three nuclear particles and test many-body methods against each other. Their method gradually transforms the problem until it becomes easy to solve, a scheme called an in-medium similarity flow.

They ran it with modern chiral forces at two levels of refinement, for both pure neutron matter and balanced nuclear matter. Rival methods agreed loosely with soft forces but diverged when the force grew harder. The authors offer their setup as fresh infrastructure for studying dense matter and other strongly bound systems.
arxiv-2501-02579:
Smashing gold nuclei together squeezes nuclear matter to extreme density, and how stiff that matter gets decides how the debris flows. Bao-An Li and Wen-Jie Xie mine flow measurements from the FOPI experiment, which fired gold at gold from 150 to 1,200 million electron volts per nucleon. Feeding the data through a Bayesian framework, they infer two hidden quantities. One is how much particle collisions are suppressed inside the dense medium; the other is the matter's stiffness.

The suppression factor climbs from about 0.7 at the lowest energy toward the free-space value of 1.0 as energy rises. The stiffness tells a two-stage story: near 220 million electron volts at low energy, marking soft matter, and near 320 at higher energies, marking stiff matter. The switch happens around 250, where both values are equally likely: the matter hardens gradually as density and temperature grow.
arxiv-2501-02979:
Zhi Qu and co-authors present a trick in 2025 that lets a small, focused translation model rival huge language models. Their model translates among many languages and is cheap to train and run. Yet models of its kind have lagged behind the giant general models in quality.

The trick adds a set of made up tokens, called registers, between the source text and the target text. The tokens name the target language. The model is set so that each new target word attends only to the registers, which carry the source meaning recast in the target language's space. That focus sharpens the output. A small model that can match a giant one would cut the cost of translation for many language pairs. The paper sets out the method and its tests.
arxiv-2501-03179:
Chardac, Norton, Touboul, and Duclos wrote in twenty twenty-five about protein patterns forming in three dimensions on floating membrane bubbles. The Min protein system drives cell division placement in bacteria. On a continuous membrane it forms two-dimensional patterns of waves. The team fragmented the membrane into tiny drifting liposomes instead. Protein interactions powered by ATP still organized across the whole suspension. Patterns emerged at scales ten thousand times larger than single liposomes.

Traveling waves, spirals, and a mixed coexistence phase all appeared. None of these forms occur on flat continuous membranes. Changing protein amounts and liposome size or density shifted the patterns. Simulations showed the fragmented membrane rescales binding and diffusion rates. Those two parameters select the pattern type and wavelength. The authors propose protein-membrane suspensions as a template for studying three-dimensional self-organization.
arxiv-2501-03279:
Haozhen Zhang and co-authors present a model that sorts encrypted network traffic without reading its contents. Sorting such traffic is a core security task, since it can flag attacks in transit. Older byte-based methods look at traffic in fixed chunks and miss how bytes relate.

Their model, MH-Net, groups traffic bits into units of several sizes at once. It builds graphs from those units, with unlike link types for unlike relations, such as header to payload. Learning over the graphs lets the model use context that flat methods drop. The design aims for finer reads of streams that stay locked to human eyes. Strong results would help guards watch networks they cannot decrypt. The work targets a growing blind spot in defense.
arxiv-2501-03779:
Andrea Cernuschi and Thomas Thuillier use computer simulation, in a 2025 preprint, to study X-rays given off inside an ion source. The device, called an electron cyclotron resonance ion source, traps electrons with magnetic fields. Hot electrons inside emit bremsstrahlung, a kind of X-ray radiation. Operators want to know what sets the temperature of that radiation. The authors focus on the weakest point of the magnetic trap.

Their Monte Carlo code follows many electrons and builds the X-ray spectrum from their motion. The simulated temperature matched past lab measurements well. It also rose and fell with the minimum magnetic field, as earlier work found. The field at the point where ions leave had no effect. Digging into the electron population, the authors propose how the trap shape creates the hot electrons behind the change. That picture may guide safer and better source design.
arxiv-2501-03979:
Luqman Saleem, Hasan Abdullah, Udo Schwingenschlögl, and Aurélien Manchon chart how magnons carry heat on the alpha-T3 lattice. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses atomistic spin dynamics runs. Further-neighbor hopping and easy-axis anisotropy keep ferromagnetic order steady against a twist term. Four phases appear as knobs turn: one plain magnon insulator and three Chern phases.

The plain phase still shows a small thermal Hall flow. In the Chern phases, the lowest band's Chern number drives the flow's size. At phase borders the flow's sign holds steady. Its size, though, jumps in clear steps. The team maps which band traits set the heat current's sign and strength. The work guides searches for lattices whose heat flow can be switched by design.
arxiv-2501-04079:
Sedanur Iyisan and three co-authors map the thin disc of our galaxy in a 2025 study of old stars near the Sun. They drew on a large space survey of star places and light. From about 39 million stars within a set range, they picked out old, bright stars with the best place data.

The final sample held more than 670,000 stars, split across 36 sky zones by their place in the galaxy. Dust dimming was stripped out with a galaxy dust map before the counts were made. The team fit the fall of star counts with height and reach, giving fresh numbers for the disc's shape.
arxiv-2501-04179:
Raman and Raman extend a young theory of how machines can generate new examples of a concept from examples alone. In the basic setup, an adversary picks a rule and feeds a generator its positive examples; the generator must eventually produce fresh positive examples it has never seen. Real streams are dirty, though. The authors let the adversary slip a finite number of negative examples into the stream, unlabeled.

The paper finds exact conditions for when a class of rules can still be generated from such a noisy stream. A striking result: for finite and countable classes, a finite amount of noise barely matters — generatability survives almost unchanged. For learning theorists, the work hardens a fragile-looking idea against realistic mess, and maps where the true limits sit.
arxiv-2501-04979:
Jae-Woo Lee, Tae-Hyeong Kim, and colleagues examine star populations inside an old cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud in a 2025 astronomy study. Globular clusters were once thought to hold one uniform generation of stars, but many show several populations with different chemistry. Whether the host galaxy's environment shapes those populations is an open question in near-field cosmology.

Photometry sensitive to calcium and molecular bands sorts the cluster's stars into generations. The first generation dominates the count, and the authors read the pattern as showing no major environmental effect for old clusters in that galaxy. Each well studied cluster sharpens the story of how these ancient systems formed.
arxiv-2501-05179:
Models that see and read at high resolution drown in tokens, the chunks they chew one by one, and their cost grows with the square of that count. Xuyang Liu and co-authors speed such models in 2025 with a commander that squeezes the token stream. It needs no retraining and plugs into models as they stand.

High-resolution models crop a big image into tiles, and past squeezers treat all tiles alike. The team's read shows a small whole-image view can judge which tiles matter. The commander lets that global view guide the squeeze of each crop. Crops also differ among themselves in what they hold. Early reads claim strong speed gains with the answer's quality held. The design fits the multi-view form of modern high-end models.
arxiv-2501-05279:
Emilia Magnani, Ernesto De Vito, Philipp Hennig, and Lorenzo Rosasco study learning convolution operators on compact groups in a math paper from 2025. Convolutions smear a signal by a kernel, the same operation behind image filters. Here the signals live on compact abelian groups, spaces like circles and tori.

The team analyzes a ridge regression estimator for the unknown kernel. The kernel is assumed to sit in a translation-invariant Hilbert space. Error bounds show how accuracy grows with sample size. Classic smoothness assumptions gain a fresh reading as limits on space and frequency spread. Computer simulations back the theory. The work serves signal processing on periodic and directional data.
arxiv-2501-05379:
Gerogiannis and co-authors present Arc2Avatar, a method that builds an expressive three-dimensional avatar head from a single photo. Past methods needed many views of a person to build a good avatar. New large models trained on human faces, though, carry strong knowledge of what heads look like from any angle.

Arc2Avatar fine-tunes such a face model on synthetic data so it can imagine the head from new viewpoints. It then shapes a fast three-dimensional representation that stays tied to a standard face mesh. That tie lets the avatar change expression the way digital puppets do, through blend shapes. Extra steps clean up the fit. The result is a lifelike avatar from one image, ready for games and virtual meetings.
arxiv-2501-05579:
Some black holes feed so fast that their own light blows gas away at a third of light speed. Chloe Taylor, Daniel Wilkins, and Steven Allen report such an outflow in this 2025 paper. The galaxy's core, catalogued as RE J1034+396, was watched by an X-ray telescope for about a million seconds in total. Its spectrum mixes a steep glow from hot gas with reflections off a searing accretion disk.

Soft X-ray excess was traced to disk light scattered by a warm plasma over the inner flow. Absorption lines in a second instrument confirmed the fast outflow independently. The wind's speed pinned down tightly, and its strength makes it exceptional among known cases. Such winds can reshape a galaxy's growth.
arxiv-2501-06079:
M D Fajardo studies functions that return sets rather than single values, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Such functions arise where a problem has ranges of answers ranked by a cone's order. She focuses on evenly convex ones, whose graph's upper region can be cut out by open half-spaces, a shape notion weaker than plain convexity.

Fajardo proves that each such function is exactly the pointwise top of its flat minorants, the set-valued affine functions that sit under it. She then builds a matching scheme for this class, pairing each function with a dual built from those minorants. The scheme obeys a double-dual law in the spirit of the classic Fenchel-Moreau theorem: applying it twice returns the function itself. The work is pure theory in convex analysis.
arxiv-2501-06379: Luiz Lopes, writing solo, asks whether an ultra compact object could be a strange star laced with dark matter, in a 2025 letter. The object is oddly light and small for a neutron star. Lopes models it with a named dark matter particle held at a set momentum. He then computes the star's top mass, spin inertia, light bending shift, and tide response. He totals its dark matter load for a set mass. The letter lays out those figures as a test of the mixed star idea.
arxiv-2501-06579:
Krishnendu Chatterjee and three co-authors prove when two random programs truly differ in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Probabilistic programs can observe data and score runs, shaping their output spread. Asking whether two such programs give the same spread is hard. Refuting sameness means finding a proof they differ. The authors build the first fully automated method for programs with conditioning.

Their trick, weighted restarting, rewrites a conditioned program into an equivalent one without conditioning. Older tools for the simpler case then apply. The method also supplies concrete evidence of the gap it finds. Program verification researchers are the audience. Reliable randomness matters in Bayesian tools and randomized algorithms alike.
arxiv-2501-06979:
John Gough examines in 2025 a claim about how path integrals set the rule for turning classic physics into quantum physics. The claim holds that one rule, the Born-Jordan rule, is the sole rule that fits the short time behavior of the propagator. That claim has shaped views in the field.

Close checks show the short time expansion holds only for a narrow class of systems. Those are systems at most quadratic in momentum, with fixed mass. In that class, other rules, such as the Weyl scheme, give the same answer. The paper thus narrows the reach of the Born-Jordan rule and reopens the question of a universal rule.
arxiv-2501-07179:
Wassim Kabbani, Tristan Le Pessot, Kiran Raja, Raghavendra Ramachandra, and Christoph Busch build a detector for fish-eye warp in face photos used for ID checks. Their paper from twenty twenty-five targets enrolment quality in face recognition systems. Radial distortion bends facial traits and drags down match scores. Self-enrolment by phone makes such flaws easy to miss.

Their model flags warped enrolment shots before they enter the system. It is cast as a face image quality algorithm, in line with field practice. The team also gauges how warp size shifts recognition scores in depth. Detection marks came out strong in their trials. The impact study yields rules for how flagged shots should be handled in live systems. The work guards the front door of identity pipelines.
arxiv-2501-07379:
Manh Hong Duong, Fabian Spill, and Blaine Van Rensburg model evolution and ecology together in twenty twenty-five. Eco-evolutionary dynamics matter for many species and even for cancer growth. They shape how populations survive pressures such as climate change. Models of this interplay often give up analytical tractability or ignore population heterogeneity.

The authors generalize a moment-based method to fill that gap. Their version allows birth and death rates that change over time. It works in the regime of small segregational variance. Both transient and long-term behavior stay within reach. They apply the results to a trait-structured predator-prey model with sexual reproduction. Readers get math that keeps heterogeneity in view without losing the ability to compute.
arxiv-2501-07479:
Yijue Ding, a solo author, simulates what happens when light tears a common solvent molecule apart, in two thousand twenty-five. The molecule is dichloromethane, and the events unfold extremely fast. Computer tracks run over accurate maps of the molecule's energy in its excited states.

After the breakup, the author simulates a second step where the charged pieces blow apart. Both steps suggest the molecule is unlikely to rearrange into its mirror form along the way. Energy estimates from a pure charge model missed the simulated values by a clear margin. The study shows how the breakup signals map onto structural changes, supporting the imaging method used to probe such reactions.
arxiv-2501-08379:
Jaychandran Padayasi, Ken Ma, and Kun Yang recast a broad class of metal-like states as a kind of quantum Hall state in an odd space. Their 2025 paper starts from states that keep a sharp surface in momentum space and obey a known count rule. Past work built such states from shared traits of symmetry and anomaly. The authors view them instead in phase space, which mixes place and momentum.

In that view, the states look like Hall fluids that resist being squeezed. A map that turns the odd space into a plain one then yields the field theory for these states. The method gives both the known special terms and the terms that set how the states respond.
arxiv-2501-08579:
Qian Wang and eight co-authors argue, in 2025 work, that fake humans played by large language models are not yet trusty. Such stand-ins now fill studies of crowds, markets, policy, and minds. The team checked those uses end to end and found wide gaps between the fakes' acts and real human acts.

The gaps spring from two roots: flaws bred into the models, and weak build of the fake worlds they act in. Both are walked through in depth. Fixes are then framed: richer base data, stronger models, and sturdier design rules. A step-by-step plan turns the frame into a guide. A shared list of past work rounds out the paper, for teams who want sound fakes.
arxiv-2501-08679:
Yicheng Li and Qian Lin introduce a kernel model that learns its own shape while it trains. Classic kernel methods fix the kernel in advance, and if that choice clashes with the target pattern, accuracy suffers. Their diagonal model adjusts the kernel's eigenvalues and the output weights at the same time, so the kernel bends toward the structure of the true function. The gain over fixed kernels is largest exactly when the starting kernel is a poor match.

The improvement, they show, comes from learning the right eigenvalues, which is a form of feature learning inside a kernel method. Adding depth to the setup strengthens the effect further. The authors frame the work as a bridge between two views of neural networks: feature learning on one side, and the quiet pull of implicit regularization on the other.
arxiv-2501-08779:
Sydney Vernon, Eviatar Bach, and Oliver Dunbar present a 2025 way to speed up ensemble Kalman inversion, a particle method for solving inverse problems without derivatives. The method can be read as a flow that follows a slope downhill, so slope-speeding tricks may apply. The team adds a Nesterov-style push to each particle.

The push is a small nudge that plugs into any variant of the method with no extra cost and no new knobs to tune. Tests on many inverse problems show the cost drops faster with the push in place. Two named variants gain the same way.
arxiv-2501-08879:
Axel Brandenburg and co-authors test how swirl changes mixing in turbulent flows in a 2025 paper. Turbulence boosts how fast magnetic fields and plain scalars spread out. When the flow also twists, with helicity, magnetic spreading is known to drop below the plain value.

Standard approximations fail to capture that magnetic drop. The new simulations show the scalar case runs the other way: helicity raises passive scalar spreading. Twisting also lengthens the time that flow patterns stay alike, a clue to the cause. Computer runs where helicity grows on its own support the same picture. Plasma and climate modelers both need the sign of this effect right.
arxiv-2501-08979:
Statistics students learn that averages settle into a bell curve, but the modern version must hold across thousands of coordinates at once. Woonyoung Chang and three co-authors bound the error of that settling in 2025 for self normalized sums, where each sum is divided by its own spread. Their bound is fully explicit, with no hidden constants.

When the third moment is finite, the error shrinks at a stated rate tied to sample size and dimension. The dimension may grow almost exponentially in the sample size before the bound stops shrinking. No such bound existed before for these statistics in high dimensions. The authors present it as a missing piece of the high dimensional limit theory.
arxiv-2501-09579:
Runzhou Mao, Juraj Fulir, Christoph Garth, and Petra Gospodnetic wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on factory surface checks. Automated inspection often stumbles on mere impurities like water stains and fingerprints, which are not defects but still fool the camera.

The team argues synthetic training data should include such stains, not just perfect parts and true defects. They build a method to paint lifelike water stains into synthetic images. High-resolution inspection photos also strain memory, so they add Sequential PatchCore, which builds its memory bank in passes and runs on consumer hardware. Pre-training on the synthetic sets, then fine-tuning on real photos, worked best. The paper also reports recall defect by defect, the measure factories care about, and shows how stains and fuzzy labels drag scores down.
arxiv-2501-09679:
Haroune Houamed, writing alone in 2025, proves that a plasma model breaks down unless its magnetic field starts in a special shape. The model couples an incompressible fluid with Maxwell's equations for the field, a system used for ionized gases. Recent work had shown the two-dimensional system behaves well for all time when the field obeys a condition called the Normal Structure.

Houamed shows that condition cannot be dropped. For starting data that break it, the system becomes ill-posed in the Yudovich class, the mild setting used in the good result. The proof works both on the open plane and on a repeating square, for any speed of light. It expands the field around a flat background and splits the magnetic force into a singular part and a smaller rest. The catalog title carries an acknowledgment note, so the clean head title governs.
arxiv-2501-09779: John Haslegrave presents a short 2025 note in graph theory. A graph's automorphism group collects all the ways its structure can be mapped onto itself. Earlier work by Barbieri showed that graphs realizing any given finite symmetry group can have unbounded genus. That result answered a question from Cornwell and others. Haslegrave gives a brief proof of a stronger claim. Those same graphs can have unbounded clique number, so they can contain arbitrarily large sets of points that are all directly connected to each other.
arxiv-2501-10079:
Christopher Añorve and co-authors release a tool for reading galaxy brightness profiles in a 2025 paper. EllipSect works beside GALFIT 3, a widely used code that fits two-dimensional models to galaxy images. Fitting alone leaves astronomers short of some summary measures they need for papers.

Built in Python, EllipSect takes the image data plus the fit output and returns clean figures and exportable data files. It grades the fit as a whole and piece by piece. It also computes measures the base code skips, like the total effective radius from multi-part fits, the cusp radius, and the Petrosian radius. Worked examples and a quick guide fill the paper, so a new user can go from a raw fit to checked numbers and plots in one sitting.
arxiv-2501-10179:
Kazuma Onishi and Katsuhiko Hayashi offer a strikingly simple method for extreme multi label learning in a 2025 paper. The task assigns each item several labels from an enormous label set. Leading models carry many knobs to tune and are painful to reimplement. Their method rests on ridge regression, a classic technique with a closed form answer and a single tuning parameter.

A frequency based weighting, added in a few lines, lifts predictions for rare labels, which carry rich information but little data. On standard benchmarks, the simple method matched or beat heavily tuned rivals. The weighting clearly improved rare label accuracy. The authors share the code and present the result as a reminder that simple baselines deserve respect in this field.
arxiv-2501-10279:
Haowei Xu and Ju Li predict, in a 2025 paper, how electric fields and light can switch on magnetism in a crystal that is not magnetic at all. The effect they study, the Edelstein effect, turns an applied field into magnetization, with a linear version and a stronger second-order one. Their test material is CoSi, a chiral crystal that comes in left- and right-handed forms.

Both effects, the calculations show, need time-reversal symmetry broken, but heat and dissipation in a real device can break it spontaneously. The two crystal hands behave as mirror images for the linear effect and identically for the nonlinear one. At field strengths near those inside atoms, the induced magnetization could reach ten Bohr magnetons per unit cell. The authors offer their method as a systematic way to hunt such effects in real materials, toward spintronic devices and magnetic memory.
arxiv-2501-10579:
Jaromir Savelka and co-authors report four years of a fast-track course that trains AI technicians for the United States Army. Their 2025 paper argues that armies and firms need many hands-on AI staff, not just degree-holding scientists. Four- and two-year degrees fill that gap too slowly, so the Army and a university built a rapid route.

Fifty-nine technicians had finished at the time of writing. Course content needs steady refresh, since Army AI use shifts fast. Tight links between Army and campus staff keep the course aimed at real posts. Other large employers facing the same hiring wall can borrow the playbook, the authors suggest.
arxiv-2501-10979:
Seven researchers present a way to keep teaching language models without erasing old skills in a paper from 2025. Continued training often causes catastrophic forgetting, where new lessons wipe out earlier ability. Their method, Control LLM, adds fresh transformer blocks beside the original ones. Interpolation aligns the hidden states of old and new blocks during training. The design lets new knowledge enter while old performance stays guarded.

On a popular open model, math and coding scores rose sharply after continued training. Multilingual scores improved as well, using far less data than rivals. Losses on original skills stayed under five percent, versus over thirty-five percent for some tuned models. The approach already runs in LinkedIn products.
arxiv-2501-11179:
Benjamin Reidys and co-authors pack more virtual machines onto cloud servers in a 2025 paper. Cloud fleets sit idle much of the time across all resource types. Renting out the slack is risky when tenants surge at once. Usage records from a major cloud showed many machines peak at opposite times.

Their system pairs those rhythms to oversell every resource safely. Each tenant gets a guaranteed slice plus a shared bonus slice. Watchers catch crowding early and shift memory before slowdowns bite. Trials hosted about a quarter more machines with minimal slowdown.
arxiv-2501-11679:
David O'Neill, Christopher Tiede, Daniel J. D'Orazio, Zoltán Haiman, and Andrew MacFadyen model pairs of large black holes in this two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. A disk of gas rings the pair and spins the other way, a set-up called retrograde. Gravitational waves shrink the pair's orbit. It breaks free of the disk, when its fall in runs faster than the disk can react. Retrograde cases have had less study than prograde ones and may merge faster.

The runs find the break-free point is the same for both kinds of disk, so signs in light should show at the same time before merger. But retrograde disks leave a smaller hole. That points to higher-frequency light and faster rebrightening after merger. Low-viscosity retrograde disks flared in a quasi-periodic way. The cause was unstable flow. That flaring could be a sign to look for.
arxiv-2501-11879:
Takahiro Morishita and colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope in 2025 to study a merging galaxy system in the most distant known protocluster, seen as it was in the early universe. Their integral field observations covered two previously known galaxies and revealed a third. Because one glowing oxygen region showed a faint temperature-sensitive line, the team could measure its metal content directly rather than by calibration.

Metal levels varied strikingly from place to place, by roughly a factor of ten, which points to rapid enrichment from intense star formation stirred by mergers. Imaging showed several bright clumps of young stars in the new galaxy. The authors warn that metal-poor regions are easily outshone by enriched ones, so surveys using combined light may miss truly pristine star formation in early galaxies.
arxiv-2501-12079:
Qingyuan Liang, Zeyu Sun, and co-authors put out a 2025 paper on teaching code models how edits unfold step by step. Most code models learn from fixed code and miss how real changes build over time. Their model, DivoT5, learns from pairs of code before and after an edit, with the path of change built into the training task.

Training mixes two task types. One type adds noise to old code and asks the model to restore the new code. The other type asks the model to move draft versions toward the final code. The team tested the model on five tasks, from code review to code repair. DivoT5 beat models of the same size and some far larger ones on most tasks.
arxiv-2501-12579:
Sergey Bravyi, David Gosset, Vojtech Havlicek, and Louis Schatzki find faster ways to compute characters, the key numerical fingerprints of the symmetric group's representations. These values appear across group theory, but for permutations they are notoriously hard: worst-case computation sits in the hardest counting class.

Their classical method encodes all the characters of one permutation in a matrix product state. That is a compact chain form borrowed from quantum physics. It uses a known bridge between characters and quantum spin chains, which they also re-derive more simply. A matching quantum circuit of polynomial size prepares the same state, giving an efficient quantum route to related sampling tasks. The authors also prove a general link between computing a probability exactly and merely sampling from it, for problems with the right grain, a result they note may stand on its own.
arxiv-2501-13079:
Francesco Pedrotti and Justin Salez prove a new test for when a random process snaps suddenly into balance, a jump called cutoff. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Cutoff was lately shown to follow from two broad traits for smooth systems. The proof leaned on a chain rule that works only for smooth generators, not step-by-step chains.

The pair show that a near version of that rule always holds. The slack depends on how rough the watched quantity is. With it, they prove the cutoff test for chains on finite sets with curved-up geometry. The single proof now covers classic cases once handled one by one. These include walks on cubes, card shuffles by random swaps, and samplers for magnet models. The work unifies a scattered corner of probability theory.
arxiv-2501-13179:
Francesca Lusetti and Adriano Tomassini build new shapes that pass a strict geometry test in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Kähler manifolds are the tidy stars of complex geometry, but many shapes lack that structure. A symplectic form can still give rich geometry, and the Hard Lefschetz Condition is a demanding test of its quality. The authors produce fresh families of non-Kähler examples that pass. Their shapes are quotients of a solvable Lie group by explicit lattices.

Cohomology computations confirm the test is met. They also compute a dimension that classifies the complex structure and list generators for two cohomology theories. New examples keep conjectures honest in complex geometry. Geometers are the audience.
arxiv-2501-13279:
Carlo Cafaro, Emma Clements, and Abeer Alanazi weigh how hard it is for a quantum bit to travel from one state to another. The states of the bit sit on a ball, the Bloch sphere, and each path across the ball has a length, a speed, and a curve. Their 2025 study picks paths by set marks of merit, from the swift best path to slower, loose ones. Each path is then scored by a new measure of cost, and by a linked length scale.

Swift, lean paths tend to cost less than loose ones. Yet length is not the whole story. A long path with the right bend can cost as much as a short, flat one, or less. Checks with swapped start and end states back the measure as sound. The work gives quantum engineers a finer scale for the true cost of a state change.
arxiv-2501-13379:
Anthony Leiva-Valverde and co-authors weigh in 2025 faster ways to compute the softmax step in neural networks. Softmax turns raw scores into class probabilities at the output layer. On small programmable chips it is costly, because it needs exponential and division steps that eat time and hardware.

The team tested shortcut methods based on polynomial series and on lookup tables with interpolation. The table method with a curved fit gave the lowest numerical error. The series shortcuts ran faster and used fewer chip resources, thanks to their simple math. On two well known image models, the series versions lost at most 0.2 percent accuracy while cutting resource use by up to 14 percent. The authors see the results as a base for adding such shortcuts to larger models.
arxiv-2501-13479:
Rishabh Agrawal set out a framework for learning from a handful of labeled cases, in a solo paper published in 2025. Few-shot learning serves fields where labels are scarce: health, robotics, and speech. Its flaws are known: shaky starts, poor jumps to new fields, and weak spots with noisy data. The framework stacks four modules to meet those flaws directly.

One module steadies the starts. One aligns the model to new fields. One hardens it against noise. One fuses mixed kinds of data, such as text with scans. Supporting methods join in: task-fitted data growth, partly labeled learning, and clear explanation tools. The author presents the stack as a scalable base for high-stakes use, where data will stay thin.
arxiv-2501-13779:
Tanya Rodchenko, Natasha Noy, and Nino Scherrer argue that AI builders should choose their training data on purpose, in a 2025 paper. The default instinct is to gather ever more data for ever larger models. The authors counter that tasks differ in whether more data can even help them. The shape of the data itself, its composition and structure, signals which tasks will reward scaling and which will not.

Being intentional about acquisition saves money and compute, and it points research toward new computing approaches for tasks where data runs out. The paper is a position piece, asking the field to match its data appetite to the structure of each problem rather than feeding every problem the same diet.
arxiv-2501-13879:
André Menezes, Andrew Parnell, and Keefe Murphy give a new view of two models for count data in this 2025 paper. The data mix counts with shares, and they hold more zeros than plain models expect. Extra mass also piles up at the top count.

The authors show both models can be written as finite mixtures, blends of simpler parts. One blend rests on a model studied before; the other is new. From the mixture form they derive key traits like means and edge cases. They also build faster Bayesian fitting steps, using Gibbs sampling where it fits the math.
arxiv-2501-14779:
Mika Setala and co-authors survey Finnish high school students on using generative AI for math in a 2025 paper. Chat style tools are entering classrooms fast, and schools need to know what drives students to accept or reject them. The study reads the answers through a classic model of technology acceptance.

Usefulness proved the strongest driver of intent to use the tools. Enjoyment mattered too, shaping both how useful and how easy the tools felt. Adding a fit measure, how well the tools match student study habits, sharpened the model's power, above all for usefulness. The authors compare their Finnish results with a past study abroad and draw lessons for rolling AI into math classes.
arxiv-2501-14879:
Martin-Gonzalez and co-authors ask how fast a two-sex population dies out when mating depends on size in two thousand twenty-five. In their model, extinction is certain in the end, so the useful question is when it will strike. Exact answers are hard, so they seek a sound estimate.

The team builds its estimate on extreme value theory, the branch of statistics that deals with rare edge events. Those tools are standard and easy to apply in practice, which suits field use. The authors prove the core claims behind the method. A few worked numeric cases show how the estimate behaves on sample populations.
arxiv-2501-14979:
Hannah Wakeling and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv document setting out green guidelines for large particle accelerator facilities. New accelerators are planned for the coming decades, and upgrades of old ones are under way. Both moments, the authors argue, are rare chances to bake lower environmental impact into the design rather than bolting it on later.

The document is a living one, meant to be updated as practice improves. It walks through every stage of a facility's life: planning, construction, operation, and final decommissioning. For each stage it collects resources, real examples from existing labs, and suggested practices for cutting energy use, waste, and emissions. Because accelerators are huge, long-lived machines, early choices lock in decades of footprint. The guidelines aim to make sustainability a design input, on par with cost and performance, from the very first sketch.
arxiv-2501-15979:
Victor Moya, Jaime Rosado, and Fernando Arqueros wrote a short physics paper in two thousand twenty-five about an upgrade to a software package called LegPy. The package simulates how particles move through matter. The upgrade adds the making of X-ray fluorescence, the glow atoms give off after being struck.

The team used a simple model for that glow and ran tests to check its accuracy. In cases where the glow matters a lot, the old package had drifted far from a trusted reference code called PENELOPE. The simple model was enough to fix those gaps. The paper reports what was added and how the checks came out.
arxiv-2501-16079:
Le Ngoc Tram and co-authors model how interstellar dust grains line up with magnetic fields, opening the GRADE-POL project. Polarized light from aligned dust is a main tool for mapping cosmic magnetic fields, but it also contaminates maps of the cosmic microwave background. The leading alignment theory says starlight torques, boosted by magnetism, spin grains into line.

Their simulations show polarization efficiency first sagging slowly as dust is buried deeper in a cloud, then dropping steeply once grains lose alignment in the dark interior. That two-stage fall explains the polarization holes seen around dense cores. Applied to a real starless core in the Pipe Nebula, the model reproduces observations at two starlight bands and one submillimeter band. The work sharpens dust physics behind magnetic field maps.
arxiv-2501-16279:
Leila Ghasemzadeh and co-authors introduce a new model for the inner layout of nucleons in a 2025 paper. Nucleons, the core bits of atoms, hold quarks and gluons in patterns that maps called GPDs describe. A good map must fit lab data on how nucleons bend probes, a trait summed up in form factors.

Their model, named GSAMA24, uses fresh settings for how the maps shift with angle and energy share. Fitted to form factor data, it beat three older models, most clearly at high momentum transfer. It also matched theory's rules for such maps better than one rival. The authors offer it as a tool for future hadron studies.
arxiv-2501-17279:
Atom-thin sheets gain new tricks when single atoms go missing in planned spots, and language models may design those defect patterns. Abdalaziz Al-Maeeni, Denis Derkach, and Andrey Ustyuzhanin apply that idea to molybdenum disulfide in a 2025 paper. A dataset built from physics calculations covers many defect types and doses. A pretrained language model proposes the layouts instead of random generation.

The model predicts how each layout shifts the material's traits. Older pipelines made random layouts and screened them afterward. Here the design step itself is learned. The authors frame the method for optoelectronics and other high-tech uses. Understanding defect-to-trait links is a stated second goal.
arxiv-2501-17379:
Henning Koehler and co-authors present a labeling method that answers distance questions on road networks that keep changing, in this 2025 paper. Traffic shifts close lanes and change travel times constantly. Older methods precompute distance labels tied to a ranking of junctions, but the labels grow large and resist quick updates.

Their method rests on a stable tree ranking of the network. Labels store distances only within small subnetworks, so a road change touches few of them. Two maintenance algorithms refresh the labels after each change. The design aims to balance fast queries against cheap updates, a trade-off that live navigation and logistics tools depend on.
arxiv-2501-17579:
An atom falling into a black hole can glow as it nears the edge, and that glow carries a form of entropy. Arpita Jana, Soham Sen, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay compute that glow for a charged black hole in a 2025 paper. Their hole is improved by quantum flow rules, where gravity's strength and the charge shift with energy scale.

The atom's chance to jump states, by shedding a virtual photon, bends slightly from the pure heat curve. That bend comes from an incomplete gamma term in the math. The entropy they derive matches the classic area law plus fix terms. One fix runs as an inverse log of area, a fresh shape for this setting.
arxiv-2501-17779:
Günay Dogan and co-authors make aligning two closed curves an order of magnitude cheaper. Shape analysis, from anatomy to cell morphology, constantly needs one outline rotated and re-started to best match another. With no natural starting point on a closed loop, the naive search over rotations and starts grows quadratically with the number of nodes.

Their algorithm runs in near-linear time by moving the search into Fourier space with the fast Fourier transform, after resampling both curves evenly by arc length. Experiments show order-of-magnitude speedups over the naive method. Plugged into elastic shape distance computations, the aligner delivers accurate distances at a fraction of the previous cost. The authors aim it at the large curve collections modern imaging produces.
arxiv-2501-17879:
Sagnik Bhattacharya, Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin, Ahsan Bilal, and John Cioffi design a speech coding scheme for wireless settings in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Augmented and virtual reality apps need a set of near devices to stream linked speech over weak and narrow links. Past autoencoder coders can not shift bitrate with no new training, miss links between sources, and miss how the rebuilt speech serves tasks that come next. The team puts forth a neural distributed principal component analysis aided coding method.

Many linked sources send to one central receiver, using their shared form. A perception-aware loss trades sound that feels real against how well tasks do. Tests showed peak signal-to-noise gains over autoencoder ways at tight bandwidth. The gains neared the top bound of joint encoding, most at low bandwidth. A rate-distortion-perception curve lets apps trade realism against bitrate as needs shift.
arxiv-2501-17979:
Tony Lelièvre, Xuyang Lin, and Pierre Monmarché prove the first exponential convergence result for a family of simulation methods used to explore molecular energy landscapes, in a 2025 paper. Adaptive biasing methods, including metadynamics and the adaptive biasing force, add a shifting push that helps simulations cross energy barriers. They have worked well in practice for decades, but proving how fast they settle is hard, especially for the realistic kinetic Langevin dynamics, which is non-reversible.

Working in an idealized setting, the authors recast the algorithm as a flow over probability distributions, a mean-field picture. The key insight is that the process amounts to gradient descent of a well-chosen functional on that distribution space. From that viewpoint the exponential rate follows. The authors are explicit that the setting is idealized, but the result gives this widely used family its first firm convergence footing of this strength.
arxiv-2501-18079:
Gregory Constantine studies the lattice of normal subgroups of a group, a topic in pure algebra. His work appeared in twenty twenty-five. He focuses on two special parts of a group, called the socle and the radical, and on what their subgroup patterns reveal.

From those patterns, Constantine derives a formula for the fewest classes of elements needed to generate the whole group. He shows that this number can be read off from the group's character table. He then uses the Möbius function, a classic counting tool, on the lattice. That step pulls out facts about the group's faithful irreducible representations, the building blocks that act on the group without losing information.
arxiv-2501-18179:
Suripto Bhuiyan and Michael Geller design a layered sensor for trace toxins in liquids in a 2025 paper. The sensor reads surface plasmon resonance, a light effect that shifts when molecules bind. Reaching toxin levels in parts per billion takes sharp tuning.

Their stack uses the classic Kretschmann layout with two-dimensional materials, black phosphorus and metal dichalcogenide sheets among them. Layer choices were tuned for sensitivity, a narrow signal width, and a strong figure of merit. Simulations checked the design rather than bench tests. A stronger evanescent field grips the sample, the authors report, lifting both precision and specificity. Uses span biochemical sensing and environmental watch.
arxiv-2501-18279:
Christina Ovezik, Dimitris Karakostas, Mary Milad, Aggelos Kiayias, and Daniel Woods sort out how to measure decentralization in blockchains, in work from 2025. Everyone praises the trait, but no shared ruler exists. Studies pick their own windows, cutoffs, and math, then compare poorly.

The team frames every past method by what resource it counts, how the split is pulled from data, and what function turns the split into a score. They then test whether the choices change the answer. Small data choices, like window size, swing scores a lot. Factor tests show work-based chains split into two signals, not one. The paper urges care in what a score really names.
arxiv-2501-18379:
Florian Fischer and Christian Rose review and extend a method for sharp inequalities on curved spaces and on graphs, in a 2025 paper. The inequalities, of Poincare and Hardy type, bound how a function can spread given its slope, and the best possible weights in them are the prize. The method is first recalled for hyperbolic spaces.

The review then covers manifolds with like traits. A known result for regular trees, which are graphs that branch evenly, gets a new proof by the same method. New results follow for graphs with a weak spherical symmetry, including fast-growing trees and anti-trees. Their optimal weights grow larger at infinity than the classic weights built by an older recipe. The paper is a technical survey and advance for specialists in analysis on spaces and networks.
arxiv-2501-18579:
Raz Rajwan and Amir Boag image moving vehicles on roads with a single radar channel flying a circular path, in this 2025 paper. Near-field radar in spotlight mode can watch traffic, but movers smear under standard processing. Their algorithm is built for exactly that case.

A fast back-projection scheme stitches together coarse images from slices of the data, using layered interpolation to stay quick. Both parked and moving vehicles come out sharp. The design assumes the radar circles the scene, a pattern drones and towers can fly. The authors present it as a step toward cheap, high-fidelity traffic radar.
arxiv-2501-18779:
Kwangmin Oh and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy study of two very bright X-ray sources in the galaxy NGC 1399. Both sources sit inside globular clusters, dense balls of old stars. One of them, called GCU7, is only the second such source known to glow in visible light as well.

The team gathered X-ray and optical data spanning two decades. GCU7 barely changed over 20 years, which rules out a one-time event like a star being torn apart. Its light shows nitrogen and oxygen but no hydrogen. Computer models match that pattern to gas flowing from a helium white dwarf onto a neutron star. The pair likely formed when a neutron star crashed into a red giant star.
arxiv-2501-18879:
Takeshi Koshizuka and Issei Sato present a 2025 theory paper on physics-informed learning. Such models blend known physics with real data to learn faster from fewer samples. Past theory leaned on full prior knowledge and straight-line systems, while real problems mix partial rules with curved behavior.

The authors give one shared form that covers the main ways physics is folded into training. In that frame, how well the model generalizes turns on the size of a shape tied to the physics rule, not on the count of model settings. They also give a way to gauge that size, and tests back the claim.
arxiv-2501-18979:
A large team of physicists designs a compact trap to hunt for a muon's electric dipole moment. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, explains the frozen-spin method. A dipole moment in a basic particle would break key symmetries of nature. Finding one in the muon would point to new physics beyond the standard model.

Muons circle in the trap while their spin is held frozen by a strong field. In the muon's own frame that field is huge, which boosts the signal. A small tilt of the spin would betray the dipole. The trap's compact size keeps the setup sharp and cheap. The paper lays out the full design for the search.
arxiv-2501-19179:
Machine learned models of molecules are fast because they keep interactions local, but real chemistry reaches across distance: charges pull, clouds shift, electrons wander. Paul Fuchs and two co-authors bolt a long range sense onto such models in 2025 with a layer called CELLI. It revives the classical charge equilibration idea, letting atoms settle their charges together, inside the neural machinery.

The layer fits any of the modern symmetry aware potentials and explains itself through the charges it assigns. On benchmarks it set the pace among strictly local models while running cheaply and scaling to large structures. The authors present it as the missing long arm for local learning. Interpretability, they note, comes free with the physics.
arxiv-2501-19279:
Pedro Sanchez Sanchez and co-authors present a 2025 paper on training AI without a central server. In decentralized federated learning, devices train a shared model by passing updates peer to peer. No server means no single point of failure. The costs are uneven data across devices, heavy traffic, and wasted compute. Their method, called S-VOTE, picks which clients train by a similarity vote.

Voting favors clients whose data add the most to the group model. A flexible local plan lets idle clients join without a big cost jump. Wide tests on benchmark data check the gains. Edge AI teams get a way to spend compute where it counts. Hospitals, banks, and phone fleets all train under privacy rules that bar central data pools. Smarter client choice can lift model quality while keeping that privacy intact.
arxiv-2502-00079:
The back of the eye shows blood vessel changes that track stroke risk, and a photo of it is quick, cheap, and painless. Aysen Degerli and co-authors build a deep learning system in a 2025 paper that reads those photos for stroke and mini-stroke. Their network looks at both eyes at once, which earlier work had not done.

The system takes views centered on the macula and on the optic nerve head from each eye. It learns features from all four views and weighs how they relate. Tested on patients with stroke or mini-stroke plus healthy controls, it reached a solid discrimination score. The authors pitch eye photos as a fast front door for stroke checks where brain scans are scarce.
arxiv-2502-00179:
Darian McLaren and co-authors present a way to gauge errors in quantum measures that use feed forward, in a 2025 paper. Such measures are key parts of fault tolerant quantum computers, where later steps depend on earlier results. Their method fits the chance that a long run of mixed up measures all give the ideal result. All data come from one long run of measures in a row.

The authors also prove that key quality scores stay the same under the mixing step. Those scores can combine with the error rate to describe the faults at play, up to one known ambiguity about timing. Readers get a simpler test for a part of quantum hardware that is hard to check in other ways.
arxiv-2502-00279:
Khiem Pham, Charles Herrmann, and Ramin Zabih tackle a flaw in learning from partly labeled data in 2025. Semi-supervised methods guess labels for unlabeled items, but the guess leans toward the labeled mix. When rare classes dominate the unlabeled pool, that lean hurts results a lot.

The authors first estimate the true class mix in the unlabeled data. Their estimator is doubly robust, a form that stays sound if one of two models is right. That estimate then guides label guessing during training. Tests show the step lifts the scores of common label-guessing methods. The fix needs no prior knowledge of the unlabeled mix.
arxiv-2502-00379:
Alexander Nikulin and co-authors test a way to teach robots from plain video, in a 2025 paper. Latent action learning lets a model guess the hidden moves behind each video frame. It can then train on the huge stock of video on the web, with no labels at all. Past work used clean clips where frame changes come from the agent's own acts.

Real video is messier, with side events that move with the action and act as distractors. The team used a test suite full of such traps and found the base method, LAPO, falters there. Their fix, LAOM, made the learned actions eight times cleaner by one probe measure. Adding true action labels for even a tiny slice of the data lifted later scores more than fourfold. They urge builders to mix in some supervision from the start.
arxiv-2502-00579:
Jongwook Kim, Chunfeng Huang, and Nicholas Bussberg present a 2025 statistics paper on modeling data that vary over the globe and through time. Weather and climate records live on a sphere, not a flat map, and their patterns shift from place to place and era to era. Standard tools assume steady behavior everywhere, which rarely holds.

The authors build new covariance models, the formulas that say how strongly two points in space and time move together, using a framework that drops the steady-behavior assumptions. They also give a method for fitting the model's parameters to data. Simulations and a real dataset of global temperature anomalies showed the models work and stay interpretable, an advantage over black-box alternatives for climate science.
arxiv-2502-00679:
Bhavesh Gupta and co-authors present a fast noise check in 2025 for transmon qubits, a leading type of quantum bit. Noise limits how long qubits hold information and how well circuits run. Standard noise tests are slow and resource heavy.

Their method runs simple pulse sequences and records how coherence fades. A neural network, trained on mock data, then predicts the noise spectrum from those traces. Tests used real superconducting qubits on a public quantum platform. The quick spectra can guide custom pulse schemes to fight noise. The method works across many hardware types.
arxiv-2502-00779:
Eun Som Jeon and co-authors write a 2025 paper on wearable sensor data. Sensors on the body stream fast, rich signals for health and activity tools. Shape-based features from topology can enrich those signals, but computing them is slow and costly.

Knowledge distillation offers a shortcut, training a small student model on the output of larger teachers. The team studies how mixup, a trick that blends training samples and their labels, interacts with that transfer. Both methods lean on smoothed targets, which links them in a natural way. Teachers carrying time-series and topology features both feed the student. The analysis maps which mixes of the two methods work best for sensor tasks.
arxiv-2502-01279:
Bernardo Maraldi, Henk Dijkstra, and Michael Ghil study short-term atmospheric swings in a small climate model as the climate drifts, in a 2025 paper. Simple models help explain how mid-latitude circulation varies and how warming might change it. The authors treat the model as a system whose rules shift with the seasons.

First they map the model's behavior under fixed forcing. Seasonal forcing then reshapes the attractor: summer patterns lose their regular rhythm while winter favors one wave route for energy transport. Under climate trends, chaos can switch off or on, and patterns can vanish and rebuild. Jet speed did not always follow the pole-to-equator temperature gap, they note.
arxiv-2502-01479:
Paul Gomez, Franck Plunian, and Thierry Alboussière wrote this 2025 paper testing a shortcut to galactic magnetism. Galaxies hold broad magnetic fields, usually blamed on turbulent dynamos. Recent theory and lab work showed a lazier route: if electrical conductivity is stronger along one direction, plain rotation can grow a field, no turbulence needed.

Spiral arms suggest exactly that anisotropy, with conductivity along the arms perhaps double the cross-arm value. But a geometric test must also pass, linking the pitch angle of the arms to the shear of rotation. Real spiral galaxies fail it: their arms trail, the wrong way round for the effect. Even NGC 4622, which sports both leading and trailing arms, fails. Simulations confirm the verdict, so arm anisotropy cannot explain galactic fields.
arxiv-2502-01679:
Bias tests for language models mostly speak American: the groups, slang, and stereotypes come from United States data. Five researchers build a local alternative in 2025, tuned to New Zealand. Their framework pulls test material from local text collections instead of crowdsourcing, and it adds two guards. One score flags when a model simply does not know a local word, so ignorance is not mistaken for prejudice. Another measures how far its answers drift between groups.

The test set tops 360,000 cases. Older model families and a small open model barely grasp the local terms. The largest model shows the biggest bias yet handles the cultural setting best. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2502-01779:
Salih Kibaroğlu and Mustafa Senay work out a next cosmology in this two thousand twenty-five theoretical physics paper. Verlinde's entropic gravity treats gravity as an emergent entropic force, not a base interaction. The team joins it with q-deformed theory. That is a stretch of particle dynamics with roots in quantum group forms. They use both on the Bianchi type-I universe, an anisotropic model where space grows at distinct rates on distinct axes.

They set out the dynamical equations for that model under q-deformation, in the entropic frame, then study a case with symmetry round one axis in depth. The point is to see how q-deformation shifts acts, where the early universe may act in new ways, and how the universe grows later. The upshots show where such shifts could leave signs that can be seen. Those signs would stand off from standard cosmology.
arxiv-2502-02179:
Jeremiah Fadugba, Isabel Lieberman, Olabode Ajayi, Mansour Osman, Solomon Oluwole Akinola, Tinashe Mustvangwa, Dong Zhang, Udunna Anazondo, and Raymond Confidence wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds a deep ensemble that cuts brain tumors out of scans, aimed at clinics with few experts.

Hand tracing is slow and rests on scarce skill, a hard lack in Sub-Saharan Africa. The team blends three net shapes, first trained on a global glioma set, then tuned on an African set. The blend beats each part on all three tumor zones: core, whole, and enhancing rim. The gains press the case for ensemble tools where staff and gear run thin.
arxiv-2502-02479:
Xiyuan Wang and Muhan Zhang present a 2025 paper on adding random noise to graph neural networks without hurting them. Such networks learn from linked data, and noise fed in the right way can make them more expressive. Fed in carelessly, though, noise can drag performance down, while noise tricks built for one task rarely travel to others.

The authors first build a theory showing why careless noise raises the amount of training data needed. Their design, called ENGNN, uses the symmetry of noise itself to cut that cost back. Across node, link, subgraph, and whole-graph tasks, the design matched tools built for single tasks, offering one general way to boost these networks.
arxiv-2502-02679:
Vera Kurkova and Marcello Sanguineti present a 2025 analysis of neural networks whose function sets have finite VC dimension, weighing the pros and cons. VC dimension measures a model family's capacity. Finite capacity helps learning theory: sample errors settle uniformly, which supports reliable learning from data. The same finiteness, though, can hurt approximation of functions drawn from the kinds of distributions real applications present.

Using concentration-of-measure effects in high dimensions, the authors show both approximation and sample errors behave almost deterministically for such networks on large data. They discuss the practical limits of the universal approximation promise. The trade-off between fitting power and learning consistency, and how network depth with ReLU units shifts it, rounds out the paper.
arxiv-2502-02779:
Weicheng Zhu and co-authors build a foundation model for spotting disease in head CT scans, in a 2025 paper. Head CT is the first-line scan in brain emergencies: fast, safe, cheap, and everywhere. Deep learning could flag many diseases at once, but scarce expert labels, above all for rare conditions, hold models back.

Their model, FM-CT, learns without labels from over three hundred sixty thousand non-contrast 3D head scans. Two self-teaching styles, self-distillation and masked image modeling, train it in full 3D rather than slice by slice, so it absorbs the skull's true structure. The goal is one adaptable model that transfers across the many diseases a head scan can show, easing the label bottleneck.
arxiv-2502-02879:
Nkiru Ede, Jens Dietrich, and Ulrich Zülicke study Maven Central in a 2025 paper on how Java software parts gain and lose use over time. Maven Central is a large shared store of Java parts that other programs build on. A small group of parts draws most of the links, and the authors ask whether that top group stays fixed.

Using several measures of use and change, the team finds that the top group does shift over time. New parts still enter and rise, though the pace of fresh ideas has slowed as the store has aged over twenty years. Readers who build or study software stores get a clear picture of a system that is mature but still active and open to change.
arxiv-2502-02979:
A drum skin and a light field can knot their states, yet the room's noise can cut the knot at a set depth. Su Direkci and co-authors find that depth in a 2025 study of a drum and light rig in a room whose noise has a past. The drive light may be plain or squeezed, in flat or bent forms.

For the flat forms, the knot dies at a depth set by the room's noise alone. The rig's own grip and the squeeze depth do not move that bar. Where drum and light start apart, bent squeeze can not birth a knot. The bar is thus a wide law of such rigs, not a tune of one build.
arxiv-2502-03279:
Teemu Säilynoja and co-authors sharpen a standard check for Bayesian inference code in this 2025 paper. Simulation-based calibration tests a method by re-running it on fake data. The classic version draws fake settings from the prior, before seeing real data.

After real data arrive, a different question matters more. Does the method work on data like the ones actually observed? Their posterior version conditions the check on the observed dataset. That focuses testing power where the analyst actually stands. A check can pass globally yet fail near the real case. Statisticians gain a sharper tool for trusting their own pipelines. Software packages can adopt the sharper check directly.
arxiv-2502-03479:
Elvis Han Cui, writing alone in 2025, studies how to estimate the chance that patients move between health states over time. Such estimates guide care research, here for stem cell transplant patients who pass through six clinical states. Models that ignore how long a patient has been in a state can blur the true path.

Cui compares two estimators on a standard transplant dataset. The one built on renewal ideas, which respect time spent in each state, drew smoother and more time-aware curves. The gap was clearest for moves out of long-lasting states. Math arguments in the paper show the estimator settles toward the truth as data grows. Future work would add patient traits and richer dynamics.
arxiv-2502-03679:
Why galaxies come in the sizes they do, and how size ties to the dark matter halo around each, remains an open question. The authors mine the IllustrisTNG simulations, pairing the full physics runs with dark-matter-only twins. They test how the galaxy-to-halo size ratio relates to halo spin, concentration, and formation time, from today back to redshift 3. Observations add pressure: big and small galaxies cluster differently on large scales, in ways some published models fail to match.

In the simulations, size ratio tracks halo concentration only above a threshold value, and it tracks formation time. The team measures size-based clustering directly in the largest run and finds the same qualitative pattern as the sky shows. Yet the halo-property links do not drive that clustering in the simulation; satellite galaxies do. They conclude that history and environment shape galaxy size alongside halo traits.
arxiv-2502-03879:
Yuanyuan Wang and co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on a change of state in the strong force under a weak magnetic field. The team studies two-flavor quark matter at a special angle value where a symmetry called CP can switch states as heat rises. They use a well-known model of quarks and add a term for a scale effect tied to electric charge.

The authors find that the switch becomes a sharp, first-order change, and that it grows stronger as the field rises. The new term builds a barrier in the energy landscape that heat alone creates, which drives the sharp change. Their result links a subtle quantum effect to how quark matter behaves in magnetic fields.
arxiv-2502-04079:
Mehrsa Pourya, Erich Kobler, Michael Unser, and Sebastian Neumayer rebuild images with a lean method rooted in classic maths, in work from twenty twenty-five. Top image rebuild tools now lean on huge, complex neural designs. Those designs can be hard to read, trust, or prove stable. The team asks if a classic frame can match them with less bulk. Their frame grows from Tikhonov regularization, a long-used smoothing rule.

The method refines a draft image by solving a chain of simple square problems. Learned filters pull out the key traits of each draft stage. An attention step then adjusts how hard each trait is penalised, place by place. Scores match top plug-and-play and learned rivals on the tests run. The method also stays readable, robust, and sure to settle. It bridges old maths and deep learning in one clean loop.
arxiv-2502-04279:
Thomas Hull, Marcus Michelen, and Corrine Yap develop a theory of random flat-foldable origami, in a mathematics paper from 2025. Given a crease pattern, each crease can be a mountain or a valley fold. A random assignment that stays flat-foldable at each vertex is the object of study, with a natural sampling chain that flips whole faces when allowed.

The chain is proved to mix rapidly for several classic tessellations, including the square grid and Miura-ori, and for a single vertex. Local and global foldability are then compared. On the square grid, a random locally valid pattern is exponentially unlikely to fold flat as a whole. The gap guides how origami samplers should be trusted.
arxiv-2502-04479:
Dmitry Chernyak and Andreas Piepke showed in twenty twenty-five that simple wiping removes much of the radioactive radon progeny from delicate detector surfaces. Experiments hunting rare events fear polonium-210: its alpha decays spawn neutrons that mimic signals, and the contamination depends on how long parts sat in air. Costly controls on air exposure follow from that fear.

The team found about half the polonium on copper wipes off with acetone-wet tissue, and similar cleaning works on silicon with acetone-soaked cotton. For copper, long-lived lead-210 came off comparably; extra wiping added little. Silicon results carried larger uncertainty. The trivial cleaning step could let experiments relax air-exposure limits during construction, saving time and money.
arxiv-2502-04879:
Etienne Gauthier, Francis Bach, and Michael Jordan study in 2025 how groups of users on learning platforms can act together to bend the platform's algorithm toward their own aims. Members of such a collective submit altered data in a coordinated way. To act wisely, the group must judge the effect before moving, since changing data carries risk, and must coordinate using only what it can observe.

The authors build a framework that treats both sides, the theory of what a collective can achieve and the algorithms it can actually run. Experiments in a product rating domain test the ideas. The work speaks to platform design, user organizing, and the rules that should govern group action on data.
arxiv-2502-05079:
Choon-Lin Ho treats a particle break-out from a trap well with a Dirac-style guess path that keeps a classic picture. Break-out, the Kramers problem, mixes heat shakes and quantum leaks under strong drag. His path bends the well with a quantum fix drawn from a trial wave form. Rest-state needs and a least-doubt rule pin that fix in the sums.

The break-out rate he lands matches the form won by a far more tangled path method. No dive into fake time is needed, a plain win for grasp. Heat and quantum pushes sit in one drift field in the read. Trap, cold atom, and chem rate teams can use the light path.
arxiv-2502-06179:
Shuning Zhang and nine co-authors model the split-second choice a driver makes when a self-driving system suggests an action. Taking over well is central to safe cooperation between humans and automated vehicles, yet the quality of those decisions had not been dissected. The team defines two scores: the gain a driver actually achieves, and the gain an optimal judge would perceive, both weighted by how accurate the system is.

A first study of 315 people measured perceived gains and losses for route choice, overtaking, and collision avoidance. Two smaller studies then varied system accuracy and decision time. Given more than about three and a half seconds, actual decisions converged toward optimal ones; under time pressure, drivers fell back on intuition and fixed habits. Small trials with voice and multi-modal alarms, triggered by deviations from optimal choices, showed the scores can guide interventions that improve decisions.
arxiv-2502-06279:
Utkarsh Tiwari and five co-authors build a debate-based benchmark for language models in a 2025 paper. Judging a full competitive debate demands long memory and structured reasoning: eight seven-minute speeches, rules to learn, and scores that must match expert adjudicators. That is exactly the kind of task that strains today's models.

The data set collects 256 speeches from thirty-two British Parliamentary debates at top tournaments, each debate over an hour and about thirty-two thousand tokens, with official speech scores and rankings attached. Models must learn the format from context, follow every argument, and produce final standings. Leading models, including top reasoning systems, struggled in early tests. The authors offer the benchmark as a hard target for long-context reasoning research. Debate, they note, compresses argument, rebuttal, and judgment into a single measurable skill.
arxiv-2502-06379:
Filip Ekström Kelvinius and co-authors run diffusion models backward with particle filters in a 2025 machine learning paper. Pretrained diffusion generators make excellent priors for Bayesian inverse problems, reconstructing hidden causes from noisy measurements, but sampling the posterior exactly is hard.

Their sequential Monte Carlo method exploits a decoupled diffusion design that permits bigger sampling steps without losing the trail. The algorithm is asymptotically exact, a guarantee many heuristic samplers lack. Tests on synthetic problems, images, and protein data showed it recovering solutions faithfully, and the team extended the machinery to discrete data as well.
arxiv-2502-06479:
Ville Rinne, Yury Nikulin, and Marko M Mäkelä sort a class of bent cost curves for rough choice tasks in a 2025 paper. The curves can bend in a loose sense tied to a shared shift map. Rough tasks use many such curves at once, in lone or set form.

The team shows the whole family can be read through its lone-curve kin, one curve at a time. That cut lets tests built for lone curves carry to the set case. The work is a tight maths note that firms the base for this curve class.
arxiv-2502-06679:
Jangho Kim, Pratitee Pattanaik, and Wolfgang Unger locate the chiral critical point of strong-force matter using an expansion that works where ordinary simulations struggle, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. At high temperature or density, quantum chromodynamics changes phase, and the critical point of that change is a major target for theory and experiment.

The strong coupling expansion rewrites staggered fermions in a dual form suited to Monte Carlo sampling. Its sign problem is mild at strong coupling, so the full density-temperature plane becomes accessible. The authors extend the expansion with first and second order corrections in the inverse gauge coupling, mapping the system to a vertex model. Simulations then track how the chiral critical point moves with the coupling. Each correction sharpens where the point sits. Such maps guide heavy-ion experiments hunting the critical point in real collisions.
arxiv-2502-06979:
Kenkireth, Sajith, and Sasidharan sort forbidden shapes in 2025 for two graph families. Some graphs can be encoded by words, a class marked by a special arrow pattern; inside it sit the comparability graphs, where arrows follow a ranking. Both families are pinned down by their smallest banned members, but the banned list for the word family stays open.

The team sorts every smallest non-comparability graph by whether words can still encode it, they report. That settles which banned shapes ban both families at once, and fully lists the word family's banned graphs that carry one all-connected point. They also show some word graphs need many comparability layers to cover, growing with size. Forbidden-shape lists are how such families get recognized fast.
arxiv-2502-07079:
Zhangkai Cao and co-authors map pairing states in electron-doped cuprates in a 2025 physics paper. Cuprate superconductors still defy a full theory, and lab results clash with Hubbard model outputs. The team adds nearest-neighbor electron interaction to the standard model on a square lattice.

Quantum Monte Carlo runs at a fixed doping level trace how pairing shifts with that added force. Attraction between neighbors drives an exotic p-wave spin-triplet pairing. Repulsion instead weakens the usual d-wave state and brings out a rival pairing form. Stronger repulsion strengthens the rival further in the middle coupling range. The map may explain why electron-doped cuprates behave oddly in the lab.
arxiv-2502-07479:
