The team joins neutron, heat, and stress models to score each shell in one test frame. Heat tests favor a silicon based shell for steady heat load. A nickel alloy shell stands out for stress strength. Heat harms the other two shells more. A smart doubt check shows which trait swings drive peak stress the most.
arxiv-2503-15079:
Ke Zhang and co-authors present LogiAgent, a 2025 system that tests REST APIs for logic flaws, not just crashes. Most API testers watch status codes and server errors. Business logic faults slip past such checks as rules evolve. LogiAgent sends model-driven agents after those deeper faults.

Three agents split the work: one drafts scenarios, one fires requests, one judges replies. The judge uses logic oracles grounded in the business rules. That setup catches wrong data, not just error codes. Modern web services lean on APIs, so logic proof matters. The system aims to raise trust in changing back ends.
arxiv-2503-15179:
Florian De Leger, a solo author, builds a ladder of algebraic structures called operads in a 2025 paper. An operad is a rule book for combining operations that take many inputs. De Leger defines operads of a given complexity, a dial that starts at one. At the first setting the structures are simple monoids in a graded world. At the second they match a known class of operads without symmetry.

He proves the rule book for each complexity level sits inside a filtered version of a known operad built from lattice paths. He then exhibits exact sequences, called fibrations, among these objects. The work extends earlier results by two pairs of mathematicians. It is pure structure theory, giving algebraists a graded family where before there were isolated cases, and a set of exact ladders linking them.
arxiv-2503-15479:
Klaus Paschek and co-authors model how the building blocks of life could have formed on the early Earth. The young planet's air may have been rich in carbon dioxide, which blocks many routes to key starter molecules. One such molecule, hydrogen cyanide, can gather in warm little ponds and help form the parts of RNA.

The team combined models of Earth's deep interior, its air, and incoming space rocks. They found that if the early air was hydrogen-rich, bombardment by carbon-rich rocks could supply enough of the starter molecule. Even if the air began oxidized, gases released by a rock-water process in the crust could slowly turn it more favorable. In both cases, pond levels of the products reached values that lab work shows are enough to assemble nucleotides, the units of RNA.
arxiv-2503-15679:
Rahul Sundar, Didier Lucor, and Sunetra Sarkar improve a modeling method for airflow around flapping wings in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their tool blends neural networks with the laws of physics. Earlier work by the group let such networks handle moving boundaries without reshaping the frame of reference. Long runs of time, though, strain these networks. Data grow sparse, spectra grow rich, and errors build up.

The authors add sequential learning to the framework. One strategy grows the time window step by step as training proceeds. Another restarts the learning in stages across the full span. They test velocity and pressure recovery for the flapping flow. The goal is a stable model of unsteady flow over long times. Such models could aid the design of small flying machines and wind devices.
arxiv-2503-15879:
DongGeon Lee and co-authors present Typed-RAG in a 2025 paper on answering non factoid questions. Such questions are open ended, carry varied intent, and need reasoning across several aspects. Standard retrieval augmented generation often retrieves poorly for them and gives thin answers.

Their framework first classifies a question into a type, such as debate, experience, or comparison. It then splits the question into focused sub queries, retrieves for each, and combines the results. A new benchmark built from wiki content covers many question types. Typed-RAG beat language model and standard retrieval baselines on retrieval and answer quality.
arxiv-2503-16079:
Chiara Rucco, Antonella Longo, and Motaz Saad present a 2025 paper proposing a design pattern for feeding data into cloud systems. Modern firms drown in data, and getting it in, fast and cleanly, is a weak point of many platforms. Patterns exist for other data tasks, but high-volume ingestion lacked a settled recipe.

The proposed pattern handles both full reloads and incremental updates. A metadata-driven frame steers the process, so switching ingestion type or changing a schema takes configuration, not surgery. The authors place their design among known data engineering patterns like data mesh and lambda architecture. They argue the pattern restores feasibility and flexibility to a step that often quietly decides whether a platform scales.
arxiv-2503-16379:
Corasaniti and co-authors wrote a paper in 2025 on how baryons, the ordinary matter that stars are made of, affect the sparsity of simulated galaxy clusters. Sparsity measures how mass is distributed within a cluster's dark matter halo. It can help constrain the parameters of cosmological models, provided its systematic uncertainties are controlled.

The team used simulated clusters from a large project, run with and without baryonic matter and with varied feedback from stars and black holes. Sparsity measures spanning the full depth of a cluster were affected by baryons the most, and they tracked the gas fraction in the cluster's core. Measures reading only the outskirts were affected far less. The team also shows how a biased mass estimate, inferred under an assumed equilibrium rule, skews the sparsity measurement and the cosmological conclusions drawn from it.
arxiv-2503-16479:
Milin Patel, Rolf Jung, and Yasin Cakir build a simulator test for the ways drivers predictably misuse driving automation in this 2025 paper. In highly automated cars the human is a backup who may misunderstand the system. Safety standards name this foreseeable misuse and demand it be tested, which is easier said in a simulator than done.

The team modeled a transverse guidance assist system and, above all, the interface between driver and machine. That interface carries the signals a driver must perceive, grasp, and act on when retaking control. A misuse scenario derived from the standard was then run in the driving simulator. The aim is a setup where the system explains itself so plainly that reasonable use follows. The authors present the interface build as the missing piece for misuse testing.
arxiv-2503-16579:
Jonas Krumme and Christoph Zetzsche ask where robots can get world knowledge in twenty twenty-five. Robots often face tasks with missing detail and no single right answer. A person stocking a fridge, for instance, must judge where each item belongs. Writing all such know-how into a robot by hand would quickly become unmanageable.

Images of the real world quietly hold answers to many such questions. They show how objects are usually arranged and grouped. The authors draw on AI image generation to tap that stored knowledge for robot control. A generated image can suggest a sensible setup before the robot acts. Readers see a way to borrow human-like judgment from pictures rather than rules.
arxiv-2503-16779:
Mengsong Wu and five co-authors taught frozen language models to call vast sets of tools. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with tool learning. Past ways tune the model so it knows just the tools seen in training. Or they stuff tool demos in the prompt, which wastes space. Their way, Chain-of-Tools, leans on the strong sense vectors of a frozen model. The model calls tools step by step inside its chain of thought.

The tool pool can be huge and can hold tools the model has never seen. The team built a new set of plain tool questions to test that case. Trials on math and fact benchmarks back the claim. Readers get tool use with no tuning bill.
arxiv-2503-16879:
Bin Li, Dongdong Yang, and Lei Liu published a paper in 2025 on smart reflective panels that can rotate to help phones offload computing. Edge servers near users can take over heavy tasks, saving battery, but weak wireless links waste that promise. A wall of tiny adjustable reflectors can steer signals, and letting the whole panel rotate adds a further gain.

The authors treat phones moving across time slots and aim to cut total energy use. Their plan jointly sets panel angle, reflector phases, server resources, sending power, and what each phone offloads. A learning algorithm from the actor-critic family handles the moving parts, while simpler rules fill in the rest. Against a fixed panel, rotation cut energy use by up to about forty-seven percent.
arxiv-2503-16979:
Free-viewpoint video lets viewers move around inside a recorded scene, but building it frame by frame has been slow and prone to drift. Jinbo Yan and co-authors present Instant Gaussian Stream in this 2025 paper, a framework that rebuilds moving scenes as a stream at about two seconds per frame.

A motion network uses anchor points to drive all the scene elements at once, predicting each new frame in a single pass. A key-frame step then refines selected frames so errors do not pile up over time. Tests inside and across data sets show faster streaming with better picture quality than earlier approaches.
arxiv-2503-17079:
Agastya Raj and co-authors use neural networks to find which user is causing interference in shared optical spectrum services, in a 2025 paper. In optical spectrum as a service, several customers rent slices of one fiber's capacity. When interference appears, the operator must blame the right customer without peeking at private traffic details.

Their convolutional network reads the spectrum shape and classifies the source of the impairment. In experiments with three simultaneous users, the model named the culprit with accuracy of about ninety-four percent. The architecture respects the blindness constraint, judging only the shared signal. For operators selling spectrum slices, the method promises faster fault hunting without breaking customer privacy.
arxiv-2503-17279:
Gaifan Zhang, Yi Zhou, and Danushka Bollegala present condition aware sentence embeddings in this 2025 paper. A sentence's meaning shifts with context, so judging two sentences as similar should depend on the condition in view. Their method, CASE, first embeds the condition with a language model encoder. The sentence steers attention while that condition embedding is pooled. A supervised step then aligns the embeddings with human similarity judgments made under stated conditions.

One simple trick helped on its own: subtracting the condition embedding improved scores across models. The authors trace the gain to a better spread of the embedding space. Their trained projection improved results further while using few dimensions. The method is both efficient and accurate on the conditional similarity task. The authors offer CASE as a fix for a gap in standard embeddings, which freeze one meaning per sentence. Context dependent tasks need the conditioned version.
arxiv-2503-17379:
Jassem Abbasi and co-authors benchmark neural solvers on equations with shock fronts in a 2025 review. Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by folding the physics into training. Sudden jumps, like shock waves in underground multiphase flow, break their smooth habits and threaten both accuracy and stability.

Two test problems anchor the study: the classic Buckley-Leverett flow and a harder fully coupled system. Two families of fixes handled the first problem's infinite gradients well. A third family failed to resolve the shocks at all. On the coupled system, errors ballooned fast for every method, a sign that loss landscape traps deepen with coupling. The review sorts the known tricks by strength and weakness and calls for fresh ideas aimed squarely at hard discontinuities.
arxiv-2503-17879:
Four mathematicians, Do Tran Van, Susovan Pal, Benjamin Eltzner, and Stephan Huckemann, tackle a hard shape problem in this 2025 work. They study curved spaces that are folded by symmetry, and ways to lift points back to the full space in the best spot. Their goal is a firm base for tests that compare two groups of shapes.

The team proves that the lifts are smooth and mostly unique, and that the mean shape sits in the top layer of the space. From this they build new two-sample tests based on the lifts of each shape. In trials the new tests beat older ones. One use is the study of thin tubes inside cells, where shape tells a story about cell health.
arxiv-2503-18079:
Dimitrios Beis and Athanasios Dedes check a consistency requirement of the Standard Model's effective extension in a 2025 paper. Effective field theory adds small higher-dimension terms to the Standard Model to hint at new physics. Chiral anomalies, quantum effects that can break gauge symmetry, must cancel for the theory to make sense.

The authors show cancellation works when loop calculations route momenta consistently: Goldstone boson terms cancel the anomalies from heavy gauge boson vertices. They then compute vertices where three neutral gauge bosons meet, finding the new terms dominate at all reachable energies. A complete model with a heavy electron-like particle confirms the picture and suggests collider searches could spot these effects.
arxiv-2503-18179:
Xiaojie Yang and five co-authors add causal thinking to the task of guessing where a person will go next. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses human mobility data, which mixes many travel habits at once. Past predictors blend user, place, and time facts, but ignore which facts cause which, so false links can creep in.

The team draws a causal graph of the inputs and uses counterfactuals to boost indirect effects for one habit type: trips not tied to anchor points like home or work. The module plugs into existing predictors of many designs. On several top models and data sets, it raised accuracy and made the models easier to interpret.
arxiv-2503-18279:
Harshdeep Singh, Sonjoy Majumder, and Sabyashachi Mishra cut the cost of quantum time simulation in a 2025 paper. A known method tracks a quantum state by tuning a circuit's knobs step by step, but tuning all knobs each step is dear. Their twist tunes one block of the circuit at a time while the rest stay fixed, a plan they call BLOP-VQD.

Each block still touches all the qubits, so the full state evolves while the tuning chore shrinks. Blocks can be picked in turn order, at random, or by a fidelity score. Tests on spin lattice models of mixed size kept the accuracy of the full method at a much lower cost. The authors pitch the plan as a path to faithful runs on bigger systems.
arxiv-2503-18579:
Sorting sounds into groups without labels is a first step toward machines that organise audio on their own. Luan Vinícius Fiorio and co-authors build a clustering model that works directly on the time-frequency picture of sound. Their design extends a variational autoencoder: sound is compressed into a hidden space shaped like a mixture of bell curves, one per hoped-for cluster, and a convolutional-recurrent network handles the spectrogram's structure.

On a spoken-digits dataset the model beat traditional clustering methods by a clear margin in both accuracy and cluster quality. The authors credit the mixture-shaped hidden space for capturing tangled audio patterns. The work, backed by an industry-academic radar collaboration, points toward self-organising sound archives and smarter hearing devices.
arxiv-2503-18679:
Squeezing video means guessing each block of a frame from its neighbours, and a good guess saves bits. Mohsen Abdoli and three co-authors add a merge mode to a guess tool in 2025. The base tool scans a strip above and left of the block to find which guess modes fit the strip best.

That strip can mislead when its texture differs from the block's own. The merge mode answers by building a list of blocks coded with the base tool across a wider zone, not just the near neighbours. The list is then ranked by the strip, and the best fits guide the block's own guess. The tool sits in the test software that probes what comes past the current video standard. Small gains here add up across a whole stream.
arxiv-2503-18979:
Elija Perrier analyzes how threshold crossings in AI systems can act as tail events for catastrophic risk. The 2025 paper studies bifurcation-driven jumps, where a small change pushes a system into a very different state.

When a control parameter fluctuates randomly near a catastrophic threshold, the outcomes can follow a heavy-tailed distribution. Perrier shows when the chance of a sudden, large-scale transition aligns closely with the tail probability of the damage distribution. That link matters for how risk is estimated. If damage tails and transition chances match, then monitoring the tail gives a direct handle on the chance of the jump itself. The work aids monitoring and control of such systems.
arxiv-2503-19079:
Bethany Terris asks what it means to say a quantum particle was present somewhere, in a 2025 philosophy paper. Weak measurements, gentle probes that barely disturb a system, have produced paradoxes: particles seem to appear and vanish along broken paths. Terris argues the paradox comes from faulty logic. Classical thinking stitches together claims from separate single-time weak values, and the stitches tear.

Her remedy redefines presence across time. Sequential weak values, chained through the particle's history, give a coherent if non-classical account of where it was. The discontinuous trajectories dissolve. Terris weighs the account's advantages and costs, then tests it against other cases of broken paths. The paper offers quantum theory a more careful language for particle whereabouts.
arxiv-2503-19379:
Chenhao Jin, Yinhua Xia, and Yan Xu present, in twenty twenty-five, a kernel compensation method for computing energy gaps in photonic crystals. Photonic crystals are patterned materials that block some light colors, useful for optical devices. Computing their band gaps means solving Maxwell's equations as an eigenvalue problem. A snag is an infinite-dimensional kernel, a space of trivial solutions that spawns fake eigenvalues. They first turn the quasi-periodic problem into a periodic one on a cube. A compensation term, built from a shifted curl operator, is then added.

They prove the term exactly fills the kernel and removes spurious eigenvalues. The discretization respects a key geometric structure of the equations. An efficient preconditioner with fast solvers allows parallel computing. Tests on three dimensional lattices confirm accuracy.
arxiv-2503-19679:
Daniele Malafarina and co-authors ask what magnetism could inflate the infant universe in a 2025 paper. Nonlinear electrodynamics bends the rules of electric and magnetic fields at extreme strengths. A magnetic early universe built on those rules might inflate on its own.

The team derives, for the first time, the exact conditions the theory must obey. The universe must start near a de Sitter state, then slow-roll gently. Models proposed so far fail to give a long enough inflation, they show. One family survives: theories that soften to Maxwell's rules in weak fields. Cosmic beginnings remain picky about their physics.
arxiv-2503-19779:
Machine learning jobs fire off thousands of tiny GPU tasks, and the chore of launching each one now eats real time. CUDA Graphs fix that by taping the sequence and replaying it in one dispatch, but in practice the tape often refuses to stick. Abhishek Ghosh and co-authors present PyGraph in this 2025 paper, a compiler layer that makes graph capture work across ordinary PyTorch programs.

PyGraph rewrites code so it can be captured, removes copying overheads inside graphs, and turns graphs on only where a cost-benefit check says they pay. Across twenty-five standard workloads it more than doubled the benefit of the standard compiler route. No programmer effort is required.
arxiv-2503-19979:
Enora Rice and co-authors untangle what makes a good transfer language for grammar tagging in this 2025 paper. Tagging parts of speech in a low-resource tongue can borrow strength from a richer one. Picking the best donor language, though, is still guesswork in practice.

The team trained rankers that score donor languages for a target. Feeds included word overlap, text statistics, family distance, and fine grammar traits. Tests ran across older recurrent models and modern pretrained ones. Word overlap and family distance topped the feature lists everywhere. Mixing grammar traits with dataset facts gave the best rankings overall. Either group alone still ranked respectably, which eases data needs for new languages.
arxiv-2503-20179:
Shijia Zhang and co-authors teach a model to spot immune therapy studies hidden in a large gene data bank. Their 2025 paper tackles a sorting task with real traps. Wording overlaps between classes, true cases are rare, and labeled examples are few. Their method joins a biomedical language model with class prototypes, which are average patterns for each class. A light tuning method adapts the model without retraining it whole.

Training uses only a few dozen labeled studies, split evenly across classes. On a held-out test set, the method beats rule-based sorting, classic learning models, and the plain tuned model. Applied to tens of thousands of unlabeled studies, it cuts manual review work by a large share. Removing parts of the design shows the prototype and tuning pieces work best together. The tool can speed curation for cancer research teams.
arxiv-2503-20479:
Robert Lupoiu and co-authors let AI agents design light-bending surfaces on their own. Their 2025 paper introduces MetaChat, a team of software agents that turn a spoken design goal into a freeform metasurface layout. Human experts now grind through slow cycles of simulation and tuning. The agents talk through steps with a shared inner monologue, calling code tools and each other.

Fast surrogate solvers, tuned by feature-wise modulation, stand in for full Maxwell simulations. On test goals spanning many aims and wavelengths, the system delivered strong layouts orders of magnitude faster than standard routes. The authors offer the frame as a blueprint for agent-led design across physics, not just photonics.
arxiv-2503-20579:
Berk Çakar and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on ways to build regular expressions, the pattern strings used to match text. Coders find these patterns hard to write well. Faults, slow runs, and security holes can follow. Tools can build them by rules, language models can draft them, and coders often reuse old ones. No past work had matched these routes head to head.

The team mined a huge bank of patterns from open code and the web. They built tens of thousands of tasks with match and non-match cases. A new reuse by example tool searches the bank for a fit. All three routes solved most tasks well. Reuse and language models led on the full set of gauges.
arxiv-2503-20679:
Tomáš Jakl reviews four areas of computing that echo a four-valued logic from the 1970s, in work from 2025. That logic lets a claim be true, false, both, or neither. It was built to handle messy, partial data in a clean way.

Only one of the four areas openly credits the link, a branch of frame theory. The other three cover linear logic, a blame system for program parts, and shared mutable values. A product trick for pairing values connects all of them behind the scenes. Jakl argues the hidden debt should be named and studied. Naming it could let each field borrow proofs and tools from the others.
arxiv-2503-21079:
Pablo Shmerkin and Alexia Yavicoli prove results about Cantor sets in a 2025 math paper. Cantor sets are dust-like sets built by removing middle parts again and again. The question is whether copies of such a set can be shifted to sit inside almost any large set.

Under a mild size condition, the authors show such sets are not universal in that sense. This strengthens a known fact for sets of positive size in the usual sense. For all Cantor sets, they build a large set that still misses shifted copies almost everywhere. The result holds even after smooth stretching of the set.
arxiv-2503-21579:
Weronika Ormaniec, Michael Vollenweider, and Elisa Hoskovec merge trained graph neural networks into one model with optimal transport, in work from twenty twenty-five. Model fusion can combine skills from separate training runs into a single network. Graph networks add structure that plain weight averaging ignores.

The team aligns weights layer by layer with transport plans and tests three cost choices. Fusion beat plain averaging in every setup tried. Yet gains were smaller and harder won than for simple feed forward networks. Adding graph structure into the transport step did not lift results further. The study maps where transport fusion helps and where graph models resist it.
arxiv-2503-21879:
Antti Rantala and Thorsten Naab simulate how dense star clusters in the young universe could forge seeds of supermassive black holes fast. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. New telescope images show early star formation was clumpy and crowded, a hint about where the giant black holes came from.

The team modeled nine massive clusters merging step by step. Stars collided and grew, then collapsed into black holes of intermediate mass. Having partner stars boosted those masses two to three times. The holes shredded about fifty passing stars in ten million years. Cluster mergers often left several seeds together, and they merged quickly by gravitational waves. The authors predict a telltale wave signal for future observatories.
arxiv-2503-21979:
One model that both reads images and makes them must hold two kinds of knowledge at once. Size Wu and co-authors build such a model, called Harmon, in a 2025 paper. Older unified models lean on codes that keep pixel detail but lose meaning, which hurts reading tasks.

Harmon starts from an encoder trained by hiding parts of images and asking for them back. That encoder proved sharp at naming the concepts in a picture. A three-stage training plan then grows both skills in one shared frame. The model hit top scores on image-making tests while matching rivals at image reading. Code and models are set for public release.
arxiv-2503-22179:
Dailan He and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on swapping faces in photos with diffusion models. The catalog creator list runs names together, but the head gives eight authors. A good swap puts the source person's identity onto a target photo while keeping the target's pose and expression. Models often blur that balance, letting identity swamp the pose or the reverse.

Their framework secures identity first, then tunes the result to match the target's traits, feeding the two kinds of guidance in apart. A final training stage with identity and adversarial losses sharpens the match. In their tests the method beat rivals on both likeness and trait keeping. Face tools raise consent concerns, and quality papers like this also inform detection work.
arxiv-2503-22379:
Rewriting a private document so it can be shared safely always spends a privacy budget, a number that caps how much protection the rewrite guarantees. Stephen Meisenbacher, Chaeeun Joy Lee, and Florian Matthes ask a question earlier work skipped. Not all words in a document are equally sensitive, so why spread that budget evenly?

The team builds a toolkit of language-based methods that hand more of the budget to the tokens that need it most and less to harmless ones. In privacy and utility tests, this smart allocation protects better than naive even spreading at the same total budget. The trade-off between hiding content and keeping meaning also improves. The work targets differentially private text rewriting, where the rewritten text must hide both plain and implied identifiers.
arxiv-2503-22479:
Simone Sartorello, Pierfrancesco Di Cintio, Alessandro Alberto Trani, and Mario Pasquato study chaos during the violent settling of a collapsing star system. When a cold cloud of stars collapses, its shared gravity field swings fast and drives the system toward a steady state. Chaos in single orbits and chaos from the swinging field are tangled in that process.

The team built a simplified model: test orbits move in a smooth, time-changing potential that mimics a full simulation, with a noise term for the graininess of real star counts. They measure chaos by the largest Lyapunov exponent, the rate at which nearby orbits split. Varying the particle count shows how each source of chaos scales. The aim is a cleaner account of how star systems relax.
arxiv-2503-22779:
Junkai Hu and Li Xia study mean variance team stochastic games in two thousand twenty-five. All agents share one mean variance goal for the whole system. Each acts on its own to lift that shared score. Variance is not additive or Markovian, which breaks classic tools.

Joint updates also make each agent's world shift under it. The team uses sensitivity based optimization to crack both snags. Formulas for performance gaps and derivatives drive the search. A policy iteration scheme updates agents one by one in order. It provably lands on a stationary point. A trust region form scales it to unknown settings.
arxiv-2503-23179:
Wiebke Heyer and co-authors described a challenge for aligning medical images in cancer care in two thousand twenty-five. Registration aligns scans from different times or machines so doctors can target tumors while sparing healthy tissue. Privacy rules mean much cancer data cannot be shared openly.

The OncoReg Challenge lets teams build methods on public data, then train on private data inside secure hospital networks. Its task aligns cone-beam scans taken during treatment with standard planning scans. Review of the entries found feature extraction was the key step. A new method proved flexible, older methods still matched newer ones, and mixing methods worked best overall.
arxiv-2503-23479:
C E Ardila-Gutiérrez and co-authors examine a family of crystals where twisted structure and magnetism meet, in a 2025 physics paper. The crystals pair a rare-earth metal with platinum and boron, and their metal atoms sit on a three-dimensional kagome lattice, a pattern of linked triangles. Such patterns can leave magnetic moments frustrated, with no simple way to align.

Using symmetry analysis and computer models, the team found the crystal's twist favors a matching twisted pattern of magnetism. That state sits lower in energy than a plain aligned one. They also found special points in the electronic structure that survive even when magnetism is switched on in the neodymium version. A predicted sideways electrical response was on par with other known materials of this kind.
arxiv-2503-23579:
Shounak De and co-authors hunt in 2025 for hidden zeros in a math object that describes how the early universe's fields behaved. The object, called the cosmological wavefunction, is built from graph shaped pieces. Recent work found secret zeros in the scattering formulas of particle physics, and the team asks if a like pattern hides here.

They show that each graph piece splits into factors near its zeros, for all tree shaped graphs. They also give proof that the same holds for graphs with loops. The team builds shape based models of the graphs that give the zeros a clear geometric and physical sense. As a bonus, one class of these pieces turns out to match a known flat space scattering formula. That match lets the new zeros reveal more about the older ones.
arxiv-2503-23679:
Mingkai Tian and six co-authors improve automatic captions for videos that the system was never trained on, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such zero-shot captioning leans on vision-language models to suggest text prompts for a language model. Older methods fix on one part of a scene and miss the rest.

Their approach builds three stores of prompts at rising detail: short noun phrases, linked scene graphs, and full sentences. A second mechanism weighs which store entries fit the topic at hand, based on how language is spread around that topic. On three standard benchmarks, the method beat prior systems by clear margins on the main caption score. The authors argue that modeling scene content openly is the key.
arxiv-2503-23779:
Ine Gevers and co-authors paraphrase a famous commonsense benchmark and watch language model scores fall sharply, in work from twenty twenty-five. WinoGrande sentences test pronoun sense through twin-sentence choices. Their WinoWhat corpus rewrites every validation item in new words. Five commonsense categories tag what kind of knowledge each item needs. Models of many sizes face both versions of the test.

Every model performs notably worse on the paraphrased corpus. That gap suggests benchmark scores overstate true reasoning skill. Training-data matches are checked to rule out simple memorisation. Memorisation, it turns out, explains little of the score gap. Surface wording, not knowledge, props up headline results. Paraphrase twins make a sterner test for machine commonsense.
arxiv-2503-23879:
Giovanni Palermo and five co-authors study how social network shape affects a newer kind of election poll, in a research paper from 2025. Social circle polls ask voters not only their own choice but also how their contacts will vote. This taps collective knowledge and can sharpen forecasts.

Simulations of voter networks show these polls usually beat standard ones. But packed, polarized networks can bias them. The authors propose an estimator that blends both poll types to correct for that. They test it on real data from the twenty sixteen United States presidential election. The method also yields an estimate of how polarized that electorate was.
arxiv-2504-00079:
A large international team presents a 2025 status report on the International Axion Observatory, a planned facility to hunt for axions. Axions are light particles proposed to solve open problems in physics, and the Sun should pour them out if they exist. The report was written as input to the European Strategy for Particle Physics.

The text sets out the science case for the observatory, where the project stands, and what is planned next. A giant magnet paired with sharp detectors would convert solar axions into X-rays that can be counted. The report makes the case for building the facility as a flagship hunt.
arxiv-2504-00379:
Zhiyuan Zhang and six co-authors present MPDrive, a method to help self-driving systems answer questions about a scene. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with driving visual question answering, which spans perception, prediction, and planning. A model must grasp where things are, and past work wrote positions as text coordinates, which fit the image poorly.

MPDrive marks positions right on the image. A detection expert stamps numbered labels on object regions, so the model predicts markers, not raw coordinates. The marked and plain images are fused, at both scene and object level, into prompts for the language model. On two driving data sets it set new best scores, above all on spatial questions.
arxiv-2504-00479: Jan Moser's short paper from 2025 deals with the Fermat-Wiles theorem, the famed result about a certain raised-power equation having no whole-number solutions. Working in the line of Jacob's ladders, Moser joins two known formulas, one by Ingham and one due to Heath-Brown from 1979. From the joined form he draws a new statement that stands or falls with the theorem itself. The paper also proves that endless finite chains of such linked statements exist. Readers need a firm grip on the cited formulas to follow it.
arxiv-2504-00679:
Sai Li and co-authors build QUEST, a training framework for spiking neural networks on brain-like hardware, in a 2025 paper. Neuromorphic chips promise huge energy savings, but each new device behaves differently, and most work stalls at proof of concept for want of training tools shaped to the hardware.

QUEST trains spiking networks directly for devices with many resistance levels, using a skyrmion magnetic tunnel junction as the test case. Device mapping patterns and sparse activation operations keep the arithmetic tiny. On the CIFAR-10 image task it reached about ninety percent accuracy with just two-bit precision, using roughly ninety-three times less energy than a standard network. The framework offers both device builders and algorithm designers a shared playbook.
arxiv-2504-01179:
The Dirac equation describes spinning electrons, and the Feshbach-Villars trick rewrites it as a pair of coupled components that behave more like a Hamiltonian system. Abdelmalek Boumali extends that rewriting to curved spacetime in this 2025 paper, where gravity itself bends the stage. He derives the Hamiltonian form of the Dirac equation under gravity and electromagnetism together.

Squaring the Dirac operator gives a generalized Klein-Gordon equation, which he also recasts in the new form. Results are given in matrix and Pauli matrix dress, in both two and three spatial dimensions, with care for the term coupling spin to the fields. The framework targets relativistic quantum mechanics where gravity cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2504-01379:
Chenyao Suo and five co-authors built a tool that hunts silent bugs in a widely used compiler framework, in a 2025 paper. Silent bugs are the nastiest kind: the compiler quietly produces wrong code instead of crashing. MLIR, a framework for building compilers, had fuzzers that found crashes but not silent mis-optimizations. Two hurdles block the hunt: test programs must avoid undefined behavior, and programs must be lowered to runnable form to compare outputs.

Their tool, DESIL, applies rules drawn from MLIR's own documentation to scrub undefined behavior from generated programs. A smart lowering strategy then picks efficient paths to executable code, and varied optimization choices create outputs to compare. Run against the newest MLIR code, it found twenty-three silent bugs and nineteen crashes. Developers confirmed or fixed many of them, the authors report.
arxiv-2504-01679:
Wan-Lu Song, Ji-Ling Wang, Bin Zhou, Wan-Li Yang, and Jun-Hong An slow the self-discharge of a quantum battery built in diamond. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses the nitrogen-vacancy center, whose electron spin stores the charge. Decoherence drains such batteries on its own, a flaw called self-discharging. That drain blocks real use.

The team finds that coherent ergotropy, the work tied to quantum coherence, fades slower than its incoherent kin. Raising the coherent share of the total thus hardens the battery. The native nitrogen nucleus in the center couples to the electron and lets that share be tuned. Both drain and yield improve at once in their scheme. The authors frame it as a step toward a working quantum battery.
arxiv-2504-02179:
The authors drew new lessons from a known law of superconductors in a 2025 physics paper. Homes' law ties the temperature at which cuprate materials start to superconduct to traits of their normal metal state. One past reading held that their metals are as thick-flowing as quantum rules allow, which is why their transition heat runs high.

The team shows the law in fact forces three things. Resistance must grow in a straight line with heat near the transition. The rate at which electrons relax must track heat with a factor near one, a famed Planckian rate. And the law holds across an oddly wide range of electron masses in these materials.
arxiv-2504-03179:
Chakraborty, Schmalian, and Fernandes (2025) show how a magnetic field can tune disorder in a class of magnets called altermagnets. These materials pair opposing magnetic arrangements in a way that blocks any direct grip by an external field. A sideways grip does exist: field and strain together couple to the magnetic order, an effect called piezomagnetism.

If the material carries random internal strain, the authors show, switching on a field creates an effective random field acting on the magnetic order. Two effects then compete: the random field suppresses order, while a strengthened link to elastic fluctuations favors it. Solving the resulting model in mean-field approximation maps out the temperature-field phase diagram. It reveals a re-entrant ordered phase that appears, vanishes, and returns as the field grows. The authors also point to measurable fingerprints, in stiffness, in heat effects, and in the order itself.
arxiv-2504-03779:
Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean and three colleagues derive a new ingredient for density functional theory from a balance-of-forces idea, in a 2025 paper. The theory predicts material behavior from electron density alone, but its correlation piece is usually borrowed from a uniform electron gas.

Starting from an older correlated wave function, the authors extract an analytical formula for the correlation energy via the force-balance equation. On atoms, the new formula beats the standard uniform-gas version. On solids it does slightly worse. Still, the result is the first practical functional from this route, and it can be improved step by step. The authors frame it as a foundation for a new family of approximations.
arxiv-2504-03879:
Jiho Kim and Cong Hao published a 2025 paper on a tool that measures how chip designs actually perform once built. Designers now write hardware in high-level languages and let software compile them onto programmable chips. Simulators predict the speed, but real chips often run slower, hiding the true bottlenecks. Existing on-chip analyzers demand tedious manual wiring into the generated code.

Their tool, RealProbe, automates the whole job. One directive line in the source code triggers it. The tool then generates all the profiling code needed to count cycles across the entire design hierarchy, inside the running chip. Because it is lightweight, it barely disturbs the design it measures. Designers get honest numbers instead of simulation promises, and can aim their fixes at real slowdowns. The paper targets a quiet productivity drain in hardware design: tools exist, but their setup cost keeps them unused.
arxiv-2504-04079:
Ashwin Vinod and Chandrajit Bajaj present a Bayesian method that groups rows and columns of a data table at the same time, in work from 2025. Joint grouping shines on sparse, high-dimensional data, where one-way grouping misses structure. Deep versions exist, but noise can break them and their inner states can collapse to a bland form.

Their model learns row and column groups directly in a hidden space, with a sharper training objective that cleans the signal. A built-in noise learning step lets one pipeline handle spoiled or missing inputs. A scale tweak guards against the collapse failure. The authors frame the result as the first fully variational method of its kind, built for scale.
arxiv-2504-04279:
Hongchao Fang and co-authors ask, in a 2025 paper, whether AI systems can trace fake images and text back to the models that made them, and explain the verdict. Machine-made content now floods public life. Abusers forge images that break rules, and lazy reviewers pass off model-written reviews as their own.

Earlier work mostly detected fakes, sometimes naming a source model. A systematic, fine-grained comparison was missing. The study spans images versus text, fully versus partly generated pictures, and benign versus malicious uses. It also tests whether a leading multimodal model can justify its attributions. Provenance tools that explain themselves would serve platforms, courts, and journals better than bare detectors.
arxiv-2504-04579:
Itay Evron and co-authors analyze forgetting in continual learning in a 2025 theory paper. Models trained task after task tend to lose earlier skills, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. For linear models fitted in sequence, the team proves that fitting each new task equals one gradient step on a reshaped objective.

That bridge lets them import fresh gradient descent bounds and derive forgetting rates that hold universally, without depending on problem size. Random task order alone, they show, prevents catastrophic forgetting over long sequences. Rates improve on the best known for regression with repeated tasks, and a matching lower-style rate covers classification on separable data.
arxiv-2504-04879:
Véronique Gayrard studies false memories in a classic model of associative memory, in a 2025 paper. The model stores chosen patterns as low points in an energy landscape. Other low points can arise by accident, acting as false memories. Their existence was long supported only by simulations and rough calculations.

Gayrard explicitly builds a family of states called mixed memories. Their traits are meant to characterize the energy landscape's low points. For three leading versions of the model, she gives growth conditions on the stored pattern count. Under those conditions, mixed memories are exact fixed points of the recall process as the network grows. She conjectures that in this regime all low points are mixed memories. The result puts a long-assumed picture on firm ground.
arxiv-2504-05379:
Indranil Halder, Daniel Jafferis, and Debmalya Sarkar study a counting tool for supersymmetric systems with disorder, in a 2025 physics paper. The tool is the Witten index, a count that stays fixed under many changes to a system. Their test case is a disordered quantum mechanics model of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev type with extended supersymmetry. Disorder means the model's couplings are drawn at random rather than fixed.

When the random couplings do not affect the index, the authors show the exact answer still comes out of averaged collective variables. Averaging over several copies of the same theory creates couplings between the copies, a surprising twist. Even so, the final index splits into separate factors, one per copy. The framework gives a cleaner route to exact results in messy quantum systems.
arxiv-2504-05479:
Gurarie studies, in a 2025 paper, a quantum particle whose position is measured at random places and random times. Measurement is usually treated as a readout, but here it becomes part of the motion itself. He built a formalism kin to the one used for systems shaken by noise.

A free particle under this random watching spreads faster than diffusion, a superdiffusive walk. A charged particle pinned to the lowest Landau level in a magnetic field instead diffuses normally. Most strikingly, a particle trapped by disorder, Anderson localized in a static random landscape, starts diffusing once random measurements break its localization. The results suggest measurement can act as a transport engine, not just an observer.
arxiv-2504-05579:
Artem Zholus and nine co-authors present TAPNext, a model that tracks any chosen point through a video. Point tracking supports robotics, video editing, and 3D reconstruction. Older trackers lean on many hand-built rules and tricks made just for tracking, which limits how far they can scale.

TAPNext treats tracking as next-token prediction, the same framing that powers language models. The model reads the video in order and outputs the point's path step by step, hiding future frames as it goes. It runs online with very low delay and needs no window of surrounding frames. Despite its plain design, it set a new best score among both online and offline trackers, the authors report. They also show that many tricks older trackers rely on appear on their own inside the trained model.
arxiv-2504-06079:
Sharath Raghvendra and co-authors speed up the offline k-server problem, a classic about moving servers to meet requests at least cost. The offline answer reduces to a cheapest partial matching between two point sets. In spaces where distance follows a power rule, older methods scale with the product of points and servers.

Their method partitions the plane into nested rectangles and grows the matching by merging neighbors, so each point joins few improving paths. The runtime drops below the old barrier. The work also settles an open question about matching with few nearest-neighbor queries, at least for server-born cases.
arxiv-2504-06179:
Varsha Behrunani and colleagues designed a control scheme in 2025 for neighborhoods of energy hubs that trade power and heat with each other. Homes and campuses increasingly generate, store, and exchange energy, and predictive controllers can run each hub cheaply, but peer-to-peer trading across a growing network creates computational and privacy strain. Worse, conventional distributed controllers must be recomputed everywhere whenever a hub joins or leaves.

Their framework clusters the network and makes trading plug-and-play: a hub entering or leaving forces updates only inside its own cluster. Trading between clusters is arranged as a two-level bargaining game, with commitments negotiated at the top level and dispatch handled below, all under economic model predictive control that respects operating constraints. The design aims to keep the efficiency gains of peer trading without the fragility that has limited its scale.
arxiv-2504-06579:
Sushanta Dattagupta and Shamik Gupta study how random pulses stir a contest between coherence and decoherence in a three-level quantum system. Two levels evolve in clean, coherent step with each other. The third level is tied loosely to the second, and pulses can knock population into it.

In their 2025 paper, the pulses arrive as a Poisson stream, each one instant and of random strength. The authors build an averaged transition operator for this noisy drive and solve for the density matrix in closed form. Starting from the first level, they track the stay-put probability over time, the survival of Rabi oscillations under the kicks. The model shows how steady random hits erode quantum beats.
arxiv-2504-06679: Gianni Arioli, Alessio Falocchi, and Filippo Gazzola prove bounds on the eigenfunctions of the Stokes problem in a cube, in a 2025 paper. The Stokes equations describe slow, viscous fluid flow, and their eigenfunctions are the natural vibration modes of such a flow in a box. The boundary condition is Navier's, which lets the fluid slip along the walls in proportion to the stress there, rather than sticking fast. The authors establish explicit bounds on those modes, feeding analysis of flow stability and numerical methods.
arxiv-2504-06779:
Daniel Angerhausen and co-authors ask in 2025 what a blank result from a far planet survey would still teach us. New space scopes will scan mild, rocky worlds for signs of life fit zones and of life itself. A survey that finds none could still bind how rare such worlds are.

Chance based math maps how the bound tightens as survey size grows. Twenty to fifty clean looks give bounds that owe little to prior guesses. Near forty looks cap the rate at a fifth, and near eighty at a tenth, at high trust. Both planned scopes aim at sizes in that range.
arxiv-2504-06879:
Arushi Sharma and five co-authors reconstruct a nuclear force from scattering data with physics-guided machine learning in a 2025 paper. When an alpha particle bounces off a deuteron, the deflection pattern encodes the force between them. Inverting that pattern is the classic inverse scattering problem.

Their reference force joins three Morse curves with ten parameters. A genetic algorithm tunes the parameters, each round solving the phase equation numerically and comparing predicted phase shifts with experiment. The recovered potentials cover single- and multi-channel cases. Phase shifts from them yield resonance energies and widths for three states that match measurements. The authors present the method as a complement to direct potential building.
arxiv-2504-07079:
Boyuan Zheng, Michael Fatemi, and nine co-authors let web agents teach themselves reusable skills. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents SkillWeaver. Human experts turn practice into portable know-how. Web agents, by contrast, start each task nearly from zero.

Facing a new website, the agent explores and spots candidate skills. It practices each one and distills the lessons into a tidy API. Repeated rounds grow a plug-and-play skill library. On a standard web benchmark, success jumps by about a third in relative terms. Real websites show a similar gain. Skills minted by strong agents also lift weaker ones.
arxiv-2504-07179:
Benjamin Elder, Giorgio Mentasti, Elizabeth Pasatembou and colleagues ask what the next generation of atomic clocks could reveal about dark physics in 2025. Many theories beyond the Standard Model predict tiny drifts in particle mass ratios, which precision clock comparisons can detect.

The team first searched published clock data for changes in the electron-proton mass ratio. They then modelled the noise of realistic near-future clock pairs and translated their sensitivity into projected bounds on theories tied to dark matter, dark energy and unification. The forecast promises much tighter limits within a few years, and the authors package their code as a tool that turns clock specifications into physics bounds.
arxiv-2504-07279:
Carosi and the ADMX team report a search for axion dark matter in a narrow radio band, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Axions are light particles that could make up all dark matter. They could also solve a long-standing puzzle in particle physics. The ADMX tool uses a strong magnet to turn axions into photons.

A tuned cavity boosts the signal at the target frequency. A deep cooler and a near-perfect amplifier cut noise to very low levels. In the latest run, the team scanned from one point one to one point three gigahertz. They reached the sensitivity needed to test a leading axion model. No axion signal is claimed in the report. The paper details the run and the setup.
arxiv-2504-07879:
AI image tools help people sketch ideas in seconds, but each generated picture costs energy, and heavy use adds up. The authors run a user study with 24 people to ask whether that cost can fall without weakening the creative support users feel. Participants generate images from prompts under different conditions while the team records energy use, prompting behavior, and ratings of creativity support. Attitudes toward designing with AI and toward its environmental footprint are also gathered.

The condition a user is in clearly changes energy consumption. It also changes the creativity support felt per prompt, though not per whole task, and image quantity per prompt looks like the main driver of both. The authors unpack how prompting habits, output counts, and energy trade against each other. They offer the results as early design guidance for creativity tools that respect both the user's flow and the planet's budget.
arxiv-2504-08379:
Yuki Amari, Muneto Nitta, and Zebin Qiu map the border between two exotic states of nuclear matter in a magnetic field. Their 2025 paper works where strong fields are routine: neutron stars and heavy-ion collisions. Theory says matter there can form a lattice of chiral solitons. It can also nest Skyrmions inside such solitons or, at high density and weaker fields, stand as a crystal of Skyrmions alone.

The authors draw the phase boundary between that crystal and the empty vacuum. A standing conjecture pictured the field squashing each Skyrmion into a pancake ringed by a superconducting loop of charged pions. Their exact solution shows the picture is nearly right in strong fields and wrong in weak ones. They also check that the Skyrmion would collapse without its stabilizing term, with the field bending the usual scaling argument. The paper firms up the phase diagram of dense magnetized matter.
arxiv-2504-08479:
Mass bends light, and the faint distortion of distant galaxies lets astronomers weigh structures too dim to see. Dutta and co-authors apply that weak lensing trick to three galaxy clusters, A115, A2219, and A2261, in a 2025 paper, using short exposures from the WIYN telescope's ODI camera.

Their significance maps recovered the clusters, most known galaxy groups in the wide field, and pieces of the filaments feeding them, including a structure over nine megaparsecs long holding A2219. Cross-checks with X-ray and radio telescopes show A115 and A2219 mid-merger, hot gas trailing away from the lensing mass in A115. A2261 looks calm in gas but is likely tugging at a neighbor seven hundred kiloparsecs away. Image depth and sharpness decided how much of the cosmic web appeared.
arxiv-2504-08879:
Zachary Scofield and co-authors ask if the most distant star candidate, Earendel, is truly a star, in work from twenty twenty-five. Earendel sits in a lensed galaxy arc behind a massive cluster. If it is a single star, its brightness demands extreme lens magnification and rare luminosity.

The team rebuilt the cluster mass map with space telescope data, joining strong and weak lensing. New multiple image systems and a dense weak lensing catalog tightened the model. Their best fit puts the magnification far below past estimates, in a modest range of tens. That drop undercuts the single star claim. Earendel may be a small star cluster or a less rare object instead.
arxiv-2504-08979:
Eugene Wu and co-authors build the first system for visualizing whole databases, not just single tables. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that classic grammars like Vega-Lite and ggplot2 assume one table. Multi-table data makes those tools clunky and their rules unsound.

A database visualization maps database constraints, such as schemas and foreign keys, to visual forms. A design counts as faithful if the picture keeps those constraints true. This view shows that chart choices are really data modeling choices in disguise. A JavaScript library called dvl puts the idea to work. Case studies show it beating both special tools and grammar languages on their own ground.
arxiv-2504-09079:
Saail Narvekar and co-authors build a remote rover frame for greenhouses in this 2025 paper. Crop studies move slowly, since each crop cycle comes once a year. A twin setup, with a fake greenhouse matched to a real one, lets teams test code any time.

Their frame links a simulated greenhouse, a real rover, and the message rules between them. Code proven in the fake house can then drive the real rover from afar. The whole stack runs on a modest laptop, the authors note. They stress how network setup, rover control, and message choice lean on each other. The frame aims to speed farm robot work in poorer lands most.
arxiv-2504-09779:
Irene Hou and six co-authors report, in a 2025 study, how generative AI tools are thinning student help networks. The team interviewed 17 undergraduate computing students at seven leading North American universities. AI help is fast and available around the clock, and its gains for solo work are clear. What it does to peer ties and classroom dynamics was less well known.

Students described a clear shift. When a peer asked for help, many now redirect that peer to a chat tool instead of helping themselves. That cuts the back-and-forth that builds skill and bonds. Students also reported growing feelings of isolation and lower motivation as their support networks frayed. The authors warn that peer interaction is a core part of learning and of a sense of belonging. Tools that replace that interaction may cost more than they give.
arxiv-2504-09979:
Teppei Suzuki and Keisuke Ozawa offer, in a 2025 paper, a shortcut for grading large vision-language models without running every benchmark in full. These models claim broad skills, so honest testing spans many data sets and costs heavily.

First, classification experiments showed no single benchmark covers all the challenges. The authors then built small test subsets by farthest point sampling, picking examples spread as widely as possible. Subsets using roughly one percent of the data tracked full evaluations with correlation above 0.96. Applying the same sampling inside one benchmark also improved its match to overall results, hinting at reduced hidden bias.
arxiv-2504-10279:
Bartosz Żbik and Andrzej Odrzywołek model small self-gravitating bodies as perfectly elastic in this 2025 paper. Working out the inner structure of asteroids and moons usually forces a choice between crude uniform density and heavy numerical recipes. Their model uses a logarithmic equation of state with a starting density and fixed bulk stiffness. The body sits in balance between its own gravity and elastic pressure.

A scaling trick reduces every case to one universal solution of a single equation, echoing classic stellar models. The mass-radius curve wiggles as it grows, giving both a maximum mass and a maximum radius. The authors derive simple formulas for center density, spin inertia, binding energy, and gravity strength. They aim the shortcuts at space mining and small body science.
arxiv-2504-10479:
Zhu leads a large team presenting InternVL3, an open-source model that reads both images and text, in a 2025 paper. Most such models start from a text-only model and bolt vision on later. That post-hoc route creates alignment headaches.

InternVL3 instead pre-trains on mixed image-text and pure text data in a single stage. A variable position scheme supports long multimodal contexts. Fine-tuning and preference optimization follow, plus test-time scaling tricks. The largest version set a new open-source best on a major multimodal benchmark. It stayed competitive with leading closed models while keeping strong language skill. The team pledges to release data and weights openly. The release aims to spur next-generation research.
arxiv-2504-10579:
Minxing Xu and six co-authors describe a 2025 chip that can sense the tiny Casimir force between two flat plates held very close. The force comes from quantum effects in empty space, and how it shifts when a metal turns superconducting is still an open question. Past tests were held back by poor alignment and stray forces. The new chip holds the plates far more parallel than past rigs did.

A scanning probe reads the motion of a thin, hanging plate with extreme care, which lets the team weed out other weak forces. The setup can sense pressure far below the jumps that theory predicts at the shift point. The authors say the chip opens a clean path to test how the force and superconductivity interact.
arxiv-2504-10779:
Ali Maalaoui, Vittorio Martino, and Lamine Mbarki study a Dirac equation with a non-local twist in a 2025 mathematics study. The equation respects conformal symmetry, meaning it keeps its form under angle-preserving changes of scale and shape. Its non-linear term works by convolution, so each point feels the whole configuration, a feature drawn from a coupled Einstein and Dirac problem.

The authors analyze compactness, bubbling, and energy levels of the related functional. They characterize ground state solutions on the standard sphere. An inequality of Aubin type then guarantees solutions exist, including for the motivating geometric problem. A linear perturbation leads to a further existence result.
arxiv-2504-10879:
Nguyen Tuan Hung and co-authors compute in 2025 how stretching a one-atom-thick magnetic crystal changes its light and quantum traits. The crystal family, written MnBi2X4, pairs magnetism with topological behavior prized for future devices. First-principles calculations tested pull in two directions at once and pull along one axis. The two pulls had opposite effects on the magnetic strength.

A measure called quantum weight tracked how the crystal's quantum geometry shifted. One-axis pull lowered that weight and made the response directional, giving designers an extra dial. Bond analysis showed where the sheets tend to crack or bend. The work guides how strain could tune such crystals in real devices.
arxiv-2504-11079:
Machine learning systems are spreading through industry, and keeping them both scalable and maintainable over their whole life is getting harder. Karthik Shivashankar, Ghadi Al Hajj, and Antonio Martini review the literature on these twin challenges. They analyzed one hundred twenty-four papers. From them they catalogued forty-one maintainability challenges and thirteen scalability challenges, along with the solutions proposed for each. The review is organized around six research questions.

The questions follow the life of a system: data work, model building, and system development. A recurring finding is that the two goals pull on each other, so gains in scale often cost upkeep, and vice versa. The authors map how each challenge looks at each life stage. They aim the overview at researchers and practitioners who need to design machine learning systems that stay sound as they grow.
arxiv-2504-12079:
Hoyer and co-authors add massive star clusters to the L-Galaxies galaxy formation model. Star cluster histories are tied to their host galaxies' pasts. Poor grasp of cluster assembly limits their use as tracers, though. The new model version grows clusters above ten thousand solar masses. It tests several physical guesses about how clusters form and fade. Galaxy traits and local star birth rates set what share of stars end up bound in clusters.

Cluster masses are drawn from a mass rule that depends on environment. Each cluster also gets a size, metal content, and place in the galaxy. Cosmic time then evolves the population. The upgrade lets simulated galaxies grow realistic cluster families.
arxiv-2504-12379:
Nico Huber and co-authors map the electron structure of the metal compound PdGa in a 2025 physics paper. The compound is a chiral semimetal, meaning its crystal twists one way and its electrons behave partly like a metal's. Tiny oscillations in magnetic response reveal the shape of its Fermi surface, the boundary of filled electron states.

The measured surface holds several pockets split by a relativistic effect that couples spin and motion. The team matches the data against computed band structures. They show the full signal can be read once two effects are included: flat degeneracies at the zone edge and electrons tunneling between pockets in strong fields. The work refines how such oscillation data are decoded.
arxiv-2504-12479:
Gritskov and Andrey Losev wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on perturbative geometry. The subject grows out of quantum field theory, where physicists expand hard problems into series of simpler terms. The authors build a formal geometry that matches that style of expansion.

In the first part, they define this geometry and prove a theorem. The theorem links neighborhoods of affine varieties, built step by step, with higher tangent bundles. In the second part, they turn to vector fields inside the new framework. These fields are finite versions of traits that appear in quantum field theory. The paper gives abstract tools for work where expansions, not exact forms, carry the content.
arxiv-2504-12779:
Keita Kishigi and Yasumasa Hasegawa probe heat capacity near a flattened Dirac cone in a 2025 paper. Dirac cones come in three tilt kinds, and at the third kind the slope dies along one direction. In the narrow sense form, even the curved terms die, which leaves a fully flat run.

The pair tilt a model cone step by step and track electronic specific heat with warmth. A crossover shows near the narrow form: heat grows with the square of temperature below a mark, then with its square root above it. The density of states shape drives the switch. The mark gives labs a probe of tilt depth.
arxiv-2504-12879:
Grigory Kovalev and co-authors present RusBEIR, a benchmark for Russian information retrieval, in this 2025 paper. Retrieval models are usually tested in English. Russian is morphologically rich, which changes how word based search behaves. A shared test set is needed for fair comparison.

RusBEIR gathers 17 datasets from varied domains. Some were adapted, some translated, and some built new for this benchmark. Word based and neural models were compared in a zero shot setting. Careful preprocessing mattered greatly for word based models. A classic method, BM25, stayed a strong baseline on full documents. Neural models won on most sets but struggled with long documents due to input limits. The framework is open source.
arxiv-2504-13679:
Daniel Rouan and co-authors image the debris disk of a young star in mid infrared light with a space telescope in 2025, using team framing for a very long author list. Debris disks are rings of dust left from planet building. The goal was to map the disk's shape, heat, and dust mass. Grain sizes were also a target.

The disk shows clearly at both wavelengths used. Its shape fits a belt with a set edge radius. Fill inside that radius argues against carving by an inner giant planet. Grain size from the flux ratio matches what starlight blows out. Dust mass agrees with ground based radio data. Belt heat averages near seventy four kelvin.
arxiv-2504-14179:
Veeranna Banoth, a solo author, proposes a new probability distribution for data that lean far to one side, in a 2025 statistics paper. The new model extends the Fisk distribution, a known curve used for skewed data. Extra settings in the model let it bend to fit a wider range of skew and peak shapes than the older curve.

Banoth works out the model's main traits, including its quantiles, moments, and measures of skew and peakedness. Tests with simulated data check how well the standard fitting method recovers the true settings. The paper then fits the model to real datasets from fields such as economics and engineering. By standard fit checks, the new curve beat rival models on the data tried.
arxiv-2504-14379:
Andrew Lee and co-authors dissect how a reasoning model checks its own answers, in a research paper from 2025. They trained a model on an arithmetic game where trained preferences collapse outputs into rigid, structured chains. That regularity makes the inner machinery easier to trace.

From the top down, they found weights that light up for words like success or incorrect. From the bottom up, attention heads that watch the previous token did most of the checking. The two views met: as few as three heads, found via the top-down clues, could switch self-checking off. Similar parts appeared in the base model and a large public reasoning model.
arxiv-2504-14479:
Xinyi Wu and Xiaocheng Shang present a 2025 method for measuring how fluids resist flow at small scales. The setting is dissipative particle dynamics, a simulation style for soft matter and complex fluids. The standard approach fixes the push on a system and measures the flow it induces. Their stochastic Norton approach flips the setup: it fixes the flow and measures the push needed to sustain it.

The team extends earlier results from a simpler dynamics to this particle method. Response curves from both approaches match, in gentle and strong driving alike. That match validates the flipped method for transport values such as mobility and shear viscosity. From small push theory they also derive a closed form for viscosity, confirmed in simulations. The flipped method showed far tighter error control, above all when friction is high.
arxiv-2504-14979:
Some particle decays carry a rare fingerprint called an anomaly, a term in the theory that no simple diagram can produce. Chao-Qiang Geng and two co-authors show in 2025 how particle colliders could pin down that term for hadrons, the particles built from quarks. They focus on the decays of two light mesons, eta and eta prime, and on kaon decays.

For one eta decay, the anomaly term rules the rate, so a collider in China could measure its strength to percent level precision, they find. Data on an eta prime decay gave a far larger share for the term than expected. In kaon decays the term fills one slot in the decay pattern, though passing states can shift it by a quarter. The authors urge fresh runs at higher precision.
arxiv-2504-15279:
Weiye Xu and co-authors build a test of visual reasoning for AI models in 2025. Many current tests let models cheat by reasoning over text alone. Their benchmark, VisuLogic, holds a thousand human checked problems that demand true looking. Problems span six types, from counting shifts to spatial relations and trait comparisons.

Leading multimodal models were scored on the full set. Most landed barely above random guessing, which exposes a wide gap. The team sorts the common failure modes behind those scores. A test that blocks language shortcuts gives builders a truer gauge of machine sight.
arxiv-2504-15379:
Lim and co-authors studied rhythmic brightness pulses in tiny solar brightenings in 2025. Small flashes in extreme ultraviolet light may share physics with larger solar flares. Flares often pulse in a near-regular rhythm, a trait called quasi-periodic pulsations, and the team asked whether the small events pulse too.

Light curves were extracted for more than twenty-two thousand brightenings in two quiet regions of the Sun. About three in a hundred showed steady pulses. Pulses were more common in larger, longer, and brighter events. Their periods ran from about fifteen to two hundred sixty seconds, much like flare pulses. Unlike in big flares, pulse period did not track event lifetime or size here.
arxiv-2504-15479:
Jeremy Goldwasser and Giles Hooker unify two ways of explaining image classifiers under one method, in a 2025 paper. Counterfactual images show what change would flip a prediction, but pixel-level edits often cheat with invisible noise. Their method, Counterfactual Attacks, edits the image's latent representation along a low-dimensional manifold instead, riding on modern generative models.

Given a side data set of image descriptors, the same framework scores which features changed between the original and the counterfactual. Averaging those scores over many images yields global explanations of what drives the model overall. Tests on handwritten digits and celebrity faces show the explanations stay faithful while remaining cheap to compute.
arxiv-2504-15679:
Brandon Panos and Ivan Milić solve the two-level atom non-LTE radiative transfer problem with reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. To read a star's air, physicists must work out how light and atoms settle into balance away from local equilibrium. Classic solvers lean on approximate operators and many rounds of iteration.

Their agent learns the depth-by-depth source function as if it were a control task. A radiative transfer engine scores each try, and a soft actor-critic method steers the policy by reward alone. No answer key and no gradient through the solver are needed. A simple setup shows the agent can find the self-consistent state.
arxiv-2504-15879:
Haotian Xu and co-authors estimate how event intensity varies across several dimensions at once, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Events such as earthquakes form point patterns whose density shifts by place and trait. Their method views the intensity surface as a large matrix or tensor with a low-rank core.

That view yields the best possible trade-off between bias and noise, with cost set by the rank. Many standard model families fit the low-rank shape, the team shows. On United States earthquake data with location, depth, and size, the method kept sharp local patterns that a kernel method blurred away.
arxiv-2504-16079:
Sara Algeri and six co-workers wrote a 2025 paper on testing models of sky patterns. Scientists often sum up such patterns with a spectrum curve. A good test must judge if a model fits that curve. Past tests needed the exact spread of the curve's estimates, which is often unknown.

Their new test skips that need. It works without fixing the spread in advance, under broad conditions. It also skips the case-by-case simulations that older tests required for each model. That saves a lot of computing time. The authors present the method as a tool for many fields that use such spectra.
arxiv-2504-16379:
Yash Akhauri and co-authors teach a small reasoning model to hand off its hardest steps to a bigger one. Long chains of thought make language models accurate but slow and costly, since every token is produced one by one. Not all steps are equally hard, though, so the team built SplitReason to keep the easy stretches in-house and offload only the tough segments.

The authors marked difficult segments in eighteen thousand reasoning traces from a public math dataset, then trained a 1.5-billion-parameter model with supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning to spot and delegate such segments itself. On a hard math benchmark the setup raised accuracy by twenty-four to twenty-eight percent while offloading only about one to five percent of tokens. Model, data, code, and logs are released openly.
arxiv-2504-16679:
Hugo Lemarquand and five co-authors map how flow breaks down inside a hypersonic wind tunnel nozzle in a 2025 paper. Quiet tunnels, which keep the test flow smooth, are prized for testing fast aircraft, but the nozzle itself can seed the turbulence it must avoid.

Working at six times the speed of sound, the team computed the base flow and tested its stability for two wall heat settings. A small separation bubble near the inlet proved able to excite a steady three-dimensional instability. Down the widening outlet, ripples of several known families can grow, plus a shear instability fed by the bubble. The study shows why a suction lip before the throat calms the tunnel.
arxiv-2504-16779:
Software engineers work under deadline pressure with their minds as the tool, and burnout stalks the profession. Cristina Martinez Montes and Birgit Penzenstadler ran an eight-week yoga program inside a software company and measured what changed. Six well-being scales were given before and after, with a weekly check-in between, plus a focus group with the organizers.

The numbers moved too little to prove anything. The stories told another tale: participants said they felt better and valued the sessions. With only one session a week, workplace pressures easily buried the effect in the statistics. The authors conclude yoga likely helps, and that context decides whether studies can see it.
arxiv-2504-17179:
Mohammad Zarei and co-authors hunt rare failure modes in self-driving car perception, in a paper from 2025. Cars trained on millions of miles still miss odd scenes that almost never occur. That long tail of rare cases is a standing safety risk. Their method grows such scenes on purpose with a guided image generator.

They first cut out the objects a car must see, like other cars. The scene around those shapes is then rebuilt from text prompts. A noise-tuning step steers the rebuild toward scenes that fool the detector. The result is a set of fresh, tricky images that expose blind spots. Plain-language notes describe each failure for engineers and rule makers. The authors say the trick can harden both training and testing of driving systems.
arxiv-2504-17279:
Xiuying Chen and co-authors evaluated bias in AI-written medical text and tested ways to reduce it in a 2025 paper. Deep learning systems now match experts on many medical tasks and draft text for clinics. Yet they can absorb human bias and serve historically neglected groups worse, a flaw that hides inside fluent prose.

The team measured how bias shows up in generated medical text, across patient groups. They then tested mitigation steps and checked whether fixes held without gutting quality. Fair generation matters because biased notes can steer real treatment. Their framework gives hospitals a way to audit medical writing tools before trusting them in records, summaries, and patient messages.
arxiv-2504-17779:
