Dan Crawford and three co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on odd swirls of current in superconductors. In a Josephson junction, two superconductors are split by a thin barrier. Here the barrier is a weak magnet with strong spin-orbit coupling, a link between electron spin and motion. The authors show this mix can spawn vortices tied to an unusual form of pairing.

A symmetry study finds a new term in the energy that allows magnet-like effects even where older theory said none could appear. Using a detailed model, they show the vortices can be moved and reshaped by tuning the spin-orbit coupling with electric gates. That control hints at a way to spot the vortices with scanning magnetic probes. The pairing itself can also twist into a texture. The work adds a fresh handle on exotic states in quantum devices.
arxiv-2504-17979:
Long space missions may need surgery with a small crew and long communication delays, so a robot arm that can work partly on its own becomes attractive. Shankar and co-authors adapt a path-planning method called Fuzzy Rapidly-exploring Random Tree for a two-degree-of-freedom surgical arm modeled on a miniaturized robotic surgery system. The arm must move through a workspace with obstacles while a human partner shares control.

The fuzzy version of the planner steers the random search with graded rules rather than hard cutoffs. That suits the soft judgments involved in surgical motion. In tests, the method cut path search time sharply, an improvement of seven hundred forty-three percent, and lowered path cost by forty-three percent over the baseline. The authors call the result a step toward semi-autonomous surgical help on missions where a surgical team cannot be present.
arxiv-2504-18179:
Lovro Sindičić and Ivica Kopriva present a clustering method that needs no labelled data and no hand-tuned settings, in a 2025 paper. Clustering groups similar items together, and one family of methods assumes the data sits inside a few overlapping subspaces. Deep learning versions of that idea work well but lean on labelled data to tune settings, judge quality, and decide when to stop. Those labels often do not exist in practice.

The new method reads information from every layer of its network, not just the last one. It also learns the data layout and the grouping at the same time, rather than in separate steps. Training runs in stages, first warming up and then refining. The design removes the need for a held-out labelled set and for label-based checks at the end, which the authors say should widen where such clustering can be used.
arxiv-2504-18279:
Neelkamal Mallick and co-authors teach machines to rebuild a charm baryon from its three-way death spray, in a study from 2025. Charm quarks are born in the first clash flash and live through the whole fire tale, so their hadrons are prime probes. To rebuild one from spray is to fight a vast sea of chance pairs.

The mark was a charm baryon that dies to a proton and a short-lived kin, which then splits to two pions. Two learn tools, a boost tree and a deep net, read the young spray's marks to sift true deaths from the sea, and prompt births from beauty-fed ones. Clean sift, they show, can be taught, not just cut.
arxiv-2504-18579:
Feng Chen and co-authors present a training method in 2025 that forces vision-language models to use far fewer tokens. Models that read images and text split input into tokens, and attending to all of them costs a lot of computing power. Trimming tokens can halve the cost, but pushing further usually hurts accuracy.

Most trimming methods just exploit the sparsity a model already has, so they stall near that halfway mark. The authors instead train the model directly to be sparse, with control over the token budget rather than rigid patterns. Their method adapts to each input and layer. The result aims at cheaper, faster multimodal models for phones and services where every token saved cuts cost and delay.
arxiv-2504-18879: Ting-Wei Chang, Song-Yun Chen, Fei-Jun Huang, and Hung-Chun Tsui define a family of series in prime characteristic, in this 2025 note given in short form. The catalog title is garbled with funding text, so it follows the head of the text. Multiple Eisenstein series come in any rank, and known multiple zeta values appear as the constant terms of their expansions through multiple Goss sums. The authors prove the series obey the same q-shuffle relations as the zeta values, lifting them from values to functions.
arxiv-2504-18979:
Duško Jojić, Gaiane Panina, and Rade Živaljević tackle a fair-division puzzle in this 2025 math paper: how many ways can a cake be split so that no player envies another's piece? Envy-free splits are a classic topic, because they show when a fair outcome exists at all.

The authors prove lower bounds in two settings. In the classic one, hungry players always value any piece, and at least two envy-free splits must exist; they show this count cannot be improved. In a mixed setting, where fairness is paired with an equal split of a second measure, they count a much larger set of fair splits tied to prime numbers. The results sharpen what theory can promise about fair sharing.
arxiv-2504-19579:
Jack Radcliffe and co-authors report progress on wide-field VLBI, in a 2025 conference paper. The technique links telescopes across thousands of kilometers for the sharpest images in astronomy, but computing limits have confined it to one small target at a time. Wide-field methods open the view to many sources at once and have already repaid the effort on galactic nuclei, supernovae, and gravitational lenses.

New workflows for correlation and calibration, including distributed processing, aim to make wide-field observing routine on all major arrays rather than a specialist stunt. The authors argue that standardizing the mode would unlock far more science from existing telescope networks without new hardware.
arxiv-2504-19679:
Benno Bock, Daniel Brady, and Michael Fleischhauer wrote a 2025 physics paper on excited atoms held in light tweezers. Excitations hop between Rydberg atoms, but the hop also shakes the atoms' motion. As that link grows, a cluster's spread changes character in stages.

First the cluster spreads freely. Then it sways back and forth like a Bloch wave. At strong link it freezes in place, a form of disorder trapping. Random quantum shakes of the motion field cause the last step. The trapped motion also lands in squeezed, non-classical states, moving in or out of step by interaction shape. The study maps a full path from motion to stillness.
arxiv-2504-20279:
Stephen Humphries and Joseph Marrow classify special group pairs in a 2025 algebra paper. A strong Gelfand pair is a group with a subgroup where every character of the subgroup lifts to the full group without repeats. Such pairs matter in representation theory, where they signal unusually clean structure.

The pair focus on the finite symplectic group of four-by-four matrices over a field with an even number of elements. They classify all strong Gelfand pairs of that group in the even case. The result completes a case split by parity, since the even case behaves differently from the odd. The paper gives the full list with proof, closing the classification for this group family.
arxiv-2504-20379:
Jongwon Lee and Timothy Bretl pinpoint where a photo was taken inside a pre-built 3D scene, in a 2025 paper. Modern scene models, built from splats of soft 3D blobs, render views from any angle. Older localization methods compare pixels directly and take over ten seconds per photo.

Their pipeline renders a synthetic color-plus-depth view from a rough first guess of the pose. It matches features between the real photo and the synthetic one, lifts the matches into 3D using the depth map, and solves for the camera pose geometrically. Across thirty-eight scenes and thousands of test images, the method ran up to a hundred times faster with lower error. It even recovered from starting guesses off by fifty-five degrees.
arxiv-2504-20479:
Elena Martinez and five co-authors build a stand in model of heart work that deals with shifts in the shape of sick folk. Heart mock runs based on physics are true but tied to one shape. They need new train for each new sick one. Their path codes heart spark runs into a form called Branched Latent Neural Maps. Those runs come from a model at more than one scale.

Shifts in shape are set through a two pouch atlas built from thirteen young sick folk. All had Tetralogy of Fallot. A stats pick way then makes fifty-two made up shapes that match those shifts. They form the train set. The stand in works back on the first sick group with firm scores and low flaw. The code is put out for all. Its aim is heart models for one sick one that wards can use.
arxiv-2504-20579:
Praharsh Nanavati, Ranjitha Prasad, and Karthikeyan Shanmugam learn representations for treatment effect estimation in a 2025 paper. Observational data mislead twice over: hidden factors confound the comparison, and treated and control groups differ in makeup. Past methods usually fix one problem and ignore the other.

Their neural architectures build a covariate representation that both qualifies as a valid adjustment and satisfies matching constraints between groups. Gradient matching across subsampled domains supplies one of the mechanisms. A common frame for both biases could make real-world effect estimates, from medicine to policy, less of a leap of faith.
arxiv-2504-20679:
Search tools for matching survey questions across decades are weighed by Wing Yan Li and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Long studies reuse near-same questions, but word drift hides the pairs. The team frames a fresh search task: spot same-concept questions and their answer sets. A survey base from 1946 to 2020 supplies the test ground.

Plain odds models, light probes of language nets, and search-tuned nets all got a run. Search-tuned nets won overall, with other tools close behind. Re-ranking added at most a hair. Experts found the tools blind to word overlap with wrong sub-concepts.
arxiv-2504-20879:
Shivalika Singh and co-authors published a 2025 paper arguing that a famous AI leaderboard does not rank models fairly. Chatbot Arena lets the public vote head-to-head on chatbot answers, and its table steers the whole field. The authors document hidden practices that tilt the table toward a few big providers.

Some providers, they find, test many private versions of a model on the arena before release. They can then publish only the best score. One company tested twenty-seven private variants ahead of a major launch. Closed models also get sampled in more battles and are removed from the board less often than open ones. As a result, two companies have received about a fifth each of all arena data. That data itself improves models, widening the gap. The paper calls the ranking an illusion and urges reforms for fair measurement.
arxiv-2504-21379:
Andreas Anastasiou and Piotr Fryzlewicz present a new change-point method in a 2025 statistics paper. Change-point tools find the moments when a data stream's pattern shifts. Many shifts at once, of any kind, are hard to locate without assuming a model family.

Their method, NPID, isolates each stretch of data so it holds at most one change, which sharpens the search. It estimates both how many changes occurred and where, for general distribution shifts. Two stopping rules are offered: a fixed threshold and an information score. Across a wide range of test cases, the method beat current rivals. An R package ships with the paper.
arxiv-2504-21579:
Stavros Anagnou, Christoph Salge, and Peter Lewis ask how shared rules ever get started. Their twenty twenty-five paper names a bootstrapping problem for institutions. People see value in joining only once a group exists, so no one wants to go first.

The authors propose that false belief can break the deadlock. If some people wrongly think a group already exists, they join and help make it real. Game models join known quirks of mind, such as bias, warped odds, and noisy views. Plain noise from distinct lives cut the needed crowd size a lot. Readers get a fresh take on a classic commons puzzle.
arxiv-2504-21779:
Valérie Gillot, Philippe Langevin, and Alexandr Polujan settle the last open case in a long running question about bent functions, special Boolean functions used in coding and cryptography. A bent function is called normal if it stays constant on a flat subspace of half the dimension. Their 2025 paper tackles eight variables, the one size left unresolved.

They prove every eight variable bent function is normal once a linear function may be added. The count of such functions is huge, around two to the power 106, so the proof rests on structure, not enumeration. Smaller sizes were already known to be fully normal, while at ten variables and up, some functions can never be made normal. The result completes a classification posed as an open problem two decades ago.
arxiv-2505-00379:
Ni Wang and Germán Morales-España reviewed how energy planners model power investments across many years, in a 2025 paper. The simple approach lumps all capacity together, ignoring the year each plant was built. The vintage approach tracks each year's builds, catching how gear improves over time, but it swells the model's size.

The pair propose a compact form that keeps the year-by-year detail while trimming the model's dimensions. It is built into an open-source energy model the community can use. The paper weighs fidelity against computing cost for long-range planning. The authors argue planners no longer must choose between detail and a model that actually runs.
arxiv-2505-00679:
Xinchen Yang and Marine Carpuat tackle style transfer with large language models in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The task is to rewrite a text so it matches the style of a sample text the user gives. The hard part is telling the model what that style is. A poor account of style leads to weak rewrites.

The authors use register analysis, a way of describing how word choice fits a setting and a goal. They turn that account into a prompt for the model. Tests across several style tasks show their prompts work well. Rewrites matched the target style more strongly than with older prompt styles. They also kept the source sense intact more often. The method needs no extra training of the model.
arxiv-2505-00779:
Junwon Seo, Kensuke Nakamura, and Andrea Bajcsy build safety filters that heed doubt in two thousand twenty-five. World models let classic safe control work from raw sensor views. But training can never cover all risky scenes. A filter on a flawed model may miss new hazards and call them safe.

Their filter uses the model's own doubt as a sign of the unseen. A threshold for doubt is set with a formal method that gives coverage bounds. Reach tests then run in a space that holds both state and doubt. Tests in simulation and on a real robot arm show early warnings. The filter steers the robot to safe, known acts.
arxiv-2505-01379:
Hao-Cheng Weng and co-authors observed the full ladder of temporal quantum correlations in a superconducting qubit, in a 2025 paper. Such correlations test whether a system behaves in a truly quantum way over time. They form a hierarchy, from the denial of macrorealism up through temporal steering to temporal inseparability.

By steering the qubit's dynamics, the team brought out each level of the ladder in turn. The rich behavior they saw, such as steering that dies suddenly or revives, gives a fresh yardstick for testing qubits on real circuits. As a sample use, they showed the memory effect in a single qubit's dynamics, a sign that its past still shapes its present.
arxiv-2505-01479:
Siheng Xiong and co-authors give language models a symbolic partner for planning. Their 2025 paper builds SymPlanner for tasks that need many steps in a fixed order. Pure text reasoning often drifts into action chains that break the rules. A symbolic world instead holds each state exactly and checks every move.

A policy model proposes actions, and the symbolic world runs and verifies them. One add-on repairs bad steps using feedback from the world. Another compares rival plans side by side before picking one. Together they mirror how people fix errors and form choices. On PlanBench, the system made plans that held together better. The plans could also be checked step by step.
arxiv-2505-01779:
Thin materials with fine inner structure need math that predicts how they bend and stretch, and a 2025 paper by Antoine Chan-Lock and Miguel A. Otaduy offers a new method. Earlier ways to sum up such a material's behavior each gave something up: some missed the look, some broke energy rules, and all handled only a few ways of deforming at once.

Their method builds the material law on the full space of membrane and bending changes, so the modes can interact in rich ways. A new kind of interpolant, written for polar coordinates, sits at the center of the design. Tests show the method fits many microstructure behaviors more closely than past work, in both numbers and look.
arxiv-2505-02279:
Ehtesham, Singh, Gupta, and Kumar surveyed four protocols that let AI agents work together and use tools in a standard way. As agents built on large language models spread, ad-hoc links between them have become hard to scale and secure. The survey compares the Model Context Protocol, the Agent Communication Protocol, the Agent-to-Agent Protocol, and the Agent Network Protocol, each aimed at a different layer of cooperation.

The protocols differ in how agents find each other, pass messages, and stay secure. One focuses on safe tool access, another on general messaging over the web, a third on delegating tasks between peers, and the fourth on open, decentralized networks. The authors propose adopting them in phases, from tool access up to open agent marketplaces. They present the comparison as a base for building secure, interoperable agent systems.
arxiv-2505-02579:
Lingxiao Kong and co-authors introduce EMORL, a framework for fine-tuning language models toward several goals at once. Balancing rival goals in reinforcement learning is slow and hard to scale or explain. EMORL instead fine-tunes separate models, each on a single objective, and then optimizes how their internal states are combined.

The method is the first to merge the hidden states of single-goal models, carrying context from each objective into the mix. A hierarchical grid search finds the best weights for the blend. Tests used counselor reflection writing, scored by text classifiers that supplied the training rewards. Across two data sets, EMORL trained with far fewer data points and less time than rival methods, and its results were steadier. Performance across the goals stayed comparable, while scaling and clarity improved. The authors offer the framework as a flexible route to multi-goal tuning.
arxiv-2505-02979:
Ruiyue Huang, Claire Heaney, and Maarten van Reeuwijk present a 2025 method to fit the settings of a land-surface model from data. Such models predict soil moisture, heat, and water flows over land. Their settings are hard to measure directly in the field. The team rewrote a simple model's equations so they can be run with machine learning libraries. That rewrite makes the model differentiable, so gradients flow through it. Settings can then be tuned by gradient methods to match data.

No separate adjoint code needs to be derived or maintained. The forward model stays pure physics, with no learned parts. Tuning minimizes the gap between model output and real or synthetic records. Settings may shift over time in their approach. The authors test the method as an inverse modeling tool. It could serve weather, farming, and flood models alike.
arxiv-2505-03279:
Enaldiev studies layer-breathing phonons in 2025, trapped inside dislocations of twisted bilayers made of common layered materials. The materials are transition metal dichalcogenides, with layers set parallel or antiparallel. Once the layers settle, dislocations form in the moire pattern and shift the gap between layers along their lines. The study looks at how these trapped modes form and where they sit.

That shift creates wells that bind one-dimensional bands of breathing modes. The parallel kind hosts several such bands inside perfect dislocations. The other kind hosts only one, for angles near the edge type. Frequencies sit above the domain breathing mode in both cases. Models at many scales supply the results.
arxiv-2505-03379:
Ishtiaque Ahmed and Leila Musavian design a hybrid wireless scheme in 2025 for networks serving two kinds of users at once. Some users want raw bits; a newer class wants meaning, sending semantic content instead. Sharing one access point between them efficiently is the puzzle.

Their scheme mixes two access styles: shared slots where users overlap under power ordering, and clean slots reserved for bit users. In mixed slots, bit messages are decoded before semantic ones. The team sets up a power allocation problem to maximize the semantic throughput under a total power cap. Simulations beat the plain one-user-at-a-time setup, showing the blend serves both camps better.
arxiv-2505-03779:
Tao Liu and co-authors present a neural method that designs fiber-based composite parts in one pass. Their 2025 paper deals with strong, light materials made of fibers set in plastic. Shape, layer layout, and fiber direction all shape how a part bears load and whether a printer can make it.

Their framework uses three neural fields to stand for shape, layer order, and fiber direction. Goals such as strength, volume, layer curve, and thickness enter the training as losses. That way, design and making limits are solved together, not one after the other. Real prints showed parts that bore notably higher failure loads than parts designed in split steps. The method fits multi-axis printing on varied hardware.
arxiv-2505-04379:
Self-driving cars sharing city streets must be safe, polite to other road users, and good for traffic flow all at once. Elayan and Kontar ask how often automated vehicles achieve that full consensus, using fine-grained trajectory data from a city test dataset.

At a signalized intersection and around people walking and cycling, they scored time-to-collision, post-encroachment time, braking patterns, headways, and flow stability. Full consensus turned out to be rare. Only 1.63 percent of the frames involving vulnerable road users met the safety, interaction, and performance conditions together. The authors argue that driving models must be built to balance these three goals openly, rather than assume they align, and they share their analysis code.
arxiv-2505-04479:
Reetika Joshi and co-authors film a solar filament in the act of rewiring itself with the loops around it. In the flat textbook picture, a flare's reconnection happens under the erupting rope. Three-dimensional geometry allows another route, in which the rope swaps partners with the arcades above it and its feet slide across the surface. A two-ribbon flare gave the team a live case to read with imaging and spectroscopy.

As the filament rose, bright points marked where it reconnected with the arcade loops, which then vanished while a hot flux rope took shape. Its footpoints slipped toward the loops' old anchors, exactly the predicted drift. Spectral lines showed gas rushing toward us at up to two hundred kilometers a second, hugely broadened, with one lopsided profile betraying accelerated particles.
arxiv-2505-04579:
Stephane Aroca-Ouellette and co-authors help AI agents team with strangers in a 2025 paper. Agents that collaborate well with known partners often flounder beside new ones, whether machine or human. People handle this by sharing task abstractions: rough, layered ideas of what the team is doing. The authors argue the lack of such shared structure is what blocks zero-shot teamwork for machines.

Their framework, HA2, uses hierarchical reinforcement learning so agents learn both high-level plans and low-level moves, mimicking the human structure. In the Overcooked kitchen game, a standard testbed, HA2 beat prior methods when paired with unseen agents and with people. It also held up better when the setting shifted. The authors present shared abstraction as a design principle for flexible teammates.
arxiv-2505-04779:
Twagirayezu, a solo author, studies in this 2025 physics paper how a smallest possible length would change the shape factors of mesons. The idea comes from a generalized uncertainty rule that adds quantum gravity hints to particle math. The setting is a light-front holography model that maps strong-force physics onto a five-dimensional space.

With the new rule folded into the model's wave functions, overlaps between particle states grow. Key coefficients turn out positive, so the net fix lifts the predicted form factors. The lift brings the model closer to measured pion data across the tested range. Sums over all states are cut at three terms for the numeric work, which still covers the data well. The result hints that grain-scale space effects leave marks on strong-force data.
arxiv-2505-05779:
Elfimov and Sharapov present a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian system whose quantization shows anomalies, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Gauge field theories often face such anomalies during quantization. They are blamed on degrees of freedom without end. A regularization scheme is then thought to be needed to complete the model.

Their counterexample is a finite system with first-class constraints. Nothing about it is infinite-dimensional. Yet quantization still yields anomalies. The authors trace the anomaly's origin to the nontrivial topology of the reduced phase space. The example tests the standard story about where anomalies come from. It suggests topology, not infinity, can be the true culprit.
arxiv-2505-05979:
Arnoldus Otto and four co-authors built a cluster model for skew, mixed data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with data that is not bell shaped. Their frame joins two parts: a shifted asymmetric Laplace law for the answers and one for the input traits, mixed across clusters. Each cluster runs its own regression on that law. Stray points can bend such fits, so a guarded twin model is built too.

The twin adds per cluster shares for outliers and leverage points, plus a grade of outlier depth. Readers in statistics get a cluster weighted tool that reads skew and dirt in data at once, in more than one trait at a time.
arxiv-2505-06079:
Shuaiyi Huang and five co-authors teach robots from human preferences without letting noisy labels poison the lesson. Their 2025 paper works in preference-based reinforcement learning, where a reward model is trained on comparisons, which is better, this attempt or that one. Human and model annotators both mislabel often, and the reward model learns the noise as faithfully as the signal.

Their framework, TREND, adds two guards. A handful of expert demonstrations, as few as one to three, anchors the training. And three reward models train together in a tri-teaching loop. Each treats the preference pairs it fits most easily as trustworthy, and passes those to a peer for its update. Suspect labels starve. On robotic manipulation tasks the method reached success rates up to ninety percent even when forty percent of the labels were wrong.
arxiv-2505-06279:
Shashwat Pandey builds a toolkit for watching reinforcement learning agents think. Agents trained by curiosity, rewarded for novelty rather than goals, learn to explore on their own, but what changes inside them is murky. His 2025 paper studies five agents, from plain deep networks to a transformer variant, all trained in procedurally generated worlds.

Using heat-map and relevance methods borrowed from image research, plus clustering of the agents' inner representations, Pandey tracks where each agent looks and how its world model forms. Two new measures anchor the work: attention diversity, the breadth of an agent's focus, and attention change rate, how fast that focus shifts. Curiosity-driven agents looked wider and shifted faster than goal-driven ones. The transformer variant paired broad attention with high exploration and tidy inner structure. The author offers the framework as a diagnostic kit for agent design beyond raw scores.
arxiv-2505-06579:
Yangguang Shao and six co-authors warn about a new attack on search-backed chat systems, in a research paper from 2025. These systems pull text from outside sources to help answer questions. The attack, called PoisonCraft, plants fake text so the system pulls it in and points users to false websites.

Older attacks needed to know what the user would ask, or needed to change the question. This one needs neither. Tests across data sets, search tools, and language models show the attack works and can move to new systems. The authors share their code so others can build stronger defenses for real-world use.
arxiv-2505-06779:
Alexander Haywood and Fatima Ebrahimi study spinning magnetized plasma in this 2025 study. Gas and plasma that spin at uneven speeds, as in disks around young stars, can turn unstable and churn. Two rival instabilities may start that churn: a local one tied to magnetic fields, and a global one driven by the curve of the flow itself.

The authors built a global math tool and checked it against a known simulation code. The global, slow mode survived when diffusion was strong, while the local, fast mode faded. Maps they drew from the tool show which mode wins for each mix of disk thickness, curve, and field strength. Flow shape mattered too: uneven spin profiles were more prone to churn. The maps can guide both lab work and star-disk models.
arxiv-2505-07179:
Corentin Delacour and co-authors present a 2025 oscillatory neural network that can handle constraints in hard search problems. Networks of oscillators settle into low-energy states that encode solutions, much like Hopfield nets. Plain versions get stuck in states that break the rules of a constrained problem, since the energy view has no way to price rule breaks.

Their design adds extra oscillators that act as Lagrange multipliers, the classic math device for priced constraints. Those extra units steer the system out of rule-breaking states across a reshaped energy landscape. The net settles only when all constraints are met. On a max-satisfiability task with three literals per clause, it solved random library cases with up to 200 variables and 860 clauses. It gives a deterministic rival to simulated annealing for coupled oscillators.
arxiv-2505-07679:
Schinina proved this result in additive combinatorics in twenty twenty-five. A sumset collects all sums formed by adding elements of a set to itself a set number of times. For sets of k elements, scholars ask which sizes the h-fold sumset can take. The full list of possible sizes is still unknown.

Known bounds place the size between two endpoints, and both endpoints do occur. Schinina shows that a short run of sizes just above the low endpoint never occurs. The ban holds for sets of at least four elements in groups without torsion. He also builds an example whose sumset reaches the next size up, proving the gap cannot stretch further. The paper tightens a long-open classification problem.
arxiv-2505-07779:
Li, Zanardi, and Zardini present a fast planner for fleets of moving robots in a 2025 paper. Warehouses need many robots routed at once without crashes. Classic planners work offline and answer slowly. Their method plans one step at a time, looking a short span ahead. Robots first draft solo routes side by side.

Robots whose routes clash are then grouped on the fly, based on clash points and reach. Fixes are worked out within each group while the rest keep moving. On standard maps the method cut time to first action by up to sixty percent. Route quality stayed high across sizes and spans. The authors pitch it for live, busy robot floors.
arxiv-2505-08779:
Patrick Ledwith, Ashvin Vishwanath, and Eslam Khalaf name the missing carriers in twisted bilayer graphene. Their twenty twenty-five paper attacks a puzzle near the filling where superconductivity appears: spectral weight vanishes at the band top, so something unseen must carry the charge.

The authors build on a picture of local moments beside a Mott semimetal. They propose Dirac trions, bound triples of excitations, as the hidden carriers. Heat data showing entropy down to low temperatures fit this view. If trions rule the normal state, the superconductor that grows from it needs a fresh theory. The claim gives experimenters a concrete target to hunt in spectra.
arxiv-2505-09379:
Ali Rida Sahili, Najett Neji, and Hedi Tabia wrote this 2025 survey of systems that turn written text into human motion. A user can type a plain request and get a moving figure, with no need for pre-made motion clips. That ease makes the approach useful for virtual worlds, games, and robots.

Older methods guessed future poses from a short start or from a fixed action label. The survey sorts the newer text-based methods in two ways: by model type, and by how motion is stored, as smooth paths or as discrete steps. The authors also review the main data sets, scoring methods, and test sets that shape the field. They close with the open problems and the paths they see as most hopeful for new work.
arxiv-2505-09479:
Nikolai Chugai offers a scenario for how some giant stars explode just after shedding their outer layers. His 2025 paper centers on SN 2006gy, one of the brightest stellar blasts ever seen. Chugai argues that heavy mass loss in the last ten to twenty years built a dense shell around the star. Heat dumped into the outer layer made the star swell a bit. That small swell let a close companion star sink into the shared outer layer.

Once inside, the pair set up the blast of the stripped core soon after the envelope was lost. The timing explains why the blast lit up so strongly when it hit the shell. Chugai puts the case forward as a path to other very bright blasts of the same kind.
arxiv-2505-09579:
P I Gerevenkov and co-authors map three ways sound and magnetism trade energy in thin magnetic films. Fast acoustic pulses can stir spin waves, the ripples that magnonics hopes to use in low-power devices. Which regime fires depends on how the sound and spin speeds line up.

Using a scanning laser pump-probe method, the team watches both wave types move in a permalloy film and a carved waveguide. At one tuning, sound and spin lock into a joint magneto-elastic packet. Detune them and the sound sheds spin waves in a Cherenkov-like spray. Detune further and the spin system just rides along, forced and non-resonant. Direct speed measures mark each border. Only in the locked regime does the sound pulse itself change shape from the exchange.
arxiv-2505-09679:
Vincenzo Cirigliano, Wouter Dekens, and Sebastian Urrutia Quiroga map where future double beta decay experiments could strike gold. They work inside a standard extension of neutrino physics. The target process emits no neutrinos at all. It can only happen if neutrinos are their own antiparticles. The team studies the three-plus-three seesaw model, which adds three heavy partner neutrinos. They scan right-handed mass scales from feather-light to very heavy. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they fold in constraints from many high- and low-energy experiments, updating several. The outlook appears as likelihood maps linking the decay half-life to neutrino masses.

Their conclusion is optimistic. In this simple model class, current and upcoming experiments hold broad discovery potential. Both orderings of the light neutrino masses are covered. The plots tell experimentalists which half-lives their detectors must reach to test the model.
arxiv-2505-09779:
Hygor Goncalves and co-authors explore how quasars flicker across cosmic time in a 2025 paper. Quasars are brilliant cores of galaxies fed by giant black holes, and their flicker betrays how feeding flows run. Light curves spanning about six years came from a sky survey telescope.

Near a thousand quasars with known masses and brightness fed the study. Brighter quasars flickered less, a trend that grew stronger at greater distances. Mass links flipped sign with distance in a puzzling way. One link held steady throughout: flicker fell as feeding rate rose. The team gives a formula for that near-universal rule.
arxiv-2505-09879:
Yupeng Yang, Xinyi Dai, and Yicheng Wang test whether dark matter density fades off the standard path in a 2025 paper. The standard model says density grows with a fixed cube law as space expands. A small exponent shift captures any drift from that law. Five data types, from sound wave rulers to supernovae, pin the shift down.

The shift lands slightly below zero with tight error bars. That offset sits about two point four sigma from the no interaction case. The authors read it as a hint that dark matter trades energy with vacuum energy. New survey data sharpened the case versus older studies. More data will judge whether the hint hardens into proof.
arxiv-2505-10079:
Deung-Jang Choi, Soo-hyon Phark, Andreas Heinrich, and Nicolas Lorente reviewed in 2025 electron spin resonance inside a scanning tunneling microscope as a platform for identical atomic qubits. The combined tool controls single spins on surfaces with electrical signals, at atomic precision and with energy detail beyond thermal limits.

The review covers how the method works, how single spins are addressed, and how their states are driven and read out through Rabi oscillations and frequency-resolved signals. Atom placement and local field shaping allow multi-qubit designs. Logic gates such as controlled-NOT and Toffoli have been built this way. Molecular qubit systems are a further direction the authors highlight.
arxiv-2505-10279:
Gabriel Palma and four co-authors estimate how many individual viewer profiles hide inside a household television account. Personalized recommendations need that count, yet providers rarely know who is watching at any moment, alone or in a group. Group viewing also needs a principled way to merge profiles, which standard systems lack.

A Gaussian mixture model averaging framework gives point estimates for the profile count. A Bayesian random walk adds uncertainty over time. Real customer data total about half a million viewing observations. Combined with chosen viewing features, the framework recovers profile counts and traits, tracks shifts over time, and quantifies uncertainty. The method supports better group recommendations for shared screens.
arxiv-2505-10479:
Giant eruptions from the Sun, called coronal mass ejections, threaten satellites and power grids, and their speed matters. Kelly Victor-French, Karl Battams, and Brian Wood ask in a 2025 paper whether the glow of the corona above an eruption site hints at that speed. They gathered every mid-to-top-class flare near the Sun's edge from 1996 to 2022, checked which ones launched eruptions, and measured both speeds and corona brightness from a long-running index.

Above a certain brightness, fast eruptions became much less likely. One famous 2014 active region fit the pattern: its unusually bright corona may explain its oddly low eruption output. Brightness, the authors argue, deserves a place in eruption forecasts.
arxiv-2505-10579:
Elodie Germani and co-authors audit large pretrained models for bias and weak generalization in breast imaging, in a 2025 paper. Foundation models learn from huge datasets and transfer well across tasks. In mammography, though, image quality shifts and label noise can teach them shortcuts. Patient traits may leak into their calls.

The team pooled datasets from many sources, including underrepresented regions and their own hospital. Classifiers were trained on the models' features dataset by dataset. Modality-specific pretraining did lift performance. Yet classifiers tuned to one dataset's features stumbled on others. The audit warns that strong average scores can hide unfair, brittle behavior in screening tools.
arxiv-2505-10679:
Jianyang Xie and co-authors ask whether graph networks for action recognition carry too many parameters, in a 2025 paper. The catalog creator field ends with affiliation text, so the head byline governs. These networks read skeleton motion well, yet many rival designs score nearly alike once inputs match, a hint of bloat.

Tests under the lottery ticket idea backed the guess: sparse subnetworks match the full models. Their generator trains a sparse form straight from a random dense start. Even with ninety five percent of weights cut, accuracy fell by under one point on four datasets. Mixing sparsity levels did better still, beating the dense model while using a third fewer weights.
arxiv-2505-11179:
Jan Brezina and Eduard Feireisl studied in 2025 boundary conditions for the compressible magnetohydrodynamics system, the equations for a conducting fluid under magnetic forces. The magnetic field spreads through a varied medium, and the right conditions at the edge of a bounded domain must come from physics, not guesswork.

By penalizing terms tied to transport coefficients and taking several singular limits, they justify a set of physically grounded boundary conditions. They also prove that weak solutions exist for any finite-energy starting data, when the induction equation holds outside the fluid as well. The work offers a sound platform for computer tests on domains with complex boundary shapes.
arxiv-2505-11679:
Zhibo Hu and co-authors tackle ambiguity when language models map text to structured data in this 2025 paper. Vague wording can lead a model to pick the wrong tool call or database query. Past fixes rely on trial and error or on task-specific training.

The team instead studies how ambiguous text sits in the model's latent space. They build a distance measure from a path kernel over concepts, not plain embeddings. Patterns in that space flag a question as ambiguous before mapping starts. A second method predicts the missing concept behind the vagueness. Both parts reached top results on their test tasks.
arxiv-2505-11879:
Reihaneh Yourdkhani, Arash Tavoosian, Navid Asadi Khomami, and Mehdi Tale Masouleh teach a Delta robot to pack catering boxes on its own. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses a two-finger gripper on a three-degree-of-freedom parallel arm. Deep learning drives the seeing and grasping. A custom image set was built for the task, the first centered on Persian-made products.

A YOLOv5 model spots each item. FastSAM then cuts out its outline. The mask yields a spin angle and a rotated box around the item. A geometry trick based on eigenvectors picks two grasp points on that box. All data flow to the arm in real time for calibration and packing. Trials packed full catering sets with a high grasp success rate. The work shows a full pipeline, from photo to packed box.
arxiv-2505-12879:
Yeonsu Kim and four co-authors speed up a method for predicting how random inputs shake a dynamic system. Spline dimensional decomposition breaks a response into smooth pieces joined at knots. Results hinge on where those knots sit, and optimizing them the standard way is expensive.

Their 2025 shortcut reads the knots off interpolated input-output profiles. Within each stretch, the knot goes where the slope is steepest. On a car control arm's vibration analysis, their knots beat uniform and random placements and a Gaussian process rival. The error in predicted spread of the first natural frequency fell to 2.89 percent. All rivals used the same 401 simulations. Larger reliability studies confirmed the method scales.
arxiv-2505-12979:
Hanteng Wang, Xingyu Li, and Chengshu Li propose a way to probe an elusive point in phase-change physics using ladders of Rydberg atoms, in a 2025 paper. At a tricritical point, lines of gentle phase changes end, and its fingerprints have resisted measurement.

The team maps out two- and three-leg atom ladders that host two kinds of tricritical behavior. By slowly sweeping the drive settings, they extract the key exponents along two kinds of paths. At faster sweeps the dynamics drift toward a nearby ordinary critical line, in a pattern they liken to a classic theorem. The plan runs on existing atom simulators, the authors note.
arxiv-2505-13079:
Xugang Lu and three co-authors improve speech recognition by borrowing knowledge from text models in a 2025 paper. A strong language model knows grammar and words, and that knowledge can coach a speech system. The hard part is aligning text features with sound features, since the two live in different shapes.

Older methods lined the two up as loose sets of points, ignoring order. The new method treats each sequence as a graph, with points for features and edges for time order. A combined distance then matches both the points and the wiring between them. Theory shows the older approach is a special case of this one. Tests on Mandarin speech recognition showed clear gains. The authors say respecting structure is what lets knowledge cross from reading to listening.
arxiv-2505-13379:
Gongfan Fang, Xinyin Ma, and Xinchao Wang teach a language model when not to think in a 2025 paper. Reasoning models shine on hard problems by writing long chains of thought. Applying that effort to every query wastes compute, since many questions have short answers.

Their Thinkless framework lets the model pick a short reply or a long reasoning pass per query, guided by two control tokens. A reinforcement learning method splits training into choosing the mode and improving the answer itself. The model learns to spend thought where it pays. Cheaper inference at equal quality is the prize, a real concern as reasoning models scale.
arxiv-2505-13679:
Heather Leitch and Alastair Kay explain a landmark family of quantum error-correcting codes in plain terms. Balanced product codes were the breakthrough that led to good quantum codes, ones that store much information while keeping errors at bay. The original papers are dense, though, and the construction's logic can hide behind abstraction.

This review retells the story with the technical load stripped down wherever possible. It assumes readers know the standard stabilizer language of error correction, then shows how parity-check matrices for these high-density codes are built. The authors aim the piece at researchers who want to actually use the construction, not just admire it. Their hope is to widen the circle of people who can design the next generation of quantum codes.
arxiv-2505-13879:
Eric Johnson and Michael Zingale, two authors writing in 2025, simulate flames on neutron stars. X-ray bursts are runaway burning in a layer of hydrogen and helium on such a star. How the mixed flame spreads, and how hot it runs, depends on the starting mix.

Two-dimensional fluid simulations varied the hydrogen share of the layer. More hydrogen made the flame weaker and slower. Whether a flame formed at all, and whether the base ran away, hinged on the starting model and the reaction network. A second flame lit late in the runs, by a route that depended on the mix.
arxiv-2505-14279:
Jennifer D'Souza, Hamed Babaei Giglou, and Quentin Münch present a framework for grading AI answers to science questions in a 2025 paper. Search engines now answer science queries with large language models, and other models are used as judges of those answers. Judges can be too rosy, a flaw called optimism bias, and their robustness is little tested.

Their open-source framework, YESciEval, grades answers against fine-grained rubrics. It also uses reinforcement learning to train judges that resist the rosy bias. The team releases science question sets across many fields, plus hostile variants made to trip judges up, with scores from several models. The method needs no paid models and no human labels, so it can scale cheaply. The authors frame it as a step toward open, trustworthy grading of science answers.
arxiv-2505-14579:
Sina Tootoonian and Andreas Schaefer ask how a brain can reason with linked guesses about the world. Sense data hint at hidden causes, and those causes often move together. Most models wrongly treat them as free of each other. Wiring every cause to every other would be costly and, in brains, implausible.

Inspired by the smell bulb, they propose sister cells as the bridge. Sister neurons share the same input but wire to local partners in unlike ways. Through those partners, causes sway each other without direct links. Math shows how to build a wanted prior from such wiring, and tests show sharp inference in noise. The prior can even be read back from cell activity.
arxiv-2505-14779:
Sabarish and co-authors present a 2025 study of dark matter clumps that fall into giant black holes. Dark matter spikes near such holes could boost clash signals or drag on merging pairs. The spikes also test how clash-prone dark matter is, since speeds there run high. The team ran the first body-by-body sims of self-clashing spikes around a lone giant hole.

The spike shapes held steady across the sim spans, as math said they should. Inflow onto the hole grew with clash strength in one regime, then leveled in the next. Both matched heat-flow math, and a small rate model caps the work.
arxiv-2505-14879:
Ali Devran Kara studies how an agent can learn to act when it cannot see the full state of its world, in a 2025 paper. Such settings are modeled as partially observed Markov decision processes. Kara pairs them with two shortcuts: values written as simple weighted sums of features, and policies that look back only a fixed stretch of past steps.

First, Kara gives a method to score a fixed policy that uses such short memory, with error bounds tied to how stable the agent's belief filter is. Next, he turns to learning near-best action values with the same setup. Learning needs extra care about how the agent explores, though the care can be eased for clean linear models or for grid-based features.
arxiv-2505-15179:
Chaozheng Wang and co-authors compare two ways to adapt code models for use inside a firm, in a 2025 study. Code completion tools guess the next lines as a programmer types. Code inside a firm uses its own patterns and parts, so a general model needs help to fit that local style.

One way feeds the model matching code at the time of use. The other way trains the model more on the firm's own code. Working with a large tech firm, the team tested both on a vast store of code files. Their study weighs cost, speed, and quality for teams that must pick one path.
arxiv-2505-15279:
Five authors led by Zixiang Ren design a secure radio system that sends data, power, and sensing signals at once. A base station with a huge antenna array sends a private message to one user. At the same time it beams power to small devices and senses a target nearby. Those devices and the target could try to snoop on the private message, so the design must guard it.

The station mixes the message beam with extra beams that carry power, aid sensing, and jam snoops with noise. Only rough place data for the devices and target are known, so the radio links are not known with full care. The team shapes the beams to lift the secret rate while still meeting worst-case needs for sensing and power. The near-field setting, where the user is close to the array, shapes the math.
arxiv-2505-15379:
Raphael Sulzer and co-authors release a large data set for drawing building outlines from sky data. Maps need crisp vector outlines, not just blobs on a photo. Their 2025 set, P3, blends three views of the same ground: laser point clouds from the air, sharp air photos, and hand-checked outline files, drawn from three continents in all.

More than ten billion laser points sit in the set, each pinned to a tight spot, with color photos at fine ground grain. Tests show laser clouds alone can drive good outline guesses. Blending laser and photo views lifts both hit rate and shape quality past each view alone. The set ships free, with code and trained weights for three top tools, so labs can build on one shared base.
arxiv-2505-15479:
Following a star's orbit for billions of years needs an integrator that neither drifts nor dawdles. Alexandre Bougakov, Melaine Saillenfest, and Marc Fouchard borrow a trick from planetary work in this 2025 paper. Planetary codes alternate exact Keplerian glides with small kicks; the authors build the stellar cousin, gliding along exact orbits of a classic solvable potential instead.

That potential, the isochrone, yields formulas for every orbit shape, bound or escaping, which the team derives in full. Split into glide and kick, the scheme stays symplectic, the property that keeps long integrations honest. Tested on stars in a Plummer sphere, the workhorse model of star clusters, the method conserved energy superbly at low cost, in both the dense core and the sparse outskirts. Settings for best efficiency are tabulated for users.
arxiv-2505-15579:
Hossein Zakerinia, Jonathan Scott, and Christoph Lampert present a computing paper from 2025 on learning across devices. In federated learning, phones or clinics train a shared model without pooling their data. Each device's data differs, so each may want a personal version of the model. Past methods needed labeled data on the device to make that personal version.

Their method builds a personal model from unlabeled data in a single forward pass. The personal weights live in a small, low-dimensional space, which keeps data transfer cheap. A new theory result backs the approach with performance promises for unlabeled users. Both labeled and unlabeled users can feed the shared training. Tests on varied data sets showed strong results against rival methods.
arxiv-2505-15879:
Yue Fan and co-authors present GRIT, a method that teaches vision-language models to reason with images, not just words, in a 2025 paper. Most such models write their reasoning as plain text, which can drift away from what the image shows. GRIT has the model point to image regions as it thinks.

Reasoning steps mix sentences with box coordinates that mark the parts of the image being used. Training uses reinforcement learning with rewards for correct answers and proper format, so no hand-labeled reasoning chains are needed. The method is strikingly cheap in data, working with as few as twenty examples. Tests show models trained this way give clearer reasoning that stays tied to the picture.
arxiv-2505-16079:
Connor Mattes, Esha Datta, and Ali Pinar study small patterns inside networks in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Counting tiny sub-networks, like triangles and squares, helps reveal how a network is organized, but raw counts can mislead because dense networks form many patterns by chance alone.

The team derives tighter mathematical bounds on how common these patterns can be, then defines a spread ratio comparing a real network's counts against what is feasible. Their bounds, built with flag algebra methods, shrink the feasible range up to threefold compared with earlier work. Testing eleven real networks, they find social networks sit unusually low in their feasible range, unlike other network types. The tool helps analysts tell which structures come from the data itself rather than from density alone.
arxiv-2505-16279:
Junjie Zheng and co-authors present a framework that dubs movies by reading the picture as well as the script, in a 2025 paper. Current dubbing tools copy a reference voice and sync it to the video. Yet they often miss dubbing style and the difference between dialogue and narration. Cues like a speaker's age or gender also get lost. The new system sends the video through a large vision-language model first.

That reading steers a speech generator, which gets the dubbing type and fine details as guidance. The team also built an annotated movie dubbing dataset carrying exactly those labels. Across benchmarks, scores for sync, speaker match, emotion match, and sound quality improved, with gains up to about 19 percent on emotion similarity.
arxiv-2505-16479:
Yuetong Liu and four co-authors tackle photo cleanup for nights with mixed bad weather. Their 2025 paper addresses rain, snow, and haze tangled with glare after dark. Real nights mix these flaws, yet past work handled one at a time. The team first builds a dataset for the harder task.

AllWeatherNight holds many night images with blended, layered damage. A generator that respects lighting creates the damage. Their ClearNight framework then removes all flaws in one pass. It leans on Retinex-based cues for lit regions and true texture. A weather-aware module picks tools matched to each flaw type. Tests on fake and real photos put ClearNight ahead of rivals.
arxiv-2505-16579:
Siqu Ou and co-authors add drawn drafts to text reasoning for moving space tasks in a 2025 paper. Text-only chains help models think, but they falter when a scene shifts step by step. The team builds a maze test bench to gauge this dynamic spatial skill.

Chains with live drawn drafts laid on the input image beat plain text chains by a clear gap. The authors then wrap the trick in a no-train frame that pairs each text step with its draft. Tests across tasks show steady gains with no fine-tuning, which sets a strong base for this kind of work.
arxiv-2505-16679:
Virtual worlds need to share 3D objects across weak connections, and squeezing a model the usual way falls apart past about tenfold. Jordan Dotzel and co-authors try a different route in this 2025 paper: semantic compression, which stores what an object is rather than its exact geometry.

Their pipeline writes the object down in plain language, then rebuilds a look-alike with modern generative models, guessing back size, pose, and placement. On a large public object set they reached compression above one hundredfold. In that extreme range their method kept quality better than classic tools, a fit for collaborative virtual spaces.
arxiv-2505-16879:
Hannah Sansford and co-authors ask what 'high-dimensional' really means for modern data analysis, in a 2025 paper. Methods that map hidden shapes in data, like topological analysis and manifold learning, often fail or succeed for reasons blamed on dimension. The authors distinguish three different quantities that all get called dimension: total spread across features, complexity across samples, and the true dimension of the hidden structure.

Using a new version of a classic concentration inequality, they show the hidden shape can still be recovered when the data's total spread merely outgrows the logarithm of the sample size. They then revisit a famous neuroscience claim, the ring-like code in grid cells, and show for the first time that the structure mirrors physical space faithfully. Clearer dimension bookkeeping could stop researchers from discarding methods that would have worked.
arxiv-2505-16979:
Zhenkun Li and co-authors present in 2025 a design strategy for multi-agent systems built on large language models, called Know the Ropes. Single agents hit limits in context size and role load. Usual multi-agent fixes bring vague task splits and heavy checking costs. Their method turns domain knowledge into a hierarchy of typed subtasks with controllers.

Each subtask gets the lightest help that works, from plain prompting to small tuning. On a knapsack task, three modest agents jumped from three percent to ninety-five percent accuracy after one bottleneck fix. A six-agent setup solved a harder assignment task fully at moderate sizes.
arxiv-2505-17479:
Olivier Toubia and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a data set for building digital twins of people. Language models can mimic a person's behavior, but real ground truth data are scarce. The team surveyed 2,058 United States participants over four waves. Each person spent about two and a half hours answering 500 questions in all.

The battery covered demographics, psychology, money choices, personality, and thinking tests. Classic behavior games and a pricing survey were replicated inside it. The last wave repeated earlier tasks to set a test-retest yardstick. Early checks suggest the data are sound and twins built on them predict behavior well. The full set is public. Social scientists can also mine it for links across traits.
arxiv-2505-17679:
Giovanni Sisorio, Alberto Cappellaro, and Luca Dell'Anna test whether simpler quantum batteries charge better in a 2025 paper. Quantum batteries store energy in quantum systems, hoping quantum effects beat classical limits. A model called SYK, with dense random links between its parts, entangles strongly and charges fast. Its complexity, though, may be fragile in practice.

The team studied a sparse version of the model, with many links removed. They found that trimming complexity need not hurt. As long as the system's chaos survives, sparser versions can charge with more power, not less. In their results, reducing links amplified the charging power of the battery. The authors frame sparsity as a design lever: less wiring, more efficiency. They place the work where quantum mechanics meets thermodynamics, the science of energy and heat.
arxiv-2505-17779:
Ultrasound scans are cheap and everywhere, but reading them well takes skill, and modern vision-language models have barely been tested on them. Anjie Le and co-authors build U2-BENCH, the first broad benchmark for such models on ultrasound. It holds 7,241 cases from 15 body regions, arranged into eight clinic-style tasks across 50 use settings, from diagnosis and view naming to finding lesions, estimating measures, and writing reports.

The team runs 23 leading models, both open and commercial, general and medical. Models handled whole-image classification well but stumbled on spatial reasoning and on writing clinical text. The authors offer the benchmark, published in 2025, as a shared yardstick to speed progress in a corner of medical imaging that models have largely skipped.
arxiv-2505-17979:
Radoslaw Klimek and Jakub Semczyszyn recheck earlier claims about software that writes logic specifications on its own. Their 2025 conference paper reproduces and extends prior results on automated logical specification for behavioral models, the kind used to verify that software behaves as intended. The team tests how robust, scalable, and repeatable the methods really are.

The main trends from the earlier work held up under reproduction. But the rerun exposed performance irregularities: theorem provers swing in efficiency depending on the shape of the problem they face. That instability matters where verification must run in real time, inside build pipelines or smart editors. The authors suggest self-optimizing solvers that adapt their strategy to the problem at hand. Their study is a reminder that in verification research, the rerun is part of the evidence.
arxiv-2505-18179:
Ata Akbari Asanjan and co-authors pretrain GAIA, a base model for sky dynamics, on fifteen years of global satellite heat images, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model mixes masked rebuilding with label-free self-teaching to learn rich sky patterns. Checks show it learns true air motion, not just day-night cycles.

Gap filling beat a masked-only base across missing data levels. Moved to new tasks, it improved river-of-moisture mapping and storm spotting, with far more early storm catches. Rain guessing stayed on par with the base. Learned traits spread across many feature axes in a tidy, object-like way. Weights and code are shared. Readers get a transferable sky base model.
arxiv-2505-18379:
Ashley Davey and Harry Zheng prove in 2025 that a near policy step method meets for a class of bound chance control tasks. In these tasks the control steers both the drift and the spread of the state. That spread link makes the twin back ward equation hard to grade.

One cost term must be strong bent, while the rest may stay unbent. Forms and bounds for the twin equation let the team show step gains run in a straight line pace. Code that pairs deep nets with plain solvers runs the method at high dims. Test cases match the proof claims.
arxiv-2505-18779:
Broestl and co-authors argue that firms must deliberately steer the viewpoints of their AI assistants in this 2025 paper. Instruction-tuned models now help with thinking work across companies. Their built-in perspectives shape decisions, teamwork, and culture.

Those perspectives come from training data biases and developer tuning goals. The authors frame in-house alignment as a strategic and ethical duty, warning about automation bias and weakened critical thinking. They propose three strategies: a supportive assistant that backs the firm's mission, an adversarial one that stress-tests ideas, and a diverse one that voices many stakeholder views. Each carries trade-offs for manager and peer relationships. The paper analyzes those trade-offs through business ethics.
arxiv-2505-19079:
Wei and co-authors study how non-Hermitian effects change the best possible precision of quantum measurements, in a 2025 paper. The key measure is quantum Fisher information, which sets the ultimate bound on how well a parameter can be estimated. Non-Hermitian systems, which can gain or lose energy, break the rules of standard quantum theory in useful ways.

Using a projected space method and a spectral split, the authors derive a formula for the measure in terms of the state and the generators of the parameter. It recovers the standard result for normal systems and adds the effect of a state norm that changes in time. A single-qubit test system and a symmetry-based system are worked through. A dilation trick that embeds the odd system in a larger normal one confirms the formula. The authors aim at better quantum sensors.
arxiv-2505-19179:
Speech recognition systems stumble on names and rare words unless they are given a bias list, and huge lists slow them down. Xun Gong and co-authors present BR-ASR, a 2025 framework that retrieves the few bias words that matter for each utterance.

The system learns to match speech against bias entries by contrast, pulling likely candidates from lists as large as two hundred thousand entries. A staged training plan tackles confusion between sound-alike words. The retrieved shortlist plugs into many recognizers without retraining them. On a standard speech benchmark, biased word errors fell by nearly half against prior methods. Even at the largest list size, speed stayed high and accuracy barely slipped.
arxiv-2505-19279:
Choudhury and co-authors published this study in 2025. It reports the first use of launched helicon waves to scatter runaway electrons in a fusion device. Runaway electrons can reach extreme energies and threaten the machine. In the DIII-D tokamak, the team fired helicon waves that met the resonance condition for these electrons. After the waves started, the electrons' pitch angles scattered widely.

Light emissions tied to the scattering jumped, while hard X-rays marking the runaway count stopped growing. Energy-resolved readings showed the highest-energy electrons, above about eight million electron volts, dropping below detection. This happened even though the driving electric field stayed strong enough to grow runaways without the waves. The authors see a new lever for capping runaway energy in future fusion reactors.
arxiv-2505-19579:
Zhanpeng Cui and Bo Hou set out a new structure, quasi-triangular Novikov bialgebras, in a 2025 paper. Novikov algebras come up in algebra linked to physics. A bialgebra pairs one of them with a split that fits it well.

The new class is built from solutions of a Novikov form of the Yang-Baxter equation. In each solution, the symmetric parts stay the same. Two key subclasses, triangular and factorizable, are mapped out in full. A factorizable case splits its underlying algebra into pieces. The double of any bialgebra also carries this kind of structure on its own. Cui and Hou also link the factorizable class, one to one, with a family of Rota-Baxter algebras. Lie bialgebras induced in this way take on the same kind of structure, when the stated conditions hold.
arxiv-2505-19679:
A team of researchers reports speech translation systems for three low-resource languages in a paper from 2025. The catalog names five authors while the head byline lists nine, so team framing is used here. The work entered a shared evaluation campaign. Systems translate Bemba and two Arabic dialects into English. Both cascaded pipelines and direct end-to-end models were built. Synthetic data plays a central role throughout.

For one dialect with no real training pairs, synthetic data alone beat the cascade trained on real data. Synthetic speech also lifted Bemba recognition and translation. A distillation trick improved every task tried. Combining systems with risk-based decoding added about one and a half quality points.
arxiv-2505-19779:
Mobina Mansoori and co-authors fine-tuned six giant vision models, built on ordinary photos, to read medical images, in a 2025 paper. Foundation models trained on massive data promise to transfer into fields short on labels. The team adapted recent leaders, from DINOv2 to SAM2, on four public test beds: mammograms, skin lesions, retinal scans for diabetes, and chest X-rays.

Fine-tuning lifted classification across the board, even with limited labeled examples. Three models led the pack. The results say progress in general vision training spills into medicine rather than stopping at its door. Code is public. Clinics with thin data sets gain a running start.
arxiv-2505-19879:
Siyuan Li and co-authors read human likes and dislikes from brain waves in a 2025 study. Judging preference matters for mental health checks and for design work, yet self-reports can mislead. The team showed volunteers mixed images of hats, fruits, snacks, scarves, drinks, and pets while recording scalp signals.

Two signal features carried the preference code. An early wave over the front of the head grew for liked items, marking quick visual attention. A later slow wave grew for both liked and disliked items, marking deeper emotional weighing. The authors combine both waves in a model that estimates how strong a preference runs and in which direction. They suggest uses from brain-computer links to product design.
arxiv-2505-19979:
Capella and three colleagues revisit the classic theory of how excited atoms shed light, asking how tangled the atom and its photon become, in a 2025 paper. The Weisskopf-Wigner framework usually tracks only the light's color, ignoring the atom's own motion.

Here the atom is treated as a moving wave packet with some starting momentum spread. Counting the mixedness of the combined system measures the entanglement between atom and photon. Two rich regimes appear. With tight momentum, the atom's recoil builds the entanglement. With loose momentum, Doppler shifts in the photon's frequency do the work. The authors map the thresholds between the regimes and explain each mechanism physically.
arxiv-2505-20179:
Hawkins, a solo author, argues that quasar light curves show signs of dark matter made of primordial black holes in 2025. Such black holes, if they form a large share of dark matter, would bend light from distant quasars.

A web of caustics from these objects would boost quasar light in a distinct pattern as quasars cross it. Simulations clarify what those crossing features should look like in a light curve. Hawkins compares them with observed curves and finds matching features present. Light curves also show the symmetry expected from lensing but not from most inner quasar changes. The author says lensing fits the data best.
arxiv-2505-20379:
Eliran Sherzer, Yehezkel Resheff, and Miklos Telek present a fitting method for phase type distributions in this 2025 paper. These distributions model waiting and service times and are prized for their tidy math. Often a model must match a set of target averages, called moments, drawn from real data.

Older methods match only a few moments or small models. The authors recast the model in a new form that lets a standard optimizer run freely, with no constraints. On many test targets, the method fit up to 20 moments with models of up to 100 phases, with errors mostly under half a percent. A queueing case study shows the method at work.
arxiv-2505-20579:
Dane Malenfant and Blake A Richards present a 2025 paper on hidden gifts, a credit-assignment puzzle for teams of learning agents. Sometimes one agent's act quietly helps another, who never notices. Standard learning struggles here, because the helped agent cannot tell why things went well, and the helper gets no readable signal either.

Their test world gives each agent a door to unlock for a private reward. A bigger group prize needs every door open, but only one key exists, so agents must drop it for others after use. Help is thus easy to hide. The paper measures how hidden gifts distort learning and what that means for cooperative AI.
arxiv-2505-20779:
Noy Sternlicht and Tom Hope build in 2025 CHIMERA, a knowledge base of science idea blends mined from papers. Human novelty often recombines old concepts in fresh ways. Their base is the first large store of such blends drawn by machine from the literature.

A new extraction task names blend cases inside paper text. Experts marked a training set, and a tuned language model then mined a broad AI corpus. The base also stretches to a biology domain in tests. Blend pattern maps and a hypothesis maker trained on the base show its worth.
arxiv-2505-20979:
Two songs can share a tune while everything else about them differs, and plagiarism checks need ears for the tune alone. Tongyu Lu and four co-authors present MelodySim in a 2025 paper, a model and dataset for measuring how alike two melodies are. Their goal is a tool that flags copied melodic fragments even when the rest of the track has been reworked.

To train it, the team started from a MIDI dataset and made altered copies of each piece. The copies keep the melody but change the dressing: notes split, runs added, tracks dropped, instruments swapped. A user study confirmed the copies still sound like the same tune. The model encodes segments of music and learns, by comparing triples, to pull matching melodies close. It beat rival models at spotting similar fragments, and its output shows where in a pair the match sits.
arxiv-2505-21179:
Dar-Yen Chen and three colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on steering AI image models away from unwanted traits. In diffusion models, this push is called negative guidance. The standard method, classifier-free guidance, works when many steps are taken, but it breaks when steps are cut to a few.

Their method, Normalized Attention Guidance, works inside the model's attention layers instead. It stretches the gap between wanted and unwanted signals, then levels it with a simple norm. No retraining is needed. Tests show it keeps image quality while the standard method fails at low step counts. It also works across varied model designs, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-21479:
Do language models judge right and wrong by outcomes or by duties? Keenan Samway and co-authors test that question in a 2025 paper. Most past work scored only the final judgments of models, not the reasons behind them. The team uses more than six hundred trolley-style dilemmas as probes.

Each model reply's reasoning trace was sorted by a scheme drawn from two classic moral theories. Step-by-step traces leaned toward duty-based reasons, such as rules against harm. Later summaries shifted toward outcome-based reasons, weighing total good. The split matters as models enter health, law, and public roles. Knowing which reasons drive a model helps builders judge when to trust its calls.
arxiv-2505-21779:
Daniel Hauck, Stefan Rex, and Markus Garst propose, in 2025, a simple magnetic setup for building devices that host Majorana states. These exotic states are prized for future quantum computing, but platforms that can create and steer them reliably are scarce. Magnet-superconductor hybrids are a leading idea.

The authors study a magnetic ribbon on a superconductor whose magnetization twists through a full turn across a domain wall. For the right settings, that wall turns the ribbon into a topological wire, with Majorana states pinned at its edges. Because such walls are easy to make and move with current techniques, the design offers a flexible testbed.
arxiv-2505-21879:
Weiting Liu and co-authors present a pretrained symbolic regressor for complex networks in this 2025 paper. Symbolic regression seeks a readable formula behind data, not just a forecast. Networks add many interacting parts, which makes formula hunting slow by hand.

Their model was trained in advance and then applied to fresh problems. It handles plain symbolic tasks, network data, and the recovery of network dynamics laws. Tests spanned physics, biochemistry, ecology, and disease spread. Equation finding ran about three times more efficiently than baseline tools while keeping accuracy. Applied to global outbreak data, it fit well and gave intuitive spread laws.
arxiv-2505-22779:
Mohammad Helal Uddin and Sabur Baidya combine phone motion data with social media posts to judge depression in this 2025 paper. Low mood often shows in how much a person moves and in the tone of what they post. The team wanted a quiet monitoring method that does not intrude on private life.

They recruited thirty-three volunteers and tracked daily activity through phone sensors. Deep learning models named the activity, such as walking or resting, with about ninety-five percent accuracy. A separate model read the tone of each person's Twitter posts with similar accuracy. Nine features from the two streams were compared with weekly depression scores from a standard questionnaire. A support vector machine sorted depression severity with ninety-four percent accuracy, beating two rival models. Several activity features tracked symptom severity closely, which supports phone-based checks as an early warning tool.
arxiv-2505-22879:
Philippe Merle and Fabio Petrillo present KubeDiagrams, a free tool that turns Kubernetes setup files into architecture pictures. Kubernetes runs most modern cloud software, but its text-heavy configuration style leaves developers and operators guessing how the pieces connect. Starting from a study of how real users try to visualize such systems, the authors derived concrete design needs and built the tool around them.

The program reads ordinary manifests, charts, and live cluster descriptions, and draws diagrams that stay faithful to the platform's core concepts. It fits into automated pipelines and can be extended for new object types. Three case studies show teams using the pictures to understand systems faster and argue about design with the whole structure in view. Users praised its automation, clarity, and easy fit with existing habits. The authors offer the tool as a remedy for a daily pain point in cloud operations.
arxiv-2505-22979:
Bengisu Guresti, Chongjie Zhang, and Yevgeniy Vorobeychik tackle a coordination problem in games where players hold private information, in a 2025 paper. With many possible equilibria, a recommender can suggest strategies, but players must gain from joining, reporting honestly, and following the advice. Earlier designs fail for stochastic games when advice must take the form of steady Markov policies.

Their bi-level reinforcement learning method designs the recommender automatically and represents it as a neural network, so it runs fast at play time.
