On repeated and stochastic test games it reached welfare close to cooperative multi-agent baselines while keeping incentives far stronger. The authors present it as a practical route to trustworthy coordination.
arxiv-2505-23179:
Sungjune Park and four co-authors present DIP-R1, a reinforcement learning framework for visual perception in complex scenes, in work from 2025. Large multimodal models read images well in broad terms, but fine detail in crowded real scenes remains hard. DIP-R1 trains a model to inspect a scene in stages before it answers.

Three rule-based rewards guide that process. One rewards a three-step pattern of scene reading, close inspection and decision. One pushes the model to look at regions where it is unsure. One weights precision and recall to improve final choices. Tests on fine-grained detection data show steady gains over baselines and supervised fine-tuning, both in-domain and beyond.
arxiv-2505-23279:
Thea Kozakis and co-authors ask whether ozone can stand in for oxygen in alien skies in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Oxygen is a key sign of life on a planet, but it can be hard to detect directly. Ozone forms from oxygen in starlight, so it might serve as a proxy, though their link is not simple.

The team models Earth-like planets around stars of many types, varying oxygen and nitrous oxide levels. Nitrous oxide matters because it feeds reactions that both destroy and create ozone. Around hot stars, extra nitrous oxide often cuts ozone. Around cooler stars at low oxygen, it can raise ozone instead. The authors warn the proxy needs care, with effects on habitability and future observations.
arxiv-2505-23779: Runbo Li proves in 2025 a number theory claim about large square divisors of primes shifted by a fixed step. For each non-zero whole step, the claim gives primes where the shifted value holds a square factor past a set size bound. The new bound lifts the best past mark by a clear step. Strong sieve tools from Harman's work drive the gain. Short as the note is, it moves a hard counting edge that past work had left in place.
arxiv-2505-24179:
Xiaodong Ji and co-authors speed up the first pass of long-context language model work, where attention cost grows with the square of text length. Their 2025 method, called SALE, skips weak parts of the attention map. Older skipping methods inspect the map too coarsely and lose accuracy.

SALE estimates attention weights finely using four-bit quantized products of queries and keys. A relative score then ranks which pairs matter, and block-sparse math does the rest. A custom chip kernel keeps the added cost near eleven percent of full attention time. No retraining is needed. On long-text tests, speed rose at least three point four times for texts past sixty-four thousand tokens, with quality held.
arxiv-2505-24379:
Xiaoyu Wu, Yifei Pang, Terrance Liu, and Zhiwei Steven Wu show that even the strongest form of machine unlearning can leak the very data it removed. Exact unlearning retrains a language model from scratch without the target data and is treated as the gold standard for privacy. The head title differs slightly from the catalog title, though both name the same study. Their 2025 attack targets a common setup where both the old and new models' outputs stay reachable.

By letting the old model's signals steer the new one, and filtering tokens along the way, the attack pulls out text that mirrors the removed data. Success rates roughly doubled on standard test suites, and the trick also worked on a simulated medical records set. The authors argue that judging unlearning only on the final model is too narrow: access to earlier checkpoints must count as part of the threat.
arxiv-2506-00979:
Changjiang Jiang and co-authors build an explainable benchmark for spotting AI media in 2025. Synthetic images and video now look convincing, yet detectors mostly give a bare real or fake verdict. Existing datasets use simple binary labels that cannot explain a call. Their benchmark, Ivy-Fake, adds rich multi angle annotation at large scale.

The framework aims for step by step reasoning that locates and explains the forgery signs. Fine grained judgment matters where a wrong call can harm trust or safety. The release targets detectors that show their work. Explainable detection could make moderation decisions contestable instead of opaque.
arxiv-2506-01079:
Long Qian and co-authors hunt flat patterns that fold into several boxes at once in this 2025 paper. A polyomino net may fold into more than one non-matching box shape. Finding and counting such shared nets at scale had stumped earlier tools.

Old encodings leaned on global rules like connectivity, which solvers handle poorly. The new approach swaps those for simple local constraints with better spread of deductions. Search size then jumps far past prior records for both finding and counting nets. The team also ruled out three candidate areas for a net shared by three boxes. That result overturns a published conjecture from 2017 about the smallest such area.
arxiv-2506-01279:
Spaces whose points are themselves probability distributions have become a meeting ground for geometry and heat flow. Rong Lei, Xiang-Dong Li, and Yu-Zhao Wang prove entropy formulas on such a space in this 2025 paper. The space is the Wasserstein space over a curved manifold, with a flexible power in its distance. A geodesic flow moves distributions along shortest paths there.

For that flow the team proves an entropy formula and a rigidity result: equality cases are pinned down exactly. They then build a deformation blending heat flow with the geodesic flow, modeled on a classic dynamics equation. On flat and compact spaces the blended flow exists, is unique, and stays smooth. Non-negative curvature yields a further entropy-information formula.
arxiv-2506-01479:
Timothy LaRock and Renaud Lambiotte study what gets lost when group data is flattened into a pairwise map, in a 2025 paper. A hypergraph records group ties: one link can join many points at once. Analysts often squash such data into a table that counts how often each pair of points shares a group. The trouble is that many unlike hypergraphs squash to the same table, so the original cannot be read back.

The pair built a search tool that finds every hypergraph behind a given table. They timed the search and checked how well it runs in parallel. Feeding it tables made from random hypergraphs, they charted when the flattening is ambiguous and when it is safe. Their tools let analysts measure how much group structure a pairwise map hides, before they trust conclusions drawn from it.
arxiv-2506-01679:
Neutrinos annihilating above a black hole's dinner plate can light a jet on their own, simulate Kyohei Kawaguchi, Sho Fujibayashi, and Masaru Shibata in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their models pair a spinning black hole with a hot torus of debris, tracked with full neutrino transport and relativistic fluid physics.

Across most spins and torus masses, colliding neutrinos and antineutrinos deposited enough energy to launch relativistic fireballs. The blasts topped out near the energy of dim short gamma ray bursts, in under two tenths of a second. Too weak for the brightest bursts, the mechanism may explain faint ones and early flashes before the main event.
arxiv-2506-01879:
Wlodek Bryc and co-authors extend formulas for a growth model on a strip using new free-probability tools in this 2025 paper. Last passage percolation tracks the best path through random weights. Confining the grid to a strip gives the model a steady state.

Earlier work found that steady state and integral formulas for its generating functions. The pair of objects introduced here, free Askey-Wilson functionals, widen those formulas. The wider range covers boundary settings that were out of reach before. With them, the full phase diagram of long-run behavior falls out. Probability models of this kind echo traffic, queues, and crystal growth. Exact phase maps help all those fields at once.
arxiv-2506-02279:
Wenzheng Zhang and colleagues published a computer science paper in 2025 introducing a system called ImpRAG. Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a language model with a search step. Usually the search needs a written query from outside the model. ImpRAG instead lets the model signal its own information needs.

The design splits one pretrained model into layer groups with different jobs. Some layers handle retrieval while others handle generation. Both tasks train together and share a single forward pass at run time. Tests covered eight knowledge-heavy tasks with varied formats. Scores improved clearly on tasks the system had not seen before. The authors argue that balancing the two jobs inside one model is the key.
arxiv-2506-02379:
Hideya Watanabe, writing alone in a 2025 paper, classifies the basic building blocks of a family of infinite-dimensional algebras called twisted loop algebras of the second kind. Such algebras are built from a simpler, well-known algebra plus a flip of order at most two. Their smallest faithful views, known as finite-dimensional irreducible representations, were sorted before by a broad theory covering many algebra types.

Watanabe reaches the same sorting by a more direct, elementary route for this family. A plainer proof can be easier to check, teach, and adapt to nearby families. Specialists in algebra will find the full argument and the cases it settles.
arxiv-2506-02479:
Kalyan Nakka and Nitesh Saxena disclose a jailbreak that hides forbidden requests inside hyphen separated bitstreams. Their 2025 paper, BitBypass, tests the safety training of five leading language models. Rather than dressing a request in a clever story, the attack recodes it at the level of bits, a representation the guardrails were never taught to read.

Across the tested systems the camouflage slipped harmful content past alignment more often, and more quietly, than rival published attacks. The authors frame the hole as structural: safety checks patrol the surface text, while meaning survives recoding underneath. The paper carries a reader warning for its examples and aims the result at defenders, arguing alignment must reckon with information itself, not phrasing.
arxiv-2506-02579:
Lorenzo Oghittu and co-authors study, in a 2025 physics paper, how tight confinement can help form weakly bound pairs of unlike atoms at very low temperatures. The pairs join an alkali atom with an alkaline earth atom. Such pairs are a step toward one dimensional gases of molecules, a prized lab system.

When two atoms are held in a narrow tube like trap, their scattering changes at certain settings, called confinement induced resonances. The team models the contact between species with a simple one dimensional strength drawn from the three dimensional case. They pay close attention to traps that hold the two species with unequal squeeze. For a rubidium and strontium mix, they find settings that labs can reach. At those settings, the resonances should let weakly bound molecules form.
arxiv-2506-02679:
Gabriele Digregorio and co-authors present FedBlockParadox, a test bench for federated learning systems that run on blockchains, in a 2025 poster paper. Such systems promise private, resilient training spread across many owners, but researchers lack flexible tools to attack them in a controlled way. The framework models the whole stack.

Users can swap consensus rules, validation schemes, and merging strategies, and dial in a menu of attacks. That makes it possible to stress a design before it meets real adversaries. The code is open source and built for extension. The authors aim it at teams developing secure, decentralized learning for settings where no central server can be trusted.
arxiv-2506-02779:
Joseph Murtagh, Megan Schwamb, and a large team of collaborators wrote a 2025 astronomy paper forecasting how many Centaurs a new sky survey will find. Centaurs are icy bodies orbiting between the giant planets. The Vera Rubin Observatory's ten year Legacy Survey of Space and Time, starting in late 2025, will inventory the solar system with unusual depth and cadence.

Using a survey simulator fed with the best current dynamical models, the team sets the first discovery limits for Centaurs across the survey's decade. They predict the known population will grow seven to twelve fold, reaching roughly twelve hundred to two thousand objects. About half should appear within the first two years. The haul will sharpen models of how these unstable worlds evolve.
arxiv-2506-02879:
Yilong Song and co-authors present a distributed training method for problems where answers must keep a fixed geometric shape, in a paper from 2025. Such set shaped problems appear in data analysis and in hardening neural networks. A recent single machine method avoids costly shape fixing steps, but it was not built for networks of machines.

Their version adds compressed messaging with error feedback, so machines share far less data. Proofs show it still converges, stays on the shape, and speeds up as machines are added, matching methods without compression. The design covers both exact and noisy gradients and extends to block shaped sets. Computer tests supported the theory.
arxiv-2506-03179:
Qi Li, Runpeng Yu, and Xinchao Wang present Vid-SME, the first membership inference attack shaped for video data in large video understanding models. Such models may train on private clips, and proving misuse is an open problem. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Text and image attacks port poorly to video, scale badly with frame counts, and catch few true members at low false alarm rates. Video frames vary in time, and model acts shift with frame count. Vid-SME uses output confidence plus an adaptive entropy gauge, Sharma-Mittal entropy, on the video. Gaps between natural and shifted inputs drive the call.
arxiv-2506-03279:
Santiago Lamata-Otín and co-authors model virus evolution in a 2025 paper on epidemics. Fast-changing viruses dodge immunity by drifting in form, and genome data show their family tree of types forms a web with clustered branches. Older models flattened that web into a simple space, losing its shape.

The team's model lets the web's shape drive both virus spread and population immunity. On synthetic webs, shape alone could flip a virus between steady presence and yearly epidemic waves. Fitted with the web of a real flu strain, the model estimated when new types emerged. The authors argue that epidemic forecasts should build in the true shape of viral family webs, not a smoothed stand-in.
arxiv-2506-03779:
Hachem Kadri and co-authors argue that quantum machine learning should move past simple number-valued kernels. Their 2025 position paper recalls the early excitement around quantum kernels, functions that score similarity using quantum states. Later studies cooled that mood, suggesting little advantage when learning from ordinary classical data.

The authors say the disappointment is partly a framing error. Scalar kernels are too rigid to use what is distinctly quantum, such as entanglement, and the tasks tested were ones classical methods already handle well. They propose operator-valued kernels, which return structured outputs and can express richer dependencies. A small proof of concept shows such kernels exposing structure that scalar versions miss. The paper lays out a roadmap toward harder, structured prediction problems. It asks the field to aim quantum tools where classical ones actually struggle.
arxiv-2506-03879:
Huan Liu and co-authors study a family of quantum states called anisotropic two-qutrit states in this 2025 paper. A qutrit has three basic levels, so a pair of qutrits can hold more linked states than a pair of qubits. The team asks how three key traits behave in these states. Those traits are entanglement, Wigner negativity, and Bell nonlocality.

The authors build the states from a pure state mixed with white noise. They then test each trait with known criteria, using both exact math and numeric work. One main lesson is that strong entanglement does not always mean strong Wigner negativity or strong Bell nonlocality. Size and noise shift each trait in its own way.
arxiv-2506-03979:
Haoxuan Chen and co-authors propose, in a 2025 paper, a cleaner way to solve inverse problems using diffusion models as prior knowledge. Inverse problems ask what hidden cause fits the data seen. Diffusion models capture complex patterns well, so they make strong priors.

Most current methods lean on rough shortcuts inside the sampling process. The authors instead build an ensemble sampler that avoids those approximations. Their route grows out of sequential Monte Carlo ideas, guided by how the prior evolves during diffusion. A derived equation steers the sampling without heuristic patches. Cleaner sampling should mean answers that reflect the model honestly, a real concern when inverse problems drive medical or scientific decisions.
arxiv-2506-04079:
Pedro Henrique Martins and a large team of co-authors report EuroLLM-9B, a language model built from scratch for Europe's languages. Most open models serve the official languages of the European Union poorly. Their 2025 model covers all twenty-four of them, plus eleven more. The report walks through the whole build: how the tokenizer was shaped, what the network looks like, and how training text was gathered and cleaned.

The team stresses data quality filters and training steps tuned for many tongues at once. A model of nine billion parameters is small enough for wide use. They frame the project as public infrastructure for citizens whose languages big labs skip. The report is written so other groups can copy the recipe for their own regions.
arxiv-2506-04179:
Anhao Zhao and co-authors present SkipGPT, a dynamic pruning method for large language models in 2025. Deep models cost a lot to run. Static pruning cuts the same layers for every input, which ignores how tokens differ and how layer types differ in role.

SkipGPT routes tokens with a global view of their import and prunes attention and feed-forward parts under separate policies. A two-stage training plan first learns the routing softly, then restores quality with a light fine-tune. Tests cut over forty percent of parameters while matching or beating the full model on benchmarks. The code is public.
arxiv-2506-04279:
Adama Nouboukpo, Kodzo Michel Aladji, and Muktar Bappa propose new ways to count the effective number of political parties in Africa, in a paper from 2025. The standard index often misses how African party systems truly work. Dominant parties, shifting loyalties, and ethnic and regional splits all blur the count.

Their two new measures stay neutral toward institutions by design. They rest on geography and demography, above all population size and land area. Both keep a floor of two parties. The authors argue the models are simpler and fit local facts better, above all where data is scarce. The approach may also help analysts streamline party systems beyond Africa.
arxiv-2506-04379:
Matthew Shinkle and Mark Lescroart showed in 2025 how a trick for picturing what AI vision models prefer can also picture what brain areas prefer. Neural networks trained on images build features much like the human visual system. The team fit models that predict brain scan responses from network features. Then they turned the usual method around, generating images tuned to excite single spots in the visual cortex.

The generated images matched known tastes of those spots and let the team survey tastes across the cortex. Images tuned for whole regions were then shown to people in a scanner. They reliably drove the targeted areas, low-level and high-level alike, across subjects. The authors say the approach maps and steers visual brain responses without needing a native image generator.
arxiv-2506-04579:
Jianfei Zhang and co-authors improve, in a 2025 paper, how examples are chosen when a language model learns a task from many demonstrations in its prompt. Showing a model dozens of worked examples can beat fine-tuning, but picking them at random wastes the chance. Picking one example at a time does not fit the many-example setting. The authors reason that good demonstrations should teach what training on the full data set would teach.

Their method picks examples whose training gradients match those of the whole task data, using a small model to do the matching. Across nine data sets, the picks beat random choice for much larger models, from a handful of examples up to well over a hundred. Gains held for both open and closed models. The result makes many-shot prompting more reliable in practice.
arxiv-2506-04679:
Raphaël Millière, writing alone, argues that today's alignment of large language models is shallow and breaks under pressure. The 2025 paper grants that fine-tuning on human preferences teaches models to favor helpfulness, honesty, and harmlessness. Attacks succeed, the author contends, by setting those taught norms against each other.

Human moral psychology offers the contrast: people deliberate about clashing norms, which makes them harder to manipulate. Models instead carry fixed behavioral leanings with no real capacity to notice or settle a conflict between them. Newer reasoning-focused models, the author argues, have not closed that gap. The conclusion presses on safety and regulation: preference training alone cannot secure ever stronger systems, so deeper forms of alignment are needed.
arxiv-2506-04879:
Yu-Feng Chen and three co-authors present a hidden trigger attack on image editing models in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models can be steered by patterns planted in their input. Most past attacks used visible marks, which users would notice before editing begins.

Their method hides the trigger inside a digital watermark placed in training images. When the trained model sees a watermarked image, it produces a preset target output. Clean images are edited normally as the prompt asks. Tests across several watermarking models gave strong attack success rates. Analysis of the watermark traits backs up the claim. The authors release code and frame the work as a security warning for editing tools.
arxiv-2506-04979:
Yadong Wang and co-authors report strong light-matter coupling in a tiny layered device, in this 2025 paper. Such mixed states, half light and half matter, may serve in quantum and nonlinear optics. Tiny antennas made of clear, high-index material trap light well, but the trapped light sits inside the antenna, away from outside matter.

The team built antennas from a layered crystal on a gold base, which pushed the trapped light outward. A one-atom-thick sheet placed on top then coupled strongly with the trapped light at room temperature. The mixed states also bent light far more strongly than the sheet alone. The work points to new hybrid devices from layered crystals.
arxiv-2506-05179:
Zoltán Guba, Aris Alexandradinata, and Tomáš Bzdušek extend delicate topology from Bloch states to hybrid Wannier functions. Topological insulators are marked by bulk states that cannot be smoothed into an atomic limit without breaking symmetry or closing the gap. Delicate insulators refine that picture: their edge states are promised only at sharp boundaries.

Their 2025 paper defines delicate Wannier insulators, whose spread-out Wannier orbitals still let the bulk deform to a one-cell atomic limit when no edge is present. Sharp hinges and corners, though, block that smoothing and host boundary states. A layering recipe lifts a delicate model in one dimension count to a Wannier one in the next, shown on three models.
arxiv-2506-05479:
Matei Gabriel Coşa and Marek Eliáš wrote this 2025 theoretical computer science paper on metrical task systems with advice from several predictors. A metrical task system handles a stream of tasks, paying to move between states and to serve each task. In this variant, the algorithm owns a set of heuristics, each tuned to a different kind of input.

The catch is limited access. At each step, the algorithm may ask only one heuristic what it would do. Worse, the cost a heuristic paid at a step cannot be judged unless it was also asked at the step before. The goal is to do nearly as well as the best heuristic in the set. The authors reach regret that grows as the two-thirds power of the best cost. They also prove a matching lower bound, so the rate cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2506-05579:
Shi and co-authors present a 2025 study on whether AI models can actually teach people what they know. Strong benchmark scores may not mean a model explains its reasoning in usable ways. Their framework, KITE, tests knowledge transfer with real people. In a two-phase setup, 118 participants first planned solutions with an AI, then solved problems alone.

Benchmark skill did track joint results, but loosely, with big outliers. Some strong models taught poorly, and some weaker ones taught well. Habits such as clear strategy talk marked the good teachers. The authors release their code and data, urging builders to optimize teaching as its own goal, not a side effect of raw skill.
arxiv-2506-05679:
Binghao Ye and co-authors give spiking neurons a wider voice by letting them fire integer values during training. Their 2025 paper addresses the main weakness of spiking networks: binary spikes carry little information per step, so accuracy trails ordinary networks despite far lower energy use. Their neuron design expands what one spike event can say.

At inference, the integer activity converts back to binary spikes spread over virtual extra steps, keeping the event-driven style. A range alignment step fixes neurons that never reach their high values. On a standard image benchmark the method set a new best for its architecture, and on object detection it also led. Accuracy matched or beat the ordinary network twin, with several-fold energy savings.
arxiv-2506-05979:
Gabriel Loiseau and four co-authors build a shared way to judge tools that hide private facts in text. Hiding names and other details keeps people safe, but it can also strip out facts that later tasks need. Their 2025 work, called Tau-Eval, weighs both sides of that trade-off at once.

The free Python kit scores hiding methods by how well they guard privacy and how well the text still works for later use. Needs differ by task, so the kit tests methods across varied uses rather than one fixed test. Guides, lessons, and code are open to all. The authors hope the kit gives the field a fair base for comparing new tools.
arxiv-2506-06079:
Yixuan Liu and Meichen Guo design controllers from data alone for nonlinear systems that must track a signal amid disturbances. Their paper from 2025 treats output regulation, where the target and the disturbances both come from a known linear generator. No full model of the plant is assumed.

The plan builds a feedback that makes the closed loop gently passive with respect to the tracking error, then links it to an internal model of the generator. The feedback is pinned down by matrix conditions drawn from data, kept apart from the internal model, which saves data and adds design freedom. The same plan settles systems at a nonzero balance point with unknown input. Tests on number cases close the paper.
arxiv-2506-06179:
Self-attention, the engine of transformer models, still lacks a full theory of why it works. Muhammed Ustaomeroglu and Guannan Qu study it as a device for learning interactions between entities, whether agents in a game, genes in a sequence, or words in a text. They show that even one layer of simple linear attention can represent, learn, and generalize functions built on pairwise interactions.

The learning works under mild conditions on how varied the training interactions are, and it extends to cases unlike the training data. Experiments confirm the theory: attention picks up interaction functions and carries them to new distributions. The authors then build two new modules on the insight. One learns couplings between feature-level interactions, and the other reaches beyond pairs to three-way and larger dependencies among entities.
arxiv-2506-06379:
Natalia Gorobey and co-authors place the observer inside quantum cosmology, in a 2025 paper. Quantum cosmology asks for the first state of the universe. The no-boundary proposal gives one famous answer. This work rebuilds that idea with a new least-action method. Watching then enters as extra rules in a small region of spacetime.

Those rules come from laws tied to the symmetries of the theory. Energy and momentum of matter move in a fixed way inside the watched region. Even the shape of that region's edge gains fixed traits. The result is a cosmos whose watched part acts in a classical way by design. Researchers in the foundations of physics gain a new route to the measurement problem.
arxiv-2506-06779:
Mirzaie asks, in 2025, how many sampled points are needed to estimate the curvature of a curve or surface accurately. Point clouds are finite samples drawn from some distribution spread over the shape. Too few points near a spot make local bending impossible to judge.

An algorithm first estimates curvature at a point of a curve from its nearby samples. The method then extends to the Gaussian curvature of surfaces. A key relation ties the number of selected points to the chance that a given point has enough neighbors. That relation lets users control how large the cloud must be before measuring. The work serves scanning and shape analysis.
arxiv-2506-06879:
Agissilaos Athanassoulis, Fotini Karakatsani, and Irene Kyza present a 2025 arXiv paper on a better numerical scheme for the von Neumann equation with power self-interaction. In ocean science the equation is the Alber equation, whose stability flip helps explain rogue waves. Only a first-order time method existed. Their linearly implicit scheme reaches second order while preserving the equation's structure.

Simulations of growing instability matched linear theory early on but showed it cannot predict peak heights or the shapes that form. Monte Carlo runs with random seas found the background state, more than the seed bump, sets the maximum, and strong instability breeds recurring hotspots.
arxiv-2506-07279:
Iris Paparelle and co-authors demonstrate memory control in an optical quantum reservoir computer in this 2025 paper. Reservoir computing suits time-based tasks, but quantum versions with real memory are scarce. Their platform uses multimode squeezed light in a fully continuous-variable setup.

Data enters by shaping the pump's phase in an optical process, and answers are read by selective detection. Feedback through phase modulators gives short-term fading memory, while spatial multiplexing holds longer dependencies. The system handled parity checks and chaotic signal forecasts with little post-processing. A high-fidelity digital twin matched the experiments. The authors say the entangled multimode structure boosts both expressiveness and memory, making a scalable photonic platform.
arxiv-2506-07379:
Bruno Moreira Coimbra and Marco Mambelli present a 2025 arXiv paper on securing access tokens in GlideinWMS, a system that farms out grid computing jobs. The platform moved from certificates to tokens between 2019 and 2022, and wider token use exposed weak spots in how credentials are made, moved, stored, and renewed.

New credential modules sort credentials by type and purpose, with flows for each. Tokens are generated on the fly with tight scope and lifetime, honoring least privilege. Storage, renewal, and invalidation steps were added to the design. The modules are built to serve sibling systems such as HEPCloud as well.
arxiv-2506-07579:
Shinnosuke Hattori and co-authors ask whether large machine-learned models of atomic forces pick up real chemical sense as they grow. Their 2025 paper uses a framework that splits a model's total energy into edge-wise parts, one for each bond. Such models are known to improve in a smooth power-law way with size, but fresh skills at scale were untested.

They probe a network trained on a large set of molecules. Without ever being taught bond strengths, the model had learned values that match published ones for how much energy each bond takes to break. The match held across data sets. An entropy-based read ties how cleanly the energy splits to how well the model scales, which hints at both limits and paths to clearer models.
arxiv-2506-07679:
Yu-Mei Wu, Yan-Chen Bi, and Qing-Guo Huang study pulsar timing in a 2025 physics paper. Arrays of pulsars can sense gravitational waves by their ticking shifts. Many wave sources interfere, which warps the expected pattern between pulsars. The team asks how that plays out if gravity has mass.

Simulations show the warped patterns still fit layered angular expansions. The quadrupole part, the two lobed term, stays dominant throughout. Heavier gravitons make that dominance stronger, not weaker. Interference adds wide scatter around the average pattern, though. A single universe snapshot may not separate massive gravity from Einstein's version. The authors warn that observation time sets a hard floor on any tighter mass bound.
arxiv-2506-07879:
The Belle II group, a large team working at a particle detector, reports a measurement from 2025. They study a decay of a charged D meson into two pions. The key value is a small imbalance between how matter and antimatter versions decay.

Such an imbalance, called CP asymmetry, helps test how nature treats matter and antimatter apart. Even a tiny gap can point to physics beyond the current model. The paper presents the measured value from Belle II data. The long author list in the head reflects the scale of the team behind the detector and the analysis.
arxiv-2506-08079:
Danny Horta and Melissa Ness read the chemical fingerprints of Milky Way star clusters to sort their births, in a 2025 letter. Stars keep the mix of their birth gas in their air. The team splits the alpha elements into two clans: those forged in calm burning and those in explosions. Their ratio, dubbed the hex ratio, tags where a star's cradle sat.

Survey data cover clusters, halo wreckage, dwarf galaxies that orbit us, and the galaxy's own two disks. Clusters and halo streams share high hex ratios across a wide span of iron content, while dwarf galaxies sit lower at the same iron. The ratio drifts with iron everywhere, and weakly with cluster age, but not with cluster mass. Home-born and captured clusters match, a null that cuts against easy labels. The authors read the pattern as a shared early kitchen for the halo's parts.
arxiv-2506-08779:
Dor Shohat and co-authors study how soft disordered materials age when they are pushed back and forth in slow cycles, in a 2025 paper. Such materials, from sand piles to foams, often fail to settle after a change and instead relax ever more slowly. The team cycled three different materials and measured how much energy each cycle wasted. All three showed the same pattern: waste fell off as the logarithm of the cycle count.

The team then tested three models that explain aging at rest. A model of linked two-state elastic bonds in a random network matched all the results, while two simpler models did not. Its success points to slow wandering through a rugged energy landscape. The authors offer cycling as a simple test that can tell competing models of these materials apart.
arxiv-2506-08879:
Krzysztof Pachucki completes a precision calculation of how radiation corrects the nuclear size effects seen in atomic spectra. Atoms feel the nucleus's finite size, its recoil, and its polarizability as tiny energy shifts. At the accuracy modern spectroscopy reaches, radiative corrections to those shifts matter. The calculation covers the relevant order in the fine-structure constant expansion, for all three effects at once.

The payoff is a cross-check between two experimental worlds. The difference of mean square charge radii between deuteron and proton, extracted from ordinary electronic atoms, agrees very well with the value from muonic atoms. That agreement is nontrivial: muonic measurements once fueled a famous proton size puzzle. Complete radiative bookkeeping of this kind is what lets atomic physics testify about nuclear structure with confidence.
arxiv-2506-10179:
In Alzheimer's research, a marker that moves with the disease is not necessarily a driver of it. Hamzah Dabool and Raghad Mustafa build a study around that distinction. They combine correlation analysis with a strong classifier and with explanation tools that show each feature's contribution. Clinical scores, cognitive tests, genes, and biomarkers all enter the mix.

Cognitive measures and known genetic risks dominated the classification. Correlation clusters grouped variables that travel together without proving any of them causes the disease. The explanation values shifted across disease stages, showing which features matter when. The authors frame the work as groundwork for true causal studies. Separating drivers from passengers, they argue, is how early diagnosis and real treatments get built.
arxiv-2506-10579:
Ali Talebi works on a model of disordered magnets known as the mixed p-spin glass model. In these systems, each tiny magnet interacts with many others through links frozen in a random pattern. The classic version counts pairs only, while the p-spin version adds groups of three or more, and the mixed form adds them all.

Talebi sets out to derive the balance equations that describe the system as a whole. The work uses a trick that copies the system many times to average out the disorder. It also finds when the simple, even answer stays stable, and when the copies in one group hold together, at the first step of a more split solution.
arxiv-2506-11179:
Md Mynoddin and co-authors present a stress detector from brain waves in 2025. Stress harms thinking and health, so a non invasive test has clear value. Brain wave records show stress directly, but the signals shift and tangle in complex ways. Their tool, called Brain2Vec, sorts stress states from raw recordings.

The model stacks three parts: layers that catch local patterns, a memory layer for sequence, and an attention step that weighs key moments. It was tested on a known emotion and stress data set. Cleaning steps such as filtering and scaling fed the model steady inputs. Reliable stress reads could aid clinics and workplaces.
arxiv-2506-11379:
Long Li and Liang Ding present faster algorithms for sparse recovery, the task of finding a signal that uses only a few building blocks. Such methods serve statistics, imaging, and signal work. Standard solvers lean on a slow repeating step that can eat heavy compute. Their 2025 paper builds two schemes around a classic matrix factorization method instead.

The classic method alone suits only square-law penalties. The new schemes extend it to stronger sparsity penalties when the sensing operator is diagonal in a suitable basis. For general operators, the team show the factorization route still works as a sound regularizer. In numerical tests, their algorithms ran faster and succeeded more often than the iterative standards.
arxiv-2506-11479:
Max Winkler and Hamdullah Yucel work on steering a system whose edge values act as the control, when input data carry chance. Their 2025 paper treats an elliptic model where the aim is to keep the state near a target on average while the control stays fixed in form. A Galerkin method that builds chance into its base functions does the math.

Error bounds are proved for both the control and the state in mean-square terms. Large linear systems arise, so the authors design warm-start solvers for both free and boxed control cases. Tests on sample problems confirm the bounds and show the solvers run well. The work serves control tasks where noise cannot be ignored, such as heat or flow systems.
arxiv-2506-11779:
Ishtiaque Ahmed and co-authors survey a new way to send data over wireless links: sending the meaning, not every bit. As user counts grow and air space runs short, that shift could save room and guide how networks share it. Their review asks how meaning-based sending can live side by side with the older bit-based kind.

The authors weigh ways for many users to share one channel, and look at systems that mix text, sound, and images. They also turn to satellite links, where saved room matters most and signals face harsh terms. The paper closes with open problems that must be solved before such systems join future 6G networks.
arxiv-2506-11879:
Zhen Qian and co-authors rebuild a global record of forest carbon above ground from 1988 to 2021, in work from 2025. Forests drive much of the global carbon cycle, yet their long term carbon balance is uncertain. Satellite data and deep learning models were joined to make a record that carries its own uncertainty.

Global forests gained carbon overall in the span. But moist tropical and northern forests have drifted toward releasing carbon since the early 2000s. In the Brazilian Amazon, intact forests came to drive most of the year to year swing in losses. Their share passed that of cleared land. The shift ties forest health to the pace of carbon build up in air.
arxiv-2506-12179:
Cunningham and four co-authors measure how fast disordered phases form at grain boundaries in metals, in a paper from 2025. Thin disordered layers at the boundaries between crystals can greatly improve a metal's traits. The team used ultrafast calorimetry, which heats and cools samples at extreme rates, to catch the change as it happens in four aluminum-based alloys.

Microscope work linked the heat signals to phase changes and grain stability. For one alloy they built a time-temperature map and found the critical cooling rate for the disordered-to-ordered switch. After a thousand repeat heat cycles, the structure stayed remarkably stable even near the melting point.
arxiv-2506-12279:
Jan Stenflo, writing alone, argues that a key piece of evidence for dark energy has been misread. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Distant galaxies appear shifted toward red light, and the pattern of that shift with distance is usually fit with a constant term. That term is taken to be Einstein's cosmological constant, the driver of dark energy.

Stenflo says the constant comes from a geometry mix-up instead. Observers measure look-back time, not the proper time used in the standard equations, and the two differ along lines of sight. Adding the term merely enforces that space looks the same in all directions nearby. His reading raises the age of the universe and eases a known clash over its expansion rate.
arxiv-2506-12379:
Zichuan Fu and co-authors merge a shelf of tuned language models into one that can do all their jobs, with no new training. Open models now spawn tuned kin for each tongue and task. Their 2025 method, Hi-Merging, trims and scales weights in two passes: whole-model first, then layer by layer. A lend score steers each pass, so clashes in weights get curbed where they bite.

Tests span pick-one and ask-answer tasks in two tongues. The merged model beats past merge tools in the race. In most cases it also beats a model tuned on all the data at once. Free code ships with the study. The pitch is thrift: one strong model from parts, with no fresh compute bill.
arxiv-2506-12679:
Sacha Greenfield, Archana Kamal, Justin Dressel, and Eli Levenson-Falk give a tutorial on the quantum Zeno effect in two thousand twenty-five. In that effect, watching a quantum system often can freeze its change, like a watched pot that never boils. Watching in other ways can also speed decay up, an effect called anti-Zeno.

The tutorial shows both effects as two faces of one process. A driven two-level system, called a qubit, serves as the teaching case throughout. The authors sort past work by how the watching is done: in bursts or nonstop, with or without reading the result. They close with uses in quantum control and error repair, and with lab routes to build each case.
arxiv-2506-12879:
Frederic Gmeiner, Kaitao Luo, Ye Wang, Kenneth Holstein, and Nikolas Martelaro ask how AI agents could help designers think more reflectively, in a two thousand twenty-five conference paper. Designers using generative AI tools often struggle to state their criteria clearly and stay mentally engaged.

The team proposes metacognitive support agents that counter intent-formulation problems and cognitive offloading. They tested the idea through a Wizard of Oz study with twenty mechanical designers trying several support plans. Backed users made more feasible designs than unsupported users, though plans differed in effect. The paper weighs opportunities and trade-offs for future AI design tools.
arxiv-2506-13479:
Chen, Hoang, Hahn, and Sarfraz argue that a popular way of recycling model parts deserves a pause. Low-rank adapters, small plug-in modules fine-tuned for one task, are often merged or routed into general models when data is scarce. The position paper asks whether such reuse truly composes knowledge or just matches surface patterns.

The authors test two data-free reuse schemes on synthetic two-hop reasoning and math word problems. The merged adapters often fail to combine facts learned in separate training sets, especially facts the base model barely knew. Their theory links the failure to the adapters' limited expressive range. They urge the field to study mechanisms and limits before inventing yet more merging recipes.
arxiv-2506-13579:
Andrew Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 text generation method that can fill gaps of any length at any place in a text. Discrete diffusion models build text in parallel and can look both ways in a sentence, unlike step by step generators. But they could not fill a gap without knowing the true length and place of the missing part in advance. Their model, DDOT, denoises both the words and their positions at once.

A coupling based on optimal transport keeps the word order intact while letting positions and gap length shift as the model works. The method can be added to existing text denoisers without changing their core. On standard infilling benchmarks, DDOT beat plain diffusion baselines. It matched leading non step by step models while training faster and handling prompts more flexibly, the authors report.
arxiv-2506-13779:
Ruoqian Zhu, Dave Love, and Scott Powers measure smooth shooting in twenty twenty-five. Coaches agree smoother free throw motions are better, but smooth was never well defined. The authors ask which part of the motion needs to be smooth. Ball tracking data from an NBA season supplies the evidence.

They fit Bézier curves to the ball path in the side plane. Different ways of computing path curvature were tested against shooting success. Both maximum curvature and terminal curvature were negatively linked to performance. Terminal curvature, the bend near release, explained far more of the gap between players. The advice follows directly: coach the end of the shot, not the start of the forward motion.
arxiv-2506-13979:
Rafal Kalinowski, Monika Pilsniak, and Magdalena Prorok prove, in a 2025 mathematics paper, a sharp bound on the colors needed to break all symmetry in a doubled graph. Start with a simple graph, and replace each edge by arrows in both directions. A coloring of the arrows is distinguishing when no nontrivial symmetry of the graph keeps every color in place.

The coloring must also be proper in a specific sense: consecutive arrows along a path must differ in color. The authors bound the least number of colors for a connected such digraph. The bound sits near twice the square root of the largest vertex degree, and it cannot be improved in general. The same bound is proven tight for a second coloring type, where only single color two step paths are banned. Symmetry breaking colorings show up in chemistry and network design, where telling apart identical looking parts matters.
arxiv-2506-14079:
Matthew Toles, Rattandeep Singh, Isaac Song, and Zhou Yu present FormGym, a test set for computer agents that fill in paper forms from images alone, in a research paper from 2025. The agents get no typed text or page code, only pictures of forms. Filling them demands image reading, fact lookup, and tool use at once.

The set holds 432 fields across 55 documents and three tasks. Baseline agents scored under one percent in most cases, mainly failing to locate the right boxes. The team adds FieldFinder, a tool that points models to where each answer goes. With that help, scores rose sharply, in one case from two to fifty-six percent.
arxiv-2506-14179:
Xiao-Xiao Kou and co-authors run a mock data challenge for a new, far more sensitive hunt for the hum of merged black holes, in a paper from 2025. Most mergers are too faint to hear one by one, yet their sum should form a steady background hum.

Standard cross checks have set only upper bounds so far. A coherent hunt that uses the phase path of each merger can do far better, at high compute cost and with strict demands on error control. The team shows the coherent route works on realistic fake data. That proof clears the way for a real search.
arxiv-2506-14779: Veronica Pasquarella presents course material on homological mirror symmetry, taught at the Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences. Mirror symmetry links two apart views of geometry, and its homological form ties them through category theory. The hosted text gathers the topics her course covers, from first ideas to uses of the theory. Beyond that opening frame, the text states little about scope or level. What stands is a structured course text on a central topic in modern geometry, offered as a guided path into a hard subject.
arxiv-2506-14879:
Csaba Csáki, Teruhiko Kawano, Hitoshi Murayama, and Ofri Telem compute how vacuum energy depends on the angle theta in a cousin of quantum chromodynamics. Their theory can be solved exactly, unlike real QCD. It is a supersymmetric gauge theory, softly broken and coupled to anomaly-mediated supersymmetry breaking, with a clear scale ladder that keeps the analysis sound.

As in ordinary QCD, the vacuum energy shifts with theta and jumps in first-order transitions as different dyons condense. With no flavors, the jump sits at theta equal to pi, as expected. With one, two, or three flavors, the jumps land at fractional values of pi instead. The result sharpens theory about vacuum structure.
arxiv-2506-14979:
Rodrigo Cádiz, Marcelo Loewe, and Renato Zamora ask how heat rewrites the Regge trajectories that organize particle spectra. Their 2025 paper works in a simple cubic field theory. Regge trajectories line up particles by spin and mass, and the team first computes them at zero temperature as a baseline.

The new part extends the calculation to finite temperature, with an analytic formula for the hot trajectories. Resumming thermal ladder diagrams shows how masses on different trajectories evolve as the medium heats. Such results feed the physics of hot matter, from quark-gluon plasma studies to the early universe, where spectra measured cold must be read in a hot world.
arxiv-2506-15279:
Qian Li and colleagues present BCRNet, a system to sharpen landmark detection in laparoscopic liver surgery. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves augmented reality navigation. Such systems align scans with live camera views of the liver. Precise detection of curved anatomical landmarks drives that alignment. Liver surgery through small incisions makes those landmarks hard to spot.

BCRNet refines landmarks by fitting Bezier curves to them. A feature module first extracts rich semantic cues from the image. An adaptive step then proposes curves with confidence scores. A hierarchical step improves those curves stage by stage. The design aims for pixel-level fit to vessel and edge lines. Better landmarks should make surgical overlays steadier and safer.
arxiv-2506-15479:
Artur Oliveira and co-authors let users steer data projections with plain-language prompts, in a 2025 paper. Projection tools flatten rich data into flat maps a person can read. Standard tools follow the raw numbers alone, so meanings a user cares about, but never labeled, stay hidden. Their framework asks a multimodal language model to sort items by the user's stated theme, with no new labels needed.

That zero-shot sorting then bends the map: items the theme joins pull together, and others spread apart. Across several datasets the steered maps split clusters more cleanly than plain ones. Users can re-prompt mid-exploration and watch the map reshape around a fresh question. The authors pitch the method as a shift from push-button charts to a driven, human-led hunt. It suits image and text banks where sense, not just stats, guides the search.
arxiv-2506-15579:
Shubham Agarwal, Sergey Sukhomlinov, Marc Honecker, and Martin Muser reviewed Langevin thermostats in twenty twenty-five. They extend them too. Molecular simulations hold heat steady by a link to an imagined bath. The Langevin equation is the classic way to do this. Good thermostats matter a lot. Crude global controls can distort dynamics in bad ways.

The authors pull past schemes into one place. They derive them in a compact way through asymptotic analysis. That holds the highly accurate Gronbech-Jensen method. They show these thermostats beat global kinetic-energy controls. Two extensions come next. One is a precise thermostat with colored noise. One is a lean thermostat that conserves momentum. The work serves those who simulate soft matter and rheology. In those fields flow and heat control meet. Fakes can look like real physics.
arxiv-2506-15679:
Sparse autoencoders dissect language models into features, and they are supposed to fire rarely. Xiaoqing Sun and co-authors defend the ones that fire all the time. These dense latents look like training accidents. The team shows they are anything but. Dense latents pair up in opposite directions, rebuilding specific axes of the model's inner space. Erasing their subspace stops new dense features from appearing in retrained systems.

The authors sort dense latents into working classes: position trackers, context binders, entropy regulators, and output signals, among others. Across layers, the cast changes from structure early to meaning in the middle to output at the end. Density, they conclude, is a job description, not a defect.
arxiv-2506-15879:
The authors build a prototype system that predicts salaries and groups similar jobs, using a large set of made-up job listings. Real market data is hard to gather, so synthetic data lets them test the full method first. The study asks which features drive pay and job type, and whether similar roles fall into clear clusters. The team stresses that the setup is a proof of method, not a tool ready for real use.

The workflow starts with exploring the data, then builds three kinds of model. Regression models predict salary, classification models predict job titles, and clustering methods group similar listings. Text from the listings is turned into features with standard language tools. The tests reveal which factors matter most for pay and roles, and they show clear job clusters. The authors argue the same framework can transfer to real job market data later.
arxiv-2506-16779:
Games among many players who share one noise source are solved by Yu Si and Jingtao Shi in a 2025 paper. The setting is a linear-quadratic mean field game, where each player's cost depends on the crowd average. Diffusion in the system also depends on states, controls, and that average.

Two routes reach the same answer: a direct method and a fixed-point method. Finite-player analysis yields exact conditions for the shared equilibrium, then feedback forms via matrix equations. As players multiply, the team builds decentralized strategies and proves they stay near-optimal. Identical answers from both routes cross-check the math. Large interacting systems, from energy grids to fleets, use such equilibrium tools.
arxiv-2506-17079:
Uros Sutulovic and three co-authors propose a cleaner way to rebuild the hidden pattern, called an attractor, that a complex system traces over time, in this 2025 paper. Measurements are usually noisy, partial, and short, so standard rebuilding methods often produce distorted copies of the true pattern. The team's tool first scrubs the noise using a device called a homogeneous differentiator, which comes with firm theory behind it.

Tests cover classic chaotic systems, two models of brain cell dynamics, and real brain wave recordings. With several kinds of noise added, the new method produced sharper, truer reconstructions than rival approaches. It also ran far faster, in some cases by orders of magnitude. The authors suggest the tool could become the standard first step for this kind of analysis.
arxiv-2506-17479:
Albani and co-authors propose listening for high-frequency gravitational waves with quartz crystals that ring like tiny bells. A bulk acoustic wave device is a piezoelectric crystal between electrodes, long used to keep frequencies steady. Pressed into service as a resonant antenna, it should strain with passing waves near ten megahertz, a band current detectors miss.

Their 2025 plan runs in two stages: first an array of off-the-shelf crystals in several modes, then custom-built ones tuned for the hunt. Shelf parts already rival running experiments near that band. Custom designs could open frequencies from a tenth to ten megahertz. Target signals include neutron star merger leftovers and dark matter candidates. The project is named BAUSCIA.
arxiv-2506-17579:
Abdullah Zafar, Lei Ni, and six co-authors simulate how magnetic reconnection heats the Sun's lower atmosphere. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, varies plasma beta, the ratio of gas to magnetic pressure. The layers from photosphere to upper chromosphere are partly ionized. Field strength shifts across those layers set the test cases.

Low beta runs spawn more plasmoids, small magnetic islands. Their frequent merging stirs turbulence and squeezes the plasma. That compression heating then dominates. Its power falls steeply as beta rises, with a layer-dependent exponent. At high beta in the low layers, friction from electron-neutral hits takes over. The results sort heating recipes by height.
arxiv-2506-17979:
Kazuhiro Kuwae, Rong Lei, and Ludovico Marini sharpen a result on subharmonic functions in a 2025 paper. The setting is symmetric Dirichlet forms, a general frame for diffusion and heat flow. Earlier theory in this frame required functions to be locally bounded before anything could be said.

That boundedness assumption is now removed entirely from the main results. Subharmonicity is characterized through stochastic processes instead of pointwise bounds. The frame allows forms that are not strongly local, which widens the reach. A parameter shifts the form without breaking the argument at any step. Readers in probability and analysis get cleaner criteria for a class of functions tied to heat flow on rough spaces.
arxiv-2506-18079:
Entangled photon pairs on a chip are the workhorses of quantum light tech, and one platform now lets users dial the exact entangled state. Andreas Maeder, Robert J Chapman, Alessandra Sabatti, Giovanni Finco, Jost Kellner, and Rachel Grange built the circuit in a 2025 paper. Two pair sources sit on thin-film lithium niobate beside programmable interferometers. The chip's pair brightness is high while false coincidences stay low.

The two sources interfered with ninety-nine percent visibility, proving the photons near-identical. Any of the four classic Bell states could be prepared with fidelity above ninety percent. Full state tomography verified the results. The authors pitch the platform as scalable for quantum photonics.
arxiv-2506-18179:
Alberto Pipitone Federico and Misha Verbitsky prove that a certain exotic geometric structure cannot exist on a torus, in a 2025 paper. A hypercomplex manifold carries three complex structures obeying the algebra of quaternions, and with them a unique torsion-free connection, the Obata connection. On a Kähler manifold, a hypercomplex structure that is not of the stronger hyperkähler kind is called exotic, and whether exotic examples exist was open.

For a torus, the pair show the Obata connection of any exotic structure would have to be flat. They then classify all complete flat affine structures on real tori. The classification leaves no room for the exotic case, so exotic hypercomplex structures on tori do not exist. The proof closes a gap in the geometry of quaternionic manifolds by way of affine geometry.
arxiv-2506-18279:
Mihailo Stojnic wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on how a good first guess shapes solvers for a hard reconstruction task. Phase retrieval rebuilds a signal from the size of its waves alone, with all sign information lost. Solvers that step downhill on a cost surface can solve it if they start well.

A companion paper maps a key shape governing what such solvers can do. The flat regions of that shape are where solvers stall. The present paper studies the best starting tools, called spectral initializers, built from the spread of the data itself. It works out how well those starts match the true signal. That match tells whether a solver can bypass the flat regions or falls into them. The unwelcome finding is that the best starts tend to land inside them. A small increase in the share of data shrinks the regions and frees the starts.
arxiv-2506-18379:
Rohit Chawla and co-authors sharpen the maths for systems that bounce off soft barriers. Their 2025 paper studies impact oscillators near a pre-stressed soft stop. The standard shortcut for mapping a path across the impact boundary leans on a linear approximation, and it misjudges impacts close to grazing.

A higher-order map is derived that catches the onset of impacts well. Flight time comes out as a quadratic, so real impacts exist only when its discriminant stays positive. The gap between old and new estimates grows for slow, near-grazing hits. A bench circuit that mimics the oscillator backs the maths with matching behaviour.
arxiv-2506-18479:
Mavis Liang, Blake Hansen, Alejandra Avalos-Pacheco, and Roberta De Vito tutor readers on Bayesian factor methods that merge many studies, in work from twenty twenty-five. Biomedical data now arrive wide, with many measures per sample. Merging studies boosts power and trust versus studying each alone. Factor models compress wide data into a few hidden drivers. Bayesian versions can split shared signals from study-specific noise.

Five advanced models are compared side by side in the tutorial. Two simple benchmarks, pooled and separate fits, anchor the comparison. Wide simulations judge speed and accuracy of loadings and factor counts. A full workflow with R code then works real nutrition and gene data. Readers see each step from raw data to readable patterns. Code and resources are shared openly alongside the tutorial. Applied teams gain a practical map of a complex model family.
arxiv-2506-18879:
Junyan Li and co-authors present CommVQ in a 2025 paper on making large language models cheaper to run. When a model reads a long text, it stores a key-value cache that can fill GPU memory fast. Cutting that cache down without hurting accuracy is a key goal for long-text use.

CommVQ squeezes the cache with a learned codebook that adds simple parts together. The codebook is shaped to work smoothly with the way models mark word position, so decoding stays fast. In tests, the method cut cache size by 87.5 percent at 2-bit storage and beat rival methods. It even allowed 1-bit storage with small loss, letting a mid-size model handle very long texts on one common GPU.
arxiv-2506-19079:
Iosif Tsangko and co-authors probe, in a 2025 paper, whether large vision-language models read emotions from faces by true cues or by shallow proxies like visible teeth. Such models now claim emotion skill with no task training, which raises fairness worries in schools and mental health. The team tested models of varied size on a face data set marked for teeth.

Scores shifted in a steady way when teeth showed versus when they did not. A close look at the best model's own reasoning showed brow position drove much of its judgment. Its inner ratings were highly self-consistent. Still, the proxy habits point to shortcut learning, the authors warn, which can bias sensitive uses. The work urges cue audits before deployment.
arxiv-2506-19179:
Qiaoqiao Ren and Tony Belpaeme study how context shapes the feel of a robot's touch in a 2025 experiment. Feeling is not just a matter of sensing emotion. It is built in the moment, shaped by what is going on around the touch. How a vibration from a robot reads as happy or upset may depend on what the person just saw.

Thirty-two people watched short videos in which a robot was treated in kind, harsh, or neutral ways. After each video, the robot sent a touch signal through a vibrating sleeve on the person's arm. People rated the robot's mood and its intensity from the video, from the touch, and from both together. The study shows how scene and touch combine to color what a robot's signal seems to say.
arxiv-2506-19279:
AI counselors can sound warm while missing where the client actually is in the session. Zhiyang Qi and co-authors fix that blindness with EmoStage in a 2025 paper, a framework that needs no extra training data. Two inference tricks do the work: perspective-taking to infer the psychological state of the client, and phase recognition to locate the counseling stage.

Responses are then generated to fit both the feeling and the phase, avoiding comfort offered too early or advice dropped too late. Experiments in Japanese and Chinese counseling settings improved the reply quality of the base models. The framework performed competitively with systems trained on large counseling corpora. Because it runs on open-source models, the authors note, it also sidesteps the privacy risks of commercial deployment.
arxiv-2506-19779:
Atul Mohan and co-authors report radio range emission from a young red dwarf star, in a 2025 paper. Cool stars shine in this band mainly from hot outer layers, and quiet emission was thought to be plain heat glow. Young red dwarfs are very active, yet their quiet glow was little explored.

The team watched the star AD Leo with a radio array in northern France. Its quiet glow ran up to seven times the heat based forecast. That points to a steady stream of fast electrons adding non-thermal light. They also caught a double humped flare that rose with frequency and flickered in seconds. Such flares hint at repeated bursts of sped up electrons.
arxiv-2506-19979:
Pierre Dehornoy and Ana Rechtman study the motion of geodesics on rounded surfaces in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. A geodesic is the straightest possible path on a curved surface. The flow of all geodesics can be called left-handed when any two steady patterns link with a negative twist. The authors work on spheres of revolution, surfaces spun from a curve. They require the surface's curvature to be pinched within set bounds.

They prove that with the tightest pinching, the geodesic flow is left-handed. For any looser pinching, they build a surface where the flow fails to be left-handed. The split supports a conjecture that the bound they use is the best possible. The paper serves dynamicists who study flows on three-dimensional spaces.
arxiv-2506-20079:
Reza Hadavian and Dmitri Truhachev published a 2025 paper on faster decoding of error-correcting codes. Digital messages are sent with extra structure so receivers can fix errors. One decoding method, ORDEPT, tests likely error patterns in order until a valid message appears, but testing many patterns is slow.

The authors add an early stopping rule based on likelihood, a measure of how well a candidate matches the received signal. Once a candidate falls below a set threshold of difference, decoding ends at once. Error performance stayed the same as before. At the same time, delay and computing cost fell several-fold compared with leading methods. The gain matters for fast, low-power communication devices.
arxiv-2506-20179:
Enzhe Zhao and four co-authors propose a new pansharpening method in two thousand twenty-five. Pansharpening fuses sharp gray images with color images to make crisp color views. Training truth is faked by a standard protocol that shrinks images. That trick rests on a flawed guess about how real blur works.

Models trained that way trade skill between shrunk and full size tests. The team's module learns the true blur by looping two sub nets. One aligns, the other degrades, and they teach each other. A second part adds fine detail through a diffusion frame. Tests beat the best past methods on sharpness and quality.
arxiv-2506-20679:
Sílvia de Sojo and co-authors give mobility research a validated yardstick for its most basic question: where does this phone live and work? Smartphone traces power studies of commuting and jobs, yet home and work detection is usually hand-rolled per data set. Their open-source library, HoWDe, standardizes the step.

The pipeline is modular and transparent, built to survive missing data, uneven sampling, and sparse users, with a few readable knobs to tune. Against ground truth for over five thousand people in sixty-eight countries, it found homes with up to ninety-seven percent accuracy and workplaces up to eighty-eight. The team also shows how settings ripple into job and commuting estimates, arguing that shared standards make mobility science comparable.
arxiv-2506-20879:
Shubhankar Borse and co-authors built a benchmark for testing how well image generators handle pictures with several people in them in a 2025 paper. Keeping each person's face recognizable while they perform actions is a known weak point, and no shared test existed. The new set, MultiHuman-Testbench, contains 1,800 prompts ranging from simple to complex actions.

The prompts are matched with 5,550 face photos chosen for balance across age, background, and gender, plus pose images picked by people to fit each prompt. Scoring covers face count, identity match, prompt fit, and action detection. The team tested many models, with and without extra layout guidance, and found that isolating regions with segmentation and careful matching lifted identity scores a lot.
arxiv-2506-20979:
Weichen Dai and co-authors build scene maps that own up to the camera's own light flaws, in a study from 2025. Pics from sundry eyes bear bends of light: dim rims, hue casts, and more. A scene build that trusts raw pics bakes those flaws in as if they were walls and goods.

Their form learns two maps at once: the scene's glow field and the camera's light law, in and out. A depth rein keeps the scene from soak up light junk as form. The pair then trains as one, so each map stays in its lane. Builds came out clean where past builds smeared the flaws. A full map, they pitch, holds the eye as well as the seen.
arxiv-2506-21279:
Houssam El Mrabet Haje and co-authors report striking optical behavior in a two-dimensional ferrielectric crystal in a 2025 paper. The material, CuInP2S6, belongs to a family prized for holding electric polarization in sheets only atoms thick. Such materials are now drawing interest for electro-optic devices, where voltage steers light.

The team found that the crystal's refractive index shifts with thickness far beyond the ultrathin limit, by nearly a quarter, even at room temperature. In blue and ultraviolet light it also shows the largest birefringence known for any material in that range. The authors tie these effects to the mobile copper ions that carry the polarization. Electrically steering the optics could serve future photonic chips.
arxiv-2506-21579:
Recommender systems learn tastes from clicks, encoding people and products as bare ID numbers, and the numbers know nothing outside their home platform. Yingzhi He and co-authors give those embeddings a language education in a 2025 paper: LLM2Rec, a sequential recommendation model built from a large language model.

Training runs in two stages. First, collaborative supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to infer item relationships from histories of user behavior. Then an embedding stage reshapes it into a producer of structured item vectors that carry both meaning and collaborative signal, what similar users actually chose. Pure text methods generalize but miss that signal; pure ID methods trap it at home. Experiments on real datasets test the blend in and out of domain. The authors argue the ideal embedding marries semantics to the wisdom of crowds.
arxiv-2506-22079:
Rijken works out how a nucleon and a quark trade a bound quark pair, a particle knot called a diquark. Such trades shape the force between nuclear matter and quark matter where the two mix, as deep inside dead stars. The note builds the math carrier for the pair's exchange from scratch. It follows the same steps textbooks use for a kindred problem.

One sign in the result flips compared with quark-antiquark exchange. The flip traces to a loop term that appears in the older case but not here. Color charge adds its own factor to the carrier. Used on a quark-nucleon swap, the carrier gives a pushing-away force. That force already serves in models of mixed nuclear and quark matter.
arxiv-2506-22179:
Wenhan Wu and co-authors teach a model to recognize body movements it has never been shown, in a 2025 paper. Zero-shot action recognition from skeleton data asks a system to name new actions. It matches joint movements to written descriptions. Similar actions, like drinking water and brushing teeth, are easy to confuse. The fine hand motions live in details earlier systems ignored.

Their model splits movement into high and low frequency parts to enrich what the skeleton conveys. It aligns descriptions at both local and global levels. A calibrated loss lets clear examples offset ambiguous ones. On standard benchmarks the approach separated look-alike action clusters more reliably. Such systems could label new activities in sports or rehabilitation without fresh training data.
arxiv-2506-22279:
Ritwik Das and Indra Dasgupta model magnetism in a layered compound in this 2025 paper. The compound, OsCl3, arranges its metal atoms in a honeycomb pattern. Such materials may host a rare state called a Kitaev spin liquid. Real materials also carry other magnetic forces that can spoil that state. The team wanted the full set of forces for this compound.

They pulled basic inputs from standard electronic calculations. Then they solved a detailed two-site model exactly to extract the magnetic couplings. Scanning the strength of electron repulsion showed how each coupling shifts. For chosen values, the ground state came out as a zigzag antiferromagnet, matching earlier results. Their route is cheaper than older energy-mapping methods.
arxiv-2506-22479:
Krisanu Sarkar introduces Hindsight-Guided Momentum, a first-order optimizer that adapts learning rates from the directional consistency of recent updates. The 2025 paper argues that standard adaptive methods use only gradient magnitude and miss geometric cues.

Methods such as Adam and RMSprop adapt from how large gradients are. Directional information, like the alignment between the current gradient and past updates, reflects curvature and path consistency. Hindsight-Guided Momentum measures the cosine similarity between the current gradient and accumulated momentum. It raises the learning rate when updates align and lowers it amid oscillation or noise. The result should converge faster in smooth regions of the loss surface.
arxiv-2506-22579:
Armin Abdolmohammadi, Navid Mojahed, Shima Nazari, and Bahram Ravani estimate digging forces for wheel loaders in a 2025 paper. Autonomous digging needs good force prediction, but gathering data for every soil type is costly and slow. Their method learns the soil on the fly, using force measures from the bucket load just completed.

A physics-based model of how tools move soil sits at the core. A staged fitting process finds the soil traits that match the last cycle, then predicts forces for the next one. Tests in a detailed simulator, across soil types and digging paths, gave errors between ten and fifteen percent. The cycle-by-cycle update could support online control and path planning without large training data sets.
arxiv-2506-22679:
Raut and four co-authors test whether large language models can spot micro-behaviors in team talk. Their 2025 paper uses transcripts from simulated space missions. Such small acts, like discouraging speech, shape how crews work. The team asks whether models can flag each turn of talk.

Several setups were tried, from zero-shot use to fine-tuning on labeled turns. Smaller encoder models missed the rare acts even when weighted. A fine-tuned Llama model did best, reaching mid-range scores. The authors argue such tools could aid crew training. They also warn that rare but key acts stay hard to catch.
arxiv-2506-22779:
Chen, Yan, and Yao blend physics laws with neural networks to model change over time. Many data sets evolve under partial differential equations set by known laws. Those laws miss small-scale effects that science has not yet pinned down. Their SemiPDE model pairs a law-based part with a flexible learned part. The law part keeps the model stable and clear to read.

A deep profiling M-estimation method fits the two parts in split steps. It leans on numeric solvers for the law part and networks for the rest. The team proves the first inference theory for this kind of deep fit. Tests on fake and real data back the theory. The method also helps name the real forces that drive the data.
arxiv-2506-22879:
Jiawei Shen and Yang Jie prove a boundedness result in a 2025 analysis paper. They study an oscillatory singular integral operator built with commutators of a special Calderón type, where a polynomial phase makes the kernel wiggle fast. Such operators sit at the heart of harmonic analysis.

Under stated conditions on the kernel, including a vanishing moment and a smoothness rule, they show the operator stays bounded on the standard power spaces of functions. The bound is uniform, not depending on the fine details. The result improves and extends earlier work on this operator family, the authors note.
arxiv-2506-22979:
Liu, Shen, Zhou, Sonke, and Gavves tune the class templates of vision-language models with odds in mind, for pixel labeling from a few shots, in work from twenty twenty-five. The task adds new classes from a few example shots, while base classes stay sharp. Fixed, one-value templates bend poorly to new shots that swing a lot, when labels are scarce. Their FewCLIP frame tunes CLIP templates with a sense of doubt built in.

Frozen text templates are honed by visual templates that learn. A rule keeps the spread of tuned templates in shape, so they do not just memorize the few shots. That shaped doubt helps the model carry to fresh swings in new classes. On the PASCAL and COCO sets, FewCLIP beats the best past scores by a clear gap. The gains hold when classes are added one by one, and on the plain splits.
arxiv-2506-23279:
Yuncheng You introduces a new notion of approximate synchronization for Hopfield neural networks linked by memristors, in work from 2025. A memristor is a device whose resistance remembers past current. Exact synchronization is a hallmark difference between artificial and biological networks, blocked by drifting weights and mismatched activations.
