The study asks whether the neurons can instead be brought within any small prescribed gap of each other.

You proves that the dynamics of the network are robustly dissipative, and he finds a sharp ultimate bound on how far the states can spread. From uniform estimates on the equations for gaps between neurons, he shows the near-match holds at an exponential rate. The key condition is an explicit threshold on the coupling strength between neurons. The result extends to networks with Hebbian learning rules, which widens its reach for unsupervised training.
arxiv-2506-23479:
Zhaojie Zeng, Yuesong Wang, Chao Yang, Tao Guan, and Lili Ju present a computing paper from 2025 on storing images. One way stores an image as a set of soft blobs that blend to form the picture. Older blob methods train slowly and use the same blob count for every image.

Their method uses a network to sketch the blobs at once, then fine-tunes in a few steps. It also sets the blob count by how complex the image is. Busy images get more blobs; plain ones get fewer. On two public test sets, the method matched or beat the older blob method in picture quality. It did so with far fewer steps and training time cut by up to ten times. The authors say the method is ready for wider use.
arxiv-2506-23579:
Ulrich Abel, Ana Maria Acu, Margareta Heilmann and Ioan Raşa study what happens when positive linear operators are composed. Their focus is on Bernstein-Durrmeyer operators and Szász-Mirakjan-Durrmeyer operators, and on the kernel functions that arise when such operators are applied one after another.

For Bernstein-Durrmeyer operators, they prove new identities for the kernel from composing two and three operators, and commutativity follows in a natural way. Using the eigenstructure of one operator, they write its repeated iterates as a linear combination of related operators. They also treat composition for the Szász-Mirakjan-Durrmeyer family and revisit a known result with a basic, direct proof.
arxiv-2506-23679:
David Demitri Africa and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how a small transformer learns modular exponentiation, a core operation in number theory and code making. They train the model and then probe its insides to see what it has learned. Tools include sampling design, pattern maps of its codes, and patching parts of its activity.

Training on reciprocal pairs brought sudden jumps in skill across related moduli. The jumps look like grokking, where a model abruptly grasps a shared rule. A small group of attention heads in the last layer proved enough for full skill on plain exponentiation. The authors say transformers build special circuits for this math, a step toward clearer and leaner models.
arxiv-2506-23779:
Maxime Massoudzadegan and a large team of co-authors report transport measurements in extreme magnetic fields in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Pulsed fields beyond one hundred tesla open new physics, but they destroy samples and sensors alike. Precise electrical measurements in such blasts were out of reach.

The team built a microwave technique for two-point measurements in semi-destructive pulses up to one hundred twenty-five tesla, at temperatures down to one point five kelvin. They tested it on several materials. Alongside a metal-insulator transition in indium arsenide, they report the first quantum oscillation signals in tungsten ditelluride above one hundred tesla. The setup pushes high-field condensed matter work into fresh territory.
arxiv-2507-00079:
Ethan Smyth and Alessandro Suglia present VoyagerVision in 2025, a multimodal agent that builds structures in Minecraft with its eyes open. Open ended learning agents pick their own tasks, a path eyed for general intelligence, and new language models can now read images as well as text. Earlier agents parsed the game world through pixels in limited ways.

Building on a known text driven Minecraft agent, VoyagerVision feeds screenshots back to the model as visual feedback while it builds. Over dozens of system rounds it created several unique structures on average, a feat its text only base could not do at all. In set building tests on flat worlds it succeeded in half its tries, with failures clustering on harder structures. The authors argue that adding sight widens the range of tasks an open ended agent can master.
arxiv-2507-00179: Tinghao Huang studies averages of twisted L-values in this 2025 number theory paper. The work takes a holomorphic cusp form and twists its central L-value by quadratic characters. It does the same for the derivative tied to a second, distinct cusp form. Huang proves, with no extra assumptions, an asymptotic formula for the product of the two quantities. The result builds on three earlier papers on moments of such twisted values and their derivatives, which it extends.
arxiv-2507-00479:
Sixiao Zhang and co-authors attack the data shortage that hobbles chat-based shopping assistants. These systems, called conversational recommenders, learn what a user wants from dialogue and suggest items. They struggle twice over: chat language varies wildly, and most items in their knowledge graphs are barely seen during training.

Their framework, DACRS, works on both problems at once. One module rewrites and enriches dialogues in two stages so the model handles varied wording. A second module strengthens item representations by swapping in related items from the knowledge graph and tying similar items closer together. A third module blends the dialogue with the items mentioned in it, guided by attention, to capture both stated and hidden tastes. On two public benchmarks, the system beat the best current rivals by a clear margin. The authors say treating sparse dialogue and sparse items together, rather than separately, is the key advance.
arxiv-2507-00779:
Fernanda Oliveira and co-authors tested a dark energy model in two thousand twenty-five. The model lets dark energy change strength over cosmic time. Fresh survey data seemed to favor it over a constant version. That support came from smooth, large-scale measures of expansion. The team asked whether it also fits the clumpy universe. Clumpiness is gauged by how strongly matter groups together.

They used a fresh set of clumpiness measures across cosmic ages. A flexible curve rebuilt the pattern directly from the data. Both candidate models were compared against that pattern. Best-fit values came from major sky survey results. The changing model faced a stricter test on this ground. Such checks matter because a winning model must fit both faces. Expansion history alone cannot settle the dark energy debate.
arxiv-2507-01379:
Miguel Yulo Asuncion and co-authors map the spacetime of spinning black holes in an alternative theory of gravity in a 2025 paper. Weyl conformal gravity changes the rules, so its rotating vacuum solution need not mirror Einstein's Kerr hole. The team charted the causal structure and ergoregions across the solution's parameter space for positive mass.

Comparisons with Kerr and its cosmological cousins show where the conformal version rhymes and departs. Extreme limits for horizons and ergosurfaces were derived explicitly. At those limits, horizon surface gravity and Hawking temperature both vanish, matching the classical pattern. The analysis gives relativists a reference map for testing whether nature's spinning holes follow Einstein or a conformal rival.
arxiv-2507-01579:
Jethro Browell and co-authors report a 2024 competition that asked teams to forecast and trade wind and solar power in Britain, in a 2025 paper. Teams handled a portfolio of farms rated at 3.6 gigawatts over three months. Each day they filed real forecasts and market bids for the day ahead, mimicking live operations.

Prizes covered forecast accuracy, trading revenue, and combined rank. Popular tree-boosting methods again proved hard to beat for day-ahead forecasts, though other approaches scored well and details of setup mattered most. Trading results showed forecast skill alone does not set earnings; strategy counts too. All data, from weather to bids, are shared openly for benchmarking and further study.
arxiv-2507-01679:
Zeyu Huang and co-authors blend two fine tuning styles for language models in a 2025 paper. Supervised tuning copies demonstrations faithfully but can generalize badly, like rote cloning. Reinforcement tuning explores and can soar, yet it drifts into odd behavior and leans on the starting policy.

Their Prefix-RFT stitches the two: training begins from demonstration prefixes, then lets exploration take over. On math reasoning problems the hybrid beat either method alone and also beat schemes that simply mix policies in parallel. Follow up tests showed the recipe tolerates swings in demonstration quality and quantity. The authors read the result as proof the two styles complete rather than compete with each other.
arxiv-2507-01879:
Pouneh Safarzadeh Ilkhchi, Amin Rezaei Akbarieh, and Ali Seraj study lasting ripples in a tachyon gravity theory in this 2025 paper. Gravitational memory is the permanent shift left in spacetime after a wave passes. A tachyon field, moving in theory faster than light, is here coupled to gravity in a nonstandard way.

The team sets the model in two frames and tracks fields far from the source. The tachyon adds a breathing mode to the radiation. That mode changes the mass loss formula and marks the displacement memory. They also derive the soft factors for gentle graviton and scalar emission. The work tests how exotic fields would sign their names in wave data.
arxiv-2507-01979:
Nelson-Archer and co-authors forecast job market shifts with a multi-scale deep learning model in a 2025 paper. Their data come from the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics: employment levels, wages, turnover, and openings across industries. Reading both fast wiggles and slow trends is the challenge such a model must meet.

The network outputs seven-day employment forecasts plus a health index for each industry that a human can read. It beat baseline models in most sectors, doing best in stable industries. Its health rankings lined up well with how volatile industries actually were. The authors review where errors cluster by sector and what would improve interpretation and reach.
arxiv-2507-02179:
Zheng Zhang, writing alone in 2025, swaps neural nets for plain polynomials to mimic the cosmos math. Simulators that map sky laws to the sky's glow are slow, so stands-in, called emulators, do the fast runs. Nets do it well but hide their math and cost much to train.

His tool, MomentEmu, projects sim data on polynomial bases through moment grids, which yields plain text forms. Cost to train is near nil, runs take a blink, and the form can be read. Two sky tools were built: one maps six laws to the glow's full spread, true to under one percent; one maps both ways twixt laws and the glow's peak traits. For smooth maps of mid span, the team pitch is a light, clear swap for black-box nets.
arxiv-2507-02679:
Gender bias in language hides in more than job titles. Ahmed Sabir and Rajesh Sharma build tools to find it in the verbs and objects around the titles too. Their dataset, GenderLexicon, catalogs these contextual cues. A scoring framework then estimates how strongly a passage leans, and can say why. That interpretability matters: a bias score without reasons is hard to act on.

Tests across five datasets, including one in Japanese, confirm biases well beyond occupational stereotypes. Actions and objects carry gendered expectations of their own. The authors aim their work at builders of language systems, who need to find bias before their users do. A lens that reads context, not just titles, sees more of the problem.
arxiv-2507-02779:
Ryan Doran and Thomas Bland model spinning vortices in a dipolar quantum gas in this 2025 paper. The gas is a Bose-Einstein condensate, matter cooled until it acts as one wave. Its atoms pull on each other over long range, which twists how vortices move.

The pair derive an exact formula for a vortex's phase that captures those sideways pulls. On that base they build a point vortex model, tracking vortices as moving points with both flow and dipole forces. The lean model matches full simulations: bent orbits, uneven speeds, and directional drift all appear. It opens cheap analytic study of turbulence in such gases.
arxiv-2507-02879:
Naimahmed Nesaragi and co-authors present Biaxialformer, an EEG decoder for predicting patient outcomes, in this 2025 paper. Brain wave readings mix time patterns inside each channel with links across channels. Transformer models that treat channels independently miss those links. Outcome prediction after brain injury needs both kinds of structure.

Their two stage attention reads time first and space second, then joins them. Joint positional codes preserve time and place together. That design fights the forgetting of cross channel ties seen in simpler models. A tokenization step packages the signal for the transformer. The framework targets neurological outcome prediction as its test task. Better decoders could sharpen prognosis in intensive care.
arxiv-2507-03079:
Shahar Hod proves a floor on how far charged matter clouds must stretch around spinning black holes. Such clouds are neat fields of charged bits that can rest, bound, near a charged and spinning hole. His 2025 work uses pure math, with no runs on a computer.

The proof sets a neat bound: the cloud's true length, scaled by the hole's mass, must top a fixed log value. The bound holds for all spin and charge mixes a Kerr-Newman hole can take. It also holds for all charge, mass, and wave shapes of the field itself. Hod calls it a no-short-hair rule for these clouds. The neatness of the bound, one clean number for all cases, is part of its draw.
arxiv-2507-03279:
Five authors present Conformal Information Pursuit in 2025, a guide for step-wise asks by language models. In chat tasks the model must ask for facts one by one, and few asks is the aim. A gain-greedy path needs true doubt grades, which model scores give in bent form.

Their path reads doubt from sure-set size at each step, a score free of shape needs. On a 20-ask game the path wins more and asks less than past paths. On a doctor chat set it ties one-shot calls while it shows its work.
arxiv-2507-03379:
Alberti and co-authors revisit fears that a classic imaging problem is plagued by false solutions. The Calderón problem asks for inner conductivity from boundary measures, usually attacked by least squares fitting, which was thought to swarm with bad local minima. Their 2025 paper tests that belief for ring shaped, piecewise constant conductivities.

For two unknown values and noiseless data, they prove no spurious critical points exist at all. A partial proof covers the general case under a condition computers can check. They also build a practical version of a newer convexification method and test it head to head. Plain least squares solvers beat it, ran faster, and needed fewer measurements, the team reports.
arxiv-2507-03479:
Alexander Frummet and co-authors make the case for explainable search in auditing. Their 2025 paper notes that chat assistants can give false or made-up sources, which is risky in fields like medicine and finance. Explainable retrieval aims to make search results clear enough that a user can judge them.

Auditing is the authors' test field, since auditors face long, complex search tasks with high stakes for error. The paper sets out why plain chat help is not enough for that work. It then maps the main challenges for building search tools that show their grounds. Last, it names future research paths that could make such tools fit for audit practice.
arxiv-2507-03579:
Assigning workers to tasks as a business runs, hour by hour, is a choice that shifts with each new state of play. Riccardo Lo Bianco and three co-authors take on a snag in how learning methods see that choice in 2025. A model must be fed the state and the options in a form it can read, yet traits can take endless values.

Their answer casts the whole problem as a graph. Tasks, workers, and their traits sit as nodes and links in one chart. They also give a way to turn a standard business process chart into that graph. Last, they adapt a learning method to run on the graph form. The frame claims no home turf: any dynamic assignment task that fits the graph can use it.
arxiv-2507-03679:
Luhman, writing solo, reclassifies two hundred candidate objects in the Orion Nebula Cluster with space telescope spectra, in a 2025 paper. Archival near infrared spectra from JWST let Luhman test which sources truly belong to the young cluster and how cool they are. Fifty three look like members, and twenty four of those are cool enough to count as brown dwarfs.

Seven targets had been announced as Jupiter mass binary objects, a sensation. Every one reads as a background source instead, not a cluster brown dwarf. The verdict matches Luhman's earlier study of the cluster's colors from telescope photos.
arxiv-2507-03779:
Jiaqi Zhang, Juntuo Wang, Zhixin Sun, John Zou, and Randall Balestriero published a 2025 paper on training a large vision model faster and more robustly. DINOv2 is a foundation model that learns from images without labels, but retraining it is very costly. That cost blocks work on private data or new kinds of images.

Their method, FastDINOv2, shows the model blurred, low-detail images first and sharper ones later, a schedule based on image frequency. A noise-based augmentation is added along the way. Training time fell by a factor of 1.6 and computing cost by 2.25, while accuracy on standard tests stayed competitive. Robustness to corrupted images matched the original model. The code is public for others to use.
arxiv-2507-04079:
Goswami and Saini test a modified theory of gravity against the way cosmic structure actually grew, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Their theory couples matter and geometry directly, through a function of both the curvature and the matter content. Such coupling changes how density ripples amplify into galaxies. The authors derive the growth equation and compute the growth-rate observable that galaxy surveys measure from distorted redshift maps.

Fresh data from big surveys supplied the comparison. The standard cosmological model stayed broadly consistent, but the modified theory could absorb small deviations that the standard one cannot, hinting at relief for known tensions in structure measurements. The authors close with what the next survey generation, including Euclid and the Rubin observatory's programme, could settle. Growth, they argue, is where modified gravity must prove itself.
arxiv-2507-04379:
Linnea Heitmeier, Olfa D'Angelo, Maziyar Jalaal, and Thomas Voigtmann watch droplets of yield-stress fluid spread, with and without gravity. Such fluids, like gels and pastes, flow only past a push threshold. Their resting droplet shape balances surface tension against that inner resistance.

The team dropped the fluid in a drop tower for brief weightlessness and ran matched tests on the ground. Droplets sat on a film of the same stuff, letting them test thin-film scaling laws head-on. Weightless runs untied gravity's pull from surface effects. Simulations with a thinning, elastic model matched the shapes well. Deviations at strong yield stress get a close discussion.
arxiv-2507-04479:
Jonas Arenhart, Raoni Arroyo, and Ederson Safra Melo pull apart two ideas that usually travel together in the philosophy of logic. Anti-exceptionalism holds that logic is studied like any other science, with theory choice guided by evidence and virtues. Many of its leading versions quietly assume scientific realism, the view that successful theories describe reality. The authors argue the pairing is a historical accident, not a logical need.

They draw a parallel with the metaphysics of quantum mechanics, where background assumptions often hide. By exposing the realist baggage, they loosen the link and sketch the opposite pairing: anti-exceptionalism built on an antirealist view of science. The paper is a metaphilosophical housekeeping job. It aims to show that debates about logic's method do not have to wait on the realism question, and that each stance can be mixed and matched on its own merits.
arxiv-2507-04679:
Ziqi Ji, Penghao Duan, and Gang Du let symbolic regression discover a turbulence model that keeps a key stress-shape term older models drop. Their 2025 paper works in a field where classic formulas barely improved for fifty years. Data-driven tools now promise fresh gains.

The learned model is an implicit algebraic stress form, written as plain formulas rather than a black box. It folds in how the local flow breeds the stress pattern's shape, a channel rivals ignore. Five test flows of varied character benchmark the model against three alternatives. Scores show sturdy behavior and wide reach across cases. The authors say the shape term is what buys the edge in hard flows.
arxiv-2507-04779:
Chien-Ming Chi presents a 2025 paper introducing a neural network design with unusually firm statistical promises. The model, o1Neuro, uses sparse neurons that fire as simple indicators. Chi proves two properties rarely found together. The deep version can fit any measurable function closely, and training is sure to reach the best fit if the updates run long enough.

A shallow version already handles additive models with two-way interactions exactly, trading depth against sparsity in a clean way. Benchmarks against popular tree ensembles and a tabular deep network, on public datasets of ten thousand rows and synthetic sets, favored o1Neuro on complex regression tasks. The paper targets users who want neural flexibility with guarantees closer to classical statistics.
arxiv-2507-04879:
Riccardo Miccini and co-authors make a speech cleaning model that can shrink or grow to fit each input, in a paper from 2025. Speech enhancement clears noise for calls, hearing aids, and voice tools. Small devices, though, force a fixed trade between quality and compute cost.

The team added dynamic slimming to DEMUCS, a known enhancement model. The slimmed model can run at many sizes, stored as one file. A small router network picks the right size for each clip, trained together with the main model. Trained to use ten percent of its full size on average, it matched a fixed model set at 25 percent. It also used 29 percent fewer operations to get there.
arxiv-2507-05179:
Pulkit Bansal and four co-authors build in 2025 a system that writes clear explanations of whether Hindi news stories are true. False news spreads fast, and languages like Hindi lack strong automated tools, so fact-checking cannot keep up.

Their method pairs Direct Preference Optimization, which teaches a model to favor better answers, with curriculum learning, which orders the training from easy to hard. Trusted fact-check explanations serve as the answers to prefer, while raw model output shows what to avoid. The goal is explanations that reason the way a human fact-checker would, in the language readers actually use.
arxiv-2507-05379:
Abhijat Sarma and co-authors show how plain snapshots from a quantum simulator can reveal the physics of defects. Snapshots, quick local reads of a quantum system, are the standard data in such labs. They are used to probe bulk behavior, while defects are usually studied by building them in.

The team's protocol needs no built-in defect at all. From bulk snapshots alone, it extracts defect traits that once seemed out of reach. In a chain of Rydberg atoms tuned to a critical point, the method reads off defect entropy. It also traces a full line of fixed points for the defect's field theory. Since one dataset serves many defect types, labs can screen defect physics cheaply before hardware runs. The trick widens what snapshot data can say about quantum matter.
arxiv-2507-05479:
G A Bobkov and co-authors study how a thin pairing of a standard superconductor and a helical magnet affects superconductivity, published in 2025. Helical magnetism, unlike plain magnetism, can coexist with superconductivity and weakens it only a little. It can also induce a p-wave triplet form of pairing, which is of interest for lossless spin devices.

The authors treat atomically thin layered systems of the two materials. They find that the strength of the proximity effect is a complex function of the magnet's exchange field and of filling factors on both sides. That includes how strong the induced p-wave pairing is and how much the main pairing is suppressed. They also show that the p-wave part can carry a spin supercurrent in conical magnet layers.
arxiv-2507-05579:
Mumford and Lewis-Swan study the long-time behavior of quantum Fisher information across dynamical quantum phase transitions. Such transitions mark sharp changes in a quantum system driven out of balance. The pair use two systems with clear classical limits: a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate and the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model.

In their 2025 paper, the long-time average of the Fisher information jumps at the transition point, which makes it a clean diagnostic. Mean-field and semiclassical methods then show that this long-time average acts in a universal way. The same pattern holds across both systems, despite their apart setups. The result gives experimenters a shared yardstick for spotting these transitions in the lab.
arxiv-2507-05879:
Suresh Chandra Joshi and co-authors probe oxygen gaps in high entropy oxide films in a 2025 study. These oxides mix many elements at one crystal site on purpose. The mix warps local symmetry and tunes what the material can do. Oxygen gaps add a second kind of disorder, in the oxygen layer itself.

The films studied are single crystals with five rare earth elements sharing one site. More oxygen gaps raised sheet resistance at room temperature. The shift from metal to insulator answered in two faced ways: small gaps lowered its temperature, while more gaps killed the metal phase. Magnet tests show weak then strong trapping of charge as gaps grow.
arxiv-2507-06079:
Sebastian Siegel and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on fitting sequence models onto small, exotic hardware. Structured state space models read long sequences with a steady, small memory, unlike the growing appetite of Transformers. That thrift suits edge devices, but the chips in question compute with analog parts that are noisy and imprecise.

The team trained the models while aware of the rounding the hardware will impose. That awareness shrank model complexity by up to a hundredfold across several measures. It also made the models tougher against analog noise and opened the door to cutting unneeded structure. Finally the authors ran the models on a real memristive analog chip and saw the expected efficiency gains. The work shows exotic chips and modern sequence models can be made to fit each other.
arxiv-2507-06379:
Haydn Belfield sketches four world bodies to govern the strongest smart tools in a 2025 paper. Chips are the choke point: no state can train a top tool with no top chips, so chip rules can bear the weight of law.

First come home rules, with risk checks, gate tests, and counts of chip hall use. Next, a world watch body, on the lines of the atom watch, to set one tune for those rules. A chip pact then bars top chips from lands with no such rules in force. Last, the lead state and its friends pool funds to train top tools as one shared work. For each body the draw is the same: a seat at the chip table. Belfield owns the build may take years, but says first steps are in.
arxiv-2507-06479:
Asefi and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on rebuilding ocean states from very sparse drift data. Ocean measures are sparse and scattered, most of all below the surface. That sparsity blocks forecasts of eddies and rogue waves. Their method pairs a neural operator with a generative diffusion model. The operator gives a first draft, and the generator refines it. The pair capture fine, fast-changing patterns even at extreme sparsity. Tests cover lab benchmarks, fake float data, and real satellite records.

The method holds up at ninety-nine percent missing data on fake sets. On real satellite data it copes with even higher sparsity. It beats other deep learning baselines under those harsh limits. The authors aim at better ocean forecasts from thin data.
arxiv-2507-06679:
Miaojing Shi and co-authors improve how vision-language models count objects named in a text prompt. Models often know the category but not the quantity. Their system, QUANet, adds quantity-focused prompts and a training loss that ties words to counts in the image.

A two-stream decoder blends a transformer path with a classic vision path, with adapters passing knowledge between them. A ranking loss keeps the two streams' counts in sane order. Tests on four standard sets show strong counting of unseen categories with no retraining. The code is public for others to build on.
arxiv-2507-06779:
Brain-computer interfaces promise control by thought, but deep learning decoders trained offline stumble when the signal must be read live, sliding window by sliding window. Martin Wimpff, Jan Zerfowski, and Bin Yang introduce in 2025 realtime adaptive pooling. Their parameter-free tweak adjusts the pooling layers of existing models. It readies them for online use and decodes consecutive windows jointly, cutting compute.

A source-free adaptation step then adjusts the model to a new user without touching the original user's private data. The result is cross-person decoding with no per-user calibration session, a step toward interfaces that work the moment they are switched on.
arxiv-2507-06879:
Gaytri Arya, Paolo Bianchini, and Alberto Diaspro tested whether optics after the source can rescue a quantum imaging method in 2025. Quantum imaging with undetected photons photographs with light that never touched the object, useful where detectors are poor. Polarization can mark which crystal a photon pair came from, and such marks can kill interference.

The team placed a two-path interferometer after the pair sources and tried to restore the lost pattern. Interference lost at birth stayed lost: no later arrangement of optics brought it back. The result pins coherence on sameness at the source itself. Designers of such imagers, they conclude, must guard indistinguishability where pairs are born.
arxiv-2507-07679:
Atsushi Ono develops a general way to read nonlinear responses out of a system's motion in a 2025 paper. When a material is pushed hard, its answer bends in ways a gentle probe cannot show. The standard route grinds through many-point correlation functions, a heavy lift.

Ono's frame rests on functional derivatives: wiggle the drive in the math, and the response functions fall out of the time trace itself. He checks the method on a classic two-band model, pulling its second- and third-order light responses. A tensor network run on an interacting many-body system shows the frame scales past toy cases.
arxiv-2507-08179:
Tomer Reiss and co-authors survey a faint ultraviolet glow from active black holes in a 2025 paper. The glow comes from neon gas stripped of many electrons near the black hole, and it may pierce dust that hides other signals. Their sample holds more than 340 nearby active galaxies picked by hard X-rays from the BASS survey.

The line showed clearly in about forty-three percent of the galaxies. Detection stayed high even for the most buried black holes, yet some of the cleanest spectra lacked the line entirely. Its strength tracked X-ray output with less scatter than a common oxygen tracer. Oddly, the line's relative strength showed no link to black hole mass, feeding rate, or burial depth, against simple model guesses. The authors offer the line as a steady, if puzzling, gauge of black hole power.
arxiv-2507-08379:
Samarth Kashyap and co-authors reviewed in 2025 where quantum techniques can help machine learning. Quantum machine learning aims to use quantum computing gains for data tasks, above all where classic methods face bottlenecks with complex data. The review covers encoding, learning theory, and optimisation, sorting methods by data type and machine design.

Known quantum gains depend on the problem, so useful directions need care. The authors weigh methods such as quantum principal component analysis and quantum sensing, plus uses in materials science, for real speed-ups and limits. Noise, scale, and encoding costs in current devices receive detailed treatment. Future work needs quantum-native methods and honest benchmarks, they argue.
arxiv-2507-08579:
Kanav Sharma and co-authors study disorder in topological insulator films in a twenty twenty-five paper. These materials carry current on their surface in a protected way, but charged impurities in the bulk disturb that flow. Doping is often used to tune the material, yet its effect on the disorder itself was unclear.

The team grew films of a three-element compound and a version doped with indium. Gate tests showed the doping raised the impurity count tenfold and shrank the puddles of stray charge. Mobility on the surface fell as a direct result. Their lesson: to build good devices, cut defects at the source, not just balance them with doping.
arxiv-2507-08679:
Rajarshi Roy and co-authors present a prompting trick that gives vision-language models a sense of depth, with no retraining, in a 2025 paper. Such models often fumble spatial questions and invent objects that are not there. Their method, ByDeWay, first estimates depth from the single photo, then slices the scene into near, middle, and far layers. A grounded vision model writes a short caption for each layer.

Those depth-tagged captions are pasted into the question prompt, so the main model reads the scene in layers. The trick is light, modular, and works even with closed models whose weights cannot be touched. On a test built to catch invented objects and on a hard reasoning test, scores rose across several models. The authors pitch depth as free context that any multimodal system can borrow.
arxiv-2507-08979:
Mahdiyar Molahasani, Azadeh Motamedi, Michael Greenspan, Il-Min Kim, and Ali Etemad present PRISM, a way to strip hidden bias from vision-language models without new data. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that models like CLIP inherit skewed links from their training sets. Past fixes need set bias classes or extra data. PRISM needs neither, and it works across tasks.

First, a language model writes scene texts from plain class prompts, surfacing the spurious links in words. Then a contrast-style loss learns a projection of the embeddings. The projection trims those links while keeping image-text alignment intact. Tests on the standard Waterbirds and CelebA sets beat current debiasing methods. Code is public. The authors stress the data-free stance: bias can be cut with the model's own space alone.
arxiv-2507-09079:
Isak Svensson, Alexander Tichai, Kai Hebeler, and Achim Schwenk apply a 2025 stats framework to the error bars of nuclear theory. Models of atomic nuclei rest on layers of cut off math, and each layer adds doubt to the results. Doubt from the force laws has been charted with care, but doubt from the solving method was left to expert feel.

Their framework treats that second doubt with the same stats tools. They ran it across many nuclei, using two and three particle forces drawn from a leading theory of the strong force. The work moves the field toward full, honest error bars on its forecasts.
arxiv-2507-09379:
Marc Bara Iniesta surveys where automatic differentiation could still change astrophysics, in this 2025 paper. The technique feeds exact gradients into searches, letting computers explore trade-offs rather than just climb them. His earlier radar work found designs four times faster by doing exactly that, and gradient methods already serve in gravity-wave and exoplanet studies.

Nine further fields, he argues, have the right math yet remain untouched, from exotic solutions of Einstein's equations to stellar and planetary systems. For each, he lays out the groundwork, and he proposes one shared framework, GRASP, for differentiable astrophysics computing.
arxiv-2507-09479:
Bhuvanesh Sundar and five co-authors ran a plasma wave test on a quantum chip. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is a first step toward quantum tests of plasmas. Strong plasmas lie past the reach of plain computers when quantum effects count. The team showed a plain plasma wave moving on a superconducting chip. They used the chip's own high grade gates plus a trick to cut errors.

They mimicked laser pulses bouncing off uneven plasmas. The key was a local spin model whose waves act like plasma waves. That model needs fewer gates than past plans, so it fits today's chips. Readers in plasma physics see a workable path to quantum tests of hard regimes.
arxiv-2507-09579:
Marc Bara proposes treating AI prompts as property in this 2025 paper. A good prompt is skilled work, yet today's platforms give its maker no ownership record, no version history, and no pay when others profit from it. PromptChain answers with a decentralized design.

Files live on a peer-to-peer store where they cannot be quietly altered, while smart contracts handle ownership and rules. A metadata standard aims to make prompts portable across models. Reviewers stake tokens on their judgments, aligning their pay with honesty, and a token economy rewards creators in proportion to their measured impact. Because prompts are decoupled from any one model, the system imagines an open marketplace of them. The author presents the blueprint as the first systematic treatment of prompts as standalone digital assets.
arxiv-2507-09879:
Tanvi Bajpai, Chandra Chekuri, and Pooja Kulkarni sharpen algorithms for covering several submodular demands at once in a 2025 paper. The task: pick a cheapest set of items that meets a target level for each of several value functions. With one function, the problem is classic. With many, past algorithms lose a factor that grows with their count, and that loss is unavoidable in general.

The authors study the case where the number of functions is a fixed constant. Their randomized method nearly meets every demand while costing close to a chosen multiple of optimal, with the trade-off tunable. For the important coverage-function case, they give an approximation close to the single-demand quality. The moral: a few demands are almost as tractable as one. They note applications that follow directly from the general results.
arxiv-2507-09979:
Anton Gerasimov, Dmitry Lebedev, and Sergey Oblezin build a global operator joining two deep mathematical worlds in a 2025 paper. On one side sit integrable systems, physics-flavored structures with hidden conservation laws. On the other sits the arithmetic of the group GL2, whose symmetries encode number theory's L-functions.

Their Hecke-Baxter operator lives in a global Hecke algebra built from the double coset space of integer matrices inside real ones. Acting on Eisenstein series, the operator's eigenvalues come out as exactly the corresponding global L-factors, the analytic fingerprints of arithmetic objects. The construction lifts the authors' earlier local versions, built field by field, into one global object. They close with a conjecture fit for the union: zeros of those L-factors should obey an arithmetic form of the Bethe ansatz equations, the spectral rules of integrable systems.
arxiv-2507-10079:
Alexander Balatsky and Saikat Banerjee build a single map for all the ways electrons can pair up in a superconductor. Their scheme sorts pairing states by how the pairing function swaps spin, orbital, space, and time labels. Those swaps must multiply to minus one, a rule from quantum statistics.

Known states, from classic pairing to odd-frequency and pair-density-wave orders, fall into sectors of one cube-shaped chart. The chart also flags allowed hybrid orders that few have studied, such as odd-frequency versions of known states. The authors sketch where such states might hide and how experiments could spot them.
arxiv-2507-10179:
Asvin G models mathematical discovery as a loop of belief updates, and asks why machines are not yet having ideas. Solving a problem, in this view, mixes stored knowledge and local search with a third act: mining the search itself for information that revises what the solver believes. His 2025 solo essay argues the loop's yield depends on the vocabulary the solver can think in.

Two kinds of concept reshape that vocabulary. Implicit concepts sharpen pruning inside a fixed language of moves. Explicit concepts add moves the language could not express before, and their creation, forced by necessity when no available computation settles the question, is the signature step of real discovery. Today's AI, even at superhuman games and theorem proving, forms only the implicit kind. The essay closes on what explicit creation would take, and how machine tradeoffs might breed alien styles of mathematics.
arxiv-2507-10479:
Max Rädler, Mark Colley, and Enrico Rukzio build a vision loss simulator with the help of people who live with low vision, in a study from 2025. Designers use such tools to feel what a screen is like for a user with poor sight. Past tools were built sans the users' own say, so their truth was in doubt.

Seven people with vision loss shaped the tool, VIP-Sim, through a joint design path. It lays 21 signs, such as field loss and light sting, over stock design apps. Most testers felt the tool matched their own sight well. They praised it, yet they flagged a risk: a tool built from a few lives may miss the breadth of the group. The work sets a bar for user-led design aids.
arxiv-2507-10579:
Ekaterina Kochmar and co-authors report the results of a shared task that graded how well AI tutors teach. More than fifty teams from around the world took part. The tutors, built on large language models, had to respond to student mistakes in teaching chats, and the systems scored those responses.

Five tracks covered the work: spotting a mistake, pinning down where it sits, giving guidance, making feedback usable, and naming which tutor wrote a reply. Scores on the teaching tracks were fair at best, with the top mark for spotting mistakes. Naming the tutor proved far easier. The hosts share all data from the task to push further work on AI teaching quality.
arxiv-2507-10679:
Gian Pietro Bellocca, Ignacio Garrón, Vladimir Rodríguez-Caballero, and Esther Ruiz present FARS, an R package to build full predictive distributions for economic series. Point forecasts hide risk. Their method instead produces conditional densities from factor-augmented quantile regressions. The factors themselves come from multi-level dynamic factor models, at times with group factors that overlap.

The package extracts global factors and factors for each group, and gives confidence regions that account for loading uncertainty. It estimates the quantile regressions with standard errors, rebuilds densities from the quantiles, and computes risk measures from the extreme tails. Users can also stress the factors to design adverse economic scenarios. The users in mind are economists and financial analysts who need scenario-ready forecasts.
arxiv-2507-10879:
Adib, Kazemi, and Kholghy present Omnisoot, a software package for designing processes that make soot and carbon black from gases. The tool builds on a chemistry library to model how tiny carbon particles form and grow. Their 2025 paper describes the package design and tests it on three cases.

The package couples several reactor types with four particle birth models and two models of particle size spread. It tracks particle birth, surface growth, and burning away, tied to detailed gas chemistry. Test cases cover methane and ethylene heating and ethylene burning. Results show that several birth and growth settings can match carbon yield while giving very different particle shapes, so shape data are needed to pin models down.
arxiv-2507-11079:
Li Wang, Qizhen Wu, and Lei Chen put a vision-language model in command of robot vehicle teams in a 2025 paper. In multi-vehicle clashes, each unit has to read the field and pick tactics fast. Hand rules crack under shifting chaos, and learning methods steer wheels well but plan poorly.

Their commander pairs a vision model that reads the scene with a light language model that reasons out strategy. Both work in one shared meaning space, much like a human commander who sees, then decides. Simulated battles gave the team win rates above eighty percent against baselines. Ablation tests showed each module earns its place. The authors stress clear reasoning as the edge over black-box rivals.
arxiv-2507-11179:
Itamar Procaccia and Tuhin Samanta report a dipole-induced phase transition in three dimensions, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Famous dipole-driven transitions, like the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, live in two dimensions, where vortices and dislocations unbind. Whether a genuine counterpart exists in three dimensions was open.

Studying how amorphous solids respond to strain, the authors find an intermediate phase between normal elastic response at high pressure and fluid behavior at zero pressure. Plastic events in this phase create quadrupolar fields, whose gradients act as dipole charges that screen elasticity and break symmetries. Angular correlations grow long-ranged at the transition, and the authors determine the critical scaling exponents.
arxiv-2507-11279:
Yujie Zhang, Sabine Struckmeyer, Andreas Kolb, and Sven Reichardt release a large photo dataset for grading tomato plants in fine detail. Breeders score plant traits by eye, which invites bias and drift between observers. Standardized images could make scoring repeatable.

Their rig photographs plants from four heights in twelve poses. The set holds over sixty-four thousand images. Boxes mark seven plant parts, and fifty growth stages follow the standard scale. A smaller subset adds pixel-level outlines. Test runs with a cascading method checked the data's usefulness. Robots and breeders both need ground truth like this. Fine-grained labels are the dataset's selling point.
arxiv-2507-11479:
Virtual and mixed reality systems guess at what users want, but they know little about who the user is. Daniel Platnick and co-authors propose a framework that gives such systems a sense of perspective. Its core is a model of each user built from their digital traces over time. That model tracks how a person's thinking and experience change. A closed loop then adapts the virtual scene to the user's state.

The team lays out the framework's parts and flow. They built two trial scenes in a Unity-based engine to show it working. The approach aims at experiences that feel personal yet stay open to inspection. It points human-computer research toward identity-aware immersion.
arxiv-2507-11879:
Jie Ding, Xiang Wei, and Shuai Ma derive the exact asymptotic behavior of the radio range at which a random wireless network snaps into connectivity. Random geometric graphs sprinkle points over a region and link those within a transmission radius. Two thresholds matter: the radius where the graph becomes k-connected, and the radius where every node gains at least k neighbors. Their setting is a unit-volume region in three or more dimensions.

The paper gives the precise asymptotic distribution of both critical radii. Such distributions tell a network designer not just the typical threshold but its fluctuations, which govern reliability margins. Higher dimensions change the geometry of nearest neighbors in ways the classical two-dimensional theory does not capture. Random geometric graphs model sensor fields, device swarms, and ad hoc networks. Sharp threshold laws are the design charts for all of them.
arxiv-2507-12179:
Abbas Ebrahimi, Mohsen Nejad-Asghar, and Azar Khosravi simulate how the density profile of a rotating molecular cloud core affects magnetic braking, the process that drains a forming star's spin. Observations show core density falls off as a power law with radius. Using particle-based simulations under ideal magnetohydrodynamics, they varied the steepness of that falloff.

Steeper profiles strengthened the twisted, toroidal part of the magnetic field. A stronger twist carried more angular momentum outward, so braking grew more effective. Across the range tested, the system's rotation dropped by roughly half from the shallowest to the steepest profile. The authors conclude that assuming uniform density understates how strongly magnetic fields slow core rotation.
arxiv-2507-12379:
Yucheng Sun, Alessandro Stolfo, and Mrinmaya Sachan read a language model's mind to catch its math slips before they surface. The team starts with three-digit addition, where simple probes decode both the model's planned answer and the true answer from hidden states. The decoding works whether or not the final output is right. Lightweight detectors trained on those signals flag errors with over 90% accuracy.

Probes trained on plain addition carried over to chain-of-thought traces from GSM8K problems. The same internal error pattern showed in the harder setting. Guiding re-prompts only at flagged steps repaired answers with little damage to correct ones.
arxiv-2507-12479:
Adam Uchytil, Milan Korda, and Jiri Zemanek steer a magnetically driven fluid in real time using a predictor learned purely from data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Electric and magnetic fields push a weakly conducting liquid around. Electrode and magnet arrays ring the fluid reservoir. Cameras track the flow surface for feedback each instant. Koopman theory lifts the nonlinear flow into linear form.

That linear predictor plugs straight into model predictive control. Two small quadratic programmes split electrode and magnet duties. The whole loop runs live on an ordinary laptop. Experiments shape the flow to match target velocity patterns. A time-varying swirl pattern is tracked successfully as well. Data-driven control tames a genuinely nonlinear flow system.
arxiv-2507-12979:
Youssef Tawfilis, Hossam Amer, Minar El-Aasser, and Tallal Elshabrawy present a way to train generative AI across many scattered devices without any device giving up its raw data. Generative models, above all GANs, need large datasets and heavy computing. Many phones and edge devices sit idle with spare power, but their owners will not share private data.

Their approach trains a GAN in a decentralized way. A clustered form of federated learning groups devices with similar data, weighted by a divergence measure. A split learning design divides the network so that weak devices carry only part of the load. No labels or raw data, real or synthetic, pass between nodes. In tests, classification scores rose by about ten percent on average, and image quality scores improved sharply on harder datasets. The authors release their code openly.
arxiv-2507-13279:
Bruno Bertin-Johannet and co-authors ask if extra ports can lift solar cells in a 2025 paper. A stock cell has two ports, one for electrons and one for holes. Sun light makes some carriers hot, and their heat dies as they cool to the band edge. Extra ports with energy gates could skim those hot carriers first. The race is clock-based: skim must beat the cool.

When skim wins, a four-port cell tops the best two-port cell, the team find. Gains run 20 to 40 percent in their math. Like gains should show in heat-power tools with skewed carrier spreads. The paper is a design proof, not a bench build. It points cell craft toward ports that sort by energy.
arxiv-2507-13379:
Niccolò Di Marco and co-authors survey how online social media behaves in this 2025 paper. Platforms record human interaction at huge scale and fine grain. That data lets researchers watch information spread, opinions shift, and crowds coordinate in real time.

Yet the field is scattered, with mixed methods and weakly checked models. The survey gathers empirical findings and formal models under one roof. It reviews regular patterns seen across platforms and judges how well models reproduce them. Gaps between data and theory get named plainly. The synthesis aims to give a fragmented field shared ground, from misinformation studies to platform design.
arxiv-2507-13679:
Anton Deitmar writes a short note that sharpens a recent result on the spread of prime geodesic traces. Prime geodesics are closed paths on curved surfaces that play a role much like prime numbers in arithmetic. A recent paper by Chatzakos, Harcos, and Kaneko measured how their traces are distributed, and Deitmar revisits that measurement with a different balance of detail and accuracy.

Using a prime geodesic theorem in the style of Dirichlet and relying on the Selberg trace formula, he improves the error term in the earlier estimate. The gain comes at a cost: the new version resolves the distribution less finely. The note is aimed at specialists who need the stronger error bound and can accept the lower resolution that comes with it.
arxiv-2507-13779:
Singh, Boubekki, Jenssen, and Kampffmeyer presented SuperCM in twenty twenty-five, a method improving learning when labels are scarce. Semi-supervised learning mixes a few labeled examples with many unlabeled ones. Domain adaptation applies the same idea when data shifts to a new setting.

Both tasks rest on a clustering idea: points grouped together should share a category. Past methods enforce this only indirectly during training. SuperCM instead builds clustering directly into the model as a module that can be trained end to end. Labeled data help set the cluster centers. Wide experiments show gains, mainly when supervision is very low. The method works alone or as an added regularizer that steadies existing approaches, the authors report.
arxiv-2507-13879:
Petr Beneš and Filip Blaschke study magnetic monopoles in a 2025 physics paper. A monopole is a lone north or south magnetic pole, the magnetic counterpart of an electric charge. Such objects can form in some field theories when a symmetry breaks. The pair work with a broken SU(2) gauge theory with a scalar field, in the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield limit, where exact solutions can be found.

In that limit they find exact monopole solutions. Some carry a new internal degree of freedom, a moduli space parameter that no earlier work on this limit had shown. Changing the parameter reshapes where the monopole's energy density sits in space. The total energy, and so the mass, stays constant while the profile shifts. The result widens the known family of exact monopole solutions.
arxiv-2507-13979:
Brian Murphy and co-authors map the coma of comet 67P in a 2025 paper. The comet, visited by the Rosetta mission, passed near the Sun in 2021. With a large telescope spectrograph, the team made maps of dust and several gases at twelve points around that passage.

Dust and gas showed distinct shapes. Two gases tracked known dust fans, hinting that dust itself may release them. In the south, one gas followed a sharp dust feature closely. Scale lengths for one gas ran larger in the north, backing an extended source there. The maps enrich the Rosetta record with ground-based context.
arxiv-2507-14179:
Dhar and five co-authors put forth a way in twenty twenty-five to guess which neurons fire in a large chat model, to save compute cost. Such models fire just a part of their neurons per input, but guessing each one costs too much at their scale. They group like fire forms into a small set of clusters.

A new input is then matched to a cluster in place of neuron-by-neuron calls. Their groups hit high truth rates and beat plain two-way groups. With more groups, score loss stayed near nil in their tests. The plan sets a base for fast sparse runs of such models.
arxiv-2507-14279:
Richter and colleagues assess whether two forbidden iron lines could open a window on the Milky Way's million-degree halo gas. That hot corona is a major reservoir of the galaxy's ordinary matter, yet nearly invisible. Singly and triply ionized iron have intersystem lines in the optical that might absorb against bright background quasars. A semi-analytic halo model plus cosmological simulations predict the expected column densities and line shapes.

Detection at three sigma would need a signal-to-noise near fifty thousand, far beyond routine spectroscopy. The team therefore stacked over seven hundred archival high-resolution quasar spectra from two great observatories. The composite reached a signal-to-noise above a thousand and still showed no lines, yielding upper limits consistent with predictions. The lines wait for future surveys with millions of spectra. Feasibility studies like this set the instrument requirements honestly.
arxiv-2507-14579:
Kester Wong, Sahan Bulathwela, and Mutlu Cukurova study human and AI joint work in problem solving diagnosis in two thousand twenty-five. The task is to spot joint problem solving signs in student dialogue. Past work used BERT on transcripts to tag such signs. A speech aware variant, AudiBERT, added sound traits to the text.

The team checks if those gains are real and where they land. AudiBERT gains were firm in the social cognitive class set. No like gains showed in the affective set. More training data linked to better recall for both models. Human coder accord linked to BERT precision. A plan for joint human AI work closes the paper.
arxiv-2507-14779:
Huaian Diao, Hongyu Liu, Qingle Meng, and Li Wang study how patterns arise in paired equations that model waves leaving a region without reflection, a setup called transparent boundary conditions. Such systems appear in several fields at once. They encode inverse problems read from a single boundary measurement, special vibration modes of layered media, and the mathematics of objects that hide from waves.

The team uncovers a new local pattern and proves a sharp link. The link ties the mismatch in the equations' lower-order terms to the geometry of the region, especially inside tube-like ends with strongly curved walls. That one result feeds back into each application area. The authors draw out new physical insight and practical consequences for scattering and shape detection.
arxiv-2507-14879:
Rizhao Fan, Tianfang Ma, Zhigen Li, Ning An, and Jian Cheng fix the scale of foundation depth maps with a few true measurements, in work from twenty twenty-five. Foundation models now guess scene depth strikingly well from one image. Their outputs come in relative units, not true metres. That gap blocks direct use in robots and other real tools. Past fixes retrain models per domain and dull their general skill.

Their method adapts scale region by region with sparse true depths. No retraining or fine-tuning touches the foundation model at all. General skill across new scenes thus stays fully intact. Sparse points from cheap sensors suffice to anchor the scale. Tests confirm the adapted maps land in true metric units. Cost stays low since only arithmetic, not learning, is added. Deployment to fresh domains becomes a light step.
arxiv-2507-15179:
Yuxi Hu and Mengran Yuan study a relaxed form of the equations that govern compressible gas flow. Their 2025 paper swaps the classic Newtonian stress law for a Maxwell law, which lets stress lag behind motion. They look for round, symmetric flows outside a ball in three-dimensional space, a setup whose boundary causes technical trouble.

The pair first build a nearby, easier system and show it has local solutions. They then craft a weighted energy measure and handle the boundary terms with care to win bounds that hold for all time. Those bounds give global solutions for the first system, and limit arguments extend them to the true one. Last, they prove the relaxation limit holds worldwide, linking the new model back to the classic equations.
arxiv-2507-15279:
Li Cai, Yangyu Fan, and Dongming She study a period integral tied to deep values of L-functions. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, works with automorphic forms on GL(2). Two exceptional theta series on a cubic cover join the form. The integral they build is called a co-period.

Locally, they prove the key space is always one-dimensional. The unramified cases are computed in full. Globally, the integral splits into local pieces for Eisenstein series. They then propose a formula, in the Ichino-Ikeda style, for cuspidal forms. It links the integral to the central value of a symmetric cube L-function. A corollary gives forms with nonzero central values.
arxiv-2507-15479:
Rami Atar and Amarjit Budhiraja study a system of many particles where only the leftmost particle gets a push, in work from 2025. The system is known as the Atlas model. Earlier work covered one special start, where particle positions follow a random pattern of fixed density, and the large-scale limit was a classic melting-type problem.

The authors allow a far wider set of starting layouts, as long as the layout grows in a controlled way. In that wider setting, the limit is a free boundary problem stated with measures rather than the classic melting form. Under an added condition that the start has some density everywhere, the boundary moves along a smooth continuous path. The leftmost particle follows that path in the limit.
arxiv-2507-15679:
János Pach, Orit E. Raz, and József Solymosi work on a classic puzzle in geometry posed by Erdős: how often can the same distance occur among points in a flat plane? A result from 1984 caps the count for the unit distance, but the true cap is thought to be much lower, near a bound Erdős himself suggested. The gap between the two bounds has stood for decades.

The three authors prove a structural result about point sets that come close to the known cap. They show that such sets must have a rigid shape in a precise sense. Using that fact, they reduce the whole problem to a single claim about rigid frameworks. If that claim holds, it would give the first gain on the 1984 bound. A weaker form of the claim has already been proved by two of the authors.
arxiv-2507-15779:
Felix Koster and Atsushi Uchida tried reservoir computing as a language model in two thousand twenty-five. Giant language models devour energy and time. Reservoir computing trains only a small output layer. The reservoir itself is a fixed, lively dynamical system. Physical versions could run fast on little power. Text modeling with reservoirs remains little studied.

Three character-level approaches were compared directly. Two reservoir designs faced a transformer baseline. Accuracy, cost, and prediction quality were scored. The gap to transformers is real but mapped now. Hardware reservoirs could suit always-on devices. Efficiency, not raw scale, is the selling point. The study gives the field honest benchmarks.
arxiv-2507-15879:
Lei Zhao studies a billiard problem with a twist of gravity in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. In Kepler billiards, a ball moves inside a closed curve under a Kepler force, as if pulled to one focus, and bounces off the walls. Zhao looks at the zero-energy case in the plane.

He assumes the curve meets each focused parabola at most twice. If the system has a curve of two-bounce orbits and a smooth first integral near it, Zhao proves the curve must be an ellipse. The Kepler center then sits at one focus of that ellipse. The proof adapts a theorem of Bialy and Mironov through a change of variables.
arxiv-2507-16279:
Junhao Su and co-authors present MAN++, a 2025 method for training vision networks in smaller local pieces. Standard training sends error signals through the whole network, which locks updates, uses much memory, and differs from biology. Local learning instead splits the network into blocks, each with its own helper network.

The weakness of local learning is that blocks cannot share what they learn. The authors add a momentum-based helper design that scales the approach up while easing that isolation. For engineers, the work tests whether local training can stay practical on larger vision tasks without full backpropagation.
arxiv-2507-16479:
Haoyang Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on how energy traders can profit by moving between local electricity markets. Households and firms that both make and use power bid in a local energy market and a local flexibility market. Past work studied bidding in one market at a time, leaving cross-market gains unexplored.

Their method gives each trading firm two cooperating learning agents, one for each market stage. Without the joint strategy, the agents work apart and chase local profit only. With it, they share information and shift energy across markets. In their test case, higher first-stage costs were outweighed by later savings, lifting total profit by about forty percent on average.
arxiv-2507-16579:
Xiao, Hu, and Wang present a diffusion model for medical image synthesis in twenty twenty-five. Clinics often lack a needed imaging modality due to time, artifacts, or patient limits. Synthesis can fill that gap by generating the missing scan type. Their model, PHMDiff, works across scales in a pyramid structure.

Random multi scale masks with high coverage speed up training. A transformer based diffusion process adds cross granularity regularization. That term keeps mutual information consistent across latent spaces at each scale. Experiments on two data sets beat rivals on two standard quality metrics. Ablation tests confirmed each component contributes to the result. The model works both across and within imaging modalities. Source code is released by the authors.
arxiv-2507-16679:
Han Jiang and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It improves a cheap way to steer language models toward human values: giving examples and instructions in the prompt itself, with no retraining. The catch is that values clash. A prompt that asks for both excitement and tradition can leave the model torn.

Their method, PICACO, rewrites the guiding instruction so the model grasps all the listed values at once. It tunes the wording by raising a measure of how much the values and the model's answers move together. Across five value sets, the method worked with both closed and open models. It beat recent rivals and held a better balance across as many as eight values at once. The approach suits products that must serve users with mixed priorities.
arxiv-2507-16779:
Aiden Ochoa, Xinyuan Xu, and Xing Wang raise the hit rate of a network that hunts flaws in electron microscope images of nuclear fuel. Their 2025 paper deals with a hard vision task: flaws at the nanoscale vary wildly, labeled examples are few, and hand labels carry errors. Standard scores can thus mislead.

Their test case is finding grain edges in images of uranium dioxide. By starting from a network pre-trained on plain photos and adding a penalty that keeps its weights small, they steered it toward simple, trusty cues. Scores tied to the flawed labels hid the gain, so they built new measures that stand apart from label quality. On those, the flaw find rate rose by more than half.
arxiv-2507-16879:
Azhar Ikhtiarudin and co-authors cut the measurement bill of an adaptive quantum chemistry method. Their 2025 paper works on ADAPT-VQE, which builds a quantum circuit step by step for molecule problems. Each step needs many repeated readings, called shots, and the count balloons fast.

Two fixes are combined. Readings taken while tuning the circuit are reused when picking the next operator, instead of being thrown away. Shots are also handed out by variance, so noisy terms get more and calm terms fewer. Tests on several molecules reached chemical accuracy with far fewer shots. Fidelity held up throughout. The authors aim the savings at today's noisy machines that cannot afford wasted measurement rounds.
arxiv-2507-17079:
Md Meftahul Ferdaus, Kendall Niles, Joe Tom, Mahdi Abdelguerfi, and Elias Ioup survey in a 2025 paper how detectors learn new classes from a few examples. Labeling video frames and 3D scans by hand is slow and costly. Few shot learning aims to spot new object types after seeing just a handful of marked cases.

For video, methods carry data across frames with tube proposals and time match nets. For 3D, sparse point clouds and weak texture force custom nets and losses that cope with class imbalance. Shared hard parts include the pull between broad skill and overfit, plus matching by class prototype. The survey maps recent gains and argues the approach can cut labeling needs for real world use, such as self driving cars.
arxiv-2507-17379:
Shen Tan and co-authors present a robot system in a 2025 paper on mobile manipulation guided by language. The task is hard: a robot must move through homes, find new objects it has never seen, and follow free-form spoken or typed orders. Their system, LOVMM, pairs a large language model with a vision-language model.

In simulated homes, the robot handled varied jobs, such as tossing food boxes into a bin or packing bottles from a bed into a box. It learned across tasks and coped with new objects without fresh training. The system also moved to tabletop jobs and beat rival methods on success rates. Readers get a clear design for flexible home robots.
arxiv-2507-17979:
Shubham Mohole and Sainyam Galhotra present SIFOTL, a method that finds which segments of a population drive a shift in tabular data. Their 2025 paper targets settings like healthcare, where privacy rules block full data access and noise clouds the signal. SIFOTL works only from privacy safe summary statistics.

Twin gradient boosted models, assisted by a language model, separate intervention signal from noise. Their outputs merge through a Pareto weighted decision tree that names readable segments behind the shift. On a benefits dataset mimicking a new drug subsidy, the method scored far above a commercial contribution analysis and standard tests. Across eighteen synthetic health datasets it held up, even with noise injected.
arxiv-2507-18079:
Frank Barrows and co-authors explain in a 2025 study why quantum annealers, built to escape memory, show magnetic hysteresis after all. These machines tunnel through energy barriers to find low states, so stuck, history-bound behavior was a surprise. Their account mixes quantum two-level jumps with classical domain-wall motion.

On D-Wave hardware, even one-dimensional rings of nearly five thousand qubits showed coercivity, a memory effect classical physics forbids there. The model reproduced loop shapes, kink counts, and sweep-rate trends across three machines, including dips where response briefly goes negative. Quantum memory, they conclude, is real and programmable.
arxiv-2507-18179:
Multiplication runs constantly inside AI chips, and every switching event in the circuit burns a little power. Felix Arnold, Maxence Bouvier, Ryan Amaudruz, Renzo Andri, and Lukas Cavigelli redesign the multiplier to waste less. Their design first converts numbers into sign-magnitude form, where the sign is stored apart from the size. The multiplication then runs in that cheaper format.

The two blocks are built and tuned separately, and the final circuit provably computes the same results as before. AI workloads cluster near zero, where the new form shines. In simulations of a small multiplier fed realistic data, switching activity fell by up to about thirteen percent. A wider allowed input range pushed the saving near a third. Smarter tuning added a few more points on top.
arxiv-2507-18479:
Ngoc Luyen Le and Marie-Hélène Abel ask language models to name prerequisite skills in a 2025 paper. Learning paths depend on knowing what must come before what. Expert lists of those links are costly to build and maintain. The pair test whether models can guess them cold, from descriptions alone.

Their benchmark draws over three thousand skills from the European ESCO taxonomy. Expert defined prerequisite links form the ground truth. Thirteen major models were prompted in one standard way. Scores covered meaning similarity, a learned text metric, and response speed. Several models, including Llama and Claude versions, tracked expert judgment closely. No fine tuning was involved anywhere. The results support model assisted curriculum design at scale.
arxiv-2507-18579:
Campbell, Shank, and Wehlau map the fixed ring of a finite right-angle group in this twenty twenty-five paper. The group acts on its own base space in odd depth and even field grade. Fixed parts of that act form a ring whose build was not yet known here.

Inside, the team builds a least set of parts that spawn the whole fixed ring. They then give the ties that bind those spawn parts to each other. The ring turns out to be a full cross form, a neat and strong build type. That build earns the ring a sound grade in the scale of ring health. The work tops a past case done just for the field of size two.
arxiv-2507-18679: Dezi Liu and Yuan Fang offer a practical guide to weight maps for CCD photometry in a 2025 note. Weight maps help astronomers judge how much trust to place in each part of an image. The note sets out full equations for data counted in electrons. It also gives equations for data in ADU units. Simpler forms cover common observing setups. Separate noise sources are treated as independent of each other.
arxiv-2507-19679:
Sellers need each product photo tagged with the right traits, and Mandar Kulkarni's 2025 paper tackles that job for online shops. Hand labels cost too much at scale, so Kulkarni works with compact vision language models of two to three billion parameters. The method starts from a small labeled set built with an outside annotation service, then trains small adapter modules on it.

The adapters then face unlabeled listings. For each item the model drafts several reasoned answers, and the answers that agree most are treated as preferred while the rest count as dispreferred. A preference training method called DPO learns from that split, and the round repeats with the updated model. Across twelve shop categories, the method beat plain supervised training and kept gaining as more unlabeled data came in, which shows a large pool of raw listings can lift accuracy cheaply.
arxiv-2507-19779:
Choudhary and co-authors study a crystal whose atoms sit on a kagome lattice, a pattern of linked triangles. The crystal mixes yttrium, calcium, manganese, oxygen, and boron. Its spins pull in rival ways, some pairing up and some opposing. That tug of war makes the material act in odd ways when cooled.

Tests show the crystal orders as a magnet at a low heat, near eight degrees above absolute zero. A small applied field then flips its state, a sign the spins sit at a slant. The crystal also soaks up heat well when a field is applied, a trait prized for cooling machines. The authors note it holds no rare earth metals, which adds to its appeal for fridge use.
arxiv-2507-19879:
Roozbeh Hazrat and co-authors lay the base for a graded counting theory for a class of algebras built from layered graphs, in a 2025 paper. These algebras, named for Kumjian and Pask, encode the paths of such graphs. A sound counting tool could help sort them into types.

The team prove that a graded count from the graph's path system matches the graded count of its algebra, with order kept intact. Two graph moves that reshape the graph leave the count unchanged and keep the algebras close kin. They also give a term under which maps between counts lift to maps between algebras. The work builds a case for the tool as a sorting key.
arxiv-2507-20179:
Giulia Bertaglia and co-authors estimate past Alzheimer disease incidence from death records alone. Direct tracking of new cases is often missing for long spans. Death data are fuller, but they reflect incidence only indirectly.

Their two-stage method starts with ensemble Kalman inversion on mortality data. An age-structured population model is fit to observed death counts. That stage yields population shape and Alzheimer death rates by age. A back-calculation then infers when cases must have begun. It uses the risk of death after disease onset. The pipeline rebuilds hidden disease history over time. Health planners gain a tool for chronic disease monitoring without case registries.
arxiv-2507-20279:
Katharina Trinley, Toshiki Nakai, Tatiana Anikina, and Tanja Baeumel ask which language a multilingual model thinks in. They studied Aya-23, a model trained on balanced data across languages, and compared it with mostly English or mostly Chinese models. Their tools peeked inside the network: one reads early guesses at each layer, the other maps which neurons serve which language.

During translation, Aya-23 lit up representations of related languages, rather than routing everything through one pivot language as English-centered models do. In mixed-language text, the base language shaped the pattern more than the mixed-in one. Its language-specific neurons for mixed inputs clustered in the final layers, unlike earlier reports. How alike two languages are, in family or in script, shaped the overlap. The findings show multilingual training reorganizes a model's inner life.
arxiv-2507-20579:
Zhixi Cai and co-authors release a giant test set for spotting deepfake video and audio, in this 2025 paper. Modern speech and face tools can fabricate clips that fool the eye and ear. Detectors need training data rich in forgery styles and in the wear that online video suffers. Their set, AV-Deepfake1M++, holds two million clips with varied manipulation and sound-image distortions.

It extends an earlier million-clip release with tougher, more realistic damage. The paper explains how the fakes were made and benchmarks current detectors against them. Results show where today's methods stand. The team also runs a public detection challenge on the data, offered under a research-only license. They hope the scale pushes detection research toward real-world conditions.
arxiv-2507-20679:
Georgios Konstantinou and Konstantinos Moulopoulos wrote a paper from 2025 on a subtle flaw in a standard tool of quantum physics. The tool, called Berry curvature, tracks how a system's states twist as its settings change. It is drawn from the states themselves by a set recipe. The pair show that the recipe can go wrong where the operator for a setting is not well defined across its whole range.

Handled with care, those problem zones can change the curvature a great deal. Even a system whose core rule shows no link to the setting can end up with a nonzero twist. The lesson is that the curvature lives in the states, not in the core rule as such. The team works the point from first steps in the standard frame for crystals, where settings are wave-like. They close by weighing what the shift may mean for solid materials.
arxiv-2507-20779:
Daniel Werner and co-authors study charge flow through a watched quantum dot with strong internal interplay. Their paper from 2025 uses a dissipative Anderson impurity model, where the dot charge or spin is tracked by its setting, causing a blurring called dephasing. A master equation method does the sums.

The Kondo state, a many body resonance of the dot, stood up to mild charge blurring but not to spin blurring. The team reads that gap as blurring heating the low energy states. In a two lead build they also sum steady current and conductance. The curved conductance traces fold onto one curve when scaled by a blurring tied Kondo scale, a neat universal mark.
arxiv-2507-21279:
Štěpán Marek and Jan Wilhelm present a 2025 method to compute how molecules answer light, step by step in time. Light response traits shape solar cells, sensors, and lasers.
