The standard route solves a response equation at set tones, which misses effects that need stronger fields. Their route runs the Bethe-Salpeter equation forward in time under a live electric field.

Electron pairing effects enter through a screened swap term, and start energies come from a prior high-grade run. Tests on organic molecules matched the standard route on tone peaks within a small margin. The time route also caught second-harmonic output and field rectification, feats the standard route can not do. Cost stays near that of common hybrid methods, which suits wide use.
arxiv-2507-21379:
Helio Takai, a physicist, rebuilds one of the most famous experiments in science inside a box. The original Rutherford scattering test, run by Geiger and Marsden under Rutherford's direction, fired alpha particles at gold foil. A few bounced back at wild angles, proving the atom hides a tiny, dense nucleus. That result overturned the picture of the atom in one stroke.

Takai's version swaps the rare gear of the original for parts anyone can buy. The setup still shows the key deflections that betray the nucleus. He offers it as a platform for classroom demonstrations and first investigations in nuclear physics. Students can watch the evidence gather with their own eyes, at low cost and with modest risk.
arxiv-2507-21979:
Workhorse Q-switched lasers fire strong, cheap pulses, but physics caps how short those pulses can be: a few hundred picoseconds at best. Peer Biesterfeld and co-authors bolted an afterburner onto one. Their multi-pass cell bounces the pulse through a glass rod again and again, broadening its spectrum each pass, so a compressor can then squeeze it in time. Half-nanosecond pulses carrying a millijoule came out at 24 picoseconds, in a compact setup.

Simulations matched the experiment and suggest a few picoseconds are reachable. The authors pitch the scheme as a bridge: ultrafast timing from a platform industry already trusts, without the size and cost of mode-locked lasers.
arxiv-2507-22079:
Leo Guo and co-authors compare two Bayesian design strategies for cellular structures that absorb energy, in a 2025 paper. The structures, called spinodoids, are sponge-like metamaterials tuned for crash protection. Computer simulations of such designs grow ever more exact but also more costly, while data-driven design wants many samples.

Bayesian optimization is a data-thrifty way to tune costly functions. Its multi-fidelity cousin exploits cheap, coarse simulations alongside dear, fine ones. The authors apply both to the same real design task, a head-to-head test that was missing. They also use variance-based sensitivity analysis on well spread samples to shrink the design space before optimizing.
arxiv-2507-22279:
Timothy Jacob Huber, Madhur Tiwari, and Camilo Riano-Rios work on predicting satellite motion in groups. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with multi-agent systems, where each craft must guess where its nearest neighbors will be. Graphs are the standard tool to model who talks to whom in such a fleet.

Their method uses EvolveGCN, a graph network that itself changes over time, to forecast how the links between agents evolve. To keep the forecasts physically sound, they add loss terms based on the Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, which govern relative motion in orbit. The mix aims for predictions that are both accurate and plausible.
arxiv-2507-22379:
Chang Liu, Bin Qian, and Ran Wang wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a heat equation driven by random noise. The equation uses a fractional Laplacian, a tool that spreads heat in a way that depends on a power called alpha. The noise is white in time but rough in space.

The authors find the exact growth pattern of the solution as time and space grow large. From that pattern they derive sharp growth rates for the Hölder coefficients, which measure how rough the solution is. The proofs rest on two known tools from probability theory. One is Talagrand's majorizing measure theorem, and the other is Sudakov's minoration theorem. The work pins down how roughness builds up in this kind of random heat flow.
arxiv-2507-22479:
Nick Haupka presents a classifier that sorts research from non-research content in OpenAlex in a 2025 paper. OpenAlex is a major open catalog of scholarly works. Its article and review sets contain editorials, letters, and other paratexts mixed with true research, which can skew bibliometric studies.

Trained on open metadata, the classifier scores very high on standard accuracy measures. Applied to tens of millions of records, it reclassified about a tenth as non-research. That is a large data quality gain for a free resource. Scholars who measure science itself can clean their samples before drawing conclusions about fields or institutions.
arxiv-2507-22779:
Ran-Chen He and five co-authors reframe a notorious computing problem through the zeros of a key function. Simulating identical particles hits the fermion sign problem: minus signs cancel the signal and wreck the math. Recent work writes the partition function as a recursion in a variable marking bosons against fermions. Their 2025 paper, the first of a series, pushes that variable into the complex plane, turning the function into a polynomial. Its zeros, read in the spirit of Lee-Yang theory, reveal the function's analytic shape.

At absolute zero, the zero pattern shows special structure. Zeros govern phase behavior in statistical physics, so the move imports a powerful lens. The authors seek understanding before algorithms. Their analysis may explain why the sign problem bites where it does.
arxiv-2507-22979:
Six researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on when the Milky Way's thin disc took over from its thick one. Using red giant stars from two big surveys, they modeled how stellar motion varies with age. The disc's structure shifts clearly with age.

Stars older than about ten billion years are compact, like the thick disc. Younger stars spread wider the younger they are, the signature of a thin disc growing from inside out. Right at the transition, scale lengths dip below even the thick disc's. A comparison simulation links that dip to the gas disc shrinking after a major merger.
arxiv-2507-23079:
Craig Gidney designs a quantum circuit that adds a known classical number into a quantum register, in this 2025 paper. Such adders are workhorses inside larger quantum algorithms, notably those that run modular arithmetic. A 2004 design handled quantum-plus-quantum addition cheaply, but the classical case stayed open.

Gidney's first adder uses only three clean spare qubits, no matter the size of the numbers, with gate cost growing in a straight line. A second version trims the gate count further by borrowing dirty spare qubits. Applying either adder under the control of another qubit costs nothing extra, which suits the big algorithms that need them.
arxiv-2507-23379:
Marra and six co-authors compute how the thermal glow of a black hole's accretion disk becomes polarized, in the first of a series. New X-ray polarimetry missions make this signal observable for stellar-mass black holes in their thermal state. The polarization should reveal the disk's tilt and the hole's spin, if the physics is modeled well.

Two stages shape the signal: scattering and absorption inside the disk atmosphere, then relativistic bending on the trip to the observer. This paper handles only the direct radiation. Two atmosphere models, collisional and photoionization equilibrium, are compared for their spectro-polarimetric fingerprints at the surface. The authors then propagate those fingerprints through strong gravity.
arxiv-2507-23679:
Teodor Parella-Dilmé, Jakob Kottmann, and Antonio Acín improve how quantum circuits are laid out on hardware where not every qubit can reach every other, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Hybrid algorithms that mix classical and quantum computing need state preparations that are both expressive and trainable.

The team first designs a routing method that works for any pattern of links between qubits. The result is a swap network that lets any pair of qubits interact directly, at a reasonable cost. They then weave that routing into the circuit layers themselves, so layout and logic are planned together. This joint design trains better and reaches good answers with fewer resources. Tests on spin glasses and on molecular ground states show the gains. The work helps near-term quantum hardware handle strongly linked problems.
arxiv-2507-23779:
Miaosen Zhang and a team of co-authors reported in twenty twenty-five on Phi-Ground, a family of models that teach computer-use agents where to click. Such agents act on screens, and grounding — finding the right button or field — decides success. Leading end-to-end models still score under sixty-five percent on hard benchmarks, too low when one misclick can ruin a task.

The report walks through an empirical study of training these models, from data collection to final tuning. The resulting Phi-Ground models top all five grounding benchmarks among models under ten billion parameters in agent settings. In end-to-end settings they also set records on two named benchmarks. The authors share their failures as well as successes, aiming to guide other perception tasks beyond screen grounding.
arxiv-2508-00179:
Keisi Kacanja, Kanchan Soni, and Alexander Harvey Nitz measure orbit oddness in six low mass wave events in 2025, using the fuller author name given in the text head. Odd, oval orbits hint at how neutron star pairs form. Reading that trait is hard, since wave models for oval orbits are young and costly. The team re ran six past events with two such models.

One event, GW200105, showed clear oval character under both models. Support for that read was moderate. The other five events fit near round orbits, with tight upper bounds. A famous mixed event showed no oval sign. The authors also flag sampling traps in these fits. Better models will sharpen such tests.
arxiv-2508-00679:
Shubham Nigam and three co-authors built a legal search tool that works the way lawyers do, from parts of a case, in a paper published in 2025. Past rulings guide new ones, but full texts are long and often only fragments are known at search time. Their tool, TraceRetriever, cuts rulings into role parts such as facts and grounds. Only the weighty parts form the query.

Three search kinds run in one pipeline: word match, vector match, and a fine re-ranking step. A rank fusion blends their lists before the final sort. The role labels come from a network trained on Indian rulings. Tests on two legal datasets show the pipeline holds up as case loads grow. The authors present it as a firm base for real-world case search.
arxiv-2508-01179: Youjiang Lin, Jiaming Lan, and Jinghong Zhou prove a set of inequalities in a 2025 paper. The results are affine fractional versions of the classic Pólya-Szegö inequalities, stated for two functions on n dimensional space. The authors show their affine forms are stronger than the known Euclidean fractional versions, which is the whole claim of the short abstract.
arxiv-2508-01379:
Gergely Nyitray studies a coupled system made of a hoop and a solid wheel joined at their centers by a spring, in a 2025 paper on the edge of complexity. When the system swings in its normal modes, the mass at the center does not stay still. Nyitray shows that this happens because of the grip forces where the two bodies touch the ground.

When both bodies have the same resistance to turning, that grip effect vanishes. With care in placing the spring ends, the center mass can also be kept at rest when the bodies differ. Nyitray derives the motion in four ways, using force laws, energy, and angular momentum. The simple setup thus shows rich behavior that suits teaching and study.
arxiv-2508-01479:
Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay, and Bugra Kilictas present a 2025 paper on rebuilding hidden trust profiles from simple trust scores. Security frameworks often publish a single score for how much two devices trust each other. The rich profiles behind those scores stay hidden, yet analysts may need them.

The authors frame the rebuild as an inverse problem with data from two watchers. Their estimator joins the paired score series with four summary features of each series. They prove the rebuild map settles to a single fixed point, using a classic contraction argument. Tests on fake data with noise kept the device layout close to the truth, and error bounds tie accuracy to series length.
arxiv-2508-01579:
Lingfeng He and co-authors propose SECA, a method that helps vision-language models learn new tasks without forgetting old ones, in a 2025 paper. Continual learning with CLIP often transfers past knowledge blindly, letting unrelated tasks interfere. Their framework instead uses the rich meaning stored in text descriptions to judge which old knowledge is relevant to each new image.

One module turns that judgment into tailored teaching signals for the backbone network. A second module sharpens the visual class prototypes using the semantic relations held in text embeddings, fixing their lack of precise meaning. Tests on several benchmarks support the design. The authors argue text priors are an underused guard against forgetting.
arxiv-2508-01879:
Edwin Tham and four co-authors distribute a quantum memory in twenty twenty-five. Their design spreads a memory over a two-row array of qubit modules. Logical information lives in the first row of modules. Ancilla modules in the second row handle error correction. A cyclic shift, carried by flying qubits, is the only connector between modules.

They prove quantum LDPC codes keep their performance in this distributed setting. Two correction strategies are offered. The cyclic layout works for any stabilizer code, widening earlier results limited to CSS codes. The sparse cyclic layout is tuned to bivariate bicycle codes. For one such code, the memory holds twelve logical qubits. Readers get fault tolerance with strikingly simple hardware links.
arxiv-2508-01979:
Lorrien MacEnulty and co-authors benchmark, in a 2025 paper, a correction term in quantum chemistry calculations of iron molecules that flip between spin states. Such spin crossover molecules are candidates for switches and sensors. Predicting their energy balance cheaply matters, and density functional theory with added Hubbard terms is the workhorse method.

The team studied four iron compounds at the strongly bonded end of the spectrum. They computed the standard correction and the Hund's J term for every relevant atomic subspace and spin state, using a minimum tracking response method. Applied in the usual sign, the J terms failed to improve on the already strong plain method, against high level reference calculations. That failure is informative: it shows where the correction's picture of static correlation breaks down in covalent systems. The paper maps the limits and points to how the terms might be fixed.
arxiv-2508-02779:
Roster and Wright lead a very large Euclid Consortium team reporting on redshift calibration for the Euclid space survey, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Euclid maps weak gravitational lensing to trace how cosmic structures evolved. That science needs accurate average redshifts for huge ensembles of galaxies, grouped into tomographic bins.

Photometric redshifts, estimated from galaxy colors, carry systematic biases. The team used self-organising maps, a machine learning technique, to check the calibration. They worked with mock samples resembling the Euclid Wide Survey. The maps help validate whether Euclid meets its strict uncertainty requirement on mean redshift. Reliable calibration underpins the survey's cosmological conclusions about dark matter and dark energy.
arxiv-2508-02979:
Peng Ding and Rick Stevens present a 2025 paper on connecting tools to large language models. Tool-using models can call outside software, but each protocol demands its own setup, schemas, and plumbing. That fragmentation slows developers and bloats code.

Their approach hides protocol differences behind one unified layer. Schemas are generated on their own, tools from many sources are managed together, and calls can run in two concurrent modes for speed. Tests showed code shrinking by sixty to eighty percent across integration cases. Speed rose up to 3.1 times through better concurrency. The design stays compatible with current function-calling standards. The authors offer it as both an architectural idea and a working fix for real projects.
arxiv-2508-03279:
Vasileios Kouvakis, Stylianos Trevlakis, Ioannis Arapakis, and Alexandros-Apostolos Boulogeorgos used spiking neural networks to assign users in drone-aided wireless networks in 2025. Drones acting as flying base stations make the network mixed and fast-changing. Poor assignment can cause congestion and weak service.

Spiking networks use brief pulses and event-driven steps, which can be fast and light on power. The team compared two plans: a central plan that sees the whole network, and a spread plan run at each node. In ray-tracing tests, the spread plan passed ninety percent accuracy, while the central plan ranged higher but varied more. Each plan trades the best choice for one user against a workable choice for all.
arxiv-2508-03379:
Wenxin Mao and co-authors teach language models to write factory software from diagrams rather than vague prose. Plain text requirements hide tangled behaviors and data flows. That is common in service-based systems. Their framework starts from a rich sequence diagram. It adds decision tables and interface specs, which removes guesswork from the wording.

Before any code is written, the system first works out a clear graph of data links between services. They frame that step as a math-style reasoning task with tight rules. That suits what the models do best. Static checks then prune the graph to keep it manageable. The authors argue that making the links clear first should raise how often the code comes out right.
arxiv-2508-03979:
Arafat Sultan and Ramón Fernandez Astudillo trim the cost of self-consistency in language models in a 2025 paper. Self-consistency samples many chains of thought and votes among them, which burns tokens fast. Long reasoning tasks make that bill hard to justify in daily use.

Their fix prunes rival drafts early while all chains still run in parallel. Two cheap signals guide the cuts: the model's own confidence, and how well a kept subset covers the words of all drafts. A fast weighted set cover algorithm makes those calls. Tests on five models and three math sets show real token savings. Parallel strength survives, since pruning never serializes the work.
arxiv-2508-04079:
Joshua Petrack and David Doty break a speed record in 2025 for simulating chemical reactions exactly. Reaction networks, where molecules meet and transform by fixed rules, model everything from cell chemistry to epidemics, and the standard Gillespie algorithm steps through one reaction at a time.

That one-at-a-time pace means simulating a long chain of reactions costs at least one unit of time per step. Petrack and Doty show how to do better: their method simulates exact random reaction sequences in less than constant time per reaction on average. Faster exact simulation lets scientists follow far larger chemical systems faithfully.
arxiv-2508-04179:
Srinivasa Varadhan and co-authors measure in 2025 how close text to speech systems come to fooling human listeners. Scores that claim human parity may not survive a deception test, so the team defines a fooling rate: how often machine speech is taken for human. They ran a large scale test across open and commercial systems.

Three lessons stand out. Claims of parity from standard scores often failed the deception test. Tests should use lively human reference speech, since flat samples set a low bar. Commercial systems nearly matched humans on fresh text, while open systems still lagged on natural talk. Tuning on fine data helped but did not close the gap. The authors call for human centered tests.
arxiv-2508-04279:
Haoyu Jia and co-authors ask in a 2025 study whether a chat model can do ordinary machine learning work on its own. Their framework, Mockingbird, tells the model to role-play the needed functions, run a task, then reflect on its mistakes and try again. The loop mimics how a junior analyst might iterate.

On several standard tasks the model reached acceptable scores without task-specific code. Yet self-reflection alone could not beat the gains from expert-written documents or human feedback. The study maps both the promise and the ceiling of handing routine data work to a talking model.
arxiv-2508-04479:
Hashini Gunatilake and co-authors explore in 2025 how empathy shows up in software work, and when it helps or hinders. Feeling with others shapes teamwork, talk, and choices in building software, yet its forms in daily practice were poorly mapped. The team ran twenty-two interviews and a large survey of 116 practitioners.

Their findings chart how empathy is expressed on teams, what drives staff to show it, and which tasks call for it most. Some activities gain little from it, and outside factors can raise or lower it. The authors draw practical lessons for teams and researchers who want the benefits of empathy without forcing it where it does not fit.
arxiv-2508-04579:
Wahei Hara proves that two mirror-image geometric spaces share the same derived category, for a recently found flop of type D4, in a 2025 paper. A flop swaps a curve between two spaces, and physicists and geometers both ask whether the swap changes the deeper category of sheaves.

Hara builds tilting bundles on both sides of Kanemitsu's local model. Those bundles bridge the two categories and settle the equivalence. A payoff follows for surfaces: general K3 surfaces of degree twelve pair up equivalently. The construction is harder than in the author's earlier G2 case. The result adds one more confirmed brick to the wall of flop conjectures.
arxiv-2508-04679:
Amit Kumar Das and Klaus Mueller present MisVisFix, a dashboard that finds and fixes misleading charts with help from large language models, in a 2025 paper. Bad charts can bend what readers take from data, and most earlier tools only flag the problem.

The dashboard checks a chart, explains each fault in plain words, and draws a corrected version. It sorts faults as major, minor, or possible concerns, and it caught 96 percent of chart faults in the team's tests, covering all 74 known types of chart trickery. A chat box lets users ask about a chart or ask for changes. Tests with chart experts and fact-checking tool builders found the flags accurate and the advice useful.
arxiv-2508-05079:
Sabrina Mulinacci and Massimo Ricci generalize in 2025 a classic equation that captures how lifetimes forget the past. Kaminsky's equation singles out the Gompertz law for one lifetime; later work carried it to pairs. The pair here lets the survival law after a shared threshold be any time-varying distortion of the plain one, not just a fixed reshaping.

The single-lifetime version yields only a trivial case, so the study centers on the weak paired version. The authors trace how the time-varying distortion bends aging behavior and the dependence between the two remaining lifetimes, using time-varying rank and tail measures. A mixing recipe builds a wide family of examples, aimed at insurance risk work.
arxiv-2508-05179:
Catherine Kobus and co-authors report the ATLANTIS team entry to a 2025 shared task on finding made up text in question answering. Language models can state false or misleading content with confidence, called hallucination. The task asked systems to mark the exact spans of text that were made up, in answers across several languages.

The team tried methods with and without outside context. They used few shot prompting of a large model, token level classification, and a model fine tuned on made up training data. Their entries took top places in Spanish and strong places in English and German. The work stresses that good context is key to catching false spans.
arxiv-2508-05779:
Pengyu Liu and co-authors present ConiQ, a compiler for quantum error correction on neutral atom arrays, in a 2025 paper. Layered codes, in which small codes nest inside larger ones, are very space efficient. Yet they lacked cheap logical gates, and they need heavy parallelism and long range links that strain most hardware.

Neutral atom arrays supply both traits. The compiler adds a gate method that uses code symmetries to cut overhead sharply against distillation based routes. A virtual atom layer lets it optimize level by level. Tests show huge cuts in space time cost and compile time against leading compilers. Layered codes look more practical for near term fault tolerant machines.
arxiv-2508-05979:
Students who ask a chatbot for answers often learn passively, and teachers worry about the shortcut. Xinming Yang, Haasil Pujara, and Jun Li flip the arrangement in a 2025 paper: students must teach the language model instead. Questions are designed with built-in knowledge gaps that only the student can fill.

Their system, Socrates, deploys the exercise with little overhead for instructors. In an undergraduate computer science course, the method produced statistically significant gains over earlier cohorts taught the usual way. Teaching forces the student to organize, check, and defend their understanding, the very work passive prompting skips. The authors present the setup as a cheap, practical framework for deeper engagement with course material.
arxiv-2508-06279:
Shamil Asgarli and Dragos Ghioca study what happens when two starting points, pushed through the same simple rule again and again, land on the same value. Their 2025 paper works over number fields where arithmetic wraps around a prime count, a setting that makes the question harder.

The rule in question raises a value to a fixed power and adds a shifting constant. The authors give exact terms for when the set of constants that force a meeting point is endless. They also probe the case where all starting points sit inside a small finite field. There, computer data point to a surprise pattern the authors offer as a conjecture. The work extends a line of questions long studied only in ordinary arithmetic.
arxiv-2508-06679:
Michael Kopreski and George Shaji build geometric models for the symmetry groups of surfaces with infinitely many holes and ends, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Mapping class groups collect all the ways a surface can be deformed into itself. Infinite-type surfaces push that group into huge, uncountable territory.

The authors take a well-behaved subgroup of such a group and construct a graph whose vertices are simple arcs and curves on the surface. The group acts on this graph, and the orbit map from group to graph is a coarse equivalence, meaning the graph faithfully mirrors the group's large-scale shape. When the group is boundedly generated, the graph becomes a Cayley-type graph and the map a quasi-isometry. For the standard big mapping class groups, they conclude the asymptotic dimension is infinite. The result completes a classification project for these groups' dimension.
arxiv-2508-06879:
Michael Dorner and co-authors ask software developers where code review is heading, in a 2025 study. Code review — colleagues reading each change before it merges — is a bedrock habit of team programming. Automation now writes, checks, and even reviews code, which puts the human ritual in flux.

The team surveyed one hundred developers at five software-driven firms. Questions covered how much time review takes today, what gets reviewed, and how both may shift over five years. Open answers invited hopes and worries in the developers' own words. Tensions surfaced between speed, trust, and learning on the job. The results give tool builders and team leads a grounded view of what practitioners expect.
arxiv-2508-07079:
Aslam and co-authors test a robot control system that predicts how pedestrians will move before choosing its own path. Safe travel through crowds is a core challenge for mobile robots. Their controller pairs model predictive control with a learned predictor called Social-Implicit. Tests ran on a real Continental Corriere robot at varied crowd densities. The learned system was compared with a simple constant-velocity model.

The learned predictor cut forecast errors by up to 76% when crowds were thin. In dense scenes it improved safety and made motion smoother. Real-world runs also showed that lab scores can mislead: the learned model gave broader, more cautious forecasts in live use. The team stresses testing the whole system, not just parts.
arxiv-2508-07279:
Vasudha Varadarajan and co-authors build MAQuA, a screening system that asks each patient only the questions that teach it the most. Their 2025 paper tackles a burden problem in mental health checks: long fixed questionnaires tire users, yet many symptoms must be screened at once. Language models make interactive screening possible, but naive chat wastes turns.

MAQuA joins language modeling of answers with item response theory, the statistics behind adaptive testing. At each step it picks the question with the highest information across several symptom dimensions at once. On a new dataset, scores settled with half to nearly nine tenths fewer questions than random order. Early stopping cut the load further. The system held up across inward and outward symptom types, from depression to eating disorders.
arxiv-2508-07479:
Veseli, Chibane, Toneva, and Koller show in twenty twenty-five that language models' place biases in long texts shift as inputs near the model's memory limit. Models often use facts near the start or end of a text better than facts in the middle, the lost-in-the-middle effect. Past long-text studies found this unevenly, so the team measured input length relative to each model's window instead of in raw size.

The middle dip was strongest when inputs filled up to half the window. Past that, the start advantage faded while the end advantage held, so the dip vanished into a plain distance effect. Reasoning scores mostly inherited the same bias from retrieval. The authors say benchmark design should reckon with relative length.
arxiv-2508-07579:
Ziqi Pan and five co-authors follow a hashtag's migration between platforms and cultures, in a 2025 paper. The tag #wlw, women loving women, traveled from TikTok to the Chinese platform RedNote when a brief United States ban scare pushed users across. The authors ran a two-phase content analysis of four hundred eighteen posts from January and April. They compared how the tag was used during its arrival and its later spread.

Arrival succeeded through bold importation by the newcomers, mutual interpretation between the two populations, and discussion among RedNote natives. Hashtags act as identity markers, so a tag's journey traces a community negotiating belonging across languages. The case offers rare evidence on how online cultures actually blend.
arxiv-2508-07779: Deepalakshmi D and Lisa Mathew open a fresh branch of pattern machines that read pictures on honeycomb grids, in work from 2025. They define two new classes of finite automata for hexagonal grids. One class sweeps back and forth across the grid. The other returns to the start of each row. The paper lays the formal base for both classes and probes what they can compute. It also maps how the language families they define relate, and where the two classes agree.
arxiv-2508-07979:
Giulia Cavalleri, Pierluigi Colli, and Elisabetta Rocca proved in 2025 that a tumor growth model with heat is well posed, meaning its math yields sound, unique answers. Their system follows the Caginalp phase-field style: one equation tracks tumor and healthy shares, one tracks heat, and one tracks nutrient spread. Pull effects toward nutrients and active transport are folded in, with sealed borders.

The proof works in two steps, smoothing the energy term and building answers piece by piece. Under stronger smoothness the team also gets strong solutions, and shows that near starts stay near, which seals uniqueness. The model is aimed at growth under heat therapy, where warmth is used to fight the tumor.
arxiv-2508-08179:
Sihan Zhao and co-authors build a score for computer-generated human motion that judges looks and physics together, in a 2025 paper. Generated motion serves games, film, sport, and rehab, but grading it is slippery: people judge by eye, coarsely, while physics checks ignore perception. Their fix starts with a new yardstick for the physical side, the smallest edit that would make a motion obey physical law.

Those edit sizes give smooth, continuous labels to train on. Their metric, PP-Motion, learns from the physics labels and from human ratings at once, with a training loss that rewards correlation with both. In experiments it matched physical law and tracked human judgment better than earlier metrics. The authors aim it at animation and virtual reality pipelines, where bad motion is easy to make and hard to grade.
arxiv-2508-08279:
Ziqi Wang and co-authors forecast water quality with rainfall built in, in a 2025 paper. Rain drives runoff, dilution, and stirred sediment, all of which swing water quality fast. Classic physics models capture this but need heavy site-by-site tuning.

Their data-driven system, RaiNet, learns water patterns at several time scales at once. A trend tool tracks irregular local swings in each station's record. Rainfall events are built per station from gridded rain data, with time lags honored. A fusion gate then mixes the streams with care for scale and delay. Long-range forecasts across sites gain a model that respects weather.
arxiv-2508-08379:
Oleksii Ihnatenko and Maksym Ovchynnikov sharpen a key number in cosmology with a new simulation tool, in work from 2025. The number, N-eff, counts the effective species of light particles in the early universe and tests the standard cosmological model.

Their method simulates cosmic neutrinos directly with a Monte Carlo solver of the Boltzmann equation. The full solver includes the electron's mass, mixing among three neutrino flavors, and quantum corrections to the hot plasma's behavior. Applied to standard neutrino decoupling, it gives N-eff of 3.0439, give or take 0.0006, matching state-of-the-art results. The tool can also explore non-standard early-universe scenarios.
arxiv-2508-08779:
Roberto Aloisio, Antonio Ambrosone, and Carmelo Evoli use a single record-breaking neutrino to test ideas about dark matter, in a 2025 paper. A deep-sea detector recently caught a neutrino with far more energy than any seen before. If super-heavy dark matter particles exist and slowly decay, they would spray out just such particles, so the event offers a rare check.

The team built a framework that weighs the new event against other evidence: neutrino counts from two other observatories, and gamma-ray limits from the sky. The combined check sets the tightest bounds yet on how long super-heavy dark matter must live before decaying. The authors also show that neutrinos from our own galaxy's center carry real weight in such tests. Future hunts in that direction, they argue, could settle whether these giant particles feed the high-energy sky.
arxiv-2508-08879:
Haeun Yu and co-authors present CulTrace in a 2025 paper, a method for watching how a large language model thinks about culture on the inside. Earlier studies judged cultural awareness only from the model's answers, which shows what goes wrong but not why. CulTrace instead traces activity inside the model layer by layer while it answers cultural questions, mapping when and where the relevant culture gets picked out.

The team finds a steady three-stage pattern: the model first takes in the question's topic, then settles on the culture involved, and only then narrows to an answer. That middle step runs late and muddy for cultures that are rare in training data, which explains many wrong answers. The authors argue that fixing cultural bias will require working on these internal steps, not just scoring final outputs.
arxiv-2508-09179:
MRI scans are slow because the machine samples less data than the image needs, and Hongli Chen and co-authors rebuild the missing picture with a state-space model in a 2025 paper. Their architecture, HiFi-Mamba, splits the signal by frequency before reconstructing it.

A W-Laplacian block decouples the data into low- and high-frequency streams. The low stream, carrying global structure, goes to the Mamba blocks, which model long-range patterns in linear time. The high stream, carrying edges and fine anatomy, is folded back through adaptive state-space modulation so detail survives. A single-direction scan replaces the redundant multi-directional scanning of earlier vision Mambas. On standard benchmarks the system beat convolutional, transformer, and other Mamba rivals in reconstruction accuracy while staying compact, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-09379:
Ting Gong, Yeqin Liu, and Yu Shen study twisted sheaves, a generalization of ordinary sheaves used in modern geometry. A twist is set by a class in the Brauer group of the space. Tensoring every twisted sheaf by one fixed sheaf gives a transformation of the whole category. The authors ask when that transformation secretly does nothing.

They prove it acts as the identity exactly when the chosen sheaf is the structure sheaf itself. Any other choice moves the category in a detectable way. As a payoff, the Picard group of line bundles acts faithfully on the derived category of twisted sheaves. That holds for any Noetherian scheme. The result pins down the symmetries of these categories. It tells geometers that line bundles leave distinct fingerprints on twisted worlds.
arxiv-2508-09679:
Quantum gravity research increasingly studies small patches of spacetime rather than the whole universe at once. Charalampos Theofilis and Wolfgang Wieland lay foundations for computing transition amplitudes inside such a patch, a causal diamond. Their account assumes only basic quantum theory and relativity, not one chosen theory of quantum gravity.

The building block is a slab of light-like surface with a past and a future corner. Each slab gets a state space that splits into interior and corner parts. With vacuum states for the bulk and boundary symmetries, and a projector onto physical states, amplitudes arise by joining boundary states along the diamond's pattern. The resulting amplitudes obey the expected symmetry identities and charge conservation. The authors close by sketching how rival quantum gravity programs could each fill in the scheme.
arxiv-2508-09979:
Sharma and co-authors measured neutron capture elements in stars that host planets in a 2025 paper, with the byline listing the team by initials. Their sample covers one hundred sixty sun like stars in the northern sky, including dozens with several planets. High resolution spectra came from a Lithuanian observatory telescope. Abundances of nine heavy elements were derived line by line against model atmospheres.

Most elements in planet hosts follow the galaxy's general chemical story. Three, though, sit higher in planet hosts than in matched reference stars. Links between abundance and planet mass were generally positive, with a few elements showing no trend. Planet hosts also skew toward enrichment in hard to vaporize elements. Older multi planet dwarf stars tended to show smaller or negative slopes, a pattern the authors note for follow up.
arxiv-2508-10079: Andrada Pojar proves a clean split for a class of matrices in a 2025 paper. The matrices at hand are the ones whose root data stays as simple as can be. Some of them split into a sum of two parts. One part returns to itself when raised to a fixed power. The other fades to zero when raised in steps. For all such matrices over fields of odd prime tone, the fade part can be taken to die at the third power.
arxiv-2508-10479:
Alexander Merkov and co-authors warn that hidden bias haunts shopping recommenders in a 2025 paper. Confounding strikes when an unseen factor drives both a choice and its outcome. Recommenders seem safe because platforms log nearly everything about a click.

Yet routine practices quietly throw logged facts away, recreating the blind spot. Feature building, A/B testing habits, and modular pipelines all play a part. Simulations show how each practice bends measured effects off course. Fixes are offered for builders who want honest product decisions. The lesson crosses fields: ignored data is as dangerous as missing data.
arxiv-2508-10579:
Katherine Bennett and co-authors report new space telescope transits of a rocky planet around a red dwarf, in this 2025 paper. The planet, GJ 1132 b, is a touch larger and heavier than Earth. It circles its small, bright star in under two days.

Past attempts to read its atmosphere gave mixed and contested results. The team add two transits taken with the Webb telescope's near-infrared tool. Combined with earlier data, the spectrum comes out featureless. A flat spectrum can mean no atmosphere or one that hides its marks. Either answer shapes how astronomers judge rocky planets near red dwarfs. More visits may settle whether air clings to this hot world.
arxiv-2508-10879:
Johanna Düngler and Amartya Sanyal work on a privacy-preserving form of principal component analysis, a standard tool for finding the main patterns in data. Their 2025 paper asks how to find not just the top pattern, but the top several, from random matrices, without leaking facts about any single person's data.

Older methods needed huge sample sizes or added so much noise that results suffered. Their repeating algorithm adjusts its noise as it goes and handles any number of top patterns. They prove error bounds that match a lower limit they also derive, up to a small factor. Tests back the theory against rival methods.
arxiv-2508-10979:
Matthew Low asks if clash rigs can run the famed test of close-held truth in a 2025 paper. That truth says near things rule near things, and far twins share no spook link. Quantum pairs break its bounds in fine bench tests.

At a clash rig no one reads a grain's spin head-on. Hands guess it from the spray of its death, a guess that lands true at a set rate. Low shows that with such a noisy read, no test of the old truth can be run at all: the gap can not be shut. Yet the twin links are still there in the spray, still read true, and still tell lore of the grains. The paper sorts what rigs can and can not claim.
arxiv-2508-11079:
Cheongho Han and a large team of co-authors weighed four pairs of stars or planets by gravitational microlensing, in a 2025 paper. Microlensing happens when a foreground pair bends light from a background star. Sharp spikes in the brightening mark the pair's edges and reveal its angular size. Long events let Earth's motion add a second measure, the parallax.

The team screened events from three survey years for both traits. Four events qualified for full mass and distance solutions. Combining spike timing, source color, and parallax pinned down each lens system on its own. Most pairs turned out to hold two low-mass components, based on the part of the analysis shown. Direct masses like these anchor models of what unseen pairs across the galaxy are made of.
arxiv-2508-11179:
Pei Liu and co-authors built PTMPicker in 2025 to help developers choose among a flood of pretrained models. Keyword search on model hubs often misses what a developer really needs. License terms, hardware limits, and bias concerns rarely appear in simple function descriptions. PTMPicker first defines a structured template of the attributes that matter for a model.

Both candidate models and user requests are rewritten in that shared format. Embedding similarity judges the function-related attributes, while crafted prompts check special constraints like licenses. The team scraped nearly 544,000 models from Hugging Face and synthesized over fifteen thousand search requests. In tests, most sampled requests found a suitable model in the top ten results. The authors offer the tool as a practical front door to model hubs.
arxiv-2508-11379:
Ramil Khafizov and co-authors present in 2025 a guided method for rebuilding 3D scenes from photos. Fast modern methods work from images alone, yet real projects often hold extra data such as depth maps, camera settings, or camera spots. Their method, G-CUT3R, extends a fast base model to use that extra help.

A small encoder for each kind of extra data turns it into features, which are blended with the image features through a zero-start link. Any mix of extra data can be fed in at run time, or none at all. Across many benchmarks the guided method scored clear gains, which shows the value of priors that projects already have on hand.
arxiv-2508-11479:
Tatiana Zemskova, Aleksei Staroverov, Dmitry Yudin, and Aleksandr Panov present OVSegDT, a robot navigation policy that finds objects named in free language, in a 2025 paper. The target object may belong to a category the robot never saw in training. End-to-end policies often memorize simulator scenes and collide often in new ones.

Their lightweight transformer grounds the goal with a mask-predicting branch and an extra segmentation loss. A second component adjusts the balance between copying demonstrations and trial-and-error learning, based on the policy's own uncertainty. Training needed a third fewer samples and collisions halved. On a standard benchmark it matched seen-category success on unseen categories.
arxiv-2508-11579:
Karina LaRubbio, Alyssa Lanter, Seihyun Lee, Mahima Ramesh, and Diana Freed study how families can shield older adults from deepfake scams, in a research paper from 2025. Faked voices and videos now mimic grandchildren in fake emergencies, pressing elders to send money fast. The realism erodes the old cues people used to spot fraud.

Focus groups with thirty-seven adults over sixty-five explored what they know and fear about such scams. Most lean on trusted relatives to check suspicious calls and build safe habits. The authors propose enlisting youth, whose likenesses are often stolen, as active partners in family defense against these scams.
arxiv-2508-11879:
Hugh Dennin, a solo author, wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on padded Schubert polynomials. Schubert polynomials are a key tool in algebraic combinatorics. Recent work showed that a certain operator expands with positive terms in this basis.

Gaetz and Tung proved a matching positivity result for a dual operator acting on padded Schubert polynomials for a dominant permutation. Dennin gives a new proof of their result. His proof uses the combinatorics of pipe dreams, which are diagram-like objects used to study these polynomials. The paper offers a more visual route to a result first shown by other means.
arxiv-2508-11979:
Agostino Capponi, Garud Iyengar, Bo Yang, and Daniel Bienstock model virtual trading in power markets. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, though the pack title names only the first author. In these markets, power is bought a day ahead and then balanced in real time. Virtual traders bet on the price gap between the two, with no power to deliver.

Without them, buyers bid low in the day-ahead market, which drags its price below the real-time price. Virtual trading shrinks that gap, and can close it when traders are many. Yet the amount bought a day ahead still falls short of true need. Data from two state grid firms back the model.
arxiv-2508-12179:
Yuta Noma and co-authors present a compact way to work with new surface formats in graphics, in work from 2025. Meshes are the classic way to store shapes, and many tools exist for them. New formats render fast and stay small, but they lack those tools.

Their method learns a small neural map from a rough mesh to the true surface. The whole store takes only a few hundred kilobytes, so it sends fast. From the map, users can pull out clean meshes for study and shape work. The method also shrinks stored field data for quick delivery. Tests show it is fast and exact enough for live, shared geometry work.
arxiv-2508-12279:
Jun Liu and co-authors adapt image segmentation networks to fit the varied hardware on self-driving platforms, published in 2025. Cars face diverse scenes, and each platform has its own limits on compute and its own needs for precision. A network that suits one car may waste resources, or fall short, on another.

Their method, TSLA, adjusts a network through three controls: a width multiplier, the depth of the final classifier, and its kernel size. This allows broad scaling, fine tuning of the last layers, and scene-specific choices. A Bayesian search with a stand-in model explores settings within tight compute budgets. The approach aims to match each deployment's cost and accuracy needs through automatic search rather than hand design.
arxiv-2508-12379:
Rongzheng Wang and co-authors published this graph reasoning study in 2025. Language models handle small graph puzzles well but falter on large real networks with hard questions. Their working memory cannot hold long-range structure through many reasoning steps. The team built GraphCogent, a team of cooperating agents modeled on human working memory. It splits graph reasoning into three jobs: sensing, buffering, and executing.

One module standardizes how graphs are written and samples key subgraphs. A second indexes the graph data across formats. A third solves the task by calling tools, or building new ones when needed. The team also released Graph4real, a benchmark spanning web, transport, social, and citation networks with twenty-one task types. Graphs there run up to ten times larger than in older benchmarks. Their system, built on a modest model, beat a far larger rival by half and cut token use sharply.
arxiv-2508-12579:
Cella Sum and co-authors report a 2025 study of tech workers who are forming unions in the United States. Tech jobs are often told as tales of prestige and comfort, yet many workers face unstable and split work lives. The team spoke with forty-four worker-organizers across roles, from engineers to gig workers.

Organizers said weak job security holds back joint action and leaves workers feeling powerless. Still, they are building ties in their workplaces and growing a shared grasp of the forces at play. The authors place these drives inside wider industry trends and ask how their own field can stand with the movement.
arxiv-2508-13579:
Language models read medical text fluently but stumble over patient records. Health records are time-stamped, high-dimensional, and structured, a poor match for prose-trained models. Yue Fang and co-authors teach the model itself to reason over records, rather than borrowing answers from outside tools. Their framework, EAG-RL, learns in two stages. First, expert-guided tree search builds step-by-step reasoning paths that train the model.

Then reinforcement learning aligns the model's attention with the features expert systems find clinically important. On two real record datasets, the method improved reasoning scores by about fifteen percent on average. It also held up better when features were perturbed and when tasks changed. The aim is a model whose clinical judgment lives inside it, not in a crutch.
arxiv-2508-14179:
Jorge L Rosa-Raíces and David T Limmer present a cheaper way to compute free energy in this 2025 study. Free energy gaps tell chemists how likely a molecule is to change form, but standard methods need long simulations to cross between forms. Their method learns from the wasted energy, or dissipation, along a fast switching path between the two forms.

A flow-based learning model is trained to match the force field behind that wasted energy. With the learned field plus short runs of data, the method gives upper and lower bounds on the free energy. If the field were perfect, both bounds would meet at the exact value. On atom models, the method cut computing cost a great deal with almost no loss of accuracy.
arxiv-2508-14579:
Salmaso and co-authors analyze, in a 2025 paper, a supernova with a triple-peaked light curve, and use it to sort a strange family of stellar explosions. Type IIn supernovae blow up inside dense shells of gas the star shed earlier. The 2009ip-like branch first flickers with a dim peak, a dying star's unrest, then erupts in earnest.

SN 2024hpj showed three peaks and spectra mixing broad and narrow lines in a complex blend. Comparing it with kin from the literature and four unpublished cases, the team found these events favor star-forming neighborhoods. Sorting the family by brightness and speed yielded four sub-classes, hinting at unlike parent stars. Shell mass and layout seem to script much of the variety. A rate count rounds out the census.
arxiv-2508-14979:
Lennart Bittel, Francesco Mele, Jens Eisert, and Antonio Mele give a fast method to measure Gaussian states of light with firm error guarantees, in work from twenty twenty-five. Such states are basic tools in quantum optics, and reading them well matters for sensing. Old methods needed more samples as the state's energy grew.

Their algorithm's sample count depends only on the number of modes, barely on the energy. That is a huge gain over prior methods. It uses tools labs already have: a squeezed vacuum helper, passive optics, and homodyne detection. An adaptive step steadily lowers the system's squeezing. The team also tightens bounds for the standard heterodyne method.
arxiv-2508-15579:
Akaraphon Jantaraphum and co-authors present a 2025 paper on searching DNA databases for relatives of an unknown person. The search weighs two options: that two people are related, or that they are not. Standard methods assume one shared genetic background for everyone, but real populations split into groups with different gene rates.

That split can bias the result. The team's new statistic adds a sorting step that guesses which group each profile comes from, using a simple classifier. Older fixes, such as using average gene rates or the highest and lowest ratios, only partly handle the problem. Tests show whether the sorting step sharpens family search results.
arxiv-2508-15679:
Eric Ye, Ren Tao, and Natasha Jaques open a playground for studying how AI agents learn from each other. Real settings are social: many self-driven agents, some of them expert, share one world. The authors argue that a learner surrounded by experts can pick up skills faster, but open-ended worlds for testing that idea were missing. Their environment lets many agents chase separate, complex goals at once.

Agents can profit from watching experts, and they may drift into cooperation against shared enemies, or into building and sharing tools for long projects. The team uses the world to measure how social learning changes performance, and whether rivalry or teamwork helps more. They offer the environment as a testbed for socially intelligent agents that must learn the way people do, from the crowd around them.
arxiv-2508-15779:
Leo Yicheng Yang presents two new ways to count grids of numbers that never decrease along rows and columns. The grids have two rows, with entries chosen from one up to a set limit. Counting such grids exactly is a classic problem in combinatorics, the study of counting patterns.

The first method matches each grid with a chemical pattern: the bond layouts of certain ring-shaped molecules built from hexagons. The second method turns the count into a count of pairs of stair-like paths that never cross. Each match lets known results from one field solve the other. Yang's paper shows how problems that look unrelated can share the same hidden structure.
arxiv-2508-15879:
Filipe Ribeiro and co-authors study how light waves travel through a twisted plasma that may fill the space between stars, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model treats the plasma as cold, even, and free of crashes, with rules that link electric and magnetic effects. New wave modes appear for right- and left-handed round waves.

Odd light effects show up, like a double flip in how the wave twists as it goes. At low rates a changed whistler-type wave with right-handed spin appears. Data from five pulsars cap the twist strength at very small values. Readers get both a rich theory picture and hard limits from real sky data.
arxiv-2508-15979:
Surajit Das and Pavel Zun present a 2025 method, described in the text as semi-unsupervised segmentation, for outlining cells in microscope images without any labeled training data. Unstained live cells are faint and unevenly lit, and deep learning tools need costly labeled sets and hardware. Their method finds the background from local brightness spread. Fuzzy logic and spatial statistics then settle the doubtful pixels, and a saved calibration profile cleans the result for reuse.

The tool runs on a normal CPU and offers a point-and-click interface for non-programmers. On unstained muscle cell images it beat two leading deep learning tools on overlap scores. On a large phase-contrast data set it also scored well, with strong expert agreement. It even handled laser-marked polymer surfaces, showing range beyond biology.
arxiv-2508-16579:
Yansong Du, Yutong Deng, Yuting Zhou, Feiyu Jiao, Jian Song, and Xun Guan fuse two depth-sensing technologies to overcome each one's limits, in a two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper. Indirect time-of-flight sensors give low resolution, narrow fields of view, and distorted structure.

The framework first reprojects the narrow time-of-flight depth map into the wide camera image coordinates through precise geometric calibration. A dual-encoder network then merges depth and color features, guided by monocular depth priors to recover fine structure. Cross-modal cues and depth consistency constraints sharpen edges and widen coverage seamlessly. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets beat state-of-the-art methods on accuracy and visual quality.
arxiv-2508-16679:
Gamal Nashed and Salvatore Capozziello work out black hole solutions in a modified gravity theory in a 2025 paper. Their setting is a spacetime with two space dimensions and one of time. The theory reshapes gravity through a quantity called non metricity, with a quadratic correction added. They solve for charged and uncharged black holes with round symmetry.

The corrections bend the solutions away from the standard form for this dimension. The team compute curvature measures to classify singularities, finding them weaker than in general relativity. Heat, entropy, and heat capacity all obey the first law of black hole thermodynamics. They also track test particle paths and photon orbits for stability. Multi horizon setups appear possible. The paper maps how this gravity theory changes black holes in low dimensions.
arxiv-2508-16979:
Valentin Leplat, Salman Ahmadi-Asl, JunJun Pan, and Ning Zheng develop, in a 2025 math paper, step by step methods to compute a special inverse for matrices whose entries are quaternions. Quaternions extend complex numbers, and their multiplication does not commute, which makes many standard matrix tricks fail. The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse is a general purpose inverse used across signal and data work.

Their methods work natively with quaternions, without translating the problem into real or complex form. One refines a classic Newton-Schulz loop, with care for left and right identities in non square cases. Higher order versions converge faster near the answer. They add a randomized sketch method, a hybrid of the two, and a gradient method on the normal equations. Each comes with convergence analysis and factorizations that cut the work per step.
arxiv-2508-17679:
Trinayan Baruah, Kaustubh Shivdikar, Sara Prescott, and David Kaeli published a computing paper in 2025 profiling how Mamba-style sequence models behave while training on graphics processors. These state space models dodge the quadratic cost of attention, suiting long sequences in text, video, and graphs. The team built a suite of representative models spanning several architectures. Profiling tools then measured where time and resources go.

Their analysis exposes the demands these workloads place on current hardware design. Findings point to concrete optimizations for keeping performance scaling as models grow. The authors frame the suite as a reference for architects designing chips for the post-transformer wave of sequence models.
arxiv-2508-17779:
Domínguez, Straniero, Piersanti, Giannotti, and Mirizzi modeled in twenty twenty-five how hypothetical axion-like particles would change the late lives of middleweight stars. Stars of three to eleven solar masses can end as white dwarfs, electron-capture supernovae, or full core-collapse supernovae, depending on delicate ignition thresholds. If axion-like particles exist, stars would radiate them away as an extra energy loss.

Computing stellar models across coupling strengths, the team found the critical masses for carbon and neon ignition shift upward. Under current coupling limits, the heaviest star still ending as a carbon-oxygen white dwarf grows by about one solar mass, and the lightest core-collapse progenitor by about seven tenths. Observed supernova data do not yet exclude such particles, though progenitor age estimates may.
arxiv-2508-17879:
Seema Chahal and Brato Chakrabarti study swirling flows in suspensions of spinning particles in a 2025 paper. Active fluids of swimming or driven particles often break into chaotic flows through a known alignment instability. Their particles are chiral: they spin under torque and propel themselves as a result.

Using theory and simulation, the authors find a different route to collective motion. Torque driven flow and self propulsion couple two kinds of order in the fluid, one directional and one orientational. That coupling, not the classic dipolar stress, drives chaotic flows in three dimensions. The results suggest ways to design suspensions that stir themselves. They also offer a framework for studying the flow behavior of chiral fluids more broadly.
arxiv-2508-17979:
Lasse Grimmelt and Jori Merikoski prove new estimates for the divisor function in a 2025 paper. The divisor function counts how many ways a number splits into factors. Its average along arithmetic progressions is a classic hard topic. Moduli with two small factors are their entry point.

Their equidistribution result reaches moduli of a high exponent for almost all cases. Two uses follow from the main estimate. One gives an asymptotic formula for the divisor sum over progressions. The other treats values of a binary cubic polynomial in two variables. Such results feed analytic number theory, where averages over sparse sets test deep conjectures about primes and divisors.
arxiv-2508-18079:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, the Virgo Collaboration, and the KAGRA Collaboration release their gravitational-wave data to the public. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. It covers the first part of the network's fourth observing run. The three detector groups form a worldwide network of observatories. Their strain data and analysis results feed many outside studies. Open release is a standing policy of the network.

Data and results are served through the Gravitational Wave Open Science Center. Outside researchers can reanalyze signals or hunt for new ones. The paper documents what the release contains and how it was produced. Calibration and data quality notes guide proper use. Open data widens the reach of gravitational-wave astronomy well beyond the collaborations.
arxiv-2508-18279:
Jeesu Jung and Sangkeun Jung propose in a 2025 paper a new way to order training tasks for large language models. Teaching in steps, from easy to hard, needs a signal for how hard each task is. Their core claim is simple: tasks that take humans more steps of thought should also be harder for models.

They define depth of thought by counting the steps in a teacher model's chain of thought. Training then runs from shallow tasks to deep ones on that scale. Three claims are set out for tests, on links to known difficulty, gains over other orders, and steadiness across teachers. The paper also sets out a test plan and names risks, such as teacher style skewing the step counts.
arxiv-2508-18779:
Salt that creeps across a surface as it crystallizes can build roses in deserts and pillars by salt lakes, and the same efflorescence eats away at buildings and soils. Wijnhorst, Prat, and Shahidzadeh dig into how these growths organize themselves.

Under controlled evaporation, the porous salt crusts turned out to be self-similar: the same crystallization pattern repeats at scale after scale. Small crystal clusters echo the shape of the whole deposit, like florets in a cauliflower. Imaging and fractal analysis showed orderly cubic microcrystals packed in a hierarchy inside the crust. A growth model then delivered a surprise. The final height of a deposit is set mainly by how much salt was there at the start, not by flow forces inside the crust.
arxiv-2508-18879:
Bengt Friman, Krzysztof Redlich, and Anar Rustamov tackle a theory problem in nuclear physics in a 2025 paper. When two atomic nuclei collide at high speed, scientists study how the numbers of particles bounce around from event to event. Those swings carry clues about the matter made in the crash, but charge rules that hold for the whole system also shape them.

The authors work out exact formulas that link swings seen in a small part of the system to swings in the whole system. They add simple terms for particles pulling together or pushing apart near each other. Matched against data from two experiments, the model shows that these local forces matter a great deal. At high energy, a push between protons fits the data, while at lower energy a pull among three particles is needed.
arxiv-2508-19379:
Anurag Chakraborty and Semih Salihoğlu make recursive graph queries run in parallel more robustly in a 2025 paper. Graph databases answer questions that walk links step by step, such as finding all reachable nodes. Using many processor cores well is vital for speed on large graphs.

Two standard schemes split work by starting node or by the frontier of each step. The authors show both can break down badly on skewed graphs, leaving cores idle while a few grind. Their approach keeps parallelism steady across shapes of data. Database builders get query engines that hold speed on the messy, uneven graphs met in practice, from social networks to supply chains, rather than only on tidy test data.
arxiv-2508-19579:
Haomiao Zhang and eight co-authors push hologram video toward full color, full high grade frames at high speed. Past learned models made phases too smooth, which muddied color. Past hand tuned methods treated each frame alone and wasted time.

Their plan pairs a color split method that shapes light spread with a light net that learns links across frames. In tests the color held true at high frame rates. The net made full frames more than twice as fast as the prior best. Lab demos back the claims for next displays.
arxiv-2508-20079:
Shivam Nadimpalli and Caleb Pascale revisit a known construction in a short 2025 mathematics paper. The topic is the Gaussian perimeter of convex sets, a measure of surface area weighted by the normal bell-shaped distribution. An earlier construction by Nazarov gave a convex set whose weighted surface area comes close to the maximum possible.

The authors give a fresh analysis of that construction. Their argument rests on a notion called convex influence, which tracks how much single coordinates sway a function. The new viewpoint aims to make the near-maximal example easier to understand. Short papers of this kind matter because clean proofs often open the way to new results in high-dimensional geometry and probability.
arxiv-2508-20179:
Dark matter may bump into itself, and a giant galaxy cluster can test that idea. Jackson H O'Donnell and co-authors studied the cluster MACS J0138-2155 in a 2025 paper. The cluster bends light from objects behind it, and it hosts two lensed supernovae. The team paired that bent light with maps of how stars move in the central galaxy.

Each method gave a mass profile for the cluster, and the two agreed well. Joined, they set an upper limit on how strongly dark matter can hit itself. The limit holds at a stated pair speed and a ninety-five percent confidence level. The authors say the joint method is the most detailed single-system study of its kind so far. It should sharpen later work on dark matter and on cosmic distance measures.
arxiv-2508-20279:
Zhuoran Yu and Lee dissect multimodal language models layer by layer to see where seeing becomes reasoning. They train simple probes on each layer's token patterns to predict fine visual classes, then stress the system with reworded prompts, negated concepts, and changed answer formats across three model families.

A steady three-act structure appears. Early layers ground the words in visual features. Middle layers blend language and meaning, where rewordings and negations bite. Final layers shape the answer for output. The acts stay in order across training recipes, but which layers play which role shifts with the base model's design. The probing kit is light and model-agnostic, a reusable X-ray for multimodal systems.
arxiv-2508-20379:
Hyeonyu Kim and co-authors present a way in 2025 to edit images with sound as a guide, not just words. Image editing tools based on diffusion models have grown strong, but some edits are hard to state in text alone. A sound, like a dog's bark or rain, can name what a word list misses.

Past sound guided methods had to be trained on set data to link sound with text, which capped their use in the wild. The new method needs no extra training. It leans on a pre trained encoder that already joins sound, image, and text in one space. Several text and sound prompts can steer one edit at once. The team shows how they close the gap between what the sound encoder gives and what the editing model expects.
arxiv-2508-20579:
Debasis Maji and Debaditya Barman read emotions from face landmark graphs in a 2025 paper. Landmark points from three dimensional alignment become graph nodes for their network. A coarsening step merges points into regions while keeping face layout. Region embeddings then feed the emotion call.

Scores hit about sixty-five percent on a hard wild photo set. A lab face set scored above ninety-four percent in their tests. Region level graphs beat several prior baselines in the study. The graph form also keeps decisions easier to trace than black box nets. Occlusion and varied expressions remain the hard cases the design targets.
arxiv-2508-20879:
Gabriele Fici, Esteban Gabory, and co-authors construct strings with fully scattered transforms in a 2025 paper. The Burrows-Wheeler transform rearranges a string to cluster equal letters, which aids compression. The worst case for clustering is a transform where no two neighbors match at all.

The authors prove such strings exist at every length for alphabets of three or more letters. Their construction uses necklaces, a cyclic form of strings. They also lower-bound how many of these extreme strings exist. The binary alphabet case stays open and links to a famous conjecture about primitive roots. The result closes a basic question in combinatorics on words. It also marks the true worst case for transform-based compressors.
arxiv-2508-21179:
Jorge Saldivar, Anna Gatzioura, and Carlos Castillo build synthetic CVs to create and test fairness aware hiring tools. Hiring algorithms rank floods of applicants, yet they can smuggle in bias by age, sex, or origin. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Testing bias fixes needs CV sets that mirror diverse real people, and none existed. The team shaped features from real CVs given through a donation drive. The result is a public set of well over a thousand synthetic CVs. The authors offer it as a shared benchmark for work on hiring bias, so fixes can be gauged before real use.
arxiv-2508-21479:
A large team builds a quantum relay chain in 2025 with a quantum dot single-photon source at its core. Quantum nets need relays to stretch links for compute, code, and measure tasks across long spans. Their design runs three middle nodes that need no trust, at a pace over 300 megahertz.

A guard-free measure plan sets safe keys over fiber runs up to 300 kilometers in the trials. The source grade lets the chain stay modular and scale to more nodes with ease. The team frames the build as a step toward wide, flexible quantum nets.
arxiv-2508-21779:
Phase reading with bent light states is studied by the authors in a 2025 arXiv paper on quantum measure tools. The setup is a split-path device that reads tiny phase shifts. The states come from bent forms of two classic algebras, built from a shifted swing system with four knobs. Those knobs add tuning range and odd quantum traits.

The team works out the best phase skill any tool could reach for such states. They then test three read-out ways, from split-beam counts to balanced wave mixing. Each way is scored against that best reach. In the right knob ranges, the states let all three ways near the top reach. The frame suits fine sensing work.
arxiv-2509-00179:
Daniel Ablin and Alon Cohen study Markov games in 2025 where a player never sees the payoffs. Markov games extend matrix games over time, with states that shift as players act. Prior work showed a player can compete in repeated symmetric matrix games without payoff data, as long as rival actions are seen.

The authors define a new class of zero-sum symmetric Markov games and formalize three notions of symmetry for it. A player who knows the transition dynamics and watches only the rival's actions can still compete, even if the rival knows the whole game. The learning problem reduces to online learning, which yields methods with guarantees. Hidden-payoff results matter for agents that must act under poor feedback.
arxiv-2509-00779:
Sachin Kumar, with two co-authors, screens perovskite materials for solar water splitting. The process uses sunlight to drive cycles that split water into hydrogen. It is a promising route to clean hydrogen production. Perovskites are a broad family of crystals. Their structure tolerates many element swaps, which aids the search.

The team uses density functional theory, a standard quantum method for materials. They examine strontium-based and strontium-cerium-based perovskites with various metals. Two mixed compounds stand out as promising candidates. One contains manganese and the other contains chromium. Both show an optimal cost for forming oxygen vacancies. That removal step is key in the splitting cycle. Both are also stable at zero kelvin.
arxiv-2509-00979:
Bhima Sankar Manthina leads a team of five authors on noise monitoring with mobile nodes. Urban noise pollution poses a significant threat to public health. Existing monitoring offers limited spatial coverage and adaptability. Their system is IoT-based and works in real time. Sensor nodes ride on a moving vehicle to gather data.

A low-cost sound sensor joins GPS modules in each node. Geotagged noise data are collected at one-second intervals. Nodes are calibrated against a reference meter in the lab. Performance degrades during collection in a moving vehicle, though. Calibration must thus use data collected in motion with the reference device. Random forest regression performs best for mobile calibration. A Hyderabad deployment ran for twenty-seven days. It captured hundreds of thousands of data points.
arxiv-2509-01179:
Yann Bernard studies equations met at the best shapes for a class of curvature energies in four dimensions. These energies do not change under conformal maps, which preserve angles, and they are measured for surfaces of any codimension placed in Euclidean space. Critical points, where the energy is stationary, obey Euler-Lagrange equations that can be hard to handle.

Using symmetries and Noether's theorem, which links each symmetry to a conserved quantity, Bernard recasts those equations into a system with a friendlier analytic form. The approach extends ideas Tristan Riviere developed for the Willmore energy in two dimensions. Better structure in the equations opens the way to proving regularity and other traits of the optimal shapes, a central concern in geometric analysis.
arxiv-2509-01879:
Aman Gupta, Aditi Sheshadri, and Dhruv Suri grade seven AI weather systems on the South Asian monsoon using real observations. Most AI weather grading leans on reanalysis, a blended data product that can hide flaws. Their MAUSAM check uses ground stations, rain gauges, and satellite images instead. The monsoon brings heavy rain and storms where sparse data make forecasts hard.

The models show strong skill on broad traits, from surface heat and winds to rain and cloud cover. Finer traits still fail, with extreme rain underdone, cyclone paths split, and small scale energy off. Errors against observations run notably larger than against reanalysis, so past grades flatter the models. One system proves most consistent overall, with two rivals close behind.
arxiv-2509-02079:
Sanatan Digal and Ajit M Srivastava predict Doppler shifted Hawking radiation from acoustic black holes in heavy ion collisions. When fluid flow turns supersonic, the boundary acts like a black hole horizon for sound. Hawking radiation from such acoustic horizons has been studied in cold atoms and electron fluids. In ultra relativistic collisions, the plasma flow pattern seemed to redshift the signal away to infinity.

Boost invariant flow holds only in a central window of the collision geometry. At large rapidities, meaning far along the beam direction, the flow must deviate from that pattern. An observer there sees a horizon with finite redshift instead. Particle momentum patterns should thus carry a Hawking imprint in that window, while central regions stay unaffected. The prediction opens a fresh observational target.
arxiv-2509-02379:
Yuheng Li and four co-authors present a 2025 medical AI paper on outlining organs and tumours in CT and MRI scans. Most current models handle one task well but transfer poorly across scan types and hospitals.

Their MedDINOv3 adapts DINOv3, a vision foundation model trained on huge natural image sets, to medical data. A plain vision transformer backbone gets multi-scale token merging, which pools features at several sizes. Domain training then uses a curated set of millions of axial CT slices in stages. Across four segmentation benchmarks, the adapted model matched or beat leading specialist systems. The results support shared vision backbones for medical segmentation instead of one model per task.
arxiv-2509-02479:
Zhenghai Xue and six co-authors wrote a 2025 machine learning paper on training language models to reason with external tools over several turns. Reinforcement learning for such tool use often collapses because tool feedback shifts the data distribution mid-training.

The team traces the failure to void turns, steps that produce neither code nor a final answer, which trigger harmful gradient spikes. Their SimpleTIR algorithm simply filters out trajectories containing void turns before each update. That one change stabilises learning without extra machinery. Starting from a base model, scores on the AIME24 maths benchmark more than doubled over a text-only baseline.
