Freed from supervised fine-tuning limits, the model also found richer strategies, including cross-checking its own work and correcting itself.
arxiv-2509-02579:
Mazyar Taghavi and Rahman Farnoosh present a 2025 multi-agent learning paper on sending drone teams to guard wildlife from poachers. Reserves are vast, views are partial, and response must be fast, which makes coordination under uncertainty the core problem.

Their method blends expectation-maximization, an iterative inference routine, with multi-agent reinforcement learning. Latent variables stand for hidden environmental factors and for how agents influence each other, sharpening exploration and teamwork. A custom simulation flies ten drones over habitat of the endangered Iranian leopard. Against standard algorithms such as PPO and DDPG, the approach scored better on detection accuracy, adaptability, and learning speed. Code, the simulation, and training scripts are released publicly.
arxiv-2509-02679:
Paarmita Pandey and eight co-authors present a 2025 astrophysics paper making the first systematic search for gamma rays from explosive dispersal outflows, violent winds thrown off when young massive star clusters interact. Such outflows may accelerate cosmic rays, the high-energy particles filling the galaxy.

Sixteen years of Fermi satellite data cover seven outflows. Three showed gamma-ray emission at the right position; the rest gave no detection. One system, DR21, stood out with a very strong signal and a spectrum cutting off at high energy. Its gamma-ray output, set against the outflow's kinetic energy, implies an acceleration efficiency consistent with shocks in dense gas. The sample spans wide luminosity range, suggesting these outflows add meaningfully to the cosmic ray budget of the galaxy.
arxiv-2509-03079:
Guangyu Yu, Tao Xiang, and Zheng Zhu reported claimed evidence in 2025 for an unusual kind of phase change in quantum Hall bilayers. A bilayer stacks two thin electron sheets. In the quantum Hall regime, strong magnetic fields force electrons into exotic collective states.

Standard theory expects phase changes to fit the Landau pattern, built on broken symmetry. A deconfined quantum critical point breaks that pattern. By tuning the gap between layers, the authors claim a direct, smooth switch between two unlike ordered states. One state flows like a superfluid of excitons, paired electron-hole units; the other forms stripes of charge. Their claim rests on large simulations, exact small-system checks, and several ground-state measures.
arxiv-2509-03179:
Alma M. Liezenga and 6 co-authors studied poisoning attacks on military object detectors in a 2025 paper. Poisoning means slipping corrupted examples into training data so a model learns a hidden weakness. Open datasets and pretrained models make that risk real, and military uses raise the stakes.

The team built a small custom dataset of military and civilian vehicles. They adapted a patch-based attack and found it could succeed, but only after a large share of the data was poisoned, which questions its practicality. They then tested existing detection ideas and found both specialized and general anomaly methods wanting. Their own detector, AutoDetect, uses an autoencoder's reconstruction error on image slices to separate clean from poisoned samples. It outperformed rivals while staying fast and light.
arxiv-2509-03379:
Guoxin Wang and 4 co-authors proposed TinyDrop in 2025, a way to make vision transformers cheaper to run by discarding unimportant image tokens. Vision transformers split an image into tokens and process them all, which is powerful but costly. TinyDrop instead lets a tiny companion model judge which tokens matter during inference.

Tokens rated low in importance are dropped before the large model performs its expensive attention calculations. The framework needs no retraining and no changes to the host model's architecture, so it plugs into many transformer variants. On standard image classification benchmarks it cut floating-point operations by up to about four fifths. Accuracy degradation stayed minimal in those tests. The authors present it as a practical route to efficient transformer-based classification.
arxiv-2509-03979:
Gilles Callebaut and one co-author devote a 2025 research paper to a low-cost, open-source system for tracking Asian hornets back to their nests. The Asian hornet threatens ecosystems and beekeeping across Europe, and destroying nests is the main control route. Finding nests usually means manual triangulation over many trips.

Their system pairs a lightweight Bluetooth Low Energy tag, carried by a captured hornet, with a software-defined radio receiver built in GNU Radio. Bypassing the standard Bluetooth stack, they embed a pseudo-noise sequence in the radio's uncoded physical layer, enabling correlation-based detection of the tag signal. A Yagi antenna and a PlutoSDR receiver sweep digitally to locate the tag. Field tests resolve its angle reliably at fifty metres, with range up to three hundred sixty metres. Everything is released open-source. The modulation raises receiver complexity, but enables future multichannel spreading and individual tag identification.
arxiv-2509-04179: Yihong Hao and two co-authors study a curvature question in complex geometry in a 2025 mathematics paper. Some Kähler spaces carry a metric, a way of measuring, whose holomorphic curvature stays squeezed below zero within a band, called negative pinching. Tied to such a space sits a disc bundle, a family of small discs packaged inside a Hermitian line bundle. The paper relates when the base space admits such a pinched metric to properties of its disc bundle.
arxiv-2509-04479:
Jing Liu, writing alone, investigates how transformers handle rare tokens in a 2025 research paper. Language models predict rare words poorly, and earlier work found specialized plateau neurons that serve them, following a distinctive influence pattern. Whether those neurons organize into dedicated modules stayed unknown. Liu probes neuron influence, clustering built on graphs, and attention head shutdowns in Pythia and GPT-2 XL models.

Rare tokens recruit extra plateau neurons beyond what common tokens need, forming a second computational regime. Those neurons scatter across the network instead of clustering into modules. Attention heads show no special routing toward the specialists either. Specialization emerges from training spreading work around, which preserves flexible, context-sensitive processing.
arxiv-2509-04579:
Subham Saha and three co-authors chart how a future muon collider could discover scalar leptoquarks in a 2025 physics paper. Leptoquarks are hypothetical particles linking quarks and leptons, the two great matter families, and many theories beyond the Standard Model predict them. The studied doublet links light quarks with right-handed neutrinos. Indirect signs appear when leptoquark exchange distorts high-momentum jet pairs, while direct searches produce the particles themselves, singly or in pairs.

With moderate coupling, indirect probes reach masses near four thousand gigaelectronvolts at a five-TeV collider and far higher at ten TeV. Single production, powered by neutrino-assisted decays, extends direct reach into the multi-TeV regime. Both channels together outrun the upgraded LHC's projections.
arxiv-2509-04679:
Simulating flows with two fluids is cheap in a one-dimensional two-fluid model, but runaway instability has long spoiled it. Alexander López-de-Bertodano and one co-author present a physics-based fix in a 2025 paper on nonlinear stability. Earlier approaches relied on unphysical fixes to control Kelvin-Helmholtz instability.

Their method adds a simple turbulent viscosity model. It gives nonlinear stabilisation and stays compatible with inertial coupling. They build analytic and numeric tools to study the dynamics that result. Those tools cover turbulent cascades, chaos, and the formation of churn or slug flow patterns.
arxiv-2509-04779:
Do decoder language models understand humour as well as encoder models can detect it? Eli Borodach, lead author with three co-authors, test that question in a 2025 natural language processing paper. Earlier checks of machine humour understanding stopped at older decoder models, leaving newer systems untested.

The authors fine-tune a decoder model, GPT-4o, and compare it with a fine-tuned encoder, RoBERTa, on humour classification. The decoder's average score nearly matches the encoder's best result in their experiments. They present the finding as evidence that large decoders perform on this nuanced task as strongly as specialist encoders, while the deeper question of understanding remains open.
arxiv-2509-04879:
Repeatedly applying a multiplication operator can generate useful families of functions, but not in every function space. Jahangir Cheshmavar examines that contrast in a solo 2025 analysis note. Earlier work showed such an operator cannot generate a frame, a stable building-block system, in the usual square-integrable space on an interval.

Cheshmavar studies the same operator on the Hardy space of holomorphic functions on the unit disk. There the iterates behave fundamentally differently in frame terms. The note reports new structural results, showing the choice of function space changes what iteration can produce.
arxiv-2509-05179:
Black holes at galaxy centres push back on their hosts through winds and jets that depend on how the holes spin. Filip Huško, lead author with eight co-authors, present a hybrid feedback model for galaxy simulations in a 2025 astronomy paper. The model includes three accretion disc states and two feedback modes, thermal and kinetic jets.

Black hole spin evolves through accretion, mergers, jet spindown, and relativistic torques, and it sets jet direction and efficiency. Implemented in a major simulation code, the model affects galaxies down to small masses. Predicted spins peak for intermediate-mass holes, matching observations, and the intergalactic medium ends up hotter than with thermal feedback alone.
arxiv-2509-05579:
Changes of a shape built from a mirrored four-sided figure are mapped out by Jaesung Bae in a solo 2025 geometry paper. The shape is a Coxeter orbifold, formed from a four-sided Coxeter figure in the projective plane, lifted one step higher and made convex.

This noncompact orbifold arises from two polytopes, a fact Bae uses to pin down its space of convex real projective structures in full. Projective structures record how the shape can bend while keeping straight lines straight. The paper then works through how that space behaves. Orbifolds extend plain spaces by allowing controlled sharp points, and this one is tied to reflection symmetries.
arxiv-2509-05679:
Training deep networks across many machines without waiting for slow workers is studied by Viet Hoang Pham and Hyo-Sung Ahn in a 2025 machine learning paper. Bigger networks and datasets make training slow, and ordinary backpropagation forces processors to lock step with each other.

Their method merges data parallelism, where machines train on different data slices, with fully decoupled parallel backpropagation, where layers update without waiting. More data is processed per round and locking delays shrink. The authors prove convergence to critical points under stated conditions. Tests training a classifier on the CIFAR-10 image set support the efficiency claims.
arxiv-2509-06079:
A caption-first trick for solving physics problems with pictures wins a major challenge in a 2025 technical report led by Hao Liang with five co-authors. Even leading models that reason well in text stumble when a problem mixes diagrams with words. The team's framework has the model describe the visual content, then reason over text and caption together.

The approach took first place in the SeePhys challenge at the ICML 2025 AI for Math workshop. Tests on the MathVerse benchmark for geometric reasoning show the method travels beyond physics. The authors release their code, presenting caption-assisted reasoning as a simple, robust bridge between seeing and reasoning for science problems.
arxiv-2509-06579:
Building new camera views of a scene one frame at a time is the advance claimed by Xin Kong and four co-authors in a 2025 computer vision paper. Multi-view diffusion models can imagine a scene from new angles, but most produce all views at once. That fixes the number of views and slows generation down.

Their model, CausNVS, works autoregressively, generating each view in sequence so any mix of input and output angles is possible. Training uses causal masking, noise added per frame, and camera pose codes based on relative positions between frame pairs. During generation, a sliding window with memory caching and noise conditioning keeps the sequence from drifting. Experiments show wide camera paths, flexible view synthesis, and strong picture quality across settings, which suits world modeling.
arxiv-2509-06879:
Phases that exist only because a system is non-Hermitian are separated from impostors by Ken Shiozaki in a solo 2025 condensed matter paper. Non-Hermitian topology comes in point-gap and line-gap flavors. Some phases reduce to plain Hermitian or anti-Hermitian ones; others are truly new, with no Hermitian counterpart.

Natural maps from line-gap phases to point-gap phases let Shiozaki draw the line precisely: extrinsic phases are those reducible in that way, intrinsic phases are the rest. Classification tables for all symmetry classes existed in earlier work, but this paper develops a single shared treatment and works through every internal symmetry class. One shared treatment matters because researchers comparing results across symmetry classes need one consistent language for what counts as an intrinsically non-Hermitian phase.
arxiv-2509-06979:
Predicting bus and tram arrivals without throwing away the patterns in irregular data is the aim of a 2025 transportation paper by Zirui Li and two co-authors. Arrival time prediction shapes passenger experience and traffic management. Deep learning models handle the nonlinear, time-varying data well, but drifting distributions degrade multi-step forecasts.

Standard practice normalizes the series to remove non-stationarity, which can also erase useful structure, a flaw the authors call over-stationarization. Their two-stage method first stationarizes for predictability, then recovers the non-stationary effect. A module extended to two-dimensional models captures hidden periodicity, and a compensation module learns scaling and shifting factors from the raw data. On a hundred twenty-five days of Dresden transit operations, the method cut standard error measures for both trams and buses compared with baselines, by small but consistent margins.
arxiv-2509-07279:
E. Rule and 4 co-authors design a quantum algorithm in 2025 for building antisymmetric states of fermions. Fermions, the particle family that includes electrons, must obey an antisymmetry rule when their labels are swapped. Preparing such states on a quantum computer is a basic step for simulating chemistry and materials, but older sorting-based methods need ordered inputs and many costly gates.

The new recursive method sets up each particle on its own, with no ordering needed first. Its cost grows gently with the number of particles and orbitals, beating rivals when the particle count stays below the square root of the orbital count. A measurement-based variant cuts the gate cost by about half. Worked circuits for two and three particles, plus a noise study, show the scheme holds up in practice.
arxiv-2509-07579:
Liya Gaynutdinova and 3 co-authors add error bounds to neural solvers for composite materials in a 2025 paper. Physics-informed neural networks solve partial differential equations by training a network to obey them. They often fail on materials whose traits jump sharply from one region to the next. Homogenization replaces such a patchy material with smooth effective traits. It is a core step in multiscale modeling.

The authors add a dual formulation to the network framework. It serves periodic thermo-conductive composites, in strong and weak forms. The dual view yields firm upper and lower error bounds. Those bounds double as a failure alarm for the network. Standard networks on smoothed materials can win in calm settings but break at jumps with no warning. The weak-form versions accept the patchy traits but need test functions chosen with care. The dual check proves a sound sign of convergence quality.
arxiv-2509-07679:
M. Boldrin leads a 15-author study in 2025 into why the perovskite La2CoMnO6 couples its magnetic and dielectric traits near room temperature. That coupling is called the magnetodielectric effect. It could serve sensors and memory devices. Yet the mechanism that rules it was not fully understood. The team probes how structure, electrons, and magnetism interact in a polycrystalline sample.

Field-dependent X-ray diffraction shows that a magnetic field shrinks the unit cell volume. A capacitive dilatometer confirms the size change. These shifts modify the octahedral distortions in the crystal. X-ray absorption studies at the cobalt edges point to two key drivers. One is the spin-orbit coupling of cobalt's outer electrons. The other is a field-driven rise in covalence. Multiplet and density functional calculations back a clear picture. Field-tuned orbital mixing and ligand-to-metal charge transfer produce the effect.
arxiv-2509-07779:
Emre Sahinoglu and 1 co-author extend decentralized online optimization to curved spaces with positive curvature in a 2025 paper. In this setting, many agents learn together while sharing only local information. Online means data arrive over time. Riemannian optimization does this on manifolds, curved spaces. Past work leaned on Hadamard manifolds. Their negative curvature gives a friendly convex structure.

Positive curvature breaks that structure. Geodesic distances may not be globally convex there. The authors first analyze a curvature-aware consensus step. That step is the averaging move that keeps agents in agreement. It converges linearly beyond Hadamard manifolds. On that step, they build an online gradient method. Its regret grows like the square root of time, the standard good rate. A two-point bandit version observes only function values. It reaches the same rate, using smoothing-based gradient estimates.
arxiv-2509-07979:
Heeji Yoon and 12 co-authors argue that multimodal language models need direct visual training signals, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Such models ace many tasks after visual instruction tuning, yet they stumble on vision-heavy jobs like counting objects or judging spatial layouts. The authors blame text-only supervision, which guides the visual pathway only indirectly and lets fine detail get discarded.

Their strategy, VIRAL, regularly aligns the model's internal visual representations with those of a pretrained vision foundation model during training. Keeping the visual features faithful to a strong vision encoder should preserve the detail that counting and spatial questions depend on. Simple regularisation of this kind is attractive because it bolts onto existing training recipes.
arxiv-2509-08179:
Aaron Herrera and 1 co-author model Parkinson's disease across brain scales in a 2025 paper. The disease plays out in a loop of brain parts: the cortex, the basal ganglia, and the thalamus. A model at one scale alone misses part of the story. Small-scale electric spread and large-scale network rhythms shape each other.

Their co-simulation joins the two scales in one run. It tracks how charge moves through tissue and how signals enter each region. Deep brain stimulation, a standard therapy with implanted electrodes, is applied in the model. Random noise keeps the rhythms lifelike. Such models may one day help doctors tune a patient's device settings on a screen first, before they touch the real implant.
arxiv-2509-08479:
Growing interfaces, from bacterial colonies to burning fronts, often obey the same rough scaling law named for Kardar, Parisi, and Zhang. Mikheil Tsitsishvili and 3 co-authors propose a concrete system to watch that law, in a 2025 research paper. Their platform is an array of Josephson junctions, superconducting devices with well-controlled behavior. The geometry is a two-chain ladder.

Numerical simulations track the roughness function of the array over time. Analytical arguments support what the simulations show. The celebrated KPZ scaling appears at intermediate times and lasts long enough to observe. At longer times, the system crosses over to a regime ruled by soliton proliferation, where solitary waves multiply. A single platform displaying both regimes gives experimentalists a rare, tunable window onto nonequilibrium physics that is usually only simulated.
arxiv-2509-08979:
Zong-Zhe Du finds a shared soft rule for rare field theories in de Sitter space in a 2025 paper. De Sitter space is a model of a cosmos that expands at a set rate. Soft here means one particle in a clash has near zero push.

A broad rule on energy saving forces a set pattern: the clash strength does not scale with that soft push at all. That pattern fixes four point clash strengths in two named theories and a six point one in a third. Du conjectures it fixes all such theories to all orders. If true, the soft rule is a shared test for the whole class.
arxiv-2509-09079:
Yunyi Zhang builds an ANOVA test for high dimensional, non-stationary time series in a 2025 paper. ANOVA checks if group means differ. Time series that drift over time and lean on their past can bias that test, which changes its size and power.

Hard fourth order terms make the spread of the new test stat hard to gauge. A bootstrap method, which resamples the data by computer, is built to run the test. Theory gives the stat's limit law when no group gap exists, and proves the bootstrap sound. Tests on fake data show good small sample traits. Side results on quadratic forms may help others who work with such series.
arxiv-2509-09379:
Rong Yang and 1 co-author published a mathematics paper in 2025 on Hardy-Carleson type tent spaces, a setting used to study functions with controlled size. Their focus falls on two linked themes. One is how a special product turns those spaces into a Banach algebra. The other is how a Cesàro-like operator behaves when it acts on them.

Inside, the authors examine a Hadamard-Bergman convolution alongside the Duhamel product, asking when the algebra structure holds. They then test the named operator for two key properties, whether it stays bounded and whether it is compact. Readers in complex and harmonic analysis get a focused account of structure and operator behaviour in this family of spaces.
arxiv-2509-09579: Dariusz Piekarz wrote a short 2025 note on a three-point interpolation question in complex analysis. Agler and McCarthy had studied when an extremal solution is unique in the bidisc. Piekarz takes up the matching problem inside the unit Euclidean ball, allowing the ball to sit in any dimension, and works toward settling uniqueness there.
arxiv-2509-09979:
Yuting Liu and Masamune Oguri measure the expansion rate of the universe in this 2025 paper, using a supernova bent by a galaxy cluster. Light from supernova Refsdal arrives by several paths, and the delays between its images depend on the Hubble constant. This time-delay route is independent of both the cosmic distance ladder and early-universe methods, which currently disagree.

The pair rebuilt the cluster's mass model using new spectroscopic redshifts from ground and space telescopes. They checked stability with a jackknife method. That method drops parts of the data in turn and refits. Combining four lens models with different assumptions, they report a Hubble constant near the middle of the disputed range, with an uncertainty of a few units.
arxiv-2509-10079:
Giuliano Lorenzon and 20 co-authors report telescope observations of old, quiet galaxies in this 2025 paper. Once a galaxy stops forming stars, textbooks say its dust and cold gas should fade fast. New finds of dusty, gassy quiet galaxies at high redshift challenge that view, raising the question of whether dust and gas fade together or on separate clocks.

Using the ALMA array, the team measured dust and carbon monoxide gas in 17 quiet galaxies seen as they were billions of years ago. Their dust-to-gas ratios spread widely, from far below to above the usual value. About half the galaxies lost dust quickly, while the rest kept high ratios for billions of years, so no single fading path fits all.
arxiv-2509-10179:
Jiří Milička and 2 co-authors benchmark how language models handle style in a 2025 linguistics paper. Human writing shifts register with audience and purpose, and the question is whether machine text shifts the same way or flattens into a house style. Their yardstick is Biber's multidimensional analysis, which scores texts along interpretable axes of variation learned from real usage.

A fresh corpus of model writing, AI-Brown, was built to mirror a contemporary British English collection, text for text. Sixteen leading models were tested under varied prompts and settings, with base models set against their instruction-tuned twins. Because training data starve every language but English, the whole exercise was repeated for Czech with its own corpus and model. Rankings on each dimension give users a style report card per system.
arxiv-2509-10279:
Pavel Plyusnin and six co-authors tackle slow software testing in this 2025 paper on continuous integration, where teams merge code changes many times a day. Running every test on every change wastes hours, so their system, Targeted Test Selection, learns to pick only the tests a given change is likely to affect.

A key choice is how each commit is described: as a bag of words over the changed files, enriched with cross-file and other predictive features, and notably without coverage maps. Already running in production, the system selects about fifteen percent of tests, cuts execution time roughly sixfold, and still catches over ninety-five percent of failures. The authors also release the implementation publicly for other teams to use.
arxiv-2509-10679:
Peter Keevash and Peleg Michaeli prove a generalized Ramsey-Turán theorem for matchings in this 2025 paper. Ramsey theory asks how much structure a colored graph must contain. Turán theory asks how many pieces a graph can hold while avoiding a pattern. Their theorem fuses the two. The pattern is a matching, a set of disjoint edges. The setting spans many colors at once.

Take a graph whose edges are colored in q colors. Each color class is banned from containing a matching of a set size. The authors determine the most copies of any complete subgraph such a graph can hold. Two explicit constructions compete for that maximum. An intricate compression argument settles the contest. It builds on the Gallai-Edmonds decomposition of each color. One construction wins. The result extends two classics at once. They are the Cockayne-Lorimer theorem and the Erdős-Gallai theorem.
arxiv-2509-10779:
Yilun Xiao, writing alone, improves drone-image object detection with a post-processing trick in this 2025 paper. From a drone's height, small objects pack densely into each frame and standard detectors miss many, hidden by overlap and clutter. Xiao's framework works after any detector runs, so no retraining is needed.

First, overlapping image tiles recover low-confidence candidates the detector dropped. Two gates then check groups of candidates, one clustering by position and one by appearance, and groups that pass get a careful confidence boost before the final merging step. On the VisDrone benchmark, recall rose clearly while precision fell, a trade the author argues suits counting and monitoring jobs where misses cost more than false alarms.
arxiv-2509-11079:
Jinwei Su and eight co-authors present this 2025 artificial intelligence paper on teams of language-model agents that split a question among several specialized workers. Fixed workflows waste effort on easy questions and fall short on hard ones, so the authors let the workflow itself adapt.

Their system, called DAAO, first guesses how hard a query is, then assembles a matching workflow from reusable building blocks and routes each step to a suitable model. Feedback on whether the workflow succeeded keeps the difficulty guesses honest. Across six test benchmarks, the adaptive setup beat earlier multi-agent systems on both accuracy and running cost, giving simple questions lean treatment and hard questions heavier machinery.
arxiv-2509-11179:
George Cherry and three co-authors wrote this 2025 solar physics paper. It tackles a long-standing puzzle. How might wave energy at the Sun's surface travel upward? Could it help heat the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere?

The team used a realistic three-dimensional simulation of the quiet Sun. They decomposed wave activity by its most significant frequency. Two signals were followed upward from the convection zone. Twisted magnetic structures change how the oscillations propagate. Swirling flows change them too. The strongest high-frequency signals mark where shocks form. Those shocks sit in the chromosphere. The two frequencies carry a large share of total wave power. At times the share reaches about half. Shocks, mode conversion, and jets join into one picture of upward energy transport.
arxiv-2509-11379:
Chen Cheng and John Duchi show that cleaning labels buys robustness raw labels cannot. This 2025 machine learning theory paper treats pipelines that distill noisy human answers into grouped labels. The authors argue that grouping changes what guarantees are even possible.

Procedures built on grouped labels win stronger guarantees. The guarantees concern the true task loss. Training still minimizes a stand-in loss. Classical instinct says to use all label doubt for best efficiency. Yet standard methods lose consistency once the loss is slightly off. Grouped-label procedures still converge to the best classifiers. The paper urges viewing the whole pipeline as one design object. Collection, fitting, and prediction belong in one frame.
arxiv-2509-11479:
Ante Bing, Donna Spiegelman, and Judith J. Lok improve a trial design meant to stop good trials from failing. This 2025 biostatistics paper treats the Learn-As-you-GO design. That design adapts a trial's intervention package as data build up. A trial can still end underpowered, though. It may be too small to find the effect it seeks.

The authors add power itself as a design goal. Two flavors are given. One is unconditional power. The other conditions on data so far. When early stages hint at low power, the optimizer strengthens the package. Final power rises. Effect estimates keep their long-run properties. The final test keeps its level. A rerun of the BetterBirth study shows the gain. More intensive care might have carried that trial to significance.
arxiv-2509-11679:
Joe H. N. Pattison, Dominic J. Anstey, and Eloy de Lera Acedo quantify a nuisance for cosmology: the Moon crossing the sky. This 2025 radio astronomy paper treats hunts for the global twenty-one centimeter signal. That signal tracks early cosmic hydrogen. Bright galactic foregrounds must be modeled and removed with extreme care. An unmodeled lunar eclipse of the sky corrupts that removal.

Toy cases were simulated. A foreground mismatch of fifteen parts per million is the Moon's scale near bright sky. It inflated recovery error by up to a fifth. With the Moon near the galactic center and in the beam's most sensitive spot, error more than doubled. Venus is too small on the sky to matter. Lunar alignments to avoid are mapped.
arxiv-2509-11879:
Banhi Chatterjee and Peter Kratzer nominate a magnetic material as a host for swirling sound. This 2025 condensed matter paper treats chiral phonons. These lattice vibrations move in circles and carry a twist. They have been seen mainly in familiar two-dimensional semiconductors. A substrate that breaks mirror symmetry helps them appear.

First-principles computing backs the nomination. The material is MnPS3, a magnetic semiconductor. It shares the six-sided structure of those semiconductors. Its unit cell is larger. In-plane chiral phonon modes appear at the valley points of a monolayer. The modes sort by which atoms trace the circles, manganese or sulfur. Each mode's twist is counted in fixed units. Light with a corkscrew twist could excite one handedness at a time.
arxiv-2509-12079:
A single flat snapshot that secretly encodes a full spectrum at every pixel is the raw material of coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging. Xiaodong Wang and four co-authors improve how that hyperspectral cube gets rebuilt in 2025, targeting the jerky behavior of deep unfolding networks.

Unfolding alternates explicit data-fitting steps with learned denoising, and quality can lurch unevenly from stage to stage. Borrowing from diffusion and flow matching, the proposed framework forces a smooth path from rough first guess to finished image, so refinement stays gradual and controllable. A spatial-spectral transformer built for the job, plus a frequency-domain fusion module, keeps the cost down. Tests on simulated and real captures report better quality and efficiency than leading earlier methods.
arxiv-2509-12979:
Dipak Rabari, Yogesh Meghrajani and Laxmi Desai share many secret images with one shared quantum piece in 2025. Image safety matters more as theft grows. Visual codes split images into shares that reveal nothing alone.

Their scheme adds quantum tools to the split. One common share serves for many secret images at once. Quantum links resist many forms of spying. Tests back strong safety for firm data and army use, among other fields. The blend aims to keep shared images safe while cutting the shares that must be stored and sent.
arxiv-2509-13579:
Momchil Tomov and sixteen co-authors present TreeIRL in 2025. TreeIRL is a planner that steers self-driving cars through city traffic. Planning must balance safety, progress, comfort, and human-like behavior at once. Purely classical and purely learned methods each handle only part of that balance.

TreeIRL pairs two techniques. Monte Carlo tree search explores many possible futures. Inverse reinforcement learning learns from human driving what good behavior looks like. The search proposes safe candidate paths. A learned scoring function then picks the most human-like one. The team tested it in large simulations and in real driving around Las Vegas. The real runs covered more than five hundred miles of dense traffic, cut-ins, and traffic lights. TreeIRL earned the best overall balance among the planners tested.
arxiv-2509-13879:
Mariano Barone and four co-authors build a biomedical fact-checker in a 2025 paper. The target is health misinformation, from vaccine hesitancy to unproven cures. Checking medical claims is harder than checking ordinary news. The terminology is technical and the stakes are high. Verdicts must rest on real scientific evidence, not on a model's memory.

Their framework, CER, combines three stages. It retrieves high-quality biomedical evidence. It reasons over that evidence with a large language model. And it predicts veracity with a supervised classifier. Grounding the model's output in retrieved sources curbs hallucination. On the expert-annotated HealthFC, BioASQ-7b, and SciFact datasets, CER reached the best reported performance. It also generalized promisingly across datasets. Code and data are released openly.
arxiv-2509-13979:
Dudley Stark extends the Chinese restaurant process to multisets in a solo 2025 probability paper. Such bags allow repeated elements, like the letters of a word. Their orderings vastly outnumber ordinary ones. The classical Chinese restaurant process builds random orderings of distinct elements seat by seat. Each permutation is weighted by its number of cycles. Knuth long ago showed multiset orderings also factor into cycles.

Stark adapts the restaurant scheme to grow multiset orderings step by step. More copies arrive over time, with each element's count fixed in advance. For a uniform random multiset ordering, the number of cycles splits into a sum of separate negative hypergeometric terms. For general weighting, under a mild condition, he proves a central limit theorem as the multiset grows.
arxiv-2509-14279:
Robert Tjarko Lange and five co-authors present robust-kbench in 2025, a stricter test for AI written CUDA kernels. CUDA kernels are the low level routines that run on graphics processors. Language models can write them, but loose benchmarks let models game the score.

Existing kernel tests have exploitable loopholes and narrow test conditions, the authors argue. Their benchmark checks performance and correctness across varied scenarios with fewer cheats. Beside it sits an agent framework that searches for, verifies and improves kernels on its own. Frontier models in the pipeline translate PyTorch code into CUDA and refine it in rounds. Harder, cleaner tests matter because a fast kernel that is subtly wrong is worse than a slower correct one.
arxiv-2509-14379:
Yochai Yemini and three co-authors tackle speech separation in 2025, pulling apart voices recorded by one microphone in noisy rooms. Noise and speech arrive mixed, so a listener hears a blend. Training only on mixes limits what a model can learn.

Their generative method models clean speech and structured noise separately, training only on single signals. A score model that watches lip and face cues as well as sound gives a strong speech prior. Separation then runs as an inverse problem, sampling backwards through a diffusion process to remove the modelled noise. Recovered voices are the clean parts left behind. Early results look promising for noisy settings where paired mixed training data are hard to gather.
arxiv-2509-14479:
Sean Foley and six co-authors release in 2025 a long form real time MRI speech data set from a single speaker. Magnetic resonance imaging can film the vocal tract while speech is produced. Long, high quality recordings of that kind are rare.

The USC Long Single-Speaker set holds roughly an hour of video and audio from one native speaker of American English. Releases include video cropped to the vocal tract, sentence level splits and cleaned restored audio. Region of interest time series are also supplied for direct analysis. Baseline tests on articulatory synthesis and phoneme recognition anchor the benchmark. Speech scientists gain a shared, richly derived record for testing how tongue, lips and jaw shape sound.
arxiv-2509-15179:
Arghyadeep Basu and four co-authors test how the assumed spectrum of the first stars changes the fingerprint they leave in intergalactic gas, in a 2025 astrophysics paper. During cosmic reionization, starlight ionized the hydrogen between galaxies, and the Lyman-alpha forest records that era's temperature and ionization. Models usually simplify the sources' spectra to blackbody or power-law shapes.

The team runs three-dimensional radiative transfer simulations on top of hydrodynamic ones, trying realistic spectra that include X-ray binaries, shock-heated gas emission, and binary stars, beside the idealized shapes. The broad layout of ionized regions barely changes between models. Harder, higher-energy spectra do stretch the partly ionized zones, enlarge regions of doubly ionized helium, and alter the forest's thermal imprint. Spectral assumptions therefore matter for reading the forest precisely.
arxiv-2509-15279:
Chi Liu and six co-authors train a medical reasoning model whose answers can be checked in a 2025 health AI paper. Clinical language models must do more than land the right answer; their reasoning has to be transparent enough for experts to trust. Fleming-R1 pursues verifiable medical reasoning through three innovations.

A reasoning-oriented data strategy merges curated medical question sets with knowledge-graph-guided synthesis, widening coverage of rare diseases, drugs, and multi-step reasoning chains. Chain-of-thought cold start then distills high-quality reasoning traces from teacher models to set strong inference habits. Finally, a two-stage reinforcement learning program with verifiable rewards, using group-relative policy optimization, consolidates the skill. The recipe targets expert-level performance on problems where the reasoning path matters as much as the conclusion.
arxiv-2509-15479:
Björn Möller leads a team that makes an open system for fake driving videos. Such systems guess how a road scene will unfold and render it as video. Past systems used large private models, gave little insight into design choices, and shared no code. The team wanted a system that others can study, copy, and check.

Their system, OpenViGA, splits the work into three parts: an image coder, a world model, and a video maker. They grade each part on its own, in both numbers and looks. All parts start from open pre-trained models, tuned on public driving data with modest hardware. They publish the code and models, so results can be fully redone.
arxiv-2509-15579:
Yun Tang and Cindy Tseng train speech models on chunks instead of whole clips. Fast reply matters more as speech tools grow, yet most training assumes the full clip is known. Streaming use gives only parts at a time, which forces awkward fixes. The pair wanted one training plan that suits both streaming and full clip use.

Their plan hides some speech frames inside a chunk and asks the model to restore them. Help comes from open frames in the same chunk and from chunks before it. A copy and append trick makes chunk training cheap. Sound traits are turned into codes by a fine grained quantizer. A grouped loss trains on the hidden frames. Tests show finer codebooks aid later tasks.
arxiv-2509-15779:
Dekuan Dong, Yingzhou Li, and Jungong Xue multiply matrices that are stored inside quantum operators. This storage scheme, called block encoding, is a standard base for quantum algorithms. Fast products of stored matrices matter for tasks like simulating physics and solving linear systems. Past product methods cost many spare qubits.

The trio give leaner methods for three product kinds: plain matrix products, Kronecker products, and entry wise products. They work for oblong matrices of any size. Their builds slash spare qubit counts, with exponential savings across chains of products. Gate cost rises only moderately. The products also unlock richer encodings, such as a squeeze gadget for time varying simulation.
arxiv-2509-16179:
Splitting an image into light and dark parts with the Otsu method is a classic step in image work, but the search over all cut points is slow. Sai Varun Kodathala speeds it up with a bisection search that homes in on the best cut in far fewer steps. The trick rests on the method's score curve having a single peak.

On forty-eight test images, the fast version cut score computations by over ninety percent. It matched the exact best cut in two thirds of cases and stayed close in nearly all the rest. The gains suit real-time image systems with tight time budgets.
arxiv-2509-16379:
Summarizing a rich data distribution by a few numbers usually throws away detail that matters. Xinran Liu, Shansita D. Sharma, and Soheil Kolouri present EMPEROR, a method that encodes a distribution through its statistical moments along many sliced directions. Each slice gets a small mixture fit, and the slice results merge into one compact descriptor.

Classical theorems back the claim that these moments pin down the distribution in full. Error bounds scale in the best known way with slice and sample counts. Across data types the descriptor held richer detail than common pooling tricks, while staying cheap to compute.
arxiv-2509-16879:
Yan-Li Wang, Shu-Ting Cai, and Yu-Kuo Hsiao study rare charm decays in a 2025 particle paper. A D meson can decay into two light scalar mesons. Short-range paths from W boson exchange turn out to be tiny here. Long-range rescattering, where products bounce and swap, drives the decay instead.

The team compute rates for these rescattering-driven decays. One key mode is squeezed by a tight mass match, which cuts its rate. The authors give a precise value with stated uncertainties. Current experiments at several labs can hunt these modes. Finding them would test how final-state interactions shape charm physics.
arxiv-2509-17479:
Alessio Pomponio and Lianfeng Yang study a coupled equation system from mathematical physics. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats a zero mass Schrödinger-Bopp-Podolsky system in three-dimensional space. An earlier study had found weak solutions by a perturbation route, and this paper completes that line of work with a more direct attack.

Using the Mountain Pass Theorem and a splitting lemma, the pair obtain a ground state solution for a stated range of the power in the system. A Pohozaev identity then yields nonexistence results for other powers, so the range is not an artifact of the method. In the radial case, they track how solutions behave as a key parameter shrinks to zero. That limit links the system to the zero mass Schrödinger-Poisson system, tying two models together.
arxiv-2509-17579:
Rahul Trivedi and J. Ignacio Cirac prove that noisy quantum simulators are sturdier than folklore suggests. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies problem-to-simulator mappings such as Trotterization and perturbative expansions. On a perfect machine, longer runs buy more accuracy. On a real one, longer runs invite more noise, so many expected the output to collapse.

The authors show the opposite for a key class of tasks: reading local observables in quantum lattice models. In all the mappings they study, those observables can be pinned to a precision that does not grow with system size. The error scales more gently than the noise rate itself. The proof holds for both digital and analog simulators. Their results give theory cover for using today's flawed quantum hardware on many-body physics, with little or no error correction.
arxiv-2509-17879:
Tu Nguyen and 3 co-authors score how strongly a prompt text can sway a language model. Their 2025 paper sets two skills side by side: use of stored facts, and use of new facts given in the prompt. A prompt that clashes with stored facts may or may not move the model's answer.

Their score, TPS, goes past just reading the top answer. It tracks how far the whole spread of likely answers moves toward a target spread. Tests show the score picks up fine shifts that blunt checks miss. That gives a sharper tool to study when models yield to context.
arxiv-2509-18079:
Hector Perez-Urbina reads the words of top AI leaders for a creed he calls techno-supremacy. His 2025 paper studies a small elite that shapes how AI is funded, built, and spread world-wide. The creed, as he defines it, trusts tech to beat hard social problems by its own nature.

He runs a two-phase close read of texts by elite members across eight years. The group is not of one mind: stances span a wide range. Pro-creed talk grew and split views more sharply after ChatGPT came out. A common move pairs bright promises with a nod to risk, then offers yet more tech as the cure.
arxiv-2509-18179:
Sai Varun Kodathala and Rakesh Vunnam measure what is lost when an image is turned into words, then back into an image. Their 2025 paper calls that loss the describe-then-generate bottleneck. Mixed AI flows now route vision through text in many creative tools, yet the cost of that detour was poorly scored.

The team made more than a hundred image pairs through such a flow. Scores for look, structure, and colour tracked how much of the first image survived. Near all pairs lost a lot in look, and most lost a lot in structure too. Text is thus a leaky bridge for visual facts.
arxiv-2509-18379:
Entangled states are key resources for quantum computing, but they are fragile and fade fast. F. Q. Guo, Shi-Lei Su, Weibin Li, and X. Q. Shao propose a way to hold entanglement steady in arrays of neutral atoms. Their 2025 paper uses engineered loss, not isolation, to push atoms toward the wanted state. The scheme runs inside a Floquet-Lindblad frame, with drives that repeat in time.

Each cycle fires a short laser pulse, then a strong pulse that links the ground state to a Rydberg state. The setup avoids slow, gentle tuning, so it stays fast and shrugs off atom motion and position jitter. The engineered loss channels speed the settle time toward the target state. The authors show the method scales and can prepare many shared graph states with high fidelity. It works at zero and at warmer temperatures, and may double as passive error control.
arxiv-2509-19079:
Edge servers close to users take jobs from several dispatchers, but their status changes fast and queues are finite. Samuel Chamoun and five co-authors study how dispatchers can keep track of those servers without drowning them in status checks. Each dispatcher learns in two ways: by paying for direct status queries, or for free when a job succeeds or fails and reports back. The goal is high throughput at low communication cost.

The team frames the problem as cooperative multi-agent learning and solves it with a MAPPO algorithm. Training is centralized while each dispatcher acts on its own stale, partial view. In experiments the learned policy beat baseline strategies across query costs, arrival rates, and dispatcher counts. The work was supported in part by the Army Research Laboratory and the National Science Foundation.
arxiv-2509-19379:
Returaj Burnwal and three co-authors survey learning from observation, where an AI agent imitates an expert while seeing only the expert's states, never their actions. Classic imitation learning copies behavior from demonstrations that include actions, but in many real settings actions are unavailable or impractical to record. Think of learning from videos of a person, where muscle commands are invisible. The survey organizes the fast-growing literature on this state-only variant.

The authors present a framework and sort existing methods by how they build trajectories, what they assume, and their design choices. They draw connections to offline reinforcement learning, model-based methods, and hierarchical learning. Open problems are identified, with directions for future work. Published in a major computing survey venue, this overview gives newcomers a taxonomy of the field and gives specialists a shared map of its gaps.
arxiv-2509-19479:
Many physics and chemistry problems share a symmetry that standard software largely ignores. Leon D. da Silva and Marcelo P. Santos built PySymmetry, a free tool in Sage and Python that uses that symmetry to shrink linear systems. The tool builds bases matched to the symmetry, which splits a big system into smaller blocks. It can also count how often each block type appears.

Three test cases show the range of the tool. One comes from chemistry, and one solves a quantum equation more than seventeen times faster than standard methods. A third case gave the first full analytic answer to a hard problem about how bodies move under gravity. The tool works with common libraries such as NumPy and SciPy. It aims to put symmetry tricks within reach of working scientists.
arxiv-2509-19879:
Speech therapists judge traits such as breathiness and strain by ear, yet labeled recordings of disordered speech are scarce. Jenthe Thienpondt and three co-authors teach a recognizer to expose phonological features, the sound traits that define speech sounds. A bottleneck layer forces the model to speak in those interpretable features at each frame. Training needs only weak labels, drawn from what phonemes are known to sound like.

Features from that layer then feed two clinical tasks. One predicts intelligibility scores; the other classifies the pathology. Both matched leading acoustic features, with accuracy near three quarters on classification. Interpretable features let clinicians see why a model judged as it did. That transparency matters before any tool can support treatment choices.
arxiv-2509-20179:
Sanchali Mitra and Santanu Mahapatra wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on a proposed memory device. Memristors made from molybdenum disulfide, a two-dimensional semiconductor, switch resistance in ways bulk oxides do not explain. Earlier work by the group proposed that single sulphur atoms pop out of the layer to drive the switching. This follow-up paper revisits that model.

The authors add new evidence from density functional theory calculations. They set the new results beside their earlier reactive-force-field simulations. The paper also tests universal machine learning potentials, a newer simulation shortcut. Those potentials, they find, fail to reproduce the earlier simulation results faithfully. The follow-up thus both strengthens the sulphur popping picture and warns against one tempting replacement tool.
arxiv-2509-20279:
Medical image analysis gets an agentic upgrade in TissueLab, a system presented by Songhao Li and thirteen co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier agent systems in this field lacked solid tools and live expert feedback. TissueLab lets researchers ask direct questions in plain language. It then plans and runs explainable analysis workflows on its own.

The system gathers tool factories from pathology, radiology, and spatial omics. Standard inputs and outputs let it decide when and how to call each tool. Experts can watch intermediate results and refine them in real time. Across tasks tied to staging, prognosis, and treatment planning, TissueLab beat end-to-end vision-language models and rival agent systems. It also learns from clinician feedback over time. With active learning, it handled unseen diseases within minutes, without massive new datasets.
arxiv-2509-20379:
Vision-language models sometimes describe things that are not in the picture. Ofir Azachi and six co-authors offer a cheap way to catch such hallucinations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Checking outputs with another big model works but adds heavy cost and delay. Their detector instead watches the model's own next-token probabilities, a direct signal of its uncertainty.

The team built a dataset of one thousand four hundred human-labeled statements drawn from model outputs. Each statement was marked hallucinated or not. Simple machine learning models trained on the probability signals matched the detection quality of strong vision-language models. Adding text-only probability features improved the scores further. Combining both signals with a judge model's score worked best of all. The approach points toward fast, lightweight reliability checks.
arxiv-2509-20679:
Fake speech is hard to spot when an attack type has never been seen before. Duc-Tuan Truong and five co-authors address that problem in a 2025 research paper on speech deepfake detection. Their method is called QAMO, short for quality-aware multi-centroid one-class learning. It was accepted for the INTERSPEECH 2026 conference.

Older one-class methods model real speech around a single center point. QAMO instead uses several centers, each tied to a level of speech quality, such as how natural the voice sounds. Quality scores come from existing assessment models. Tests reported by the authors show the multi-center design models real speech better and improves detection of unseen fake attacks.
arxiv-2509-21379:
Removing a concept from a diffusion image model is harder than it sounds. The concept is split across many latent features, so erasure is costly and imprecise. Enrico Cassano and 5 co-authors address that problem in a 2025 paper. Their answer uses supervised sparse autoencoders, which learn compact internal codes for images.

The method, SAEmnesia, labels concepts during training to bind each one to a single neuron. That one to one mapping makes erasure targeted and fast. Search over settings dropped sharply compared with past sparse methods. Scores on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark improved for objects. Sequential erasure also scaled better, with higher accuracy when nine objects were removed one after another.
arxiv-2509-21479:
Synthetic data can ease data scarcity, but poor generations can bias a model. Zixuan Wu and 4 co-authors propose a filtering method in a 2025 paper. Good augmentation expands the training set with diverse samples from the same distribution. It should add little bias while cutting estimator variance. Conformal prediction supplies the filter, with provable risk control.

Conformal data augmentation screens synthetic samples and removes low quality ones. The method is simple to implement. It needs no access to internal model logits and no large scale retraining. Tests across multiple tasks demonstrate its effectiveness. The authors present the approach as a principled way to keep augmentation diverse yet safe, so synthetic data helps rather than harms.
arxiv-2509-21779:
Yun Zhao and Xian-Qiao Yu compute how a rare particle, the Bc meson, decays in this 2025 particle physics paper. They study decays where the Bc turns into a J/psi particle plus either an axial-vector meson or a tensor meson. Four such partner particles are covered. The work is driven by steady observations of Bc decays at the LHCb experiment.

The authors use a method called perturbative QCD, which splits the decay into parts that can and cannot be computed directly. Helper curves, called light-cone distribution amplitudes, tame the parts that resist direct math. Their results give decay rates for each channel, and the axial-vector ones look within reach of future experiments. They also predict how the spin of the products lines up, finding that the lengthwise pattern should dominate.
arxiv-2509-21879:
Chaoyang Luo, Yan Zou, and Nanjing Huang address a tension in neural ordinary differential equations, models that treat a network as a continuous flow. Such models are naturally sturdy, but methods that force stability on them often lose accuracy. Their 2025 paper traces the problem to rigid stability conditions: the region a model settles into does not match its decision borders. Their framework, Zubov-Net, joins the dynamics and the decision in one design.

The team uses learnable Lyapunov functions, which measure a kind of energy, directly as the classifier. That makes the settling regions match the classes by construction. A second step, driven by Zubov's equation, reshapes the prescribed regions toward the true ones through a training loss. The authors prove the combined loss guarantees the alignment, plus stable paths and a certified safety margin. They also give probability bounds that justify the convex shape of their energy functions.
arxiv-2509-22079:
Catarina S. Monteiro and five co-authors present a fiber-optic sensor that both locates a vibration and records its waveform. Fiber sensors suit large sites and harsh settings, since they are cheap to install, small, and sturdy. Existing distributed systems, though, are costly and trade sharpness of location against frequency range. Their 2025 paper breaks that trade by combining two ways of reading the same fiber.

One reading uses speckle, the grainy light pattern inside a multimode fiber, which shifts when the fiber is disturbed. That part pinned down vibration sources to within centimeters. The second reading tracks the polarization of the light, and it rebuilt waveforms faithfully across a wide band, from low rumble up to high-pitched tones. The authors present the pairing as a general blueprint: using several readouts at once can lift the limits that any single readout faces.
arxiv-2509-22179:
Yuxi Meng and eleven co-authors ask whether living in a cosmic filament gives a galaxy more satellite companions. Filaments are the thread-like strands of the cosmic web, and their influence on galaxy growth is a live question. Using the IllustrisTNG simulation of the universe, the team compared central galaxies in filaments, traced from the galaxy distribution, with matching galaxies in the open field. Across all brightness ranges, the filament galaxies hosted more satellites, echoing telescope survey results.

Much of that excess turned out to be indirect: galaxies in filaments tend to sit in heavier dark matter halos, which naturally hold more satellites. After the authors rebalanced the two samples to share the same halo masses, most of the enhancement vanished. The tracer used to draw the filaments mattered too: tracing them from dark matter instead of galaxies shrank the gap further.
arxiv-2509-22379:
Stefano Carlo Lambertenghi, Mirena Flores Valdez, and Andrea Stocco compare four ways to test self-driving software. Tests in pure simulation are safe, but results may not carry to real roads. The team built each setup around a small car with real camera and LiDAR sensors, plus its digital twin. The setups ranged from full simulation to mixed reality to real runs indoors.

Two system designs faced real obstacles and road layouts. Pure simulation missed key traits of sensing and motion. Mixed reality gave more true sensing while staying safe. The team maps which failures move across setups and which do not, and why.
arxiv-2509-22479:
Yuqing Zhang and 4 co-authors built a lab of neural agents to watch word meanings change. Corpus studies can track change but cannot show its causes. Human experiments are hard to stretch over the long spans that change needs. Their framework, NeLLCom-Lex, grounds agents in a real lexicon like English, then shifts what the agents need to say to each other.

The test bed is color naming, a classic task in this field. Agents trained to speak an existing language copied human-like naming patterns closely. Changes in communicative need then reshaped both behavior and vocabulary. The results support using such agents to probe the mechanisms behind semantic change.
arxiv-2509-22579:
Jaewoo Joo and 3 co-authors give a recipe for simulating relativistic particles on near-term quantum computers. Their first-quantized approach stores the wavefunction on a grid held in system qubits. It handles two edge rules: periodic, where the grid wraps around, and Dirichlet, where the wave vanishes at the border. The squared momentum operator is built from finite differences using quantum translation steps.

The relativistic kinetic energy is then expanded as a series with higher momentum terms. Variational optimization of trial states can estimate ground-state energies, with or without relativistic effects. The authors present the method as a practical route for quantum physics and chemistry on current devices.
arxiv-2509-22779:
Paz Beniamini, Hagai B. Perets, and Jonathan Granot explain an ultra-long gamma-ray burst as a small-scale tidal disruption. GRB 250702B fired for hours, with an X-ray pre-peak a day before, an off-center host position, and hard, fast-varying gamma rays. Standard progenitors, from collapsing blue supergiants to white dwarf disruptions, fit that mix poorly. The authors propose a micro-tidal disruption: a stellar-mass black hole or neutron star tearing apart a normal star.

Three pathways give the day-long delay between precursor and main flare. A grazing pass, a natal kick, or a mix of both can set the timing. Fallback accretion then explains the long duration and variability. The paper lists observations that can tell the channels apart.
arxiv-2509-23179:
Post-quantum crypto keys and signatures are far longer than classic ones, and cache bandwidth becomes the bottleneck. Jingyao Zhang and Elaheh Sadredini put compute next to the cache to break that limit. Their Crypto-Near-Cache design adds SRAM arrays with bitline computing beside cache slices. Virtual addressing works natively, which eases system fit. An instruction set extension exposes the hardware to software.

Internal bandwidth runs high while data movement stays short. The pair discuss core and cache datapath details for implementation. Older in-cache designs struggle to integrate with modern systems, they argue. Their paradigm aims for speed and energy gains without those frictions. Post-quantum algorithms are the prime target.
arxiv-2509-23379:
Radiology models invent findings that the scan does not support, a risky failure in medicine. Xi Zhang and 3 co-authors curb that with Clinical Contrastive Decoding. Their analysis blames prompt-driven hallucinations on over-sensitivity to clinical text sections. The fix needs no training and no retrieval. Structured signals from task-specific radiology expert models enter at decode time.

A two-stage contrastive step refines token scores during generation. Clinical fidelity rises while the base model stays untouched. On MIMIC-CXR, a key graph-based score rose by up to seventeen percent for top report models. Tests spanned three data sets and several models. The approach is pitched as light and general.
arxiv-2509-23479:
Two people talking means two brains shaping each other, a hard case for models of single brains. Maria Glushanina and 4 co-authors apply CEBRA, a method that learns compact codes from neural data, to EEG recorded from pairs at once. Their data come from structured social exchanges between partners. The goal is to code joint activity, not just one person's response to a stimulus.

The learned codes captured who was speaking and who was listening, plus other measures of behavior. The team frames this as a step toward foundation models for social brain data. Such models would need to scale and to work across new pairs of people, with possible uses in clinics.
arxiv-2509-23579:
Turning a plain request into a Jira query is a daily task in big firms, yet no public test measured it well. Kevin Frank and 4 co-authors built Jackal, a benchmark of one hundred thousand request-and-query pairs checked by running them on a live Jira system. Each query comes with four request styles: long, short, similar in meaning, and exact. A snapshot of the Jira instance ships with the set for repeatable scoring.

On a five-thousand-pair subset, twenty-three models were graded by whether their queries ran correctly. The best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, managed about sixty percent overall. Long and exact requests scored high, while short and merely similar ones fell sharply.
arxiv-2509-23779:
Mamba, a state-space sequence model, rivals transformers at in-context learning, but the theory of how it learns in context lagged behind. Jiarui Jiang and 4 co-authors study Mamba's training dynamics on in-context linear regression, a standard test bed. They develop tools for the non-convex training problem shaped by Mamba's structure. The results give an exponential convergence rate to the in-context solution and a loss bound comparable to the transformer's.

The mechanism they uncover differs from the transformer's usual story. A trained Mamba turns out to emulate a variant of online gradient descent on the hidden function. Simulations confirm the theory.
arxiv-2509-23979:
Text games make tidy test worlds for language models, if the game code itself is clean enough to extend. Haonan Wang and 4 co-authors refactored the ByteSized32 corpus into a modular library. A shared foundation file centralizes common logic across all thirty-two games, abstracting seven base classes into reusable modules. Total code shrank from about twenty thousand lines to ten thousand compared with the original corpus.

Experiments with GPT-4o gave mixed results: generated games for unseen scenarios improved on two of four quality dimensions and slipped on two. The authors read the hierarchy as both a help and a new challenge for models, and offer the corpus as a scalable evaluation environment.
arxiv-2509-24079:
Tomasz Kania refines a classic question about which lists of numbers can arise as the spectrum of a symmetric doubly stochastic matrix. Such a matrix has rows and columns that each sum to one, with matching entries across the diagonal. The lists in view have one at the head and the rest at or below zero.

Kania sharpens a Fourier-based template and computes an exact threshold that depends on matrix size. A new phase-aligned basis removes a quirk for sizes divisible by eight and improves the bound for every size from three up. On special group settings, a Walsh-Hadamard basis settles all such lists at once. The same holds in every Hadamard order, including Paley cases.
arxiv-2509-25279:
Jiecheng Zhou and co-authors study how a popular AI training method behaves in real deployment, in a 2025 paper. The method rewards models for answers that can be checked as right or wrong. It has surged as a way to boost reasoning. Its data flows are complex, though, and little was known about its system demands.

The team profiled live training jobs across tasks and steps. They found graphics processors sitting idle when answer lengths skewed. Set parallel plans wasted effort as workloads shifted. Data handling and load balance also lagged. The paper lists these bottlenecks from direct observation. System builders can use the findings to design training setups that waste less costly hardware time.
arxiv-2509-25479:
Zhenfeng Deng and co-authors show that a binder protein can be designed from just the patch it will grip, not the whole target. Their 2025 paper tackles a cost problem in protein design. Big targets, or patches that span two parts of a protein, take heavy computing and fail more often.

Their bet rests on how folding networks work: they seem to care most about local contacts near the grip site. Keeping only the loose surface bits around that site lifted success rates in tests by up to eighty percent. Each win also took far less time, up to forty times less. The team adds search steps that tune the design, and shows wins on targets once thought out of reach.
arxiv-2509-25579:
Miroslav Krstić and three co-authors develop in 2025 new steering laws for unicycle robots, the simple vehicles that roll forward and turn like a bicycle wheel. Working in polar coordinates, a companion study built such laws through backstepping; here the authors show a second method, integrator forwarding, can do the same job.

For a unicycle moving at steady speed, like a Dubins car, both methods yield the same family of parking maneuvers that finish in finite time. The team also builds the control Lyapunov functions behind the laws. Having both routes widens the toolbox for inverse optimal control design.
arxiv-2509-25779:
Siyu Zhu and co-authors train travel-planning agents with shaped rewards in a 2025 paper. Their system, Planner-R1, learns by reinforcement on the TravelPlanner benchmark. It reached a high final-pass rate with only a small set of training queries, beating a strong general model baseline.

Small models responded best to dense, step-by-step reward signals. An eight-billion-parameter model matched larger rivals while using far less compute and memory. Big models were steadier under sparse rewards but gained less from shaping and varied more between runs. Curriculum learning added no clear gain. The lesson is practical: reward design can matter more than model size for agent work.
arxiv-2509-26379:
Alois Altenburger and co-authors compute how jets spread in the first instants of a heavy-ion collision, in this 2025 paper. Fast partons plow through hot matter and lose energy, a process called jet quenching. Standard tools assume the matter is already in thermal balance.

The earliest stage is far from balance, and jets cross it anyway. The team derive the collision kernel and dipole cross section for that stage. They then compute gluon splitting rates from the new kernel. For mid-range parton energies, the rates differ clearly from thermal estimates. Jet readings are a main probe of the early fireball. Sharper early-stage inputs should sharpen what those readings mean.
arxiv-2509-26479:
De Sousa and co-authors develop, in a 2025 paper, machine learning tools to read the traits of laser cooled atoms without destroying the sample. Atoms held in a magneto optical trap glow as they cool, and photos of that glow show the cloud's shape. Traits such as temperature, though, are not obvious from a snapshot.

The team built a labeled data set spanning about eight thousand settings. It ranges from large, dense clouds to no atoms at all. They trained a range of models to predict atom number and temperature from the glow images alone. A plain linear model on total glow did poorly. Deep neural networks did far better, pinning number and temperature to within about ten and twenty percent. The method lets a lab gauge a cloud in place, without the usual destructive probe.
arxiv-2510-00079:
Hai Huang wrote this 2025 theory paper on choosing which text chunks an AI model should read. Modern AI tools work from a limited window of context, so picking the right chunks matters. Huang proposes a test based on directed information, a measure of how well one chunk predicts another. If one chunk nearly covers another, the second can be dropped with little loss.

The method turns chunk choice into a covering problem and solves it with a greedy algorithm. Huang proves the algorithm keeps query-relevant content within a bounded loss. The covering is built once, offline, so answering each new question costs nothing extra. On the HotpotQA question dataset, the method beat a strong keyword-search baseline. Its edge was clearest in hard cases, such as tight compression and single-slot prompts.
arxiv-2510-00479:
Ke Zhou and Samuel Grauer published this 2025 paper on squeezing more information out of particle tracking in fluid flows. Cameras follow tracer particles through a volume, but the tracks are sparse and noisy. The open question is whether the flow field and the particles' own properties can both be recovered. Their neural data assimilation framework couples an Eulerian flow model with Lagrangian particle physics.

Three flow regimes served as test beds for joint recovery. In a turbulent boundary layer, noisy tracer tracks still yielded flow states and true particle positions. In isotropic turbulence with heavier particles, the method recovered particle diameters alongside the flow. A shock-dominated compressible case pushed further, reconstructing velocity, pressure, density, and particle traits together. Sensitivity studies mapped how seeding density, noise, and particle inertia govern accuracy. The authors frame the results as design guidelines for future experiments.
arxiv-2510-00679:
Li and Wang, at Xiamen University, study an affine vertex operator superalgebra built from the Lie superalgebra sl(2|1) in this 2025 arXiv paper on representation theory. Vertex operator algebras encode the symmetries behind two-dimensional conformal field theory, and rationality is the prized property that only finitely many basic modules exist. The authors conjecture that at boundary admissible levels their superalgebra is rational in category O, with exactly the admissible modules appearing.

They prove the conjecture at the boundary level minus one half. They also compute the Zhu algebra for a family of rationally graded versions and show those are rational and C2-cofinite. A contrasting example at level one half produces infinitely many irreducible weak modules, so the algebra there is not rational. The boundary condition in the conjecture is therefore essential, not decorative.
arxiv-2510-00779:
Marson and Malaspinas propose a kinetic closure for turbulence in this 2025 arXiv letter on fluid dynamics. Simulating turbulence means filtering out small scales, and standard models must then guess the effect of those missing scales with an added stress term. The famous Smagorinsky model is one such guess, and it needs scale separation assumptions. The authors instead start from the filtered Boltzmann-BGK equation, a kinetic description of the flow.

Their closure builds the subfilter stress tensor in naturally, with no explicit modelling ansatz. A generalized collision operator handles the turbulent diffusion in the non-conserved moments instead. Chapman-Enskog analysis shows the model's large-scale limit is exactly the filtered Navier-Stokes equations. Lattice Boltzmann simulations of the Taylor-Green vortex and a turbulent mixing layer showed better stability and less dissipation than the Smagorinsky benchmark.
arxiv-2510-00879:
Azrieli, Chambers, Healy, and Lambert study a trust problem in statistics in this arXiv paper, whose current version dates to September 2023. A principal hires an analyst to produce a statistical study, but the analyst can quietly manipulate the results. The principal cannot watch the work, yet holds a small set of trusted data from an independent source. Payments tied to that trusted data might reward honest reporting.

The authors characterize exactly which information such payment schemes can draw out of the analyst. Full honesty turns out to be hard, since complete elicitation can demand as much data as perfect estimation itself. When the parameter space is finite, though, a bounded number of trusted observations always suffices. They also define an ordering for comparing experiments by elicitation power. Data that are better for estimation are also better for elicitation, but the reverse fails.
arxiv-2510-00979:
Koopman, Bisseling, and Scholz use category theory to build parallel algorithms for tensor products in this 2025 arXiv paper on high-performance computing. Supercomputers split work across many processors with private memories, and the Bulk Synchronous Parallel model organizes that work into alternating computation and communication supersteps. The authors study linear algorithms in that model and ask what happens when several functions must be combined into their tensor product.

By translating each superstep type into linear algebra through functors, they compute tensor products superstep by superstep and translate back. Functoriality then reassembles the pieces into a correct parallel algorithm for the combined function. They state the recipe with minimal algebra so practitioners can apply it directly. A higher-dimensional Fourier transform algorithm derived earlier this way serves as the running example, and they add a new parallel discrete cosine transform.
arxiv-2510-01179:
Xu and co-authors release Toucan, a very large public dataset teaching language models to use real software tools. Open agent research starves for realistic, permissively licensed practice data with genuine tool calls. The team synthesized one and a half million task trajectories from nearly five hundred live tool environments.

Five models drafted diverse queries, filters removed weak ones, and three teacher models solved the survivors. Rule-based and model-based checks guarded quality throughout the pipeline. Extensions stretch tasks into multi-turn conversations for realism. Models fine-tuned on Toucan outperformed rivals on standard tool-use benchmarks. Real tool execution grounds the trajectories in actual system responses. Two agent frameworks produced the demonstrations, adding stylistic variety. Multi-tool chains appear throughout, not just single calls. Permissive licensing removes the legal friction that blocks open research. Scale plus realism is the dataset's whole claim to fame.
arxiv-2510-01279:
Chen and co-authors run a committee of tool-using agents in parallel and let them argue their way to better answers. Models can reason in text, write code, or search, yet nobody knew how to blend the three well. Their framework, TUMIX, assigns each agent a distinct tool-use strategy.

Agents share drafts round by round and refine each other's answers. Accuracy rose by several points over the best single-strategy baselines at similar cost.
