arxiv-2602-00479: Shaohong Liang and colleagues give two new accounts of the bounded lower oscillation space, known as BLO, via the Gaussian heat semigroup. From these they prove a lower-envelope bound for solutions of the heat equation under BLO boundary data, plus a Gaussian John-Nirenberg test, and sharp estimates of the BLO norm. They also use the semigroup method to re-prove that the Littlewood-Paley g-function maps BMO to BLO. The work ties heat-semigroup tools to BLO theory and its uses.
arxiv-2602-00579: JiaKui Hu and colleagues tackle universal image restoration, clearing varied degradations from low-quality images to recover clean, rich results. Their BDG approach first discriminates degradation types and levels with a gray-level co-occurrence matrix across angles and scales, MAS-GLCM. Diffusion training then runs in three stages — generation, bridging, and restoration — preserving textures while folding MAS-GLCM data into the process. Without changing architecture, BDG gains a lot on combined restoration and real-world super-resolution, raising fidelity without losing perceptual quality.
arxiv-2602-00779: Wai-Kiu Ricky Wong and colleagues tackle geocoronal H-alpha in Galactic H-alpha data, which varies with shadow altitude, the geometry of sight lines relative to Earth's shadow cone. That relation predicts that emission for removal from observed spectra. The method thus enables reliable H-alpha studies in mid-resolution integral field surveys. Early evidence also links that emission to solar activity and Earth-Sun distance.
arxiv-2602-00879: Hao Mark Chen and colleagues propose Dynamic Expert Sharing, shifting tuning from token-centric pruning and expert skipping to sequence-level coreset selection. Diffusion language models combined with Mixture-of-Experts architectures suffer expert explosion: as parallel tokens grow, distinct experts used grow nearly linearly. The resulting memory traffic pushes inference into a memory-bound regime. To maximize reuse, DES picks a compact, high-utility expert set for an entire parallel decoding block. Two strategies follow: Intra-Sequence Sharing, fitting allocation to the sequence level, and Saliency-Aware Voting.
arxiv-2602-00979: Xueyi Li and colleagues expose how easily grading agents can be tricked in live classrooms. Their GradingAttack frame tests short-answer grading agents with two attack styles: token-level tweaks and prompt-level tricks. Both styles shift grades while staying hard to spot, with prompt-level attacks winning more often and token-level attacks hiding better. Trials across several data sets show both routes work, revealing that current grading agents lack strong defenses. The authors call for secure, trustworthy grading systems for high-stakes school use.
arxiv-2602-01179: Zhichao Chen and co-authors rethink flow-based slow domain shift via semi-dual transport. Slow shift moves a model from source to target through mid domains, but real mid domains often miss or fail, forcing made mid samples. Flow plans that lean on odds math toss out good info and dent shift scores. Their entropy-tuned transport plan builds mid domains straight from samples, dodging odds math. Entropy tuning then turns shaky min-max training into calm step-by-step training, with steadiness proofs.
arxiv-2602-01379: Zachary Cooper-Baldock and co-authors launch WAKESET, a huge high-Reynolds flow set for machine learning of turbulent wakes. Machine learning could speed fluid sims and sharpen turbulence models, but progress stalls on thin, small, low-fidelity sets, above all for wild turbulent flows ruling real engineering. WAKESET captures underwater recovery of a self-driving sub by a bigger sub, with 1,091 high-fidelity sim runs boosted to 4,364 cases. Speeds reach Reynolds numbers of 1.09 x 10 to the power 8, spanning wide turn angles for flow and navigation tests.
arxiv-2602-01479: Xueqing Peng and co-authors introduce Ebisu, a benchmark testing Japanese financial language. Japanese finance mixes agglutinative head-final structure and high-context norms. Ebisu holds expert-annotated tasks: JF-ICR, testing implicit commitment and refusal recognition for investor Q&A, and JF-TE, testing hierarchical extraction and ranking of nested terms from disclosures. The team tests open-source and proprietary models: general, Japanese-adapted, and finance ones. Even the best systems struggle; scale helps little, and adaptation does not reliably help. Its datasets and scripts are public.
arxiv-2602-01679: Raghavasimhan Sankaranarayanan and colleagues automate sterile tray setup, where sorting, checks and packing of instruments wastes time, invites errors and risks contamination and breakage. Their robotic system sorts and packs instruments into sterile trays. It trains on a custom set of 31 instruments and 6975 labeled images. Detection uses YOLO12, and a ResNet model classifies. A vision module, a rule based packing algorithm, and a Staubli arm with an electromagnetic gripper run the system. Tests show high perception accuracy and far fewer tool collisions than human assembled trays.
arxiv-2602-01779: Rui Hua and colleagues build LingLanMedBench, a benchmark for judging large language models in traditional Chinese medicine, where tests are narrow. It holds over twenty five thousand expert checked items in thirteen subtasks across five domains, spanning knowledge, language, extraction and diagnostic therapeutic choices. Fourteen open and proprietary models took a zero shot test, with scores varying widely by domain, family, task form and difficulty. The leading score drops on hard subsets, and prescription generation lags far behind decision recognition, revealing a gap between knowledge and clinically faithful reasoning.
arxiv-2602-01979: Fabio Stano and colleagues study how digital workers find flow, foregrounding daily habits workers already use. From a reflexive analysis of open ended survey responses from 160 people, they surface 38 items across task shaping, environment, organization and personal readiness. An online survey of 121 people validates this set, showing broad versus polarizing endorsement, and gathers visions of tech support. The work contributes empirical insights into how digital workers find flow, situates them in existing literature, and derives design opportunities for future digital flow interventions.
arxiv-2602-02079: Daniil Orel and colleagues offer AICD Bench, the biggest AI-made code benchmark, spanning 2M cases, 77 models, 11 groups, 9 codes. Large language models write working source code, raising credit and security concerns, while older benchmarks are narrow, limited to binary sorting. Beyond scale, AICD Bench adds three real tasks: robust binary sorting under shifts; model family credit by design lineage; and fine-grained sorting of human, machine, and hybrid code. Tests on neural and older tools show scores far below real use, notably for hybrid or hostile code.
arxiv-2602-02179: Marina Mastroleo and others present SurvKAN, a fully parametric survival model built on Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for predicting time-to-event outcomes in medicine. Deep survival models gain flexibility at the cost of clarity. SurvKAN feeds time straight into a network predicting the log-hazard function, allowing training straight on the full survival likelihood without the proportional hazards constraint. Learnable univariate functions keep the model readable, showing how each feature shapes risk.
arxiv-2602-02279: Thomas Birbacher and others present NICE, a cryogenic nulling interferometry testbed for the LIFE exoplanet mission. Earlier testbeds proved deep stable nulls but never combined high contrast with high throughput and cryogenic operation. Results from the Warm Bench precursor show required null depth with a polarized source and required throughput through one nulling channel.
arxiv-2602-02479:
Ni Annie Yuan and 1 co-author analyze over three million posts in a 2026 arXiv paper. They track how moralized political content spread on TikTok and Instagram during the 2024 United States presidential election. Moralization turns a policy dispute into a clash of good and evil. The authors argue issues are not moralized by nature; audience demographics, platform design, and partisan framing do the work.

Supply-and-demand analysis plus moral foundations scoring surfaces three findings. TikTok's algorithm pushed moralized abortion and immigration content viral despite low supply, while Instagram amplified economic talk where supply matched demand. Cryptocurrency discussion, supposedly pragmatic, invoked loyalty and authority more than any other topic. The platforms also reacted to different events: TikTok surged after Harris's nomination, Instagram around crypto policy news. Network analysis shows TikTok's circular structure spreads exposure across camps.
arxiv-2602-03079:
Yu-Feng Luo and 8 co-authors pin down the orbit of a rare gamma-ray binary in a 2026 paper. The system pairs a pulsar with a Be star, a hot star with a surrounding disk. It is the only gamma-ray binary showing gamma-ray pulsations. Earlier work suggested a highly eccentric, extremely long orbit, with closest approach in November twenty seventeen.

Sixteen years of Fermi satellite monitoring cover eight years on each side of that passage. Analyzing pulse arrival times yields the orbital parameters precisely for the first time. The period is about fifty-two years, with very high eccentricity. The semi-major axis and inclination range are also determined. The timing analysis additionally revealed a small glitch in the pulsar during twenty twenty-one.
arxiv-2602-03279:
Hard thinking problems are synthesized by an agent rather than annotated by humans in work led by Zhengbo Jiao with 7 collaborators. High-quality verifiable datasets drive complex thinking gains, but human annotation is costly and hard to scale. Synthesis methods trade off validity against difficulty, producing either simple valid problems or harder inconsistent ones that cannot train a solver reliably at scale.

Their Agentic Proposing system treats synthesis as a sequential decision process. A specialized agent selects and composes modular thinking skills, reflecting internally and using tools iteratively. The resulting proposer makes verifiable trajectories across mathematics, coding, and science. Solvers trained on its data beat leading earlier methods and generalized across domains. A mid-size solver trained on a small synthesized set reached state-of-the-art score on a competition math benchmark.
arxiv-2602-03379:
Sangyeon Yoon and 3 co-authors ask why erased knowledge keeps coming back in large language models. Their 2026 paper studies benign relearning, the effect where fine-tuning on harmless data makes a model recover content that unlearning was supposed to remove. The usual explanation blames topical closeness between the new data and the forgotten material.

Across several benchmarks, the authors show that sentence structure matters more than topic. Data that merely shares syntax with the forgotten content triggers recovery, because the two align inside the model. They answer with syntactic diversification, which rewrites the forget queries into varied sentence shapes before unlearning. The change suppresses relearning, speeds up forgetting, and softens the trade-off between erasure and general usefulness.
arxiv-2602-03479:
Sajjad Taravati presents a metasurface built from Josephson junctions that converts the frequency of arriving photons. The 2026 talk describes a device working at millikelvin temperatures, deep in the superconducting regime. Josephson junctions carry supercurrent with zero loss, and their nonlinearity lets the surface reshape waves in ways ordinary materials cannot.

The talk walks through how the surface converts frequencies. It is nonreciprocal, meaning waves behave differently by direction. The same structure can also amplify incident photons, a valuable trick for faint quantum signals. Such devices could serve quantum tools that need to shift and boost microwave photons without adding the noise that ordinary electronics bring.
arxiv-2602-03879:
Ali Bayeh and 2 co-authors rework a young neural network design in their 2026 paper. Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks replace fixed activations with learnable curves, usually built from B-splines, which are smooth but costly. Their version, TruKAN, swaps in truncated power functions, a simpler family from spline theory.

Each layer pairs a truncated power term with a polynomial term, using shared or separate knots. Built into an EfficientNet-V2 vision framework, TruKAN beats rival KAN variants on accuracy, training time, and memory. The simpler curves also make the model easier to interpret than its spline-based cousins.
arxiv-2602-03979:
Ariel Kwiatkowski and 4 co-authors simplify how reasoning models earn rewards. Standard reinforcement learning needs a separate checker for each benchmark, and its yes-or-no rewards give sparse feedback. Their 2026 paper instead rewards the model by how probable it finds the reference answer.

Several variants of likelihood-based reward were compared against standard baselines. Only one, the log-probability of the reference answer, performed well everywhere. It worked on math benchmarks and on long-form answers where no external checker exists. Such rewards need no verifier engineering and exist wherever training data does, making them cheap to deploy at scale.
arxiv-2602-04079:
What stops inside a colliding nucleus carries clues about its skin. Grégoire Pihan and 1 co-author analyze baryon and charge stopping in heavy-ion collisions with a statistical model. Their 2026 paper starts with isobar collisions at RHIC, where ruthenium and zirconium nuclei have the same mass but different charge.

A stopping parameter they define can be extracted from upcoming measurements of stopping ratios. They then generalize across collision systems and energies. A new oxygen-baseline observable proves sharply sensitive to the neutron skin, the extra reach of neutrons over protons at a nucleus's edge. That thickness constrains the physics of neutron stars.
arxiv-2602-04279:
Fluent but wrong heart readings are worse than none. Jiarui Jin and colleagues built ECG-R1, a multimodal language model that reads ECGs and is built for reliability, in a 2026 paper. Current models often produce plausible readings that fail clinical checks.

Three innovations ground the system. Protocol-guided data building ties readings to measured features and published thresholds. A split architecture with interleaved dropout stays consistent when the signal or the image is missing. Reinforcement learning rewards evidence for a diagnosis, not just conclusions. The team also tests current closed and open models head-on, mapping how far ECG reading still has to go.
arxiv-2602-04479:
Demyan Yarmoshik's 2026 paper, written with 3 co-authors, studies optimization problems spread across a network of computers. Each node holds part of the problem. Some limits apply to local variables, while others couple variables shared across nodes or differ between nodes.

Such setups appear in federated learning, resource allocation, and distributed control. The authors analyze smooth and non-smooth cases, for both strongly convex and general convex functions. Convex here means the problem has a bowl-like shape with no false low points. Their main result is an optimal algorithm for the smooth, strongly convex case. Its speed matches known lower bounds. They also give near-optimal methods for the remaining cases.
arxiv-2602-04579:
Sameh Khattab's 2026 paper, written with 5 co-authors, presents AIANO, a tool for building search datasets with AI help. Such datasets are in growing demand for retrieval and retrieval-augmented generation, yet standard labeling tools make the work slow and awkward.

AIANO pairs human judgment with language model tips while leaving final calls to the annotator. Fifteen participants built question-answering datasets using both AIANO and a baseline tool. Labeling with AIANO was nearly twice as fast. Users also found it easier to use, and the data that came out raised retrieval scores. The study supports AI-augmented labeling, where the model assists rather than replaces the human labeler.
arxiv-2602-05079:
Emergency braking systems must decide in a split second, and camera-based learning systems often miss the scene's meaning. Vinal Asodia and 2 co-authors propose a neuro-symbolic upgrade in this 2026 robotics paper. Their aim is braking that reads context the way a careful human driver would, with special attention to vulnerable road users.

The pipeline builds features that combine semantics, spatial layout, and shape from segmentation maps, with dynamic objects boosted in importance. A soft first-order logic reward then scores actions by linguistic rules, balancing human values against raw driving goals. In the CARLA simulator, across traffic densities and occlusion levels, the representation and reward together improved robustness and safety metrics over baseline designs. The authors present the work as evidence that holistic features plus soft reasoning make driving policies more context-aware.
arxiv-2602-05179:
Stochastic programming plans under uncertainty by averaging over many scenarios, but solving an exact hard subproblem for each scenario is ruinously slow. Jingyi Zhao and 4 co-authors move that work onto graphics processors in this 2026 optimization paper. Their move is to rewrite dynamic programming, classically a sequential method, as GPU kernels built for scenario-based sample average approximation.

The kernels expose parallelism at three levels at once. They work across scenarios, across dynamic programming layers, and across route or action choices, clearing Bellman updates for over a million scenario realizations in a single pass. Two testbeds, a split operator for stochastic vehicle routing and a dynamic program for inventory reinsertion, show near-linear scaling in the count of scenarios. Speedups ran from tens to tens of thousands of times. More scenarios per second means more first-stage candidates evaluated, and consistently stronger decisions.
arxiv-2602-05279:
Security teams would love an LLM's help writing incident response plans, but a hallucinating planner is worse than none. Kim Hammar and 2 co-authors build a guardrailed framework in this 2026 paper, accepted at a major network operations and management symposium. The language model proposes actions; the framework refuses to trust them blindly.

Each candidate action is checked for consistency with system constraints and with lookahead predictions. When consistency falls below a threshold, the system abstains and gathers outside feedback instead, for instance by trying the action in a digital twin of the network. That feedback refines the next round of proposals through in-context learning. The authors prove the hallucination risk can be dialed down by tightening the consistency threshold, and bound the learning regret under stated assumptions. On four public datasets for incident response, recovery times fell by up to 30 percent against frontier models used directly.
arxiv-2602-05379:
Past-run replay lets a reinforcement learning agent learn again and again from its past, but standard replay treats a lucky guess and a hard-won lesson as equals. Hua Zheng and 3 co-authors propose Variance Reduction Experience Replay in this 2026 statistics paper, 46 pages long. The scheme reuses past observations selectively, choosing the samples that most reduce the variance of policy gradient estimates.

The method is method-neutral and plugs into current policy tuning, yielding a combined method the authors study in depth. Their theory is itself a contribution: it tracks the links that Markovian dynamics and behavior policies create between samples, something earlier replay studies ignored. Finite-time settling guarantees follow, along with a mapped trade-off, since older samples cut variance but add bias. Tests show faster learning and better final performance than leading policy tuning methods.
arxiv-2602-05579:
Fluid antennas can shift their radiating point to find a better signal, but mapping the radio field they move through takes costly measurements. Mu Jia, Hao Sun, Junting Chen, and Pooi-Yuen Kam propose a physics-aware way to rebuild radio maps from sparse samples. Their method treats the signal field as a three-way tensor and fills in the missing entries, a task known as tensor completion.

Two kinds of structure guide the filling: the environment's low-rank pattern, and antenna physics drawn from a theory of effective aerial degrees of freedom. That physics is turned into a gain map used as a prior. An ADMM-based algorithm solves the resulting optimization. In simulations, it gained a clear margin over baselines at a low sampling rate and kept sharp shadowing edges that other methods blur. The authors aim it at low-overhead beam management for fluid antenna systems.
arxiv-2602-05679:
Planning under uncertainty is hard enough, and camera images make it harder, since classic solvers cannot reason over raw pixels. Miriam Schäfers, Merlijn Krale, and 3 co-authors present a framework that bolts a perception model onto traditional solvers for partially observable Markov decision processes. An image classifier turns each visual observation into a probability distribution over states, and that distribution feeds the belief update directly.

The authors show the update matches the standard one when the classifier is exact. Because real classifiers err, they add uncertainty quantification and two ways to adjust the update when perception is shaky. Tests with two classic solvers beat end to end deep reinforcement learning methods. Adding the uncertainty handling also made the system more robust when images were corrupted. The work was accepted at an autonomous agents conference. It offers a bridge between learned perception and principled planning.
arxiv-2602-05779:
Deep networks train best when signals neither explode nor vanish across layers, and a body of theory called edge of chaos guides the choice of starting weights. Emily Dent and Jared Tanner study a less explored case: activations that induce heavy sparsity, zeroing a large region of values near the origin. For near linear activations, the classic theory pushes the layer variance toward zero with depth.

The authors prove a new phenomenon for the sparse case: starting points that lead to larger fixed Gaussian processes are actually better for training stability. That finding informs a simple new initialization strategy for fully connected and convolutional networks. With it, they train networks whose hidden layers run at up to ninety percent sparsity. The result matters for efficient computing, since sparse networks promise cheaper inference. In the sparse regime, shrinking variance is the wrong target.
arxiv-2602-05879:
Europe's tongues are ill-served by open language models, and Miguel Moura Ramos and 17 co-authors present EuroLLM-22B, a model trained from scratch to serve them. It covers all twenty four official European Union tongues plus eleven more. The tech report walks through the full build: word-piece design, shape, data sifting, and training steps.

Across a broad set of many-tongue tests, the model does well in reasoning, instruction following, and translation, matching models of like size. The team puts out the base and instruction tuned models, the many-tongue web training data, updated instruction data sets, and the training and test code. That openness is part of the point: Europe's research groups gain a base they can inspect and extend. The report logs choices in enough detail to redo the pipe. It should catch builders of local and public interest language models.
arxiv-2602-06179:
Diseases of the female pelvis are often diagnosed late, partly because anatomy varies so much between patients that MRI scans are hard to read. Anika Knupfer and 11 co-authors set up a benchmark for spotting such disease without labeled examples of illness. Their model learns only what healthy scans look like.

A variational autoencoder trained on healthy scans flags regions it cannot rebuild well, marking them on heat maps as suspect. Extra synthetic scans, made by a diffusion model, hardened the training. On a public uterine fibroid data set, detection scores were moderate, and clinician review covered several other conditions. The system runs in real time, fast enough for live scanning sessions.
arxiv-2602-06379:
Clinical trials that peek at results early and adapt the design break the rules of classical statistics. Alexandra Sokolova and Vadim Sokolov write a practical guide to e-values, a newer tool that stays valid under such peeking. E-processes allow optional stopping and continuation without a preset schedule of looks.

The guide builds e-processes for two-arm randomized trials from a betting martingale idea, and shows how they handle combined hypotheses and futility checks. It also advises when older tools, like group sequential or Bayesian designs, serve better. In a numerical study of a two-arm trial with a binary outcome, naive repeated testing inflated false alarms badly. Valid methods differed in power, with the e-value rule offering robust anytime protection.
arxiv-2602-06679: Wadim Zudilin writes about a kind of number identity in which sequences agree to very high powers of a prime. These are called supercongruences. Building on the work of Guillera, he pushes the classic Ramanujan-type cases one step further. In the new setting, the Fibonacci and Lucas sequences show up next to the Apéry numbers and their kin.
arxiv-2602-06879:
Ruchika Chavhan and five co-authors shrink a large text-to-image model down to phone size. State-of-the-art image generators keep growing, widening the gap with on-device solutions that must run fast on limited hardware. Their model, NanoFLUX, is a 2.4-billion-parameter flow-matching model distilled from a 17-billion-parameter teacher, built through a progressive compression pipeline designed to preserve quality.

The pipeline prunes redundant parts of the diffusion transformer, cutting it from 12 billion to 2 billion parameters, and adds a downsampling mechanism so middle blocks work on lower-resolution tokens. A new text encoder distillation step uses visual signals from the denoiser's early layers during sampling. The result generates 512 by 512 images in about 2.5 seconds on mobile devices, showing high-quality on-device generation is feasible.
arxiv-2602-06979:
Baishun Lai, Ge Tang, and Ziying Xu study weak solutions of the magnetohydrodynamics equations with large initial data in the critical L3 space. The natural slip boundary condition on the magnetic field breaks the standard Leray-Schauder fixed-point approach used for the Navier-Stokes equations, so the weak solution theory for this system needs a different route. The authors turn to Leray's approximation technique combined with perturbation theory.

Their strategy yields a global weak solution to the Cauchy problem for magnetohydrodynamics with large L3 initial data, and the solution is unique under some restrictions. As a bonus, the same approach gives a simple self-contained proof of the weak L3 solution theory for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. The work extends the classical weak solution program to a system where the standard tools fail.
arxiv-2602-07279:
Vertical federated learning lets parties holding other traits of the same people analyze data, but clustering in that setting has mostly meant distributed k-means with central coordination.  Bruno Belucci and three co-authors present VertCoHiRF, a fully decentralized option.

Each agent clusters its own local view with a method suited to that view. The agents reconcile their proposals through identifier-level consensus built on decentralized ordinal ranking, without exchanging feature-dependent statistics or relying on noise for privacy.  The design tolerates heterogeneous views and adversarial action better than centralized variants.  Federated learning teams get a clustering method that stays peer-to-peer from start to finish.
arxiv-2602-07379:
Voice agents now handle banking, customer service, and IT support, yet their security has never been tested as a full deployment pipeline.  Xiang Li and two co-authors present Aegis, a red-teaming method for the governance, integrity, and security of AI voice agents.

Aegis models real deployment and designs structured adversarial scenarios covering privacy leakage, privilege escalation, resource abuse, and more.  Case studies in banking call centers, IT support, and logistics show access controls mitigating data-level risks while other risks persist.  Security teams deploying voice agents get a thorough test suite for threats that text-only tests miss.
arxiv-2602-07579:
Ensembles of neural networks for time series classification usually train identical models and hope diversity emerges, but identical training breeds redundant traits.  Javidan Abdullayev and five co-authors build a diversity-driven ensemble that explicitly encourages members to learn other traits.

A decorrelated learning strategy applies a feature orthogonality loss to learned representations, pushing ensemble members apart in feature space so their combination adds real information.  The method targets time series classification, where ensembles already lead but often waste their members.  Users get an ensemble method that earns its extra models through enforced diversity rather than mere replication.
arxiv-2602-07679:
Feed-forward networks need frequency-rich expressivity without losing stability, a tension exposed by spline-based Kolmogorov-Arnold networks whose grid refinement bloats weight counts and brittles tuning.  Jusheng Zhang and seven co-authors present Spectral Gating Networks, a drop-in spectral reparameterization for standard MLP layers under fixed setting and training budgets.

A compact spectral pathway built from trainable random Fourier features joins the standard activation pathway. Learnable gates that start from stable base action and progressively allocate capacity to spectral features during training.  Network builders get spectral expressivity that grows safely, rather than a parameterization that must be tuned to stay stable.
arxiv-2602-08279:
If-based freedom is central to chance, and if-based mutual freedom widens it, including working link as a special case. Laigang Guo and two co-authors tackle two basic questions for such claims over finite discrete factors: when are two if-based mutual freedoms same, and when does one imply the other?

They obtain needed and enough rules for both, put through a set form given for if-based mutual freedom. The accounts give chance fans and information theorists a complete, checkable account of the logic of these freedom claims, clearing links that before needed ad hoc case. Graph-model teams gain tools for thought strictly about freedom structure.
arxiv-2602-08379:
Heavy quarks plowing through quark-gluon plasma lose energy by collisions, and the plasma itself may follow nonstandard statistics. Bing-feng Jiang and two co-authors compute that energy loss for a nonextensive plasma, where a parameter q reshapes the usual thermal distributions. Their arXiv paper derives the plasma's dielectric response first, then applies two established loss formulas.

Loss grows with q in both formulas, more so at high quark momentum and less so for heavier quarks. The thermal-field-theory formula predicts substantially larger loss than the plasma-physics formula, and its q-dependence is stronger and less mass-suppressed. Readers get a clear statement of how far from ordinary statistics a plasma must sit before heavy-quark probes can tell.
arxiv-2602-08779:
Crawling cells move by actin networks that push and pull in waves, regulated by signaling proteins and lipids. Jack M. Hughes and two co-authors study a model in which filamentous actin feeds back negatively onto a GTPase switch. Their arXiv paper explores cell shapes and motility across polar, oscillatory, and traveling-wave regimes of a mass-conserved equation model.

Guided by bifurcation analysis, the authors use cellular Potts simulations to trace how each regime shapes cells and motion, and how cells switch between modes under noisy stimuli. States include resting cells with uniform activity, polar cells with static active zones, and traveling waves along the cell edge, sometimes coexisting. Readers get a map linking feedback sign to the shapes and gaits of crawling cells.
arxiv-2602-08879:
How old are Alpha Centauri A and B, our nearest Sun-like neighbors? F. Thévenin and six co-authors apply a mapping technique that treats the pair as twins: same age, same starting chemistry. Feeding in fresh measurements of mass, radius, brightness, and composition, they solve for age plus starting helium and heavy-element shares.

The answer depends on the assumed solar mixture. With a high solar heavy-element ratio, the age comes out near 7.8 billion years; with a low one, near 8.7 billion years. Tiny mass errors of 0.002 solar masses shift the age by 0.6 billion years, showing why better stellar models matter ahead of the PLATO mission.
arxiv-2602-08979:
Podcasts, lectures, and long videos are easier to navigate with chapters, yet most chaptering research still leans on text transcripts. Fabian Retkowski and four co-authors ask what sound itself can add. They compare text models with acoustic features, a new audio-only architecture called AudioSeg, and multimodal language models, on the YTSeg data set.

AudioSeg substantially beats text-based approaches, and pauses turn out to be the most valuable acoustic cue. Multimodal models are held back by context length and weak instruction following, though they show promise on shorter clips. The paper also formalizes fair evaluation protocols, contrasting transcript-dependent scoring with transcript-free, time-based scoring.
arxiv-2602-09079:
Deciding who most needs costly obesity therapies starts with risk, and body mass index alone is a blunt tool. Zachary N. Flamholz and eight co-authors present PatientTPP, a neural temporal point-process model. It is trained on over 500,000 real clinical trajectories of diagnoses, labs, and medications, extended with static and numeric features plus clinical knowledge for event encoding.

Its learned patient representations predict obesity-linked outcomes even in low-risk people, including events never explicitly modeled in training. In health-economic tests, PatientTPP beats body mass index at ranking patients by future cardiovascular costs, finding higher-risk patients more efficiently. Modeling both event type and timing gives an interpretable foundation for obesity-related care.
arxiv-2602-09179:
Moving a spin qubit across a chip offers bendy wiring for error fixing, but only if its linked state lasts the trip. Jan A. Krzywda and eight co-authors show steady noise cutting during shuttling in a silicon-germanium quantum-dot device. First, quietly flattening magnet-field slopes halves charge-noise coupling, doubling the space-averaged fade time from 4.4 to 8.5 microseconds.

Timed shuttling then uses motion narrowing, lifting linked-state life to 11.5 microseconds, and adding active uncoupling over shuttles beyond 200 nanometers reaches 32 microseconds. Dressed-state shuttling guards against low-rate noise for 21 microseconds without pulsed-control extra cost, even on one-way trips. The tricks keep linked states past typical gate and readout times, backing mobile spins for scalable silicon chips.
arxiv-2602-09679:
Chang Qin and four co-authors present a full review of recent gains in bent sifting methods in their 2026 paper. The review is set into three main groups: Kalman-type methods, Monte Carlo methods, and the Yau-Yau method. For each group, the authors join theory gains, method variants, and usable uses that have emerged in recent years.

Both smooth-time and discrete-time system forms are covered, giving a unified review across frames. The work also reveals the changing influence of machine breakthroughs on the entire bent sifting field, most in areas such as learning-based sifters, neural network-boosted methods, and data-driven ways. Real-time sifting thus appears as a field remade by both classic theory and modern machine learning.
arxiv-2602-09879:
The Frobenius stratification measures how bundles in a moduli space grow unstable when pulled back by the Frobenius map. Lingguang Li and Hongyi Zhang study rank-two stable vector bundles with fixed determinant in their 2026 paper. The bundles sit on a smooth projective algebraic curve of genus at least two, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic two.

Their question is whether any Frobenius stratum in this setting is covered by Hecke curves. The answer is yes: the authors show that there exists a Frobenius stratum in the moduli space that is covered by Hecke curves. This gives a concrete geometric description of one layer of the stratification, linking the instability measured by Frobenius pullback to a classical family of curves. The result supplies a foothold for further study of how these strata are shaped.
arxiv-2602-10079:
Image forgery detection usually hunts for artifacts in the altered region alone, but that can mislead, as when a duplicated act is inserted into a peaceful crowd. A 2026 paper by Soumyaroop Nandi and Prem Natarajan introduces Forensim, an attention-based state-space framework that localizes both manipulated target regions and their source regions together. Its masks carry three classes: pristine, source, and target.

A visual state-space model with normalized attention maps finds internal similarities, while a region-based block attention module separates manipulated regions. One architecture handles both splicing and copy-move forgery with end-to-end training. Forensim leads standard benchmarks, and the team releases a new data set, CMFD-Anything, fixing limits of existing copy-move collections.
arxiv-2602-10379:
Duhamel's principle turns a forced partial differential equation into its unforced counterpart, but fractional derivatives depend on the whole past, so they break the classical argument. A 2026 paper by Sabir Umarov extends the principle to fully coupled fractional systems, building on two decades of partial fractional versions. The result gives a general way to reduce forced fractional problems to unforced ones while keeping the structure of the classical method.

When derivatives return to integer order, the version restores the classical principle. It also exposes effects found only in coupled fractional systems, among them effects from coupled fractional impulses. The paper therefore supplies a general tool for workers on coupled fractional systems. It lets them transfer unforced-problem methods to forced settings without redoing the theory case by case.
arxiv-2602-10479:
Mamdouh Alenezi charts the shift from chatbots to goal-directed AI systems in a 2026 paper. Agentic AI marks an architectural break: instead of answering one prompt at a time, systems perceive, plan, act, and adapt through control loops. The paper connects older agent theories, including reactive, deliberative, and belief-desire-intention models, with today's tool-using language models.

Three contributions anchor the survey. A reference system separates mind thinking from execution through typed tool interfaces. A taxonomy of multi-agent topologies maps their failure modes and mitigations. An enterprise hardening checklist covers governance, observability, and related safeguards. Jointly they give builders a shared words for moving agents from demos into production.
arxiv-2602-11079:
Post-training can plant bad conduct that only odd prompts reveal. Frank Xiao and Santiago Aranguri propose probe-based data attribution, which traces conduct shifts in tuned language models back to culprit training examples. They rank examples by matching signal-difference vectors for test prompts and preference pairs.

Applied to OLMo 2 preference tuning, the method surfaces distractor-triggered compliance, where harmless formatting notes make the model obey dangerous requests. Removing top-ranked examples cuts that conduct sharply, and flipping their labels cuts it further, at far lower cost than gradient or judge rivals. The case gives safety work a realistic, in-the-wild test bed born from tainted data, not staged injection.
arxiv-2602-11179:
Prompting has become a core skill, yet its methods lack a shared frame. Munazza Zaib and Elaf Alhazmi survey prompt engineering for natural language making, where instructions in plain language draw structured knowledge from language models. They review recent methods and their effects across making tasks.

The survey presents prompt design as input-level control that complements fine-tuning and decoding. It offers a taxonomy of prompting paradigms, a decision frame for choosing prompts, and a map of trends and challenges. A final frame links design, tuning, and tests, aiming for making that is more controllable and generalizable across tasks and models.
arxiv-2602-11279:
Maps of hot gas in the universe are a cosmological tool. A. S. Maniyar and a large team present thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich Compton-y maps from two years of South Pole Telescope data combined with Planck data. A straight combination pipeline yields several reconstructions with other trade-offs.

Minimum-variance, cosmic-microwave-background-deprojected, and dust-deprojected maps balance sensitivity against foreground contamination. Checks through power spectra, cross-links with large-scale structure, and cluster stacking confirms robust signal recovery across a wide survey field. The high-detail, low-noise maps will feed power spectrum work, cluster pressure building, and studies of cosmic baryons and their thermodynamic state.
arxiv-2602-11879:
Heavy-to-light decays underpin mixing measurements, but precise predictions need high-order QCD corrections. Long Chen and three co-authors present the first complete second- and third-order perturbative corrections to all five heavy-to-light structure functions behind triple-differential semileptonic decay rates. A hybrid strategy combines interpolation on layered points in one variable with differential equations in the other, plus reduced numerical dependence on a cutoff.

The authors highlight a prediction for a B meson decay rate in the kinetic-mass scheme. They report how the first three orders converge for spectra and moments in different quark-mass schemes, insights for improving mixing-element and non-perturbative parameter determinations. A subtle boundary finding is also discussed. Certain terms first appear at third order and must be included to preserve total moments, requiring binning from that order onward even in pure perturbation theory.
arxiv-2602-12279:
Unified models can both read and make images, yet they usually run in one pass without checking or fixing their own work. Leon Liangyu Chen led this work with 13 co-authors, presenting UniT, a frame for multimodal chain-of-thought test-time scaling. One unified model reasons, checks, and refines across several rounds, handling spatial layouts, many objects, and changing instructions.

UniT joins agentic data synthesis, unified training, and flexible test-time inference to spark checking, subgoal splitting, and content memory. Three findings stand out: short reasoning training generalises to longer test-time chains, sequential reasoning scales better than parallel sampling, and training on generation and editing lifts out-of-distribution visual reasoning. Test-time scaling thus becomes a real lever for unified models.
arxiv-2602-12479:
Odd Radio Circles are a newly found class of huge radio rings whose origins remain unclear. Yiting Wang led this work with one co-author, Sebastian Heinz. They test a model where the rings are synchrotron-emitting vortex rings formed by Richtmyer-Meshkov instability, when a shock hits a low-density fossil radio lobe in the intergalactic medium. Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations track the rings as their initial oscillations damp over time.

A new scale-free method models inverse-Compton and synchrotron cooling at high frequencies, allowing wide parameter tests against observations. Shock strengths of Mach 2 to 4 fit the data, as expected for accretion, merger, or active-galaxy shocks. Bubble sizes of 140 to 250 kiloparsecs are required to explain the rings. Energies near 10 to the 57 to 59 ergs match fossil lobes from moderately powerful radio galaxies, in low-density group outskirts aged 70 to 200 million years.
arxiv-2602-12679:
Generative inbetweening aims to make plausible frames between two keyframes, and image-to-video diffusion models have advanced that field a lot. Wooseok Jeon led this work with three co-authors, noting that inference-time sampling tricks using priors of large-scale pre-trained image-to-video models without extra training have become popular. Yet old tricks often suffer time gaps and unwanted visual flaws.

The cause is misalignment between forward and backward made paths, whether fused in parallel or alternated in sequence. Their method, Motion Prior Distillation in Time Reversal Sampling, distils motion priors to align the two paths during time-reversed sampling. That cuts gaps and flaws. Tests on inbetweening tests show improved time consistency and visual quality over prior inference-time sampling rivals.
arxiv-2602-12779:
Language models now grade writing, but their feedback is often vague, generic, and disconnected from what the user actually asked for. Jingwen Bai and three co-authors propose iRULER, a tool that scaffolds review with user-defined rubrics. It gives reasons for each score and concrete revisions aimed at different quality levels. A rubric-of-rubrics loop even refines the user's own criteria step by step.

In controlled tests on revision and rubric creation, iRULER improved validated review scores more than read-only rubrics or plain text feedback. Users also rated it most helpful and best aligned with their goals. Interview findings back the design choices behind it. The contribution is a practical set of interactive rubric tools for making machine review of writing clearer, fairer, and easier to act on.
arxiv-2602-12979:
Reconfigurable surfaces can help locate and track objects indoors without line of sight, but near-field effects complicate the geometry. Thomas Zemen and seven co-authors study position and velocity estimation with a compound surface of four tiles, each cell offering 1-bit phase control. Simulations over a 3-by-3-metre area, including antenna patterns, show that a far-field grid search fails at small distances from the surface centre.

The authors propose a more robust three-step algorithm that accounts for near-field geometry and antenna-pattern effects, which otherwise inflate errors. Under a realistic propagation model, the method reaches 7 millimetres position error and 0.12 metres per second velocity error at 2 metres from the surface centre. For indoor tracking with reconfigurable surfaces, the result shows near-field-aware processing is essential, not optional.
arxiv-2602-13179:
Many-mode pull systems assume visual queries are clean, but real queries arrive distorted, degraded, or ambiguous, causing catastrophic pull failures. Jiankun Zhang and six co-authors propose V-QPP-Bench, the first benchmark for visual query pre-processing as agentic decision-making: many-mode models must spot imperfections and use perceptual tools to improve queries. Testing spans 46,700 imperfect queries across diverse pull paradigms.

Three insights emerge. First, imperfections severely degrade pull recall and end-to-end scores. Second, oracle preprocessing nearly restores scores, but off-the-shelf models struggle to pick tools and predict settings without specialised training. Third, supervised fine-tuning lets compact models match or beat larger proprietary models. The benchmark thus diagnoses a real vulnerability and shows a training path toward robust many-mode pull.
arxiv-2602-13279:
Rumors spread through social networks in tangled paths, and detectors often miss how meaning flows along a whole chain of shares. This framework adds a language model as a structural helper for graph-based rumor detection. The model reads subchains of shares, then the system inserts a virtual node into the graph to turn hidden semantic links into visible structure. That gives graph networks access to textual coherence they normally cannot see.

A structured prompt design reins in model bias while keeping graph learning strong, and the setup is model-agnostic, working with different language models and graph methods without rewriting them. The plug-and-play design means future tuned models can slot in directly. Jiran Tao leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13479:
Wearable video assistants that answer questions about text face a squeeze. Reading text needs high-resolution video, but streaming it drains battery and overheats the device, while text across frames must stay coherent in time. This paper exploits an asymmetry: optical character recognition needs fine detail, while scene understanding tolerates coarse features. Its hybrid design runs selective high-resolution OCR on the device and streams low-resolution video for visual context.

On a benchmark of text-based visual question answering across five task categories, the system reached 72 percent accuracy at 0.49 times the power of full-resolution streaming. That efficiency enables sustained question-answering sessions on constrained wearables without giving up text understanding. Akhil Ramachandran leads the work with ten co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14179:
Khyodeno Mozhui and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv problem on word-representable graphs. In such graphs, vertices are encoded by words, and the representation number measures the complexity of that encoding. Graphs with representation number up to two were already characterized, but no full picture existed for number three.

The paper proves melon graphs need a representation number of three at most. It also sorts melon graphs that are comparability graphs, showing their permutation-representation number caps at three too. Finally, it sorts the word-representable line graphs of melon graphs, again capping at three. The results fill a gap for this graph family.
arxiv-2602-14279:
Ruomeng Ding and five co-authors study a 2026 arXiv problem in tuned group asking. Surveys and group checks must cut doubt about group traits under tight budgets, costs, and missing data. Old methods usually fix the person pool and tune only what to ask, ignoring who should answer.

The offered setup picks both questions and people across rounds. A language-model info-gain score rates candidate questions, while a mixed graph neural net spreads seen answers and person traits to fill missing answers and guide person choice. That closed loop asks a small, telling subset each round, tuning to partial data as it lands.
arxiv-2602-14379:
Nai-Hui Chia and three co-authors prove a 2026 arXiv hardness result for quantum problems. The local Hamiltonian problem is Kitaev's canonical QMA-complete problem.

It cannot be cracked classically in time order 2 to the (1 minus epsilon) n, for any epsilon above zero, under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis. Quantumly, it cannot be cracked in time order 2 to the (1 minus epsilon) n over 2, under the quantum form of that guess. Those bounds, built from size-keeping circuit-to-Hamiltonian builds, hint current old and quantum methods for local Hamiltonians cannot gain much. The paper also gives fine-grained lower bounds for guessing the quantum partition function with fixed relative error. That task is the same as roughly counting the answer-space size of QMA problems, plus a quantum method for that guess.
arxiv-2602-14479:
Samaneh Sojudi and one co-author builds a 2026 arXiv form of conditional means in mean-field stochastic differential equations with jumps. The joined approach mixes plain means with strictly set weight factors, using Malliavin calculus on Poisson space and direction slopes to lift guess exactness.

The method is used for number pricing of American put options in a jump-spread mean-field setting, where early-use traits pose hurdles. Full number tests show big lifts in pricing exactness over old tricks. The work offers a new guess tool for mean-field models with jumps, bridging random study and real option pricing.
arxiv-2602-14579:
Indranil Biswas and one co-author proves a 2026 arXiv result on Brauer groups of moduli stacks. For parabolic stable principal PGL(r, C)-bundles on a curve, with a broad weight system along any parabolic divisor, the Brauer group of the moduli stack matches a key group.

That group is the Brauer group of the smooth part of the matching coarse moduli space. That match ties stack and space invariants together. The paper also shows that for any simple, simply linked complex linear algebra group G, the analytic and algebraic Brauer groups of the moduli stack of quasi-parabolic main G-bundles vanish. Those vanishing results simplify the math and shape of parabolic bundle moduli, dropping Brauer blocks in a wide class of cases.
arxiv-2602-14679:
Text-guided image editing can be misused for deepfakes and unauthorized edits. Chanhui Lee, with four co-authors, proposes a universal immunization that blocks diffusion-based editing. Most defenses need per-image optimization or extra networks at run time.

Their method crafts one image-agnostic perturbation that pushes the editor toward a chosen semantic target. It also suppresses the original content, steering attention away from what should stay private. Experiments show it beats several baselines as the first universal approach of its kind. The goal is practical protection that scales to many images at once.
arxiv-2602-14879:
Qingqing Zhu and colleagues introduce CT-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal lesion understanding in computed tomography, answering a shortage of public CT data with lesion-level annotations. Its lesion image and metadata set holds 20,335 lesions from 7,795 CT studies, with bounding boxes, descriptions, and sizes. Beside it stands a multitask visual question answering benchmark of 2,850 pairs on localisation, description, size, and attributes.

Hard negatives mirror real diagnostic difficulty, and several state-of-the-art models are evaluated on the new tasks. Radiology AI gains a shared test that asks not just where a lesion is, but what it is and how big. Lesion understanding becomes measurable at scale.
arxiv-2602-15079:
Liu investigates the link between getting answers right and staying steady in classical and quantum learning algorithms under noise and attack. The chapter introduces and clarifies several definitions, including corrupted-instance robustness accuracy and prediction-change robustness, and sets them apart from conventional measures. Theory and toy models then pin down when trade-offs between the two qualities appear and when they can be avoided.

The framework highlights how model bias, noise character, and attack type interact, including relevant versus irrelevant kinds. Liu explores what the results imply for incompatible noise, adversarial quantum perturbations, and the no free lunch theorem, and suggests studying these problems next through the lens of dynamical systems.
arxiv-2602-15179:
Fassarella and Loray study moduli spaces for Higgs bundles on an elliptic curve that carry two poles. They give a full account of the Hitchin map's singular fibers, with the nilpotent cone among them. For this, they use a modular map sending Higgs bundles on the Riemann sphere with five poles up to Higgs bundles on the elliptic curve.

That map is a two-sheeted covering, and the team analyzes its Galois involution. They prove surjectivity for the modular map and pin down its ramification locus. In particular, they give a fully explicit account of where the moduli space becomes singular, rounding out a detailed portrait of its singular geometry.
arxiv-2602-15279:
Moriamé and colleagues test pairwise Hamiltonian control to break sync in the higher-order Kuramoto model. Sync of oscillators appears in natural systems and emerges from links within them. It can help power grids and harm in seizures. In the latter case, efficient break-up methods are crucial. Studies show links are not always pairwise, but higher-order, meaning many-body, greatly affecting dynamics.

Higher-order links raise the linear stability of synchronized states yet shrink their attraction basin, pulling control in opposite directions. The team tries a minimally invasive pairwise Hamiltonian control on phase oscillators with higher-order interactions, checking how well it works. When starting phases sit near the synchronized state, higher-order links make breaking sync harder. Otherwise, intermediate higher-order strengths impede breaking sync while larger ones facilitate it. Across all cases, the control breaks sync with enough controlled nodes and intensity.
arxiv-2602-15379:
Shu and colleagues offer FlashMem, a flowing setup for running large modern deep brain nets and multi-DNN jobs on mobile GPUs while cutting memory use and cutting run lag. Current setups mostly use an early loading plan, loading all model weights into memory before runs. The team argues this method is weak for modern jobs holding very large models and maybe some other models in a row.

Instead of fully preloading weights, FlashMem sets model loading plans ahead and flows them live on need. It uses two-and-a-half-dimensional surface memory to cut reshapes and boost speed. Test findings on 11 models show FlashMem hits 2 to about 8 times memory cut and about 2 to 75 times boost versus current setups. That allows lean runs of large-scale models and multi-DNN aid on tight mobile GPUs.
arxiv-2602-15679:
Davidov works alone on hypothesis tests under order restrictions, where inequality constraints can buy large gains in power and clarity. The catch is misspecification: when the imposed constraints are wrong, inferences can mislead or fail outright, and Type III errors can occur, rejecting the null when neither null nor alternative is true. The paper introduces safe tests to close that hole.

A safe test is, heuristically, a procedure asymptotically free of Type III errors. It comes with a certificate of validity, a pre-test checking whether the original hypotheses fit the data, so the null is rejected only when warranted. The approach aims at principled inference without systematic error risk. Simulations and analyses of well-known illustrative data sets show strong protection against Type III errors while keeping power comparable to standard procedures, and the ideas extend beyond order-restricted problems.
arxiv-2602-15979:
Ikuta and colleagues compare three ways of reading the young Sun like star EK Draconis, a star already caught firing prominence eruptions with superflares. They map starspots from TESS light curves, image magnetic fields with Zeeman Doppler imaging, and track brightness changes across optical, hydrogen alpha, and X ray bands at the same time.

Spot positions from photometry mostly match the magnetic maps, except for a polar spot. The hydrogen alpha curve follows the TESS rhythm because that line shines from chromospheric gas around spots. The X ray curve shows no such link, likely because many active regions and extended coronal structure blur the signal. Together the methods trace how flares connect across heights of the stellar atmosphere, and help gauge the high energy radiation bathing young exoplanets.
arxiv-2602-16179:
CoreCraft is a fully working enterprise simulation of a customer support organization, built by Sushant Mehta and coauthors as the first environment in EnterpriseBench. It holds over twenty-five hundred entities across fourteen types, with twenty-three tools, and it tests whether AI agents can do the multi-step, domain-specific work real jobs demand. Frontier models solve fewer than three in ten tasks when every expert rubric criterion must be met.

Training GLM 4.6 in this environment with group relative policy optimization lifts held-out task pass rates markedly after a single epoch. More notably, the gains transfer to out-of-distribution benchmarks in tool use and retail tasks. The authors credit three environment traits: task-centric world building for diverse, hard tasks; expert rubrics that make rewards reliable; and workflows that mirror realistic professional patterns. Environment quality, diversity, and realism thus appear central to generalizable agent skill.
arxiv-2602-16279:
Michael Knierim and coauthors test a popular assumption: that social media appeal comes from flow, a state of deep absorption and effortless engagement. Prolonged use has also been linked to distraction, fatigue, and lower mood. That paradox stays poorly understood, partly because prior studies rely on habitual or one-shot reports that ask people to directly credit social media with flow. The team ran a five-day field study with forty participants, combining objective smartphone app tracking with daily reconstructions of flow-inducing activities.

Across hundreds of reported flow occurrences, participants rarely linked flow to social media, in only about two percent of cases. Heavier social media use predicted fewer daily flow occurrences. The team further traces that link through effects on fatigue, mood, and motivation. Their findings suggest flow and social media may not align as closely as assumed, and might even compete.
arxiv-2602-16379:
Mohammad H. A. Monfared works with Lucie Flek and Akbar Karimi on making synthetic training data for aspect-based sentiment analysis more trustworthy. Their agentic method builds examples through repeated generation and verification, aiming for high-quality data that keeps its labels. To isolate what the agentic structure adds, they also build a matched prompting baseline using the same model and instructions.

Both methods are tested across three subtasks, aspect term extraction, aspect sentiment classification, and aspect sentiment pair extraction, on four SemEval datasets and two encoder-decoder models, T5-Base and Tk-Instruct. The agentic augmentation beats raw prompting at preserving labels, especially where tasks require generating aspect terms. Combined with real data it gives higher gains, consistently beating prompting-based generation. Gains are largest for T5-Base, while the more heavily pretrained Tk-Instruct improves less, and augmented data helps T5-Base match its counterpart's performance.
arxiv-2602-16479:
Bálint Tóth, writing alone, strengthens a central limit theorem for random walks in degenerate divergence-free random environments. The paper enhances a result by Kozma and Tóth from 2017. It proves the central limit theorem, in probability with respect to the environment, for the displacement of a random walker in a divergence-free, or doubly stochastic, random environment. Ellipticity assumptions are substantially relaxed.

Only integrability of the reciprocal of the symmetric part of the jump rates is assumed, rather than their boundedness as in previous works on this type of random walk in random environment. Loosening ellipticity forces major proof changes, yet the proof stays conceptually basic, avoiding Nash's inequality in every form. The paper thus extends the central limit theorem to a broader, less regular class of environments.
arxiv-2602-16579:
Maria Luisa Taccari and co-authors introduce AIFL, a deterministic LSTM model for global daily streamflow forecasting. The task is central to flood readiness and water management. Data-driven models often stumble moving from historical reanalysis to live forecast products. AIFL uses two-stage transfer learning to bridge that gap. It is pre-trained on four decades of ERA5-Land reanalysis across thousands of Caravan basins. It is then fine-tuned on operational IFS forecasts to absorb their biases.

Ablation tests show the two-stage route beats an IFS-only baseline. It also beats a mixed single-stage alternative. On an independent recent test period, the model reaches solid skill scores. Its accuracy is comparable to current state-of-the-art global systems. Hydrologists get a streamlined baseline for global flood forecasting, and the first such model trained end to end in Caravan.
arxiv-2602-16779:
Shin Toriumi reviews how NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory links solar and stellar physics. The solar-stellar link offers a frame for grasping magnetic activity and air heating across many star types. The observatory's three tools enable detailed Sun-as-a-star studies. Those studies turn fine solar views into whole-disk data that can be set beside distant stars.

The review highlights recent work using all three tools to map active zones, gauge universal heating laws, and rebuild stellar X-ray and ultraviolet spectra. Those results advance knowledge of stellar magnetic activity. They also give predictive tools for exoplanet settings. The paper closes with next steps for applying solar-based frames to varied stellar groups, from quiet dwarfs to active giants.
arxiv-2602-16979:
Divyam Madaan, Sumit Chopra, and Kyunghyun Cho propose PRIMO, a supervised latent-variable model gauging the predictive impact of modes. Despite recent success of multimodal large language models, existing approaches predominantly assume multiple modes are on hand during training and inference. In practice, multimodal data is often incomplete because modes may be missing, collected asynchronously, or available only for a subset of examples.

PRIMO quantifies the predictive impact of any missing modality within the multimodal learning setting. It enables use of all available training examples, whether modalities are complete or partial. It models the missing mode through a latent variable capturing its relationship with the observed mode in the context of prediction. Tests on a synthetic XOR dataset, Audio-Vision MNIST, and MIMIC-III for mortality and ICD-9 prediction show scores comparable to unimodal baselines when a mode is missing.
arxiv-2602-17079:
Dylan Munson led a three-author team making agent-based models practical for environmental policy. Coupled human-environment systems behave as complex adaptive systems, where small interactions yield emergent outcomes, and agent-based models capture that richness well. But such models cost so much compute that optimizing policy over them is often out of reach.

The authors answer with a statistical framework that pairs machine learning with reinforcement learning: first a sensitivity test for the optimal policy, then an efficient search for that policy. They trial the framework on Sugarscape, the classic resource-harvesting model, where it quickly found optimal, interpretable policies that beat baselines. Sensitivity and dynamic analyses tie the results back to economic theory, showing policy designers a faster route to defensible choices.
arxiv-2602-17779:
Antoine Maillard and team explore the topology of high-dimensional empirical risk landscapes, with an application to phase retrieval. They study risk minimization for high-dimensional Gaussian single-index models, where an unknown signal must be recovered from a loss function built on label pairs. The regime with sample count comparable to dimension is the focus.

Using the Kac-Rice formula, they analyze landscape complexity, defined as the expected number of critical points, across types including local minima. Variational formulas from the literature simplify drastically to explicit problems over finitely many scalar parameters, solvable numerically. The frame also predicts critical point traits, including Hessian spectra and label spreads. Applied to real phase retrieval, it yields full topological phase diagrams, including BBP-type transitions where the Hessian at local minima turns unstable toward the signal. Tests against gradient flow dynamics agree excellently.
arxiv-2602-18079:
Masoud Jamshidiyan Tehrani and colleagues study why adversarial attacks on autonomous-driving perception often fail in a full driving stack. Such attacks tend to be spatially or temporally short-lived, since vehicle dynamics blunt them, so they rarely change vehicle behavior. The authors answer with a system-level attack in which two pedestrians carry adversarial patches on their clothing and jointly amplify the effect through coordination and motion.

They evaluate the attacks in the CARLA simulator with a state-of-the-art autonomous driving agent. Single-pedestrian attacks fail in all ten runs, while dynamic collusion by two pedestrians forces full vehicle stops in up to half the runs. Static collusion yields no successful attack at all. The results show system-level failures arise only when adversarial signals persist over time and amplify through coordinated actors, exposing a gap between model-level robustness and end-to-end safety.
arxiv-2602-18179:
Denis Marti compares two ways of counting holes in spaces that look like smooth shapes. His 2026 paper sets singular homology, built from maps of triangles and their kin, beside homology built from integral currents, a tool for generalized surfaces. The spaces in question are metric spaces shaped like smooth manifolds.

Marti gives conditions under which a map from the current-based group onto the singular group exists in codimension one, meaning the current view covers the singular view. He also shows that a one-dimensional isoperimetric inequality for currents forces the two one-dimensional groups to match exactly. The results pin down when two quite different hole-counting machines agree, a useful bridge for geometry in rough spaces.
arxiv-2602-18279:
The CMS Collaboration makes the first measurement of jet axis decorrelation in photon-tagged events. Their 2026 paper compares lead-lead and proton-proton collisions at five point zero two tera-electron-volts per nucleon pair. The decorrelation is the angle between two ways of defining a jet's axis, a quantity sensitive to how jet pieces scatter in quark-gluon plasma.

Events pair a lone high-energy photon with a recoiling jet in set momentum windows, and lead-lead results are tracked against collision centrality and the proton-proton baseline. Lower-momentum jets look alike in both collision types, but higher-momentum jets narrow in central lead-lead collisions. Comparisons with JEWEL, PYQUEN, and HYBRID models, each with its own energy-loss picture, test how partons shed energy in plasma.
arxiv-2602-18479:
Wei Yang and colleagues build an AI agent that mines catalytic reaction data from chemistry papers. Their 2026 paper presents AgentCAT, a large language model agent that extracts and analyzes reaction data for catalysts from chemical engineering papers and supports live natural-language analysis. The agent addresses the data bottleneck in chemical engineering.

AgentCAT also offers a formal abstraction of extraction in AI-friendly terms. The complex catalytic process creates tangled links across reaction steps, molecular behaviors, and measured evidence. That structure makes full correctness hard to guarantee. AgentCAT answers with four parts. First, an extraction pipeline governed by an evolving schema. Second, a knowledge graph tracking links among catalysts, active sites, synthesis labels, mechanistic claims with evidence, and large-scale outcomes. Third, a query module for searching and viewing data across papers. Fourth, a test on about eight hundred peer-reviewed papers showing it works.
arxiv-2602-18579:
José Aldo Silva da Costa and seven co-authors watch novices read code. Their 2026 paper notes developers often extract methods to improve readability and understanding, while inlining keeps logic together. Prior static-metric work showed no clear differences, leaving comprehension and navigation underexplored.

The team studies Inline Method versus Extract Method refactorings with eye tracking, comparing visual effort, reading behavior, time, and attempts. A controlled experiment has thirty-two Java novices solve eight tasks across four programs in both versions, plus a survey of fifty-eight novices. Effects vary with task difficulty. In two tasks extraction improved performance and cut visual effort, with time falling seventy-eight point eight percent and regressions eighty-four point six percent. For simpler tasks extraction hurt, with time rising one hundred sixty-six point nine percent and regressions two hundred percent. Preferences favored extraction for readability yet did not always match performance.
arxiv-2602-18779:
When people form groups, some ties hold and others break. The rules for stable ties change when a tie can link more than two people at once. Rémi Castera, with two co-authors, extends network stability theory in 2026 to weighted hypergraphic networks. There, connections vary in strength and each person faces a budget on total connection intensity.

The work generalises pairwise stability, first set out for unweighted networks and later for weighted ones. That keeps it meaningful for multi-person relationships under budget limits. It then adds a stronger notion, full stability, in which agents may adjust several connections at once, borrowing insight from matching theory. Existence results, explicit solutions or algorithms, and counterexamples together give an almost complete theory. It bridges network formation and fractional matching.
arxiv-2602-19179:
Gaussian work on surfaces supports robots, but exact methods break down. Junghoon Seo, with two co-authors, studies tangent-linear Gaussian work in 2026 and derives direct non-asymptotic error bounds. Mapping sums and surface-measure tuning are both covered. Bounds separate local second-order geometric warp from nonlocal tail leakage.

For Gaussian inputs, closed-form diagnostics follow from mean, covariance, and curvature or reach surrogates. Circle and planar-pushing tests validate a predicted calibration transition. Normal-direction uncertainty dominates when locality breaks. Diagnostics thus trigger switching from single-chart linearisation to multi-chart or sample-based inference. Practical guidance replaces blind trust in linearised methods.
arxiv-2602-19379:
Microwave linear analog computers promise to run multiple-input multiple-output processing directly in the radio-frequency analog domain. Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx note that existing studies use idealized channel models and ignore antenna mutual coupling, yet coupling matters precisely because processing happens at radio frequency. It alters the operation the device implements, not just the channel it sees.

The authors develop a physics-compliant model using multiport network theory, covering devices at the transmitter, the receiver, or both. They formulate and solve a coupling-aware optimization problem, deriving a closed-form solution, globally optimal, that maximizes received signal power. Results show coupling helps on average, and that these devices can match digital architectures with matching networks while using fewer radio-frequency chains.
arxiv-2602-19479:
Rare kaon decays offer a sensitive probe for light bosons with vector and axial-vector couplings to non-conserved currents. Matheus Hostert and two co-authors study three- and four-body kaon decays. Searches for one neutral decay mode constrain light boson couplings to light quarks to about ten to the minus fifth power. Charged-pion modes give weaker limits near ten to the minus fourth power, but constrain complementary quark combinations.

Double emission of the boson in kaon decays adds further constraints, thanks to a double enhancement factor in the rate. For a 17 megaelectronvolt boson, these limits add to the tension between spin-1 boson interpretations of the ATOMKI experiment results and meson decay data. The paper also comments on negative pion capture, rounding out a systematic survey of kaon decay constraints.
arxiv-2602-19979:
Type IIB superstring amplitudes are organized by the number of external states and their charge under the theory's R-symmetry. A 2026 arXiv paper by Emiel Claasen and Mehregan Doroudiani analyzes the low-energy series of one-loop five-point amplitudes across all charge sectors.

The representative processes involve five gravitons, or four gravitons plus one dilaton. The authors compute one-loop contributions to moduli-dependent couplings in the effective action up to high-derivative interactions. Their results satisfy S-duality constraints in every charge sector. They display rich arithmetic structure. That structure includes single-valued multiple zeta values. It also includes logarithmic derivatives of the Riemann zeta function, evaluated at odd integers and combined in affine linear ways, plus a new constant whose nature is currently unknown. The paper thus maps five-point one-loop physics with unusual arithmetic depth.
arxiv-2602-20279:
Elias Furrer and Jan Manschot compute correlation functions in a twisted form of supersymmetric gauge theory. Their 2026 study treats SU(2) Yang-Mills theory with up to three massive matter fields, on a smooth, compact, oriented four-dimensional space with a stated topological condition. In that setting, the correlations reduce to a finite set of universal functions, whose mass dependence records intersection numbers of instanton moduli spaces.

The authors derive closed formulas for those functions by combining Seiberg-Witten geometry, the u-plane integral, and the blowup formula. When the space is a complex algebraic surface, the correlations match generating functions of Segre invariants for sheaf moduli spaces. The results agree with earlier formulas by Göttsche and Kool for those generating functions. The paper thus ties gauge-theory correlations, instanton geometry, and sheaf counting into one consistent picture.
arxiv-2602-20779:
Florian Lux and two co-authors tackle a flaw in 3D nano-printed lens scanners: the printed polymer creeps and drifts with heat, so open-loop moves lose accuracy over time. Their fix is closed-loop control, with a built-in sensor that tracks the lens position as it moves.

A tiny magnet around the microlens drives motion and also supplies the sensing signal, read by a commercial three-axis Hall sensor placed between a pair of drive coils. Subtracting the coil field recovers the magnet position. The loop holds mean accuracy to 0.86 micrometers and precision to 0.49 over a 150-micrometer range, wiping out creep and hysteresis.
arxiv-2602-20979:
AI agents now write code on their own, but the software world around them was built for humans. Mark Marron argues that world itself must change in this 2026 arXiv paper, sketching an Agentic Infused Software Ecosystem. The vision rests on three pillars: the agents, the languages and tools they use, and the runtime environment they operate in.

Agents have moved in the past five years from simple code completion toward independent development work, and that trend will continue. Languages and APIs increasingly serve as the shared medium through which humans and agents collaborate. The paper insists all three pillars must advance together, in ways that suit present agents, future agents, and the human developers beside them.
arxiv-2602-21079:
Thermal transpiration moves gas through a temperature gradient, a phenomenon Knudsen studied in 1909.
