Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Mr. Haldeman on 14 June 1861. It stands as Document 279 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d79:
On 10 September 1861, William H. Seward sent a short note to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 79 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid September found Seward juggling the West, the border states, and Europe at once. His London letters stayed short because his days were full. This note is a brief pull on the most vital thread of all, the tie to Britain. Short notes like this one kept the London envoy from ever working in the dark. No envoy who works in the dark can hold a great post for long.
frus-1862-d179:
Secretary of State William H. Seward answered London on 30 October 1862 with a dispatch printed as Document 179 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Its reader was Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

Crossing letters were the norm in Atlantic diplomacy: Seward wrote against Adams reports already two weeks old. Both men knew the flaw and wrote to last, framing orders that could survive changed facts. A dispatch from the last day of October belongs to the effort to hold Britain steady while France pushed its truce scheme toward a decision. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d279:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 16 May 1862 in a letter printed as Document 279 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote eleven days after Puebla, when the French press was explaining away a rare defeat. How the emperor's government handled embarrassment abroad bore directly on its American policy. Reports like this one gave Seward a feel for the court's temper that no newspaper could supply. And they guided his answers to the French minister in Washington. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d379:
Viscount Treilhard wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 October 1862, in a letter printed as Document 379 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is the last letter of the Treilhard run in this file.

By October, Antietam and the Emancipation Proclamation had changed the ground under every foreign channel in Washington. Britain and France were weighing a joint truce proposal that would soon fail. Treilhard's closing letter in the sequence belongs to that altered season, when the Union's position abroad was slowly strengthening. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d479:
James E. Harvey sent this report from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 August 1862, two days after his previous dispatch. It is Document 479 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

A two-day gap between reports signals pressing business at the post, and in August 1862 the pressing business at Atlantic ports was the Confederate cruisers. Harvey's Lisbon letters kept Washington informed of Portuguese rulings and rumors touching belligerent ships. Seward used such reports to protest, to warn, or to thank, as each case required. The dispatch is a small but pointed piece of the maritime file. In that file the Civil War was fought with notes and port rules as much as with guns.
frus-1862-d579:
James Watson Webb wrote from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 August 1862. His report is Document 579 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's printed record.

Late August 1862 found the Alabama at sea and the cruiser question rising in every Atlantic capital, Rio included. Webb, never a passive observer, reported Brazilian feeling and pressed the Union's interests with his usual energy. His letters also remind the reader of a hard fact. Brazil and the United States were then the two great slaveholding powers of the hemisphere. That fact shadowed their wartime dealings. The dispatch is part of the thin but telling Brazilian file in a volume dominated by Europe.
frus-1862-d679:
The China file for this stretch closes with a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Anson Burlingame, dated 1 August 1862. Burlingame was the American minister to China, and Seward's letters to him close the China file for this stretch. The letter is document 679 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

With this note, the year's back-and-forth between Washington and the China legation rounds off in the printed volume. The exchange shows the two men at work: one reporting from the treaty ports, the other guiding from a capital at war. For readers now, the full run is a clear window on how the United States dealt with China in the early 1860s.
frus-1862-d79:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 9 June 1862. It stands as Document 79 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d179: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 May 1863. It is document 179 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d279:
Writing from London on 4 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 279 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d379:
On 30 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to one of Her Majesty's consuls, whose post the printed title leaves blank. The instruction is document 379 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

British consuls in American ports watched over British ships, sailors, and trade, and reported up to Lyons. Orders from the minister told them how to handle arrests, seizures, and protests on the spot. Seward obtained and printed such papers because they showed how British officials were directed inside the Union. The note is a glimpse of the consular network that fed the bigger fight in Washington.
frus-1863p1-d479:
On 25 April 1863 a formal note passed from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d579:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 30 June 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d679:
A second Seward letter to London bears the date 30 November 1863. It went to Charles Francis Adams, the United States minister in Britain, and it is kept as document 679 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. Two notes on one day hints at a busy week in Washington.

By late 1863 the war had turned in the Union's favor on the field, but Europe still held back from full trust. Seward kept Adams supplied with facts and lines to use with British officials. The reader sees that work at the sentence level. It is a short, direct record of how a government spoke to a key envoy in wartime.
frus-1863p1-d79:
On 13 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 79 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

Adams's mail was the Union's window on the British mind. He wrote of what the cabinet did and what the street felt, and Seward read both to plan his next moves. This dispatch holds the middle of a busy day's work. Read with its mates, it shows the legation sorting a city's worth of news into three clean sheets for a reader an ocean away.
frus-1879:
Specie payments resume at the front of the 1879 volume. Hayes reports United States notes redeemed in coin since January. Trade revival follows, he tells Congress. The correspondence then runs its full annual course. Britain takes the longest European file. Mexico leads the American side. Japan adds a curious block on imperial telegraphs.

Hawaii appears twice, in file and addenda. One addendum prints a British-Hawaiian treaty text. Its clauses equalize duties and port charges between the two. China, Chile, and Colombia hold solid sections. Spain shrinks to a single document plus a circular. Turkey and Tunis close the volume. The tone is prosperous and settled. Money, not war, frames this year.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d179: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 31, 1943, in a letter the editors placed in the Moscow section as Document 179 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A companion Churchill note of the same date stands in the main sequence. The record gives the date and the two names and no subject. Read together, the pair shows the prime minister reacting on paper as the Moscow results came in.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d279:
For a Cairo conversation of late November 1943, no official record has been found, and the volume prints an editorial note in its place. The only reference to it sits in notes by John Davies recording what Harry Hopkins told him and General Stilwell on 6 December, after the Tehran trip.

On Davies' notes, Hopkins said he had talked with the Chiangs for three hours on the evening before leaving for Tehran. Of the subjects discussed, Hopkins named only one: the Chiangs had raised the question of the return of Outer Mongolia, a question first brought up at the dinner meeting of 23 November. Hopkins' own notes, printed facing the editorial note, may belong to this same conversation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d379:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the plenary session at Tehran on 1 December 1943 at six in the evening. Roosevelt names Poland and the treatment of Germany as the two main questions, but Molotov first asks for an answer on the Soviet request for Italian ships.

Roosevelt holds that the Italian merchant and war ships should serve the three nations in common until the war ends. Title can be divided then. Molotov accepts use now, with possession settled later. Delivery is set for about the end of January 1944. It will be made in the Black Sea if Turkey enters the war, otherwise to northern ports. Care will be taken to avoid mutiny or scuttling in the Italian fleet. On Poland, Stalin charges the exile government with German ties and with killing partisans, while Churchill recalls that Britain went to war over Poland's invasion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d479:
John J. McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant, on December 4, 1943. The Second Cairo Conference opened that day, and Hopkins was traveling with the President while McCloy minded the War Department. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

McCloy and Hopkins were two of the great staff operators of the wartime government, men who settled problems that never reached a cabinet table. Their channel linked the War Department directly to the President's side. A message between them shows the informal wiring of Roosevelt's Washington, where personal trust often moved business faster than formal procedure.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d79: General Brehon Somervell, who commanded the Army Service Forces, wrote a memorandum dated October 30, 1943, preserved as Document 79 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Somervell ran the vast supply machine behind the American armies, and his papers in a summit volume mark the weight of logistics in grand strategy. The record gives the author and the date and no topic. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d179:
The Combined Chiefs met again at 2:30 p.m. on September 13, 1944. They approved the previous day's minutes with a small correction from Marshall about the Plough Force and its sleds in southern France. A proposed directive on control of the strategic bomber forces in Europe was put off until the next day, Portal not having had time to study it fully.

Coordination with Moscow moved forward: the chiefs agreed to dispatch the messages drafted for Generals Burrows and Deane, the mission chiefs in Moscow. They took note of the intelligence committee's report on the enemy in the Pacific and of an American progress report on Pacific operations. The meeting then turned to strategy for the defeat of Japan.
frus-1944-quebec-d279:
Churchill's memorandum of September 16, 1944, accepts the Mountbatten directive while pleading to limit the Burma jungle fighting. His government was in full accord on securing the air route and opening overland communications with China. But sickness had cost 288,000 men in six months, and the burden fell almost wholly on the Imperial armies.

The remedy was Dracula, the stroke at Rangoon, to be brought on by March 15 by straining every nerve. Five or six divisions were essential: the 6th Airborne from England and a British-Indian division from Italy would start at once. Churchill asked America for two light or ordinary divisions as well. Without Dracula, he warned, Britain would feel exposed to unnecessary sacrifices in disease-ravaged operations.
frus-1944-quebec-d79:
Viscount Simon, Britain's Lord Chancellor, prepared a memorandum dated September 4, 1944. Simon was the government's senior legal officer. His paper reached the files of the Quebec Conference. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume.

British legal thinking mattered as the allies planned Germany's defeat. Questions of law surrounded surrender terms and occupation duties. Simon's memorandum put a top lawyer's view into the record. For readers, it shows legal advice crossing the Atlantic before the summit. Lawyers, like generals and treasurers, helped prepare the leaders' choices at Quebec. The conference opened at Quebec City on September 12.
frus-1945-50-intel-d179:
Formal minutes cover the 12th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 17 December 1946. It is document 179 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. Later fights over who agreed to what often end with a page like this one. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d279:
The Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) on 25 May 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 279 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d379:
The Chief of the Intelligence Coordinating and Planning Staff (Childs) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 6 April 1949. Readers meet it as document 379 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Two years into the CIA's life, the question in these papers is less how to build it than how to fix it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d79:
Benton answered McCormack the next day, 24 October 1945. A reply within a day shows two office heads settling a shared border while the wartime agencies were being wound up. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Benton's public and cultural office grew from the same wartime root stock as McCormack's intelligence service. Their exchange is a small treaty inside one department. Readers can use the pair of papers to see how functions were divided in practice: by letters between chiefs, each guarding his charter. The speed of the reply hints at good will, or at urgency. The volume's later papers show how long that will lasted between State's growing offices.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d179:
Britain and the Soviet Union pressed Washington to help move King Peter, and Grew summed up the pressure on 28 January 1945. His secret report to the traveling Secretary of State is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It covers a crowded day of calls and cables.

Ambassador Stevenson, at Eden's request, was pushing Patterson for instructions to say something helpful to the King. A British memorandum reported that Stalin wanted the agreement in force at once, with recognition by the three chief allies and no reservations of any kind. Halifax telephoned in person. From London, Winant passed on Cadogan's hope that Washington would join in recognizing the united Yugoslav government. The British feared that American talk of temporary representation in Belgrade was keeping the King from giving way.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d279:
Feeding freed Europe for six months is the business of this American-British agreement. The memorandum records the agreed views of the two governments' authorities. It covers shipping supplies to liberated countries in the first half of 1945. The text is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

The Supreme Commander in Europe has agreed to set aside port space and inland clearance for the French and Belgian governments' own import programs. These run apart from, and in addition to, the military programs. A four-party committee, seating France, the two allies, and SHAEF, has reviewed and recommended the French program. Belgium's is expected to follow the same road. For Italy, UNRRA has put in a program, which the Mediterranean commander has endorsed so long as his own needs are not hurt.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d379:
Two hands share this exchange of February 7, 1945. Hopkins wrote first, puzzling over Churchill's resistance to calling the United Nations conference early. Something lay behind the talk that the Americans did not know, he warned. Better, he advised, to wait until later that night to learn what was on Churchill's mind.

Roosevelt answered on the same slip. All this is rot, he wrote — local politics. He was quite sure Churchill was thinking about the next election in Britain. The note, half in the President's own hand, shows the two men gossiping on paper while the plenary ground on.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d479:
Seven countries are ticked off in Grew's cable of February 6, 1945, on the Associated Nations question. Ecuador, he reported, had declared a state of war with Japan dating from December 7, 1941. Paraguay's action was expected momentarily. Peru's executive might act soon. Venezuela showed no change, though its ambassador was traveling home to press the matter.

Uruguay's government was looking for a justification to act. Chile showed no change since the delegation left. Favorable action, Grew judged, might be expected from all except Chile within a reasonably short time. The tally mattered: declarations of war by March 1 meant seats at San Francisco.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d79:
Leo Pasvolsky wrote down what happened when the Dumbarton Oaks papers reached the President on 15 November 1944. Pasvolsky was a special assistant to the Secretary of State. His record of the talk is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Stettinius walked the President through the six unsettled questions. He stressed that voting and membership had to be settled among the three allies first. Roosevelt then studied the voting paper closely. He held that a middle course was needed, since the United States would never accept having no vote in a grave crisis touching itself. He approved the attached plan as the American position.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d179:
H. Freeman Matthews recorded a British visit about the revised agenda in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The memo is document 179 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. British Minister John Balfour called with Nevile Butler and left an aide-mémoire revising London's suggested topics for the Berlin meeting, with comments on each.

Balfour added that the Foreign Office hoped the United States would take the lead in presenting several named points. Matthews could not comment until Truman and the new Secretary of State had studied the Department's papers. On his own level, he found the British list ran parallel to American thinking, though he noted it said nothing about the Far East. Some original items had plainly gone stale and were dropped by both sides.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d279:
Ambassador Harriman reported a blockage at the Austrian zones in a telegram from Moscow on July 2, 1945. The urgent message is document 279 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Soviet commanders in Austria had refused to let American troops enter the proposed occupation zones.

The local commanders said they had no instructions, Harriman reports. General Deane was trying to learn from the Red Army staff why no orders had gone out. In his June 16 reply to the President, Stalin had set July 1 as the occupation date. The date covered both the German and Austrian zones. Stalin had described the interval as time for the European Advisory Commission to finish its work. Harriman asks for urgent advice on the state of the commission's decisions, since Deane wants his support with Molotov. He wants it for a SHAEF request to start the troop movements.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d379:
Reparation is the sixth topic in Dunn's extracts of his July 14, 1945 talk with Cadogan at Potsdam. The British official Coulson, Dunn reports, was skeptical of moving capital goods out of Germany before basic reparations decisions were reached. He also dissented from the proposal that large interim deliveries of capital goods be made while decisions were pending.

Cadogan agreed the allies should strive for a narrow definition of booty of war. He also felt Britain and America should secure as high a percentage of reparation as possible. If they later failed to use their full shares, they might reallocate part to others. The extract shows London guarding its claim.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d479:
The future of Allied Force Headquarters in the Mediterranean is taken up in a United States Chiefs of Staff memorandum of July 7, 1945. The American chiefs agree in general with the views already set out in the combined paper. They note one complication: since that paper was written, the question of combined command in Austria has been discussed in another series.

With operations ended and American and British forces redeploying out of the theater, they argue, the headquarters can be reduced progressively. Field Marshal Alexander should be directed to restrict its activities to essentially allied matters. He should shrink it as the troops in the theater and its commitments diminish. The memo keeps a combined staff, but on a diet.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d579:
Joseph Grew, the Acting Secretary of State, sent Secretary Byrnes a top secret memo on July 13, 1945. It is document 579 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Attached is a study of the Yalta deal and what terms China might fairly accept.

Grew flags one striking fact at the start. The Department holds no copy of the Yalta Agreement and no record of the talks behind it. The study was thus built from memory of what it said. Its first part takes up Outer Mongolia, which China claims as its own. It notes that China lost control there in 1911 but never dropped the claim. Treaties of 1913, 1915, and 1924, it says, all won outside backing for that claim.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d679:
George Elsey traced the Dardanelles dispute in a top secret memo filed July 1, 1945. It is document 679 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The Straits, linking the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, were governed by the Montreux Convention of 1936.

Elsey recalls that Stalin raised revision of that pact with Churchill in Moscow in October 1944. Stalin wanted free passage at all times for Russian warships. Churchill did not contest the bid, saying revision was clearly needed since Japan was a signatory. The two agreed Moscow would send formal notes setting out its wishes. No notes ever came. The subject surfaced next at Yalta on February 10, 1945, where Stalin called the treaty outmoded. Elsey's memo gives Truman the full paper trail before Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d79:
Admiral Leahy reported a delicate staffing question to President Truman on June 20, 1945. His note is document 79 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. At the joint request of General Marshall and Harry Hopkins, Leahy had asked Ambassador Harriman to sound out Stalin on the American Chiefs of Staff coming to Berlin with the President.

Leahy adds the private doubts behind the question. Both Marshall and Hopkins question whether a staff meeting in Germany is wise or needed at this time. They also fear Stalin would not like it, and that Japan might read the gathering the wrong way. Early word on Stalin's reaction was wanted. The note shows how carefully Washington weighed even the guest list for Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1079:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh sent this despatch from Athens on July 24, 1945. It transmits a War Department report by Captain William McNeill on violations of the Greco-Yugoslav border. The incidents have grown more serious, MacVeagh warns, and seem directed from a base near Monastir. Their aims are stirring trouble inside Greece and spreading Communist propaganda.

One British soldier has been killed, one wounded, and a third captured by such a band. Yugoslav guards also crossed the border on July 12, attacked a Greek post, and seized a guardsman. Some thirty reports of armed bands cluster around Florina. MacVeagh sees a war of nerves, meant chiefly against Turkey, but keeping Greece simmering too.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1179:
Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote a fourth memorandum on 8 August 1945. His post-summit paperwork ran on through that week: more filing, more certifying, more closing of the books. The secretariat had served the talks; now it served the record of the talks.

Each of his notes fixed some part of the conference's paper trail for the archive. The series, read in order, shows an office method at work. This one is another step in that effort. It may look like routine, but the archive it built is the reason the summit can be studied at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1279:
The United States Chiefs of Staff wrote to the Soviet Chiefs of Staff on 24 July 1945. A message from one high command to the other crossed the alliance's widest seam. The two staffs had worked as allies in war; the peace was already testing that tie.

Military channels between Washington and Moscow handled the practical joins of the alliance: zones, movements, and the war still shared against Japan. This note belongs to that traffic. It shows the soldiers of two powers still doing joint business in the summit's second week, whatever the envoys argued about above them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1379:
George Allen's papers to Assistant Secretary James Dunn continue with a note dated 25 July 1945. The volume prints several Allen notes from that single week, a sign of how full the Near East file had grown. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Readers meeting Allen again here should note the pattern: the Near East desk never left the summit's agenda for long. Each note pressed the claims of a region that produced oil, held holy cities, and bordered Soviet lands. This one adds a further piece to the file Dunn carried. Taken together, the Allen notes form one of the clearest staff-level threads in the whole Potsdam record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-79:
Department of State minutes record the plenary session of July 23, 1945, at 5 p.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov presented the morning foreign ministers' report as rapporteur.

On reparations, the two Soviet drafts went to the economic subcommittee for preliminary study. The ministers would take the matter up after that examination. On German economic principles, three paragraphs were in dispute. Molotov had withdrawn his amendment to paragraph 13 at the morning meeting. He suggested deleting paragraph 18, leaving its questions to the Allied authorities in Germany. If the Control Council could not agree there, the governments would decide. No agreement was reached, and the point went to the Big Three. Byrnes had already called the new Soviet paragraph 19 unacceptable that morning. Molotov answered at the plenary by submitting yet another paragraph on the question.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d779:
Kirk wrote again from Rome on July 22, 1945, in document 779. The ambassador in Italy reported to the Acting Secretary as the conference entered its second week. Italy's hopes for a soft peace hung on these weeks. The report entered the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

Serial reports build a moving picture. Kirk could correct earlier views as events shifted. Readers watch an envoy adjusting his counsel in near-real time. The document also shows the burden on posts outside the room: Italy's fate was being weighed by men it could not address. Kirk's letters were its voice by proxy.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d879:
Britain's delegation circulated this memorandum on political principles for Germany at Babelsberg on July 24, 1945. It returns to two points the Economic Sub-Committee had raised but the foreign secretaries had not taken up. The Soviet side had argued both points were political, not economic.

The British ask that both points be written into the agreed text. One new clause would call for uniform treatment of the German population across all zones, so far as practical. A second clause would allow free travel by land and air for citizens of the four powers in every zone. The paper quotes the earlier sub-committee report to make its case.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d979:
William Clayton and Emilio Collado sent this secret telegram from London to Willard Thorp on August 16, 1945. Like its companion message, it explains the German economic decisions taken at Potsdam. The two men resist a reading they see growing in Washington: that the reparations operating deal means the end of four-power treatment of Germany.

The economic principles, they point out, still charge the Control Council with common policies. Those policies cover deindustrialization, reparation deliveries, import and export programs, living standards, and food distribution. Common rulings are still needed on external assets, restitution, Allied property, and gold. General Clay, they add, trusts he can win some shared policies, and that effort should not be dropped early.
frus-1958-60v19-d79:
A memorandum records President Eisenhower's talk with Secretary Dulles on September 11, 1958, on the Taiwan Straits crisis. They shape the President's radio and TV talk together. The bind is stated plainly: firmness abroad, yet an over-commitment to Chiang Kai-shek.

Eisenhower grants that Quemoy might have to be let go, though not in public. The Chiefs now doubt the islands can be held. Convoys under fire would ease off. A detected flight over the mainland had drawn protest. The talk shows a crisis managed by speech, pause, and private doubt.
gao-gaoreports-b-295579:
On March 28, 2005, GAO issued its ruling in file B-295579, the protest of Systems, Studies, and Simulation, Inc. The Army had rejected its quotation in a buy of advisory and assistance services for the Army Aviation and Missile Command. The Army meant to award at least four blanket purchase agreements. The firm's pricing structure was rated as posing moderate risk. GAO denied the protest. That rating was fair on the record.

The firm had quoted its Federal Supply Schedule labor rates. Those rates ran slightly to far below the Army's own past rates for like work. For highly complex services, such low rates fairly raise a risk flag.
gao-gaoreports-b-295879:
On April 25, 2005, GAO issued its ruling in file B-295879, the protest of United Valve Company, a small business. The Army Materiel Command had awarded Logistical Support, LLC, a contract for flutter dampeners, a part for the UH-1 Huey helicopter. The firm attacked the winner's standing as an approved source. GAO denied the protest. The winner ran a previously approved source: the same plant, machines, trained staff, and test stands. That sameness fairly supported approval.

A second point covers schedule. The agency had eased the delivery schedule for both firms. The protester's own asked schedule was longer still, and its price higher. No prejudice was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-297879:
BAE Systems Norfolk Ship Repair protested a Navy award in GAO decision B-297879, dated March 29, 2006. The winner was Earl Industries. The work was ship fix and refit work in Norfolk, Virginia. Ships were dock landing and transport dock class. Cost bids had to rest on test work items. State cost views set hours and goods costs for those items.

GAO denied the protest. Shifts from state views needed clear and strong proof. Soft fixed-price quotes did not meet that bar. That call was sound. Same top marks for both bids were also sound. Past work was the least key tech point. The notes showed true gaps were weighed in the pick.
gao-gaoreports-b-400379:
John Gage, acting for federal staff as their named agent, protested a Transportation Security Administration award for human resources work. GAO ruled in B-400379 on August 4, 2008. The award went to Lockheed Martin Integrated Systems, Inc. It came under a request issued on October 18, 2007. Gage said the deal moved federal staff work to a firm with no fair test.

GAO dismissed the protest on power grounds. By law, it cannot hear protests of TSA buys run under a request sent out before June 23, 2008. This request predates that line. The ruling rests on that date rule alone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-179:
Homeland Security, GAO-05-179 of March 29, 2005, grades the Department of Homeland Security as it builds one buying shop from many. The department spends billions of dollars a year on goods and services for its guard work. Two years in, its parts still buy in the ways they brought from their old homes. One set of rules and tools has yet to form.

GAO names spots where teamwork in buying has grown. It names spots where the split still hurts. It also grades the review path for big, complex buys. Wins and gaps share the page, with a push for one strong review gate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-379:
National Energy Policy, GAO-05-379 of June 10, 2005, stocks the shelf of federal energy work and grades a famed plan's wake. The May 2001 policy held over 100 counsels for the land's energy path. Demand climbs and prices bite. Each home and firm feels the strain. Congress weighs new energy law in that plan's light.

GAO names the major federal energy plans in force. It tracks where each of the 2001 counsels stands: done, in train, or stalled. It tells how the cash tied to such work has moved since the plan came out. The sum runs long; it is a map, not a plea.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-479:
How the government bars bad contractors is examined in GAO report GAO-05-479, dated July 29, 2005. Federal purchases of goods and services had grown past $300 billion a year. Rules let agencies suspend or debar firms that fail badly or act against the public trust. GAO reviewed shared rules, the add-on rules of 24 agencies, and 6 large agencies in depth.

In fiscal year 2004 the six agencies suspended 262 parties and debarred 590 parties. Five of them also signed 38 deals that let firms stay eligible if they met set terms. The shared database of barred parties was weak, though. About 99 percent of its records for those agencies lacked the ID numbers needed to match firms. That gap raised the risk that a barred firm could win new work by mistake. GAO urged better data reporting and wider sharing of waivers and side deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-779:
Drug price trends from 2000 to 2004 are charted in GAO-05-779, a report released August 15, 2005. Drug spending was the fastest-growing part of health costs. A new Medicare drug benefit was about to raise the federal stake. GAO tracked the prices people without drug cover pay at pharmacies. It used data from two state help programs and a federal staff health plan.

GAO found that average prices for 96 widely used drugs rose 24.5 percent over the span. Twenty drugs drove nearly two-thirds of that rise. Brand drug prices rose three times as fast as generic prices. The same steep pattern showed in maker prices and list prices. A small set of drugs drove about half of each index's rise.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-879:
Graduation rates under the school law are studied in GAO-05-879, dated September 20, 2005. About one-third of students who enter high school do not graduate. The No Child Left Behind Act makes states use graduation rates to grade schools. GAO asked how states define the rate. It checked what shapes the accuracy of the data. And it looked at programs that may lift rates.

Section headings give the findings. Many states are moving toward a definition that follows one student group over time. Federal guidance on the law's demands is limited, GAO found. Data quality remains a key challenge to accuracy. Few programs meant to lift rates have been rigorously tested. The Education Department has done little to test or spread the research that exists. GAO made recommendations to close those gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-979:
A trade offset law's workings are assessed in GAO-05-979, issued September 26, 2005. From fiscal years 2001 to 2004, the law paid over $1 billion from import duties to U.S. firms hurt by unfair trade. Backers call it fair relief. Critics call it a windfall. Eleven trade body members filed a complaint against it. GAO covered the law's rules, agency problems, and who got paid.

GAO found the law limits payments to firms that filed or backed a relief petition. That is narrower than normal trade relief. The customs agency must pay within 60 days of the fiscal year's start, which strains its checks. Its claim process is labor-heavy, with no standard forms or e-filing. Firms need not back their claims, and the agency does not verify them. About half the duties meant for payment went uncollected in fiscal year 2004. Half the payments went to five companies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-379:
Federal workers face hazards on the job, and the repair bills are large. Dated April 21, 2006, GAO-06-379 looks at workplace safety in federal agencies. Federal workers' compensation costs topped $1.5 billion in 2004. About 148,000 new claims were filed that year. GAO described agency safety programs and the problems they face.

The study then grades the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. It checks how that agency oversees and helps federal safety programs. GAO found OSHA could do more with a more strategic approach. Readers learn what strong agency programs look like. They also see gaps in federal oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-479:
Embassy support work can sometimes be done far from the embassy itself. Report GAO-06-479, issued May 2, 2006, reviews remote support for U.S. posts abroad. The President's Management Agenda stresses a rightsized overseas presence. Rightsizing means moving some support tasks to the United States or to regional centers. Such moves can be cheaper, safer, or more effective. The State Department is the focus here.

GAO reviews the department's efforts to provide support from remote sites. It names the challenges in doing so. It outlines gains and concerns tied to remote support. Cost studies and performance measures are needed, GAO said. Readers see a staffing idea tested against proof.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-579:
Towns need hundreds of billions for clean water works, and a loan fund helps pay. GAO's June 5, 2006 report, GAO-06-579, studies the Clean Water State Revolving Fund program. Through fiscal year 2005, states used the funds to provide over $52 billion for water projects. The Clean Water Act lets states fund standard wastewater works. It also lets them control diffuse pollution and protect designated estuaries. States have wide choice in how they spend the money.

GAO measured how states split funds among those uses. It described strategies states use to allocate dollars. It also reviewed measures states use to judge results. Readers get allocation patterns across states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-79:
Housing bias complaints and how they are handled fill GAO-06-79, published on October 31, 2005. Each year, the Department of Housing and Urban Development and state and local partner agencies take in several thousand complaints of housing discrimination. Federal standards direct how staff receive complaints, guide callers, and try to settle cases. GAO tested whether intake and investigation work was consistently thorough.

GAO found that staff often responded promptly and gave useful guidance. Yet intake work was not always thorough or timely. Some would-be complainants had trouble even making first contact. Missing or inconsistent data also weakened a tracking system meant to control the process. GAO said the department needs better assurance that its standards are met in every office.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-979:
Aging Coast Guard vessels for navigation aids and icebreaking are surveyed in GAO report GAO-06-979, dated September 22, 2006. The fleet tops 200 craft, from 225-foot buoy tenders to 21-foot boats. After the attacks of September 11, 2001, many took on added security patrol work.

Many craft near, or pass, the span they were built to serve. GAO tracked how much time the fleet spends on missions. It weighed craft state and its effect on mission results. It checked Coast Guard steps to keep the work going. State had slipped for some craft, GAO found, while mission effects looked mixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-379:
Global trade talks collapsed in July 2006 and restarted six months later with the same fault lines. GAO briefed Congress on the stakes in GAO-07-379, a report dated March 5, 2007. The Doha Round began in November 2001. Farm trade sits at the center of the deadlock. The trade chief suspended talks when members could not agree. Formal talks resumed in February 2007. Positions had not moved.

The United States demands deep tariff cuts abroad, GAO found. It offers subsidy cuts only for strong market access in return. The European Union and developing nations want U.S. subsidies cut below current spending. Brazil and India lead the developing bloc. A deeper split concerns what a development round means. Poor nations resist paying for subsidy reform with their own openings. Missing the 2006 window cost the talks fast-track cover in Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-679:
Knowing what a program truly costs is a skill agencies hold unevenly, and GAO-07-679, dated July 20, 2007, sums up five studies. Laws and standards over the past 16 years have pushed managerial cost accounting on the government. Since 2005, GAO has reviewed the practice at 10 large civilian agencies. Those reviews filled five reports. This one draws their lessons together.

Few agencies use cost data in daily choices, GAO finds. Where the method lives, it often serves one program, not the whole shop. Broken finance systems are part of the cause. Culture is the rest: managers run budgets, not costs, by habit. Full use needs strong leaders, better systems, and time. The reward is real, the report argues. An agency that knows its unit costs can price its work, spot waste, and defend its budget with facts instead of habit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-79:
Hospital accreditation and a linked consulting firm are examined in GAO-07-79, dated December 15, 2006. Most hospitals prove they meet Medicare rules through accreditation. The Joint Commission grants that accreditation to over 80 percent of hospitals. In 1986, it set up Joint Commission Resources as a nonprofit affiliate. The affiliate sells advice to the same hospitals on how to improve. GAO studied how the two bodies relate. It checked the walls they built to keep data apart.

The two share a mission and close governance ties. Commission leaders sit on the affiliate's board, and the bodies trade services. Since 1987, they have built a firewall to stop improper data sharing. They added more rules and training after 2003. Staff can report suspected breaches of the wall. Oversight of the firewall has also grown since 2003. The aim is to keep consulting work from swaying accreditation calls. GAO lays out each safeguard in turn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-879:
Loans for manufactured homes are studied in GAO-07-879, dated August 24, 2007. The Federal Housing Administration runs the Title I loan program for such homes. Pending legislation would raise loan limits and insure each loan. It would also tighten underwriting and set up-front premiums. GAO profiled manufactured housing and its owners from census data.

Most manufactured homes sit in rural areas of southern states. Lower-income owners, not renters, live in most of them. Sales of new homes fell sharply from 1996 to 2005. Owners get stronger protections when homes count as real property, GAO found. Rules on repossession are weaker than those on foreclosure. Park closures add risk for owners on leased land. GAO urged the housing agency to assess the bill's effects before acting. It also urged a plan to gather the data needed to run the program. The agency agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-379:
Contract termination costs in defense programs are studied in GAO report GAO-08-379, issued March 14, 2008. The Defense Department plans to invest $1.6 trillion in new weapon systems, a sum GAO calls unsustainable. Some officials fear that ending a contract costs more than finishing it, and GAO tested that fear.

In the cases GAO reviewed, termination costs were rarely the driver; shifts in warfighter need and budget pressure mattered more. GAO found eight fully ended contracts worth over $100 million each with usable data, and none cost more to end than to finish. When programs stop, the department can still shift finished work or materials to other efforts. GAO recommended clearer guidance on when ending a program is the right call. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-79:
Census counting leans on computers to gather and process forms. The Census Bureau plans to spend about $3 billion on such systems for the 2010 count. GAO-08-79, dated October 5, 2007, checks four big system buys and how well the bureau handles the risks tied to them.

Two of the four projects run behind schedule, and some features will be delayed. A fourth contract, due in 2005, was only awarded in September 2007. One project also ran over cost. Since the dress rehearsal will miss the full system set, later testing matters more. Risk lists and fix plans vary by team, GAO found.
george-progress-poverty-1879:
Henry George published Progress and Poverty in 1879 in San Francisco. George, a self-taught economist and journalist, asked why poverty deepens as wealth and progress grow. His answer made the book the best-selling economics work of the nineteenth century.

George blamed private ownership of land: rent rises with progress, so landlords gain what labor and capital earn. His remedy was a single tax on land value, replacing other taxes and leaving buildings untaxed. Millions read him, and land reform movements rose on several continents in his name. Critics disputed the remedy, but the question he posed, why progress and poverty travel together, still has force.
habeas-corpus-act-1679:
England's Parliament passed the Habeas Corpus Act in 1679 to stop prisoners from being held without answers. Under the old writ, a jailer had to bring a prisoner before a judge and explain the arrest. In practice, officials had found ways to delay, move, or hide prisoners.

The act sets firm deadlines for producing a prisoner and gives penalties for officials who dodge the writ. It also bars sending prisoners to distant places beyond the court's reach. These rules made unlawful detention much harder to sustain. The statute became a model for legal systems far beyond England.
haeckel-freedom-in-science-and-teaching-:
Ernst Haeckel, the German naturalist who did more than any man to spread Darwin's teaching in his own land, wrote Freedom in Science and Teaching as a blow in that fight. The English edition of 1879 carries a prefatory note by T. H. Huxley, Darwin's famed advocate. Huxley asks whether any responsible teacher would admit he had not done his best to separate facts from hypotheses in the minds of his hearers.

Haeckel argues that science must be free in the schools and universities, against the claims of the churches to bind it. The book grew out of the fierce German dispute over evolution in education. Its tone is bold, learned, and combative. For English readers it was a dispatch from the front line of the Darwinian wars, with Huxley's name as a flag of approval.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol1-1879:
Constantine Hering spent a lifetime gathering drug symptoms, and The Guiding Symptoms of Our Materia Medica began appearing in 1879. Volume I opens his great American materia medica, a work his students finished after his death. Hering tested remedies on healthy volunteers and recorded every change they felt.

The symptoms are sorted by part of the body, from mind and head down through the frame. Marks show which signs Hering trusted most, confirmed in practice again and again. Prescribers prized the set as a storehouse drawn from real provings, and the first volume sets the pattern the rest follow.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol2-1879:
Volume II of Hering's Guiding Symptoms, issued in 1879, carries the great symptom record forward. Constantine Hering had died with the work unfinished, so his students and family saw the volumes through the press. The plan stays the same: remedies in order, their signs grouped by region of the body.

What sets these pages apart is the grading worked into the text. Strong marks flag the symptoms seen most often and cured most surely, the true guiding signs. A prescriber could scan a remedy and find its heart at a glance. The volume keeps Hering's lifetime of proving work within easy reach.
heroic-romances-of-ireland-translated-in:
Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume 2, translated by A H Leahy into English prose and verse, gathers the shorter tales that once introduced the great cattle raid. Leahy explains in his preface that ancient Irish storytellers recited lesser Tains before the central story of the heroic age. A list names fourteen such preludes, three of them lost, and this volume prints the five that editors had so far prepared.

The five are the raids of Dartada, Flidais, Fraich, Regamon, and Regamna. The Fraich tale stands longest, as long as the other four together, and works as a story in its own right. Each tale appears in verse with a literal prose translation, and a short introduction names the manuscript it comes from. Cattle, in this world, are wealth worth fighting wars over, and every raid sets kings and champions in motion.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
Chapters forty-seven and forty-eight of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands send a Dutch fleet against Spain itself. Admiral Heemskerk sails for the Spanish coast, carrying the war home after forty years. Motley then turns inward, to the internal condition of Spain under Philip III. The inquisition's influence, degraded labour, and expelled Moors fill his indictment.

Venality, he writes, is the special characteristic of Spanish polity. The Duke of Lerma rules by a system of bribery and trafficking. Population, revenue, church income, and an insolvent government are reckoned in turn. The chapter is Motley's explanation of the whole war's outcome. Spain still looked like the world's leading power, he says, although foiled in all its undertakings. Appearances deceived; the truce merely signed the truth.
hume-dialogues-natural-religion-1779:
David Hume wrote his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion in his last years, and they were published in 1779, after his death. Three speakers carry the debate: Cleanthes, who defends the argument from design; Demea, who speaks for orthodox faith; and Philo, the skeptic who asks the hard questions. Their topic is the being and nature of God.

Philo presses the design argument until its likeness between world and machine wears thin. Suffering, disorder, and rival causes all enter his case. Cleanthes answers with warmth, and the dialogue never quite declares a winner. The work became the classic demolition of natural theology in English, and the most readable of Hume's philosophical writings.
jevons-theory-political-economy-1879:
W Stanley Jevons published The Theory of Political Economy in 1879 in its second edition, first issued in 1871. Jevons, a Manchester economist and logician, helped start the marginalist revolution. That turn rebuilt economics on the value of one more unit, not on labor alone.

Jevons argued that utility, the satisfaction a good gives, rules value, and that each added unit gives less than the last. He cast exchange and labor in math, treating economics as a calculus of pleasure and pain. Ricardo and Mill had stressed cost; Jevons stressed the buyer. His theory, with Menger and Walras abroad, remade the science, and the second edition spread it in a fuller form.
jewett-old-friends-new-1879:
Early tales fill Old Friends and New, under copyright of 1879. Jewett was still in her twenties and finding her voice when she wrote them. A later list of her books shows how wide her output grew, from Deephaven to The Tory Lover.

Old neighbors, summer visitors, and village oddballs people these gentle New England stories. Readers can watch a fine writer take shape page by page. Her ear for local speech, her love of place, and her pity for plain folk are all here already. The book offers a warm window on the start of a classic American career that lasted three more decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abbassid-califs:
The Abbassid Califs ruled for five centuries, from 750 to 1258, and the entry weighs the place of the Jews under them. Their stance differed from that of the Ommiads before them. When Al-Mansur founded Bagdad, the seat of rule came near Sura and Pumbedita, the two centers of Jewish learning. Bagdad itself was allowed to keep a Jewish community in its walls.

Peace was not steady, the entry stresses. Old limits on dress and riding were brought back by Harun-al-Raschid, who ruled from 786 to 809. Under Al-Mutawakkil, from 850, synagogues were turned into mosques. Yet later califs put Jews into state service. By the middle of the twelfth century Bagdad held one thousand Jewish families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigail-father-:
Abigail is the name of two women in this entry, and the second fills most of it. The first was a daughter of Jesse and a sister of David. She wed Jether the Ishmaelite and bore Amasa. The great Abigail of the entry was the wise and fair wife of Nabal, a rich but grasping noble of Carmel, in southern Judah.

When Nabal refused David pay for his guard work, Abigail went out on her own to meet the outlaw prince. She brought gifts and a soft speech, won his favor, and saved her husband from the attack he faced. Nabal soon died, and she became David's wife. At Hebron she bore him a son, Chileab, who seems to have died young. Rabbinic lore counts her among the four great beauties, and as a prophetess.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-adolphe:
Adolphe Abraham was a French colonel born at Thionville on March 21, 1814. At eighteen he joined the 52d Regiment as a volunteer and went to the siege of Antwerp. He rose from the ranks step by step.

He won the Legion of Honor after the Paris rising of June 1848. He fought in Crimea and at Sebastopol, then in Italy in 1859. Wounded at Magenta, he took Casa Nuova and four guns at Solferino. He served again in 1870 and under the Commune. Retired for good in 1879, he stayed loyal to Judaism and led the Versailles congregation till 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jos: Abraham ben Josiah ha-Rofe was a Karaitic scholar and physician born at Troki, near Wilna, about 1636. He died there in 1688 and ranked among the leading scholars of his time. Karaite tradition calls him a pupil of Joseph Solomon Delmedigo. In later years he served as physician in ordinary to King John Sobieski, who reigned from 1674 to 1696. He wrote a number of works on medicine and natural science. None of them was ever printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-she: Abraham ben Sherira was gaon in Pumbedita. He followed Rabbi Joseph bar Abba in that post, holding it from 816 to 828. He leaned toward mysticism, the entry states. People said he could foretell future events by watching the motion of tree branches. He is quoted in the Aruk, under a root entry. No work, family, or death account is given beyond those few lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-of-csarea-: Adda of Cæsarea was a pupil of R. Johanan. He taught in the third amora line. His town tag has caused an error. Some take him for a son of R. Abbahu of Cæsarea. The entry says that take is wrong. Cites in the Jerusalem and Babylonian Talmuds back the point. The hosted text is short. It gives his teacher, his rank, and the false link it clears up. It names no saying of his and no school that he led in his own right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-afghanistan-879:
Afghanistan is a land of Asia northwest of India. Its folk hold a lore that they spring from the lost Ten Tribes. A home chronicle tells of a people called Bani Israel in the land of Ghor. About the year 622 they took Islam at the hands of a man called Kais. That tale sheds no light on today's Afghan Jews, the entry says.

Those Jews are said to number 40,000 in about sixty flocks. Most live at Kabul, Herat, Kandahar, Ghazni, and Balkh. Each town keeps a Jewish quarter shut at dusk and opened at dawn. They speak Persian, and their books and teachers come from Persia. They dress like their neighbors, save a black turban. They skip army service and pay a war tax in its place. In 1880 a levy on Herat's Jews drove many to flee to Persia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahiezer-kinsman: Ahiezer, meaning "Kinsman is Help," is the name of two men in the entry. The first was a son of Ammishaddai. He led the tribe of Dan in the second year after the Exodus. He brought his offering at the dedication of the Tabernacle on the tenth day. The second was a chief among the men who came to David at Ziklag. No further detail is given for either man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albelda-sometim: Moses Albelda, whose name is sometimes miswritten Albilda or Albeylda, was a Bible commentator. He died in 1549. His name came from the town of Albelda, where he or his forebears must have lived. Early in the sixteenth century he settled at Salonica, in Turkey. He stayed there until his death at an advanced age. His known work is a supercommentary on Rashi's comment on the Pentateuch. It was printed, probably at Constantinople, about 1525. The book itself names neither the place nor the date of its printing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almazan-almacan: Miguel de Almazan was a Marano of Saragossa in Spain. He served as private secretary to King Ferdinand of Aragon. He was burned at the stake on a charge. The charge was that he held to Judaism in secret. The entry is very short and gives no year for his death. One month later, on March 18, 1486, Manuel de Almaçan of Saragossa met the same fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ambrosoli-1379:
Ambrosoli was a church dignitary of Rome. His fame rests on sermons for fair treatment of Jews. He preached in a Rome church in 1848. That year a drive rose to drop the Roman Ghetto. Hearers said his words made crowds want to tear the walls down. His sway helped bring an edict that year.

Pope Pius IX signed that edict on April 17, 1848. It called for the walls and gates to come down. A tale told by a Roman Jew fills the close. On the night the walls fell, Ambrosoli stood in the crowd. A cross lay hid under his coat. He held it ready to stop any harm in the name of his faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antigonus-son-o:
Antigonus, son of John Hyrcanus, was born about 135 B.C. and died in 103. Though young, he proved a fine soldier in his father's lifetime. With his brother Aristobulus he besieged and took Samaria about 109, beating off Syrian and Egyptian relief forces.

When Aristobulus became king about 105, he jailed his other brothers but kept Antigonus free and near the throne. That favor woke court jealousy, led, the entry says, by Queen Alexandra. Slander made the king fear that Antigonus aimed at the crown. Orders went to the guard to cut him down if he came armed before the king, and a court plot ended in his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ar-or-ar-moab-1:
Ar is a name that occurs in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah, always tied to Moab. It is often explained as the Hebrew word for city, making Ar Moab the city of Moab, a supposed old capital of the Moabites. The entry tests that reading against the verses themselves.

In Deuteronomy, God says he has given Ar to the children of Lot as a possession. Israel is told to pass through Ar, the border of Moab, and the Moabites are said to dwell in Ar. A city alone fits those lines poorly, the entry argues. Ar is simpler read as the name of a country, or its chief part, from which Moab's capital took the name Areopolis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ark-of-moses-te: Hidden by his mother for three months, the infant Moses could be concealed no longer, so she made a box and set it on the Nile, as told in Exodus chapter 2. The box was made of rushes and lined with slime and pitch to keep water out. A note from the Midrash on Exodus adds that the pitch was placed on the outside, so its smell would not trouble the child inside.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asarelah-or-ash: Asarelah, also spelled Asharelah, was one of the Asaphites whom David set over the Temple service, by First Chronicles chapter 25. In verse 14 of the same chapter he appears as Jesharelah. The entry prefers the readings with an s sound. It compares the shift in Jesse's name, written Yishai but once Ishai. The name itself may be a bent form of Israel with a strong ending added. A note in Kittel's Bible commentary is cited for the point.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-meir-:
Meir Ashkenazi of Kaffa was an envoy of the Tatar khan in the sixteenth century. Pirates killed him on a voyage from Gava, near Genoa, to Dakhel in Upper Egypt. The killing fell between the 15th and the 25th day of Tammuz, in July 1567. His death is known from witness testimony in a widow's case.

Elias ben Nehemiah testified before the rabbis at Safed for the widow and heirs. His account fixed the facts: Meir lived at Kaffa, his parents still lived there, and his brother studied at Brest-Litovsk. He had brought prisoners of war from Egypt to Gava. The khan had named him envoy to the king of Poland. On the last leg of the journey, pirates slew him with all the ship's passengers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athaliah-2079:
Athaliah was a daughter of Ahab, and presumably of Jezebel. She married Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. That match tied the two royal houses together. When her son Ahaziah was killed by Jehu, she seized her chance. She had all the royal seed killed and made herself queen of Judah.

Her rule lasted six years, given as 842 to 836 B.C. In that time she pushed the worship of Baal in Judah. In her seventh year the high priest Jehoiada brought out Joash, a hidden son of Ahaziah, and crowned him in the Temple. Athaliah rushed in and cried, Treason! Treason! Jehoiada ordered her taken out through the ranks. She was killed at the entry of the horse-gate by the king's house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-avitus-of-auver:
Avitus was bishop of Clermont-Ferrand, France, in the sixth century. He stood out among the bishops of his day for zeal in forcing Jews to convert. Other bishops dealt gently with Jews, and Pope Gregory the First warned against force. Avitus pressed the Jews of Clermont again and again, with no result. The Franks around them felt no such hatred, and Jews and Christians mixed freely.

At last one Jew was baptized, on Easter Day, April 5, 576. In the street procession a Jew sprinkled the convert with rancid oil. A mob then tore down the synagogue on Ascension Day, May 14. The next day Avitus gave the Jews a choice of baptism or exile. After three days of delay and attacks, over five hundred asked for baptism on May 18, 576. The rest fled to Marseilles, where, the entry notes, force met them again later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babel-tower-of-:
The Tower of Babel story stands in the eleventh chapter of Genesis. All mankind then spoke one tongue and formed one people. They settled in the land of Shinar, near the Euphrates. There they built a city and a tower. Their aim was to hold together, win a name, and avoid being scattered. God came down to see the work. He confused their speech. The people scattered, and the city was left unfinished.

Jewish tradition read the building as revolt. The Midrash calls the builders the generation of secession. In one account they meant to set an idol with a sword atop the tower, as if to make war on God. The entry traces the tale through rabbinic and Muslim hands. Muslim lore took up the Jewish story of two angels who taught magic at a well in Babil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakbuk-sons-of-: Sons of Bakbuk are named in the Bible as a family of Nethinim, temple servants, who came back with Zerubbabel. The entry is only two sentences. It points the reader to Ezra ii. 51 and the matching list in Nehemiah vii. 53. It adds one caution: whether these are the same as "the sons of Acub" in I Esdras v. 31 is doubtful. No person, place, or deed beyond the two lists is given for the family here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barach-rosa-247: Rosa Barach was an Austrian author and educator born at Neu-Rausnitz, Moravia, on May 15, 1841. She was educated at her home town and at Vienna, and settled in Vienna, where she founded a high school for girls. In 1882 she toured Germany as a reciter. The entry lists her novels, from "Aus Eigener Kraft" in 1880 to "Alle Drei" in 1893. It adds her patriotic songs of 1882, a biography of the Emperor Franz Josef I. in 1889, and a sketch of 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-joshua-b: Joshua Boaz ben Simon ben Abraham Baruch was a prominent Talmudist who lived at Sabionetta, later at Savigliano, and died in 1557. Of an old Judæo-Spanish family, he probably settled in Italy after the banishment from Spain. At twenty-three he began publishing useful works on the Talmud. His "Massoret ha-Shas" indexes parallel passages of the Talmud and halakic Midrashim. His "'En Mishpaṭ, Ner Miẓwah" indexes halakot quoted in Maimonides and the Turim. His "Torah Or" indexes Biblical passages in the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bayonne-2679:
Bayonne is a fortified city in the far southwest of France, split by the Adour and Nive rivers. Its Jewish community began at St. Esprit, a suburb across the water. Refugees from Spain and Portugal founded it after the expulsions from the Iberian lands.

These families first lived as New Christians, keeping their old faith at home. Royal letters guarded their stay for more than two centuries. The entry follows suits with the city, open practice of Judaism, and full citizenship in 1789. Later pages cover schools, charities, and a shrinking community. Letters patent from French kings, renewed across the years 1550 to 1777, guarded their right to stay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrens-sir-jac:
Jacob Behrens was a town leader at Bradford, England, born at Pyrmont, Germany, in November 1806. He died at Torquay on April 22, 1889. He learned trade in his father's Hamburg firm, moved to Leeds in 1834, and settled at Bradford in 1838.

Bradford's worsted trade grew up with Behrens at its center. He founded its Chamber of Commerce and spoke as an expert on tariffs and trade treaties. Queen Victoria knighted him in October 1882 for help on a French treaty. He also founded an eye and ear hospital in the town. He backed free trade with force and aided Cobden in the talks that led to the French treaty of 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berkowitz-benzi: Benzion Judah Berkowitz, a Russian Hebrew scholar, was born on July 23, 1803. He died at Wilna on May 11, 1879. All his books serve the study of the Targum Onkelos, the Aramaic rendering of the Pentateuch. Four titles are listed, printed at Wilna between 1843 and 1877. Specialists such as Berliner praised the worth of his work on that Targum. He also wrote for several Hebrew journals of his day, and the entry names four of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-besancon-3179:
Besançon is a city and county of France in the department of Doubs. The entry traces its Jewish history from the fourteenth century. Jews were expelled from the region in 1321. Some later returned. In 1348 the Black Plague brought new attacks. Jews were blamed, persecuted, and executed. Survivors were exiled in 1360.

Five Jews entered the city itself in 1320. They paid a heavy monthly poll-tax to stay. They had to wear a white and red cloth. They lived on one street behind nightly closed gates. The entry also describes a Hebrew Bible manuscript in the city library. It was sold in Yemen in May 1492.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-andre-337: André Bloch was a French musician. He was born at Wissembourg in 1873. His father was a rabbi there. At seven he composed a piano waltz. A publisher printed it. His parents moved to Paris for his training. Prizes came in a steady stream at the Conservatory. Solfeggio came in 1884, piano in 1889. Harmony followed in 1890. In 1893 he won the prize of Rome unanimously. Massenet was among his teachers. His cantata and "Poëme Nomade" lead his works. He also studied astronomy with Flammarion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bolaffio-leone-:
Leone Bolaffio was an Italian jurist born at Padua on July 5, 1848. He studied at Padua, where Luzzatto taught him at the Talmudic college. He then read law at the university there.

Bolaffio practiced law at Venice for fifteen years and taught at its technical institute. Chairs at Parma and Bologna followed. He sat on the royal commission to reform the commercial code. His chief work comments on that code, in a second edition of 1899. He also pushed shorthand teaching in Italian schools and founded shorthand societies. He also urged an end to bankruptcy suits against business men of small means. Since 1876 he edited Temi Veneta, a judicial paper he founded himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bornstein-paul-:
Paul Bornstein was a German author born in Berlin on April 8, 1868. He took his doctorate at the university in that city. He has lived in the German capital since his graduation.

Bornstein's first book retold the memoirs of Cagliostro in 1892. A novel followed in 1896, and that year he founded a monthly on new literature and art. He edited it till 1898 and wrote many essays for it. He also rendered French works into German. His largest task was editing a survey of German life in the nineteenth century. By 1902 it ran to twenty-three volumes with a young staff.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bremen-3679:
Bremen is a free city of the German empire. It stands out as a place where few Jews have ever dwelt. A baptized Jew, Paulus, is said to have taught alchemy there in the eleventh century.

Traveling Jews could stay in Bremen only one night. They had to report to the burgomaster and pay the Jews' tax. Market days alone allowed a longer stay, for a special fee. Attempts to settle there met repeated expulsions for centuries. Some thirty families settled during the French occupation of 1811-13, then were banished after 1814. A small community formed in 1848. By 1902 the city held 947 Jews, with a synagogue opened in 1876.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brux-3779:
Brüx was a town of Bohemia, 14 miles north of Saaz. Documents show Jews living there as early as the fourteenth century. Notes from 1393 onward record loans from named Jews of Brüx. A Jewish cemetery there is mentioned in a document of 1456. In 1464 the king of Bohemia barred Jews from living in or near the town.

For four hundred years Brüx had no Jewish community, and Jews were kept out of Bohemian mining towns. Nearby congregations at Harreth and Lischnicz became the parents of a new one, founded in 1868. A synagogue followed in 1873 and a cemetery in 1878. The entry credits leader Joseph Spitz, in charge from 1885, for the congregation's standing. About 1,000 Jews lived there, most of them merchants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-isaac:
Isaac Hayyim Cantarini was an Italian poet, writer, physician, and rabbi born Feb. 2, 1644, at Padua. He took his medical diploma there in 1664. He preached often in the Ashkenazic synagogue, taught in the yeshivah, and sang as cantor on the Day of Atonement. His legal rulings were sought for his deep Talmud knowledge. He died at Padua in 1723.

His chief Hebrew work tells of the attack on the Padua ghetto on Aug. 20, 1684, in which he took part. It prints government documents and opens with community statistics. Other works treat the Messiah's coming time and the tax collectors' oath. In Latin he answered a blood accusation work in 1681. The entry stresses his rare tolerance toward Christians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-church-councils:
Church councils, the law-making synods of the Roman Catholic Church, are traced here through their long record on the Jews. The entry counts twenty general councils alongside national, provincial, and diocesan meetings. Many of them legislated about Jews: cutting Jewish influence on Christians, blocking converts from returning to Judaism, and pressing Jews to convert instead.

A plain pattern emerges. Rulings grew harsher toward the end of the Middle Ages, with only a few kind resolutions on record. The survey starts with the synod at Elvira in the early fourth century, which barred Christians from having field fruits blessed by Jews. Later canons take up usury, a tax on Jewish families, and special dress for Jews and Saracens.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-hermann-4:
Hermann Cohen, a German philosopher, was born in Coswig, Anhalt, on July 4, 1842. He trained at the Dessau gymnasium, the Breslau Jewish seminary, and three universities. His deep study of Kant made his name early. In 1873 he became a privat-docent at Marburg, then assistant professor in 1875 and full professor a year later.

He stands, the entry says, among the ablest voices of the neo-Kantian school. His books work through Kant on experience, ethics, and aesthetics, and through Plato's theory of ideas. Later pages list his writings on Judaism, from a piece on the Sabbath in 1881 to essays on Jewish moral teaching. His System of Philosophy began with the Logic of Pure Knowledge in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cortissos-don-j: Don José Cortissos was a Spanish army contractor, born in 1656. He died in London in 1742. He had served as ambassador of the emperor Charles to Morocco. In 1706 he agreed to supply food to the allied armies in Spain. British commanders promised that Britain would stand behind Portugal's payment. Reports say he saved the army from starvation. Payment in full never came. He moved to England in 1712 to press his claims and won only a fraction of the sum owed. He died in poverty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cunus-petrus-al: Petrus Cunæus, also known as Peter van der Kuhn, was a Dutch Christian scholar. He was born at Flushing in 1586. He died at Leyden on Dec. 2, 1638. From 1617 he taught law and politics at the University of Leyden. His fame rests on De Republica Hebræorum, three volumes printed in 1617. The book treats the Hebrew kingdom as a pure theocracy. God alone ruled, made laws, and led the people. Cunæus ranked Hebrew law above Greek and Roman law. He drew on the Rabbis and Maimonides.
