Such surgery, using an endoprosthesis, saves the leg, but lasting strain in daily life is common. The team reviewed records for 75 patients treated from 2000 to 2020, then traced 44 who were alive and available for follow-up.

Follow-up came at a mean of 9.7 years after surgery. Two sets of patient-reported scores gauged daily function. Older age at surgery raised the risk of poor scores on both sets. A leg length discrepancy after surgery also raised the risk on one set. The threshold for age sat at 29 years, and for leg length gap at about eight millimeters. The authors urge frank discussion and strong support for older patients, and reconstructions that match the lost bone length.
pmc-10694879:
Good research often fails to change care in the places that need it most, a gap called knowledge translation. Robert Borst and co-authors studied their own project that tried to close that gap in Cameroon, Jordan, and Nigeria. Local teams led the work and chose what to study, following cycles of asking, acting, and reflecting.

The team interviewed sixty-three people involved and watched hundreds of hours of the work in action. The flexible design often let local teams bend methods to local needs, which worked well. Yet the project's own rules sometimes clashed with other values in play, forcing constant small adjustments. The authors distill three design principles and three working sensitivities for future projects. Flexibility plus supported alignment work, they argue, is what makes such projects land.
pmc-10695379:
Alexander Shayesteh, Antonia Boman, Emil Hawas, and Bo Carlberg test whether frozen leftover botulinum toxin works as well as fresh toxin for excess armpit sweat, in a study from 2023. Clinics often keep mixed toxin in the freezer for later use. Whether that hurts results or safety had not been checked with care.

The clinic in Umeå, Sweden, gave fresh toxin in each patient's right armpit and frozen, thawed toxin in the left. Records and surveys from 106 patients covered the time before treatment and 24 weeks after. Scores for sweat severity and patient ratings showed no gap between the two sides. Side effects also matched across products and brands. The authors back the frozen practice.
pmc-10696079:
Stereocenters with four bonds are routine targets for catalysts. Centers with five bonds, where a fifth group widens the space of forms, were not. The four authors report catalyst control over pentavalent phosphorus centers. A bifunctional iminophosphorane thiourea catalyst steers the making of phosphoranes with both enantio- and diastereocontrol. It separates stable enantiomers and diastereomer families that spring from one center.

The target dioxophosphorane isomers arrive in up to 99 percent yield. Their mirror-form ratios reach 96 to 4, and their paired-form ratios reach 99 to 1. Stereodivergent catalysis sends the same reaction to each form the center can take, on demand. The authors expect this trick to work for other high-valent main group species too. That would widen the range of forms chemists can build in fact.
pmc-10696779:
Behnam Ghorbani Nejad and co-authors published a review in 2023 on a food toxin and child growth. The toxin is a poison made by mold that can grow on stored food. The team asked if contact with the toxin is linked to poor growth in babies and young children.

The team searched three large databases and pooled the results of past studies. They looked at wasting, low weight, stunted growth, and standard growth scores. Pooled results linked the toxin to lower weight and height scores. Cohort studies also linked it to higher risk of low weight and stunting. The authors say the toxin may be a real risk for child growth.
pmc-10697179:
Rita Fernandes and co-authors report in 2023 the case of a 48 year old woman whose blocked gut vein was treated without surgery. The condition, a clot in the vein that drains the intestine, is rare and easy to miss. Exam findings often look mild next to the patient's pain, so doctors underrate it.

The woman had high blood pressure, blood fat trouble, heavy obesity, and an underactive thyroid, plus a family history of gut cancers. She came to primary care with pain in the upper left belly and flank. The report follows how the clot was found and how blood thinning care alone carried her through. Such cases remind front line doctors to image early when belly pain outruns the exam.
pmc-10698179:
Pihlainen K and co-authors present a 2023 review on how long military operations change soldiers' bodies and fitness. Deployments lasting three months or more mix hard work, poor sleep, and uneven training. The team gathered studies on performance, body composition, and training habits during such operations.

They screened over four thousand records and kept twenty-four studies. Endurance dipped slightly, the most consistent finding across studies. Max strength of the legs and upper body rose a little, as did push-up and sit-up endurance. Body composition barely changed overall. Training volume varied widely between soldiers, and cuts in endurance training tracked with worse results. Soldiers who started fittest tended to lose the most ground.
pmc-10698479:
Stefano Kaburu and co-authors check whether the way scientists watch monkeys changes the social maps they draw. Social network analysis measures how animals connect through grooming, huddling, and aggression. Two watching styles are common: following one animal at a time, or noting every event of a behavior as it happens across the group. Their 2023 study compares the two across three macaque species.

Direct measures, such as how many partners each animal has, matched well between the two styles for all three behaviors. Finer measures of status and bridging matched for grooming and aggression in all species. For huddling, some measures matched only in the tolerant bonnet macaque and not in the stricter rhesus macaque. Group shape measures mostly agreed, with a few exceptions. The authors give guidance on when each watching style is safe to use.
pmc-10698879:
Yasir Elhadi, writing alone in 2023, reviews Sudan's record on long-term disease policy. Diseases such as diabetes and heart disease are the top cause of illness and death worldwide, and Sudan's share has grown fast. The study reads published papers and reports to judge how far policy has come and what blocks it.

Deaths from these diseases rose from 32 percent of the total in 2015 to 54 percent in 2022. Of nineteen world target signs, eight had never been fully met, and only five were fully met in 2022. War, staff shortages, weak data systems, and low funds all slowed progress. The author urges that rebuilding after war put these policies first.
pmc-10700479:
Raanan Meyer and co-authors measured in 2023 what drives major complications after bowel surgery for endometriosis in the United States. Removing diseased bowel is among the heaviest operations for the condition, and patients deserve honest odds. The team mined a national surgical quality registry for resections done from 2012 to 2020.

Of 755 women, about two thirds had keyhole surgery and a third open surgery. Major complications struck 13.5 percent overall, and ran about twice as high in the open group as in the keyhole group, in the counts reported. Adjusted analysis began naming risk factors, starting with a higher rate for Black patients in the finding reported. Readers get a counseling table built from national data: the risks, and who carries more of them.
pmc-10701079:
Mäki-Marttunen and co-authors scan the brains of chronic migraine patients before and after they stop overusing headache medicine, hunting for network changes that track recovery. Ninety-nine patients had resting-state MRI scans, then again after three months of withdrawal therapy. Their brain connectivity was compared with healthy volunteers and with patients who had episodic migraine, chronic back pain, or depression.

One region kept standing out: the visual cortex. Its connections with major brain networks differed in chronic migraine, in the same direction across the comparison groups. Patients who responded to withdrawal, halving their headache days or better, showed reduced visual cortex connectivity afterward. Strikingly, responders already differed from non-responders at the first scan. The authors read the pattern as a marker of migraine becoming chronic, and possibly reversible.
pmc-10701979:
Wang Liao and co-authors study a blood sugar ratio as a warning sign after a severe heart attack in a 2023 paper. The ratio compares blood sugar at the time of care with the usual sugar level over past weeks. Past work linked a high ratio to worse outcomes, but the ratio can be figured in two ways.

The study followed 1,643 patients treated at two centers for a blocked heart artery. Both versions of the ratio, one based on albumin and one on hemoglobin A1c, tracked with higher death rates in hospital and over time. Each version added useful warning power to standard risk scores, and both performed much alike.
pmc-10702079:
Lei Ouyang and co-authors map a gene family in peanut in a 2023 study. The genes make enzymes that attach sugars to plant compounds, a step that changes how those compounds act. Peanut is a major oil and food crop, yet this gene family in it was barely known.

The team found 267 such genes, sorted into 15 groups, with one group grown far larger than the rest. Paired copies along the genome drove much of that growth. One gene, tested in the lab, attached sugar to a class of healthy plant compounds. Plants given extra copies of that gene bore drought and salt better, with less cell damage.
pmc-10703779:
Kanokwan Dekham and colleagues published an aquaculture study in 2023. They tested a helpful bacterium against shrimp disease. White spot virus kills farmed shrimp very fast. Losses hit shrimp producers around the world hard. The team used a Lactobacillus strain called KD1. Young shrimp received it before virus exposure. Survival, virus levels, and immune genes were measured. The full genome of the strain was also read.

Treated shrimp died far less often after challenge. No virus copies were detected in treated shrimp. Several immune genes switched on more strongly too. Genome reading showed one chromosome and one plasmid. Only one resistance gene was found overall. Related strains came from very different animal hosts. Special genes may help it survive and fight viruses. The strain looks promising for shrimp farming.
pmc-10703879:
Yan Sun and colleagues show how a myeloma cell therapy's receptor turns up its own volume by clustering on contact with its target, in this study from twenty twenty-three. The therapy, cilta-cel, which the team helped develop, arms T cells with a receptor carrying two tiny binding heads against BCMA, a myeloma marker. Receptors in nature often amplify signals by grouping; the team asked whether this engineered one does too.

Crystal structures and solution measurements said yes. When BCMA molecules engage the twin heads, receptors draw together into multimers on the T cell surface. That clustering bought real power: stronger killing of myeloma cells, tighter immune synapses, and richer release of killing cytokines. The authors name the principle antigen-induced multimerization and offer it as a design lever for the next generation of cell therapies.
pmc-10704679:
Alyssa Spomer, Benjamin Conner, Michael Schwartz, Zachary Lerner, and Katherine Steele test how sight and sound biofeedback shapes calf muscle adaptation while walking in children with cerebral palsy. Biofeedback is a gentle route to better gait training, but how the cue type sways response was unclear. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Teens walked on a treadmill under sight and sound cues, body sense cues, or both, before and after practice sessions and at a later check. Both systems targeted the calf push muscles of the weaker leg. The sight and sound system read muscle signals live. The body sense system used a resistive ankle brace. Response paths were tracked at each visit.
pmc-10705879:
Tamer Abdelrehim, Daniel Fried and their co-authors present an algorithm to auto-segment and measure early enamel decay in optical coherence tomography images in 2023. Such imaging can assess mineral loss in teeth, but clinic software still supports mainly visual, qualitative reads.

Their MATLAB tool processes batches of scans of artificially decayed human enamel and splits decay zones by intensity thresholds. It reports average decay depth, profile lines and total reflectivity for an exact assessment. Checks on real and simulated frames showed automated depths matched known measurements very closely. The authors aim at a real-time probe tool for dental diagnosis.
pmc-10706679:
Eugenia Mazzara and co-authors compared the chemistry of sumac fruits from five Sicilian sites, hunting for the best source of a natural food preservative, in a 2023 study. Sumac's sour red fruits brim with antioxidant tannins, phenolic acids, and pigments. Water extracts of each site's fruit were tested for antioxidant power and read by liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry. A principal component analysis helped visualize the differences among sites.

Two towns stood out. Fruit from San Biagio Platani carried the most of two prized compounds, the flavonoid isoquercitrin and gallic acid, at striking levels per kilogram of dry extract. Fruit from Giarratana led in red anthocyanin pigments. The authors name these two populations as the best bets for planting sumac orchards and developing sumac-based foods and supplements. Site, in short, writes the recipe.
pmc-10707879:
Eduard Levin and co-authors chase surface area in copper coatings grown for catalysis in a 2023 study. Oxide-derived copper, made by reducing a copper oxide layer, is a prized catalyst for turning carbon dioxide into useful products. Comparing catalysts fairly needs their true active area, and roughness factor is the yardstick the field had rarely measured for these coatings.

Two recipe baths, acetic and lactic acid, grew oxides with opposite characters: dense column films from one, fine porous grains from the other. After reduction, roughness grew in a straight line with deposition charge in both, but the porous route climbed far faster. Its best films reached a roughness factor of six hundred fifty, among the highest ever estimated for this catalyst family. The authors stress that recipe choice, not just chemistry, sets a catalyst's working surface.
pmc-10708479:
Chang-Hua Zhao and co-authors turn lab filter paper into a strong tool for cleaning oily water, in work from 2023. Oil and water mixes from factories are hard to split with cheap filters. Costly membranes foul and break down with use.

The team coated paper with titanium dioxide grains wrapped in a sticky natural polymer. The coat made the paper love water in air but repel oil under water. It split plain oil and water mixes and fine emulsions with over 99 percent success. After seventeen rounds of use, success still held at that level. The cheap base and lasting strength suit large-scale cleanup where budgets are tight.
pmc-10708779:
Qiancheng Tan and co-authors build a layered classifier to tell apart human activities that look nearly identical to body sensors, in a 2023 paper. Phones and watches infer activities from motion sensors, but similar motions, sitting versus standing still, typing versus writing, confuse them. The team collected accelerometer and gyroscope data during such look-alike activities and stacked three methods in sequence.

A boosted random forest first selects the most informative features. A kernel discriminant method then pulls the similar activities apart in a transformed space where their differences grow. A support vector machine makes the final calls. Tested on their data and four public benchmark sets, the model improved recognition of the confusable classes. The authors offer the layered design for health monitoring and smart environments where fine distinctions matter.
pmc-10708979:
Danilo Pizzo Kitagaki and co-authors count how often a small forearm tendon is missing in this 2023 Brazilian study. The palmaris longus tendon runs down the front of the forearm, and some people are born without it. Surgeons often harvest this tendon for grafts, so knowing how often it is absent matters for planning operations.

The team tested 1,008 adult volunteers in a multiethnic Brazilian city between October 2017 and April 2018. Each person performed a standard hand test on both sides. The tendon was missing in about twenty-six percent of the volunteers. About twelve percent lacked it on both sides, while fourteen percent lacked it on one side only. Missing on one side was more common in men, and the right side was the usual gap. Rates did not differ by sex when both sides were missing.
pmc-10709479:
Lucie Auffret and co-authors wrote a study from 2023 defining a new subtype of diffuse midline glioma, a deadly brain tumor of children and young adults. These tumors carry a signature change in a histone gene and resist all current treatment. A rare few also carry switches in one of two growth genes, and those patients seemed to fare better. The team gathered twenty-nine such tumors plus thirty-one published cases and profiled them deeply.

Patterns in the tumors' chemical tags grouped nearly all the co-altered cases into one family, apart from other glioma kinds. Scans and tissue showed unusual traits: chalky deposits and solid lumps rarely seen in this disease. Tumors favored the thalamus, and patients lived a median beyond three years, far past the norm. In one case the histone change came first. The authors argue this subtype needs its own handling in trials and care.
pmc-10709579:
Gopinadh Konda and three co-authors grade ten-year past casts of hard rain in India's monsoon heart. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Year-span casts serve year plans, and the world set of such casts was tried on June to late-year rain. Raw models low-balled rain swings by a lot. A count-map fix was laid on to set them right.

Past the fix, casts caught hard rain counts, force, and spread far more true, with gains near four fifths. Small and mid rain zones are cast to grow most in the next span of years. A fixed cast set is put forth for use.
pmc-10709879:
Andrew Stuart Lane and co-authors tested whether genetic information can sway young doctors toward a diagnosis too quickly. People tend to treat genes as destiny, a bias called genetic essentialism, even when a gene only nudges risk. The team gave 102 senior medical students a case of gut symptoms; half were also told the patient carried HLA-DQ2, a gene linked to coeliac disease but far from proof of it.

Students who saw the gene result were more likely to recommend a gluten-free diet, the management for coeliac disease, while investigation choices barely differed. Interviews showed the students understood the gene was not decisive, yet still leaned on it, though some said they were guessing what examiners wanted. The authors say the bias deserves testing in real clinical settings.
pmc-10710179:
Razan Bosly and six colleagues report cases where braces slowly pulled damaged upper front teeth outward to save them, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Badly broken front teeth are hard to restore, and their look matters greatly. The team fitted custom posts joined with brackets and gently moved the teeth to the wanted level. They took care not to harm the bone edge or root tips.

Patients were checked for three months before final crowns were built. X-rays showed a normal gum outline and fresh bone near the root tips in all cases. No root or bone loss and no nerve problems appeared. The authors recommend the method for the visible front zone, where it can also keep bone ready for later implants.
pmc-10712279:
Jiale Hu and seven co-authors report ten child cases where a common childhood tumor first showed as a lump under the skin, in a 2023 paper. Neuroblastoma grows from young nerve cells and is among the most frequent tumors of childhood. Spread to soft tissue as the first sign is rare, with only four such cases in print before this series. The team reviews scans of their ten cases and the older reports.

On ultrasound, the lumps looked dark and solid, or speckled with bright flecks. Such lumps sit in odd places and look much like harmless growths, which can fool both doctors and scan readers. The authors warn clinicians to keep this tumor in mind when a child's surface lump has an odd look or spot.
pmc-10712679:
Gang Guo and co-authors evaluate an electronic directly observed therapy system for lung tuberculosis in Xinjiang, China. Patients must take antibiotics for six months without gaps. Watching each dose in person is costly across wide rural areas.

The system joins smart medicine boxes, mobile phones, and a central platform. Patients from villages and a city joined the study. Some used standard observed therapy, and others used the electronic system. Chest X-ray scores and adherence rates judged the system. Village patients on the electronic system adhered far better. City results added a second test of the approach. The findings support digital tools for long drug courses. They may help cut relapse and drug resistance.
pmc-10712879:
Rameeza Rashed and co-authors set out the plan for a systematic review asking which physical tests can foretell how well people with low back pain will do. Back pain is very common and often limits what people can do. If plain tests of how the body works can foretell who gets better, care teams could tailor plans early instead of guessing.

No past work had pulled together such tests as prognostic factors. The review is logged in a world-wide register kept for such reviews ahead of time. It will search past studies, judge how sound each one is, and pool what they find. The tests cover walking speed, how much weight a person can lift, and how long the trunk muscles can hold out. A plan set out in advance keeps the review honest and lets others check it. Care teams await its results.
pmc-10713279:
Bernauer and co-authors describe in 2023 a fast, low cost way to raise antibodies in mice without first purifying the target protein. Antibodies are key tools for research and new drugs, and pure protein shots are the standard route. That route is slow when antibodies are needed in a hurry.

Their method shows the target on the surface of human cells, held by a cell anchor system. Shots of those cells raised antibodies against a range of proteins. A key target was the binding part of the virus that causes COVID-19. The approach could speed early steps in making new antibody drugs.
pmc-10713579:
Qian Shen and co-authors describe a surface wave that carries terahertz signals in one direction only, with an unusually large field area, in work published in 2023. One-way surface waves on magnetic materials draw much interest, and some dispute, because stray effects can leak the signal. The team builds a layered stack: metal, a near-zero material, silicon, and the compound InSb, under an external magnetic field.

The wave's field spreads almost evenly through the thick middle layer, so that layer's thickness sets the wave's size. Because most of the energy sits in that layer, leakage from stray effects drops by about a factor of ten compared with older designs. The wave can be launched by terahertz beams from open space. The authors also show uses such as squeezing and trapping wave energy, and build a free-space isolator for terahertz signals.
pmc-10713679:
Dong Lin and co-authors published this 2023 lab study on weak rock layers found under deep water. Such layers are loose, mixed, and prone to collapse, which makes drilling risky. Crews need to learn the rock's traits without hauling up endless samples. Sound speed through the rock may offer a shortcut, so the team tested how it links to other traits.

They made model rock samples and varied sound pitch, density, grain size, and strength. Sound speed rose in a straight line with pitch and with crushing strength. It fell as grain size and pore space grew, and rose with density in a curved pattern. Sample height also mattered, since tall cores slowed the wave a bit. The links let crews read rock traits from sound checks.
pmc-10713979:
Wu leads a team studying a DNA-damage gene, CHEK2, as a prognostic marker in clear cell kidney cancer in a 2023 paper. The gene helps cells respond to genetic damage and is tied to several cancers. Its role in this kidney cancer was murky.

Tumor data from a major cancer atlas were mined for expression and outcome patterns. CHEK2 levels predicted survival on their own, beyond other factors. Enrichment analysis tied the gene to immune-related processes. Immune cell infiltration in tumors tracked with its expression. High levels also linked to resistance against some targeted drugs. The authors propose CHEK2 as a biomarker for prognosis and immune status. More work is needed before clinical use.
pmc-10714479:
Vadood Javadi and four co-authors studied web searches in Iran in a 2023 paper. They tracked how often people searched Google for a rare illness that causes rash and internal bleeding in children. Search habits can mirror real health concerns in a community, so the team treated them as a signal worth reading.

Using a trends tool, they gathered over a decade of search data for the illness and its symptoms. Searches peaked in winter and fell in summer, matching the known seasonal pattern of the illness. Searches also rose and fell with terms for joint pain, vomiting, swelling, and seizures. The authors say such data can hint at outbreaks in Iran.
pmc-10714679:
Hui-Ying Sun and four co-workers wrote a 2023 study on a parasite worm that causes schistosomiasis. Two worm groups in China shed their young at distinct times of day. Each timing suits its local host. The team read the full genomes of both groups to find the genetic base of that split.

Samples came from a hilly site and a marsh site in Anhui. The two groups showed clear genetic distance. Far more genome parts showed signs of selection in the marsh group than in the hill group. A small set of enriched genes stood out in the hill group, tied to DNA binding and cell signals. Some may relate to its late-day shedding.
pmc-10715979: Tamara Kubba and co-authors describe the care of a pregnant woman who fled war in Ukraine. She had a severely narrowed heart valve, a known fault that made pregnancy high risk. She reached the United Kingdom at thirty-two weeks of pregnancy. She spoke little English at the time. She needed urgent joint care from heart, birth, and newborn teams. That care covered late pregnancy, the birth, and the weeks after.
pmc-10716079:
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a fatal muscle wasting disease of boys, in which strength drains away year by year. Victoria Brown and co-authors interviewed forty-six patient and caregiver pairs to hear how the disease is lived daily. The patients, aged four to twenty-two, included those still walking and those no longer walking. Hour long video interviews were analyzed for themes, and the team compared experiences across the walking divide.

Loss of strength and fatigue topped the symptom lists in both groups. Physical function was the hardest hit area of life: climbing stairs, running, writing, buttoning clothes, and getting up from the floor all faded as the disease advanced. For those no longer walking, transfers and daily care tasks dominated. Families shared what they hope future treatments will do. The authors offer the accounts as ground truth for judging what new therapies must improve.
pmc-10716179:
Muddy coasts feed people, shelter wildlife, and blunt the sea's attack on land. Yet nobody had mapped them worldwide or tracked how they change. Romy Hulskamp and co-authors train an automated classifier on satellite imagery and coastal datasets. It learns to pick muddy shores out of the planet's coastline.

The census finds that about fourteen percent of the world's ice-free coastline is muddy. Sixty percent of that lies in the tropics. More sobering, most muddy coasts are eroding. Many have retreated faster than a meter per year over the last three decades. Sea level rise and human pressure will squeeze these zones further. A global baseline like this one gives coastal managers the map they need to defend them.
pmc-10716379:
Sandra Montaño-Salazar, Elena Quintanilla, and Juan Sánchez track how the microbe mix on a sea fan coral shifts with warm and cold ocean phases, in a study from 2023. The coral lives near Malpelo, a remote island in the eastern Pacific with little direct human impact. Its microbes can signal how the host copes with stress.

Samples came from 2015, 2017, and 2018, spanning phases of the El Niño cycle. Warm and cool phases held similar microbe mixes, while the neutral phase stood apart. Shifts in core members such as Endozoicomonas and Mycoplasma drove the pattern. The authors read this as the coral and its microbes adjusting as one unit, keeping the host viable under heat and cold alike.
pmc-10716479:
Ting Fan and co-authors review the state of therapeutic cancer vaccines, in a 2023 paper. Unlike preventive shots, these vaccines treat an existing cancer by teaching the immune system to attack it. They aim to raise fresh T cells that target markers found on tumour cells. Other immune treatments have already changed cancer care, and vaccines could widen the army of tumour-fighting cells a patient can call on.

The review covers how vaccine targets are picked, how they are delivered into the body, and how the dose is presented so the immune system notices. It then surveys clinical trials, judging how strongly the vaccines stirred immune responses and shrank tumours. Results so far have fallen short of a breakthrough. The authors close by weighing the main hurdles and the paths most likely to clear them.
pmc-10717379:
Daisy Massey and co-authors survey how common COVID-19 and long COVID were among United States college athletes from spring 2020 to fall 2021, in work from 2023. Lasting symptoms after infection have been reported in young, healthy people. Their rate in student athletes had not been pinned down.

The team surveyed administrators at eighteen colleges, covering about seven thousand athletes. Most schools replied for each term in the span. The survey asked how many athletes tested positive, how many had symptoms, and how many developed long COVID. It also asked how many did not return to their sport. The results give a first broad estimate for this group.
pmc-10717979:
Dan Liang, Chang Liu, and Mei Yang ask whether belly fat predicts kidney stones in United States adults. Their 2023 study uses national survey data from 2007 to 2014, covering 9,886 people. A visceral adiposity index, built from waist size, body mass index, and two blood fat measures, stands in for deep belly fat.

Stones were reported by 9.24 percent of participants, and about 3 percent had suffered them again. Both rates climbed steadily as the fat index rose. People in the top quarter of the index faced roughly half again the risk of stones compared with the bottom quarter. The link held across age, sex, and other subgroups. The authors suggest that trimming deep belly fat may help prevent stones and their return.
pmc-10719279:
Guy Fincham, Clara Strauss, and Kate Cavanagh run a careful trial of slow breathing for mental health in this 2023 paper. Breathwork is widely promoted as a simple stress tool. Their trial, the largest of its kind, tested breathing at about five and a half breaths per minute against a matched placebo pace of twelve.

Four hundred volunteers practiced about ten minutes a day for four weeks, without knowing which pace they had drawn. Stress, anxiety, depression, and wellbeing all improved over the study in both groups. Yet the slow-breathing group gained no more than the placebo group on any measure, right after the course or a month later. Expectations of benefit were equal, so the tie cannot be put down to weaker belief. The authors found no added effect from the slow pace itself. They close with advice on designing tougher breathwork studies.
pmc-10720179:
Scalas, Lodi, Magnano, and Marsh test an Italian version of the Well-being Profile, a scale that scores many sides of well-being. Their study is from two thousand twenty-three. The scale covers both feeling good and living with purpose. It can be used for one person or for groups.

The Italian form was built by back-translation, then given to more than fourteen hundred adults. Tests kept the scale's fifteen-factor shape. That shape held across sex, age, and schooling. The authors also checked how the scale relates to other measures and tried short forms. They note that a few items on clear thinking could be worded better. Still, they back the scale for study and for work with clients.
pmc-10720279:
Mykola Zhovmir and co-authors (2023) study whether straw can be cleaned up enough to serve as fuel pellets. Straw is abundant, but burning it in stoves is limited by rules on ash, chlorine, nitrogen, sulfur, and heavy metals, plus the need for ash that does not melt easily. Washing the straw, a process called leaching, can remove the chlorine and salts. Earlier studies, though, did not check when the chlorine had finished washing out.

The team soaked straw with heating to 100 degrees and rinsed it in a flowing stream, testing the runoff until no chlorine remained. They measured ash, chlorine, nitrogen, sulfur, and metals in raw and washed straw, and how the ash behaves when heated, including the temperature at which it deforms. Comparing both versions against the pellet specification shows what leaching buys. The study gives pellet makers a verified endpoint for washing, rather than a guess.
pmc-10720679:
Ferdinando D'Amico and co-authors argue for a deeper treatment target in Crohn's disease in a 2023 review. Crohn's damages the full bowel wall, not just its lining. Goals have already moved from symptom relief to healing of the lining seen on scope exams. The authors push one step further: transmural remission, healing through the whole wall, judged by bowel ultrasound or MRI.

An expert group has proposed a working definition based on wall thickness and blood flow signals. Reaching that state is hard: at best half of patients get there, even on advanced drugs. A recent study they discuss used a tight-control strategy, watching a stool marker and raising treatment when it stirred. That approach lifted transmural remission rates, most of all in early disease. The authors present tight control as the future path. They call for shared definitions and trials to settle the target.
pmc-10720779:
Kang Xue and co-authors published a pooled analysis in 2023 on pancreas surgery with artery resection for advanced pancreatic cancer after prior treatment. This cancer often wraps around major arteries, blocking full removal. Pre-surgery therapy can shrink tumors, but guidance on then cutting arteries was scarce. The team searched major databases for studies of this combined path.

Nine studies with just over two hundred patients met their rules. Complication rates were high, at about half of patients, while death rates were low. Clear-margin removal was reached in most cases, and more often than without prior therapy in comparisons. Survival data varied widely. The authors see promise but call for prospective controlled studies.
pmc-10722379:
Heather McCormack and co-authors test in 2023 whether tweaks to a clinic's computer system can lift testing for sexually transmitted infections among young Aboriginal patients in Australia. The work sat in a health service run by the Aboriginal community in New South Wales, during a syphilis outbreak in nearby states. Young people aged 15 to 29 were the focus.

The change had several parts. The record system prompted staff and grouped the right lab tests in yearly health checks. Nurses and Aboriginal health workers were also cleared to run the tests on their own. The team used mixed methods to judge whether testing rose and whether staff found the new setup acceptable. System tweaks like these can lift screening without new buildings or large budgets.
pmc-10723579:
Deborah Cristine Bonetti Rosa and co-authors test a training course that helps university students speak better in class presentations, in a 2023 paper. The course mixed social skills, voice projection methods, and mindset coaching. Thirty-eight students took part at their university, learning through active exercises rather than lectures. Each student recorded a short talk on a topic of choice before the course and again after it.

Classmates and a panel of three judges, two speech therapists and a psychologist, scored the talks. Students also rated themselves. The scorecard covered word choice, formality, body language, planning, and emotional control. Every participant improved after training, the authors report, across speaking style, audience hold, and composure. The results back short, structured voice courses as a cheap way to raise students' presentation skills.
pmc-10725079:
Francisco Muñoz-Vela and eight co-authors answer critics of their study on anxiety in pregnant women during COVID in a 2023 response letter. Their survey had measured fear and anxiety among expectant mothers in Spain. Readers praised parts of the work and pressed on its limits.

The authors concede the main points and explain their choices. Online forms, unsupervised, may have bought honesty at the price of control. Sampling only certain Spanish locations narrows how far results stretch, and they accept the call for broader reach. The exchange, framed by their aim of improving pregnant women's quality of life, maps how the research line should grow next.
pmc-10725679:
Wenfeng Xu, Hao Tang, Ying Chen, and four colleagues report a four-year wrong diagnosis in this two thousand twenty-three case report. A sixty-five-year-old man carried a stomach tumor diagnosed as adenocarcinoma and received chemotherapy combined with PD-L1 immunotherapy. Doctors believed it worked, yet the tumor never shrank and his symptoms never truly improved. A repeat biopsy at the authors' hospital, checked by form, markers, and genome sequencing, gave a different answer: an epithelioid gut stromal tumor.

Epithelioid stromal tumors make up about twenty percent of these tumors and mimic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma and lymphoma under the microscope, a known diagnostic trap. The authors draw two lessons. Tissue doctors should lean on site, form, and the right markers for this tumor family. Clinicians should judge response by symptoms and lab proof rather than trusting a tissue label too far.
pmc-10726079:
Gauri Pande and Jayant Vagha review bleeding inside the brains of babies born too early, in a 2023 paper. The bleeding starts in a fragile growth zone of the preterm brain and breaks into the fluid-filled chambers. The zone's vessels are immature and dense, and the baby's brain lacks supporting cells and proteins, so bleeds happen easily. Early birth itself may follow infections in the womb or emergencies such as dangerous blood pressure in the mother.

Doctors grade the bleeds from one to four using head ultrasound and MRI scans. Care ranges from drugs that calm seizures to surgical washing procedures that drain and rinse the chambers. The harms can last for life: cerebral palsy and learning disability are among the outcomes the review catalogs. Prevention starts before birth, with treating infections and giving steroids that mature the baby's organs ahead of an early delivery.
pmc-10730979:
Rui-Lian Ding, Yu Zheng, and Jin Bu explore, in a 2023 study, why psoriasis and bowel inflammation so often occur in the same person. The two diseases are linked both ways, and that link shapes how doctors treat patients. The team hunted for shared gene markers that could explain the overlap and guide screening.

Working from public gene data sets, they found 271 genes that change in both diseases. Tests on those genes pointed to responses to bacterial products and cell signals. They built a gene network, picked hub genes, and narrowed them to a small marker set. A screening model based on those markers sorted patients from healthy controls well, and the markers also tied to patterns of immune cells in tissue.
pmc-10731279:
Qiuping Jin and Kun Yu adapt a scale for success in moving from university to work for Chinese graduates in 2023. No full measure of that shift fit many settings. Three studies tested the adapted scale. The scale holds twenty four items in four parts. They cover career joy, income freedom, faith in the future, and fit at work.

The four part shape matched the source scale. Scores tied in expected ways to career adaptability and adult identity. The scale also added forecast power beyond adaptability alone. Men and women read the items the same way. The authors back the scale for research and practice in China. It gives the school to work shift a shared yardstick.
pmc-10731479:
Alaa Youssef and co-authors explore what makes health organizations willing to share clinical data for artificial intelligence, in a 2023 study. AI tools can only be as fair as the data behind them. When shared data miss whole patient groups, the tools fail those groups. Readiness to share varies across sectors.

The team ran twenty-seven interviews with leaders in sharing roles. Cases spanned academic, government, nonprofit, and private groups. Talks probed motives, fears, and practical barriers. The study maps the factors that push an organization toward or away from sharing. Wiser sharing policies could widen the data pool and make medical AI safer for everyone.
pmc-10735379:
Lisa Hollis-Sawyer and Laura Donorfio sum up a set of talks on learning across the ages in a 2023 paper. The talks share class designs that mix older and younger learners so each side gains, in a spirit of age fairness.

One talk used joint talks in class to spur shared learning among older adults, students, and teachers. A course in Scotland took the theme abroad. A third program paired young and old online to make art and to break down clichés of age. A fourth brought retired staff into a first course on aging. The last set out rules for class design that serves all ages. The roundup frames such mixes as a boost to learning that lasts a whole life.
pmc-10735479:
Patricia D'Antonio and co-authors frame a session on policy language for aging services in this 2023 piece. The Older Americans Act has funded community social services since 1965. Its reauthorization was due in 2024, and word choice can sway that debate.

The session is led by national centers that study how to reframe aging. Speakers use the Act as a live case for communication strategy. The Act backs a network of state and area agencies plus thousands of providers and tribal groups. Framing tools aim to tell a fairer story of aging in America. Attendees learn to apply those tools to their own advocacy writing.
pmc-10735679:
Karon Phillips and Megan Wolfe describe age-friendly public health systems in action in a 2023 symposium paper. Trust for America's Health leads a national movement to make healthy aging a core job of state and local health departments. Public health helped add years to American lives, and the movement asks it to improve those years too.

The organization has worked directly with health departments to test its framework. That work produced first-hand lessons on policy and systems change. The paper shares what departments actually did, offering a model for aging work shared across health care and aging services.
pmc-10735779:
Lynn Snow and seven co-authors describe a sleep program for nursing home residents with dementia, run during the pandemic, in this 2023 paper. Poor sleep harms residents, but trials in care homes often collapse under staff load. The team worked with three nursing home firms to shrink every step of a planned trial into small bites.

Trainings became five-minute sessions. Site visits went virtual, with thirty-minute weekly calls. Forms were streamlined so floor staff could keep up amid shortages and rising resident needs. The team tracked every change with a standard reporting frame and coded interviews with site leaders. The trimmed package proved workable, acceptable, and durable in all three firms. The authors suggest the small-bites craft may serve the wider nursing home research field, pandemic or not.
pmc-10735879:
Oluwaseun Adeyemi, Mauricio Arcila-Mesa, Crystalinda Rapozo, and Joshua Chodosh study diabetes medication de-escalation in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Their patients were older adults living with both diabetes and dementia. When such patients have low blood sugar control values, they risk harm from drugs that push levels lower still. The data came from a multicenter cluster-randomized trial in primary care.

The team checked whether reducing antihyperglycemic medication over twenty-four months helped patients reach a desired, safer hemoglobin A1c range. Only about a tenth of the population had medications de-escalated, and about a fifth reached the desired range. After adjustment, de-escalation was linked with roughly double the likelihood of attaining the target range. Metformin was the drug most often kept after other medications were cut.
pmc-10735979:
Torres reviews in twenty twenty-three how research on ageing handles racism for older migrants and racialised minorities. Two broad reviews frame the piece: one on minority ageing studies, the other on three decades of work on older migrants. The older field, she notes, often sorts people by race while barely naming racism, and dwells on inequality without asking about justice.

Migration scholars centre being a migrant instead, yet even they seldom study lived experiences of racism directly. The migrant review found recognition that oppression may shape later life, but few studies that actually traced it. Torres argues the blind spot blocks understanding of how race, ethnicity, and migrant status, alone and combined, shape old age.
pmc-10736079:
Atami De Main and co-authors measure social engagement among older people living with HIV in a 2023 study. Over half of Americans with HIV are now over fifty, often juggling chronic illness and fragile support networks. Social activity guards health, yet little was known about what drives it in this group.

The study surveyed 349 New Yorkers aged fifty to eighty-four with a thirteen-item leisure scale. Media-based pastimes scored highest, while social and cultural-physical outings lagged. An AIDS diagnosis, stigma, loneliness, and depression all tracked with lower social engagement. Neighborhood vulnerability and money strain cut cultural outings, and depression alone cut media activity. The authors say the patterns map where support programs should aim.
pmc-10736279:
Bryce Van Vleet and co-authors use a poetry method to explore why some older adults hesitate over vaccines, in a 2023 study. Older adults in the United States vaccinate at higher rates than younger groups, yet many stay under-vaccinated for flu, shingles, pneumonia, and COVID-19. Eight hesitant adults in North Dakota were drawn from a larger interview study.

Each person answered how they decide on a given vaccine. Their I-statements were woven into a shared poem, sorted into stanzas by theme. Themes covered practical barriers such as allergies and side effect fears, faith in natural immunity and healthy habits, and distrust of agencies and of vaccine power. The authors say first-person verse can help clinicians grasp patient unease.
pmc-10736379:
Joshua Novak led this two thousand twenty-three methods session on matching research questions about pairs of people with the right statistical models. Dyadic data, collected from two linked individuals, raises special questions about shared experience. Newer dyadic methods let researchers ask more kinds of questions than before. The session targets researchers writing grants, planning data collection, or reusing existing datasets.

Novak walks through several named models, including the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model, the Common Fate Model, and dyadic growth curve approaches. He covers how to handle the statistical non-independence between partners. The session also addresses comparing self and partner reports of the same trait, such as health agreement or disagreement. Attendees leave with pointers to resources for learning each method in depth.
pmc-10736679:
Veronica Garcia Walker interviews women aging with schizophrenia to learn how they see healthy aging across their lives. Severe mental illness can shorten life and add health burdens, yet older women's own views are rarely heard. She spoke with a small group of women repeatedly over about a year.

Four themes stood out. Women felt aging had made functioning worse, said they need medicines and care to live healthier, voiced fear of dying, and wondered who would help them as they grow old. Walker argues that care for this group needs experts who communicate well, act genuinely, and earn trust, so women can live long lives with good quality.
pmc-10736879:
Deborah Ejem tested a web program that helps older adults name their care goals in a solo 2023 paper. The group in focus is older African Americans in the Deep South with many chronic ills. They get early comfort focused care less often than peers, in part since care teams rarely draw out their own values in a way that fits their culture.

Twenty patient and caregiver pairs from one clinic were being recruited to try the self guided program. Early pairs said the program helped them think and speak about their values. They also flagged gaps: too little content on faith, and a sample character they could not see themselves in. The finds will shape a pilot grant for a tuned version.
pmc-10737179:
Jeffrey Gregg, Rachel Rodriguez, Priyanka Mehta, Josea Kramer, and Christine Gould describe a personal learning plan program for psychologists who treat older veterans, in a 2023 paper. The psychologists belong to a national Veterans Affairs training track in geropsychology, serving rural elders with layered physical, mental, and cognitive illness. After an advanced workshop, each participant drafted an individual learning plan and carried it out over six months, with advice from a seasoned geropsychologist on call.

Fourteen of nineteen participants filed final reports and reflections. Every one of them found the plan useful, clinically or personally. Themes included new confidence, sharper skills for complex patients, and career movement. Most found the plans feasible and the resources easy to reach. About a third named real barriers, above all lack of time. The authors present the model as a light way to keep specialist growth going after formal training ends.
pmc-10737279:
Emily Kinkade and Heather Fuller follow widows and widowers over eight years to see whether social connection softens the blow. Losing a spouse is known to drag down body and mind, and support is thought to cushion the fall. Using five survey waves from 2013 to 2021 with about 245 older adults, the team modeled how well-being changed after widowhood at different levels of social integration.

Integration made a clear difference for mood. Widowed people whose social ties grew saw their depression scores fall faster than those of the still-married. It also protected daily physical functioning, as measured by basic self-care tasks. No such cushioning appeared for happiness or for the count of diseases. The authors conclude that staying woven into social life is one of the few levers that measurably eases the long adjustment to widowhood.
pmc-10737479:
A common belief in aging research says strength fades much faster than muscle itself. Peggy Cawthon and seven co-authors tested that belief in 220 men in their eighties, followed for about six years, in a 2023 study. Unlike older work that estimated muscle indirectly, they measured muscle mass directly with a labeled creatine drink, alongside grip strength, walking speed, and chair stands.

Muscle mass fell about 13 percent, close to grip strength's 15 percent loss, with walking speed down 18 percent. Yearly rates were similar across measures, and muscle loss tracked strength loss. The authors conclude shrinking muscle itself plays a bigger role in weakening than often assumed.
pmc-10737579:
David Reiter surveys MRI methods for measuring blood flow and tiny-vessel function in aging skeletal muscle, in a 2023 talk. Muscle oxygen use can rise fifty-fold from rest to heavy exercise. Even at rest, capillary flow shifts constantly under many controls. MRI offers several noninvasive ways to watch that flow. Each method carries distinct strengths and weaknesses.

The overview compares current and emerging techniques side by side. Aging and age-related disease studies anchor the examples. Perfusion measures may flag decline before strength is lost. Clinicians and physiologists share the audience. The talk format favors breadth over one experiment's depth. It maps a field that links imaging to healthy aging.
pmc-10737679:
Channing Tate wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on why older Black adults in the United States use hospice care less than others, even though hospice can help them. The paper tests a tool meant to close that gap.

Tate ran a small trial with Black adults aged sixty-five and over. Half received a hospice decision aid, a guide that explains hospice and helps people weigh choices. Half did not. The study tracked what people knew about hospice, how they felt about it, and how sure they felt making end-of-life choices. The group with the aid improved on all three measures over one month. The paper also reports that users found the aid clear and easy to use.
pmc-10737779:
Emma Baillargeon, Theodore Huppert, Caterina Rosano, and Andrea Rosso wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It studies brain activity in the front of the head while older adults walk, and how much that activity differs from person to person.

The team tested 173 adults aged sixty-five and over. A light-based brain scan measured activity while each person stood, walked, and walked while reciting every other letter of the alphabet. For about a third of the group, brain activity rose during walking. For others it fell or stayed flat. Those whose activity fell walked faster and ramped up activity more when the second task was added. The results show older walkers use their brains in quite different ways.
pmc-10737879:
Barbara Hanratty and Graciela Muniz-Terrera outline a symposium on inequalities in healthy ageing, asking which research approaches help policy most. Five studies take unlike routes to the same problem. They use frailty as a personal trait, polypharmacy as a care pattern, digital access to services, social care data, and evidence synthesis methods.

Talks cover digital exclusion during the coronavirus pandemic, links between social and economic measures and frailty-free life expectancy after fifty, and the effect of years of education on polypharmacy. One talk builds a framework so reviews weigh inequalities from the start. The closing talk compares the routes and asks how they can be joined for policy use.
pmc-10738179:
Zhou wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-three on how three cell systems age together: protein quality control, the lysosome, and the mitochondria. Loss of protein balance, failing mitochondria, and lysosome defects are classic marks of aging. Oddly, clumps of stray protein in aging cells attach to the mitochondrial surface.

The work traces that attachment to Tom70, a receptor that imports proteins into mitochondria. Tom70 also seeds the clumps, using fresh mitochondrial proteins as nuclei. Cells balance making and importing those proteins through a feedback path. Restoring Tom70 in old cells repaired mitochondrial protein building and even rescued lysosome function.
pmc-10738279:
Franziska Zuniga and co-authors studied in 2023 how a Swiss nursing home program worked in day-to-day care. The INTERCARE program had already cut unplanned hospital trips across eleven homes. Its six parts joined closer team work, a nurse with deep old-age training, full health checks, care plans made ahead, proven tools, and data-led quality work. The team read talks and notes from five homes to see which parts were used and how change came about.

Four change paths stood out, some by shifting how staff think, some by freeing tools already at hand. Staff reacted faster to shifts in a resident, checked more fully, and spoke with each other better. The team offers the map to tune the parts for wider roll-out.
pmc-10738479:
Kelly Brotherhood, Julia Newton, and co-authors map how old folks use social care in one English town zone from past files, in a 2023 study. Past files hold vast untapped clues on care paths and gaps. Files span four decades for tens of thousands of old folks in that zone.

Each folk had a mid count of care packs with short mid spans. Care came in homes, own houses, and aid flats, for rest or long terms. Paths end by death, home turns, or care shifts in most cases. Wide path range shows how split needs are in old age.
pmc-10738579:
Tam Perry, Janelle Taylor, and Yasir Mehmood study housing paths of older adults with dementia who have no close kin in a 2023 paper. Staying home or moving is a hard choice in aging. Dementia makes stating wishes harder, and a lack of spouse or children removes the usual helpers.

They followed 64 people in a long aging study who were kinless when dementia began, at a mean age of 87. Medical chart notes traced where each person lived over time. Themes showed housing weaving into health and social well-being at every step. The authors also argue that medical records, read with care, can reveal housing needs that surveys miss.
pmc-10738679:
Hyesu Yeo examines what jobs are actually available to older workers in one local market, in a study from 2023. Most past work looked at the workers themselves, their skills and choices. This study flips to the demand side: the postings employers offer.

Job ads from three search engines in late 2021 yielded over five thousand postings across hundreds of occupations. Health care, transport, and sales led the list, and most openings wanted some experience. Survey data showed the local older workforce leaned toward education, office, and sales roles, often with degrees. Every occupation asked for technology skills. The mismatch between open jobs and the older workforce is the core finding, with downward moves a real prospect for many.
pmc-10738779:
Terence Lau and Angela Leung review in 2023 how people with Parkinson ill feel about tech aids built for them. Such aids now span apps, wear gear, and home kits. Yet how users take to them, and what mind and social gain they feel, was not well summed.

The team kept a set of sound studies from six archives and wove their tales into themes. One theme ruled: how well a user copes with the aid. That coping hung on how at ease the user was with tech at the start. Well-run roll-outs did lift mind and social health. Aid makers gain a rule: train and back the user, not just ship the kit.
pmc-10738879:
Rhoodjinie Mentor and co-authors argue that nurses are the natural drivers of sensory stimulation for brain-injured patients who cannot respond, in a 2023 paper. Patients with disorders of consciousness sit in intensive care with little input to their senses, and older patients fare worst. Stimulation through touch, sight, sound, and smell aims to wake awareness by stirring brain activity.

Because nurses are at the bedside around the clock, they can tailor sessions to each patient's state and reactions. The paper gathers evidence-based strategies for neuro intensive care units, reviews what is known about nurses' attitudes, and lists workable interventions. The authors frame sensory care as nursing work that should be planned, not left to chance.
pmc-10739479:
Qiyu He and co-authors report a 2023 study of kidney harm after heart surgery done with a bypass pump. High blood sugar and high lactate during surgery are faults that staff can act on, yet their link to later kidney harm was unclear. The team checked records for more than four thousand adults.

About one in six patients developed kidney harm after surgery. Both high sugar and high lactate during the operation tied to a higher rate of that harm. The team ran many checks, from group splits to curve tests, to see how firm the link is and where it is strongest.
pmc-10741479:
Sumita Raha and three co-authors test the lipid-lowering drug gemfibrozil in a mouse model of Tay-Sachs disease, in work from 2024. The disease stems from loss of a lysosomal enzyme, which lets GM2 ganglioside build up in the brain. It brings motor trouble, loss of skills and early death, and it has no cure.

Oral gemfibrozil cut glial activation and inflammation, and lowered stored gangliosides in the motor cortex. Treated mice also behaved better and lived longer. The benefit vanished in mice that also lacked the receptor PPAR-alpha, whose brain levels the drug raised. The authors present a receptor-dependent path that may slow the disease.
pmc-10741979:
A brain chemical receptor that helps set blood pressure may be blunted by the same peptide that builds up in Alzheimer's disease. The authors test that link in rats in this 2023 study, watching pressure jumps triggered by NMDA, a receptor activator, in a brainstem control center. One amyloid form, Aβ1-40, was washed into the brain's fluid spaces at two doses.

The higher dose clearly shrank the pressure response within ten minutes; the related Aβ1-42 form did nothing. Two blocker drugs prevented the effect, and a phosphate tag on one receptor part rose in step. The Aβ1-40 also lingered longer in the fluid than its sibling. The findings hint that amyloid may disturb pressure control early in disease.
pmc-10742879:
Roya Binaymotlagh and co-authors build a gel that holds tiny titania particles, in a research paper from 2023. Titania can kill germs when light hits it, but loose particles are hard to keep in place. The team traps them in a soft gel made from a short peptide, which is a small chain that sets on its own.

Tests show the gel gets stiffer and swells less when more particles are added. The mix killed lab Staphylococcus aureus and two drug-proof strains from patients. Light boosted the effect. The work points to wound covers or coatings that fight germs with the help of light.
pmc-10743279:
Chenyu Liang, Lei Shi, Baocheng Li, and Zhiyu He ask how muscle loss links activity and falls in older Chinese adults in this 2023 study. Low activity and weak muscles both raise fall risk. The chain between the three was not clear in this group.

The team drew on a national aging survey with 3,592 adults aged 60 and over who live at home. Activity came from a standard survey form. Muscle loss was judged by grip strength, body performance, and muscle mass. Their study tests whether muscle loss sits in the middle of the path from low activity to falls.
pmc-10743679:
Alessandro Nani and co-authors tested a supplement mix in 2023 for people with type 2 diabetes, with the catalog adding one author absent from the head byline. Seventy-five patients took either the mix, two forms of inositol plus a milk protein, a plant extract, and zinc, or placebo. Blood sugar and fat profiles were tracked.

Sugar measures did not differ between groups. After three months, total cholesterol and the harmful LDL fraction fell in the supplement group. Among patients whose diabetes drugs stayed unchanged, those gaps persisted at six months, with extra weight loss at three months. Within the supplement group, protective HDL and triglycerides also improved. The mix looks a safe add-on for lipid control.
pmc-10743779:
Zota and a large team review how cuff based training affects the stiffness of arteries in twenty twenty-three. The training ties a strap or cuff on a limb to cut blood flow during exercise. It builds muscle even at light loads, which suits older or untrained people. Stiff arteries, though, are a known risk sign for heart disease.

The review weighs short and long term studies of vessel health. Brief spikes in stiffness and blood pressure show up right after sessions. Long term effects look mild or neutral so far. The authors urge care with older patients and those with high blood pressure. Longer studies are needed to judge lasting risk.
pmc-10743979:
Wenqiang Xin and nine co-authors studied a growth factor in two thousand twenty-three that calms brain immune cells in a lab model of stroke. When oxygen and glucose run out, microglia, the brain's immune cells, flare up and load with fat droplets. How those two responses interact was poorly understood, and the factor TGF-beta1 sits at their crossroads.

Raising the factor suppressed inflammation and cut fat droplets in microglia hit by an inflammatory trigger. Blocking it did the reverse under oxygen-glucose deprivation. A drug that stops droplet formation also pushed microglia toward a calm state. In co-culture, tuning either lever changed how well neurons survived beside the microglia.
pmc-10744279:
Allysa Dijkstra and co-authors told in 2023 of a boy whose newborn screen missed a grave liver disease. The disease, tyrosinemia type 1, poisons the liver when a food protein is broken down. A waste mark in blood is the screen's flag, and it was long held to rise in all cases. The boy's screen at birth read just below the Dutch cut line. At age nine he came in with liver cancer in a scarred liver, and tests then found the disease.

The team knows of no past false miss of this kind on that mark. Mild forms of the disease may shed less of the mark and slip the screen in any land, they warn. They urge doctors to weigh the disease in odd liver cases and lands to re-check their cut lines.
pmc-10744579:
Huan Wang and co-authors made, in 2023, a sacrificial agent that keeps concrete loose when clay is in the mix. The flow aid here is a superplasticizer, known as PCE. Left alone, the PCE soaks into clay in place of cement grains. The paste then loses its help to stay loose. The new agent is built from maltitol, a sugar alcohol. It soaks into the clay first, in place of the PCE.

With the agent in, the paste flowed about 19% more freely at the start. Tests of charge and of form show how it works. The agent sticks to the clay by electrostatic attraction. It does not go into the clay or puff up its layers. With the clay blocked in this way, the PCE stays free. It coats the cement grains as it should, and the clay mix can be worked with ease once more.
pmc-10744779:
Shanmugam Muthu and co-authors speed up the growth of oxide layers on nuclear fuel tubes in 2023, using team framing since the head byline is shorter than the catalog list. The tubes sheath fuel in a Canadian reactor type. Dry storage safety checks need tubes with a set oxide depth. Normal growth takes years in reactor like water. Their method cuts that wait.

Three steps build the layer. Hot pressurized water corrodes the tube first. Air baking follows at high heat. A second hot water step tops the layer to target depth. Checks with X-rays and microscopes show the layer matches normal ones in shape and phase. The shortcut can supply test tubes for storage studies.
pmc-10744879:
Iacopo Franconi and Antonella Lupetti review lab tests that go beyond the standard drug threshold for Candida fungi in a 2023 paper. Resistance to the main antifungal families is climbing worldwide, and invasive infections grow harder to cure. The minimum inhibitory concentration still anchors management, but it tells only part of the story.

Other bench tests measure whether a drug actually kills the fungus and whether the fungus merely tolerates it, waiting out treatment. Such tests live mostly in research labs today. The authors argue they could add real value in resistant, hard-to-treat cases, sharpening drug choice and dosing. Bringing them into routine practice is the review's plea.
pmc-10745079:
Soeren Buchholz and co-authors report one center's experience using gene tests to find a drug target in advanced colon cancer, in this 2023 paper. The gene, ERBB2, also known as HER2, drives growth in some tumors and is already targeted in breast and stomach cancer. In spread colon cancer it is altered in about three to five percent of patients, with no approved therapy yet. The center screened 107 patients from 2019 to 2022.

Four patients carried usable ERBB2 changes, and stain tests agreed with the gene results. Two received a targeted antibody-drug, trastuzumab-deruxtecan, after heavy prior treatment. The paper presents two of the cases in detail to show the drug's effect. The authors press for early gene profiling so targeted therapy can start sooner.
pmc-10746079:
Maria Peres and co-authors review trial evidence from 2023 on diets built around foods that raise blood sugar slowly. Such low glycemic diets are often advised for people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes. The team searched for trials from the past ten years. They wanted to see what health effects the evidence actually supports across many outcomes.

The review covers 14 trials with just over one thousand people, most of them middle aged adults with type 2 diabetes. The diets helped short term blood sugar control, weight, and body fat. Effects on blood fats were mixed, while some trials also found gains in blood pressure, markers of swelling in the body, kidney function, and gut microbes. The authors call for longer trials to test whether the gains last.
pmc-10746479:
Amir Hussain and co-authors built decision tools in 2023 for group choices under deep uncertainty, and applied them to medical diagnosis. Their data values blend two fuzzy frameworks with a flexible family of averaging rules named for Aczel and Alsina. Fusing opinions from several experts is the core problem.

Three weighted averaging operators were defined for these blended values, in plain, ordered, and hybrid forms, and their basic properties were proven. The operators then drove a multi-attribute group decision procedure. Results were checked across the rule family's parameter range and compared with existing methods. The authors argue the added flexibility helps when expert judgements are rough and conflicting, as in diagnosis panels.
pmc-10747079:
Teerapong Lertassavakorn and six co-authors validate a lab method for measuring two industrial chemicals in human blood in a 2023 study. The chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, belong to a long-lasting family used in coatings and foams. Data on levels in the Thai population were missing, so a trusted test had to come first.

Their method uses a simple protein clean-up step and a sensitive mass-based detector, checked against international guidance for accuracy and repeatability. They then tested plasma from fifty Thai Red Cross blood donors. Levels of both chemicals were lower than those reported in many other countries. The split between straight and branched forms of PFOS was also recorded, giving Thailand a baseline for tracking exposure.
pmc-10747279:
Fitri Lestari and co-authors published a review in 2023 on nanohydrogels as carriers that improve the solubility and activity of natural products. Natural compounds, especially from plants, show pharmacological activity, and herbal medicine is widely used because it is seen as safer and cheaper. Yet many such compounds dissolve poorly, are unstable, have low bioavailability, and degrade quickly. Those defects limit their therapeutic use.

Nanohydrogel is a tiny water-swollen network that can carry cargo. As a delivery system, it increases a compound's solubility, activity, and bioavailability. It also improves stability and distribution in the body, reduces toxicity, slows release, and protects the cargo from degradation. The review examines twenty-five plant-derived compounds that were encapsulated in nanohydrogel. In each case, solubility and therapeutic activity improved over the plain compound. The authors also discuss remaining challenges for plant-based nanohydrogels.
pmc-10747979:
Hu leads a team testing fertilizer mixes that keep rapeseed yields high with less nitrogen in a 2023 field study. Blending slow-release nitrogen with ordinary fast nitrogen is the strategy. Trials used direct-seeded rapeseed at a reduced total rate.

Mid-range blends, with slow-release making up roughly a third to a half of the mix, matched the full-rate control for pods, seeds, and yield. Nitrogen use efficiency peaked at the middle blend. Soil enzyme activity and microbial biomass also rose under the blends, above all at flowering. Soil nitrogen stayed available for key growth stages. The authors recommend the middle blends under a quarter cut in nitrogen. The approach promises savings without yield loss.
pmc-10748079:
Breast cancer needs new weapons, and Eid Salama and co-authors forged a family of them from an indole starting material. Reacting it with several nitrogen partners produced six new compounds, whose structures were pinned down by spectroscopy and X-ray crystallography. Cell tests against a standard breast cancer line found three standouts, each killing cancer cells at lower doses than the reference drug.

The best compound also slowed cell migration, pushed nearly forty percent of treated cells into programmed death, and blocked a panel of growth-driving kinases. In mice, it cut tumour volume almost in half. The authors put the family forward as leads worth developing, with the champion compound first in line.
pmc-10748179:
Tomoya Okada and three co-authors studied the structure of comb-shaped polymers with crystallizing side chains, in a 2023 paper. Such polymers have many uses, and their heat traits depend on crystal forms. The team varied how many side chains could crystallize. They probed structure from atomic to visible scales.

Heat tests showed melting energy rose in a straight line with the crystallizable share. X-ray checks found a six-sided crystal layout. Rich samples formed ball-like structures with radiating lines. Lean samples showed no such large-scale forms. Small-angle X-ray work caught layered crystals in rich samples and small crystals in lean ones. Above a transition heat, density ripples from correlation effects appeared. The authors conclude the side-chain share strongly steers structure at every scale.
pmc-10748279:
Hong Liu and Chuansheng Wang present a 2023 study of die metals for rubber extrusion. Extruder heads shape hot rubber into final forms, and long runs wear them down, which hurts product quality. The team sought a head metal that lasts while it leaves the rubber at its best.

They rubbed a common rubber mix against four candidate metals and scored the rubber after each test. One nickel alloy head left the rubber with the best spread of fillers and top tear strength. It also gave the lowest rolling drag and strong wet grip. The other three metals each cost the rubber more in spread, drag, or wear. Picking the right head metal, the authors say, lifts rubber quality and head life.
pmc-10748479:
Marcos Herrera and co-authors dissect, turn by turn, a breakthrough moment in a psychoanalytic therapy session in Peru, in a study from 2023. Therapy lore credits insight from interpretations, but newer theory honors moments of meeting, brief encounters that remake the relationship itself. The team applied conversation analysis to the final session of a brief therapy with a woman who had survived domestic violence.

A challenge moment arose when the client, long passive, stepped forward to animate the dialogue herself. The therapist's response ratified her move, and for a moment a new way of relating stood in the room. The authors call the shared practice co-animation. They argue that such change is built sequentially, in talk and timing, not delivered by one side.
pmc-10749479:
Acid in the air may change how clouds form, since tiny droplets freeze differently as their acidity shifts. Ziying Lei, Bo Chen, and Sarah Brooks tested that link in lab droplets in this 2023 study. The droplets mixed salts and organic matter like those found in real air particles. The team paired a freezing test rig with a laser method that reads a droplet's chemistry.

Across a wide acidity range, some mixes froze the same way throughout, by a uniform path. Other mixes split into a core and a shell, and freezing started in the core by a surface-led path. Stronger acidity weakened the droplets' power to start ice. Shifts in the salt's chemical form tracked the change. Cloud models may need that acidity effect to get high cloud ice right.
pmc-10750079:
Zixi Liu and five colleagues track how the eco-health of the Yangtze River Basin changed over twenty years, in a twenty twenty-three study. The basin is a key zone for both nature and growth in China. Using satellite data and a remote sensing eco index on a cloud platform, the team mapped quality across the whole basin from two thousand to twenty twenty. They also tested which forces drove the changes.

Overall quality sat at a good grade and rose over the period. Good areas clustered in parts of two sub-basins, while the upper reaches clustered low. Human action mattered more than any single natural factor. The strongest driver was the blend of species richness with population density. The results guide where protection work should focus.
pmc-10750379:
Ruth Ayaß links conversation analysis with genre theory to explain set forms of talk, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Conversation study began in the nineteen sixties with fine study of talk turns, gaze, and body use. Genre theory treats set talk forms as shared fixes for shared talk problems.

Three genre families carry the argument. One covers talk about the past, one covers moral talk about others, and one covers talk about the future. Each family is shown at work in real studies, with the problem it solves made clear. Readers gain a bridge from close talk study to broader social questions in sociology.
pmc-10751079:
A 2023 drug appraisal weighs tirzepatide for adults with type 2 diabetes that diet and exercise alone do not tame. The drug, sold as Mounjaro, is a weekly shot under the skin. It fires two gut hormone switches at once, both of which lower blood sugar and curb hunger.

Approval rests on five large trials that set the shot against a dummy or a rival drug, alone or added to standard pills. At each of three upkeep doses, sugar control fell by more than in the match groups. The piece sets out when the drug fits: alone when the standard first pill cannot be taken, or stacked with it.
pmc-10751179:
Eun Jeong Cho, Kyeongmin Byeon, and Young-Hoon Jeong warn in 2023 that a second kind of heart attack hid inside COVID-19 deaths. The virus does more than infect lungs, they write: it stokes swelling, harms vessel linings, and makes blood clot more readily. Those shifts can trigger clots in veins and arteries alike.

A pooled analysis they cite, over 102 studies and 64,503 patients, found clots in about fifteen percent of hospitalized patients' veins. Artery clots ran lower but still real, they note. Survivors kept a raised risk of heart and clotting trouble long after the illness. Their point is that heart attacks from oxygen mismatch, the type two kind, add a hidden layer to the pandemic's death toll.
pmc-10752579:
Dominic Recco and colleagues followed aortic arch repairs in infants over decades in 2023. Patch surgery rebuilds the narrowed arch. Ideal reconstructed size remains unknown today.
