Too small and too large both harm. Growth records covered twenty years here. One centre reviewed its experience retrospectively.

Mid-term size depended on starting size. One segment tended to stay undersized. Reintervention risk trended higher there too. Moderate oversizing at surgery held steady. Scores near normal persisted at follow-up. Targeted sizing at first operation matters most. The isthmus segment needs special focus. Planning can cut later reoperations.
pmc-10753179:
Marta Araujo-Castro and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-three on the return of rare hormone-producing tumors. These tumors grow in the adrenal gland or nearby nerve tissue and can raise blood pressure sharply. After full surgical removal, some return nearby or spread, and doctors need to know who is at risk.

The team followed three hundred three patients at nineteen Spanish hospitals. After a median of just under five years, about eight percent had recurrent disease, most of it spread to distant sites. A harmful variant in one gene strongly raised the risk. Higher levels of a hormone byproduct in urine and larger tumor size also mattered. The findings support close, long follow-up for high-risk patients.
pmc-10755479:
Hao Xie and co-authors published this neuroimaging meta-analysis in 2023. Parkinson's disease alters brain activity and blood flow, but studies examine one or the other. The team combined two resting-state measures: the strength of slow spontaneous activity, and cerebral blood flow. They gathered thirty-one trials with thirty-seven datasets. Software mapped where patients differed from healthy controls on each measure, then sought regions where the two changed together.

Activity strength fell in the left striatum and a thalamic pathway in patients. Blood flow fell in the right superior frontal gyrus. No region showed both changes at once, suggesting the two signals decouple in this disease. Both problem spots sat in circuits linking the striatum, thalamus, and cortex. Their declines also tracked lower cognitive scores. The authors highlight the left striatum and right frontal region as sites most tied to thinking problems in Parkinson's.
pmc-10756079:
Richard Oude Voshaar argues that low mood in old age is not always an early stage of depression, in a 2023 review. Doctors often treat depressed mood and depressive disorder as points on one scale of severity. That view drives screening and drug treatment in older people. Oude Voshaar proposes a discontinuity hypothesis instead, with two distinct paths for late-life low mood.

In people prone to depression, low mood may indeed grow into a disorder. In others who are resilient, it may be a side effect of physical illness tied to aging itself. He backs the split with three points on life course, screening accuracy, and health outcomes. The idea could curb drug overtreatment of mild cases and push care toward full assessment of body and mind together.
pmc-10757079:
Xiao-hui Li and co-authors test adding immune therapy to chemotherapy after bile duct cancer surgery, in work from 2023. This cancer returns and spreads often, even after complete removal. Standard drug therapy after surgery leaves much room to improve.

Records covered 101 patients treated at one cancer center from 2015 to 2020. Matched groups compared chemotherapy alone against chemotherapy plus immune therapy. The combined group stayed relapse-free significantly longer. Overall survival also favored the combined approach. Nerve invasion by tumor stood out as a risk factor in adjusted models. The findings support testing the pairing in larger trials.
pmc-10761179:
Prethish Sreenivas and co-authors uncover how a key cancer gene stays switched on in a childhood muscle tumor. Their 2023 study deals with rhabdomyosarcoma cells stuck short of full muscle form. The gene drives self-renewal and blocks that maturation, but its upkeep was unknown.

Two DNA-binding proteins share a peak past the gene that marks a domain edge. Cutting that peak kills the gene's output and the cells' survival. Restoring the gene's active form brings cells back. Removing one protein also wipes out most tumor cells. The rare survivors switch the gene back on yet stay fragile to radiation. The authors name the edge-keeping pair as a fresh target.
pmc-10761279:
Raif Alan and Betül Melek Alan write a 2023 commentary on AI in dental patient education. Chatbots backed by AI now answer health questions in two way conversation, any time and anywhere. For dentistry, that promises stronger patient communication, which itself drives treatment success. Patients can check facts about their condition in minutes instead of waiting for a visit.

The piece also casts chatbots as assistants that ease dentists' heavy workloads. It surveys how such tools function in practice and where they fit the clinic. Enthusiasm is tempered by the field's need for accuracy, since wrong advice in health carries real cost. The commentary maps an early moment in a shift still unfolding.
pmc-10765579:
After a stroke, what patients say about their arm does not always match what clinic tests show. Ronnie Baer and co-authors compared three kinds of measures in twenty-six people recovering from stroke. Patients filled in self-rating surveys, took standard clinical tests, and did reaching tasks tracked for speed and force. The team then checked which measures agreed with each other and with later self-rated function.

Survey parts about hand use matched motion measures of the arm. Only hand-focused surveys matched the clinical tests. Hand speed, average and peak, matched other measures most strongly. Two to four years later, self-ratings still lined up with the earlier measures in set ways. Clinics may need all three views to judge recovery fairly.
pmc-10773579:
Andrea Nicolò, Mathieu Gruet, and Massimo Sacchetti introduce a journal collection on breathing in sport in a 2023 editorial. Breathing during exercise has been the quiet variable of sports science, long dismissed because the lungs were thought overbuilt for the job. The editors argue that neglect is ending, for four reasons.

Breathing frequency reacts sensitively to fading exercise tolerance. Frequency and breath depth answer to different control inputs, so measuring both separately doubles the information. Cheap sensors to track breathing outside the lab now abound. And breathing strategies themselves can be trained as interventions. Sixteen articles fill the collection, grouped into physiology, pathophysiology, and applications, with deliberate overlap. The editors' pitch is practical: the breath is a readable signal and a trainable lever, and sport science should use it as both.
pmc-10783679:
Mohammed Alrawi and colleagues report bleeding in both basal ganglia of a two-year-old child, an exceedingly rare event. Their 2023 case description presents, to their knowledge, the first such paediatric report.

Basal ganglia haemorrhage affects deep brain structures including the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus, but bilateral involvement is extremely infrequent. The young girl presented with decreased consciousness, seizure, and fever. Imaging revealed spontaneous bleeding on both sides with a distinctive extension pattern. The bleed ran from the head of the caudate into the putamen, globus pallidus, and the front limb of the internal capsule. The case documents presentation, imaging extent, and rarity for clinicians.
pmc-10808379:
Jinyang Li and co-authors published a study, with the head dated 2023, on spotting weeds in soybean fields with drones to cut herbicide use. Cutting spray use is a goal for greener farming, but checks still rely on slow hand work. The team ran field trials with four levels of reduced spraying. A drone gathered field images for a detection model.

Their improved model beat the base model and an enhanced variant on all measures. One spray method with a ten percent cut controlled weeds well without hurting soybean growth, judged by leaf area and dry weight. The authors present drone detection plus tuned spraying as a path to less herbicide with sound weed control.
pmc-10810979:
Samantha Taylor, Sylvain Charlebois, Tammy Crowell, and Bryce Cross present a case study published in 2023, though the catalog lists 2024, on the ethics of large grocers in Canada. Food prices had risen sharply, and grocers stood accused of using inflation to pad profits. Shoppers grew doubtful as costs climbed and firms stayed vague.

The team read data from shoppers, watchdog groups, and industry sources to trace how public views shifted in 2022. They used a paradox frame for corporate sustainability, extended with a historical view. The study asks what the public now demands from grocers in openness and fair conduct.
pmc-10815279:
Daniah Albokhari and co-authors present a 2023 case report tracing one patient's long road to a rare metabolic diagnosis. Dihydropyrimidinase deficiency, an inherited fault in a breakdown enzyme, ranges from severe brain and gut disease to total silence. An 18-year-old patient sat at the severe end, with bone features never reported before that answered to bisphosphonate treatment.

Urine and blood chemistry flagged the disorder, and gene testing found a brand-new harmful variant in the DPYS gene, confirmed by metabolic work. The authors pair the case with a literature review and urge combined genetic and metabolic testing for such puzzles.
pmc-10822879:
Hai-li Wang, Zhi-yun Wang, Jie Tian, Dong-rui Ma, and Chang-he Shi test in a study whose head gives 2023 as its year if bowel disease raises Parkinson's risk. Both are long, progressive disorders, and past studies split on the link. A giant UK cohort offers a clean place to settle it.

The cohort holds 468,556 people from the UK Biobank, tracked to June 2023. Overall, bowel disease showed no effect on Parkinson's risk in the main model. That null held for Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, and mixed types alike. Careful matching and lag checks that drop early cases agreed with the null. Subgroup signals did appear in women and in those with top gene risk scores.
pmc-10822979:
Dung Tran and co-authors published a study in 2023 on the microbes that live on and in soybean roots. Microbes help plants grow, fight disease, and take up nutrients. The team asked how the root microbe mix differs between soybean types, and how it shifts when a major pest attacks. The pest is the soybean cyst nematode, a tiny worm that feeds on roots.

Plants bred to resist the worm, and plants it can attack, were grown in fields and in a greenhouse. Samples came from bulk soil, the soil hugging the roots, and the roots themselves. Gene sequencing showed root and soil communities overlap partly but keep distinct members. Three large bacteria groups dominated the root mix. The year and sampling time shaped the community most. Plant type had a small but real effect under worm attack in the greenhouse. Those shifts may flag helpful microbes tied to resistance.
pmc-10825579:
Tomonari Matsuda and colleagues showed in 2024 how to predict which alpaca antibodies will bind a target, by tracking how the antibody pool changes during immunization. Antibodies mature as mutations that raise binding strength are picked out again and again. The team guessed that watching this process in sequence data would reveal the winners without lab screening.

An alpaca was given repeated shots of an IgG fragment, and its antibody genes were read over months. The most common sequence groups were built and tested, and more than four in five picks proved right. Traits such as steady turnover and mutation build-up marked the good groups. The method also worked on data from a second alpaca.
pmc-10851779:
Hanin Afzal and co-authors build learning models that predict chronic illness from childhood adversity, in a study published in 2023. Hard experiences in childhood are known to raise adult disease risk through behavior and social conditions. The team asked how well machine learning could turn that history into forecasts.

Using a 2021 national survey of more than fifty-two thousand adults, they trained five kinds of models. Inputs covered childhood adversity, habits, social conditions, and background facts. The targets were thirteen chronic conditions. Adding the adversity data matched or beat earlier models that lacked it. Diabetes, lung diseases, and heart attacks were predicted best. The models also rank which inputs matter most, keeping them readable.
pmc-10861779:
O'Laughlin and a large team of co-authors compare long COVID burdens across ethnic and racial groups. Their study follows American adults after a first infection. Symptoms and lost work were checked at three and six months. The text is dated 2023, though the catalog lists 2024.

Over three thousand people joined, including a comparison group never infected. Odds were adjusted for income, health history, and other social factors. Each group was set against non-Hispanic white participants. Outcomes spanned single symptoms, general health, activity, and missed work. Such adjusted contrasts show where the pandemic's tail fell heaviest. The data guide clinics toward groups carrying the longest burden.
pmc-10862379:
Zhiai Hu and co-authors build tiny spheres that act as a smart barrier for gum tissue regrowth. Their paper from 2023 deals with guided tissue regeneration, where a barrier keeps fast gum and skin cells out of a healing defect. Results with plain barriers swing wide, thanks to narrow fit cases, skill demands, and side effects.

The spheres self build from nanofibers and carry a short peptide on their surface. That peptide draws in bone marrow and ligament stem cells while blocking skin and gum fiber cells. In tests the spheres helped the stem cells settle in the defect, lifted new bone growth, and cut root exposure and tissue loss. The team reads them as a step past standard barriers.
pmc-10868579:
Haifa Alhaithloul, Zakaria Mohamed, Abdullah Saber, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It tests a water extract of moringa seeds as a natural treatment for removing toxic algae and their poisons from treated city wastewater.

The target is Microcystis aeruginosa, a widespread cyanobacterium that releases microcystins, toxins dangerous to water life and to people. The team tried four doses of the seed extract in standard clumping tests. They tracked how many algal cells were removed, how cloudy the water stayed, and where the toxins ended up: dissolved, in the remaining particles, or trapped in the sludge. Chemical analysis measured the toxin in each fraction. The study weighs moringa, a cheap plant material, as a greener stand-in for chemical coagulants in water treatment.
pmc-10879579:
Kun Wang and co-authors track gut barrier recovery after radiation in a 2023 study. The work was published in 2023, before its catalog year. Colorectal cancer often gets chemo-radiation before surgery. Radiation injures the intestinal lining and invites complications. Timing surgery to barrier recovery could help patients.

Over forty patients gave tissue and saliva samples for study. Some had no radiation, others waited varying intervals. Antibody levels in the gut lining were measured first. Inflammatory proteins were blotted in the tissue. Immune cell proportions were counted by flow methods. Saliva bacteria were profiled by gene sequencing. The team hunts for the best surgery window. Oral microbes may signal gut barrier state indirectly. Probiotic or immune treatments could grow from the findings. Reducing complications after radiation is the clinical goal. The study links two body sites rarely examined together.
pmc-10948479:
John Massey and colleagues review robotic mitral valve surgery in a 2024 paper. Robotic repair is the least invasive surgical option for mitral valve disease. Patients recover faster than after open chest surgery. Hospital stays shorten and complications drop in reported series. Survival and repair durability match the classic operation at mid-term.

The review weighs advantages and downsides of the robotic route. Operative setup details receive close attention. Repair techniques for the valve itself are also covered. Case selection and team training shape safe adoption. Robotic heart procedures keep rising in number worldwide. Newer systems and patient demand drive that growth. More surgeons are gaining skill with the innovative approach.
pmc-10957779:
Cécile Aubert and four colleagues ask whether antibiotics taken during bladder cancer therapy weaken that therapy, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. The therapy places a weakened germ, BCG, into the bladder to train the immune system against high-risk tumors. Antibiotics are often needed around the doses and could disturb bladder germs or kill the therapy germ. The team reviewed 126 patients who finished the starter course.

About a third took antibiotics during treatment, most often one drug family. Tumor return rates did not differ by antibiotic use, type, or length. Long courses did stretch the schedule and delay more doses. The authors conclude antibiotics can be given when needed without clear loss of cancer control.
pmc-11025379:
Mikołaj Spytek and colleagues introduce survex, an R software package for explaining survival models, in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Survival models predict how long until an event, such as death or failure, occurs. Machine learning versions often beat classic statistics on accuracy. Yet they act as black boxes, which slows their use in fields like medicine. Users cannot see why a model predicts what it predicts.

Survex applies explainable AI methods to any survival model. It shows which variables drive a prediction and how they push risk up or down. That helps users judge whether a model is sound and spot hidden bias. The authors frame the tool as a step toward open, responsible modeling. Researchers who build survival models in R are the main audience.
pmc-11041479:
Max Rollwage and co-authors test a conversational AI that handles first mental health assessments in England, in a 2023 study. Therapy services face rising demand with flat budgets, so time saved at intake frees clinicians for care. The tool, Limbic Access, chats with patients at referral and sorts their needs.

Data came from nine NHS Talking Therapies services and 64,862 patients. With the AI in place, clinicians spent less time on assessments. Patients also waited less, dropped out less, and landed on the right treatment path more often. Recovery rates improved as well. The authors trace gains to better information gathered up front. Services gain real-world proof that intake AI can lift both speed and outcomes.
pmc-11182179:
Deep in the retina, rod and cone light sensors are wired together by tiny channels that let signals flow between them. Christophe Ribelayga and John O'Brien review the science of that junction in 2023, honoring the work of Steve Massey. The coupling between rods and cones shapes how the retina handles dim and bright light, and it can be dialed up or down by light and time of day.

Massey's turn to connectomics, the mapping of wiring at fine scale, pinned down the rules of who connects to whom. That work let the team compute the junction's top possible coupling, and tests showed real junctions can reach it under drug treatment. The review frames the junction as a model system for electrical synapses everywhere in the brain.
pmc-11532479:
A small enzyme that stamps two methyl marks on the ribosome's RNA turns out to matter for how a tough bacterium handles stress and antibiotics. Kamonwan Phatinuwat and four co-authors delete the ksgA gene in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and compare the mutant with normal cells across a wide panel of chemicals.

Without the marks, the bacteria grew more sensitive to a superoxide generator, partly because a protective enzyme's protein level fell even though its gene message did not. The mutant also became sensitive to two antibiotics, tied to lower levels of elongation factor genes, yet oddly resistant to kasugamycin. The authors say the work ties a conserved RNA modification to stress defense and drug response. The study appears in 2024.
pmc-11535179:
Li and six co-authors gauge how much gelatin-chewing action dentin shows once bonding glues are laid on it, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Enzymes that live in dentin can eat at glue bonds over time if they switch on. The team ran gels, in-place imaging, glow tests, and bond strength pulls. They asked if two gold-standard adhesives, the top glues in the trade, switch those enzymes on.

Dentin dust etched with acid does show gelatinases, the chewing enzymes. Yet the glues spark no switch-on that tests can pick up. Action at the join line matches blank controls, so no switch-on can be found. In liquid, both glues curb enzyme action by a lot. A week of soaking and the heat of curing switch the enzymes all but fully off. Even a strong dose of enzyme leaves bond strength as it was.
pmc-11535479:
Marc Argilés and co-authors test whether color and pace in animated films tire viewers' eyes, in this 2024 paper. Animated films are hugely popular with children and teens. Makers pick bright palettes and fast scenes for impact, but the cost to eye comfort was unmeasured.

Thirty young viewers watched a fast, vivid superhero film and a calm pastoral one, each in color and in grey. Surveys and eye tests tracked fatigue after each viewing. The fast film tired eyes more on most measures. The authors advise producers to weigh pace and color load when designing films for young audiences.
pmc-11535679:
About half of American adults with diabetes used telehealth in 2022, and five researchers ask who they are and whether the care felt as good. They draw on a national health trends survey covering 1,116 adults with diabetes, standing in for 33.6 million people, in a 2024 study. Video visits, phone visits, and mixed use are counted separately. Reasons for using or skipping remote care are also recorded.

Users skewed younger, female, urban, and higher income; adults over 65 were far less likely to connect. Provider advice and convenience drove use, while privacy worries and tech trouble held others back. Reported care quality matched in-person care across every group. The authors call for closing the access gap for older adults.
pmc-11536579:
Ruaa Al Juboori studies why Iraqi women accept home violence in a 2024 survey study. Such views shape how wide the acts spread, who tells, and who seeks help. Data from a 2018 national survey hold 19,443 wed Iraqi women, read through trait splits by class, place, and power.

Near half, 48.4 percent, held that home violence can be fair in some cases. South and central zones ran far higher, at 62 to 73 percent. Low school years and weak tech reach tracked with high marks, and the study frames tech as a power path. Rural home life and wed kin ties also tracked with high marks in the counts.
pmc-11543779:
Nilles and eight co-authors present PEPITA, a fast screen for drugs that damage hearing, in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Many antibiotics can injure the inner ear, and harmful drug combinations often surface only after approval because testing every pair is slow and expensive.

PEPITA uses zebrafish larvae, whose lateral line hair cells closely resemble human inner ear cells. Larvae are exposed to drug combinations, their hair cells are dyed, and microscopes measure the glow as a stand-in for cell health. The workflow is cheap, repeatable, and runs many tests in parallel. It promises systematic checks of drug interactions that protect hearing before new combinations reach patients.
pmc-11545479:
Snezhanna Kandrashina and co-authors study in 2024 how acid swings in blood change the shape and build of red blood cells. Such cells shift their inner work when the fluid round them turns more acid or more base. Form shifts can then change how well each cell does its job.

Past the sound point, shifts both ways turned disc cells into spiked forms. Skin rough ness, inner frame build, and spring marks all changed in step. Hard acid and base states also tied to a rise in harsh oxygen bits in the cells. The work links fluid state to cell health in a direct way.
pmc-11546579:
Henriett Butz and a large team of co-authors study forms of the glucocorticoid receptor in breast cancer tissue. These receptors respond to steroid drugs often given with cancer care. One form, GRbeta, acts against the main form, but its role in real tumors was unknown. Their 2024 study stained lab cells and two sets of tumor samples, one with one hundred ninety-four cases across subtypes and one focused on triple-negative disease.

Where the receptor sat in the cell, and which form was present, varied by subtype. High levels of the beta form in the cell body tracked with longer survival in triple-negative cases. High main-form levels in the nucleus tracked with faster return of disease. The authors urge care with steroid drugs for some patients.
pmc-11546779:
Adriana Ana Trusculescu and co-authors review eleven years of status asthmaticus cases at a Romanian hospital, in a 2024 study. The condition is asthma's worst hour: an attack that will not break and can kill without urgent care. Records from 2013 to 2023 in Timiș County were mined for who was hit, where, and when. A network analysis of accompanying conditions sorted patients into clusters.

Women and older adults bore a disproportionate share. Triggers and geographic patterns emerged from the records. Five clusters appeared: two of the allergic-leaning T2-high type, two T2-low, and one mixed. The authors argue for personalized asthma plans and public health action aimed at the county's specific demographics and hot spots. They offer the study as a template for similar regions counting their own severe asthma burden.
pmc-11557179:
Xi Zhang and co-authors study a traditional plant root as a multi-target treatment lead for type 2 diabetes, in a 2024 paper. Computer analysis first mapped the root's active compounds against diabetes genes drawn from public databases. Overlap pointed to shared targets worth testing in cells.

Four active compounds and 141 shared targets were found. Network analysis put three signal proteins at the centre. Virtual docking showed the lead compound fits each protein well, and motion simulations held the fits stable. In pancreas cells, the root extract lowered those three proteins, raised insulin release, cut cell death, and tuned self-cleaning. The authors say the mix of computing and lab proof gives a base for further study.
pmc-11563179:
Santiago Hasdeu and co-authors study how health technology advice shaped COVID choices in Argentina in a 2024 paper. During the emergency, the WHO and local bodies issued rapid assessments of drugs and tools. Provinces still diverged widely in what they backed and paid for. The team ask why advice and action split.

Records span 2020 and 2021 across all twenty-five health ministries. Documents, surveys, and interviews triangulate the story. Seven technologies were tracked from advice to reimbursement. Some weakly backed items, from ivermectin to convalescent plasma, spread widely against WHO guidance. The study shows evidence is one voice among many in crisis policy.
pmc-11568579:
Rey Chaves and co-authors reviewed twenty years of spleen removal outcomes at one Colombian center, in a study published in 2024. Taking out the spleen is sometimes unavoidable, after injury or in blood diseases. Life without it, though, carries a lasting risk of severe infection. The team gathered every adult case at their hospital from 2003 to 2023. They recorded patient traits, surgical details, and infections that followed.

Outcomes were tracked at 30 days, 90 days, and one year. The authors compared open and keyhole approaches, and planned versus emergency surgery. Emergency and open cases usually fare worse, and the data let them test that pattern locally. A two-decade single-center record is rare in the region. It gives Colombian surgeons benchmarks and shows where prevention, like vaccination, needs shoring up.
pmc-11569479:
A racing, irregular heartbeat after heart surgery, called postoperative atrial fibrillation, strikes up to forty percent of patients. Yuichi Koga and five co-authors asked in 2024 whether an extra drain behind the heart, clearing fluid that fuels inflammation, could prevent it after valve replacement.

The study compared patients at one Japanese center across two eras: 27 who got the posterior drain after 2017 and 52 earlier patients without it. The rhythm problem appeared in about 26 percent of the drain group against 48 percent without, though the gap fell short of statistical significance in this small sample. Adjusted models weighed the drain's value against body size and other factors.
pmc-11571879:
Eman Abu El-Naga and co-authors test feed recipes for buffalo embryos grown in the lab, in a 2024 study. Buffalo breeding often relies on eggs fertilized outside the body, then raised in culture dishes. The mix in those dishes can help or hinder early growth, so the team tuned the recipe.

Two base media were tried with added energy sources, spare amino acids, and antioxidants. Rates of cell splitting and growth to later stages were tracked for each mix. Energy additions helped one medium more than the other. In the second medium, antioxidant additions lifted the share of embryos reaching the morula and blastocyst stages by wide margins. The authors name a best mix for future buffalo work.
pmc-11572979:
Simon Boje Hansen and a large team pinpoint a motif in plant receptors that root nodule symbiosis cannot do without, in this 2024 Europe PMC paper. The symbiosis starts when plants sense bacterial Nod factors through receptor kinases called NFR1 and NFR5. NFR5 lacks normal kinase activity, so how it signals was a puzzle.

The team solved the crystal structure of the NFR5 inner domain from Lotus japonicus. A well-defined juxtamembrane region forms two helices carrying an exposed hydrophobic motif. That motif promotes binding between receptors and is essential for symbiotic signaling. The same motif appears across NFR5-type receptors and is needed in barley too, hinting at a broad role in plant-microbe partnerships.
pmc-11573579:
Zhi Zhang and four co-authors present a 2024 computer simulation study on orthodontic treatment for patients born with a one-sided cleft lip and palate. Moving the upper jaw in these patients interacts with the bone graft that fills the cleft, and chewing forces complicate the picture. The team built eight virtual models with grafts at different heights, then simulated jaw protraction, expansion, and both together under biting loads.

Grafted models shifted less on the non-cleft side than the ungrafted one during both maneuvers. Grafts placed in the upper or middle third of the cleft, though, produced more lopsided movement and stress. The authors stress that chewing forces belong in such simulations for realism. They suggest high grafts may need a supplementary second graft to keep jaw movement even and effective.
pmc-11573979:
Omar Mabrouk, Doaa Abdel Hady, and Tarek Abd El-Hafeez use machine learning to predict how shoulder blade exercises help college students with shoulder pain, in work from 2024. Non specific shoulder pain is common in students and can lower quality of life. Therapists use stabilization exercises to improve blade control and motion.

The study fit many regression models to link exercise traits with pain relief. Several tuning methods then refined the exercise plans for best results. The authors report that the exercises, when optimized, helped manage pain. The approach shows how data tools can personalize a standard therapy rather than give one plan to all.
pmc-11574279:
Hua Guo and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 hunting gene markers that flag the shift of multiple sclerosis into its progressive form. The disease often starts with relapses, then turns steadily worse, and the biology of that turn is murky. The team mined public gene data comparing healthy-looking and damaged tissue from one brain region.

Hundreds of genes differed between the tissues. Network analysis and two learning algorithms converged on four genes tied to immune response as candidate markers. Tests of their predictive strength looked promising for telling progressive disease apart. Immune cell patterns in the tissue added support. The authors offer the four genes as leads for diagnosis research.
pmc-11574879:
Gemma Garcia-Vicién and co-authors compare the cell neighborhoods of colon cancer spread to the liver, in a 2024 study. These deposits grow in two patterns. One builds a rim of new tissue around itself. The other blends into the liver without a rim. Patients with the rim pattern live longer. The team stained samples from one hundred patients. Three panels marked immune, scavenger, and support cells at the tumor edge.

The rim pattern held more killer T cells in tumor areas. The blending pattern held more macrophages and helper cells of a certain type. Support cell mixes also differed between patterns. One collagen-bearing support type clustered in rim tumors. Oddly, one scavenger cell type marked better outcomes inside the worse pattern. Those patients also showed richer scavenger mixes overall. The study maps two distinct landscapes. It may help predict which patients need stronger treatment.
pmc-11577379:
Yu-Bin Guo, Yue-Ming Wu, and Zhi-Zhao Lin test a way to make radiation work better on colon cancer in a 2024 paper. Cancer cells make extra amounts of an enzyme that builds a cell chemical. The team lowered that enzyme in lab grown cancer cells. They tracked growth, death, and harm after radiation.

Cells with less of the enzyme grew slower and died more readily. After radiation, those cells showed more DNA harm and more self cleaning of worn parts. A growth control path in the cells also quieted down. Blocking that path seems to drive the extra harm. The results point to the enzyme as a drug target for stubborn tumors.
pmc-11577579:
Guangda Xin and four co-authors compared two kidney function formulas head to head in a 2024 study of Chinese adults. Both formulas estimate filtration rate from cystatin C, a blood marker: one from the CKD-EPI group in 2021, one from a European consortium in 2023. The team followed 6,496 adults from a national aging study for up to seven years, logging 473 deaths and 1,996 new cardiovascular cases.

Low estimated function by the CKD-EPI formula, below sixty units, came with clearly higher risks of death and of new heart and vessel disease. The European formula's levels, by contrast, showed no significant link to either outcome. The authors recommend the CKD-EPI cystatin C equation for risk tracking in this population, while calling for more validation.
pmc-11577879:
Temesgen Wondmeneh and Zelalem Solomon pool studies on common mental disorders in Ethiopia after COVID-19, in a review dated twenty twenty-four. Twenty studies fed their meta-analysis of adults. The pooled share with a common mental disorder came to about forty percent.

Risk ran higher for women and for people out of work. Weak social support, substance use, and past mental illness in self or family also raised the odds. Long-term body illness added risk as well. The authors frame the pandemic's mental shadow as wide and call for care aimed at the most exposed groups.
pmc-11578479:
Shahryar Razzaghi and co-authors test whether dirty air on a given day sends more stroke patients to hospital in Tabriz, Iran, in a study from 2024. Tabriz is a major factory city, so air quality is a long-standing health concern there. The team used records from the city's main large hospital.

The data covered 1,821 days and 4,865 stroke cases, matched with daily readings from eight air sensors across the city. The team used a time-series model that allowed effects to show up over three days. None of the gases or dust measures they tracked linked to more stroke visits in a clear way. Only a marker for the COVID-19 period showed a clear link, a result that differs from many past reports.
pmc-11579479:
Alaa Khalifa, Mohamed Fanni, and Ahmed Khalifa design a force sensing control scheme for a flying robot arm in a 2024 paper. Such systems are prized but tricky: they tip easily, move fast, and shift as loads change.

Their scheme reads contact force with no force sensor, using a disturbance watcher paired with a fast learning fit. A firm control rule then holds the arm's touch stiffness at the set level while it tracks a path. Math checks back the scheme's steadiness. Tests show clean path tracking and touch control, which suits remote handling jobs where a human steers from afar.
pmc-11580179:
Jinha Kim, Kung-Hui Chu, and five co-authors link soil microbes to the breakdown of long-lasting chemicals. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, covers fluorotelomer-based PFAS precursors. These man-made compounds degrade in hard-to-predict ways, which complicates cleanup. Soil cultures were fed different carbon foods, from alcohols to a surfactant.

All cultures stripped fluorine from the test compounds and grew on one as a sulfur source. A butanol-fed culture did the most stripping. It held the widest microbe mix and the most breakdown genes. One surfactant-fed culture built up a distinct byproduct, tied to two named bacteria. Mixing cultures boosted breakdown, except with two of the feeds.
pmc-11581779:
Huaming Zhong and six co-authors census the genome's stutters across reptiles in a 2024 paper. Microsatellites are short DNA phrases repeated end to end, scattered by the millions. They mutate fast, making them handy markers, yet reptiles had never had a full count.

The team scanned thirty-six species, from crocodiles to lizards. Counts ran from under two million to over seven and a half million repeats, up to eight percent of some genomes. Bigger genomes held more repeats but spread thinner. Snakes and lizards carried the richest, most varied load; crocodiles the leanest. Single-letter repeats ruled in crocodiles and turtles, longer motifs elsewhere. The map aids conservation and evolution studies.
pmc-11582679:
Junyu Chen, Xueping Zou, Daniel Spencer, and Hywel Morgan published a 2024 microfluidics paper on a device that reads both the electrical and mechanical traits of single cells at high speed. A cell's stiffness and electrical behavior reflect its inner structure and can mark its type or state. Measuring both at once, without touching the cell, is the advance.

Cells flow through a channel in a viscoelastic fluid whose shear stretches them by varying amounts. Electrodes along two axes measure each cell's impedance as it deforms. From the signal, the system infers shape change and dielectric traits together. The team validated the device on cells stressed by salt shock, chemical crosslinking, and skeleton disrupting drugs. Deformed cell images confirmed the readings.
pmc-11585579:
Zhe Meng and co-authors propose a recycling method in 2024 that heats spent battery parts with waste plastic to pull out prized metals. Used lithium ion battery cathodes and PET plastic are both growing waste streams. The cathode metals, such as nickel, cobalt, and lithium, are worth recovering for new batteries.

When the two wastes are heated together, the plastic helps break the cathode down. At a set heat, the cathode splits fully into a lithium salt, a manganese oxide, and a nickel cobalt alloy, in about half an hour. The mix ratio of the two wastes is tuned for that full change. A route that treats two wastes at once and yields raw stuff for new batteries has clear appeal. The team reports the terms under which the change runs best.
pmc-11585979:
Awab Saad and co-authors ask, in 2024, whether simple body measurements can flag high blood pressure in teenagers. Measuring blood pressure in every adolescent is not always practical, so cheap stand-ins matter. In eastern Sudan, four hundred one adolescents had a battery of measurements taken, from body mass index to waist and arm sizes.

Thirty-six had hypertension. Upper arm circumference was the best single predictor, followed by waist size and body mass index, each with a usable cutoff point. Ratios based on waist and height performed poorly. The authors give local cutoff values that community health workers could apply with a tape measure alone.
pmc-11586779:
Anna Pan and five colleagues describe a forty-three-year-old man whose liver held two different cancers at once. Imaging showed multiple liver lesions but could not characterize them: the usual scans were inconclusive, and two PET tracers showed no uptake in the smaller lesions. A third tracer, targeting fibroblast activation protein, lit those lesions clearly.

The largest lesion proved to be ordinary hepatocellular carcinoma, while the smaller ones were a rare vascular tumor, epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, confirmed by tissue staining. Only two similar synchronous cases appear in the worldwide literature. The authors argue the newer tracer has strong potential for detecting and staging this rare tumor, and that it belongs in the differential diagnosis.
pmc-11586979:
Cezar-Ivan Colita and co-authors review how the time of day a psychiatric drug is given can change how well it works, in a survey published in 2024. Care that times doses to the body clock is called chronotherapy. Many clinics now give drugs in the morning or evening for ease, not because the clock was part of the plan.

The review links disorders such as depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia to broken daily rhythms in sleep, hormones, and clock genes. It then traces how the body takes in, moves, breaks down, and clears drugs across the day. Timing a dose well can raise its effect and cut side effects, the authors argue. They propose watching cortisol, melatonin, and clock genes to set dose times for each patient.
pmc-11588779:
Mariana Castells, Michael Madden, and Carole Oskeritzian review a mast cell switch behind many allergic reactions in a 2024 paper. Mast cells can be triggered without the classic allergy antibody, through a receptor called MRGPRX2. Interest in that route has grown as patients show reactions to anesthetics, antibiotics, and opioids that fit no antibody story.

The review covers the receptor's structure, where it appears in the body, and how it signals. It also explains how this route can amplify the classic antibody route in the same cell. New candidate blockers and triggers get surveyed. The authors aim to connect fresh biology to bedside puzzles like non-histamine itch, hives, and asthma, and to guide the search for drugs that calm this switch.
pmc-11588979:
Sophia Winkler-Schor and co-authors assess discipline diversity inside a conservation society in 2024, using team framing for a long author list. Good conservation needs many ways of knowing. A task force formed in 2020 to gauge inclusion in the society. It read past rule books and surveyed members and outsiders. Near eight hundred people replied in all.

Non biologists saw the society as less diverse and less fair. Most outsiders felt their work fit its mission. Yet they saw a biology first focus. The authors urge hiring and leadership steps to widen the mix. Partnerships that flatten rank between fields are also proposed. Knowledge justice is framed as core, not decoration.
pmc-11589079:
Mark Mohan Kaggwa and four co-authors review self-harm cases at emergency units in Northern Uganda, in this twenty twenty-four paper. They read the charts of patients admitted after harming themselves on purpose during twenty twenty-one. The aim was to learn the patterns and how many survived.

Of more than two hundred and fifty patients, about one in eleven died, most often from farm poison taken by mouth. Care differed between public and private hospitals, including the use of antidotes. The authors call for wider study and a joint effort across health, farming, and community groups to prevent self-harm and improve its care.
pmc-11589679:
Ying Huang and six co-authors proposed in two thousand twenty-four a way to track progress toward the global development goals in China. Their method rests on ecosystem services, the gains people get from nature. They linked those services to the goals and scored progress at both country and province level.

From two thousand to two thousand twenty, scores for eleven goals and the overall index fell in China. Scores also varied a lot across the thirty-one provinces. Health and green goals stood out as top national needs. The authors say their method can help leaders compare places, set local steps, and shape policy.
pmc-11590479:
İsa Taş and co-authors show blocking one enzyme defeats smoke driven immune escape in lung tumors in a 2024 paper. Benzo[a]pyrene, a smoke toxin, wakes a cell sensor in lung cells. That wake lifts shield proteins that hide tumors from immune attack.

Lung cell tests traced the shield lift to that sensor at work. The sensor reroutes a food amino acid through enzyme paths. Blocking the TDO2 enzyme in that path cut the shield lift. In mice with lung tumors in place, TDO2 blocks shrank tumor growth. The path names a drug target for smoke linked lung cancer.
pmc-11591279:
Chengfeng Zhao and co-authors test a mulberry leaf extract as a feed additive for chickens under chemical stress in this 2024 study. Oxidative stress harms gut health and growth in broiler farming. The extract is rich in a compound called DNJ, drawn from mulberry leaves long used in folk practice.

The team raised 240 broilers in six groups, some stressed with peroxide injections and some fed graded doses of the extract. At the lowest dose, gut lining height and structure improved, and key antioxidant enzymes rose in parts of the intestine. A gut-protective gene also switched on more strongly at the two lower doses. The authors judge the extract promising below eighty milligrams per kilogram of feed, and they call for work on how it acts inside the bird gut.
pmc-11591479:
Nilakshi Barua and A K Buragohain review, in a 2024 paper, whether silver nanoparticles could help treat tuberculosis. The lung disease remains a global health threat, in part because some strains now resist the standard drugs. New drugs are in trials, but the bacterium's complex cell wall and its life inside host cells slow that work.

Silver nanoparticles kill a wide range of microbes, and tests show they can act against the tuberculosis bacterium, including drug-resistant strains. Combined with standard drugs, they may raise the drugs' effect and shorten treatment. The review weighs these gains against open problems. Delivering the particles to the right site is hard, their killing power inside host cells varies, and harm to the body is a concern. The authors map where the field stands and what must be fixed, such as targeted delivery and safe dosing.
pmc-11593679:
García-Gamboa and five co-authors compared gut bacteria in bowel disease across two countries for this paper from twenty twenty-four. Inflammatory bowel disease ties closely to the gut microbe mix, which shifts with place and diet. The study covered seventy-nine patients and healthy controls from Mexico and Spain. Stool gene sequencing mapped their bacteria, alongside diet and body measures.

Diversity ran lower in the disease groups. One genus appeared only in the Mexican groups, and another only in the Spanish groups. A common anti-inflammatory genus was actually richer in patients here. Diet links emerged too: one genus tracked meat and protein intake, another tracked calorie intake. The authors stress that place and food must frame microbiome research.
pmc-11594579:
Krzysztof Greberski and co-authors study, in 2024, whether simple blood measures taken before heart bypass surgery can predict who will live or die afterward. The team reviewed five hundred twenty patients who had one of two forms of the operation. They recorded age, other illnesses, hospital details, and blood samples taken before surgery.

After adjusting for other factors, some blood values stood out. Counts linked to white cells and platelets, and the spread of red cell sizes, tied to higher death rates at one year and at five years. The authors suggest these cheap, routine measures could help doctors flag patients who need closer care.
pmc-11595079:
Won-Kyung Cho and co-authors test a plant compound against flu viruses in a 2024 study. The compound, amentoflavone, is found in many plants as a double flavonoid. Using a glowing tagged flu virus, the team measured how much infection fell as the dose rose.

At a mid dose, viral glow fell to about thirty percent of untreated infected cells, and viral protein levels dropped in step. Timing tests showed the compound blocks the virus from attaching to cells by interfering with its surface spike. It also directly inactivated virus particles, blocked effects of flu B and a flu A subtype, and slowed the viral release enzyme. Computer analysis supported binding to both viral proteins.
pmc-11596779:
Sanjeevamuthu Suganthi, Khursheed Ahmad, and Tae Hwan Oh review a class of flat materials called MXenes in two green tech roles, in a paper from 2024. MXenes are sheets just atoms thick, with strong light and electric traits. The review gathers past work on sensors built from these sheets. It also covers solar cells that drop costly platinum from one part.

On the sensor side, the sheets help detect phenolic compounds, a group of common pollutants. Mixed with other materials, they make electrodes that are quick and sensitive. On the solar side, MXene blends serve as the counter electrode in dye-based cells. Those cells are cheaper than standard panels but need a good stand-in for platinum. The authors say the survey should help labs design better sensors and cells.
pmc-11597479:
Sunil Wimalawansa and co-authors argue that vitamin D guidance should cover far more than bones in a 2024 paper. Vitamin D supports immune function and general well-being, and higher blood levels are linked in many studies with lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, infection complications, autoimmune disease, and death overall.

The authors review endocrine, genomic, and extra-skeletal benefits of the vitamin. They propose folding that evidence into national and regional clinical guidelines. Their case rests on a wide base of ecological, observational, prospective, and trial evidence gathered across many conditions.
pmc-11599379:
Su-Jin Shin and co-authors compare immune cells inside two kinds of breast cancer with high immune cell counts. Their 2024 paper uses tissue from 32 removed tumors, split between triple negative cases and hormone-linked cases. Stained slides let the team count cell types and map where they sat.

Triple negative tumors held more killer T cells in both the tumor core and the rim around it. They also held more of a helper cell type linked to immune control. A surface marker called PD-L1 changed the cell mix in both cancer kinds. In marker-positive triple negative cases, control-type cells packed more densely near tumor cells. The maps may help guide immune care choices.
pmc-11599579:
Tianjian Zou and co-authors track fast table tennis balls in video using a graph neural network in this 2024 paper. The ball is tiny and moves very fast, which defeats most trackers. Sports analysis needs its path for judging technique and tactics. Their method pairs a detector with a smart discriminator. The detector is a refined frame-difference tool for video. The discriminator reads the ball's likely path as a graph problem.

Messages pass along the graph to pick the true trajectory. False blobs from noise and clutter get filtered by that logic. The design leans on how table tennis balls actually move. Real match footage is the test bed described. The paper is a computer vision methods study. It targets a niche where standard trackers fail.
pmc-11599779:
Kornienko and co-authors report a 2024 study on bacteria that resist virus-based treatment. As standard drugs fail more often, doctors look again at phage therapy, which uses viruses that infect bacteria. The team studied Staphylococcus aureus strain ST239, a hospital germ, and strains of it that resist Herelleviridae phages. They combined gene, RNA, and protein data to find what sets the resistant strains apart.

Resistant strains formed their own branch on the family tree, hinting at built-in traits. In one strain, hundreds of genes changed activity within minutes of phage attack. Shifts hit energy pathways, transport systems, and genes from older resident viruses. Known surface-based defenses did not explain the pattern, the authors note.
pmc-11600579:
Sabrina Hoppe and ten co-authors lay out the OptiCor project in a 2024 protocol paper. The project aims to help general practitioners give very brief activity advice to patients with chronic ischemic heart disease, a narrowing of the heart's arteries. Moving more is proven care for these patients, and German guidance asks family doctors to advise it, yet advice stays rare, in part for lack of training.

The plan runs in three phases. First, a national survey and talks with doctors and patients map how advice is given and what blocks it. Next, a training built from those findings is piloted in a randomized trial. Finally, a full trial tests whether trained doctors advise more, with cost and process data gathered alongside.
pmc-11600679:
Houshang Bavandpour Karvane and nine co-authors published a cross-sectional nutrition study in twenty twenty-four on metabolic syndrome and a new heart-protective diet score. The cardioprotective index summarizes how protective a person's diet is, but its link to metabolic syndrome had never been tested. Three hundred forty-eight overweight or obese patients with the syndrome were recruited.

Patients were ranked into thirds by diet score and compared on blood fats, pressures, and two appetite-related hormones, nesfatin-1 and omentin-1. The lowest-scoring third had worse cholesterol, triglycerides, and blood pressure than the highest. After adjusting for age, sex, weight, activity, and calories, most differences held, though one cholesterol contrast faded. The study connects everyday diet quality to the syndrome's measurable parts.
pmc-11602879:
Taiga Shimura and co-authors report a womb cancer that hid as colon cancer in a 2024 case paper. Spread of endometrial cancer to the colon is exceptionally rare. Their patient was a seventy-nine-year-old woman with belly swelling and constipation.

Five years earlier she had surgery for serous endometrial cancer. A scope found her sigmoid colon ringed by a narrowing growth. Scans showed thick walls, swollen nodes, and fluid spread in the pelvis. Two metal stents opened the blockage. Surgeons then removed the left colon and the spread tissue. Under the microscope, the growth proved to be the old womb cancer, not a new colon one. Six months on, no return was seen.
pmc-11603179:
Yang Zhang and co-authors automate sand grading checks for concrete work in a 2024 paper. Sand grain sizes shape concrete strength and handling, but sieve tests are slow. Camera systems struggle because the finest grains need close, narrow views that miss most of a sample. Their fix samples small patches at random, many times, on a vibrating flexible disk that spreads grains evenly.

Software then builds the full size spread from the patch data. Tests show patch grading closely mirrors whole sample grading, they report, and repeated sampling shrinks the error further. The method targets the full construction sand range, from dust fine to nearly five millimeters.
pmc-11603679:
Javier Sanchez-Cerezo and co-authors count new cases of a restrictive eating disorder in children across the UK and Ireland in a 2024 study. The disorder, called ARFID, involves food avoidance not driven by body image. Its true rate in the young was unknown.

Doctors reported cases through two national watch systems over 13 months in 2021 and 2022. They confirmed 319 new cases in children aged 5 to 17, with a mean age near 11. The rate was about 2.8 cases per 100,000 children per year, slightly higher in boys. Anxiety and autism were common alongside the disorder. Over half the cases had improved at one-year follow-up.
pmc-11603979:
Joseph Lasong, Yula Salifu, and Jonas Kakungu surveyed tramadol use among university students in Ghana, in a 2024 study. Misuse of the pain drug is rising in poorer countries. It can harm social life, body, and thinking, above all with other drug use. Data on Ghanaian undergraduates were scarce. Six hundred students at one university answered the survey.

Nearly one in five students had used tramadol in their lifetime. Most of those had also used at least one other substance. Students aged twenty to twenty-four and first-year students were prominent among users. Improving study performance was the top reason given for starting. Male sex and past cannabis use linked clearly to tramadol use. The authors call the pattern a public health threat. They urge school and community campaigns plus stronger government policy.
pmc-11604779:
Arpita Das and seven co-authors studied diet patterns in pregnant women in a 2024 paper. Iron and vitamin D both matter in pregnancy, and anemia is common. The team asked whether one eating pattern tied to iron stores in the blood also relates to vitamin D levels.

They used a national nutrition survey of 1,423 pregnant women from 2017 to 2019. A statistical method distilled a diet pattern rich in fish, soy, nuts, organ meat, and sea plants, scored against blood measures. pmc-11604879:
Xiang Yuan and a large team of co-authors weigh two blood transfusion strategies for brain injury in a 2024 review. Trials have pointed both ways, leaving the choice unsettled.

The team searched the major trial databases through late 2024 and pooled the randomized trials that compared the two strategies head to head. Five trials met their rules. The pooled analysis speaks to death rates, to brain outcomes six months on, and to how much blood each strategy uses. The authors present the work as the firmest summary yet of a daily dilemma in neuro-intensive care, where both too little and too much blood carry risks.
pmc-11605079:
Michael Torrens-Spence and co-authors work out how a plant enzyme speeds the making of a defense signal. Their paper from 2024 deals with salicylic acid in the mustard family of plants. The enzyme, EPS1, is new found and belongs to a wide enzyme family with other jobs.

The team solved the shapes of the enzyme alone and with a stand in for its target held in place. Long molecule motion models plus quantum sums led them to a ring shift type plan for how the enzyme works. They rebuilt the whole path in yeast to test which parts of the enzyme matter. Putting the enzyme into soybean raised its base levels of the defense signal.
pmc-11605479:
Xuan Li and colleagues examine bright spots on brain scans after mild head injury, in a 2024 study. These spots, called white matter hyperintensities, mark small-vessel damage in the brain's wiring. The work ties a scan marker to network disruption after injury.
pmc-11605579:
Takashi Kon and co-authors report in a 2024 conference study four brain tumor cases where a glow test changed its mind between first and second surgery. Patients take a drug, 5-ALA, that makes tumor tissue glow under the knife, guiding removal. All four had radiation and drug therapy between operations.

In two cases the glow flipped from absent to strong at the second surgery; in two it stayed strong. One flipped case proved to be radiation damage, not tumor, and the others kept their first diagnosis. Tumor change alone does not explain the flips, the team notes; prior treatment may alter the glow.
pmc-11605879:
Lin-Yu Yang and co-authors track gene activity after death in silkworms in this 2024 study. Death ends life, yet some gene signals switch on or carry on afterward. The team read both gene messages and their tiny regulators in young, old, and dead worms across the hours after death.

At two hours post-death, a drop in genes that run writing and control marks reshaped the whole pattern. Five gene-regulator pairs linked to stress hormones and signal paths were picked out. Tests with mimics in live worms backed their roles.
pmc-11606079:

Both forms worked in the normal pressure range up to a set limit. The changed form proved easier to make, since one build step could be dropped. The design can be shaped to fit varied implant sites.
pmc-11606179:
Yurii Bezsmertnyi and co-authors report stress fractures in both leg stumps of an amputee in a 2024 case paper. A twenty-eight-year-old soldier had lost both lower legs. pmc-11606979:

pmc-11607079:

pmc-11607879:

pmc-11608479:

pmc-11608979:

pmc-11609879:

Older age, male sex, immune-suppressing drugs, and a second skin cancer type all raised risk. Badly changed early lesions turned into cancer faster than mildly changed ones. pmc-11610279:

Scores ran lower in the mix group at 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours. Sedation and recovery quality scores were tracked as well. Pump press counts and rescue drug use were logged. Adverse events over 48 hours were compared by group. The authors call the mix a stronger option for this surgery.
pmc-11610379:

Ning asks the authors to clarify these points.
pmc-11610579:

pmc-11611279:

pmc-11612279:

Pain scores tied at each check, day one, day two, and day seven. Pain end day also tied twixt the arms. Crust fall day, though, came first in the leaf arm by a clear edge. The leaf gel may serve as a swap for the stock cream, the team reads.
pmc-11613379:

pmc-11613779:

pmc-11613879:

pmc-11614579:

One group had mild asthma without daily steroid inhalers. The other, larger group had moderate persistent disease on regular inhaled steroids. Blood interleukins and eosinophil products were set against exhaled inflammatory measures. The question is which cheap signals track the severity split that doctors already see. pmc-11614779:

The results lay a base for breeding ducks with better meat traits.
pmc-11614879:

pmc-11614979:

Seventeen patients took part, with a mean age of 55.5 years, and twelve were women. Answers were sorted by qualitative content analysis. The final scheme had three clusters. One cluster covered the type of therapy and how the process runs. The study shows the therapy traits that sway a patient's choice, beyond survival numbers alone.
pmc-11615079:

pmc-11616279:

The hit rate fell to 54.7% in 2020, the first year of tight rules. It then rose to 79.1% in 2023 after the rules eased. Most cases held one germ, while 13% held more than one.
pmc-11616879:
Kasey R Boehmer and co-authors trial a discussion aid meant to improve care for people with long-term conditions. Their 2024 study tests the ICAN aid in primary care, where visits must weigh illness burden, treatment burden, and what matters to the patient.

Eight clinics in four health systems were split by lottery, and ninety-eight clinicians with more than seventeen hundred patients took part. Most headline outcomes showed no clear gain. A deeper analysis did find better confidence among patients in managing illness and speaking with clinicians, and better clinician ratings of chronic care. Chart checks showed the aid reached only about a fifth of eligible visits. Where it was used as designed, both sides valued the talks it opened.
pmc-11617179:
Erin Hoare, Nicky Couston, Lilli Burdon, Claudia Vella, and Kate Hall tested a wellbeing program for teenage footballers in Australia's elite pathway, in a 2024 paper. Young high-performance athletes face heavy pressure, yet proven programs are scarce. The program mixed three parts: a wellbeing curriculum drawn from positive psychology, stronger local support staff in football communities, and a personal wellbeing plan for each athlete aged sixteen to eighteen.

The team judged feasibility and acceptability through interviews with athletes, coaches, and wellbeing coordinators. Acceptance grew over time, with participants reporting rising connection and support as the program ran. Two barriers stood out: squeezing sessions into packed training schedules, and travel time for regional athletes. The authors conclude the program can work in this setting, provided delivery bends around the realities of elite junior sport.
pmc-11617579:
Beihui Huang and co-authors profile multiple myeloma patients who survive past ten years, in a study from 2024. They reviewed 168 patients treated at one center from 2004 to 2014, when modern drugs and stem cell transplants became standard. Forty-four patients crossed the ten-year mark; 124 did not.

Long survivors were more often younger than 57 at diagnosis, with healthy neutrophil counts. Lacking high-risk genetic flaws raised the odds of long survival about sevenfold. Getting a transplant up front also helped. Staying free of measurable residual disease for at least two years tracked with long survival even in patients with risky genetics. The authors read the pattern as a guide for early, deep treatment.
pmc-11617779:
Katharina Steeg and co-authors test a privacy risk in medical imaging in a 2024 paper. Head MRI scans are often shared for research after names are removed, on the belief that faces cannot be recovered from them. New free AI tools have changed that picture, and the team set out to measure the current risk.

Volunteers with a verified online presence had standard head scans. Using free software, the team built 3D face renders from the scans and ran them through public face-search services. Half of the volunteers were correctly matched in under ten minutes, with minimal skill or computing power needed. Adjusting hair or head angle to match real photos improved results further. The authors urge much stronger protection for shared scan data.
pmc-11618279:
Duk Ki Kim and co-authors study sepsis care in very old patients across South Korea, in work published in 2024. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection. Care follows a bundle of timed steps, such as measuring blood markers, giving fluids, and starting drugs that raise blood pressure.

The study drew on a national database with close to twelve thousand sepsis patients, about a third of them aged 80 or older. Patients who survived were younger, less frail, and had less organ failure on arrival. They were also more likely to get key bundle steps within the first hour and the right antibiotics within a day. Death was linked to age, frailty, organ failure scores, and other health problems. The authors call for care plans shaped to very old patients.
pmc-11618479:
Crandall and co-authors reported this engineering feat in twenty twenty-four: turning carbon dioxide into printable carbon material. Their system first uses electricity to convert the gas into carbon monoxide. A heated reactor then grows carbon nanotubes, tiny tubes prized for strength. Those tubes are printed into dense composite parts.

The setup ran for more than forty-five hours and made thirty-seven grams of nanotubes from the gas. A cost study suggests the route could cut nanotube prices by about ninety percent at industrial scale. The printed parts held a high share of nanotubes, aligned to boost strength. The authors argue the process could turn a waste gas into a valuable product at scale.
pmc-11618979:
Yuemei Ye leads a team that tests gas from food wrap in landfill like tanks. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with PFAS, a group of tough chemicals. Much plant fiber food wrap is thrown in landfills.

The team screened many wrap types for fluorine and one PFAS form. High fluorine wraps gave off far more PFAS gas in tests. One form made up nearly all the gas that was released. Low fluorine wraps and town waste gave off very little. The tanks mimicked no air break down in landfills. Wrap choice may shape PFAS spread.
pmc-11619179:
Han and co-authors track new mind-ill rates in Korea through the COVID years. Few past works used ward visit data for a whole land mass. Korea runs a must-join health scheme that spans all its folk. First-time codes for each mind ill were pulled from that bank. The span ran from 2015 to the start of 2023. Month rates were set by age to a stock form.

A split-time read built the no-plague path for each ill. Real rates were then set next to that built path. Brain-worn ills fell near 14.6 percent next to the old span. Drug-linked ills fell near 12.9 percent in the same span. Worry ills rose near 8.8 percent in the plague years. The read stays a plain sum, not a cause claim.
pmc-11620779: A 2024 retraction notice withdraws a meta-analysis on hydrocolloid dressings for pressure ulcers in ventilated patients. The journal and publisher state that an investigation found the article was accepted solely through a compromised peer review process. The probe also found large unattributed overlap with an earlier published article. The notice names the paper and its authors and records that they did not respond. The dressing study itself is not described; the notice is the record.
pmc-11621279:
Tianhua Chen asks if a full day of heartbeats from a wrist watch can flag a student's mind state in a 2024 study. Stress marks in most work come from short lab shocks, not real days. Here, students at a British university wore watches through free days with no set routine.

Signal tools turned the beat runs into forms a learning model can read, both raw and wave-split. The models beat a plain base line by a clear edge. The work hints that beat runs alone can sketch day-long mind states. More data is still being gathered for wider tests.
pmc-11621579:
Aqsa Iqbal and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on breaking down a violet dye pollutant in water with light-driven chemistry. The dye, Acid Violet 49, resists plain treatment. The team tried ultraviolet light with peroxide, plus three powder catalysts, and tuned each knob: catalyst dose, peroxide dose, acidity, and dye strength.

One pairing, zinc oxide with light and peroxide, cleared ninety-six percent of the dye in ninety minutes at the best settings. Blood cell tests checked whether the leftovers stayed toxic. Spectral and mass tools traced what the dye broke into, and the team sketched the likely path of its fall. The recipe may suit dye-house waste streams.
pmc-11621679:
Kai Zhang and co-authors report a gentle way to tune blue light devices in a 2024 study. The devices use a crystal class called perovskite. Blue forms are hard to make well, since the usual way to shift their color can harm the crystal and add flaws that waste light.

Their post treatment swaps one part of the crystal for another in a smooth, step wise way. The swap shifts color across the blue range while keeping flaw counts low. Devices made this way reached high yields of light for sky blue, pure blue, and deep blue. The method could help make brighter, cleaner blue screens and lamps.
pmc-11622479:
Kubra Gurler, Sehnaz Yilmaz, Aysin Dumani, and Oguz Yoldas compare how three single file root canal systems tire after real clinical use, in work from twenty twenty-four. Nickel titanium rotary files reshape canal work, but snapping inside a tooth stays a top worry. Files weaken with repeated bending in curved canals.

One hundred twenty patients needing molar root canal care were split among the three systems. Files were fatigue tested fresh, after one use, and after three uses. One system lasted longest in every group by time and by cycles to fracture. After three uses it and a second system clearly beat the third. Broken fragment lengths also differed by system.
pmc-11622579:
Baraa Alghalyini and four colleagues present a 2024 public health study of vaccine hesitancy among Syrian refugee parents in Canada. The team interviewed 540 parents living in Ontario who had at least one child under 18, asking about the COVID-19 vaccine and their resettlement experience. Parents who were unsure or unwilling were classed as hesitant.

About 15 percent of parents were hesitant. Good mental health lowered the odds of hesitancy, while lacking a family doctor raised them sharply. Parents who needed an interpreter but were rarely offered one were also more hesitant. Acceptance among these refugees was far higher than in Syria itself, which the authors credit to health care access and settlement support.
pmc-11622679:
Fang, Wu, and Tong wrote a letter in twenty twenty-four about a study that linked mouth habits to jaw joint pain. The first study asked people in the general public about habits such as teeth grinding. It found links between those habits and pain in the jaw joint. The letter writers praise the work, then raise four points of doubt for readers to weigh.

They note that self-reports can be wrong, since people may not know they grind their teeth in sleep. They also say a one-time survey cannot prove which came first, the habit or the pain. Missed factors and a short pain checklist add more doubt. The letter urges care in reading the first study.
pmc-11623079:
Debayan Dutta and Ravi Yadav review in 2024 what is known about dystonia when it stems from immune system disorders. In dystonia, muscles contract on their own and twist the body into odd postures. It can arise from gene faults, infections, drugs, or the immune system turning on the body.

Immune linked cases can appear alone or mixed with other movement problems, and they can start fast. The pattern for spotting and treating them has never been set out in a structured way. The pair gathered 103 papers, most of them case reports, and summed up the shared traits of patients, signs, and tests. Their aim is a clear approach a doctor can follow when immune disease is the suspected cause. A firm map of a rare problem can cut delay in care.
pmc-11623479:
Jingfa Ma, Hu Liu, and Lingxiao Chen simulate shared self-driving electric cars as a cure for city congestion, in a 2024 study. Their model runs on the MATSim platform with a Shanghai baseline. The team varied vehicle range, charging speed, and power supply style to see what drives uptake of the shared fleet.

Longer range and faster charging slightly cut use of the shared cars, by 2.5 percent, since current specs already cover daily trips in the city. Swapping battery packs instead of plugging in did not shift travel habits much either. The lesson cuts against hype: once a fleet is good enough, more hardware brings little. City planners may gain more from service design than from bigger batteries.
pmc-11624279:
Juarez and co-authors publish in a 2024 author correction a completed acknowledgements section for their radiation safety model of the ITER fusion reactor. The correction states that some funding information had been omitted from the original article. The replacement text credits the partners who built the reactor model across nine countries.

It details the ITER contract under which the work ran, a consortium led by a Spanish distance university with two engineering firms, and regional and university funding lines for the team. Only the acknowledgements change; the model and its safety findings are untouched by the notice.
pmc-11624779:
Children with developmental coordination disorder move clumsily and lose balance, and without help the struggles follow them into adult life. Jiaxin Gao and seven co-authors set out a 2024 trial protocol testing Baduanjin, a gentle traditional Chinese exercise set, as therapy for these children.

Sixty children will be split by lot: one group adds Baduanjin training to health education, the other gets education alone, for eight weeks. A standard motor battery and a balance platform measure movement change, while a brain-scanning cap records blood flow in movement areas during tasks. The team will test whether brain activation and connection changes track the motor gains. The protocol is registered in advance, as trial reports should be.
pmc-11625079:
Rodrigues and co-authors review past studies in this 2024 paper on two beam treatments for a rare skull base tumor. The tumor grows slowly but comes back often, and surgery near the skull base is risky. Both beam types aim strong doses at the tumor while sparing nearby tissue, so the team compares their results.

The authors pool fourteen studies with more than a thousand patients in total. Five-year tumor control and survival were much the same for both beam types. One beam showed a small edge in tumor control at three years. Checks for hidden bias in the pooled data raised some care flags. The authors call for case-by-case choices and more direct head-to-head studies.
pmc-11625679: Allahdad Khan and co-authors present a 2024 case report on small cell lung cancer. The cancer appears here with two serious problems at once. Fluid builds up around the lung, and the large vein to the heart is blocked. Both problems can threaten breath and blood flow. The authors call the pairing rare. Care needs speed and teamwork across specialties, as the short report stresses.
pmc-11626479:
Carolina Amelunxen and co-authors tested in 2024 whether simple fact boxes help doctors judge lung cancer screening. The boxes lay out benefits and harms in plain numbers. The team surveyed 136 Austrian physicians online. Each doctor gave estimates before and after seeing a fact box, with some also seeing a picture array of icons.

After the fact box, doctors were far more likely to give estimates in the right range. The gain was largest among those who had not favored screening at first. Adding the icon array brought no clear extra gain. The authors say clear formats can sharpen the advice doctors give patients. They call for tests in other settings.
pmc-11628379:
Jingqi Lin and co-authors review a rare inherited brain disease, published in 2024, tied to a gene that moves lipids between cell membranes. VPS13A disease, also called chorea-acanthocytosis, causes progressive brain degeneration plus spiky red blood cells. The gene's protein forms bridge like channels at membrane contact sites, yet how losing it produces both blood and brain signs remains unclear.

The review gathers recent work on the protein's role in cell lipid traffic and on how its loss may injure neurons and red cells. It also catalogues wet biomarkers, measurable substances in blood or spinal fluid, that could track the disease. For a disorder this rare, the authors aim to give clinicians and researchers one clear map of mechanism and measurement.
pmc-11628579:
Pablo Gumiel-Campos studies the water pipes of El Escorial monastery in a 2024 article. The vast sixteenth century site in Spain held many fountains and tanks. A large pipe network fed them all, yet its full layout was not well known.

Gumiel-Campos pairs old written sources on water with a list of the stone remains still on site. From those two strands he draws a fresh map of the supply network with mapping software. The map gives a sharper, fuller view of how water moved through the royal house. It adds plumbing to the known design skill of the famed building.
pmc-11628979:
Violence from patients and visitors is common in Chinese hospitals, yet nurses rarely file reports. Jianzheng Cai and co-authors surveyed 3,363 nurses in Jiangsu; over half had faced such violence in a year, but only about sixteen percent of those reported it. The study maps what helps and what hinders.

Reporting rose in specialized hospitals, in emergency, outpatient, and pediatric posts, and where hospitals visibly encouraged reporting and protected staff. Male nurses and those who had heard of the problem before also reported more. The pattern frames silence less as personal reluctance than as a system property, something management can redesign.
pmc-11629679:
