Wiesje Pelkmans and Juan Domingo Gispert comment on the role of astrocytes in Alzheimer's disease in a 2024 paper. Astrocytes are support cells in the brain that react to the plaques and tangles of the disease. Their reaction is now seen as a driver of decline, not a side effect.

The commentary discusses a study linking a blood marker of astrocyte reaction to disease signs and thinking loss. The marker rises early, even before symptoms, alongside plaque build-up. New diagnostic rules now count inflammation markers beside the classic plaque and tangle signs. The authors argue that astrocyte reaction helps set the pace of the disease and may guide early detection.
pmc-11629879:
Alexandra Musten and Patrick O'Byrne read HIV self-testing's popularity as a symptom in a 2024 commentary from Canada. Their Ottawa program, GetaKit, mails self-tests ordered online, launched as clinics closed during the pandemic and the device won approval, with goals of appropriate, accessible testing linked to care.

Uptake stayed strong, and a steady stream of users had never tested before, often younger people from the communities most affected by HIV. The authors argue the demand says less about the gadget than about primary care: many people at risk simply lack a regular clinician. Self-testing fills a gap the system left open.
pmc-11631479:
Subas Neupane and co-authors follow how satisfied midlife workers feel about juggling job and family across sixteen years. Their 2024 study uses a Helsinki survey of city employees first interviewed at ages forty to fifty and re-surveyed three times. Growth models sorted the workers into satisfaction paths rather than assuming one average trend.

Two paths appeared: a low satisfaction group holding just under half of women and over half of men, and a high group. Young children pushed women toward the low path, while school-age children oddly eased men's membership in it. Strong emotional well-being protected both sexes from the low path. Good physical functioning helped women as well. The authors show reconciliation is a long arc, shaped by children's ages and the worker's own reserves.
pmc-11631979:
Tianhao Wang and seven co-authors upgrade aluminum scrap into a high-strength alloy without melting it, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Recycling scrap aluminum by melting saves energy but locks the metal into middling grades. Their solid-phase method alloys the scrap while it stays solid.

Starting from a common extrusion-grade scrap, they blended in copper, zinc, and magnesium. The result matched a premium aircraft-grade alloy in makeup and behavior. Tiny clusters and nanoscale strengthening particles packed the structure, more than tripling yield and peak strength. Because the process is scalable and can be tuned on demand, the authors offer it as a model for upcycling many metals from scrap.
pmc-11634079:
Xianghui Zeng and co-authors chart twenty years of research on autophagy in heart muscle disease, in this 2024 paper. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, and its role in cardiomyopathy has drawn intense study. A map of who publishes what, and where the field heads, had been missing.

The team mined a major database for papers from 2004 to 2023 and charted them with mapping software. More than twenty-two hundred papers came from seventy countries and over ten thousand authors. China produced over half the output, while the United States led in influence measures. The analysis names hot topics and frontiers for the next wave of work.
pmc-11634379:
Lucas Gallo and co-authors write a letter on analysis choices in aesthetic surgery research. Their letter replies to a survey study of how well people can spot labiaplasty from images. That study asked lay adults and surgeons to judge operative status from photos. Both groups had trouble telling who had surgery. The letter grants the work merit but faults two of its stats choices.

First, the study used a correlation tool built for smooth numeric data on rank-scale answers. Rank-based tools fit such data better, the letter argues. Second, the study leaned on P values alone to claim or deny links. Small P values can mark trivial links, above all in large samples. Effect sizes should ride beside them so readers can judge real weight.
pmc-11634779:
Andreas Apseros and co-authors present a three-dimensional X-ray method that maps crystal grains and defects inside solid materials, in a 2024 paper. What a material can do depends on its grain layout and flaws. Older tools could only probe surfaces, thin slices, or coarse scales, and often destroyed the sample.

The new method uses polarised X-rays to read crystal direction voxel by voxel without cutting the sample. A catalyst material key to acid production was mapped at fine scale throughout its bulk. Grains and three kinds of grain boundary were located, and the birth and death of defects were watched. The authors say the method opens studies of working materials under real conditions.
pmc-11634879:
Wei-wei Zhu and seven co-authors published a cardiology study in twenty twenty-four on why patients with chronic coronary syndrome run out of breath and strength on exertion. Ninety patients underwent exercise testing with simultaneous heart ultrasound, letting the team watch the heart work at peak effort rather than only at rest.

Patients split by whether their oxygen uptake reached eighty-five percent of predicted. The exercise-intolerant group showed weaker squeeze and relaxation at peak and less stroke volume reserve. Two measures, a peak filling-pressure ratio and the change in stroke volume index, independently flagged intolerance, with defined cutoffs. Resting measurements, including myocardial work, mostly failed to separate the groups. The lesson: hearts must be judged under load.
pmc-11635179:
Seagrass meadows host small shrimp-like animals called amphipods, whose mix of species shifts with the seasons. Sandra Navarro-Mayoral and ten co-authors track those shifts across a sweep of coast where temperate water turns subtropical, in this 2024 study. Nine meadows of the same seagrass were sampled four times a year from 2016 to 2018, along about two thousand kilometers of latitude.

The team split change over time into species replacement and species loss, then asked what drives each. Both the meadow's own structure, a living driver, and plain environmental conditions were put to the test. Their title names the headline: how stable the habitat stays shapes the pattern of change over time. The study argues that forecasts of coastal life under climate pressure must track the meadows themselves, not just the water around them.
pmc-11635379:
Halpin, Heatley, and Price wrote a reply, published in 2024, to comments on their study of flare-ups in a chronic lung disease. The disease, known as COPD, damages the airways and flares in episodes that can land patients in hospital. Their study had asked whether flare-ups before diagnosis predict later ones. Two commentators raised the known point that, in patients already diagnosed and treated, past flare-ups best predict future risk. The reply accepts that point and sharpens what was new.

Their study was the first, they note, in people not yet diagnosed. Even a single flare-up before diagnosis marked higher risk over the next year. More or worse early flare-ups meant still higher risk. Blood cell counts before diagnosis added further signal. The reply argues for acting on that early warning, rather than waiting for the diagnosis to make the risk plain.
pmc-11635479:
Hannah Thieron and a large consortium offered practical guidance in two thousand twenty-four for isolating tiny membrane bubbles, called extracellular vesicles, in plant and microbe research. These bubbles carry messages between plants and microbes, but plant material brings special pitfalls that animal-cell guides do not cover.

Advice runs step by step through study design, fine-tuning, quality checks, and ways to raise yield and purity while keeping results repeatable. The guidance distills recent papers plus the group's own experience across many plant and microbe systems. Newcomers to the field gain a field-tested starting protocol, and the wider community gains shared standards to compare results.
pmc-11635679:
Rodrigo Duarte and co-authors synthesize glowing dye molecules that latch onto a blood protein in a 2024 study. The carboxylated merocyanine dyes were built by joining a benzoic acid piece to three different charged ring systems. Such dyes serve as probes whose light shifts when they bind targets.

The dyes absorb near-ultraviolet to blue light and fluoresce blue to green with wide Stokes shifts. Quantum calculations mapped their electronic character, and heat tests showed stability to two hundred degrees. Electrochemistry placed their energy levels in a narrow band gap window. Quenching tests proved strong, static binding to serum albumin, and docking simulations agreed. Probe development gains candidates.
pmc-11635879:
Ting-Wei Kao and co-authors pool past studies to judge a blood test ratio used to screen for a hormone disorder in this 2024 paper. The disorder, primary aldosteronism, is a treatable cause of hard-to-control high blood pressure. The ratio compares two hormones, but cut-off values vary between clinics.

The team gathered eighteen studies with over seven thousand patients with high blood pressure. About fifteen percent of them had the disorder. The ratio caught most true cases and cleared most healthy ones, giving strong overall accuracy. Its performance held steady across regions, sexes, and ages, and whether either form of the second hormone was measured. The authors back the ratio as a sound first screen and call for work to fine-tune its use.
pmc-11636179:
Toan Thanh Vo and six co-authors checked how well MRI finds meniscus tears when the knee's cruciate ligament is also torn, in a 2024 study. Meniscus damage often travels with anterior cruciate ligament injury, and missed tears grow harder to repair. The team ran a prospective study of 185 patients at a Vietnamese hospital whose ligament tears were confirmed by keyhole surgery, then compared scan readings against what the scope actually showed.

Overall agreement on whether a meniscus tear existed was 69 percent, a low match. Naming the exact spot agreed only 57 percent of the time. Region and tear-shape calls scored higher, above 85 and 89 percent accuracy, but still modest statistical agreement. The authors advise caution in ruling meniscus injury in or out from MRI alone in these knees.
pmc-11636779: Lindsay Key reports on children's exposure to phthalates and their replacement chemicals through everyday skin care products such as soaps and lotions. The central finding highlighted is that racial and ethnic differences in these exposures appear to begin in childhood, mirroring patterns seen in adults. The piece draws attention to personal care products as an early-life source of these chemicals and to the unequal exposure burden that starts young.
pmc-11637479:
Borja Gracia Tello and co-authors built a score that reads nailfold scans for disease patterns, in a study published in 2024. The scans show tiny blood vessel loops at the base of the nail and help identify a hardening skin disease and its relatives. Expert eyes sort the scans, but judges often disagree. The team took 851 scans whose patterns nine experts had agreed on, and let software measure each feature.

Set thresholds for loop counts, shares of abnormal loops, giant loops, twists, and bleeding separated the patterns well. The four-rule score distinguished the main disease from the rest with high accuracy. Finer rules separated early, active, and late stages, and separated normal from abnormal scans in the remaining cases. Scores rose further when the experts had fully agreed. The authors present the score as an aid for clinics that does not depend on a single judge.
pmc-11638079:
Zeyad Khalaf Maded and co-authors test a skin gel for psoriasis in rats in this 2024 study. The gel holds two drugs that calm a skin enzyme linked to the disease. The drugs are packed into tiny drops and mixed into a gel so they stay on the skin and pass into it better.

Rats were split into seven groups and treated for 16 days after skin disease was triggered with a cream. Groups got the mixed gel, single-drug gels, a plain mixed gel, or a standard ointment. Blood and skin were checked at the end. Early results point to the mixed form as a strong option, and the study sets out how each group compared.
pmc-11638479:
Yang Zheng and five co-authors hunt vessel-growth gene marks for osteoarthritis through gene reads and learn tools. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Vessel growth plays a key role in joint wear growth. Gene sets from sick and well joint pads were sifted with group and vessel gene lists.

Six genes were picked by three learn ways from a small start set. Four genes scored high truth on two data sets as test marks. Path and immune reads tied the marks to cell waste paths and two immune cell kinds. Drug guesses and lab checks on fresh pads backed three marks in full and one in part. The team flags them as test and cure aims.
pmc-11638579:
Akshatha Bhat and Venugopalan Krishna Kumar report an Ayurveda case for cluster headache prevention in this 2024 paper. Their patient had suffered attacks for thirteen years: sudden, maximal pain once or twice daily for forty days each winter season. Standard scores showed severe impact on life and mood.

Treatment combined a leech therapy session, medicated ghee drops in the nose for seven days, and three oral preparations. After treatment, the seasonal attacks stopped. Headache impact scores fell to the lowest range, and depression, anxiety, and stress scores all dropped to zero. No side effects were noted. The authors present the case as a preventive path worth further study.
pmc-11638779:
Essy Mozaffari and co-authors check an antiviral's real world record in a 2024 study. Patients with weak immune systems face the worst odds from COVID-19, yet trials enroll few of them. Hospital records from a large US database filled the gap. The study covered the Omicron era, from late 2021 into early 2024, matching treated and untreated patients by their risk profiles.

The main readout was death in hospital from any cause. Subgroups by immune condition type were also examined. Real world evidence of this kind guides doctors who must treat exactly the patients trials leave out. The matched design tries to keep the comparison honest despite the messy source data.
pmc-11639779:
Lisa-Marie Walther and co-authors measure immune cell shifts under social stress in a 2024 study. Stress is thought to redistribute immune cells in the blood. Past work lacked a fair placebo-style control for the stress task itself. The team compared a lab stress test with a matched low-threat twin task.

Sixty-four healthy young men took part in the study. Thirty-eight faced the stress test and twenty-six the control task. Blood and saliva were sampled before and up to thirty minutes after. Total white cells, monocytes, and lymphocytes rose more under true stress. One cell type rose under both tasks, showing it was not stress-specific. A stress hormone, epinephrine, drove most of the rise and fall pattern. Blood volume shifts also helped explain the later decline. The authors stress the value of active controls in stress research.
pmc-11639879:
Martina Anto-Ocrah and four co-authors survey US women of child bearing age on COVID vaccine doubt and future will. These women faced a paradox, wary of the shot yet at higher risk from the illness. Near one thousand women across the land filled the survey.

Doubt ran higher in younger parents, non white women, and those with less school. Long term smokers doubted more than never smokers. Doubt clustered in the Southeast and Midwest. Top fears were side effects and fertility. High felt risk and stress from COVID each foretold future will to take the shot.
pmc-11639979:
Ismail Gumussoy and co-authors measure a skull bone joint in patients with jaw mismatch, in a study published in 2024. The joint, the occipital condyle, links skull to spine, and its growth ties into how the whole face and skull base form. The team compared people whose lower jaw juts forward with those whose bite is in the standard class.

They measured seventy-six scans, half from each group, for the joint's width, length, height, and angle. The forward-jaw group had a clearly smaller joint angle and a shorter joint length than the standard group. Other measures matched between groups, and the left joint's angle exceeded the right in everyone. The authors call this early evidence that skull base shape and jaw class grow together.
pmc-11640079:
Francesca Farina and Nicola Cirillo weigh what oral cancer screening can truly deliver, and where its numbers mislead, in work from twenty twenty-four. The mouth is easy to inspect, which makes screening look obviously wise. Yet proof that it saves lives is oddly thin.

The one large randomized trial shows only limited mortality reduction from population screening. Detection rates can climb while deaths barely move, a gap the authors tie to familiar screening biases and flattering metrics. They call for sharper dentist training and new tools to support judgment calls. Screening should fold into wider oral health programs rather than stand alone, they argue.
pmc-11640179:
Manash Sarma, Subarna Chatterjee, and Mohammad Shahadat Hossain reviewed late-onset Alzheimer disease in 2024, covering causes, biomarkers, and machine learning for staging. The condition appears after age sixty-five and slowly impairs thinking, behaviour, and learning. Unlike the early-onset form, which is solely genetic, the late form has many contributing factors, making early diagnosis both harder and more important.

Sections weigh how well different biomarkers detect the disease and which stage a patient has reached. Deep learning, especially convolutional networks, dominates the machine learning work surveyed. The authors also discuss generative tools and oversampling methods that create more training data where real cases are scarce.
pmc-11640279:
Dorota Olczak-Kowalczyk and co-authors measure gum disease and its causes in young children in Poland. Gingivitis shows as red, swollen gums that bleed on probing, yet it causes no loss of tissue attachment and often goes unnoticed. The study covers healthy children aged three, five, and seven years.

In total 3,558 children were examined, and 12.25 percent had gingivitis. Parents answered questions on income, dental visits, hygiene, and diet, and dentists scored tooth decay. Gum disease linked to decay load in older boys and was more common in young boys than girls. The findings stress early plaque control and regular dental visits in preschool and early school years.
pmc-11640379:
Guillermo Fondevila leads a team in a 2024 study of bread by-product and maize silage as feeds for mealworm larvae. The larvae of Tenebrio molitor are farmed as a source of protein. What they are raised on sets both their growth and their cost, so cheap farm leftovers are worth a close test.

Four matched diets were set: a control of grain, bran, and soybean meal, and three where part of the grain and bran gave way to bread by-product, with or without silage. Larvae on the control and bread diets grew best. The bread group also ate the most, and the no-silage diets turned feed to weight with the best ratio.
pmc-11640479:
Serena Reggi and co-authors profile a biochar made from vine pruning waste in two thousand twenty-four for use in animal feed. Biochar can aid gut health and cut farming's footprint, but its effects vary with feedstock and production, causing uneven results between farms. A full chemical profile helps predict how a given batch will behave.

Using advanced mass spectrometry, the team mapped the extract's molecules, finding rich phenolic compounds among several classes. The extract slowed two harmful Escherichia coli strains by about twenty-nine and sixteen percent and interfered with their chemical chatter. It also fed beneficial Lactobacillus strains unevenly by species, a prebiotic signal. The authors argue such profiling should precede in vivo trials so feed trials start from a known material.
pmc-11640679:
Ekaterina Olkhov-Mitsel and co-authors validate two gene sequencing panels for finding gene amplifications in solid tumors. Such extra gene copies can guide cancer treatment, but detection must be trustworthy in real-world samples. The team checked the panels on hundreds of preserved tumor samples of varying purity. Standard quality metrics gave near-perfect positive predictive value.

Sensitivity fell sharply when tumor cells made up less than 30 percent of a sample. Richer samples yielded far more amplification calls per sample. In a focused test on 121 uterine cancers with known ERBB2 status, a threshold blending amplification and tumor purity reached 79 percent sensitivity with perfect specificity. It could spare about a third of uncertain cases from extra confirmatory testing. A second cohort confirmed the pattern. The authors present both the strengths and the limits of panel testing for copy number changes.
pmc-11640879:
Tiny membrane bubbles harvested from fruit can carry useful cargo for food and cosmetics, and what clings to them may be as valuable as the bubbles themselves. Maria Gomez-Molina and co-authors study vesicles from lemon fruit in this 2024 paper, asking how two farming sprays change the cargo. One spray adds zinc; the other is a plant hormone signal that wakes defense chemistry.

Zinc spraying raised the fruit's phenolic compounds, including three named acids and the flavonoid hesperidin, by about a fifth. The hormone spray boosted citrate and vitamin C, which bound tightly to the vesicles and tracked with stronger antioxidant action in lab tests. The bubbles thus arrive pre-loaded with health-linked compounds, and the loading can be steered from the field. The work adds value to one of the world's most grown fruit crops.
pmc-11641279:
Resveratrol, a plant compound in grapes, shows promise against memory loss but absorbs poorly. Maria Lazarova and co-authors pack it into tiny polymer bubbles called micelles. Rats given a dementia-like drug injury received the micellar form or the plain compound. Maze tests measured spatial memory. Brain chemistry was checked in the cortex and hippocampus.

The micelles, about 33 nanometers wide, loaded the drug at 79 percent efficiency. The packed form protected memory better than the plain drug. It also beat it on a key enzyme target and on a survival protein balance in brain tissue. The authors present micelle delivery as a way to rescue a fragile natural compound.
pmc-11641379:
Lorenza Brusini and colleagues link patterns of cortical shape change in Alzheimer's disease to gene expression. The disease builds up amyloid-beta and tau proteins in set parts of the brain, but how that links to cortical remodeling was not clear. The team built networks of morphometric similarity, mapping how alike brain region shapes are, in over a hundred amyloid- and tau-positive subjects and a larger negative group.

With gene data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas, the team matched gaps in regional similarity with gene expression. The gene tied most strongly to the changes was BCHE, linked to amyloid balance. Enriched terms flagged the immune response as a key process. The cell types named were astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocyte precursors, the brain's support and immune cells.
pmc-11641579:
Premature babies on ventilators need their airways cleared, and two hands-on techniques compete for the job. Jacqueline Carla de Macedo and co-authors randomized forty-three ventilated preterm infants between standard chest physiotherapy and a gentler method that prolongs the outward breath to move secretions. Each baby received four sessions over consecutive days.

Both methods raised oxygen levels and breathing volumes in every session. Heart and breathing rates also rose briefly after treatment in both groups. The gentler technique finished ahead on the measures parents would care about: higher oxygen saturation afterward and clearly lower pain scores. Breathing rate also settled better across sessions. The authors recommend it as the kinder option.
pmc-11641679: Tamás Visnovitz offers a short overview of extracellular vesicles, in a 2024 article on their biology and medical uses. Vesicles are tiny particles wrapped in a fat-based bilayer that sit in the space outside cells. The text stresses one plain trait: they cannot copy themselves. The overview's title frames the two themes it covers, how these particles work in the body and how they might serve as therapy tools.
pmc-11641779:
Selma Lancman and co-authors review how writers define mental health in relation to work, in a study published in 2024. The link between health and work has picked up many meanings over time. Those meanings are not always the same, yet they are often treated as if they were.

Following set review rules, the team searched six data bases and chose a small set of papers for close reading. Most of those papers did not define the core concept at all. Few treated job terms or the work setting as a source of stress. The authors warn that weak, unclear ground terms weaken both study and practice in the field.
pmc-11641979:
Dewan Md Sumsuzzman and co-authors compare glucosamine pairings for knee osteoarthritis pain in a 2024 review. Glucosamine is a popular supplement for sore knees, yet studies and guidelines disagree on whether it works, alone or combined.

The team pooled thirty trials with over five thousand patients in a network analysis. Glucosamine with omega-3 oils cut pain the most against placebo, with glucosamine plus ibuprofen close behind. A triple mix with two other supplements also helped, on weaker evidence. No other pairing passed the bar for a meaningful gain. The omega-3 pairing also ranked best on side effects, the authors report.
pmc-11642179:
Joan Lorente-Piera and co-authors map a rare ear disorder across its forms in a 2024 cohort study. Third mobile window syndrome arises when extra openings appear in the bone capsule of the inner ear. Its symptoms and test results can mimic Ménière's disease, which makes diagnosis tricky.

Records from a specialist ear center over several years covered varied opening sites. Hearing and balance tests charted each form, and four treatment plans were compared for response. The team also checked scans for fluid swelling inside the ear, called endolymphatic hydrops. Grouping cases by anatomy may explain why the same label behaves so differently. Better maps should lead to better matched treatment.
pmc-11642279:
Goran Malenkovic and co-authors present a 2024 pilot study on scan staging for early cervical cancer in Serbia. Before surgery, doctors need to know tumor size and whether nodes hold cancer. The team looked back at 62 patients who had a PET-CT scan before treatment from 2016 to 2020. Most tumors were of the common squamous type and at an early stage.

Scan tumor sizes matched exam sizes closely. For finding the main tumor, scan accuracy was near 89 percent, with perfect scores on ruling in disease. Agreement with tissue results was good for the main tumor and moderate for nodes. Node checks were weaker, with lower sensitivity. The authors back the scan for staging before surgery.
pmc-11642379:
Jihye Lee and Hee-Young Yoon studied in 2024 links between air pollution exposure and white blood cell counts in South Korea, using a national health survey of nearly fifty-five thousand people. White cell counts reflect inflammation, but how pollution timing matters was unclear. Exposure was averaged over spans from one day to five years for six pollutants.

Patterns split by pollutant and by time span. Some fine particles linked to lower counts over short spans but higher counts over years. Nitrogen dioxide and carbon monoxide mostly linked to higher counts, while ozone and sulfur dioxide leaned the other way in short spans. The authors stress that pollution's effect on inflammation depends on both the pollutant and the exposure window.
pmc-11642479:
Manuela De Michele and co-authors study secondary injury around a brain bleed in human patients, focusing on oxidative stress and a vessel-tightening substance. After bleeding inside the brain, the tissue around the clot can suffer low blood flow and further ischemic damage, worsening outlook. The team tracked blood markers at three points after onset.

A marker of oxidant enzyme activation was higher at admission in patients who went on to show ischemic lesions around the bleed, and it tracked with worse swelling later. Lesion development also went with larger bleeds and more swelling and shift. The vessel substance showed an opposite link with later bleed size, which the authors tie to its tightening effect on the torn vessel. They propose oxidant activation helps drive the secondary injury.
pmc-11642679:
Djilani Belila, Belal Khaldi, and Oussama Aiadi put forth a wavelet grain tool to sort flaws on the face of steel. Their 2024 study aims at true, fast grade checks that hold down the cost of steel work.

Wavelet steps split a pic into parts at more than one size scale, and catch both broad and fine grain in the pic. Facts and grain traits are drawn from those parts, and then a pick step keeps the traits that split best. Tests ran on two known sets of steel flaw pics used as a yard stick. The new way beat the best known ways on both sets, with right calls past ninety-eight in each hundred in each case. It stayed true with just a small set of taught pics, which fits shops and plants where large sets of tagged pics are hard to get.
pmc-11643079:
Three engineers in Poland offer a fast way to judge how much load a crumbling concrete manhole can still bear, in a paper published in 2024. Sewage manholes decay in uneven ways, and a full three-dimensional computer model of the damage takes millions of elements and too much time. The repair they study lines the manhole with plastic layers and foam to restore its shape. The question is how much strength that repair really returns.

Their method averages the wall's properties section by section, so a few hundred shell elements can stand in for the full model. Surface scans of the damage feed the calculation. The repaired sections regained up to seventy-six percent of their bending stiffness in the worst-corroded spots. Even so, the repair never fully restored the original strength. The authors pitch the shortcut as a practical tool for city maintenance crews.
pmc-11643279:
Zeming Sun and Minxia Shi set out in 2024 lab methods to prepare and test transformer oil with set levels of plant fiber particles. Transformer oil boosts insulation and cools power units. Fiber bits are a main factor in how the oil breaks down under high voltage, so labs need sound test routes.

Voltage tests can reveal oil quality and guide ways to raise insulation strength. The authors base their method on national standards and field practice. Steps cover both making oil with varied fiber levels and running the voltage test in the lab. The method aims for faster and more rigorous lab work.
pmc-11643479:
Sunlight can break down leftover antibiotics in water if the right catalyst is present, and a 2024 study by Haitao Ren and co-authors builds one from farm waste. The team coated thin sheets of a bismuth compound with carbon dots made from discarded corn stalks, adding a small amount of nitrogen.

The best mix destroyed 85 percent of a common veterinary antibiotic in forty minutes of visible light, four times the rate of the plain sheets. The dots pull electrons away, which keeps the light driven reaction running longer. Tests confirmed which reactive species did the damage. The work points toward cheap, green cleaners for polluted water.
pmc-11643579:
Xianbin Zhang and co-authors create a new thickener for the salty fluids used in oil and gas drilling. Calcium-based fluids are prized because they are dense and keep clay from swelling, but they lack gels strong enough to carry rock cuttings out of the well. The team built a branched polymer, called PAD-B, by linking two building blocks with a branching agent.

Tests show the branched version forms a web of interacting strands, giving it more shear strength than a straight-chain version at the same thickness. It also held up better under heat and in calcium-rich fluid. The authors say the stronger gel could help crews control fluid behavior in complex wells, where weak gels cause trouble.
pmc-11643679:
Pyszka and co-authors tweak light-cure fill blends for fixed tooth fills and test mass hold. Each year, vast host counts face tooth ills, chiefly rot and kin ills. That drives keen want for new blend fills that meet tooth rules. The team bent the fluid part of the blend in the work set. New spark parts, DQ1 to DQ5, rest on two ring frames in the work. A co-part based on a sulfur acid joins them in the set.

Stock parts gave way to a three-arm part, TMPTA, in the blends. Plain tooth glass served as the hard fill part in blends. Fifty-four round bits were made by the ISO 4049 guide line. Bits sat in fluids that fake the mouth in meal times. Soak, melt loss, and mass shifts were scored for each bit.
pmc-11643779:
Dandan Wang and co-authors brew silver nanoparticles with a medicinal root extract and test them against cancer cells and bacteria, in a 2024 study. Silver particles damage DNA and flood cells with oxidative stress, killing microbes and tumour cells alike, but chemical manufacturing is harsh. Green synthesis uses plant extracts as the factory. Here the extract came from the root of Chuanminshen, a traditional herb.

The resulting particles were fully characterised for size and charge. They fought bacteria, quenched free radicals, and killed several cancer cell lines in dishes, including stomach, colon, lung, and liver lines. Colon cancer cells responded best, dying by programmed cell death, and were studied in depth. The authors present the particles as a three-in-one candidate, antibacterial, antioxidant, and anticancer, made by a gentle route.
pmc-11643879:
Aggeliki Triantafyllou and co-authors feed fish oil to rats modeling postmenopausal bone loss in a 2024 study. Omega-3 fats help the heart, but skeletal effects wobble between studies. Forty rats, with or without ovary removal, took fish oil or corn oil daily for four months.

Fish oil blunted bone density loss in the ovary-removed group and made thigh bones significantly harder to break. Blood cholesterol fell in both fish oil groups. An inflammatory signal dropped sharply where measured, while other immune markers barely moved. Not every parameter improved, but the pattern leans protective for bone strength and blood lipids in this model.
pmc-11643979:
Zhang and co-authors build a better air cathode for microbial fuel cells that eat pesticide wastewater and make electricity from it. The cathode's job, pulling oxygen into the reaction, stalls without a good catalyst. Their 2024 design grows an iron-based catalyst inside hollow carbon shells made from a leaf-like scaffold, trapping metal particles as the scaffold's zinc boils away.

The finished catalyst offers mixed-valence iron, a large surface, nitrogen doping, and a junction that speeds electron flow. Cells fitted with it reached a peak power density about eighty-three percent above bare carbon cathodes. They also cleared eighty percent of the pesticide glyphosate from the water, against twenty-three percent for the bare version. The authors present the confined-structure recipe as a route toward practical, self-powered wastewater treatment.
pmc-11644279:
Juan Yang and co-authors asked in 2024 whether losing weight can offset a genetic tilt toward fatty liver disease in Chinese adults. More than ten thousand people joined the snapshot analysis and six thousand the follow-up. Genetic risk was scored from four known gene variants, and weight change patterns were tracked between visits.

Risk rose in steps with both body mass and genetic score. Losing weight cut the risk of fatty liver by about seventy percent versus staying overweight, and liver enzyme risks fell by similar shares. The absolute gains from weight loss ran largest in people with the highest genetic scores. Genes and weight also interacted on enzyme levels. The authors conclude a healthy weight protects everyone, and protects the genetically loaded most.
pmc-11644379:
Rui Zheng and co-authors build, in 2024 work, a way for guard robots to find their place when smoke and dust blind cameras and lasers. Short-wave radar can see through such air, so the team built the robot's sense of place on radar, with a method that finds the centre of a sparse cloud of points.

Radar alone left an error of about eleven units of length in their tests. They then fused radar with motion sensors that track the robot from inside, joined by a filter that weighs both streams. The fused system cut the mean error to about eight units, and its weights settled as the runs went on. The team says fusion gives the steadier, sharper fix that patrol work in bad air needs.
pmc-11644479:
Yi-Cheng Lo and seven co-authors design a sound monitor that fits on tiny factory chips, in a 2024 paper. Listening for odd machine sounds can flag failure early. Prior systems were accurate but too hungry for small devices.

The team first tackles signal variation, which confuses sound detectors. Light signal processing steps steady the input without heavy cost. They then prune the model with memory limits in mind, so it fits a microcontroller. Tests on a standard machine sound dataset showed good accuracy with small resource use. The design suits the tight budgets of industrial edge devices.
pmc-11644679:
Do-Yun Jung and co-authors tuned a sound-based crack measure for nuclear plant piping in a 2024 study. Acoustic emission sensors listen to the tiny sounds cracks make as they grow. The team bent welded samples that mimic a reactor's cold leg pipe, loading them in steps while recording emissions. Stable and unstable crack growth showed distinct signatures tied to the Kaiser and Felicity effects, two classic behaviors of stressed material.

The b-value, a slope summarizing the emission sizes, worked best when computed from signal energy rather than peak height, since energy resists fading over distance. The authors propose adding this simple analysis to the plant's leak monitoring system for real-time, quantitative crack tracking, with wider industrial use in view.
pmc-11644779:
Bruno Valades-Aguilar and co-authors test how cleaning chitosan changes its effect on human immune cells in a 2024 study. Chitosan, a natural polymer, must be cleaned of protein for medical use. Source and cleaning can change its weight, chemistry, and leftover protein, which in turn shape how it steers immune cells such as monocytes and macrophages.

Two brands were cleaned and made into nanoparticles. Cleaned chitosan gave smaller particles, since the cleaning cuts the polymer chain. At a low dose, particles from cleaned chitosan lowered two surface marks tied to cell change. A signal linked to a pro swelling cell type was also detected. The work helps guide safe, useful biomaterials.
pmc-11644979:
Li Zeng and co-authors present a 2024 paper on an automated visual inspection system for cutting inserts made of cubic boron nitride, one of the hardest tool materials. Flaws on an insert's surface can ruin both the tool and the parts it machines, so factories inspect them closely. Human inspection is slow and inconsistent at this scale.

The system pairs a high-resolution industrial camera, tuned lighting, and a support board, then runs image-processing algorithms over the pictures. The authors compare several detection algorithms, studying how settings and dataset variety change accuracy. The goal is precise sorting of good inserts from flawed ones at production speed.
pmc-11645079:
Elena Barulina and co-authors design a tiny lens for sensing single molecules in 2024. Fluorescence from single molecules reveals their motion and count, but bench gear is bulky. A chip-sized version would suit bedside and field testing.

Their flat lens, built on a waveguide chip, focuses guided light at two colors into liquid samples. Segmented design makes the two focal spots overlap despite color shifts along the guide. Sensitivity should reach thousands of photons per second per molecule at modest drive rates. That suffices to measure molecule counts and diffusion in tiny samples, they show.
pmc-11646379:
Elliot Teo and co-authors review a light-based brain monitor in this 2024 paper. After severe brain injury, catching decline early saves lives and function. Exams and scans often spot trouble only after damage is done. Probes inside the skull work but are costly and risky. The optical brain pulse monitor offers a surface alternative.

The device shines light through the head and reads the pulse signal of the brain. It runs continuously at the bedside without breaking the skin. The review covers its design, working principles, and trial results from the past five years. Early findings support it as an early warning tool. Larger trials will decide its place in care.
pmc-11647179:
Miguel Angel Balbuena Madera and four co-authors report a heart attack with a surprise second finding, in a case report from 2024. A 56-year-old woman with rectal cancer arrived with chest pain and breathlessness and was confirmed to have a major heart attack. Three drug-coated stents opened her right coronary artery.

Scans during her stay then revealed a large hole between the heart's upper chambers, present since birth. Clots on imaging raised the idea that one had crossed the hole to cause the attack, a paradoxical embolism. The hole was closed through a catheter in the same admission, and she recovered without early problems. Full checks in cancer patients are the lesson.
pmc-11647379:
Wang and co-authors set out in 2024 the plan for a trial of added pre surgery training for older patients having spine fusion in China. Older patients often face poor diet, weak function, and memory loss on top of illness. Those traits drain reserves and slow healing after spine surgery.

The trial will enroll 164 patients aged 75 and older at three teaching hospitals. One group gets standard teaching and enhanced recovery care. The other gets a multi part training plan before surgery plus the same recovery care. Staff who score results will not know group labels. All patients are followed for 90 days after surgery.
pmc-11647879:
Lukas Köbbing, Yannick Kuhn, and Birger Horstmann model in 2024 why silicon battery particles show a slow voltage drift that lasts for days. Silicon is a high capacity material for the negative side of lithium ion batteries. It swells hugely as it takes in lithium, and its voltage lags in a loop that wastes energy as heat and clouds the charge gauge.

Oddly, after rest periods the voltage keeps relaxing for several days at least, which no past model explained. The team built a model that couples chemistry with mechanics in a core and shell picture. The silicon core takes in and sheds lithium each cycle, while the shell stands for the crust that forms on the particle. Their model accounts for the loop and the slow drift. Better physics for silicon could speed its use in real cells.
pmc-11648279:
Keli Kuang and co-authors publish a 2024 correction notice for their study of a platinum complex that targets G-quadruplex DNA structures in cancer. After publication, the team found that the captions for Figures 1 to 5 were mismatched. The notice prints the correct captions in full, replacing the wrong ones.

The corrected captions describe tests in ovarian cancer cells over 96 hours of treatment. They cover how three platinum compounds enter cells and reach nuclear and mitochondrial DNA. They also cover changes in mitochondrial DNA copy numbers and RNA levels. The study argues the lead compound harms cancer mitochondria by hitting G-rich DNA in two places.
pmc-11648879:
Thirumalai and co-authors reviewed how cell growth is controlled by contact and mechanics in 2024. Cells in a tissue stop multiplying when crowded, a brake called contact inhibition known for decades. What sets the brake's strength across tissues is still murky.

Contacts between cells depend on chemical signals and on physical forces from the surroundings. A broader idea ties the brake to feedback between sticky cadherin links and mechanical stress. Cell density looks like a master variable, yet density itself shifts with growth, division, and the stiffness of the surface below. Untangling those loops is the hard part. The review pairs dish experiments on kidney cells with theory to sort the factors.
pmc-11649379:
Hesham Tayel and co-authors tell a 2024 case story of a man with two heart valve narrowings at once. A stiff aortic valve sat above a thin membrane that also blocked flow, a rare pair that is hard to grade and treat. The patient was 78 years old and had long-term heart failure.

Heart scans and a camera study through the food pipe confirmed both blocks and their severity. Open surgery carried high risk for this patient, so the team placed a self-expanding valve through a tube instead. Guidance came from the camera study during the procedure. Three months later the man was doing well with no problems. The case shows tube-based valve care can work even when a membrane shares the block.
pmc-11649579:
Han Wang and co-authors study microbes living on the surface of a green seaweed in a 2024 paper. The seaweed needs nitrogen to grow, and nitrogen is often scarce. Whether surface microbes help the seaweed capture and use nitrogen was unclear.

The team isolated many bacterial strains and tracked how surface groups shifted with nitrogen levels. Two families stood out as central to nitrogen cycling and to the web of microbe links. A built community of four strains raised seaweed growth and its uptake of nitrogen and phosphorus. Sugar, protein, and green pigment rose as well, and genes for key processes became more active.
pmc-11649979:
Daniel Kolpek, Jaechang Kim, Hisham Mohammed, John Gensel, and Jonghyuck Park published a review in 2024 on how polymer nanoparticle traits shape immune effects, with spinal cord injury in view. Such particles can reprogram immune cells after injury, drawing them away and calming harmful signals. The review asks which physical traits drive that behavior.

Size, surface charge, weight, shape, surface decoration, and polymer makeup each steer how particles meet immune cells. The authors connect each trait to the immune shifts seen in injury models. They argue that tuning these properties could yield a real therapy for spinal cord injury and maybe other inflammatory diseases. The review maps design choices for future work.
pmc-11650079:
Nong and five co-authors evaluated digital screening for high blood pressure and diabetes among older adults in Vietnam in twenty twenty-four. Community self-help clubs for older people ran the screening using an app on tablets. Volunteers recorded participants' details during checks and health activities.

The team analyzed two screening rounds from fifty-nine clubs, covering about six thousand seven hundred screenings. Data completeness was very high, and measurement errors were under one percent. Yet risk factor details went unrecorded in nearly thirty percent of screenings. Volunteers praised the app for easier reporting and safer data. Barriers included poor age-friendliness, partial translation, tablet display issues, and limited digital skills. The authors recommend steady training, app fixes, and help from younger members.
pmc-11650179:
Erin Kaufman and nine colleagues compare health records of people with borderline personality disorder who died by suicide against several other groups, in a twenty twenty-four study. This disorder brings deep instability and a high suicide risk, with up to ten percent of patients dying by suicide. The team drew on a large suicide death resource and biobank with hundreds of diagnosis codes per person.

Those with the disorder who died by suicide carried more extra mental health diagnoses than suicides without it. They also had more recorded self-harm before death. Trauma-related stress disorder stood out against suicides with other personality disorders. The authors say these profiles sharpen the search for warning signs in a very high-risk group.
pmc-11651079:
Alberto Arcia and co-authors report a swallowed fishbone that pierced a man's stomach and reached his pancreas, in a case report from two thousand twenty-four. The man, aged fifty-two, arrived with belly pain and fever. Most swallowed objects pass safely, but sharp ones can tear the gut.

A scan found the bone stuck through the stomach wall into the sac beside the pancreas, with an abscess formed. Fast care matters once a tear occurs, the team stresses. Surgery removed the bone and the patient recovered well. Readers get a neat save from a rare tear, plus a reminder to scan early.
pmc-11651179:
Jitendra Mangwani, Claire Brockett, and Elise Pegg present a 2024 review editorial on osteochondral lesions of the talus, the ankle bone. These injuries damage cartilage and the bone beneath, usually after sprains or repeated trauma, most often on the inner dome of the bone. They are increasingly caught as imaging improves. Up to seventy percent of ankle sprains and fractures may leave such a lesion.

Left untreated, the lesions cause lasting pain, limit activity, and can lead to arthritis. Diagnosis is a weak point: a lesion hides easily behind a simple sprain label when imaging is skipped or unclear. The authors note that lingering pain after fracture surgery may often trace to a missed lesion. They survey causes, noting trauma links run stronger for outer-side lesions, and discuss how pain seems to arise from the damaged bone beneath.
pmc-11651479:
Gamze Demircioğlu and Hazal Genç test whether elastic therapeutic tape instantly eases a painful shoulder condition, in a randomized trial published in two thousand twenty-four. Rounded shoulders from imbalanced muscles can pinch structures under the shoulder blade, causing impingement pain. Kinesio taping is widely used but evidence for immediate effects is contested.

One hundred fourteen patients were randomized to real taping or a sham procedure, fifty-seven each, under double blinding. Pain was rated on a visual scale. Joint position sense was measured with an inclinometer, and posture scored on a standard chart. Everything was assessed immediately around application. Sham-controlled designs matter here because tape is conspicuous and expectation effects are strong.
pmc-11651679:
Lum Kastrati and co-authors built a home-based tool that estimates when menopause will start on its own, in a 2024 study. The tool looks ten years ahead and uses simple facts a woman can supply herself. It was shaped with data from a Swiss group of women. A Dutch group was then used to test it from the outside.

The team started with 11 known factors drawn from past research. They trimmed the list with two methods and checked the model with resampling. Scores showed how well the tool sorted women and how close its odds were to real outcomes. A home tool of this kind could help women and doctors plan care well before the change arrives.
pmc-11651979:
Chunxue Wu and co-authors compare two scan methods for picturing tangled blood vessels in the brain, in a study from 2024. The tangles, called arteriovenous malformations, can bleed and need careful grading before treatment. A newer silent scan method may show them better than the standard time-of-flight method.

Eighty-five patients had both scans on the same machine. Images were graded for quality, and the features and severity grades from each method were checked against a catheter-based reference. Patients were split by traits such as recent bleeding, prior treatment, tangle size, and tightness. The study weighs where the silent method helps and whether those traits change its edge. Such detail guides which scan to trust for planning.
pmc-11652279:
Wen-yuan Li and co-authors review deep brain stimulation for walking recovery after spinal cord injury in this 2024 paper. Electrical stimulation of deep brain spots can restart stepping circuits below an injury. Evidence from people and animals has grown quickly since the nineteen-nineties.

The review maps the brain targets in play, from the midbrain stepping region to thalamic and gray-matter sites used after injury. New tools like light-based cell control and whole-brain wiring maps are clarifying how the stimulation works at cell level. Scan-guided tuning plus classic rehab now forms an effective pairing. The authors call for standard animal protocols and more trials to firm up safety and benefit.
pmc-11652679:
Young Chan Kim and co-authors build vaccine particles for Mayaro virus in a 2024 study. Virus like particles are empty shells that train the immune system without causing disease. Under a cryo microscope, their Mayaro shells matched the true virus shape closely, with surface proteins in native form. Loose protein alone lacks that faithful shape.

Shots of the particles raised strongly neutralizing antibodies in animals. Two viral vector vaccines carrying the same proteins did so as well. Faithful shape seems to be what teaches the immune system best. Mayaro, a mosquito borne virus of the Americas, lacks a licensed vaccine, so a sound shell platform is a real step.
pmc-11653179:
Mestet Yibeltal Shiferaw leads a large team on skull base tumor surgery deaths. Their study from twenty twenty-four is set at two large centers in Ethiopia. They ask what traits link to death three months after surgery.

The team looked back at past cases of tumor removal. They used charts and stats tests to sort risk traits. Skull base tumors are hard to treat and can kill or harm. Clear risk marks could shape a strict care plan. The work also gives a base line for care upgrades in a low income setting.
pmc-11653579:
Masha Zee and co-authors follow how appreciation for end-of-life caregivers rose and fell during COVID. Their twenty twenty-four Dutch study, CO-LIVE, tracks the arc from public applause to letdown. Surveys ran at four points across eighteen months with three hundred two providers; interviews added depth.

The team measures how valued staff felt and how that shaped their well-being. Early cheers faded while workload stayed high. Providers describe what real appreciation would look like: staffing, voice, and thanks that last. A healthy workforce needs more than clapping. The findings warn leaders that praise without change curdles, and the cost lands on retention.
pmc-11653679:
Keumkyung Kuk and co-authors watch soft films dry, using tiny jelly spheres packed at a surface as their test case. Such films, from living membranes to paint coats, act in complex ways as they dry, with stakes for wound care, coatings, and printed goods.

Video and particle tracking show how two forces fight as the film dries: the spheres' grip on the base and the pull of the thin water film. A water shy base kept a truer copy of the packed pattern than a water loving one, above all with softer spheres. Tests in a balance that mimics drying, plus computer models, back the same read.
pmc-11653979:
Luis Miguel Martin-delosReyes and co-authors track how crash harm for car drivers in Spain changed from 1993 to 2020. Their 2024 study draws on the national traffic register, with more than two million drivers in crashes with injuries. The team splits trends by age, by calendar period, and by birth group.

Death risk fell in the first decade of this century, then leveled off after about 2013. Age showed a bent curve, with risk high for the young and the old. Drivers born in the early and middle 1950s carried the highest risk, and later birth groups did better. Women faced lower risk than men throughout. The authors link the birth group gain in part to better safety teaching.
pmc-11654179:
Pinyan Liu and co-authors present a 2024 paper on grouping patients when their data mix numbers with categories. Standard clustering handles one kind or the other, yet clinic records hold both lab values and yes-no traits. Their method upgrades the Gower distance, a classic mixed-data yardstick, by weighting each feature according to its importance.

The algorithm, called DAFI, keeps continuous and categorical features from drowning each other out. Five simulated data sets with shifting shares of important features tested its accuracy. Real nutrition survey records from the United States then tested its cohesion, including a look at gum disease links. Against thirteen rival techniques it held its own or better. Fair weighting, the authors argue, is what mixed data needed.
pmc-11654279:
Yin Lu and co-authors describe, in a 2024 case report, a rare kidney cancer whose cells take a signet ring shape, an odd form for this tumor type. The cancer lacks a working form of an enzyme that helps cells handle a waste acid. Such tumors are aggressive and often spread fast, with many deaths.

The patient was also suspected to carry an inherited syndrome tied to the same gene fault. Four months after diagnosis, the cancer had spread to the lungs. The authors say this is the first such case with signet ring features in this tumor type. They warn that the shape can mislead doctors toward other cancers, so this rare type belongs on the checklist.
pmc-11654379:
Saguin and four colleagues validate a teaching model for judging simulation based psychological first aid courses in twenty twenty-four. All trainers of the operations course in France were sent a fifteen point survey. The points span ease of use, usefulness, and acceptance. Fifty-nine trainers, over half the national pool, replied.

The three dimensions hung together well in the checks. Each tied to trainer motivation, and motivation tied to how many sessions ran per year. The full model explained most of the spread in motivation. The authors back the model for judging health teaching tools. It may travel beyond military settings, they add.
pmc-11654979:
Simon Schwab and co-authors built EXAM, a free dashboard for watching over donor kidneys while they travel. Kidneys from deceased donors suffer without blood during transport, and cold machine perfusion cuts the risk of a slow start after transplant. Yet no free software existed to analyze the perfusion data these machines record.

Written in R, the dashboard reads data from the LifePort kidney transporter and charts pressure, flow, resistance, and temperature over time, flagging odd runs for quality checks. The authors summarize two hundred fifty-five kidneys perfused in Switzerland between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-three, with a median perfusion of about five hours. Transplant centers can deploy the tool quickly, and an online viewer is public.
pmc-11655179:
Christian Liebsch and co-authors report a 2024 lab study on how scoliosis surgery hardware changes spine movement. Surgeons fix a curved spine with rods and screws, but how much the stiff gear alters motion in all directions was not well known. The team used six donated human spines with full rib cages. They bent each spine gently and tracked every segment with cameras.

Each spine was tested bare and then with rods fitted in two common patterns. The rods cut motion in the chest part of the spine in all directions. They also weakened the natural linked motion, where side bending pairs with twist. The authors warn that this loss of linked motion may, over time, cause the curve fix to fade or new bends to form near the hardware.
pmc-11655279:
Theresa Robertson and co-authors map what science knows about horse housing in a 2024 review. Horses are social, free-ranging animals, and stalls that deny movement and company can compromise welfare, yet the research base behind stable design had never been charted globally.

Screening two databases down to sixty peer-reviewed studies, the review found the work concentrated in Europe and the United States and growing fast, over half published in the last eight years. Studies favored more natural systems, especially keeping horses with companions. Most trials were short, so the authors call for longer studies and standardized welfare measures.
pmc-11655479:
Fatty liver disease and acid reflux often appear together, but which one drives the other has been unclear. Su and co-authors used genetics to test the direction of the link in 2024, in both European and East Asian populations. Their method treats gene variants as natural instruments, letting them probe cause in both directions.

In Europeans, fatty liver did not raise reflux risk, but reflux did raise liver fat and disease risk. In East Asians, a liver enzyme tied to fatty liver showed a two-way link with reflux. A second enzyme showed no clear effect. The authors say the pattern differs by ancestry and gives fresh leads for cross-population genetic research on the two conditions.
pmc-11655679:
Ahmed Alqutaibi and co-authors warn on vaping and mouth health in a 2024 article. Vapes are sold as a safer swap for smoking, and youth take them up fast. The mouth meets the vapor first, so it bears the first harm.

Vape use tracks with more tooth decay in the work they cite. Vapor shifts mouth germs toward the harmful kinds, which weakens gum hold. Gum health in users runs below that of non smokers. Mouth sores add to the list of harms. The authors press that safer than smoke is not the same as safe.
pmc-11655779:
Yi Li and co-authors predict heart-disease death risk in young breast cancer survivors in a 2024 study. As cancer therapy improves, more survivors die of heart disease than of cancer, yet young patients are rarely the focus. Knowing who carries the risk could target protection.

From a national cancer registry, the team modeled competing risks for patients under fifty. Older age within that band, low income, rural residence, Black race, being unmarried, a hormone-sensitive subtype, larger tumors, chemotherapy, and no surgery each raised cardiac death risk. Five machine learning models were trained to score individuals, and the gradient boosting one performed best, with strong accuracy in both training and test sets. Income, marital status, race, and age drove its predictions most.
pmc-11655879:
Hong-Man Chen and co-authors present a full genome for the Banna miniature inbred pig in a 2024 paper. This pig line is bred to be uniform, which makes it prized for medical research and for organ transplant studies. No reference genome for the line existed, so work on its traits had a weak base.

Using long-read and chromosome-contact methods, the team built a genome that spans the full set of chromosomes with high completeness scores. They mapped tens of thousands of genes and found that nearly half the genome is made of repeated stretches. The line stems from another miniature pig but has drifted in clear ways. The authors say the genome will support study of inbreeding and wider medical use of the line.
pmc-11655979:
Tsamitros and a team of colleagues test virtual reality craving sessions for alcohol dependence in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Facing drink cues in a safe setting is a proven therapy step; it teaches coping before real bars and bottles. Virtual reality offers such cues on demand. Twenty-one patients in inpatient rehabilitation took one session with alcohol-linked scenes. Craving, mood, and side effects were tracked before, during, and after.

Craving rose during exposure and settled back within twenty minutes. Patients felt present in the scenes and reported only mild cybersickness. Craving tracked with cybersickness strength. The trial shows the method is workable and tolerated. Addiction therapists exploring digital tools are the readers.
pmc-11656579:
Fateen Ata and co-authors reviewed eight years of care for cancer patients who got immune checkpoint drugs. Their paper was published in two thousand twenty-four. These drugs help the immune system attack cancer, but they can also harm hormone glands. Data from the Middle East on this harm were scarce.

The review covered six hundred forty-nine adults treated from two thousand fifteen to two thousand twenty-three. About one in four had a hormone problem, most often an underactive thyroid. Age, a low white cell count, and two named drugs were linked to higher risk. Having such a problem did not seem to change the death rate in the group.
pmc-11656979:
Sun, Lau, Cheung, and Choi scan recent evidence on whether metal joint implants raise cancer risk. Regulators in Europe classed pure cobalt as a likely carcinogen in 2020, forcing makers to justify its use in implants. Lab and animal work hints at risk, but human data stayed unsettled. Their 2024 scoping review gathers studies from 2010 onward covering over seven hundred thousand implant patients.

Across up to eighteen years of follow-up, no rise in overall cancer appeared. Three spots did tick up in some studies: prostate cancer, skin melanoma, and blood cancers. The authors conclude the evidence shows no consistent cancer increase for any implant type. They frame the review as a calm counterweight to alarm.
pmc-11657279:
Naser Darvishi Tabas and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, two ways of reflecting on work experience among emergency medical technicians in Iran. Reflecting in a structured way is thought to build self-regulated learning and motivation. Fifty-four technicians from thirty ambulance centers in South Khorasan province took part. Centers were grouped and assigned to solo reflection, group reflection, or a control arm.

For four weeks, the solo group wrote weekly reflections in notebooks using a standard reflective cycle. The group arm met in small teams with chosen leaders to reflect together on the same cycle. Everyone's learning strategies and motivation were measured with standard questionnaires before and after. The authors set the two formats against each other and the control to see which better serves busy front-line staff.
pmc-11657579:
Samiullah Shaikh and a large team compare, in twenty twenty-four, two regional anesthesia blocks for pain after breast surgery, in a meta-analysis of randomized trials. Many breast surgery patients suffer post-operative pain that limits function and quality of life. The two blocks numb different tissue planes near the spine and chest wall: the erector spinae plane block and the serratus anterior plane block. Evidence comparing them was limited. The team searched three databases through May twenty twenty-four, after registering the review.

Pooled statistics compared pain and safety outcomes across trials. Standard tools graded bias risk and evidence quality. Forest and funnel plots summarized the pooled effects. The review aims to guide block choice for breast cancer surgery pain control.
pmc-11657779:
Persson, Hughton, and Herzig van Wees study life after stroke in urban Ghana, in work from twenty twenty-four. Stroke is a pressing problem across sub Saharan Africa. Survivors often face disability, mental strain, and stigma, yet their own views are rarely recorded.

Fourteen survivors who attended a physiotherapy clinic in Accra gave in depth interviews. Four themes came out: limits on mobility, psychosocial burden, limits on work, and money burden. Many survivors felt seen as non functional members of society, the authors report. Hearing these views directly can shape rehab and support that fits local life, not imported models.
pmc-11657879:
Hande Yigit and eight co-authors asked how often feverish young infants with viral infections also carry serious bacterial ones in a 2024 paper. Babies under ninety days with fever worry doctors because bacterial infection can hide behind a viral one. The team reviewed 208 such infants at four Turkish university hospitals during 2020 and 2021, all tested for COVID and cultured.

Fifty-five infants had COVID and 153 did not. Serious bacterial infection appeared in 16.4 percent of the COVID group, and the paper compares that rate with the COVID-negative group and with infants positive for other respiratory viruses. The aim is practical: knowing how often the two coincide tells clinicians how hard to keep hunting for bacteria once a virus is found.
pmc-11657979:
Seven Dutch researchers catalogue the symptoms of stroke and its warning form, the transient ischemic attack, to test the famous FAST checklist. FAST covers face droop, arm weakness, and speech trouble, and campaigns built on it sped up care for major strokes but not for milder events. The team studied 900 patients from a long-running population cohort and projected their findings to the whole country.

At least one FAST symptom appeared in 98.3 percent of major strokes, but only 73.2 percent of minor strokes and 62.2 percent of warning attacks. The missed cases most often involved vision loss, dizziness, poor coordination, or numbness. Adding visual symptoms to the checklist lifted its catch rate for mild events from 66.4 to 80.8 percent. Dizziness pushed it further, to 86.1 percent, at the cost of many more false alarms. The authors weigh that trade-off for future public campaigns.
pmc-11659479:
Luqman and a large team (2024) studied whether a blood enzyme and a gene variant together can flag coronary artery disease early. The enzyme, known as Lp-PLA2, is found in unstable artery plaques, and its gene has been linked to the disease before. The team recruited 125 people in South India, 75 with artery disease confirmed by imaging and 50 matched controls, measured blood markers, and read the gene variant in 100 of them.

In patients, the enzyme level rose together with fats in the blood and a heart injury marker. It fell as protective cholesterol rose. A doubled copy of the variant, together with high enzyme levels, was most common in patients with all three main arteries diseased, and it stood out as an independent risk predictor. The enzyme also gave the best test performance of all markers tried, leading the authors to suggest gene testing for risk grouping.
pmc-11659679:
Radice and co-authors present a 2024 audit of research on mesophotic ecosystems, the dim ocean zone between thirty and one hundred fifty meters deep. Long hard to reach, these reefs and rocky habitats now draw growing study. The team catalogued fifteen hundred papers in a public database. Four skews stand out in where and how the work gets done.

Studies cluster in a few regions and depth bands. Organism choices and platforms add more tilt, and few projects track change over time. Temperate systems have joined tropical reefs in the recent surge. The authors stay hopeful but urge wider, longer, more even coverage so management can rest on balanced evidence.
pmc-11661979:
Sattar Soltani, Nhan Huynh, and Kirst King-Jones offer a 2024 lab method for putting drugs and other matter into fruit fly young. Flies are a key model for growth and for human ills, but tests of how matter acts inside the body have been rare. Their method aims to make such tests fast and safe for the young flies.

A skilled worker can treat 150 to 300 young flies in three to five hours, and most of them live. As a test, the team put an iron store protein into mutant flies that lack it. The treated flies were saved, which shows the method can deliver real goods into the body.
pmc-11662179:
Parham Elahinia and co-authors compare, in a 2024 clinical trial, a nettle plant oil with ibuprofen for pain after root canal treatment. Standard pain drugs in this class can cause side effects, so a plant-based option taken before treatment is worth testing.

Sixty patients with painful, irreversibly inflamed molars were assigned at random to ibuprofen, nettle oil capsules, or a placebo, taken half an hour before the procedure. Pain was scored on two scales before treatment and at set points up to a day after. The three-way comparison shows whether a herbal premedication can match a standard drug in keeping post-treatment pain down.
pmc-11662279:
Li Chen, Xiu-Ling Zhu, Jie Lin, and Dong-Liang Li ask whether adding Chinese herbal medicine to a standard liver cancer procedure helps in a 2024 analysis. The procedure threads chemotherapy into the tumor's artery; herbs are widely paired with it in China, on claims of better results and gentler side effects.

Thirty-nine randomized trials fed a network meta-analysis that ranked the pairings. The combinations beat the procedure alone on response and safety in the pooled verdict. The team then traced the frequent herbs' active compounds to their gene targets, mapping the pathways involved and docking key pairs in simulation. The two lenses, clinic and molecule, point the same way.
pmc-11662679:
Yun Wu and co-authors survey, in twenty twenty-four, drug-resistance gene changes in a fungal pneumonia pathogen among non-HIV patients in China. The fungus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, kills many non-HIV patients it infects, yet resistance data for them are scarce. The team analyzed two genes tied to drug response in samples from forty-five patients. Fourteen had infection; thirty-one had colonization, meaning the fungus was present without disease. Clinical traits, fungal burden, treatment response, and outcomes were also considered.

Infected patients showed altered blood indicators, higher fungal burden, and worse prognosis than colonized patients. They also had more co-infections with viruses and bacteria. No known resistance mutations were found in one gene. Ten changes of unknown effect were found, the head text notes, in the other gene region discussed.
pmc-11663379:
Shih-Hsuan Pi and four co-authors build and test a scale that lets dying patients judge whether they near a good death, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. The idea of a good death grew from deep interviews with patients who had terminal cancer. Experts sorted the talks into three themes about living, selfhood, and dying.

From those themes the team drafted an index with fifteen topics. One hundred forty-four patients completed it, and the scores hung together well as one scale. Patients could use it to weigh their own state. The design fits the Confucian culture of East Asia, the authors note. They offer the tool for care planning and talks about end-of-life wishes.
pmc-11663879:
Madiha Fatima, Fengmei Huang, and Xiaohong Fu review how chemical edits to RNA shape the joint lining in rheumatoid arthritis. Their 2024 paper describes the synovium, the tissue that cushions and feeds the joint, as the disease's main battleground. In arthritis it thickens, fills with immune cells, and drives the remodeling that destroys joint function.

The review gathers recent work on RNA modifications, marks added after the RNA is written that steer its stability and movement within the cell. Faulty marking, above all faulty methylation, feeds the disease process. The marks link the joint's resident macrophages, fibroblasts, and immune cells into one network, part of a feedback loop among bone, cartilage, and synovium. The authors argue these modifications are a promising drug target: correcting them could restore balance in the joint lining rather than only damping inflammation downstream.
pmc-11663979:
Whiteleg shrimp are widely farmed, often in biofloc systems where helpful microbes keep the water clean and support growth. Edward Akange and co-authors asked which dose of probiotic works best in such a system. Standard tests answer this poorly, because the microbes multiply and blur dose differences. The team raised shrimp indoors for eighty-four days at three dose levels and recorded growth and water quality measures. A basic comparison of group averages found clear differences in only a handful of measures.

The team then used principal component analysis, a method that weighs how strongly each dose shapes the pattern across all measures at once. By that method, the middle dose showed the strongest overall contribution, marking it as the optimum in this setup. The authors conclude that this approach can pick out the best probiotic dose for shrimp growth and water quality where simple comparisons fail.
pmc-11664279:
Yeong-Geun Lee and co-authors test a plant compound against liver cancer cells in a 2024 study. Bakuchiol comes from the seeds of Cullen corylifolium and is known for hormone-like and germ-fighting traits. Its power against liver cancer was untested. The team compared it with three cousin flavonoids from the same plant on HepG2 cells.

Bakuchiol stood out, driving the cancer cells into apoptosis, programmed death. Both death pathways, internal and external, switched on, judged by their protein ratios. The compound also froze the cell cycle early, lowering two driver proteins while raising three brakes. It woke an energy sensor and a cleanup pathway, and damped a growth signal. The authors conclude bakuchiol kills liver cancer cells by twin routes, death and self-digestion. They present it as a lead worth developing for this hard cancer.
pmc-11664579:
Huijie Zhang and ten co-authors published a 2024 study on tiny synthetic cells that make hydrogen gas from light. The cells, called nanoreactors, copy photosynthesis in a simplified form. A bacterial enzyme inside each reactor makes hydrogen, but it needs a supply of energized electrons from outside.

A multi part protein from a bacterium forms a wire through the reactor wall. Carbon dots outside absorb light and pass energized electrons to that wire, with no helper chemicals needed. Under light, the reactors produced hydrogen at a steady rate for hours. Adding a common helper chemical roughly doubled the rate. The design shows how synthetic cells can harvest light energy across a membrane, a step toward artificial photosynthesis.
pmc-11665279:
Jesus Antonio Perez Jimenez and co-authors swab surfaces across a veterinary teaching hospital in Madrid to find drug-resistant bacteria lurking in the environment, in a 2024 study. Hospital surfaces can shelter germs that infect patients, and animal hospitals have been studied less than human ones. The team took 183 samples from twenty-six areas and grew what they could.

They recovered 109 strains, mostly gut-family bacteria plus some hardy non-fermenters, including genera known for carrying resistance genes. The horse area yielded nearly two-thirds of all isolates. Many strains resisted at least five of sixteen drugs tested, and genetic fingerprints hinted at spread within the building. The authors call for stronger prevention measures in veterinary hospitals.
pmc-11665379:
Jinyu Xu and co-authors studied milk spoilage in 2024 using a method called peptidomics. Long life milk can break down on the shelf when cold loving bacteria release enzymes that cut milk proteins. Normal tests miss low levels of this damage. The team added these enzymes to milk and tracked how quality changed over time.

As storage went on, enzyme activity and protein breakdown both rose. The team found thousands of small protein pieces and linked them to a smaller set of source proteins. Those pieces may serve as early signs of spoilage. The work could help dairies catch bad milk before shoppers notice a fault.
pmc-11665479:
Medical students cram biochemistry early, then rarely open the book again. What survives matters for clinical reasoning. Nimer Mehyar and co-authors surveyed students at a health sciences university in Riyadh about the long-term retention of the subject.
