They asked what teaching styles, review habits, and clinical exposure keep the knowledge alive.

Their framing is familiar: interactive, integrated teaching beats lectures for durability, and knowledge used on the wards sticks. The survey explores students' own sense of what faded and why, at a school where the curriculum can still be adjusted. Retention, the authors argue, is a design problem, not a student failing.
pmc-11665779:
Beerend Gerats and colleagues present neural fields for tracking anatomy and surgical tools in laparoscopic video. Their 2024 paper uses video from a single camera view. Tracking tools can support skill assessment during surgery. Tracking anatomy is needed to place virtual overlays in the right spot. Past work often treated the two tasks as separate problems.

A neural field learns a continuous model of the scene over time. From one 2D clip, it builds 3D tracks of all surfaces seen in any frame. Tools cover little of the image, so their tracks tend to be weaker. Stronger class weighting was added to lift tool accuracy. Tests on gallbladder surgery clips gave high accuracy for both anatomy and instruments. Depth maps from the reconstructions were also assessed.
pmc-11666379:
Jeremy Davidson Bailoo and co-authors describe in 2024 a water maze built to test learning and memory in lab mice with less stress than the standard maze. The standard test, a round pool, is the most used assay of its kind. Reviews have found that its methods vary a lot between labs, and that the swimming is stressful in each trial and across days.

Stress clouds attention and the fixing of memories, which can warp results. Behavior in the round pool is also hard to read, since mice hug the wall or float. The team's T shaped water maze and its protocol aim for steady, repeatable results with clearer behavior to score. A calmer, more standard test would help drug and brain studies compare results across labs. The paper sets out the design and the steps in full.
pmc-11666879:
Seohyeon Im and six co-authors reviewed virus infections spread by biting insects in organ transplant patients, in a 2024 paper. Such patients take drugs that blunt their immune system, so infections can hit harder. These viruses are spreading as the climate warms and travel grows.

The review gathered cases for six viruses, with West Nile and dengue by far the most common. Fever was the top sign in both. West Nile cases died at a rate near one in four, while dengue deaths were far lower. Some infections came from the donated organ itself. Care often meant cutting back the immune drugs. The authors call for better guarding, faster diagnosis, and clearer care plans.
pmc-11668579:
Yuwen Liu and co-authors train machine learning to spot bloodstream infection early in children with bone and joint infections. Such infections can seed the blood, a life-threatening turn that blood cultures confirm only slowly. Working from three Chinese hospitals, the team gathered 601 children treated between 2012 and 2023, of whom 181 had bloodstream infection. Sixteen measurements available early were fed to eight learning algorithms.

A random forest model won, reaching an area under the curve of 0.947 and about 90 percent accuracy. Four signals did most of the work: procalcitonin levels, neutrophil counts, white cell counts, and days of fever. The authors argue the model could help doctors act before culture results return, cutting the danger from delayed or misleading tests. They frame it as decision support, not a replacement for clinical judgement.
pmc-11668679:
Chengxu Zhou and co-authors advance remote control of legged robots in a 2024 paper. Bomb disposal is deadly work that robots should take over. A four-legged robot with an arm forms the platform.

The operator wears a motion capture suit to guide the robot. Depth cameras give the operator a view of the scene. Human judgment stays in charge while the robot takes the risk. The system is designed to be cost-effective for real teams. Smooth arm and body control are key technical aims. Readers see a practical blend of human intuition and machine strength for hazardous tasks.
pmc-11668979:
Sean McClaine and co-authors measured how well chemotherapy patients stick with remote monitoring over ninety days. One hundred sixty-two outpatients were asked to file daily symptom surveys by phone, let their smartphones collect passive sensor data, and wear a fitness tracker. On average they completed surveys on about sixty-one percent of days, and gathered enough phone and wearable data on roughly seventy percent of days. Engagement was not random.

Non-White patients engaged less with surveys and the wearable than White patients. Patients with stage four cancer reported symptoms less often, and everyone reported less on weekends. Older patients and those with better thinking scores wore the tracker more; depressive symptoms went with less phone data. The authors warn that monitoring systems can widen gaps if the patients least likely to engage are also those with greater needs. Designing for them is the study's practical message.
pmc-11669679:
Xuanchun Huang and co-authors asked in 2024 which swelling factors may cause heart failure. They used a genetic method that tests causal links in both directions. Data covered ninety-one swelling factors from large gene studies and heart failure data from a Finnish database.

Seven factors showed causal links in the forward test. Two raised risk and two looked protective among the firm results, with three more as likely links. Reverse tests suggested heart failure itself may shift levels of four factors. Checks found no sign of bias in the main results. The authors name the firm factors as targets that still need further proof.
pmc-11669879:
Phongphat Wiwatthanasetthakarn and co-authors built, in a 2024 study, a tool to speed the screening of papers for systematic reviews. Such reviews sit at the top of the evidence scale, but screening takes a huge amount of staff time. Their tool uses few-shot learning: it learns from just a few known relevant papers and ranks the rest by how similar their texts are, using sentence embeddings.

The team tuned the tool on nine past reviews, then tried it live on four new ones. With four to six training papers, the tool cut the pile by half or more while keeping all relevant papers in tests. In live use, though, it missed some relevant papers, from about two in a hundred to about one in eight. A human second reader missed more. The authors plan a web application, and they warn that full recall is not yet safe to assume.
pmc-11669979:
Yu-Jie Wang and six co-authors test a blood index as a warning for heart rhythm relapse in a 2024 study. Burning a small patch inside the heart can cure atrial fibrillation, yet the erratic rhythm often returns. Smoldering inflammation is a suspect, and a new index blends three blood cell counts into one immune gauge.

Records covered 457 patients with the non-valve kind of the disease who had their first burn procedure. The team split them by whether the rhythm returned. They weighed the index alone, then stacked it on a known clinical score, to see if the pair calls relapse better than either alone.
pmc-11670279:
Hannah Resetarits and three co-authors study how to farm a methane-cutting seaweed in this two thousand twenty-four paper. The red seaweed Asparagopsis taxiformis slashes methane output when fed to cattle in small amounts. The catch is supply: almost none is grown at commercial scale. Little was known about its best growing conditions. The team ran closed-culture experiments on seaweed gathered in southern California.

They varied water temperature and added carbon dioxide, alone and in combination. They tracked growth, light use, and the level of bromoform, the compound behind the methane effect. Knowing what boosts both growth and bromoform guides farm design. The work links climate goals to seaweed aquaculture practice.
pmc-11671579:
Tang and six co-authors study a feedback loop in rheumatoid arthritis in work from twenty twenty-four. The disease swells and harms joints. White blood cells called neutrophils can cast out web like traps of DNA, which may drive more swelling.

The team tested joint tissue and fluid from arthritis and osteoarthritis patients. A signal called IL-33 proved able to trigger the traps. In lab work, the traps then stirred joint lining cells, which drew in more neutrophils. That loop could explain why swelling sustains itself. Blocking the loop at either step is a possible future treatment idea the work supports.
pmc-11671879:
Jessica Campos and co-authors report results for a wide catheter built to reach deep into the brain's blood vessels. Brain procedures that fix aneurysms or open blocked vessels need a stable base tube to deliver devices. Older setups stop in the neck, leaving the last stretch unsupported. The device reviewed here, the TracStar LDP, is wide enough to travel into the skull itself.

The team reviewed 125 cases treated between 2020 and 2023 at the senior authors' centers. Most cases treated aneurysms; others opened narrowed vessels or stented veins. In every case, the catheter reached its target zone and the planned device was delivered without complications from placement. No vessel tears occurred in any case. The authors conclude that direct deep access with this catheter is workable across many procedure types, with a strong safety record in this series.
pmc-11672479:
Ibrahim Dagci and co-authors coat yeast cells with magnetic nanoparticles to boost protein output, in a 2024 paper. The particles are iron oxide, and adding polymers during synthesis changed their shape, size, and surface charge. Coated cells can be held and handled with magnets, which eases industrial processing.

One polymer coating gave the best results. Cells stayed healthy at high particle doses, and the particles bound to cells with high efficiency. Smaller particles wrapped cell surfaces evenly, while larger ones clumped. The best coating raised output of a test protein by about a third over free cells. A light based fingerprinting method, read by machine learning, revealed the chemical signature of that boost. The authors propose the system for biotech production.
pmc-11672579:
Bin Sun and seven co-authors design a smart warming box for nursing piglets in a 2024 paper. Young piglets need local heat, but lamps and covers waste energy and cannot adjust to age or weather. Their box uses a strip heater and a programmable controller. It watches temperatures in real time and changes power to match the target for the piglets' age.

Lab tests showed steadier, more even warmth than a lamp setup. In a barn trial with eight sows, the box kept the resting area much warmer across three weeks. Total energy use fell by well over half. The authors present the design as a win for piglet health and barn efficiency.
pmc-11672879:
Xiang Li and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, whether berries and their active compounds can help prevent age-related macular degeneration. The disease is a top cause of vision loss in older adults, and no treatment can undo the retinal damage once done. Care therefore aims to slow the middle stages. Berries carry compounds that fight oxidation, calm inflammation, and curb abnormal vessel growth.

Animal studies show extracts of aronia, honeysuckle, black currant, goji, and bilberry easing retinal stress. Human trials are few, but early results hint that eating these compounds may support visual function and slow decline. The review sorts which berries have real backing and which are only promising. It also breaks down the key chemicals, such as carotenoids and anthocyanins, and how each acts on the eye.
pmc-11672979:
Chang Joo Oh and colleagues test a protective drug against kidney damage from cisplatin chemotherapy. Their animal study from twenty twenty-four uses sodium phenylbutyrate in mice. Cisplatin harms kidneys often enough to limit cancer care. No approved drug yet prevents that injury.

Mice received the protector for days around the cisplatin dose. Treated mice kept healthier kidney tubules than untreated ones. Blood waste markers stayed near normal levels with treatment. Inflammation signals in the kidney fell as well. Cell tests showed less cell death and healthier powerhouses. The protector also lowered a metabolic enzyme tied to the injury. The results support human trials, though mouse success alone proves little.
pmc-11673079:
Andrés Moya and Jukka Finne wrote a 2024 editorial essay on the state of biology as a science and its long road toward a full theory of life. Biology, launched as a journal in 2012, takes all of life as its object. The authors sort the science two ways: by the kinds of beings studied, and by the scales of organization from molecules to ecosystems.

Each branch, from microbiology to ecology, seeks its own laws for its own level. The old debate asks whether those laws reduce to the laws of lower levels. The authors set that debate aside and stress a plainer fact: biology is still building the power to treat its findings as one whole. The essay frames that open road as the defining trait of the science, not a flaw in it.
pmc-11673579:
Aitor Garcia-Ruiz and Ming-Hao Liu studied what a strong electric field does to two stacked layers of molybdenum disulfide twisted at a small angle. Twisted bilayers form moiré patterns, large-scale interference patterns that reshape how electrons move. Applying a voltage across such a stack is a standard way to tune its behavior. The pair found that current flowing through one layer acts like electrons moving under a nanoscale patterned potential.

The field direction decides the pattern's symmetry: one way gives a hexagonal arrangement, the other a honeycomb. Under magnetic fields the two versions produce different transport behavior and different Hofstadter spectra, the fractal energy patterns of electrons in a lattice. The result suggests a new way to build tunable artificial lattices in stacked materials.
pmc-11674079:
Alexandru Garaba and co-authors reviewed in 2024 what is known about cancer spread to the brain that hardens with calcium deposits. Such deposits in the brain have many causes, and hardened spread from a tumor elsewhere is uncommon and easy to miss.

Spread to the brain is the most common tumor type in adult brains, and hardened cases are seen mostly after radiation treatment. The review set out to measure how often these deposits occur, which source cancers they link to, and whether they appear before or after radiation. The team searched three large databases up to January 2024. Missing data, they warn, can lead to wrong diagnosis and delayed care.
pmc-11674579:
Sound waves aimed through the skull can nudge brain activity without surgery, and the method can reach deep areas with fine aim. Marilyn Gatica and co-authors test what this stimulation does to brain networks in macaques. They use a new measure that separates two kinds of teamwork among brain areas: backup-style overlap and combined, synergy-style processing.

The team stimulated two targets, a motor planning area and a front area tied to emotion circuits. Each target changed its own network most, and both changed sensing, timing, and frontal networks in similar ways across animals. The link between brain structure and activity weakened after stimulation. The network layout also shifted: the motor target loosened its backup-style grouping, while the frontal target strengthened combined processing. The results map how gentle ultrasound reshapes high-level brain organization.
pmc-11674679:
Merve Yilmaz and co-authors design a drug that attacks the protective caps on cancer cell chromosomes, in a 2024 study. The caps, telomeres, help cancer cells divide forever, and an existing agent that damages them is already in trials with immunotherapy. The team attached a fatty tail to that agent, making a new molecule with better solubility.

The new compound killed many cancer cell lines at low doses. In mouse colon cancer models it shrank tumors alone and worked even better paired with immune checkpoint drugs. Treated tumors showed the expected telomere damage marks, and immune profiling found more active killer T cells and fewer suppressive ones. The authors see promise for wider testing.
pmc-11675279:
Dali Kekelidze, Mari Malazonia, David Tsereteli, and Iagor Kalandadze published this public health survey in 2024. It measures what adults in the country of Georgia know about lead poisoning, a serious and preventable harm, above all for children. Interviewers spoke with 384 adults on the street in three municipalities, Batumi, Ozurgeti, and Zugdidi, between March and June 2024.

Most people knew that children face high risk from lead. Toys were widely recognized as a source, but few knew lead also hides in jewelry and cosmetics, with the gap largest in Ozurgeti. Many were unaware that lead poisoning can cause heart and blood vessel disease, anemia, and kidney failure. The authors call for more education campaigns that name the hidden sources and the full range of harms.
pmc-11675879:
Xinyu Chen and co-authors set out a fresh way to build continuous probability distributions, in a 2024 paper. Their generator folds an exponentiated odds ratio into a survival analysis frame, aiming for models that bend to modern data's twists. One child family, the Type 2 Gumbel Weibull-G set, carries the show.

The paper works out the family's core traits: density shapes, moments, hazard and quantile forms, entropy, order statistics, and ranking rules. Five fitting methods are put to the parameters. Three real data sets then test the family against rivals, where it posts sharp accuracy. The authors offer the generator as a gain for both theory and applied work.
pmc-11675979:
Nuria Peña and co-authors hunt for bacteria that make natural germ killers in poultry plant waste water, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Drug-resistant germs are a growing threat in food chains. The team screened over eight hundred strains from eight stages of a slaughter line.

Gene reads on twelve chosen strains found many killer-making gene sets. One strain yielded a brand new killer compound that worked on a major food germ. Most strains also carried drug-resistance or harm genes, which limits their use. One strain lacked those flags and stands out as a safe candidate for food use.
pmc-11676079:
Evgenia Panou and a team of co-authors published this 2024 study comparing the chemistry of three Greek Onosma species, plants with folk medicine roots that science had looked at below ground. Methanol extracts of the aerial parts went through high-resolution liquid chromatography, with molecular networking software helping name 94 phenolic compounds across seven groups.

Each species had a strength: one richest in flavonoid glycosides, another in hydroxycinnamic acids and neolignans, the third in lignans. Total phenol counts and the flavonoid count, antioxidant strength, and enzyme blocking were checked side by side. One species led on phenol content and antioxidant power, another on flavonoid levels and on blocking acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme tied to Alzheimer's disease. The results back the long folk use of the plants with hard numbers.
pmc-11676279:
Leticia da Costa and co-authors report a 2024 study of an invasive water plant and its native rivals. The invader grows fast in lakes and rivers and can crowd out local plants. Plant-rich native groups are often thought to resist such invasions, and the team tested that idea directly.

For six months, the invader grew alone or with two native water plants in tank setups. The team weighed leaves and roots over time to see where growth went. With rivals present, the invader put more growth into leaves and less into roots. Native plants thus shift how the invader grows, even when they do not stop it.
pmc-11676479:
Rafaela de Sousa and her co-authors present a 2024 study on using gene editing as eye drops against herpes virus in the brain. Herpes simplex virus type 1 can invade the nervous system, and standard antiviral drugs carry toxicity and resistance problems. Earlier dish work showed that editing one viral gene with CRISPR/Cas9 cut replication sharply. The team tested the editor, delivered through the eye, in infected mice.

The treated mice carried a lower brain virus load a week after infection than untreated ones. Their brain tissue also showed no inflammation or the cell damage seen in other groups. A standard topical antiviral served as a comparison treatment. The authors present eye-delivered gene editing as a novel route to protect the brain from this virus. More work is needed on safety and timing, they note.
pmc-11676779:
Lijun Chen and a team of co-authors studied how a plant hormone helps white sweet clover handle salt stress, in a 2024 paper. The plant is grown worldwide as a rotation crop and green manure, and it carries useful medicinal compounds. The hormone, abscisic acid, is a central signal in plant stress defense, yet its network in this plant was unmapped.

The team sprayed the hormone on plants and tracked body chemistry and gene activity in shoots and roots. Within hours, levels of a protective amino acid, soluble protein, and a reactive oxygen signal all rose. Nearly 20,000 genes changed activity across the plant. Network analysis found two gene groups that tracked the treatment closely. Those groups center on protein making, energy use, and defense chemistry, which suggests the hormone wakes the plant's whole stress system.
pmc-11676879:
Anqi Chen, Chenwei Pan, and Jian Chen compared bread made with yeast strains from drinks production in two thousand twenty-four. Yeasts used for wine, beer, and spirits might also raise bread, but strain choice affects loaf quality. The team tested commercial strains against a standard baker's yeast.

They measured loaf volume, hardness, acidity, leftover sugars, and organic acids. One strain, ACY158, made bread very close to the standard, with good volume and a balanced acid profile. Another, ACY9, gave a small, dense loaf far from the standard. The results show some drink yeasts could match or beat baker's yeast, which could widen choices for industrial baking.
pmc-11676979:
Muhammad Khan and co-authors breed soybean lines that accept foreign genes more readily, aiming to speed up crop engineering, in a study from 2024. A standard method uses a soil bacterium to carry new genes into plant cells, but soybeans take the delivery poorly. Success depends on plant chemistry that attracts the bacterium and lets its cargo settle into the genome.

The team crossed a line prized for research use with a line rich in flavonoid compounds that draw the bacterium. The goal was one line combining both parents' gifts. Hand pollination produced the hybrids, and the study assessed the offspring for transformation readiness. Better uptake would cut the time and cost of making improved soybean varieties for trials and farms.
pmc-11677079:
Rais Pavlov and co-authors review how skin-fuse steps govern gene runs into cells by fat sacs, in a survey from 2024. Fat sacs bear genes well and kind to cells, but the gene must cross two fat skins to land. Fuse of the sac skin with the cell skin is the gate.

The review walks the gate: how sacs near the skin, meet it, and merge so the load slips free. Virus sacs cheat with fuse proteins; fat sacs must earn fuse by mix and by the bath they sit in. New mix tricks and bath tweaks that raise fuse are graded. The pair-plus team frames fuse, not load, as the yield step: raise fuse, and the same sac fleet lands more genes per run.
pmc-11677179:
Gissel García and colleagues put a candidate probiotic bacterium through a full safety workout, in this trial from twenty twenty-four. The strain, Heyndrickxia coagulans AO 1167B, makes lactic acid and straddles two bacterial families in its traits. Early evidence hints at gut benefits, but a supplement must first prove it is harmless.

The team sequenced the strain's genome and found no worrying resistance or toxin genes. Dish tests showed no drug resistance, no damage to cells, and no bursting of blood cells. Then came a phase one trial: healthy adults took the strain or a dummy capsule for sixty days, with neither side knowing which. Blood tests and health checks stayed level in both groups. Gas was the commonest complaint and faded with time. The authors judge the strain safe enough to earn deeper clinical study.
pmc-11677379:
Minjee Han, Kyungsook Woo, and Kirang Kim combine past studies, in two thousand twenty-four, on protein intake and muscle loss in older Koreans. Sarcopenia means weak, shrinking muscle, and advice on how much protein prevents it still varies. The authors set out to pool what Korean studies show for adults aged sixty-five and up.

They kept twenty-three studies, and nine fed into the pooled math. Adults eating the least protein faced a higher risk of sarcopenia than those eating more. The low group also faced a higher risk of weak hand grip. Other measures, such as gait speed and balance, showed no clear link. The authors call for strong trials that pair protein with resistance training.
pmc-11677479:
Jaedong Lee, Hyosoung Cha, Yul Hwangbo, and Wonjoong Cheon build a dual retrieval system to cut false claims by medical language models. Their 2024 study grounds answers in the latest diabetes guidelines from Korea and the United States. Fast-moving fields make fixed model knowledge go stale.

The system pairs dense search over eleven embedding models with sparse word search tuned per language. Best parts were then merged into combined retrievers for each guideline set. Multilingual embedding models beat single-language ones in both tongues. The merged retrievers widened coverage while keeping precision. The authors present the setup as a base for more trustworthy AI help in care.
pmc-11677579:
Lijuan Wang and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, soil treatments that keep toxic metals out of potatoes grown near mines. Cadmium and lead in such soils can move into the crop. The team used a potato variety known to soak up both metals readily.

Seven treatments were compared, from plain fertilizer to biochar and mineral blends. All treatment mixes improved soil traits compared with the untreated control. The aim was to lock the metals in the soil so roots take up less. Safe use of farmland near mines protects both harvests and the families who eat them. The trial ranks which passivator blends deserve wider use on contaminated fields.
pmc-11677679:
Laima Malachauskiene and co-authors test whether a pain monitor improves care during breast surgery in this 2024 trial. Breast operations bring tricky pain control problems. Nausea and long-term chest pain are known after-effects. Too much opioid painkiller was suspected as one cause. A monitor that reads pain level from the body could guide dosing. Sixty women having breast cancer surgery joined the trial at one hospital.

Half were dosed with the monitor's guidance, half by standard care. The course before, during, and after surgery was compared. Objective dosing aims to give neither too much nor too little. The trial was randomized and prospective. Its setting is a regional hospital's operating suite. Results bear on anesthesia practice for a very common surgery.
pmc-11677879:
Katarzyna Korecka and co-authors present an algorithm that stages sun-damage skin spots automatically from two kinds of images, in a 2024 preliminary study. Actinic keratoses appear on sun-exposed skin of older, fair-skinned people and can precede skin cancer. Fifty-four patients at a Polish university clinic had clinical, magnified skin, and ultrasound examinations, giving one hundred and sixty-two image pairs.

The pipeline first outlines the lesion in the ultrasound image with a neural network, then extracts crafted features. Skin surface images contribute both crafted and neural features. A classifier blends the two streams to assign the stage. Surface images alone reached about eighty-one percent accuracy, and adding ultrasound gave about seventy-nine. The authors say the tool could help judge progression risk, and they expect more images to lift accuracy.
pmc-11677979:
Julian Wilhelm Weiss and three colleagues study a tidy family of glowing crystals to learn how structure dictates light emission. The materials are alkaline-earth tetrachloroaluminates doped with ytterbium ions, which emit broad blue-violet bands. Swapping calcium for strontium or barium changed the emission in an unexpected order.

Emission peaks shifted from the calcium compound toward barium, the reverse of the usual trend, which the authors attribute to local symmetry around the emitting ion. The barium material showed a second emission band at low temperatures. All samples quenched strongly with heat, giving short decay times. The authors offer the system as an ideal testbed for structure-luminescence relationships in phosphor research.
pmc-11678179:
Maria Kepsha and co-authors review blood tests based on microRNA for cervical cancer, in a review paper from 2024. The cancer is tied to human papillomavirus, and early finding lifts outcomes. Standard smear tests and virus tests have limits in accuracy and repeat results, so better tools are still needed.

A liquid biopsy checks cancer-linked material in blood or other fluids, with no cut to tissue. It can track tumor growth, spread, and response to care over time. Small RNA strands carried in tiny cell packets get special focus here. The review weighs their promise for screening and follow-up, and calls for more study.
pmc-11678479:
Mohsan Subhani and co-authors counted how many hospital patients in Nottingham had an alcohol use disorder, and how often the diagnosis was missed, in a 2024 study. Heavy drinking drives admissions and feeds more than two hundred illnesses. The team looked back at eleven years of admissions to one large hospital. A short drinking survey was on file for nearly every patient, which gave the study a rare, near-complete screen.

One in six admitted patients met the bar for the disorder, and about one in fifty was alcohol dependent. Yet most of those patients left without any alcohol diagnosis on their record. Two-thirds also carried a mental or behavioral disorder. Risk ran highest in men, in patients in their sixties, and in emergency admissions. The authors say screening works, but hospitals must act on what it finds.
pmc-11678579:
Agata Jankowska and Krystyna Szymandera-Buszka test flour foods enriched with iodine carrying dried vegetables, in work from 2024. Iodine lack is a public health problem, and flour products are eaten widely. The team added dried pumpkin, cauliflower, carrot, broccoli, and beetroot, each loaded with one of two iodine salts, to gnocchi and ciabatta.

They measured iodine content and antioxidant activity in the foods. A vitamin level was checked in the rolls. Tests ran before and after cooking or baking and after storage. Both foods proved good iodine sources that could help prevent iodine deficiency. A single roll covered a small share of daily need.
pmc-11678679:
Santmartí-Oliver and co-authors review the evidence on placing orthodontic miniscrews with guidance rather than freehand. Miniscrews give braces a firm anchor, but a poorly placed screw can damage a tooth root. The review gathers studies up to March 2024 comparing freehand placement with radiographic guides and computer-assisted methods. Eleven studies covering 652 screws met the criteria, and safety results were pooled where the data allowed.

Static computer-assisted placement cut root damage sharply compared with freehand work and reduced angle and position errors. No dynamic-guidance studies were available to analyze, and most included studies carried real limits on bias. The authors conclude that static guidance is the safer, more accurate route today. They call for better protocols and proper studies of dynamic systems. For orthodontists, the review sums up what guidance buys and where the evidence is still thin.
pmc-11679379:
Mateusz Mądry, Bogusław Szczupak, Mateusz Śmigielski, and Bartosz Matysiak present a 2024 sensor study. Their device measures heat and damp air at the same time, a pair that is hard to split with one probe. The sensor uses light sent through thin glass fibers. One fiber is bare, and one has a coat that reacts to damp air.

A machine learning model reads the light signals and sorts out the two values. Tests gave small errors for both heat and damp air over a short sensor length. The authors also checked how sensor length and data size change the errors. The method skips slow hand work and may suit sites that need both readings at once.
pmc-11679679:
Worawat Traiwattanapong, Vandana Molahalli, Apichart Pattanaporkratana, and Nattaporn Chattham published this systematic review in 2024. It surveys transparent thin-film heaters, see-through coatings that warm a surface when current flows through them. Such films matter for smart windows, displays, actuators, and sensors, where heat must arrive without blocking the view. A good film must also survive high temperatures without degrading.

The review covers how these films are structured, which materials they use, and how they are made. It compares properties across material families and describes methods for raising efficiency. The authors also look beyond the lab, summarizing the size and growth of the market for thin-film heaters. They close with an outlook on where the technology is heading. The result is a single map of a fast-moving corner of materials engineering.
pmc-11679779:
Ayana Haku, Hitoshi Kaneko, and Junko Kawahito examine how the personalities of new parents relate to postpartum depression, in fathers as well as mothers. Most research stops at the mother. This study enrolled eighty-two Japanese couples and assessed both partners at the one-month check-up with a depression scale, a ten-item Big Five personality inventory, and a marriage quality index.

One trait dominated the mothers' risk: neuroticism was strongly tied to maternal depression. A cross-partner effect appeared as well, with more extraverted mothers having partners less likely to be depressed. Mothers' depression also tracked with lower marital satisfaction in simple correlations, though that link faded in the full structural model. The authors urge practitioners to screen and support both parents after birth, and to remember that the personality-depression relationship does not run the same way in mothers and fathers.
pmc-11679879:
Pan and co-authors developed a wireless, battery-free way to measure metal thickness with ultrasound, aimed at corrosion checks in petrochemical plants. Standard probes need contact points and costly insulation removal, so thinning spots are easy to miss. The team modeled and built a system that sends power wirelessly to the sensor and reads the echo, then cleans the echo with a pulse compression method borrowed from radar.

In lab tests on metal samples of varied thickness, shape, and material, the processed echo gave thickness readings about ten times more accurate than the raw echo. The authors say the gain makes dense networks of fixed measurement points practical, so plants can watch many spots for corrosion without repeated manual inspection.
pmc-11679979:
Self-driving cars that share control with a human driver must know who that driver is. The authors build a shared control system that personalizes itself on two human measures. One is driving capability, which guides how much authority the machine should take. The other is driving style, which the automated side learns to anticipate.

They set up simulated scenarios to measure capability fairly, and they characterized styles in field tests. On top of that sits the control framework, judged on safety, comfort, and driver workload. Tests ran both in a human-in-the-loop simulator and in a real automated vehicle on the road. Across drivers of differing skill and style, and across complex scenarios, the personalized system beat both human-only and automation-only driving on the team's measures. The authors present personalization as the step that makes shared control acceptable to real drivers.
pmc-11680179:
Meningitis bacteria carry a weapon, an enzyme that chops up a key antibody guarding the nose and throat. Yuri Prokopenko and eleven co-authors built vaccine candidates from pieces of that enzyme in a 2024 study. They picked fragments using maps of the spots antibodies and immune cells recognize, then stitched single and joined pieces into lab-made proteins.

Tested in mice, the proteins raised immune responses and protected the animals against three major meningitis groups. The authors argue the enzyme's structure is a sound base for a vaccine that could cover several bacteria sharing the same weapon, not just one strain.
pmc-11680279:
Karadağ and co-authors study how a hormone implant used to delay puberty in dogs changes reproductive signaling in the ovary and uterus. The implant releases deslorelin, and vets use it to postpone breeding. Two hormone systems, GnRH and kisspeptin, normally switch puberty on, so the team measured them after treatment.

Tissue from twenty-five young female dogs was compared across dogs that came into heat, dogs that did not, and untreated controls. Deslorelin lowered some gene signals, and the pattern differed between groups. The authors conclude the implant cannot be relied on to trigger a fertile heat in late-prepubertal dogs, while noting that larger studies are needed to settle the question.
pmc-11680379:
Savannah Grace, Kristen Wilson, Rayann Dorleans, and thirteen colleagues survey coronavirus in Florida deer in this two thousand twenty-four study. White-tailed deer elsewhere showed substantial SARS-CoV-2 infection, raising zoonotic concern. The team compared farmed deer, with heavy human contact, against free-ranging deer. Swabs, lung tissue, lymph nodes, and serum came from over nine hundred animals between twenty twenty and twenty twenty-two, tested for active infection and antibodies.

Infection prevalence was under one percent in both groups, about zero point eight five percent farmed and zero point seven six percent free-ranging. No farmed deer had neutralizing antibodies; one wild deer tested antibody-positive. Viral sequences matched human case peaks and circulating variants, indicating human-to-deer spillover, but at lower frequency than reported elsewhere. The authors conclude spillover risk in northern Florida looks reduced and call for wider study of transmission dynamics across North America.
pmc-11680479:
Pig gut organoids could cut the need for live animal tests, and a 2024 study by Camille Duchesne and co-authors asks how the donor pig's age shapes them. The team grew organoids from gut stem cells and compared their growth, shape, and cell makeup across ages.

Stem cells came from the jejunum and colon of pigs aged one day to six months, and the organoids were passed three times. Colon cells made more and larger organoids than jejunum cells. Age mattered for growth and shape: cells from young piglets gave a higher share of organoids over round spheroids. Yet age did not change the cell makeup of the organoids. The study helps labs pick donor ages for this model.
pmc-11681279:
Shirin Hasavari and Pouyan Esmaeilzadeh reported this health systems study in 2024. When a patient must move between hospitals, staff must pick the right grade of ambulance care. That pick is hard when the crew cannot see the patient's records in time. Privacy rules and clashing record systems block the flow of data.

The pair built ITC-InfoChain, a web platform that shares patient data on a locked chain of records. Hospitals load coded patient facts to a shared ledger. The ward that will take the patient, and crews on the road, can open the facts through an app. Tests showed the system stayed quick even as loads grew, with most deals done in a few seconds. The authors say wider trials could spread the tool across regions.
pmc-11681579:
Dennis Pieper, Anja Sandek, Ann-Kathrin Schäfer, and a team of co-authors test whether a protein in urine can warn of failing kidneys in people with heart failure. The two organs fail together so often that doctors speak of a cardiorenal syndrome, and catching kidney decline early opens a window to act.

They measured the protein, called DKK3, in several hundred heart failure patients and a small control group, then tracked kidney function for up to five years. Levels ran much higher in the patients, and those above a cutoff lost kidney function notably faster over the next year. The signal held even in patients whose kidneys were still healthy. The authors call the marker promising for early warning.
pmc-11682779:
A large team of co-authors reports a study from two thousand twenty-four on the fine structure of a parasitic worm's larvae. The worm, Toxocara cati, infects cats and can cause disease in people. Hosts that carry its larvae without maturing them, called paratenic hosts, pass the infection along, so the larval stages matter for diagnosis.

The team used mice as stand-in hosts and a scanning electron microscope to picture the larvae in three dimensions. Eggs were fed to pregnant mice, and larvae passed to their young. Larvae at the second stage were gathered from the mothers and at the third stage from the pups, then compared in detail.
pmc-11683079:
Jingjing Dou and her team tell of a rare self-attack ill tied to tumours, with anti-Yo marks in the blood, that was treated with good ends by ofatumumab. Their 2024 case takes in an ill that harms poise and speech.

The sick woman came in with a spun head, odd eye moves, blurred speech, and shaky steps. Tests found weak anti-Yo marks and brain flesh tests that backed the find. A first round of self-attack care eased the spun head. Pills of steroid drugs kept care up. Signs then grew worse step by step once she left care. More tests backed marks aimed at brain flesh proteins. When a next steroid round failed, care switched to ofatumumab. Two doses brought part relief of her signs.
pmc-11683279:
Belén Ríos-Sánchez and co-authors share a data set on more than twelve hundred lung cancer patients from a Madrid hospital, in a 2024 paper. Records cover diagnosis, treatment, and personal and medical history taken at intake. Gene and body traits of each patient are joined in one file.

The authors argue that such joined data can reveal how treatment choice, disease course, and side effects hang together. A sharper view of those links could raise hopes for patients and cut toxic harm. The set is offered for reuse by other teams. It comes from a single hospital's oncology ward, which both grounds it and bounds its reach.
pmc-11683579:
Leifa Mayers argues that the politics of reproductive rights and reproductive justice, long treated as rivals, can be brought closer together. The standard story says rights campaigns centered the choices of white, middle-class women not to have children. Justice organizing, in contrast, focused on the racial, gendered, and classed barriers to having and raising children. Assisted reproduction is where Mayers sees an opening.

Human rights bodies and scholars increasingly note how infertility and access to treatment are unevenly spread. Courts have begun naming assisted reproduction as part of a basic right to reproductive health. Mayers reframes the chance to choose assisted reproduction as a justice question rather than a private consumer choice. Doing so unsettles the old split between the two political logics. The essay invites rights advocates and justice organizers to work from shared ground on fertility care.
pmc-11688079:
Sonmez and co-authors count how wide urine leak runs in a town set and what it costs life grade. Folks who came to family clinics fill three forms: a life-grade scale, a leak score form, and a three-ask sort form. Just under a third of the set leaks, their 2024 study finds. Women form the bulk of those who came.

Leak score ranks split hard by leak state and by leak kind. Life grade drops with leak in the pooled sums. Scores for those free of leak sit near the scale's top. The forms cost a clinic visit just minutes yet sort kinds clean. Wide town counts of a hushed ill can steer aid, pads, and physio spend. Shame keeps counts low, so clinic asks are a fair first well.
pmc-11688179:
Junhua Wang and co-authors report in 2024 on brain and spine tumors in children aged three years or younger at one hospital. The team treated one hundred seventy one young patients over about seven years and followed most of them over time. Boys made up more than half of the group.

The most common tumor types were early cell tumors, gliomas, and growths near the hormone gland. Care often mixed surgery with drug or beam treatment based on tumor grade. Low grade cases lived a median of about forty one months, while high grade cases lived about fifteen months. Tumor grade and how much was removed shaped survival.
pmc-11688279:
Jiangqi Wu, Haiyan Wang, and Guang Li test how added nutrients change gas loss from wet alpine meadows in a 2024 study. The meadows sit on a high cold plateau and often take in the gas at stake, a strong heat-trapping gas from soil. Plots got nitrogen, phosphorus, both, or none over two growth years.

Added nitrogen raised gas loss from the soil, while phosphorus alone showed no clear effect. When both were added, phosphorus made the nitrogen effect stronger in early growth of the second year. Soil nitrogen forms and soil germ genes were the main controls the team found on the gas flow.
pmc-11688879:
Linda Waite and Hui Liu introduce a set of papers on how to study older LGBT adults in the United States, in this 2024 overview. The population numbers roughly nine to eleven million people and faces wider health gaps than peers, gaps that grow across a lifetime. A national academy has called for research that explains where those gaps come from.

The session's papers tackle method head on. One presents a fresh way to recruit a nationally fair sample of this hard to reach group. Another reports early health findings from a pilot using that method. A third compares social traits and health against other older adults in two national samples, and a fourth extends the comparison to the United Kingdom. The overview argues better design will bring better answers.
pmc-11689079:
Mei and co-authors (2024) explored how older couples, both partners living with illness, support each other in hospital after a repeat stroke. One partner's survival often depends on the other, yet how they help each other is poorly understood. The team interviewed 21 couples aged 61 to 72 in five large hospitals. They analyzed the transcripts with a standard descriptive method.

One thread ran through everything: the wish not to drag the children down. The analysis grouped their experience into three themes. The couples kept their bond alive through mutual support. They supported each other precisely to spare the children. And they struggled between ideals and reality while doing so. The authors urge health professionals to notice this cultural commitment when they plan support, and to offer each couple help fitted to its own tensions and differences.
pmc-11689179:
Alison Phinney and co-authors build dementia-friendly communities by taking the lead from people who live with dementia, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Social citizenship frames people with dementia as full community members with rights. A four-year project asked what that means in practice.

An action group of people with dementia named stigma as their top concern. With researchers, they built an online toolkit to flip stigma on its ear. Local groups such as libraries and churches then tried the toolkit. Hearing real voices, spotting stigma, and gaining confidence to change stood out in the feedback.
pmc-11689279:
Josphat Martin Muchangi and colleagues review how government policy shaped handwashing and vaccine uptake in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania during COVID-19. Government action on vaccine supply and hygiene practices was key to control the spread of the virus. The team used standard review guidelines. They screened past work and read nine of 136 candidate papers in depth.

The findings confirm that governments shaped uptake in all three countries, through distinct levers. In Uganda, public health campaigns and communication plans raised vaccine acceptance and hand hygiene. In Tanzania, government work to make hand hygiene accessible raised handwashing uptake. In Kenya, work to raise access to soap and clean water raised adherence. That work was in informal settlements and markets. The shared lesson is that policy works through both persuasion and provision. Messages change minds. Soap and water change what is possible.
pmc-11689579:
Eight researchers explored how video-based mental health visits for older veterans affected their family caregivers, in a 2024 study. Rural caregivers face thin local services, long drives, and weak internet. A veterans' health service began offering remote visits with old-age mind specialists, and caregivers often sat in on the calls.

The team interviewed thirteen caregivers, mostly spouses or adult children, across two regions. Caregivers said the visits made their role feel normal and shared, not lonely. Staff gave them practical tips and resources for handling hard behavior. Home visits saved long trips and let staff spend more time on both patient and caregiver needs. Easy follow-up by phone was prized most of all. The authors suggest that folding caregivers into such visits can ease their load and lift their well-being.
pmc-11689679:
Da Jiang and co-authors present a 2024 trial of phone based help for lonely older adults in Hong Kong, delivered by older volunteers. More than a thousand low income recipients who lived alone took part during the pandemic. Volunteers were trained in one of three styles: activity planning, mindfulness, or friendly befriending calls.

The volunteers themselves gained: less loneliness, less stress, wider networks. Recipients of activity planning did best, with gains in loneliness, mood, support, and sleep lasting six months. Mindfulness calls helped loneliness at three months. Befriending, the control style, lagged. The dual design, helping both ends of the line, is the study's signature.
pmc-11689979:
Kerry Jordan and co-authors evaluate a student-run activity program for people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Drug-free programs can help maintain thinking and daily function, but access is scarce. The program, called STAP, sends health science students to lead weekly three-and-a-half-hour sessions mixing exercise, therapy drills, thinking games, and social time.

Over two twelve-week rounds, participants were tested before and after on thinking, quality of life, and physical function. Most measures held steady without significant change, which the team reads as maintenance rather than decline. One scale, covering independent daily activities, improved significantly. The authors suggest the model can widen access to beneficial activity while giving students hands-on training with dementia care.
pmc-11690079:
Jiamin Yin and Christopher Seplaki study, in twenty twenty-four, how COVID-19 changed social isolation for older adults in the United States. Isolation is measured here by facts, not feelings. Their score covers living alone, talk about key matters, and taking part in faith and other group acts. They compare change before and after twenty twenty for two age bands, those eighty and older and those sixty-five to seventy-nine.

The oldest group was more likely to be isolated in twenty twenty than the younger group. The gap was driven by a drop in group acts. Oddly, the oldest group was less likely to live alone that year. Other parts of the score showed no clear gap.
pmc-11690279:
Ladda Thiamwong and five co-authors describe a fall prevention program called PEER for low-income older adults. Their twenty twenty-four trial used a balance tool that gives quick feedback on how steady a person stands. It also helped people rethink their own fall risk. Peer leaders then led balance and strength exercise for eight weeks in Central Florida homes.

The trial compared forty-five people in PEER with fifty-two in a control group. More PEER members moved toward a sound view of their fall risk. Fewer moved toward a poor view than in the control group. The team says low-cost tech may help close health gaps.
pmc-11690379:
Molly Lawrence and co-authors survey Rhode Island primary care doctors on how memory screening actually happens in their offices. These physicians are the first line for catching cognitive decline, yet visits are short and crowded with other problems. A fourteen-question survey went out through the state family physicians' academy, drawing forty-eight replies, about half of them substantially complete.

The MMSE, MoCA, and Mini-Cog were the tools in use, and most doctors felt fairly or very confident using them. Time was the villain at every step: no time to test, no time to counsel. Referrals snagged on long waits for specialists, thin local resources, and patients who refused. The authors read the results as a systems problem, not a knowledge problem, in early dementia care.
pmc-11690579:
Tamar Wyte-Lake and co-authors explored in 2024 how old ties between health groups can carry disaster aid to home health agencies. Such agencies are a lifeline for older adults at home, yet they run lean and sit outside most emergency plans. Care groups called coalitions already share gear and staff in disasters. The team spoke with nineteen people from six veterans' health centers and their partner home agencies.

Veterans' staff were keen to partner on emergency work. Shareable help ranged from news bulletins to staff training and joint plan drafting, at low and higher effort. The team frames a support pipeline through ties that already exist as a model other systems can copy to harden home care.
pmc-11690679:
Michelle Shardell, Chixiang Chen, and Jason Falvey study recovery after hip fracture in a 2024 paper. Their patients are nursing home residents with Alzheimer disease, a group rarely studied. Check-up timing in the national Medicare data set is irregular, and sicker patients get checked more often, which can bias results.

The team built a joint model that treats visit timing as part of the data. Among more than nine thousand five hundred residents, Medicaid coverage and weaker cognition linked more strongly to poor function under the new model. Readers get a fairer way to learn who recovers and who needs more help.
pmc-11690779:
Mushira Khan shared a 2024 study of strength and resilience in the stories of older adults from South Asia now living in the United States. Healthy aging, in one school of thought, grows from what people and their communities have at hand, not from what they lack. How that plays out for this group was little known. This study asked them directly.

Khan held in-depth interviews with more than thirty of them, split in rough halves by sex. The interviews lasted up to an hour and a half. Themes came out of the analysis. Strong networks of family and friends, near and far, held together by messaging apps and cultural feast days, fed a sense of purpose. Ties across the generations did the same. Calm mindfulness practices, a sense of grit, and creative coping in hard times all fed it too.
pmc-11691079:
Marguerite Daus and seven co-authors published a study in 2024 on who pays for veterans' post-acute skilled home health care after a hospital stay. Costs of this care have grown for the veterans' system; how financing is divided among the veterans' system, Medicare, and Medicare Advantage had not been mapped.

The researchers assembled a cohort of more than sixty-four thousand veterans aged sixty-six or older, treated at 114 veterans' hospitals from 2017 to 2019. All received home health care within fourteen days of discharge. The strongest factor was enrollment in a Medicare Advantage plan: those veterans were far more likely to have the veterans' system pay for the care. Earlier home care paid by that system, an earlier stay in its hospitals, and sepsis, a blood infection, raised the odds. The discussion turns to why cost-sharing rules and plan checks may shift the bill between payers.
pmc-11691179:
Sojung Park and three co-authors track how life in senior housing links, over the long term, to being cut off from others and to loss of thought. Their study is from two thousand twenty-four.

Senior housing in the town is said to build a sense of shared life. The team used twelve waves of a national aging study, over more than a decade. They matched older adults in senior homes to peers in plain homes. In both, being cut off rose and thought fell over the span. The team weighs how being cut off moved thought, split by pay band. They give a sharp look at the years of the recent plague.
pmc-11691279:
Men on the far side of prostate cancer can feel alone in a crowd, a loneliness tied to the disease itself. Kerri Winters-Stone and seven co-authors probe that tie in 2024, inside a group-exercise trial. In all, 145 men filled in the scales before six months of live online group exercise.

The scales join a loneliness form made for cancer to marks of worry, low mood, and social and body function. A subset of sixty-eight men filled them in again after the course. Three exercise styles ran side by side, all in supervised groups. The team's hunch is that the group itself, not just the sweat, does the healing. Shared strain may be the drug. The read can guide how such trials are built.
pmc-11691379:
Caroline Stephens, Jacqueline Telonidis, and Katherine Ornstein introduce a four-part symposium on rural aging and family caregiving, in a 2024 summary. Rural Americans age faster, carry more illness, and face the thinnest formal services. The first talk mines cancer registry and claims data for town-versus-country gaps in palliative care across six cancers. Two talks use a Utah caregiving study to ask how family size shapes end-of-life care for nursing home residents and people with dementia.

The last talk evaluates a joint-agency program backing rural caregivers directly. Together the talks map who rural elders are, where care falls short, and what fixes look promising. The editors frame the set as groundwork for rural health practice and policy.
pmc-11691579:
Gul Seckin studied how older adults use online health tools in a 2024 study. Looking up health facts online is among the most common web acts, and people over 50 lead in using tech for health ends. Seckin asked how much these adults trust web health sources and what that trust travels with.

A national sample of 499 older adults answered the survey. Trust in web sources was set against skill at finding and judging web health facts, how much such content people take in, and their sense of control over their own care. The study frames the links with theories of aging well. Its map can guide sites that serve older readers.
pmc-11691679:
Limei Chen and Megumi Inoue study how Japan fights isolation and loneliness among older adults with dementia, in a 2024 paper. Japan has a rapidly aging population, so the problem is pressing there.

The study looks at programs that build social capital, or community power, in local areas. Among them are dementia cafes, training for dementia supporters, community social workers, and dementia friendly community schemes. The authors find that active social life and strong networks in a defined local area guard against isolation. A sense of belonging and real bonds in the community can ease much of the harm that loneliness brings.
pmc-11691779:
Christopher Engeland and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on whether fasting status affects blood-based biomarkers of neurodegenerative disease in older adults. Such blood tests could detect Alzheimer's disease early, so accurate measurement matters. Factors such as recent food intake might distort the results and need to be understood.

Thirty older adults, most of them women with an average age in the late sixties, attended two laboratory visits. Each participant had fasted for more than eight hours beforehand. Blood was drawn four times at each visit, with a meal served after either the second or the fourth draw. Two biomarkers held steady after eating. Two declined after a meal, one with strong evidence and one with less. A fifth declined with weak evidence. The team concludes that laboratories should record when a meal was last eaten for some of these tests.
pmc-11691979:
Morgan Taylor and Margie Lachman published a study in 2024 on how people's outlook on their own health and energy predicts their functional health twenty years later. Positive self-perceptions of aging are associated with better cognitive and health outcomes. Few studies, however, had followed the relationship across the full adult lifespan.

The researchers used a national midlife study that first surveyed adults in the mid-1990s and again nearly twenty years later. At the first wave, participants rated their health and energy in the past, the present, and the future. The difference between past and future ratings formed an outlook score. People with a more positive outlook had fewer health limitations at the final wave, such as trouble climbing stairs or carrying groceries. The association held at all ages, after accounting for education, sex, and starting health.
pmc-11692179:
Nahyun Kim and Keiko Katagiri study how taking part in group activities may ease loneliness in older adults. Their 2024 paper draws on an online survey of Japanese adults aged sixty to seventy-nine. The analysis centers on the 570 people who were active in some form of social participation.

Close bonds inside a group were linked to lower loneliness in a direct way. Reaching out to new communities helped less directly, by widening the circle of casual neighborhood ties such as greetings and short chats. Those wider ties were in turn linked to less loneliness. The authors argue that programs should build both deep group ties and light local contact.
pmc-11692279:
Chatura Senadheera and co-authors test the safety of a daily ketone drink in healthy older adults in this 2024 paper. Ketones are body fuels made during fasting, and ester drinks can raise them without diet changes. Such drinks had not been tested in older adults before.

Thirty adults with an average age of seventy-six took part for twelve weeks. Half got the ketone drink and half a matched dummy drink, with neither side knowing which. Reports of nausea, headache, or dizziness on more than one day were rare in both groups. Symptoms were most common in the first two weeks, then faded. Lab tests and vital signs stayed steady, and the authors call the drink safe and tolerable for this group.
pmc-11692379:
Radha Dhingra and six co-authors published a study in 2024 on racial and ethnic disparities in how cardiovascular risk factors change with age in United States adults. The harms of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, and smoking are well documented. Less is known about how these factors change together across middle and later life.

The researchers used six waves of a large longitudinal survey from 2006 to 2016, covering more than ten thousand adults. They identified eight distinct trajectories of change between the ages of fifty and eighty. Just over a third of adults maintained optimal cardiovascular health levels. Black and Hispanic adults were far more likely to follow the high-risk trajectories. Education, household income, and, for Hispanic adults, being born in the United States explained much of the excess risk.
pmc-11692479:
Messay Kotecho, Abraham Kassay, and Margaret Adamek studied social isolation among older adults in Bishoftu Town, Ethiopia, in a 2024 study. Research on elders is growing in Ethiopia, but isolation had been overlooked. The team used in-depth interviews and observation with ten people aged sixty and above, chosen on purpose to cover varied lives.

Participants described shrinking social ties driven by stigma about ageing, lost relationships, money hardship, and poor health. The results included distress, unmet basic needs, and a sense of worthlessness about the future. Coping took many forms: prayer and spiritual practice, help from younger family members, and traditional savings groups, alongside excess sleep. The authors urge stronger ties between generations and richer community support for Ethiopia's elders.
pmc-11692579:
Shamatree Shakya and co-authors compare movement and blood markers between older women with heart disease who feel fatigued and those who do not in this 2024 study. Fatigue is common in cardiovascular disease and can warn of frailty. Activity is thought to ease it, partly through three growth-related blood proteins.

The data came from 253 women over sixty-five entering a movement trial. Seventeen percent reported fatigue. They logged fewer minutes of hard activity and fewer daily steps than the rest, measured by a wrist-worn tracker. Sedentary time, light activity, and fitness scores did not differ, and none of the three blood proteins separated the groups. Once background traits were counted, no activity measure still predicted fatigue. The authors call for deeper work on strength and other markers behind the gap.
pmc-11692679:
Lisa Hartnell, Alexander Maltsev, and Luigi Ferrucci use AI image analysis to measure the power-plant networks inside aging human muscle. Their 2024 study draws on an ageing research cohort and on older patients with narrowed leg arteries. Muscle samples were imaged in three dimensions at near-membrane sharpness by an ion-beam microscope, producing volumes too large to trace by hand.

Deep learning segmentation split the mitochondrial web into measurable parts. In healthy muscle the web forms an orderly continuum hugging the fibers near where energy is spent. Comparing old healthy muscle with diseased muscle shows how that web frays. The work links the shape of the energy network to mobility and thinking in later life.
pmc-11692779:
Rachel Crossdale and Nehle Penning explore how health shapes retirement planning in four European countries. Their study came out in 2024, based on a hundred life-history interviews with older workers in Germany, Poland, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.

Health worked in both directions. Good health could keep people working longer, or bankroll an early exit. Poor health pushed people out, and a partner's health pulled decisions too. All four countries shared a double bind: the workers who most need to keep earning are the ones whose health least allows it. Differences by sector, gender, and education ran through the accounts. The authors argue for preventive health policy across the working life, not treatment only at the end.
pmc-11692879:
Jieyu Mao, Miyae Yamakawa, and Yasushi Takeya published a study in 2024 on drug harms in people with dementia. People with dementia often take many drugs and face higher harm risk. They also struggle to report pain or odd feelings, so harms can be missed.

The team mined a United States harm-report database from 2013 to 2024. After cleaning, 23,519 reports tied to dementia remained. Reports peaked sharply around 2023. Buyers of the drugs filed the most reports, then doctors. The median time from drug start to harm was twenty days. Hospital stays followed in about thirty-eight percent of reports, and death in about twelve percent. One skin patch drug was most often named. The authors stress watchful care by nurses and doctors.
pmc-11693079:
Lok Man Leung and Elsie Yan compare mental health among older Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people who use aged care in Australia, in a research paper from 2024. The data cover the years from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-two. They compare people who get care at home with people who live in residential care.

Mental health problems were far more common in residential care than in home care. Mood problems were the most common kind in both groups, followed by anxiety and stress. Rates rose over the five years in both settings. The authors say residential care needs targeted mental health support built for this group.
pmc-11693279:
Aarohee Fulay and seven co-authors built in 2024 an index that grades how fairly older adults can reach healthy food. The index blends food security, physical access and personal limits, drawn from a long-running health study in Pittsburgh and Memphis. Older adults with low or middling equity scores ate worse than those with high scores. Once race was counted as a marker of structural forces, the link faded.

That fading suggests race-linked structures shape who the index flags. The team is now extending the work to two largely Black Pittsburgh neighborhoods with fresh survey data. New items will add distance to main shops and more function measures. The authors aim to expose which structural pieces of food access most need fixing. Their index treats healthy eating as an equity problem, not a willpower one.
pmc-11693379:
Clay Jackson and seven co-authors report a 2024 interim analysis of a two-question screening tool for agitation in Alzheimer’s dementia. Agitation often goes unnoticed or unreported, which delays treatment. The screener, called AASC, is the first tool built on the international definition of agitation in cognitive disorders.

In this early phase, 44 caregiver and clinician pairs took part across several sites. The screener and the full criteria agreed in about 70 percent of cases. The main source of missed cases was caregivers downplaying how much agitation affected daily function. The authors say the tool can start better conversations between caregivers and clinicians. A final analysis with 150 pairs is planned to confirm the results.
pmc-11694079:
Extended reality headsets can ease pain without drugs, and reviews gathering many trials guide doctors toward what works. Susan Persky and Megan Jiao asked a plainer question: do those reviews even describe the treatment well enough to judge? They gathered English-language reviews from 2021 to 2023 that tested such headsets for pain in any setting. Sixty-one qualified, and the team scored how each described the treatment's content and hardware.

Nearly half, twenty-nine reviews, described the treatment content only minimally, and fourteen described it in depth. The rest did not describe the content of the studies they gathered at all. Hardware reporting split similarly: a quarter minimal, just under half substantial, and thirty percent absent. Among thirty-nine reviews that pooled results numerically, only ten checked whether treatment features changed how well therapy worked. Such patchy description limits what readers can conclude about where results apply.
pmc-11694679:
Alexandra Manson, Brittany Johnson, and colleagues compare how school meal services actually reach children in a 2025 public health study. A school food service is the machinery, kitchens, staff, contracts, and rules, that turns a menu into lunch on a tray, and it differs enormously between countries and regions. Those differences decide whether healthy meal policies survive contact with reality.

Multiple cases from different countries are studied side by side to find what helps or blocks delivery. Lessons that travel across systems can guide governments designing or reforming school meals, a front-line child health intervention.
pmc-11695879: Josef Finsterer argues, in this short letter from twenty twenty-four, that a case of acute liver failure should not be blamed on high altitude until the usual causes have been ruled out. The letter's title states its whole case: altitude is a diagnosis of exclusion, not a first guess. Readers get a caution about reaching for an exotic explanation while common, testable causes of liver failure remain unchecked.
pmc-11699579:
Sri Melia and co-authors report a 2024 study of fermented goat milk boosted with two added ingredients. One is honey from stingless bees, and the other is an extract of butterfly pea flowers. Both are seen as functional foods, and adding them can change the traits of the milk.

The team varied the dose of each add in during ferment and then ran lab checks. Measures covered basic composition, acid level, color, live lactic germ counts, and defense strength against free radicals. The adds shifted composition and raised both carb content and germ counts. Acid level and pH stayed put. Brightness and yellowness rose with honey, while the flower extract cut some color values. Defense strength rose with dose.
pmc-11702379:
Xiaoting Liu and co-authors examine how arthritis links to daily disability and low mood in United States adults in a 2024 study. The data come from national health surveys run across three decades. Arthritis care, the authors argue, must cover both body and mind, not joints alone.

More than twenty-two thousand older adults fed the disability analysis, and over thirty-two thousand adults fed the mood analysis. Arthritis was self-reported, and knee arthritis was also graded from X-ray images. Disability covered daily self-care, household tasks, and mobility, while mood was scored with a standard health questionnaire. Even after full adjustment for other factors, arthritis stayed tied to more disability and more depressive symptoms. The team calls for care plans that screen for both burdens together.
pmc-11707379:
Ratika Parkash reviews how to give blood thinners safely to heart patients whose kidneys work poorly, in a 2024 article. The patients have atrial fibrillation, a faulty heart rhythm that raises stroke risk. Blood thinners cut that risk, but weak kidneys change how fast the drugs leave the body. Parkash weighs newer pills against the older drug warfarin for this group.

Newer pills are now favored over warfarin for most patients with this rhythm problem. Large trials found the pills cut stroke at least as well, with bleeding risks that vary by drug. Kidney function, though, sets the dose and can rule some pills out as kidneys fail. The review walks through trial results drug by drug so doctors can match the choice to each patient's kidneys. Heart failure, not stroke, is the top heart cause of death after such patients reach an emergency room.
pmc-11709479:
Luca Marie Michel and co-authors link brain sugar use to money-handling ability across the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, in a study from 2025. People in early decline often lose financial capacity, and with it quality of life. Whether brain function tracks that loss was unclear.

The team drew on a large Alzheimer's dataset, selecting well over a thousand people with both a financial capacity score and brain scans of glucose use. Sugar use in seventy-nine brain regions was tested against the score. Twenty-six regions correlated with financial capacity. The strongest ties sat in the caudate nucleus and the fornix, deep structures for memory and drive. Adjusted models confirmed several links. The work ties a daily-life skill to brain energy patterns.
pmc-11709579:
Women face a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease than men, and midlife is a time to cut the risks that lifestyle can change. Jessica Caldwell studies 207 women in a clinic program for lowering that risk, all with a family history of the disease. She scores each woman on fifteen risks, from diabetes, high blood pressure, and head injury to stress, sleep apnea, drinking, exercise, and schooling. She then checks whether the mix shifts across the menopause transition.

Stress, depression, and a body mass index above 30 were the most common risks. Total risk scores and lab values did not differ between women before and after menopause, whether stage came from self-report or a blood hormone test. Lab results often ran high in women who reported no matching diagnosis. Caldwell suggests that silent findings could flag chances for screening and care, and that stress and mood deserve focus in midlife.
pmc-11709679:
Elianne Pauli Quiros and co-authors set out a trial plan for older adults in Panama, in a study paper from 2025. Dementia affects tens of millions of people and is a top cause of disability in later life. Drugs have done little to slow decline, so the team tests training for the mind and body instead.

The trial plans to enroll sixty adults aged sixty to eighty and split them into three groups. One group gets health talks only. A second gets mind training, in a group and on a software platform, plus weekly walks tracked by a smartwatch. A third group does the walks only. Early checks were under way when the paper was written, with part of the group already assessed. Results will compare thought, mood, and health across the groups.
pmc-11709779:
Jeremy P Rouanet and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on amyloid tracer binding in Down syndrome brains. People with Down syndrome build amyloid early, and scans bind first and strongest in the striatum, unlike late-onset disease. The team used a glowing form of the tracer on donated tissue to ask what sits under that early signal.

Tissue came from 43 donors aged 42 to 70, in the putamen and frontal cortex. Tracer load did not grow with age and was no higher in the putamen than in cortex layers. Loads in the two regions tracked together. The tracer overlapped partly with amyloid stains, more in shallow layers.
pmc-11709879:
Isabel MacKenzie Sarty and co-authors track spinal fluid markers of Alzheimer disease and inflammation before symptoms begin. Inflammation sits at the heart of the disease process. Astrocyte reactivity rises as amyloid and tau appear in the brain.

The cohort held symptom-free adults with a family history of the disease. They have been followed for over a decade in a prevention study. Hundreds of fluid samples were drawn across those years. Standard tests measured amyloid and tau forms in the fluid. A broad panel assayed cytokines and their receptors together. The team sought which signals move earliest in the disease. Such early maps could guide prevention trials.
pmc-11709979:
Stefan Wendt and co-authors model Alzheimer disease in human cell grown spheres to study how immune cells protect neurons over time, in work from 2025. Mouse models have taught much, yet their lessons often fail to become human treatments. Human cell cultures may close that gap.

The team grew 3D spheres from human stem cell derived neuron precursors. The spheres matured over sixty days. Brain immune cells were added for the last ten days. A form of amyloid, the protein that builds plaques in the disease, was added over a long span. The setup lets them watch neuron, immune cell, and amyloid interplay.
pmc-11710079:
Jiacheng Ma and co-authors report, in a 2025 paper, on a drug target shared by two brain problems. Chemo for cancer can leave patients with lasting trouble in thinking, and it may raise the risk of dementia. The team focus on an enzyme called HDAC6, which acts on parts of the cell that move goods along nerve fibres.

In mice, they gave a brain-reaching blocker of the enzyme after cisplatin treatment. Tests then checked thinking, nerve fibre health, and tau buildup. Blocking the enzyme had earlier been shown to keep transport along fibres working and to guard their energy supply. The team also crossed a tau-disease mouse line with another line to test the target for Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-11710179:
