Seven researchers search for genes that shape how memory and thinking change with age, and whether those genes act differently in men and women. Two-thirds of Alzheimer disease cases are women, and earlier work hints that women may keep sharper minds longer but then decline faster. The team tracked five thinking skills plus overall ability in 3,021 adults aged sixty-five and older from three long-running studies.

Analyzing men and women apart, the team found a gene region on chromosome 4 tied to memory decline in men alone. A second region on chromosome 12, near a gene involved in cell energy production, was tied to decline in planning and control skills in women. Both findings add to the case that the genetics of late-life thinking differ by sex, which matters for how future studies and treatments are designed.
pmc-11710279:
Yan and co-authors report that tau, a protein that builds up in Alzheimer disease, can carry a little studied tag called UFM1. The tag system helps cells handle DNA damage, protein stress, and immune tasks, and it matters for healthy brain growth. Their 2025 study tests the tau link in lab samples and in human brain tissue.

In Alzheimer brains, one enzyme that removes the tag was lower in its soluble form, while total tag levels were higher. Tau was shown to bind two parts of the tagging machinery. Tests on tissue found tau carrying the tag under natural conditions. A detailed scan found 17 sites on tau where the tag can attach.
pmc-11710379:
Jurij Rosen and Frank Jessen test who truly qualifies for new Alzheimer therapies in a 2025 study. Antibody drugs that clear amyloid now offer hope in early disease. Trial entry rules are strict, though, and real patients may not match. The team check a large real-world dataset against those rules.

The dataset held over forty thousand patients, with post-mortem brain reports for a subset. Among those, 887 had a memory-led Alzheimer syndrome at first visit. Trial rules from three drugs left small eligible groups. The authors then check how many of those truly had Alzheimer pathology at death. The study shows how narrow the door to these drugs is in practice.
pmc-11710479:
Yiyang Wu and co-authors present a 2025 study of sex gaps in Alzheimer disease at the single cell level. Two thirds of cases are women, and past work found sex linked factors in the disease. The team used single cell gene data from a brain area tied to planning.

Data came from a long running study of aging and memory, with more than four hundred donors. The team ran sex split and sex interaction tests for diagnosis, disease signs, and decline. They found many sex specific effects, most male ones in vessel cells and most female ones in active nerve cells. One gene showed opposed links by sex. Women with the disease also showed weaker cell to cell signals overall.
pmc-11710579:
Evan Fletcher and co-authors used machine learning to model what drives memory performance in a 2025 study. Thinking health rests on many factors, some changeable like activity and sleep, and some fixed like age and genes. Untangling their joint effect is hard with standard statistics.

The team applied a decision-tree boosting method that handles tangled, interacting inputs well. It can rank which factors matter most for episodic memory, the recall of personal events that fades early in dementia. Such rankings help target prevention trials at the strongest levers. The approach also shows where factors only matter in combination, a pattern single-variable studies miss entirely.
pmc-11710679:
Elaina Smith and nine co-authors compared verbal and visual short-term memory in mild cognitive impairment, in a 2025 study. Sixteen impaired and eleven healthy adults took standard memory tests. Digit span covered number memory in three modes. Word lists and shape drawing covered the two main channels. Groups matched on age and schooling.

General screening scores did not separate the groups. Trail making, a speeded attention test, did. Sequencing digits backward in order was weaker in impairment. Simple forward and backward spans were not. Word and shape recall both lagged in the impaired group. Both groups improved with repeated trials at similar rates. Delayed recall gaps were wide and consistent. The authors say learning capacity survives while storage fades. Word list testing looked most sensitive to the impairment.
pmc-11710779:
Keith R Cole and co-authors link grip strength and walking speed to brain volume in a 2025 study of older adults. Both simple measures predict later dementia, but their ties to brain structure were less clear. The team studied 570 adults aged fifty to ninety-two from a Vanderbilt ageing project, 158 of whom had mild impairment.

All took brain MRI scans plus grip and walking tests. Weaker grip tracked a smaller hippocampus, but only in men. Slower walking tracked a smaller frontal lobe in everyone. Thinking status did not change either link. The authors say these two cheap clinic measures flag different parts of the brain, and they may help spot risk early.
pmc-11710879:
Mohammed Al-Shehari, Yasser Obadiel, Matheel Abdulwahab, and Haitham Jowah study leaks after stoma closure surgery in Yemen, in a 2024 paper. A stoma lets bowel waste leave through the belly wall, and closing it means joining the bowel ends back together. If that join leaks, patients face grave infection and longer hospital stays.

The team reviewed fifty patients treated at two large hospitals in Sana'a between 2020 and 2024. Six patients, twelve percent, developed a leak. Smoking stood out: two-thirds of the leak cases were smokers, a far higher share than among patients who healed cleanly. The authors also weighed age, other illnesses, and surgical technique. In low-resource hospitals, knowing the top risks helps teams guard the patients most likely to leak.
pmc-11711979:
Jennie L DiGrado reports a case study of how occupational therapists use the built setting in a skilled nursing facility in a 2025 session summary. Therapists adapt rooms and spaces so residents with brain disorders can manage self-care and leisure. The study gathered the views of therapists who do this work daily.

DiGrado shares what the therapists said about shaping light, layout, and cues to support person-centred care. The findings back non-drug strategies that use the physical setting itself as a tool. Such changes aim to raise quality of life for residents with dementia. The session also draws on earlier research that supports therapy advice on adapting surroundings.
pmc-11712079:
Stina Saunders and seven co-authors ask in 2025 what Americans over 50 care about most in their brain health, using an electronic person-specific outcome survey. Drugs and lifestyle programs for dementia often measure what researchers value, not what patients do. Free-text answers let people name their own priorities.

Seven hundred sixty-four participants sent more than eleven thousand responses between May 2023 and January 2024. Word patterns were compared across social groups and against British data from the same program. Confidence in managing personal priorities was compared between those with and without a dementia diagnosis. The results help trial designers pick outcomes that patients themselves would notice and value.
pmc-11712379:
Dympna Casey and co-authors report carer views of an education program in a 2025 Irish study. The program sat inside CREST, a support project for people with mild to moderate dementia who live at home. Its six weekly two-hour sessions aimed to build carer knowledge, confidence, and time for their own health.

Nine carers finished the program, with average attendance above ninety percent. All agreed the sessions were helpful and matched their needs. Carers valued most the facts about dementia and the communication strategies they learned. They also prized meeting peers, sharing hard moments, and being urged to care for themselves. The authors say such programs help carers manage stress and build a support network.
pmc-11712479:
Juliana Baldo and co-authors validate remote brain testing against clinic standards in a 2025 study. Classic paper tests for thinking skills are slow, costly, and prone to scorer bias. Patients far from clinics may never get tested at all.

The California Cognitive Assessment Battery moves testing onto computers at home. It can score spoken answers, a gap in most rival batteries. The study checks its scores against the trusted manual measures. Remote testing also records fine details of how answers unfold. Valid home testing could widen dementia screening to whole regions at once.
pmc-11712579:
Mathias Sauer and co-authors build a new test for a synaptic protein that fades in brain degeneration. Their twenty twenty-five paper measures neuronal pentraxin 2 in spinal fluid. The protein supports synaptic plasticity, and its drop tracks thought decline.

Mass spectrometry can read it, but that gear is too scarce for wide clinic use. The team built a single-molecule array test that works with a tiny fluid sample. Shop antibodies were checked for the home-built assay. The test was then run in an Alzheimer disease group. A simpler, sensitive assay could bring synaptic health checks into routine memory clinic work, where they are now rare.
pmc-11712679:
Olivar, Barreto, Mendez and colleagues report on a cognitive rehabilitation workshop for people with mild cognitive impairment in Buenos Aires in 2025. Fifteen participants, thirteen women and two men, met twice a week through 2023 for group sessions.

A test battery covering verbal fluency, trail making, naming, symbol coding and word learning was given at the start and end. About 73 percent improved their MMSE scores, and test results were broadly better. Two thirds of those with high depression scores improved, and daily living skills rose too. The team concludes that early group work can support mood, social life and quality of life.
pmc-11712779:
Raquel N Taddei and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on blood proteins tied to synapses, the tiny links between brain cells. The team asked whether these proteins could tell apart the three most common forms of dementia and track how memory fails in each one.

They tested blood drawn from 100 people whose dementia type was later confirmed by autopsy, plus a small group with no dementia. More than eighty such proteins showed up in blood. Fourteen differed between the ill and the well, and some shifted in only one form of dementia. A few also tracked memory scores. The authors say these blood signs could one day help doctors name the right disease sooner.
pmc-11712879:
Christian Mirescu presents a 2025 profile of a first in class small drug that switches on a brain immune receptor for Alzheimer disease. The receptor, TREM2, senses fats and helps the brain's guard cells live, shift shape, and move. Broken forms of it raise disease risk, which marks it as a drug aim. Antibody drugs chase it too, but a small pill could reach the brain better and dose by mouth.

The drug, VG-3927, was tested across human cell systems. Mixed dishes of guard cells, star cells, and neurons grown from stem cells gave one test bed. A mouse model bred with the human receptor gave another. Readouts tracked guard cell action and disease marks. The work backs the pill as a disease altering hope.
pmc-11712979:
Sarah Bauermeister describes a 2025 workshop program called Your Beautiful Brain, which uses art to teach brain health in Black African and Caribbean communities in the United Kingdom. These communities are often left out of dementia research, so new treatments may never be tested with them in mind. The program aimed to close that gap in a fun and fitting way.

Each workshop opened with a short talk on healthy habits, then gave out colouring sheets that showed community members jogging, walking, and eating well. A free art session let people show what they had learned, and refreshments kept the mood social. Six workshops drew more than fifty adults aged fifty and over.
pmc-11713079:
Ylauna Penalva and co-authors hunt for a cause of low brain sugar use in Alzheimer disease in a 2025 paper. Early disease brings falling glucose metabolism in the brain. A glucose transporter at the blood-brain barrier is reduced in patients.

The amyloid precursor protein sits at the center of the disease story. Mice lacking that protein show faults in mitochondria and insulin action. Whether the protein also controls the glucose transporter was open. The team traced a regulatory link between the two. Readers learn a new mechanistic thread tying a famous disease protein to brain fuel supply.
pmc-11713179:
Alice Grazia and co-authors set out a process evaluation for a German study of amyloid PET imaging in Alzheimer's care in this 2025 protocol paper. The parent study tests whether the scan changes patients' function at eighteen months. This sub-study asks how the intervention lands in real practice.

Interviews, surveys, and checklists will track acceptance among patients and providers, adherence to follow-up, and delivery fidelity. The team will also record context changes and the mechanisms that let the scan fit routine care. A mixed-methods analysis ties barriers and facilitators to outcomes. Expected findings include perceived utility and implementation hurdles. The authors say the lessons can guide similar evidence-development studies across Europe and beyond amyloid imaging.
pmc-11713279:
Bafaloukou and co-authors sort episodes of agitation in dementia into types, in this 2025 paper. Agitation affects about thirty percent of people with dementia, but its triggers vary a lot. Knowing the type could help carers pick the right response for each person.

The team used home sensor data from sixty-one people in a monitoring study. They logged two hundred thirty-five episodes and built sixty-seven features from activity, sleep, and body signals. Several sorting methods were compared, and the best one found two clear subtypes. A follow-up model tried to predict the subtype from room sensors alone, which could one day alert carers early.
pmc-11713379:
Marian Sulvaran and eleven co-authors report early safety results for a cannabis-based drug aimed at agitation in Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 study. The formulation pairs THC, the main active compound in cannabis, with melatonin. THC is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called CYP2C9, whose gene varies between people: some versions clear the drug slowly, which could change its side effects.

Thirteen Puerto Rican patients joined a phase-one trial, receiving the drug once, twice, or three times a day across successive two-week rounds. The researchers genotyped each patient as a normal or intermediate metabolizer and compared the frequency of adverse events between the groups. Early safety work like this decides whether a drug proceeds at all, and whether dosing should one day be tailored to a patient's enzyme type rather than set the same for everyone.
pmc-11713479:
Zeyu Zhu and co-authors ask how age and sex shape the spread of tau in the brain, in this 2025 paper. Tau build-up drives much of the harm in Alzheimer's disease. Scans show that its path differs by age and sex, but the reasons are unclear.

The study covered three hundred thirteen people from a national data set, some healthy and some across the disease range. Each had amyloid scans and repeat tau scans over time. The team mapped yearly tau change in two hundred brain areas and used brain wiring maps from other adults. They test how age, sex, and amyloid jointly steer where tau grows and spreads.
pmc-11713579:
Loss of synapses, the tiny junctions where brain cells connect, tracks closely with failing memory in Alzheimer's disease. Alexandra DiFilippo and fifteen co-authors ask how that loss relates to tau, a protein that tangles inside cells as the disease advances, in this 2025 study. Brain scans can now measure both in living people, using tracer dyes that light up synapses and tau.

Earlier scan studies covered narrow groups and found no link between the two measures within each group. This team widened the lens, enrolling people with no impairment and people with Alzheimer's, drawn from Wisconsin aging studies and the local community. Each person received full clinical and memory testing plus both scans. The authors compare synapse and tau levels across all participants and within groups set by amyloid status and thinking ability.
pmc-11713679:
Manas Chakraborty and co-authors test whether a ginkgo compound can shield brain-like cells from amyloid damage. Amyloid beta clumps are a core harm in Alzheimer's disease, draining cell energy and killing neurons. Bilobalide, a plant compound from Ginkgo biloba leaves, may guard several cell pathways at once.

The team grows human neuroblastoma cells and matures them into neuron-like cells. Cells get bilobalide at five dose levels for a day, then face amyloid for a day. Survival, oxygen use, and harmful oxygen byproducts are all measured. The design reads both whether cells live and how their energy engines fare. Early cognitive decline lacks good drug options, so plant compounds with broad action draw real interest. Results here set up whether bilobalide earns tests in fuller disease models.
pmc-11713779:
Lori Beason-Held and co-authors study why older adults forget, in a 2025 paper drawn from a long Baltimore aging study. The team scanned 297 cognitively normal adults, with an average age near seventy-four, while they learned pairs of faces and scenes. An hour later, the adults picked which face had gone with each scene. The team then sorted brain data by what was later remembered or forgotten.

Both remembered and forgotten items lit up a visual path and the memory core regions, such as the hippocampus. The split lay in links between regions. Remembered items showed stronger ties between the memory core and the visual path, while forgotten items lacked that pattern. The results pin encoding success on teamwork between brain regions, not on single hot spots.
pmc-11714079:
Faith Simushi and co-authors measure unmet care needs among people with dementia and their carers in Lusaka, in a study from 2025. In Zambia most care falls to family members, since formal day care and home support are scarce. The team visited thirty three pairs at home and scored needs with a standard tool for dementia care.

On the whole, well over half of the needs of patients went unmet, and the share was higher still for carers. Unmet needs ran higher for those with a degree level of schooling and for those whose type of dementia was not known. The authors say both patients and carers lack help in many areas of daily life, and that local services need to close the gap.
pmc-11714279:
Aniek van Gils and co-authors use a decision support program to route memory clinic patients through the fewest tests that still settle a diagnosis, in a 2025 study. With dementia rising and new drugs on the horizon, clinics need leaner pathways. Drawing on two cohorts with over 880 patients and controls, the team ordered tests from quick digital screening to scans and spinal fluid markers. Testing stopped whenever the program's probability score crossed a certainty threshold.

Three goals were tested: naming the syndrome, naming its cause, and judging fitness for disease-modifying treatment. Stepwise testing reached firm answers with fewer procedures than testing everyone fully. The approach aims to spare patients needless tests while clinics face growing demand.
pmc-11714479:
Yan Wang, Fang Xie, and Yihui Guan study a cell receptor tied to synapse work and its link to tau in mild Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. The receptor, called mGluR5, helps nerve cells send signals and adjust their links. Loss of synapses is an early step in the disease, so the receptor may be part of the story.

Fifteen patients with mild disease and thirteen healthy adults had combined scans for the receptor, amyloid, and tau. Patients showed less receptor binding in the hippocampus, a key memory area, and more tau in that area and beyond. Tau load there moved against receptor levels. Both measures also tracked with thinking scores. The authors say the receptor deserves study as a treatment target.
pmc-11714579:
Maryam Naseri, Owen T. Carmichael, and Sreekrishna R. Pillai wrote this research article in two thousand twenty-five. It asks whether brain studies that use positron emission tomography, or PET, can be repeated by other labs with the same results.

The authors compare PET work with MRI work on five points: shared rules, plans filed in advance, shared data and code, ready-made software, and standard pipelines. MRI scores far ahead on each point. No PET study in their search had a plan filed in advance, and shared PET data sets were rare. As a test, the team rebuilt a well-known Alzheimer's study pipeline in their own lab. The numbers matched well, but weak records made the rebuild slow. The paper argues that PET work needs shared rules and tools to catch up.
pmc-11714679:
Gemma Salvado and co-authors examine a 2025 blood test that could help find people for Alzheimer's trials. The trials need people whose brains hold amyloid clumps but who still think clearly. Tests that prove those clumps are costly or involve a needle in the back. The team asked if a blood mark called p-tau217 could do the first screen instead. Their sample held close to fifteen hundred such adults from eight groups.

About one in four of the adults proved to have amyloid on brain scans. Blood test cut-offs set in one group sorted the rest fairly well. Most people the blood test flagged did prove to have amyloid on scans. Adding a spinal fluid test for those flagged raised the hit rate further. The authors say a staged screen like this could cut trial costs and spare many people needless scans.
pmc-11714979:
Aldo Camargo and Ze Wang ask whether the brain's connection patterns change shape as Alzheimer's disease advances. They used resting-state brain scans from a large Alzheimer's study and built, for each person, a map of how 400 brain regions connect. The groups were healthy controls, people with mild memory problems, and Alzheimer's patients. From each map they extracted gradients, axes running from low to high connection similarity, and compared the first three across groups.

The main gradient ran lowest in the vision area at the back of the brain. It rose through movement and temporal regions, then fell toward the front, shrinking step by step along the disease path. It was lower in mild impairment than in healthy brains, lower still in Alzheimer's, and reduced at the front only in the Alzheimer's group. The authors read this as shared network damage that deepens as memory and thinking decline.
pmc-11715279:
Jessica Alber wrote a 2025 paper on whether eye scans can flag Alzheimer disease before symptoms start. Scans of the retina can measure the thickness of its layers. Past work links thin retinal layers to the disease. Alber asks whether those changes predict a blood marker of the disease in healthy older adults.

The study enrolled 120 adults aged 55 to 80 with normal thinking scores. Each person had retinal imaging and a blood test for a tau protein marker. Models weighed age, gene risk, and family history as well. Layers that thin in clear disease got special focus. If eye scans prove sound, they could offer a cheap early warning tool.
pmc-11715379:
Michael Slee and five co-authors review whether insulin resistance sits in the middle of how exercise guards the aging brain. Diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, and insulin paths can shape the two proteins that mark it. Their 2025 review gathers animal and human studies that touch all three threads at once.

The search found 21 studies that fit. In animals, exercise cut insulin resistance and brain disease marks side by side, again and again. Human work was thin: few studies saw both gains at once, and just one hinted the middle role is real. No study tested that role with sound shared methods. The authors call for direct tests of the chain in people. The prize is a clearer sense of how activity cuts disease risk.
pmc-11715479:
Shijia Bian and co-authors report a 2025 study of spinal fluid proteins in Down syndrome. Almost all people with Down syndrome develop Alzheimer disease by their seventh decade of life. The team asked whether the fluid changes in this group match those seen in other forms of the disease.

The study measured more than a thousand proteins in fluid from five groups of people. Some changes were shared across all forms of the disease, such as signs of immune activity and lost nerve contact markers. Most shared changes tracked with two proteins tied to brain plaques and tangles. The Down syndrome group also showed early rises in some defense proteins that set it apart.
pmc-11715679:
Suhrud Panchawagh, Sumedha Mitra, and Jonas Sundarakumar test pesticide links to cognition in rural South India in a 2025 study. Farm chemicals may harm the aging brain, but evidence from rural India was thin. Their cohort gathers older adults in a farming district.

Over four thousand three hundred participants took a full computerized thinking battery. About a third of the farmers used pesticides, for a median of ten years. After strict corrections, no thinking domain tied significantly to heavy pesticide use. The authors urge caution: exposure was self-reported and the snapshot design cannot catch slow effects. Planned follow-ups will watch whether decline accelerates over time.
pmc-11715779:
Andrea Benedet and co-authors search blood and spinal fluid proteins for Alzheimer signals beyond amyloid and tau in a 2025 study. Current blood markers spot amyloid early with high accuracy, but markers for later stages and other disease processes are still needed. The team used brain scan data to sort people by amyloid and tau status.

Samples came from a cohort spanning healthy aging, mild impairment, and dementia. Groups held 242 people with neither marker, 27 with amyloid only, and 113 with both. Protein panels were compared across groups with age and sex accounted for, and network methods grouped proteins into modules. Early shifts tied to amyloid alone began the map of what changes next.
pmc-11715879:
Anna Mammel and six co-authors compare two blood markers for Alzheimer's disease inside a working clinical laboratory, in this 2025 study. The markers are two forms of the tau protein, pTau181 and pTau217, and both rise when the disease is present. The lab ran each marker on two different testing platforms to see which pairing performs best.

Clinical checks used samples from 260 people with scan confirmed amyloid status and 119 with tissue confirmed diagnoses. The pTau217 marker sorted patients more accurately than pTau181 on both platforms. It also showed a wider working range and steadier results between batches. The authors conclude that pTau217 is the stronger choice for clinical screening, whichever platform a lab runs.
pmc-11716079:
Klodian Dhana and co-authors check whether well-known dementia risk scores work fairly across racial groups, in a 2025 study. Spotting high-risk older adults early allows timely steps that may slow decline. Four popular prediction models were put to an external test in the Chicago Health and Aging Project.

The study followed 2,130 people without dementia at the start, 1,159 Black American and 971 white participants. For each model, the team computed predicted risk from published scores, then judged the predictions against real clinical diagnoses. They measured how well each score separated future cases from non-cases and whether its risk levels matched reality, a fairness check for tools used in mixed populations.
pmc-11716179:
Duygu Tosun and co-authors ask what a spinal fluid test for Lewy body pathology means for the brain scans of Alzheimer's patients, in this 2025 study. The test detects seeds of alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Lewy body disease, which often coexists with Alzheimer's. The team, working with the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, studied amyloid-positive people with cognitive impairment.

Participants had spinal fluid tested and, within a year, brain scans measuring amyloid, tau, and shrinkage. Those testing positive showed more amyloid and tau signal in several temporal and frontal regions, and more shrinkage in others, even after adjusting for age, sex, and genetic risk. Follow-up scans were fewer, but positive patients lost tissue faster in middle frontal and parietal areas. The authors read the pattern as a sign that mixed pathology shapes how Alzheimer's unfolds.
pmc-11716379:
Marlies Oosthoek and co-authors report a 2025 study on blood and spine fluid proteins and a known risk in Alzheimer's care. Some new drugs for the disease can cause odd spots on brain scans, grouped under one short name. Risk is higher in people with small bleeds in the brain, a gene form, or low levels of a plaque protein.

The team read 288 proteins in spine fluid from 156 people with the disease. They split people by each risk trait and by a high risk and low risk mix. Each split showed its own set of changed proteins, and most were lower in the high risk group. The sets barely overlapped, which hints that each risk trait works in its own way.
pmc-11716479:
Agathe Vrillon and a large team of co-authors published a study in 2025 checking a tau brain scan against what autopsy later found. The scan tracer is approved for spotting Alzheimer's tau in patients with thinking problems. The team asked how faithfully scan readings match the tangles counted in the brain after death, including at early stages.

They studied fifty-nine patients with various brain diseases who were scanned and later autopsied in San Francisco. Healthy volunteers without autopsy served as a reference group. Scan values in two key regions were set against diagnoses and tangle stages. A blood tau marker was also compared. Checks like this tell doctors how much trust a scan deserves.
pmc-11716579:
Maria da Silva and co-authors put a standard ruler on amyloid brain scans in suspected Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid PET readings vary by tracer and lab, so the Centiloid scale rescales them onto one zero-to-one-hundred ladder. The team implemented the scale for Florbetaben scans, reworking a reference data set's pipeline in imaging software.

Twenty-eight anonymized scans were processed with MRI-guided registration and atlas normalization. The resulting spread was wide: eight people fell in the low band, nine in the intermediate band, and eleven in the high band. The authors argue the choice of cutoff genuinely moves diagnosis, and that a common scale makes those choices comparable across clinics. A worked example contrasts a clearly positive and a clearly negative brain.
pmc-11716679:
Remington E Schmidt and Yogesh Shah published a review in 2025 on a blood test for dementia of any cause. The test measures a protein released when nerve fibers are damaged, so it rises in many brain diseases rather than just one. The authors pooled the evidence on how well it separates healthy people from patients with dementia.

They combined fifty-eight studies that measured the protein on the same platform. Levels ran about twice as high in patients, and the test sorted the groups fairly well. It proved better at ruling dementia out than at ruling it in. The authors say it may help most when patients first report mild memory worries.
pmc-11716779:
Anthony J Griswold and co-authors test whether blood tests for Alzheimer's disease work as well in people of non-European ancestry. Their 2025 study measures two plasma markers, a modified tau protein and the ratio of two amyloid pieces. Three admixed cohorts took part: African Americans, Peruvians, and Caribbean Hispanics, well over seventeen hundred people in all.

The tau marker did its job everywhere. Its levels in patients did not differ by cohort, and it was clearly raised in Alzheimer's against controls in the pooled data and in each group alone. The amyloid ratio differed little, trending only the expected way. Judged by accuracy curves, the tau marker beat the ratio, and combining both did better still. The authors conclude these blood markers travel across ancestries, a needed check before clinics lean on them for diverse patients.
pmc-11716879:
Rebecca Price describes two brain sample banks in 2025 that share tissue and cells for nerve disease research. Sample access is a top block for work on Alzheimer disease and kin ills. One bank, BioSEND, holds body fluids and DNA from many disease groups, while the other holds skin and stem cell lines.

Stock spans Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, and many more, with spinal fluid, blood, urine, and saliva among the types. Cell lines cover control donors and patients with set gene faults. Both banks ship to labs world-wide and keep adding new cohorts.
pmc-11716979:
Cassandra Blew and co-authors report a 2025 study of a blood protein called GDF15 and its links to dementia. Earlier work tied the protein to dementia risk, but its value across groups and its ties to brain change were still unclear.

The team drew on three large cohorts in the United States and Britain. Higher levels of the protein went with higher dementia risk in both midlife and late life, and the pattern held in a second cohort. In one aging study, higher levels also went with smaller brain volume and more white matter damage. The findings support the protein as one signal among many for tracking risk.
pmc-11717979:
Harshavardhan Jampuram, Aneet Mahendra, and Sanjeev Gupta study cosmetic contact dermatitis in this 2024 paper. Cosmetics can trigger an inflammatory skin reaction in some users. Patch testing is the standard way to find the culprit chemical. The reaction can also weigh heavily on quality of life.

The study enrolled 65 patients with the condition. Their product histories and skin findings were recorded in detail. Patch tests used Indian cosmetic, fragrance, and standard allergen sets. Hair dye was the most common product in use, reported by about seven in ten patients. A dermatology life quality questionnaire measured daily impact. The work gives clinics a profile of typical patients and the allergens most often involved.
pmc-11718379:
Ning Jia and co-authors chart leg and foot disorders tied to work in key industries in China, in a report from two thousand twenty-four. Data spanned two thousand eighteen to two thousand twenty-three across major job groups. Such disorders drive absence from work and add to disease costs worldwide.

Near eighteen percent of workers in the groups studied had such a disorder. Toy making had the highest rate, followed by medical staff and car making. Metal smelting and coal mining rounded out the top five. The report maps risk factors by industry to guide prevention. It aims to give big-data support for control efforts in these trades.
pmc-11726979:
Ho-Hsiang Chang and co-authors studied a muscle protein called myostatin and blood vessel function in kidney disease in 2024. Myostatin slows muscle growth and has been linked to obesity, insulin problems, and heart disease. Its link to vessel lining health in people with chronic kidney disease was not clear.

The team studied 136 patients with stage three to five disease who were not on dialysis. Fasting blood tests measured the protein, and a finger heat test gave a score for vessel response. About one in five patients scored in the poor range, and near half scored in the middle range. Readers get a focused look at whether a muscle signal tracks vessel health in kidney patients. That link, if firm, could help flag heart risk in this group.
pmc-11727579:
Hemi Luan and three co-authors map which proteins a gut-derived bile acid touches in a 2023 paper. Bile acids are made in the liver and reshaped by gut microbes. Their imbalance shows up in brain diseases, but their protein targets in nerve cells were largely unknown.

The team used a heat-based profiling method: proteins that bind a compound often withstand heat differently, revealing the binding. In a human nerve cell line, a major gut bile acid bound sixty-five proteins. Two stood out. One is part of the enzyme complex that clips a precursor into amyloid beta, the peptide that piles up in Alzheimer's disease. Tests showed the bile acid, acting through that subunit, boosted amyloid production. The work draws a concrete line from gut chemistry to a hallmark of brain degeneration, and names targets drugs might aim at.
pmc-11727979:
Sofia Ruiz-Salcedo and five co-authors set out a trial protocol testing whether prescribed exercise helps smokers quit when added to a proven stop-smoking drug. The drug, cytisinicline, is funded for certain heavy smokers in Andalusia, Spain. The multicentre study will randomize 150 such smokers, all highly dependent and motivated, with a failed quit attempt in the past year, into two arms.

One arm gets targeted physical exercise prescribed alongside brief advice and the drug; the other gets a general exercise leaflet with same advice and drug. Everyone is followed for twelve months to see who stays quit, and how fitness and smoking-related illness change. The protocol, run by a multidisciplinary primary care team, estimates the added value of exercise as a formal prescription rather than a suggestion. The authors argue that if synergy is real, quit programs should write exercise into the care pathway.
pmc-11728079:
A heart attack's harm does not stop at the heart: the kidneys and liver pay for the lost flow and its return. Işın Güneş and six co-authors dosed rats in 2024 with a nano dust of cerium oxide before tying and freeing a heart vessel. Four groups split the tale: plain, dust alone, attack alone, and dust before attack. Blood marks and flesh cuts told the story.

The attack-only rats showed crowded dead cells and swelling crowds in the liver, and wrecked tubes in the kidney. The dust-first rats fared softer on each count, in the cuts the team could see. Blood rust marks were read as well. The team call the dust a shield worth more work, far from a clinic claim.
pmc-11728279:
The authors present ways to measure unevenness inside metals and ceramics in a 2024 paper. Grain size and crystal direction shape how a material behaves, yet simple averages hide patchiness. The paper offers numeric indicators for both grain unevenness and texture unevenness, then tests them on synthetic samples with varied grain patterns.

The grain measures track well with spread statistics and inequality indexes. The texture measures expose shifts that averages miss. Tests on real observed samples confirm the tools work outside simulations. Readers in materials science get a fuller dashboard for judging polycrystal quality.
pmc-11728579:
Micah Hebert and co-authors compare, in a 2024 study, leg strength and balance in people who have had knee ligament surgery with people who have not. Anterior cruciate ligament injuries strike up to a quarter million Americans a year and can waste muscle and unsteady balance long after repair.

Twelve surgical patients and thirty controls were measured for leg muscle mass, thigh size, and sway while standing on one leg. The team expected bigger gaps between legs in the surgical group, but found none. Surprisingly, controls showed the clearer pattern: their dominant leg carried more muscle and a thicker thigh. Rehab may have evened out the surgical patients' legs.
pmc-11728679:
Maria Angela Romeo and co-authors review digital tools for dry eye disease tied to screen use, in a 2024 paper. Long hours at screens cut blink rates and leave many blinks half-finished. The tear film then dries faster, and the glands that oil the tears work worse. Screen light can also strain the eyes and disturb sleep. The review asks whether apps and digital programs can retrain eye habits.

Teaching material, better desk setups, and blink exercises all ease the strain, past work shows. Digital tools can deliver that teaching in a targeted way and prompt healthier blinking. The findings reviewed here link such tools to steadier tear films and better comfort. The authors still call for longer studies across wider groups of people. They frame the tools as a low-cost aid that can sit beside standard care.
pmc-11728779:
Xiaokang Li and co-authors showed, in a 2024 study, that a notorious crop pest moth also moonlights as a pollinator on its long migrations. Spodoptera litura adults fly far between regions, and pollen rides along on their bodies. The team checked 1,253 migrants caught over four years on an island in the Bohai Strait, a known flyway.

Just over half the moths carried pollen in an average year, with rates shifting by sex and season. Lab work named pollen from 40 plant species across 21 families. Flight simulations traced autumn trips from northeast China across the sea to the north China plain. The authors argue the pest's pollination service deserves a line in the ledger beside its crop damage. Migration ecology, they note, moves genes as well as mouths.
pmc-11748979:
Renny Ssembatya and thirteen co-authors report how they gathered trustworthy data for a pregnancy ultrasound study in rural Uganda. The hosted text dates the study to 2024. Deaths of mothers and newborns stay high in poor countries, and weak data hides both the scale of the problem and the effect of fixes. Their project brought prenatal ultrasound to small rural health centers.

Local clerks were hired, trained hard, and backed by frequent oversight visits. Of 2,397 women enrolled, 82.5 percent ended with complete outcome records. An expert audit found the data over 80 percent accurate on 10 of 11 measures, and about 90 percent accurate overall. The authors conclude that careful hiring, training, and supervision make solid research data possible even in low-resource rural clinics. Their lessons can guide similar studies.
pmc-11749779:
Lucia Guilabert and Enrique de-Madaria weigh a new idea to stop a common harm from a gut scope test in a 2025 piece. The test, which checks bile and pancreas ducts, can leave the pancreas sore and swollen. Salt water given fast by vein is the usual guard, but too much fluid can harm some patients.

The authors review a trial that swapped part of the salt water for albumin, a blood protein. That mix did no better than plain salt water at a mild rate. Rates of pancreas harm were near the same in both groups. The piece urges care in picking who gets fast fluids.
pmc-11769679:
Yuekai Li and five colleagues build Funmap, a fine-mapping tool that lets hundreds of functional clues vote without drowning the signal. Fine-mapping sorts genome-wide association hits to find the variants truly driving a trait. Genome annotations can help, but piling on hundreds makes rival tools cry wolf.

Funmap ties each annotation to causal odds through a random effects model that resists overfitting. False alarms stayed calibrated in simulations where competitors lost control, while power held or improved. On four blood lipid traits with 187 annotations, its picks replicated in fresh data fifteen to twenty-six percent more often than the runner-up. A fast solver keeps the method practical.
pmc-11772179:
Qian Jiang and co-authors study a cell-death process in diabetic foot ulcers in this study, published in 2024. Foot ulcers are a common and stubborn complication of diabetes. The team asked whether ferroptosis, a form of iron-linked cell death, tracks how these wounds heal.

They followed patients with foot ulcers and patients with ordinary traumatic wounds. Blood and tissue kits measured signs tied to ferroptosis in both groups. The levels were then set against diabetes severity and healing progress. The study ran at a hospital in Gansu province over three years. A clear marker could help doctors watch risky wounds and choose care sooner. The team also note what care teams can watch in clinic.
pmc-11772479:
Sara Svensson argues that shared norms deserve a central place in the study of European cross-border regions. These are border areas where towns and authorities from two or more countries govern shared problems together. Since the 1950s, local and regional bodies have set up joint organizations to coordinate across these borders. Svensson, writing in 2024, reads these bodies through institutional theory, where norms are shared expectations that guide behavior.

Her first claim is that a focus on norms can sharpen what researchers know about how cross-border cooperation starts and how it works day to day. Her second claim runs the other way: these regions are a good testing ground for learning how norms themselves can be studied. Together, the two claims present border regions as both a puzzle to explain and a tool for building better theory about social rules.
pmc-11778179:
Cao and co-authors profile gut microbes and metabolites behind calf diarrhea, in work from 2024. Diarrhea is common in young calves and stunts their growth. The losses hit farm output and income directly.

Male Holstein calves of like birth weight were tracked from birth to weaning. Stool samples from sick and healthy calves aged one to four weeks underwent gene sequencing and chemical profiling. Diarrhea was widespread in that early window and cut daily weight gain markedly. Certain bacterial groups surged in sick calves at specific ages. Chemical shifts in the gut tracked the illness as well. Key microbes and compounds are named as control targets.
pmc-11783679:
Aklilu Getachew, Nathan Suga, Jochebed Suga, and Nuhamin Kiflemariam report a rare extra kidney found by chance in two thousand twenty-five. The hosted text dates the report to two thousand twenty-four. A supernumerary kidney is a full extra organ, and single extra kidneys favor the left side.

Their patient was a man aged thirty-five in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, with pain in his left lower flank. Scans by ultrasound and by CT with contrast confirmed a left extra kidney, with no other faults found. Blood pressure was high at the first visit, while exams and lab tests were otherwise plain. Pain care and a follow-up plan were set, since symptom-free cases need watching rather than surgery.
pmc-11790579:
Asma Pourtaheri and co-authors present a study, published in 2024, of the drivers of girl child marriage in Iran. Early marriage breaches rights and harms health, and it stands as a development challenge. The team sorted the drivers with a socio ecological model that spans the person to society.

Interviews in Bam City drew on women married under age 15, family members, informants, and policy makers. Guided content analysis sorted the factors into five levels. Solo factors covered body, mind, and background traits. Family factors covered weak support and poor interaction. Wider levels named gaps in school and care systems, the economic state, and cultural rules.
pmc-11797879:
Some children are born with enamel that forms badly, a hereditary fault called amelogenesis imperfecta. One variant, Polynesian amelogenesis imperfecta, is common among Māori and other Polynesian peoples. Michelle Martin and co-authors ask how living with it affects daily life. They survey thirty Māori children and teenagers with the condition and sixty matched peers without it, using a nineteen-item scale of oral health quality of life.

The children with the condition scored clearly worse on the scale than their peers. The gap stayed firm even after the team accounted for age and deprivation. Poorly formed enamel can mean sore, sensitive teeth and a smile a child may hide, and the scores reflect that burden. The authors call for earlier spotting of the condition, better training for dental staff in recognizing it and easing sensitivity, and more research across Polynesian communities.
pmc-11801779:
Letters to the editor are where a field argues with itself in public, and Bhalchandra Rane and co-authors join such an argument in a 2025 letter. They respond to a large Indian study of how far real prescriptions stray from treatment guidelines. The study covered thirteen centers, yet found guideline adherence in only about 55 percent of prescriptions.

The letter writers note the study ran at rational-use centers, where prescribing should be better than average, which makes the gap more worrying. They cite still lower adherence abroad, between 16 and 26 percent in one report. Outpatient practice, they suggest, may stray further and deserves its own study. Their prescription is repeated continuing education on the rational use of medicines.
pmc-11804979:
Kumar and five co-authors read jaw X-rays in twenty twenty-four to count stuck eye teeth among dental patients in Hyderabad, India. Stuck teeth can block brace work and need care plans that know how oft they come. They read near three thousand wide jaw films from one year.

Forty folks had stuck eye teeth in that set of films. Men past age twenty were the most hit group, at near half of cases. Women past twenty were next, and young folks were a small share. Zone maps sorted the stuck teeth by their tilt and depth in the jaw.
pmc-11805079:
White spots on teeth can be sealed with resin, but whitening later may roughen that seal. Aidel Abdullah Alshahrani and Afra Elrashid test that risk in a 2024 lab study. They treat 96 pulled premolar teeth in four ways.

The four ways mix one or two etch rounds with one or two resin coats. All teeth are then bleached. A light-based scanner reads surface roughness after each stage. The method of sealing changed how rough the surface became. Bleaching raised roughness in a clear, measured way. Dentists may warn patients that whitening can dull a sealed spot.
pmc-11811079:
Muslim Qadir and co-authors dissect what sets the number of ovules in an oilseed rape ovary, in this 2024 study. That count caps how many seeds a pod can hold, so it feeds straight into yield. In a bred population of two hundred lines, counts spread widely and steadily, suiting gene hunting.

The team mapped ten gene regions, two of them strong and repeatable enough for breeding markers. Hormone readings and gene activity in high- and low-count ovaries pointed to fresh candidates. Fifteen known ovule genes and hundreds of active genes inside the mapped regions now await cloning work.
pmc-11821479:
Mehmet Ali Oktay and co-authors report growth hormone care for a teen with a rare gut disease, in a paper whose text is dated 2024. The disease blunts the gut lining and causes lasting diarrhea from birth. The patient, a girl of thirteen, also had short stature, so the team tried growth hormone and tracked her height, growth pace, and motor skills.

Growth pace rose during care, and motor skills improved as well, the team reports. A review of past reports frames the case for readers. The authors suggest the hormone may lift both growth and quality of life in this disease. They call for more study of long-term gains and safety in wider patient groups before firm claims can be made.
pmc-11888679:
Priyadarshani Sarkate and co-authors test, in 2024, whether fingerprints can flag people at risk of precancerous mouth conditions. Fingerprint patterns are fixed early and can hint at genetic susceptibility. Eighty people were split into four groups: two mouth conditions, tobacco users without lesions, and healthy controls.

Ink fingerprints were compared for pattern types. Loops dominated everywhere, but whorls were more frequent in the fibrosis group than in the white-patch group, while arches ran lower in the white-patch group. The authors conclude fingerprint reading might serve as a cheap early marker for spotting people prone to these disorders, pending wider validation.
pmc-11897479:
Andrija Savić and co-authors report long-term outcomes after surgery for rare peripheral nerve lesions, published in 2024. Such lesions mix tumor and non-tumor types and appear rarely. Their varied look makes diagnosis and care hard. Past reports lacked long follow-up with quality of life data.

The team reviewed records from 2012 to 2022 at their center. Eight cases met the study rules. Patients were examined a year after surgery with imaging and self-report forms. Four lesions proved benign growths. Results cover both function and daily life quality. Rare-case series like this guide surgeons facing the same odd finds.
pmc-11932379:
Qisheng Wu and eight co-authors survey sleep among petrochemical workers on Hainan Island in this 2024 study. Nearly forty-two percent of the 952 workers who answered reported sleep disorders, a high share the team set out to explain.

After matching workers by background traits, four job factors stood out. Working more than forty hours a week raised the odds of poor sleep. So did working in high temperature areas. Job stress nearly tripled the odds. Roles in storage and transport carried over three times the risk of operational roles. The authors urge health policymakers to weigh hours, heat, stress, and job type when they plan sleep protection for this workforce.
pmc-11970179:
Pregnant women in much of sub-Saharan Africa miss many of the clinic visits that keep mothers and babies safe. The trial randomly assigned 16 local health sites to calls or to routine care.

The team followed 160 women from their first visit until delivery. Half of the women who got calls finished all four advised visits, against just over a third in the routine care group. The calls did not clearly change use of iron and folate pills or lab tests. Phone reminders look like a cheap way to lift visit numbers, though more work is needed.
pmc-12082679:
Omotayo Fagbule and co-authors built and checked in 2024 tobacco-control posters and notebooks for Nigerian teens. Tobacco is a top preventable killer, and teens start young where facts run thin. The team shaped the materials on a health-belief frame, drawing messages from a World Health Organization school manual and fitting them to local life. A mixed expert panel judged clarity, culture fit, and theory fit.

One hundred fifty teens in Ibadan then pre-tested the drafts, and their notes drove fixes. The final pieces cover tobacco forms, harmful contents, health harms, and refusal skills. Near nine in ten teens rated the content very good, and four in five backed school use. The team offers the set for classroom roll-out.
pmc-12110479:
Oluwaseun Oluwafunmilayo Abiodun and Timothy Aghogho Ehwarieme survey awareness of type 2 diabetes risk factors among students at a private university in Nigeria, published in 2024. Diabetes is a chronic condition of high blood sugar, and its global case count is projected to climb steeply by 2045. Knowing the risk factors is a first step toward prevention.

Just over three hundred undergraduates answered a self-administered online questionnaire. About seventy percent showed high awareness of the factors that predict the disease, while thirty percent scored low. Regression analysis identified age, a persistently unhealthy diet, and heredity as independent predictors of awareness. The authors conclude that awareness was generally good in this group, while noting the gaps that remain for the less aware third.
pmc-12490479:
Mila Vasilj-Mihaljević and seven co-authors wrote a 2024 study testing whether thyroid antibody levels predict progression to hypothyroidism. In chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, the immune system attacks the thyroid. Antibodies against the enzyme TPO mark that attack. The team asked how antibody concentration relates to the gland's hormone output.

The cross-sectional study began with 144 patients, mean age about 46. After exclusions for out-of-range values, treatment, and other conditions, 85 remained, split between normal and low thyroid function. Antibody levels rose together with TSH, the pituitary signal that climbs as the gland fails. They moved opposite to free thyroxine, the main thyroid hormone. No clear tie to the second hormone, free T3, headlined the results. The authors suggest the pair of measures could flag at-risk people early.
pmc-12660679:
Yongmei Zhou, Ziqin Pang, Wen Wang, and Ray Ming published this study in 2025. It pinpoints the gene that gives male papaya trees their long flower stalks. Papaya has young sex chromosomes, and this stalk trait helped the species shift toward separate male and female plants.

Together with the sex-determining genes, CpMp proves essential to papaya's breeding system and its evolving sex chromosomes.
pmc-12663379:
Timothy Kayode Samson and Francis Olatunbosun Aweda compared deep learning models for daily rain forecasts in African cities in 2025. Erratic rain under climate change threatens farm planning and food security. Four single models and three stacked hybrids were trained on daily weather records.

Single models each catch part of the pattern: shapes in space, order in time, or both. Hybrids pair strengths, such as memory networks with plain ones. The comparison shows which build forecasts best for the cities studied. Farmers and water planners gain a clearer pick for local early warning.
pmc-12663579:
Wenjie Liu and co-authors build an open microscope method that strips background haze from live-cell super views, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Pattern-lit scopes are fast and gentle but blur badly on packed inner cell parts. Their lock-in twist sorts signal by how structures modulate.

The method cuts depth cleanly and holds fine detail with true counts. Power-unit splits and organelle handshakes were filmed in living cells. Remodel steps of inner parts came out crisp and timed. Full code and design are open to all labs. Readers get a clearer window into the cell's inner rooms.
pmc-12685179:
Straightening a bowed shinbone eases arthritis on the inner side of the knee, but surgeons worry it may wear the kneecap joint instead. The authors of a 2025 study measure that wear with three-dimensional MRI in 13 knees. Scans before surgery and after hardware removal give cartilage thickness at the kneecap and its groove. The team splits each surface into inner, middle, and outer thirds to see where loss lands. Changes over a tenth of a millimeter count as real.

Over half the knees lost cartilage in the groove, the kneecap, or both. Every loss leaned toward the inner third. Kneecap height and tilt also dropped after surgery. The authors say the 3D method can track this side effect precisely for future care.
pmc-12691079:
A liver-targeted drug perfusion extends life in eye melanoma that has spread to the liver, Reiner and co-authors report in a 2025 study. This cancer spread pattern leaves most patients with about a year to live under standard care. Thirty-eight patients at one center got close to one hundred perfusion rounds over ten years.

The method floods the liver with a high-dose drug while shielding the rest of the body. Median survival after the first round reached over twenty-nine months in this group. Survival curves are tracked with standard methods and hazard models. The result, from real clinic use rather than a trial, supports the method's 2023 approval and helps centers counsel patients on likely gains.
pmc-12691179:
Ivana Gorbaslieva and co-authors review a 2025 topic on heat therapy for cancer, judged against the hallmarks of cancer. Deliberate heating of the body or tumor is used beside standard care, and it may shift many of the traits that let cancers grow. The team searched two databases for reviews across twenty-five years.

Of more than two thousand records, about a hundred met the rules. Heat shifted seven of the ten hallmarks in the gathered proof. The best-backed paths were immune wake-up at mild heat and blocked DNA repair at a touch higher heat, which together frame where heat helps most.
pmc-12691879:
Mohsen Nemat-Gorgani, Michael Anthony Jensen, and Ronald Wayne Davis argue in 2025 that a brain waste clearing system may play a key role in a disabling fatigue illness. The illness brings deep fatigue, brain fog, and crashes after effort, and most patients are never diagnosed.

The glymphatic system is a lymph like network in the brain that clears toxic waste built up during the day, mostly during sleep. Faults in that system have already been linked to Alzheimer disease. The authors propose the same kind of fault could help drive this fatigue illness. If they are right, drugs that tune the clearing system could offer a new route to treatment.
pmc-12695479:
Christopher Gonelli and co-authors test whether seasonal flu shots stir memory cells against bird flu strains, in a 2025 study. Bird viruses threaten a pandemic against which people carry almost no immunity. Leftover cross reactive memory from past flu exposure might blunt a first wave.

After seasonal vaccination, only three of nineteen donors showed any boost in those cells. T cell responses rose weakly at best. The authors conclude current vaccines barely touch bird flu memory.
pmc-12695879:
Ji Liu and a large team of co-authors chart how poorly the world's major crops use nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizer. Better use would cut reliance on mined and manufactured fertilizer and ease pollution. The team built a global database of more than three thousand observations across two hundred five countries, spanning nineteen sixty-one to twenty eighteen.

Efficiency remains low in most places, above all in developing regions. Maps show strong dependence on crop and climate: rice fares best in tropical zones and wheat in temperate ones. Maize wastes the most, with large surpluses in China and the United States. The authors call for region specific strategies rather than one global fix.
pmc-12696279:
Alessia Lozito and eight co-authors reported in 2025 a rare skin reaction in a young woman treated with a biosimilar of adalimumab for plaque psoriasis. After switching products she developed painful, ulcerated plaques on her thighs, buttocks and elbows. Tests confirmed acquired perforating dermatosis, a condition where damaged collagen pushes through the skin. No usual triggers such as diabetes or kidney failure were present.

The authors suggest the reaction may stem from disturbed fibronectin or sugar-damaged proteins unsettling skin cells. They urge doctors to count this reaction among the rare harms of this drug class. Early recognition and withdrawal can stop it worsening, they note.
pmc-12698579:
Parul Nasra and co-authors build a deep learning system to spot diseases in lettuce leaves from photos. Lettuce is prone to bacterial and fungal infections that cut yield and quality. Fast, accurate detection helps growers act early and use fewer chemicals.

Their network joins a proven image model with added parts that trim extra features, reason over them, and refine them. Trained on a public set of leaf images in three classes, it beat standard image models on accuracy and related scores. It is also small and fast. The authors see uses in greenhouses, drone surveys, and phone-based tools for farmers.
pmc-12698679:
Jan Schmitz and co-authors tested how well resuscitation works inside a cramped airliner cabin, in a manikin trial published in 2025. Heart attacks in flight are rare but deadly, and tight space can degrade chest compressions. Twenty health professionals performed ten-minute resuscitation rounds in a mock cabin and in open space, alone and in pairs.

Counter to instinct, working in pairs produced long pauses without compressions and more incomplete releases, in both settings. The confined cabin worsened the pair method's pauses further. Compression depth and rate, though, stayed within guideline ranges under all conditions. The authors recommend that, where access to the patient is limited, a single trained rescuer start alone to keep compressions early and steady.
pmc-12699579:
Boeke and co-authors report in 2025 how COVID-19 test and treat programs were set up fast in seven low and middle income nations. A global group worked with governments in Ghana, Laos, Malawi, Nigeria, Rwanda, Uganda, and Zambia. Work covered 776 health sites and training for over 5,000 staff.

A donation supplied over eleven thousand courses of an oral antiviral drug. From each nation's start date to June 2024, programs ran near 732,000 tests. About 6,700 tests were positive, and 3,041 patients were prescribed the drug. The report sums up what helped, what blocked progress, and counts of tests and treatment by nation.
pmc-12699679:
Stefano Giannoni-Luza, Daniele Urso, and Giancarlo Logroscino counted in 2025 how much dementia worldwide could in theory be headed off. About fourteen changeable risks, from low schooling to vision loss, are thought to drive near half of cases. Using global health stores, the team worked out the share of cases tied to those risks for the world, its regions, and each nation. Those shares were then set against wealth and care quality.

About a third of cases looked preventable worldwide. South Asia carried the largest share and Western Europe the smallest. Vision loss was the top single risk, then low schooling and inactivity. Richer, better-served lands carried smaller shares. The team maps where prevention buys most.
pmc-12699879:
Godfried Dougnon and Hideaki Matsui wrote this 2025 review of a waste pigment that builds up in aging brains. The pigment, called lipofuscin, gathers as glowing granules inside neurons and immune cells of the brain. It was long dismissed as inert trash left by cell breakdown.

The authors argue it may act as a slow time bomb in diseases like Alzheimer's. They pose sharp questions: why does it gather in old brain cells, what happens when those cells die, and why do plaques start in grey matter late in life? The review gathers proof that the pigment may sway how nerve disease unfolds, not just mark it.
pmc-12700879:
Jamal Barvestani designs a biosensor in a 2025 optics paper. The sensor reads the refractive index of a liquid, a value that shifts with what is dissolved in it. Its core uses states that form where two patterned crystal slabs meet, capped by a porous layer.

Math modeling and computer simulation both check how the states behave as cap settings change. Across the index range found in water-based samples, response stayed near seven hundred forty-five nanometers per unit. When the sample itself filled the porous layer, response rose higher still. A glucose test case beat prior designs on response, sharpness, and lowest detectable change. The author pitches the design for wide biosensing use.
pmc-12702279:
Changmei Wei and seven colleagues test a blood protein called gasdermin D as a marker for heart failure. The protein helps drive a fiery form of cell death, and its levels in blood had not been judged for this use. Early, accurate diagnosis of heart failure remains a clinical need.

The team compared patients with heart failure, patients with other heart disease, and healthy controls. Gasdermin D levels rose as heart function class worsened, and they tracked other standard measures. Alone, the marker sorted cases with fair accuracy. Joined with the standard hormone marker and pumping fraction, accuracy rose near the top of the scale. The authors call it a sensitive candidate marker.
pmc-12703879:
Peter Nestor and co-authors run a first safety test of scanning ultrasound as a brain treatment for Alzheimer's disease, in work from 2025. In mice, the method lifted thinking skills even without clearing the sticky protein blamed for the disease. That hint led the team to try it in people.

Twelve patients joined the open test and got four sessions spaced two weeks apart. A portable, image-guided device aimed sound at a memory-linked area at the back of the brain. Some patients got fewer, stronger pulses and others more, weaker ones. The main aim was to judge whether the method is workable, safe, and bearable. The team also tracked thinking, behavior, and brain signals as side measures.
pmc-12704079:

Single-cell gene data from fracture sites flagged a gene tied to the harsh type of macrophage. The team loads the packets into a gel that reacts to cell stress signals. A fat tag on the packets steers them to macrophages. Lab and animal tests show the gel is safe and helps steer healing.
pmc-12704879:
Leila Jafari Khouzani and co-authors predict in a 2025 study not just whether a drug touches a target, but how: switching it on, blocking it, or not at all. The framework aims to make repurposing hunts faster and more honest.
pmc-12706079:
Elfiky and co-authors use machine learning to link space weather with the power health of Egypt's first Earth observation satellite, in this 2025 study. Storms from the sun can upset satellite electronics, but the exact wiring between weather and wobble is tangled. EgyptSat-1's power subsystem gave them a test case.

Their four-stage workflow cleans the data, picks features in two passes, and trains six learning models on voltage, current, and temperature targets. Inputs included proton flux, cosmic rays, and solar wind density. A final stage hunts anomalies and cross-checks them against the predictions. The authors aim at forecasts an operator could act on. The method should travel to other satellites.
pmc-12706479:
Deep brain stimulation helps Parkinson's patients, but what happens when the same brain later needs radiation for tumors? Adel Azghadi and co-authors report such a case in a 2025 paper. pmc-12706879:

pmc-12706979:

Three small teams then built prototypes, one a choose-your-own-adventure game for test choices. pmc-12707679:

In comparisons, their algorithm processed about sixty-nine frames per second with recognition in about four and a half milliseconds. Average precision neared ninety-nine percent and accuracy about ninety-eight percent, beating rival models. Road tests confirmed good detection in practice. The work supports real-time driving perception.
pmc-12708779:

pmc-12708979:
Hiba Elhaj and co-authors report a stubborn skin case tied to high eosinophil counts in this 2025 paper. A man in his mid-twenties had six years of whole-body red, scaly skin with raised counts of the allergy-linked blood cells. Tests ruled out cancer, autoimmune disease, and other causes.

A targeted antibody drug slashed his cell counts but eased symptoms only a little. Adding a second drug, useless alone before, brought fast and lasting relief of itch and scaling. Stopping the first drug let symptoms return. The authors suggest both cell control and wider signal blocking are needed in such cases.
pmc-12709079:
Jeza Muhamad Abdul Aziz and four co-authors give an overview of the Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever outbreak in Iraq. Their perspective piece was published in twenty twenty-five. The tick-borne viral disease is a growing public threat in the country.

Cases rose during the COVID-19 pandemic years. The authors tie the rise to climate change and to close human-animal contact during festivals, when livestock are slaughtered. The virus spreads through infected people and animals and through Hyalomma ticks. They call for a One Health approach that joins human, animal, and environmental work. Rural care, tick control, and public awareness all need strengthening. They also urge cross-border teamwork and more research on diagnosis, treatment, and vaccines.
pmc-12709179:
Damilare Dabiri, Warren Rouse, and Walter Moss hunt for folded structures hidden in the RNA of respiratory syncytial virus type A. The virus is a major cause of lung infections in infants and other at-risk groups. Its genome is a single strand of RNA about 15,000 bases long, carrying instructions for eleven proteins.

Using software that predicts and compares RNA shapes, the team found 123 stable folded regions in one strand direction and 113 in the other. Most of these shapes were shared across virus strains, which hints that they do real work. Key folds sat in genes for the copying enzyme, the fusion protein, and other parts, plus a short tail region. The authors say such folds may guide how the virus copies itself, and could offer targets for future antiviral drugs.
pmc-12710879:
People with diabetes catch infections more easily, so flu shots matter a great deal for them. Walid Al-Qerem and co-authors asked whether knowing about vaccines tracks with getting the shot, in Iraq in 2025. Four hundred seventy-three adults with diabetes took a survey on vaccine knowledge, life details, and shot history. The survey ran from January to August 2025.

Just over half the group had taken a flu shot. Higher knowledge scores tracked with a higher chance of being vaccinated. Women and lower-income patients were less likely to have the shot. Lower schooling also tracked with lower knowledge scores. The authors urge teaching programs aimed at vaccine knowledge. Such programs, they argue, could lift uptake in this high-risk group.
pmc-12711079:
Heather Hamilton, Natalie Yarish, and Kristin Heron survey 187 female endurance athletes about how menopause symptoms bear on training. Runners, cyclists, swimmers, and triathletes aged forty to sixty answered an anonymous online questionnaire with a standard symptom rating scale. The catalog creator field repeats one name three times, so the clean head byline governs here.

Symptoms were common: sleep problems led at eighty-eight percent, then exhaustion, sexual problems, anxiety, irritability, low mood, and weight gain. The symptoms athletes blamed most for hurting training were joint and muscle discomfort, weight gain, poor sleep, and exhaustion. Those who felt a strong drag on performance also carried higher total symptom scores. The authors note that fitness does not exempt women from menopause's load, and urge clinicians to ask athletic patients about symptoms so they can keep them active.
pmc-12711379:
Camera traps miss small animals: a mouse crosses below the frame while the camera waits for deer. Jahiya Clark and co-authors built a fix in a 2025 paper, the SiMPL wildlife magnet, a baited station that draws creatures of many sizes into view. It is cheap and simple to construct, meant for passive monitoring.

The team tested it for two years at nine stations along an elevation gradient in the White Mountains of the northeastern United States. Adding the magnets raised detection odds for the whole mammal community and for species like red squirrels, American marten, and fisher. Flying squirrels, bears, moose, owls, and other birds also appeared more often. Beyond animal counts, the stations capture plant and snow timing. The authors recommend the design for rodents and mid-sized carnivores especially.
pmc-12711879:
Masazumi Onuki and co-authors show, in a 2025 study, how a large immune protein slows hepatitis B virus growth. The protein, MxB, is switched on by interferon and sits in the dynamin family. Lowering MxB in liver cells that make the virus changed the shape of their mitochondria, the cell's power hubs. Those cells then shed far more whole virus bits. Their virus coat proteins rose, and the surface mark in the fluid rose four to ten fold. A test signal that should wake the RIG-I alarm path fell flat as well.

The work backs a model in which MxB helps form clusters of a relay protein on those hubs. Those clusters are what the alarm path needs to fire. More MxB means a loud alarm and less virus.
pmc-12711979:
Orathai Thongjuy and nine colleagues tested a three-herb essential oil blend against Escherichia coli that resist drugs, taken from dogs with diarrhea. The bacteria make broad spectrum beta-lactamases, defeating many antibiotics, and they form biofilms that entrench infection. The blend mixes oils from three aromatic plants known by their initials. Its chemistry was profiled by chromatography and mass tests. Rectal swabs came from fifty-six dogs, thirty healthy and twenty-six diarrheic.

Bacterial isolates were named by lab tests and an automated system. The team confirmed which isolates made the resistance enzymes and formed biofilms. The oil mix was then tested for killing and antibiofilm power in the lab. Vets urgently need non-antibiotic options for such cases. Plant oils that break up biofilms could back up failing drugs.
pmc-12712279:
Giulia Morano and co-authors report early results for biopsies guided by contrast-enhanced mammography with the patient lying face down. Some breast lesions light up after contrast dye yet stay invisible on plain mammograms and ultrasound. Those spots still need tissue sampling, and the contrast scan itself can guide the needle. The team ran a prospective study on 36 patients with suspicious enhancing-only lesions.

Thirty-five of the thirty-six procedures succeeded, a rate just over 97 percent. The median procedure took 29 minutes, with a modest radiation dose and gentle compression. Of the lesions sampled, one in five were masses and the rest spread-out enhancements. Lab results showed just over half were malignant. The authors present the prone setup as a workable route to diagnose lesions that other imaging cannot reach.
pmc-12713279:
Demoze and colleagues map in twenty twenty-five what is known about climate literacy and mental health among students in Africa. Young Africans face heavy climate harm with thin support systems. Knowing climate facts can build coping strength, yet heat, crop loss, and disease fears also strain minds. The team searched seven databases for studies over a ten-year span.

Just over twenty studies from twelve countries, with over twenty thousand students, met their rules. University students knew more and held warmer attitudes, while younger students showed more false beliefs and less action. Students linked climate change to disease, hunger, and heat stress. Anxiety and distress appeared in several studies. The authors flag gaps for future teaching and policy.
pmc-12713679:
Qian Wang and co-authors study gut microbes in patients with sudden pancreas swelling, in work from 2025. A severe body wide response can follow this illness and raise the risk of organ failure. Shifts in gut microbes are tied to how the disease starts and grows.

The team took rectal swabs from eighty-eight patients and nineteen healthy controls. Patients were grouped by whether that severe response was present and by organ failure scores. Gene based tests mapped microbe mix and function. Patients had lower microbe richness and diversity than controls. Models were built to test whether microbe traits could help sort severity.
pmc-12714179:
Jacek Mazurek and four colleagues at the CDC count deaths tied to coal workers' pneumoconiosis in the United States from 2020 to 2023, in a 2025 report. The disease, caused by breathing coal mine dust, is preventable yet still disables and kills miners. Using national death records that list usual industry and job, the team found the disease on 1,754 death certificates.

Most of these deaths, 1,255, were among mining industry workers, and underground mining machine operators stood out with by far the highest relative rate. Construction and extraction jobs also showed raised rates. The authors argue the deaths justify continued dust control, early detection, medical care, and ongoing surveillance.
pmc-12714679:
Hyelim Kim and co-authors build a lung on a chip to study scarring after infection in a 2025 paper. Post-infection lung fibrosis lacks good human-like models. Their chip combines vessel cells, connective cells, and macrophages in one device. A T cell factor called TOX, which rises after severe infection, was flowed through the vessel side.

The factor weakened the vessel barrier and raised a stickiness marker. Through the macrophages, it then switched the connective cells into scar builders laying down matrix.
