Blocking the factor's receptor beforehand protected the barrier and halted the whole chain. Mice given the same treatment survived better with less scarring. The same signature appeared in patient lung wash samples, tying the chip story to real disease.
pmc-12714779:
Aoi Katayama, Hiroki Takekata, Itsuki Kunita, and Akihiro Takemura published a chronobiology study in twenty twenty-five on whether barnacles keep tidal time with an internal clock. The intertidal barnacle Fistulobalanus albicostatus sweeps its feathery legs to feed. The team watched that activity under controlled light regimes for two weeks each.

Under a normal light-dark cycle, activity peaked once daily. In constant darkness or constant light, the rhythm split into two daily peaks about twelve hours apart, betraying a tidal clock underneath. Activity onsets also locked to particular tidal phases. The day rhythm often vanished in darkness, showing the clock is flexible. The authors call it a plastic circatidal rhythm tuned to a harsh shore.
pmc-12715679:
Konstantina Manoli and Jared Ching report surgery for a rare tear at the very center of vision in a 2025 case paper. A horseshoe tear in the macula, following the vitreous gel's detachment and a long-standing blocked retinal vein, threatened sight as it slowly progressed. No established treatment existed in the literature for so rare a lesion.

Scans at each visit tracked fluid gathering beneath the retina, the sign that waiting had run out. The repair borrowed from detachment surgery: a vitrectomy that removed the gel, amputated the tear's flap, and sealed the area with a short-acting gas bubble while the patient held a face-down posture. Notably, no laser or freeze sealing was needed. The authors conclude that macular horseshoe tears can be repaired with standard vitrectomy craft, widening the options for a pathology most surgeons will meet once, if ever.
pmc-12715779:
Jerome Tullo and co-authors run a 2025 feasibility study on predicting how many lymph nodes a neck dissection will yield, before and during surgery. For mouth and throat cancers, removing neck lymph nodes is standard, and a higher node count tracks better survival. No validated tool predicts that yield in advance.

The pilot enrolled 12 patients having a standard levels two to four neck dissection by one experienced surgeon. Before surgery, CT scans gave volume estimates of the tissue to be removed. During surgery, the resected specimen was weighed at closure. Node yield was then recorded by a standard method. The question is whether scan volume or specimen mass can forecast the count. A reliable forecast could flag a dissection that falls short while the patient is still in the room, letting the surgeon extend the clearance on the spot.
pmc-12716479:
Shih Sheng Jiang and co-authors followed 734 Taiwanese patients with precancerous mouth lesions to see whether a common yeast predicts which ones turn cancerous, in a 2025 study. The yeast, Candida albicans, has long been suspected in oral cancer, but its role in progression was unclear. Swabs from each lesion were cultured to measure the yeast burden, and patients were tracked for about 2.4 years.

About 6.8 percent of the lesions became cancer. A high yeast burden nearly tripled the risk overall. Two lesion types carried high risk on their own, and the combination with heavy yeast growth pushed risk far higher. The strongest effect appeared in leukoplakia, where risk rose about twelvefold. The authors call the yeast a context-dependent risk factor.
pmc-12716579:
Ming Ren Toh and co-authors study how weather and air quality drive asthma emergencies in Singapore, in a 2025 paper. Asthma attacks send many adults to emergency rooms, and local triggers in a tropical city may differ from those elsewhere.

Records covered 5,337 visits from 2016 to 2024. Dirty air matched more visits on the same day. Rain and humid heat matched fewer visits a few days later. Haze episodes and pollution-linked festivals also raised visits, though each later haze drew fewer visits than the last. The rainy monsoon season peaked despite cleaner air, so weather matters beyond pollution. After full adjustment, the same-day pollution link faded, the authors note.
pmc-12716779:
Wu and co-authors build a score that predicts outlook for glioma, the most common malignant brain tumor, from genes tied to DNA repair faults. Faults in one repair system may shape how these tumors vary and grow. Their 2025 study mines two large tumor databases and tries many machine learning methods to find the best recipe.

The winning method picked seven genes for the score, dubbed the HRD Index. The score sorted patients by outlook with strong accuracy in checks. Lab tests showed the seven genes switch on at different levels across tumor cell lines. Groups split by the score differed in mutations, immune cell mix, and drug response. The authors say the score could guide care choices for glioma patients.
pmc-12717079:
Hui Wang and co-authors (2025) trace a zinc transporter's role in cervical cancer's aggressiveness. Cancer cells in this study run their mitochondria hot, and the transporter, SLC30A9, keeps zinc balanced inside those powerhouses. Single-cell sequencing of tumors showed the gene strongly overactive in the malignant epithelial cells. The team confirmed high levels in patient samples and in several cervical cancer cell lines, then asked what the gene does there.

Silencing the gene with RNA interference, or deleting it with CRISPR, slowed the cancer cells sharply: they grew less, stalled in their cycle, migrated less, and died more readily. The driver behind the overactivity turned out to be a regulator protein, PRDM1, which switches the gene on. The chain the authors draw, from a transcription factor to a zinc pump to over-revved mitochondria, offers two possible points of attack against a cancer that still kills many women.
pmc-12717679:
Ibrahim Alghannam and co-authors reviewed brain injury outcomes in babies under three months who had minor head knocks, in a 2025 study from a Riyadh hospital. Judging injury in this age group is hard, and a common decision rule may not fit well. The team looked back at seventy-seven infants seen within a day of the knock over about four years. Cases of suspected non-accidental harm were left out.

Just under a third of babies had a head scan, and most scans showed injury, chiefly skull fractures. Injury that changed care was rare, at two babies in the whole group. A scalp bruise on the side or back was a strong warning sign for injury on scan. Falls also raised the odds. Most unscanned babies fit low-risk marks. The authors back targeted scans when warning signs cluster, with watchful waiting for the rest.
pmc-12719879:
Dounia Louaguef and co-authors tune the size of core-shell magnetic nanoparticles to make them heat tumors better, in work from 2025. Tiny iron oxide particles can warm cancer tissue under a magnetic field, a gentle therapy route. Their heating power depends on build and size.

The particles pair a zinc-bearing core with a manganese-bearing shell in faceted shapes. Size was varied on purpose, and shape and makeup were checked by microscopy and light tests. A nuclear method confirmed the iron phase. Magnetic measures then picked the size that turns field energy into heat best. The hybrid build improved that conversion at least tenfold over plain particles. The work targets safer heat therapy doses.
pmc-12720479:
Apsara Babu and Bhaskara Rao test a protein from a marine microbe against tuberculosis bacteria. Their twenty twenty-five paper draws on Streptomyces from mangrove mud, a little-searched habitat. Drug-resistant TB strains have shrunk the list of working treatments.

The cell-free extract of the microbe was screened in plate and dye assays against TB strains. The active part proved to be a protein, which the team isolated as a drug candidate. Toxicity was checked in animal models to set early safety. A protein drug from the sea would be a fresh class for TB care. The work joins the hunt for agents that resistant strains have not yet learned to beat.
pmc-12722379:
Abby Barlow, Sarah Penington, and Ben Adams model a mosquito control method at the scale of one home, in this 2025 paper. Releasing mosquitoes that carry Wolbachia bacteria can block dengue spread, since the bacteria stop the virus from passing to people. Most past models look at whole towns, but these mosquitoes live in and around single houses.

The team built a random, time-based model for small home populations of normal and infected mosquitoes. They derived the chance that released insects take over, the expected wait, and the chance of falling back to normal. Chance plays a big role: releasing the bare minimum that works in a smooth model succeeded only about twenty percent of the time. Far larger releases were needed for ninety percent success. Release planners can use these odds to size real drops.
pmc-12722779:
Jaeeun Song and co-authors gauge how the two thousand twenty-four Korea medical crisis shifted hard surgery across hospital tiers and regions, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Trainee doctors quit en masse over a reform plan, and the state pushed hard cases toward top hospitals. Insurance claims for over nine hundred hard procedures were compared before and after.

Claims fell by a tenth overall, with top hospitals down near a fifth. General hospitals and small clinics took up part of the slack, and cancer surgery shifted out of the capital. Heart, brain, and image-guided work barely moved between tiers. Most hard surgery capacity did not recover, the authors find. Readers see system strain in hard numbers.
pmc-12723479:
Eunjeong Kim and co-authors probed two small spots on a copper-carrying protein in this 2025 study. The protein, amicyanin, ferries electrons between two partners in a soil bacterium. Each spot sits in the loop that holds the copper atom, the heart of the protein's work.

Swapping the first spot for a serine left the protein steady but made it grip its partner far more tightly. Swapping the second spot raised the protein's voltage and made it fall apart more easily. Computer models traced the second effect to a reshaped bond pattern around the copper. The authors assign each spot its own job: one sets grip, the other sets electron flow.
pmc-12727179:
Barry Sessle and Greg Murray test a pain theory on face and jaw pain in 2025. The face sensorimotor system drives chewing, speech, swallowing, and expression. Pain can warp all of those acts, yet the two way links were unclear. Several older theories each captured only part of the picture.

The authors weigh a theory of pain and movement interplay against face pain cases. They stress the wide mix of body, mind, and social factors at play. Sex and personal differences in response also get close attention. A fuller theory can steer both research and clinic care for stubborn face pain.
pmc-12727879:
Bo Huang and co-authors present a light model to sharpen satellite images in a 2025 paper. Clearer images help people read land, crops, and cities from space. Transformer models do this well, but fixed small windows limit their view, and full attention costs too much compute for large images.

Their design stacks blocks that look at windows at several scales at once. A new attention step mixes space and channel cues while keeping cost in line with window size. A gated step then adds more spatial detail. Tests on several standard sets beat top prior methods on both scores and how the images look.
pmc-12728179:
Hadi Asghari, Laura Miller, and co-authors rank which in terms rule push, stress, and shift in a wet bone post model, in a 2025 study. Bone acts as a wet stiff stuff with juice in its pores. Which terms rule its marks was the ask for heal and build tales.

A Sobol rank runs on the post solve marks in bone term spans. Time rules all marks most of all in the ranks. One bend term beats the shear term for push calls in the post. Shear rules side stress marks more than rest terms in the runs. Pair ties twixt set terms steer juice push in key ways.
pmc-12729079:
Xiaoyan Zhang and colleagues published a case report in 2025 about eye problems in a young man with hydatid disease. Hydatid disease is a parasitic infection that forms cysts in the body. It rarely involves the eye. This patient had lived with the disease for seven years on long-term drug treatment.

He came in with a month of blurred vision. Scans showed raised areas in one eye's choroid layer. Dye imaging confirmed inflamed retinal blood vessels in both eyes. Surgeons entered the eye to inspect the raised areas directly. They found no parasite cysts, only a dark green lesion. Lab tests and gene sequencing were also negative for the parasite. Steroid treatment followed the surgery.
pmc-12729179:
Jian Zhang and co-authors studied a protein called DPP4 and a cell death path in the womb lining of rats and human cells with polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2025 paper. This syndrome can make the womb lining less ready for an embryo, harming fertility. Past work by the team tied DPP4 to a form of cell death driven by iron, called ferroptosis, but the mechanism was unclear.

In their models, the womb lining showed iron build up, weak antioxidant defense, and damage to cell power units. Blocking DPP4 with a known drug improved lining readiness markers in rats before pregnancy. In human lining cells, lowering DPP4 curbed hormone receptor levels and death markers. A lab implantation test recovered as well. The authors conclude that DPP4 driven ferroptosis worsens lining function in this syndrome, and that blocking it may restore implantation capacity.
pmc-12729279:
Wenting Qin and co-authors build a tool to grade motor loss after stroke from muscle signals. Their 2025 paper uses dense surface sensors on the skin to record hand muscle activity. Fair, numeric grading can guide rehab plans. They draw eight broad features and two fine motor-unit features from each signal.

Recordings came from 11 stroke patients and 8 healthy people doing seven hand gestures. The hurt side showed weaker and less coordinated signals than healthy controls. The other side sat in between. Models built per gesture sorted recovery stages with high accuracy for wrist extension. A pinch gesture best predicted a standard arm score. The authors say gesture choice should match the clinical aim.
pmc-12730179:
The study of blood fats is being remade, writes Pablo Corral in this 2025 editorial. Decades of work on clogged arteries once centered almost entirely on LDL cholesterol. The field now embraces a wider cast: lipoprotein(a), fat-rich particles, and control pathways such as ANGPTL3 and apoC3, each a player in artery disease and metabolic illness.

New drug classes are arriving fast, from RNA-based therapies aimed at lipoprotein(a) or triglycerides to small interfering molecules against PCSK9 and potent oral LDL-lowering pills. Corral argues the rich pipeline makes care more personal and precise than a decade ago seemed possible. Writing for a journal of diabetes and metabolic disease, he invites researchers to share trials, mechanism studies, and reviews, so today's momentum becomes tomorrow's clinical gains.
pmc-12730379:
Rosa Pello and a large team tested mass spectrometry for telling drug traces from disease traces in myeloma blood tests, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Modern antibody drugs can mimic the abnormal protein that marks this blood cancer, fooling standard tests into seeing leftover disease.

Serum from patients was checked at start of treatment and three months later, by both the standard method and the new one. The new method, guided by a library of drug signatures, matched or beat the standard test. It credited interference to specific drugs in many cases and found no drug peaks for others. It also caught disease protein at baseline and avoided false alarms later. The authors support adding the method to routine labs.
pmc-12730979:
Supansa Buakaew and co-authors test whether a citrus compound can undo oxidative damage in kidney cells, in a 2025 study. Oxidative stress, when corrosive molecules outnumber defenses, accelerates aging and chronic kidney disease. Hesperidin, a flavonoid plentiful in citrus peel, fights oxidation and inflammation, but reversing damage already done is a stronger claim than preventing it.

The team first injured human kidney tubule cells with hydrogen peroxide, then treated them with hesperidin for a day. The compound restored antioxidant defenses and shifted genes tied to longevity and cell aging back toward health. Cell-level rescue is only a first step toward therapy, yet it reframes hesperidin from shield to repair crew. The work supports testing citrus-derived compounds in animals with kidney disease driven by oxidative stress.
pmc-12731779:
Maria Karhu and co-authors report a brain lesion that wore a tumor's disguise in a 2025 case paper. A sixty-three-year-old woman arrived with headache, worsening speech trouble, and hard swallowing. Her scan showed a large frontal lobe lesion with a signature pattern, the T2/FLAIR mismatch sign, that usually points to a slow-growing astrocytoma tumor. Other features argued the other way: little swelling effect, no classic ring pattern.

A biopsy was planned, but the patient declined. Steroid treatment began instead, and the lesion shrank markedly within two weeks and nearly vanished by two months. That speed is the mark of a demyelinating lesion, inflammation stripping insulation from nerve fibers, not a tumor. The authors urge clinicians to keep such mimics in mind before reaching for the scalpel.
pmc-12732279:
Rahul Shah and colleagues published a laboratory study in 2025. They tested how bone graft mixes affect implant surfaces. Wetting behavior, called hydrophilicity, matters for implant success. The diabetes drug metformin was added to graft materials. No earlier work had tested this combination directly. Three implant surfaces were compared in the tests. Two graft types were used, from cattle and algae. Each mix was tested with and without metformin. Droplet angles measured how well liquids spread.

Hundreds of droplet measurements were taken in total. Each surface and mix behaved somewhat differently. Statistical tests compared groups for each surface type. The setup isolates surface effects under controlled conditions. Results can guide later biological testing steps. Better wetting may support stronger bone integration. Animal and human studies would still be needed. The in vitro design is an early step only.
pmc-12732879:
Safae Skenndri and co-authors build a fast field test for a poultry disease germ, in a 2025 study. The germ is a non-swimming strain of Salmonella that causes fowl typhoid and hits chicken flocks hard. Standard tests are slow. Many also cannot separate this strain from its swimming cousins.

Their test uses a color-changing amplification method that works at one temperature, with two separate reactions. One flags any Salmonella through a shared gene, and the other flags this strain alone through a private gene stretch. It scored perfectly on specificity checks and matched the sensitivity of laboratory PCR, catching very low germ counts. On swabs from infected chickens it beat culturing, finding up to a quarter more positives early in infection. The authors pitch it for on-farm checks and flock surveillance.
pmc-12733079: Andrea Zille and Ana Isabel Ribeiro review research progress and application prospects for gel electrolytes in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. Gel electrolytes have become key parts of modern electrochemical systems, such as batteries and other energy devices. They bridge the performance gap between liquid electrolytes, which conduct well but can leak, and solid electrolytes, which are stable but often conduct poorly. The review surveys recent advances in these materials and where they may be applied next.
pmc-12733479:
Muhammad Ali Ibrahim Kazi, Sanmeet Singh, and Nowreen Haq study gallbladder safety of popular diabetes drugs in patients who also have inflammatory bowel disease, in a 2025 cohort paper. Both conditions raise the risk of bile duct and gallbladder trouble. The safety of GLP-1 based drugs in this combined group was uncertain.

Using a global health records network, the team matched about sixteen thousand users of semaglutide or tirzepatide with the same number of non-users. Gallstones, gallbladder inflammation, and duct stones all occurred notably less often in users. A rarer duct infection showed no clear difference. The authors describe a protective pattern rather than the harm some had feared.
pmc-12733879:
Shown Tokoro and co-authors mapped in 2025, at five-micron sharpness, exactly where each skin fat sits across the layers of human skin from the lower back. Skin fats build the barrier that keeps water in and the world out, and their misplacement marks diseases like eczema. The imaging method paints each fat species in place.

Ceramide ruled the outermost layer. Cholesterol and free fatty acids filled the horny layer but thinned at its surface, while a sulfate form peaked deeper and faded upward, matching its known role in shedding. Membrane fats stayed in the living layers below. The authors call the atlas a healthy baseline. Disease studies can now measure their maps against it.
pmc-12733979:
Hafiza Gözen, Serkan Usgu, and Yavuz Yakut ran a small trial in 2025 on balance training for children who are hard of hearing. One group trained while wearing glasses that flash on and off, which makes balance harder. The children also had to do a second task at the same time.

Thirty-one children took part, split into three groups, and training ran twice a week for sixteen weeks. The flashing-glasses group did best on a child balance scale and on a timed stand-up-and-walk test. Both training groups got faster on a step test. Many other measures did not change much. The authors say this training helps some parts of balance and movement in these children.
pmc-12734079:
Carolina Donà and colleagues ask how often clogged heart arteries ride along with a stiffening heart disease of old age, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The heart disease is cardiac amyloidosis, where misfolded protein clogs the heart muscle. Both it and coronary artery disease are common in the elderly, yet how they interact was little studied.

The team reviewed 255 amyloidosis patients who had their coronary arteries checked. Eighty-one, nearly a third, had significant artery disease. They were older and more often male, with more high blood pressure and blood fats. Heart scans showed the scar pattern was almost always the amyloid pattern, even in those with artery disease. That makes judging live muscle by scan hard. Death rates over follow-up did not differ by artery status. The authors conclude the artery disease matters for care, but not for survival here.
pmc-12734279:
Jakub Szrama leads a team comparing pressure-prediction software against standard monitoring during major aortic surgery. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Blood pressure crashes during such operations invite organ damage. A prediction index promises warning minutes before a crash lands.

They reviewed one hundred elective cases, half managed with each approach. The main measure, time-weighted pressure below the danger line, did not differ significantly. Secondary measures told a softer story in the prediction group's favor. Total time spent hypotensive looked about half as long there. Episodes also seemed shorter, though corrections for multiple testing erased significance. The authors call the trends clinically relevant but unproven. A prospective trial with more patients would settle it. The study models honest reporting of borderline results.
pmc-12734379:
Hussain Al Akam, Asaad Abduljawad, and Basel Abozor present a 2025 dental study on whether treating an infected tooth root calms inflammation throughout the body. Three hundred healthy patients with apical periodontitis, infection at the root tip, had root canal treatment or retreatment at a Jeddah clinic. Blood levels of C-reactive protein, a standard inflammation marker, were measured before and two weeks after.

The marker fell sharply in both patient groups, from about seven to two in those with painful infections. In silent cases it fell from about five point four to one point six. The painful group improved more, and age and sex did not predict the change. The authors read the result as fresh evidence that mouth infections feed whole-body inflammation.
pmc-12734479:
Nurulamin Abu Bakar and co-authors present Malaysia's first case of an ultra-rare sugar-processing disorder, pieced together with layered lab tests, in a 2025 report. The two-year-old boy showed global developmental delay, floppy muscles, a small head missing its central bridge, repeat infections, and poor growth. A transferrin test pointed at a type I glycosylation defect. Deeper tests showed sugar chains missing from their usual protein slots and widespread chemical imbalances.

Gene sequencing found a new, truncating change in the SSR4 gene on the X chromosome. The gene helps move new proteins into the cell's processing machinery. The authors say the multi-omics workup nailed a diagnosis that standard tests had missed. They offer the case as a template for solving similar mysteries in rare disease.
pmc-12734579:
Liangliang Wu and co-authors test how a printed titanium alloy holds up under repeated load at high heat, in a 2025 study. The alloy is made by laser melting of powder, a method with strong prospects for aircraft engines. Hot engine parts face both heat and long service demands.

Samples were cycled at 400 degrees Celsius under five levels of load balance. Cracks tended to start at flaws near the surface, and lifetimes varied widely, above all at the harshest balance. The team built models that mix wear from cycling with slow damage from heat and steady stress. Combined models, joined by a simple damage rule, matched real lifetimes best. The best model gives engineers a firmer way to predict part life.
pmc-12734879:
Mehman Ahmadli, Tor Berge Gjersvik, and Sigbjørn Sangesland published a 2025 study of a new coating for the gate valves that seal undersea wells. A failed seal under the sea costs much in money, time, and risk. Sand in the flow grinds the seal face down. The standard coating is a hard tungsten mixture. The team tests a diamond compact coating in its place.

First work showed the new coating cuts friction and wear, thanks to its hard face and heat stability. The team then built a full valve in code and ran a sand test in a flow simulation: a five-inch gate in a thin sand stream. The new coating cut erosion depth by over three in four. Its lifetime ran over four times that of the standard coating. The conclusion supports the coating for undersea valve use.
pmc-12734979:
Shufang Yang and co-authors compare two green algae as factory sources of the red pigment astaxanthin, in work from twenty twenty-five. Astaxanthin is a high-value antioxidant used in health products. One alga packs pigment densely but grows slowly with thick walls. The other grows to extreme density in fermenters but holds little pigment. Paths, engineering tricks, and industry prospects are weighed side by side.

The dense pigment holder remains the natural benchmark despite its costs. Light-only growth and slow pace raise its production price sharply. The fast grower flexes across light, mixed, and dark feeding modes. Its pigment flux stays low, which caps its yield per batch. Patent maps show fierce global rivalry across synthesis and engineering routes. Green solvent-free synthesis and engineered strains trend upward in filings. Industry strategy now hinges on closing the yield gap.
pmc-12735679:
Zinn and co-authors audit a style of diabetes care used in three New Zealand primary care practices, built on eating fewer carbohydrates within a whole-food, coach-supported model. The audit looks back over several years of routine care.

Data covered 106 adults with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes, followed for a median of nineteen months. Blood sugar control improved overall, with a median HbA1c drop of 3 mmol per mol. About 32 percent of those with type 2 diabetes reached reversal, and 44 percent of those with prediabetes returned to normal blood sugar. Weight loss tracked with bigger gains, while blood pressure and triglycerides stayed broadly stable. The authors caution that the audit had no control group, so results need care in reading.
pmc-12735779:
Christopher Frewin and co-authors review silicon carbide as a material for devices that link directly with the brain. Their 2025 paper notes that standard silicon probes often fail over time: mixed materials swell, crack, and stir up inflammation where they meet tissue. Silicon carbide avoids many of those flaws, being strong, chemically calm, and friendly to the body.

The review gathers progress from several labs, with emphasis on the authors' own probes built entirely from one silicon carbide system. Single-material devices dodge the failures that start at internal seams. Early tests also hint at cleaner MRI scans than silicon probes give, though safety at high field strengths still needs live study. The authors see a durable platform for long-term brain recording.
pmc-12735879:
Qi Sun and co-authors build a fake synapse that answers to ultraviolet light, in a 2025 paper. Brain-like chips use such parts to learn, and layered materials called dichalcogenides make stable ones. Yet those layers barely sense ultraviolet, so their synapses miss that band. The team pairs one such layer, WSe2, with a glow phosphor that drinks ultraviolet well.

The phosphor soaks up the light and re-feeds it to the layer, quadrupling the reply current to a single pulse. The after-current also lingers nearly ten times longer than in the plain layer. Pulse patterns tune the part's memory-like behavior, and a drill of learning and forgetting ran clean. Fed into a digit-reading net, the part's weights scored over ninety-six percent.
pmc-12736179:
Eva Scarcelli, Domenico Iacopetta, Jessica Ceramella, and five colleagues review wheat as an antibiotic option in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Resistance to antimicrobials is a global health challenge fed by careless use, pushing research toward natural compounds. Wheat, among the world's most grown crops, is rich in candidate molecules: polyphenols, small peptides, benzoxazinoids, benzoquinones, and alkylresorcinols. Screening Google Scholar and Scopus, the authors found the latest findings on these compounds across wheat varieties and by-products.

Lab studies show the plant chemicals act broadly, against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and various fungi. The review names the key compounds responsible and weighs their potency and spectra. The authors argue wheat and its milling by-products could serve as a lasting source of new antimicrobial agents, giving value to an abundant crop. They present the work as a map for researchers developing plant-based strategies against resistant infections.
pmc-12736879:
Sanbi Luo and Xiansheng Guo present a 2025 study of an AI agent that builds personal virtual exhibits from drone sensor data. Static displays cannot adapt, and general chat agents are slow and shaky in real time. Their agent aims to sense what a visitor wants and build a fitting show on the fly.

The design pairs broad search over stored material with a funnel that pins down intent and weaves a story. A test exhibit covered a wetland's wildlife. The agent answered more than twice as fast as a standard design, with far higher task success and search precision. A small user study found higher engagement too. The authors call it a shift from lookup to shared curation.
pmc-12737179: Rawan Alansari and co-authors made glowing carbon dots in a single microwave step in a 2025 paper and used them as sensors for two metal ions. The dots form from a simple carbon starting material, dissolve well in water, and stay stable. Under ultraviolet light they shine bright green, and their light yield is high. Mercury and iron ions dim the glow in proportion to their amount, with very low detection limits for both. The authors propose the dots as practical sensors for those metals in water.
pmc-12737279:
Yidong Shen and co-authors harden in 2025 the startup routine of an underwater navigation system against bad data. A strapdown inertial system knows where it points only after an initial alignment, and a Doppler velocity log helps by measuring motion through water. Underwater, that help arrives contaminated: currents and echoes inject outlier readings that can tilt the whole alignment.

Their method watches the stream of observation vectors for anomalies using a smarter distance measure, one that accounts for how the measurements naturally vary together. Suspect readings are not deleted but downweighted, through an adaptive factor folded into the observation math, so a few wild points cannot steer the result. Simulations and real experiments both showed cleaner alignment than existing methods when outliers were present. For vehicles that navigate blind under the sea, a trustworthy first fix is the difference between a mission and a search party.
pmc-12737379:
Aitor Somoano and co-authors measured harmful elements in water voles that live in two low-input apple orchards in Asturias, Spain. Their 2025 study is presented as the first full check of this kind for the species. They tested kidney, liver, and muscle tissue for lead, cadmium, and mercury, plus selenium.

Levels mostly matched the natural levels in local soils, but cadmium in the kidney rose above soil levels. The kidney held the highest levels for several elements, and body condition was linked with some of them. The authors argue that this vole can serve as a useful sign of trace inputs in farm land, if organs are tested one by one.
pmc-12738079:
Sophie Cohen-Bodénès and co-authors set out a protocol that tests a sense organ of young zebrafish by watching them hold place in a flow. Fish sense water movement through a line of hair cells along the body, kin to the hearing cells in human ears. The protocol uses rheotaxis, the urge to face and fight a current, as the readout. It gives a fine-grained check of the sense at work.

The steps cover building a small flow tank and filming larvae as they hold station. Software tracks each fish and sorts its behavior in bulk. That lets labs compare large groups with gene faults or chemical harm against normal fish. The authors say the test is a sharp tool for work on hearing loss genes and cell damage.
pmc-12738579:
Xuhui Xiong, Zhengwang Liu, Ruixuan Zhang, Liting Yang, Guisheng Liang, Ke Pei, and Renchao Che present a 2025 study of a battery electrode built on ordered gaps. Graphite and the safe titanate standard each trade off charge, speed, and life. The team took a cerium titanate crystal and set its missing cerium atoms in a strict super-pattern. The micron grains then held over two hundred milliamp-hours per gram at a handy voltage near 0.8.

Fast charging ran to fifty times the base rate, and cycles passed ten thousand at high rate. Live probes caught the crystal flipping between long and short order as lithium moved, a flip that keeps the frame whole while paths stay easy. Ordered gaps join the design kit for electrodes.
pmc-12738679:
Jannes Hohl and co-authors build a fast perfusion model for vessel trees that deform as tissue moves, in work from twenty twenty-five. Detailed vessel networks can hold millions of segments per organ. Simulating flow through every segment is far too costly. Their fix replaces the tree with layered continuum compartments. Each compartment mimics one resolution level of one vessel tree.

Flow inside a compartment follows a Darcy-type law with fitted permeability. Compartments trade mass through pressure-driven exchange everywhere at once. Key parameters come straight from the synthetic vessel segments. Spectral tricks and sample segments keep the fitting cheap. When tissue deforms, a geometric map updates parameters without refitting. A full liver case with three separate trees proves the approach. Accuracy holds while cost drops sharply.
pmc-12738879:
Adriano Nobre Arcos and co-authors count bite flies cross a Brazil grass hub as tree skin thins. The study appeared in 2025. Tree loss can shift which flies thrive, pests and plain kinds alike. Near seven thousand flies were logged cross the slope of loss.

More tree skin meant more flies as a whole. Plain kinds fell hard where skin ran thin. Pest kinds that bear ills to man and beast ran high where skin was thin. Cut marks for the shift split wide by kind, from low to high shares of skin. The team warns that more tree loss breeds more pest flies.
pmc-12741079:
Tong Li and six co-authors showed in 2025 how a helpful gut bacterium boosts a protective fat signal in injured intestines. When blood returns to a starved gut, the rush itself wounds the tissue. A fat-derived messenger called MaR1 calms inflammation, and gut bacteria help convert its raw material into the active form.

In mice with clamped gut arteries, the messenger, its food source, and the bacterium each eased damage, and together they curbed a fiery form of cell death. Deep profiling of gut genes and microbes traced the pathway. Feeding the right microbes may shield guts through surgery.
pmc-12742079:
Colas Tcherakian and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on the total mix of exposures, called the exposome, behind severe flare-ups of chronic lung diseases in France. Air, weather, and neighborhood all press on asthma and chronic obstructive disease, but their joint weight was unclear. The team linked hospital records with open environmental data for 2018 to 2022.

Hundreds of thousands of patients were matched with peers by sex, birth year, and first admission date. Cold snaps and air pollution above world limits raised flare-up odds for the obstructive disease. City living and nearby livestock farms also raised risk, while water, wetlands, and green space lowered it. Only one pollutant clearly mattered for asthma.
pmc-12742179:
Megan Simmons and ten co-authors survey primary care providers in British Columbia about helping patients quit smoking. The project drew 198 complete answers, from 154 family doctors and 44 nurse practitioners, gathered through professional newsletters. Questions covered what providers know, what training they want, and what blocks them from offering quit support. Time pressure stood out as the top barrier, followed by weak referral routes, thin local services, and poor pay for the work.

Providers asked for quick reference sheets on resources and best practice, training in counseling skills, guidance on vaping cessation, and workflows built into their record systems. The team argues quit support should be wired into everyday tools like electronic records and a single information hub. The findings show where the support system, not the providers' will, falls short.
pmc-12742379:
Qaiser Mukhtar and nine co-authors describe a program in two thousand twenty-five that helps new authors in low- and middle-income countries publish research. Local data in journals is vital for knowing disease burdens and shaping policy. Yet such countries bear most heart disease deaths and produce very few of the publications.

The Emerging Authors Program, run with the United States CDC and partners, gave mentorship and virtual writing tools. It also offered training, technical support, and funds for open access fees. From two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-three, thirty-three authors from eleven countries took part. They published thirty-one manuscripts in six journals, guided by twenty-three mentors. The authors credit mentor commitment and local teamwork.
pmc-12742579:
Yuan Li and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, how acupuncture may ease allergic diseases by calming mast cells. Mast cells drive asthma, hay fever, and skin allergies when they burst and spill signal chemicals. The review gathers proof that needle therapy steadies those cells.

The team screened studies from 2010 to 2025 and kept 365 papers on people and animals. Acupuncture cut mast cell bursting and lowered histamine and IgE levels. It also lowered pro-swelling signals and raised a calming one, through known inflammation pathways. Clinic results improved asthma airflow and eased nose and skin symptoms. Animal work showed fewer invading immune cells and less fiery cell death. The authors back acupuncture as a safe add-on for allergy care.
pmc-12742779:
Kim Hébert-Losier and co-authors ask male recreational runners how two very different racing shoes actually feel. Eighteen runners each ran three short outdoor trials: in their own shoes, in minimalist racing flats, and in carbon-plated advanced shoes, then talked through the experience in interviews before and after.

Five themes ran through the answers, from novelty and feel to performance, body mechanics, and injury worries. Their own shoes won on comfort and felt safest, being familiar. The flats felt light and natural but raised fears about soreness and injury from thin cushioning. The advanced shoes felt bouncy and fast yet unstable to some. Runners often chose performance over comfort for racing anyway. The authors advise gradual transitions to unfamiliar shoes and designs matched to the individual.
pmc-12743479:
Ying Li, Dandan Hao, Xiuru Qi, and Bijia Song lay out a trial protocol in 2025 testing anesthesia without opioids for gallbladder keyhole surgery. Nausea and vomiting after this surgery are common and often blamed on the opioids in standard anesthesia. Their trial asks whether dropping opioids cuts that misery and speeds recovery.

Ninety-six patients are split evenly and by chance between standard anesthesia and the opioid-free plan, with assignments hidden, the protocol states. Main measures are a standard nausea index and the counts of nausea and vomiting at six and twenty-four hours after surgery. The trial cleared its ethics board in April 2025, with a year of recruiting planned. Protocols like this lock the rules before results can bend them.
pmc-12744579:
Alice Raphael Karikachery and co-authors build tiny protein carriers for ketone fuel, in a 2025 study. Ketones can serve as a backup energy source when sugar is low. They may also help in weight and brain disorders, but the body takes them up poorly when they are simply swallowed.

The team wrapped a ketone compound inside pea protein particles, joined with plant based chemicals. They give full steps for making the particles and report tests in cells and in animals. The carriers are meant to help the fuel slip into cells and stay available longer. Such delivery could widen the use of ketone based diets and therapies.
pmc-12745679:
Deanna Kaplan, Roman Palitsky, and Charles Raison coin a term for a habit they see growing among scholars and clinicians: the machinal bypass. At a meeting on mental health, they heard peers ready to hand core human work to chatbots. The term names the use of smart tools not to support human contact, but to skip it.

They borrow the idea from spiritual bypass, where faith language is used to dodge hard feelings. Examples include a student dropping a bold thesis idea after a tool advised a safer path, and a colleague using a chatbot to write an apology. The authors urge readers to weigh what is lost each time a tool stands in for presence, thought, or care.
pmc-12747379:
Zibusiso Ndlovu and co-authors review task sharing for point-of-care testing in nineteen African countries in a 2025 paper. World health guidance backs trained lay workers doing quick tests when skilled staff are scarce, yet use stays low.

The team ran a survey, read over two hundred policy files, and spoke with lab leaders. Most health plans praise lay workers, but few name task sharing, and most lab plans skip lay roles. HIV plans use the idea more than lab plans do. The gap helps explain slow uptake. Readers get a clear map of where policy must change to widen test access.
pmc-12747979:
Yuanyi Feng, Dan Li, Yifu Weng, Chenfang Song, Zhenhe Huang, and Hualiang Lin wrote a 2025 paper on muscle loss in people with chronic kidney disease. Weak, shrinking muscle is called sarcopenia, and it is common when kidneys fail. The team asked whether patients with both problems go on to collect more other diseases.

They followed nineteen thousand five hundred two patients for a median of about ten years. Muscle state was judged by grip strength, muscle amount, and physical performance. Over the follow-up, thousands developed one or more added diseases, such as heart disease or diabetes. The paper also estimates how much of that burden could be avoided if grip strength improved across the group. The numbers argue for checking muscle health in kidney clinics.
pmc-12748579:
Waag and nine co-authors study how mouse brain gene activity adapts to repeated stress, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Chronic stress raises risk for mental illness, so adaptation matters for health. It was unclear whether brains simply blunt their response or build a new one. The team restrains mice repeatedly and reads genes in the lower hippocampus.

Across many time points, stress-driven gene changes grow blunt with repetition. No new response pattern emerges, and resting gene levels stay flat. Single-cell reads confirm blunting across all cell types, with cell-specific twists. Two mechanisms stand out, one via fewer activated cells and one via shorter responses. An interactive app shares the full resource.
pmc-12748679:
Peng Chen and co-authors use satellite laser data to rethink winter plant growth in the Southern Ocean, in a 2025 study. Tiny floating plants there pull carbon from the air and seed the spring blooms. Winter growth has been hard to measure, since normal satellite sensors fail in low light and ice cover. The team turned to a space laser instrument with sixteen years of records.

The laser data lifted ice-free ocean coverage from about one eighth to about four fifths. It showed winter growth rising much faster than past estimates said, over the last decade or so. Gains were strongest in the seasonal ice zone, in the Weddell and Ross Seas. Thinning ice, more light, and mixed nutrients drove the rise, shaped by large climate patterns. The authors say carbon models must add winter growth to stay accurate.
pmc-12748779:
Kuni Iwasa models in 2025 how coupled oscillators may extend ear amplification to high frequencies. Outer hair cells boost faint sounds and sharpen pitch sense in the mammal ear. Those cells are far softer than the membrane they must move, a mismatch that grows with pitch.

Pairs of coupled oscillators serve as the simplest multi-mode test bed. Some pair setups do let the soft cell act as a true amplifier past the mismatch. The rich structure of the hearing organ may thus be the key to high pitch power. The model gives a plain frame for that long puzzle.
pmc-12749079:
Md Arifuzzaman and co-authors report a 2025 material that pulls toxic hexavalent chromium out of polluted water. Their solid is a nanoscale mix of iron, titanium, and zinc oxides, made by a simple water based route. Lab checks with X-ray, light, and imaging tools confirmed its crystal form and even nanoscale shape.

Batch tests varied acidity, contact time, dose, and heat to find how uptake changes. The material held a large amount of chromium per gram and kept most of that power after five reuse cycles. Rate and heat measures pointed to chemical binding as the main step, in a process that ran on its own and took in heat. The authors present the solid as a reusable option for water cleanup.
pmc-12749279:
Canan Tastimur presents a defect finder for steel sheets in a 2025 paper. Hot-rolled steel with surface flaws loses value and buyer trust. Factories want flaws caught early in the making process. The new method, MSPro-Net, sorts flaw photos into classes. It builds on a network style that learns a model example, called a prototype, for each class.

The twist is how the prototype is picked. A mean shift method, which nudges the center toward the densest spot, gives a prototype that fits all class members better. The method shines when training photos are few. On one set with six classes and 25 shots each, it hit 98.67 percent accuracy. The older style reached only 50.67 percent on the same test. Two more sets showed like gains.
pmc-12749979:
John Guillamon, Cheng-Zhen Wang, Zin Lin, and Tsampikos Kottos steer light and radio waves inside chaotic scattering rooms by computing with the room itself, in a 2025 paper. In spaces where waves bounce hundreds of times, tiny changes ripple everywhere, making control seem hopeless. The team treats that sensitivity as an amplifier instead.

Their method performs adjoint optimization, the standard trick for computing how to tune a system, physically in place rather than in a simulated copy. Small, well-chosen tweaks then produce outsized effects through the many bounces. They demonstrate targeted emission down a chosen channel, perfect absorption of an incoming wave, and camouflage of an object. Indoor wireless is an immediate market. The broader claim is that complex wave hardware can do its own math.
pmc-12750479:
Shaibaan Mulla and co-authors compare one corneal cut with a paired cut in cataract surgery, in a 2025 trial. The surgery removes a cloudy lens through a small cut in the clear front of the eye. A second cut placed across from the first may correct a focusing flaw called astigmatism.

One hundred thirty patients were split by chance into the two groups, and checks ran for three months. The paired cut group showed a clear drop in corneal astigmatism by the end. The single cut group showed no clear change. The gap between groups was also firm. The authors conclude that the paired cut helps patients who start with this flaw.
pmc-12750579:
Manish Kumar and five co-authors evaluate a team based simulation course for medical and nursing students facing child emergencies, in this 2025 study. Health students are usually taught inside their own professions, so they reach real crises with little practice at working across roles. The course ran a child cardiac arrest scenario with rapid rounds of practice and feedback.

Seventy-two third year students, forty-six in medicine and twenty-six in nursing, trained across twelve sessions. Knowledge scores rose clearly after the course. Team clinical exam scores jumped from a median of six to seventeen. Observers also rated team performance higher in all five areas they scored, covering leadership, communication, and mutual support. Student feedback on learning side by side was gathered as well. The authors back the format for undergraduate training.
pmc-12750879:
Wang and three co-authors identify a switch protein that pushes macrophages toward their aggressive, germ-fighting state during a lung fungus infection. The fungus, Aspergillus fumigatus, can cause invasive disease in the lungs. The team combined a mouse infection model with human macrophage-like cells in dishes.

Infected lungs filled with the aggressive M1 macrophages and high levels of the switch, STAT1. In dishes, fungal spores raised STAT1 and M1 markers too. Blocking or silencing STAT1 calmed the response, while boosting it inflamed the cells further. Quiet M2 markers barely moved throughout. The authors propose STAT1 as a drug target for steering immunity in this infection.
pmc-12751179:
Danhua Zhao and co-authors published a 2025 trial comparing two schedules of a freeze-dried rabies vaccine grown in human cells. Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so vaccination after exposure must be reliable. The classic schedule takes five doses; a four-dose version would mean fewer clinic visits. The trial asked whether four doses protect as well as five.

The study ran in two stages at one center, with participants aged ten to sixty. A small first stage checked safety, including in teenagers. The main stage enrolled 1,800 people, split among the five-dose schedule, the four-dose schedule, and a control vaccine. Blood tests measured rabies-fighting antibodies, and side effects were tracked. Two weeks after the first dose and after the full course, protection rates matched between schedules, with no gap. The authors conclude the shorter schedule is not inferior.
pmc-12751379:
Shuang Yang and co-authors compare three arthroscopic stitching methods for a torn knee meniscus in a 2025 study. The tear sat in a tricky zone near a tendon passage, in the meniscus's well-supplied outer bands. All-inside repair avoids extra incisions, and the study asks whether combining two devices beats either alone.

Seventy-two patients were split evenly among a combined method, a suture device alone, and a suture hook alone. Knee scores and motion were tracked for a year, with MRI checks of healing after six months. The combined group improved clearly at both six and twelve months, with function scores climbing steeply from their start. No major complications arose. The authors favor the combined technique for this tear zone.
pmc-12751479:
Fatemeh Ammari and three co-authors compare helpful bacteria in the breast milk of mothers by weight, in a 2025 study. Two bacterial genera, Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus, seed a baby's gut with benefits. Their counts in milk shift with many factors. The team drew milk from twenty obese and twenty normal-weight mothers four months after birth, and asked each mother what she ate.

One genus, Bifidobacterium, ran far higher in the normal-weight group's milk, about nine tenths higher after other traits were weighed. A mother's weight before pregnancy shaped the counts most. Eating more energy, protein, carbs, and fiber went with more of the genus, while more fat went with less. The second genus showed no such clear split in the report.
pmc-12751579:
Ji-Yoon Lee and nine co-authors published a study in 2025 on brain wave patterns that mark severe arm weakness after stroke. Survivors whose arm barely recovers face a long, uncertain rehabilitation. A resting brain recording that flags severe cases early could guide therapy choices and honest expectations, so the team mined such recordings with machine learning.

They studied thirty-four chronic stroke survivors, split by a standard arm score into milder and severe groups. Links between brain sites were computed across six wave bands for both halves of the brain. One lean model, pared to fourteen features, sorted severe from milder cases with about ninety-one percent balanced accuracy. A short, painless recording may carry more forecast power than clinics currently use.
pmc-12751979:
Zhiqiang Wang and colleagues survey thousands of medical master's students in China on what builds research skill, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Their focus is psychological capital: a bundle of hope, confidence, optimism, and resilience. Whether it feeds research ability, and how, had not been mapped in medical graduate training.

Nearly thirty-nine hundred students from seventy universities answered online. Students richer in psychological capital showed stronger research ability, in part because they invested more in research: more time, effort, and persistence. Good mentorship strengthened both links, helping capital turn into investment, and investment into ability. The chain suggests two levers for schools: build students' inner resources, and train mentors to guide well. The authors offer the model as a base for policy on cultivating medical researchers.
pmc-12752379:
Paolo Magni, Giulia Ricci, Marco Narici, and Francesca Ferranti review what spaceflight does to hormones, metabolism, and the kidneys. Flight has long been tied to shifts in endocrine and kidney function. The authors gather the best current proof on the heart-metabolic system, the heart-kidney link, and the reproductive axis.

Their 2025 review stresses that these changes do not sit apart from the rest of the body. Each shift feeds into others, so a whole-system view is needed to grasp the health stakes of space travel. The authors call for multi-omics methods in future work, joined with machine learning and data mining. Open questions and candidate countermeasures round out the survey.
pmc-12752579:
Gas molecules can kill cancer cells, but tumors drink up too little of them for gas therapy to stand alone. The authors build a platform answering with an electric field. Metal nano-berries carrying several gas donors sit in the tumor; a field then speeds gas release and raises yield. The released molecules react with reactive oxygen species in the tumor, forming stronger killers, including reactive nitrogen species. The team names the combined assault an electro-stress storm.

The storm does a third job beyond direct killing: it wakes the immune system, which hunts tumor cells escaping the local attack. In their tests, the platform ablates even large solid tumors and suppresses spreading ones. They present the cascade design as a way to turn gas therapy from a supporting act into a main treatment, and as a route toward tumors with unclear borders.
pmc-12753379:
Haixia Lu and co-authors test in 2025 whether two plant derived fibers can cool the chronic inflammation of type 2 diabetes by way of the gut. Diabetes is increasingly read as an inflammatory disease, and the gut's microbes and their bile acid products are one control panel. The candidate prebiotics are inulin, a fiber from roots, and polysaccharides from goji berries.

Diabetic rats, made so by a fatty diet plus a pancreas straining drug, were split into groups receiving either fiber alone, both, or neither for eight weeks. The proposed chain runs through a named signaling axis: microbial bile acids talk to gut and liver receptors, which in turn switch on regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers. Work of this kind matters because it tests a mechanism, not just a supplement: if the axis carries the effect, each link becomes a drug target in its own right.
pmc-12753479:
Yuxuan Dai and Yu Chen review how a wound that will not heal is often a wound stuck in inflammation, in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Healthy healing moves through inflammation and out the other side. In chronic wounds, immune cells misfire and the alarm never stands down, so repair stalls.

The review centers on two cell families: macrophages, the cleanup and signaling crews, and T cells, the targeted arm. It traces the molecular switches that lock each into overdrive, and the cross-talk that keeps them there, each feeding the other's alarm. From those switches the authors list drug targets meant to restore balance rather than silence immunity outright. Their hope is precise calming: end the persistent activation, restart the repair sequence, and give tissue engineering a saner field to work in.
pmc-12753879:
Dan Ye and co-authors hunt for shared genes between two women's health disorders in a 2025 study. One is polycystic ovary syndrome, a common hormone disorder. The other is cancer of the womb lining. Women with the first face higher risk of the second. The team mined public gene data sets with network tools and gene-link tests.

Eight genes stood out in both disorders, among them MMP9, PECAM1, and CYBB. One shared path, type I interferon signaling, ranked as the key link. Gene-based cause tests also pointed to a true link between the two disorders, not just overlap. The authors say these genes and this path could serve as marks or drug aims that span both disorders. They note the work rests on data banks, so lab checks should follow.
pmc-12754879:
Khalid Khadoura and three co-authors measure how widely hepatitis A spread in the Gaza Strip during the 2023 to 2025 conflict, and what drove it. The virus thrives where water and sanitation systems break down. Their online survey reached four hundred forty residents aged six and older between March and June 2025. It recorded diagnoses, symptoms, and living conditions such as water source and toilet access.

About thirty percent reported a hepatitis A diagnosis during the conflict, with the young and the displaced, especially in North Gaza, hit hardest. Living in shelters raised the odds of infection twelve-fold. Trucked water, skipped handwashing before eating, and poor toilet conditions also sharply raised risk, while secondary schooling lowered it. The authors call for urgent water and hygiene fixes, targeted vaccination, and better sanitation in shelters and camps.
pmc-12755779:
Dan Li, Mi Zhou, and Xiaomei Song study how older adults divide their day among activity, sitting, and sleep. Their 2025 paper uses a European survey of health and aging in later life. A day is a fixed budget: more time in one behavior means less in another, so the authors analyze the mix as a whole rather than piece by piece.

They link the daily mix to vision, hearing, activity limits, and self-rated health. Sight and hearing showed weak, non-significant ties to the mix. Activity limits mattered clearly: people without limits spent more time in stronger activity and less time sitting. The compositional approach respects how days actually work and can shape advice for aging well.
pmc-12755879:
Huaxia Zhou and co-authors ask whether science journals have grown more global and more mixed in subject over time. Their 2025 study uses records from OpenAlex, a large open database of published work. They compare subject journals in the natural, life, and social sciences with journals that publish across many fields.

The team finds that work from many nations has become more common in almost all journals. Medicine journals stand out as less global, and their share did not rise. Physics journals split, with some turning more global and others less so. Journals that span many fields shifted their subject mix a great deal over the past century. Subject journals, by contrast, kept much the same mix.
pmc-12756079:
A rare lung lymphoma that grows slowly can look, on scans, like infection or inflammation, and small biopsies often miss it. Jian Tang, Bijun Yang, and Yang Bai describe in 2025 a 36-year-old woman, a non-smoker with no symptoms, whose routine chest X-ray showed patchy shadows in one lung. Over eighteen months the patches spread to both lungs, yet she still felt nothing.

Standard bronchial biopsy and fluid tests found only nonspecific inflammation, and a course of antibiotics changed nothing. The diagnosis came from an ultrasound-guided cryobiopsy, which takes larger, well-preserved tissue: dense B-cell growth with a monoclonal gene pattern confirmed the lymphoma, and staging scans showed stage IV disease. Because she felt well, doctors chose watchful monitoring over treatment. The authors review the literature and stress larger tissue samples when this cancer is suspected.
pmc-12756379:
Yan Li, Ute Kunzmann, Philipp Kanske, and Margund Rohr probe how felt success at managing emotions ties to couple happiness. Their 2025 study spans 37 younger couples and 41 older ones. Each partner rated their own emotion control success, their partner success, and relationship quality.

The team models actor, partner, and similarity effects across gender and age. Higher felt success links to better relationship quality overall. The link stands out most among women and older partners. For men, one quirk predicts quality: how close their self-view and partner-view of success sit. The authors suggest that helping women notice their own control, and men share a common read, can strengthen couples. The work adds age and gender nuance to emotion research.
pmc-12756779:
A clay called montmorillonite is cheap, natural, and can act as an acid catalyst for building useful molecules. Eva Vrbková, Lucie Stoupová, and Eliška Vyskočilová tested it in 2025 for a reaction that makes bicyclic ethers from limonene, a citrus oil, and crotonaldehyde. Such compounds smell pleasant and may act on estrogen receptors, which makes them interesting for fragrances and medicine.

Treating the clay with common acids boosted its performance, giving over eighty-five percent conversion of limonene in a day. Heat, solvent, and ingredient ratios all shifted the balance between conversion and selectivity. Adding stronger acid compounds raised conversion but lowered selectivity. The authors conclude acid-treated clay is the better, cheaper green option.
pmc-12757379:
Zhihui Li and a team of co-authors hunt for the liver-protecting parts of a processed traditional herb, in two thousand twenty-five. The raw herb can harm the liver, yet processing lowers that harm and raises its protective effect. A liver receptor tied to bile flow is the key target in this kind of injury.

The team built a screening system that fishes out parts of the herb that bind that receptor. Two compounds stood out, and both were richer in the processed herb. In mice with bile-related liver injury, both compounds eased damage and calmed swelling. Blocking the receptor undid their benefit, which supports the proposed path.
pmc-12758079:
Nils Thorm Milman presents a 2025 study of blood iron markers in Danish patients with a gene fault that causes iron overload. He focuses on transferrin, a protein that carries iron in the blood. Patients with two copies of the fault had lower transferrin than healthy controls, and the reason was not clear.

Nearly all patients had lower transferrin, and their iron and ferritin levels moved against it. A measure of transferrin loading also moved strongly against transferrin itself. Many patients kept low transferrin even after excess iron was removed. Milman asks whether the liver makes less of the protein or the body breaks it down faster, and calls for more work.
pmc-12764079:
Albert Muñoz-Vendrell and a team study a migraine prevention pill in everyday practice in Spanish headache clinics. The pill, atogepant, had done well in formal trials. The open question was whether it helps patients who failed newer injected antibody drugs. The study enrolled two hundred fifty-two adults starting the pill after at least one such failure, and followed them for six months.

Most had chronic migraine, and many had pain nearly every day. At three months, about thirty percent had cut their monthly migraine days by half or more, and about twelve percent by three quarters or more. Side effects hit just over half of patients, most often mild bowel or stomach complaints. The team tracked how long patients stayed on the pill and which traits predicted a good response. They present the results as real-world support for the pill after antibody failure.
pmc-12764879:
Abbey Figliomeni and co-authors profile the gut and immune signatures of Parkinson's disease, focusing on patients troubled by constipation. Digestive problems are the most common early non-motor symptom of the disease, and some evidence suggests the illness may begin in the gut. The team compared thirty-one patients with twenty-eight healthy controls.

Stool and blood samples revealed shifted chemistry: several energy-related compounds fell in stool while others rose in blood. Immune profiling showed fewer T cells, more natural killer cells, and B cells tilted toward memory types, with the shifts tracking a metabolite called succinate. Sorting the blood data split the patients into two subtypes. One carried stronger gut symptoms and T cell patterns pointing to travel between gut and brain. The authors say these paired immune and metabolic signatures define meaningful subgroups within Parkinson's.
pmc-12767479:
Ghazal Aftab and colleagues compare eye surface microbes in cats with two viral infections. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses Persian cats in four groups. Healthy cats were compared with cats carrying one or both viruses. Feline immunodeficiency and leukemia viruses weaken cat immunity.

Eighty cats gave conjunctival swabs for bacterial and fungal culture. Lab tests confirmed virus and other pathogen status. Healthy eyes carried mainly Gram-positive bacteria like staph. A gut bacterium appeared only in infected cats eyes. Co-infected cats showed the highest rates of that invader. Virus status clearly reshapes the eye surface community. Eye infections in positive cats may need different vigilance.
pmc-12767579:
Babesia ovis is a blood parasite of sheep spread by ticks, and one route of spread is from a mother tick through her eggs to her larvae. Mehmet Can Ulucesme and Munir Aktas test that route in the field in Türkiye. They collected 751 ticks from sheep and goats, then let engorged females of two Rhipicephalus species lay eggs under controlled conditions.

Parasite DNA appeared in about 19 percent of females of one species and 8 percent of the other. Every larval pool from positive mothers of the first species also tested positive, which proves natural egg transmission there. No larvae of the second species carried it, despite positive mothers. The findings separate a true vector from a mere carrier in local sheep country.
pmc-12767979:
Connor Tupper, Peter Silberstein, and co-authors compare survival for a muscle cancer in arms versus legs, in a 2025 study. This cancer in limbs has a poor outlook, in part since it spreads more often. Past checks of arm versus leg cases were few.

The team drew cases from a large United States cancer data base for two decades. More than six hundred cases fit, with about a third in arms. Arm cases lived more long at one year than leg cases. Once other traits were weighed in, that gap lost force. The team calls for direct tests in future work.
pmc-12768679:
Carla Gottgtroy and Rosangela Caetano present this 2025 conference abstract on how Brazil judges the budget impact of pricey biologic drugs. Brazil's public health system decides which new drugs to fund through a national committee, CONITEC. Biologics for rheumatic diseases strain that process with their cost and special handling needs.

The authors reviewed nine committee reports from 2012 to 2023 and checked them against national budget impact guidelines. Economic adjustments were fully adequate everywhere; the cost of introducing a new drug was missing everywhere. Interviews with five experts added color. Nine problem themes emerged, including analyses too simple for the scenario and tangles around biosimilar drugs. Everyone interviewed doubted the analyses matched the decisions' complexity.
pmc-12768779:
Sonia Muñoz-López and co-authors wrote a 2025 study on policy for melanoma in children and young people in Europe. Melanoma is a serious form of skin cancer, and it is rare in the young. Few plans exist to prevent it or catch it early in this age group.

The team ran a group session with 15 people from seven countries in Europe. The group held patients, carers, advocates, and health staff. They talked through weak spots in current policy and the role of advocates in shaping new plans. They also weighed 20 policy ideas from national cancer plans, sorted into early diagnosis, sun safety, and gene-based care. The study gives policy makers the patient view on where change is most needed.
pmc-12769579:
Yanyun Wu and colleagues review how multi-omics profiling and AI could sharpen risk prediction in the early states of multiple myeloma. MGUS and smoldering myeloma precede myeloma on one spectrum, but progression is hard to predict. Current risk models rest on clinical, laboratory, and cytogenetic markers and miss the molecular complexity driving progression, capping accuracy.

Genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics now expose molecular drivers in depth. Machine learning can merge these layers into live risk prediction for each person, finding new biomarkers and forecasting outcomes far better. The authors argue such tools could transform stratification, letting doctors watch each person and treat earlier. Uptake faces real obstacles: merging complex data types, one protocol set, data privacy, bias in the math, and shifting regulation. The clinical stake is timing: treat too early and patients endure toxicity for nothing; too late and a curable window closes.
pmc-12770479:
Weijun Fan presents, in 2025, a framework for finding tiny surface defects on composite materials when examples are scarce and some defect types have never been seen. Two paths work together. A diffusion model learns what defects look like by rebuilding them from noise, while a zero-shot path matches images to written attribute descriptions.

The paths share features at several levels and train jointly. On benchmark sets, the zero-shot side matched supervised methods without any labeled samples for the new defect types, cutting labeling cost. Results held across different composite materials. The author offers the design for smart quality control in composite manufacturing.
pmc-12770879:
Buasawat and six colleagues train machine learning models to predict severe mouth sores from head and neck radiation in twenty twenty-five. The sores are a harsh side effect that can halt treatment and ruin eating. The team used records from one hundred forty-eight patients at Thai centers. They mixed clinic facts, dose measures, and image based traits from scans.

Sixteen mixes of trait picking and model type were tried. The best mix called severe cases with high accuracy on held out patients. Dose to the mouth lining and to spit glands ranked among the top signals. Clinic and dose traits worked best, but image traits alone did nearly as well. Early warning could let doctors shield the mouth sooner.
pmc-12771579:
Minwoo Bae and co-authors find the gut enzymes that make a health-linked compound in this 2025 study. The compound, urolithin A, comes from a plant chemical found in berries and nuts, and it is tied to slower aging and less swelling. Gut bacteria make it through several hard chemical steps, but the enzymes at work were largely unknown.

Using gene activity tests, lab-made proteins, and enzyme assays, the team found two distinct enzyme families that can do the key steps. Each family needs different starting traits, which hints they work by different routes. In a human group, patients with bowel disease had lower levels of the compound and of the genes that make it.
pmc-12771879:
Platzgummer and co-authors map what is known of sand flies in five lands of mid-Europe. Sand flies spread Leishmania germs and some flu-like germs by bite. Known most in warm south lands, they now push north in Europe. One type, Phlebotomus mascittii, bears cold best and lives most far north. Yet maps for Germany, Austria, Czechia, Slovakia, and Hungary stay patchy. The team pairs a full text sweep with field hunts for the flies.

Field work adds rat checks for germs the flies may bear. Code reads, meal tests, tree charts, and land scans round out the work. Six fly types were pinned down across the five lands. Just Ph. mascittii showed in all but Czechia, with peak flight in July. Three more types showed in Hungary in the finds.
pmc-12772079:
Jing-jing Huang and co-authors modeled what drives multiple chronic diseases in rural southwest China in two thousand twenty-five. Having several noncommunicable diseases at once is rising fast in China and hits poorer areas hard. The authors wanted the pathways that link social position, lifestyle, and disease.

They surveyed adults aged thirty-five and over with interviews and physical exams. Raised blood pressure was the most common condition, and about nineteen percent had several diseases at once. A structural model found social position, age, ethnicity, inactivity, and diet each had direct and indirect effects. Obesity and family history linked directly to multimorbidity. The authors urge prevention aimed at low social position and unhealthy lifestyles.
pmc-12779979:
Luthfi Lulul Ulum and six co-authors study how a protein controls an RNA made at chromosome ends, in a 2025 paper. Chromosome tips, called telomeres, shorten with age and are guarded in cancer cells by two lengthening routes. An RNA copied from the tips, named TERRA, influences both routes, and both the tips and the RNA can fold into knots called G-quadruplexes.

The team found that a protein first known from Ewing sarcoma grips those knots in both the tip DNA and the RNA, competing for the same hold. In cells, its grip depended on a flexible tail region, and it switched on a chemical mark that opened the region for copying. Variants of the protein that gripped DNA only raised TERRA levels further. The authors conclude the tug-of-war between DNA and RNA on this protein keeps TERRA output in balance.
pmc-12783179:
Chen and co-authors trace how a key receptor reaches the primary cilium, a tiny cell antenna. The receptor, EP4, sits on both the cilium and the cell surface and shapes inflammation and cancer growth. How it gets to the cilium was not clear.

Work in zebrafish, mouse tissue, and human cells showed EP4 in cilia. Two parts of the protein guide that trip, and a short LPG motif acts as a key signal. Changing one amino acid in that motif blocked the trip and cut signaling. A screen named Rab23 and IFT43 as helpers.
pmc-12784579:
Yusef Ahmed and four co-authors asked young people at family risk of bipolar disorder how they see their own risk. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with children of parents with the disorder. Such youth face higher odds of mental ills. Counts of their signs are well known, but their own views are not: how they read a parent's illness, their own weak spots, and the role of family ties.

Fifteen youths from age fifteen to twenty-four sat for deep talks. The talks probed life with an ill parent, views on heredity, and what early help they would take. Readers who design family help get the youth view first hand, a base for care that fits their felt world.
pmc-12784779:
Alexander and Vladimir Dvoretsky published a marine biology note in two thousand twenty-five on a worm living on red king crabs. The introduced crab is valuable in the Barents Sea and hosts many hitchhiking species. Polychaete worms were already known among its lodgers.

Twelve threadworm specimens were found in the gills of two crabs in a Barents bay, in July two thousand fifteen and two thousand twenty-five. The species, Amphitrite cirrata, had never been recorded in this partnership before. The worms gain food, transport, and shelter from the crab. The crabs pay with damaged gill tissue and trapped sand. The authors document the new association as the first of its kind.
pmc-12785279:
Zuzda, Walczak-Wieteska, Andruszkiewicz, and Malyszko review kidney injury markers in surgery care, in work from twenty twenty-five. Acute kidney injury is a common problem around surgery, with high death and cost burdens. Standard tests based on creatinine and urine output detect it late.

New markers can flag injury earlier and show its type. They fall into function, stress, and damage groups. The scoping review mapped research on these markers in surgical settings. It weighed accuracy, patient outcomes, approval status, and barriers to routine use. Gaps between promising tests and daily practice are the central concern.
pmc-12785479:
Zacharias Papadakis reviews lifestyle medicine for the joined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The three systems fail in linked ways, so care must be joined too. He blends past reviews and fresh studies on how far habit care can be carried into clinic.
