Six pillars frame the care: food, motion, stress, sleep, social ties, and shunning risky goods. Work on them lifts blood pressure, fats, sugar, and weight, at times to a drug-like degree. New drug kinds may pair or queue with habit care in ways still to test. Blocks are drug-first habits and thin set plans. Fair, culture-fit care for the worst-hit groups is urged.
pmc-12785579:
Arshad Husain Rahmani and Amjad Ali Khan review chrysin, a plant flavonoid found in fruit, vegetables, honey, and propolis, in work from 2025. The compound calms oxidative stress and swelling in the body. It also steers cell signals tied to growth, death, and blood vessel formation.

The review gathers work on heart, liver, blood sugar, nerve, bone, and germ effects, plus cancer studies. Pairing chrysin with other drugs or plant compounds often boosted gains and cut toxicity in the cited work. A key limit is that the body absorbs chrysin poorly, which holds back clinic use. The authors map what is known and where better delivery could help.
pmc-12785679:
Venkata Polaki and co-authors show that exercise rebalances immune cells in belly fat of hypertensive mice, in work from twenty twenty-five. Macrophages gather in visceral fat during high blood pressure. Their inflammatory slant may drive tissue damage there. Renin-driven hypertensive mice exercise for eight weeks. Fat shape, scarring, and macrophage types are measured afterwards.

Exercised mice show smaller fat cells and less collagen in depots. Immune cell infiltration into the fat actually rises with exercise. The inflammatory-to-calming macrophage ratio, though, corrects downward. Protein markers confirm the polarisation shift inside the tissue. Vessel and fat function improve alongside the immune rebalance. Exercise fights hypertension partly through fat immunology.
pmc-12786279:
Mingyang Du and co-authors review the cell's recycling pathway in brain disease and cancer in a 2025 paper. The pathway, autophagy plus the lysosome, breaks down worn parts and keeps cells in balance. When it fails, toxic proteins pile up, a mark of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

Tumors bend the same machinery to feed growth and resist drugs. The review details how acid loss, membrane leaks, and failed merging of the pathway's parts drive each illness. New treatments aim at the lysosome itself: drugs that puncture its membrane in tumors, particles that fix its acidity, and tools that tag proteins for disposal.
pmc-12786779:
Yuming Guo and co-authors study how sea airport pavements lose their wear strength, in work from 2025. Salt spray and repeated plane impacts grind the rigid surface down and shorten its life. The team hit concrete samples with falling weights, then ran abrasion tests and read the inner changes with X-ray and scope tools.

More impacts sped surface loss a lot and let the samples soak up more water through fine cracks. Mild salt fog at first hardened the surface, as salts filled the pores. Long fog flipped the gain into loss. Mixed salt and impact wore the surface fastest of all.
pmc-12786879:
Abu-Farha and five co-authors wrote this 2025 study testing whether AI chat models can spot drug errors in children's prescriptions. Drug errors in child care are a real risk, and the team built sixty case scenes, half of them hiding an error. The cases spanned four body systems: breathing, hormones, nerves, and infections.

Four models took the cases in both English and Arabic under one shared prompt. One model, Copilot, scored best overall, near eighty-seven percent in English and eighty-five in Arabic. GPT-5 came next, while Gemini scored lowest. Arabic runs scored lower than English for most models. Copilot also gave the steadiest repeat answers. The authors say the best models could back up human checks, with a clear edge for English cases in this test.
pmc-12788479:
Priya Gupta and Ratnesh Singh compare two socket aids for healing after lower back tooth removal. The trial appeared in 2025. Such removals often bring pain, swelling, and slow tissue growth. Both aids are used to speed the mend, but head-to-head proof was thin.

Sixty patients were split at random into two groups of thirty. One group got a blood-based plug in the socket, while the other got a collagen sheet. Pain, swelling, and healing were checked on days three, seven, and fourteen. The plug group had less pain and swelling on day three. By day fourteen its tissue scores were higher, and no harms were seen.
pmc-12789679:
Jéssica Catarino and co-authors ask how much of a medical AI's skill is decided before the model ever sees the image. Deep learning pipelines begin with pre-processing, resizing, normalizing, orienting, yet its effect on breast image segmentation is barely studied. Their 2025 paper runs one standard U-Net model over two public breast datasets, mammography and MRI, while varying the preparation systematically.

Two pipelines compete. One applies the generic habits of image analysis; the other is domain-specific, handling breast metadata carefully to preserve anatomy. Each technique, intensity normalization, spacing harmonization, resizing and padding, orientation standardization, is isolated and scored for its effect. The authors identify which preparation choices genuinely help segmentation in this domain and which are ritual. The study is a first step, they concede, toward treating pre-processing as an experimental variable rather than a house style.
pmc-12790679:
Osama Abdalla and co-authors report a long-term heart infection tied to a pacemaker lead, in a case report from 2025. A man in his seventies had fever and chills for three months. Two rounds of drugs given without a firm cause had not cleared the illness, and early tests found no clear source.

Blood tests later grew a skin germ from the blood after drug treatment stopped. A scope scan of the heart then pointed to infection on the device lead. The case shows why device infection stays on the list when fever lasts. It also shows the value of repeat blood tests and heart scans.
pmc-12795579:
Ha-Neul Yu and colleagues studied diabetic retinopathy as a marker of neurodegenerative disease. Their 2025 paper uses the All of Us research database. Eye damage from diabetes has been linked to brain diseases before. Whether it adds signal beyond diabetes itself was unclear. Three matched groups were built from health records.

One group had both retinopathy and diabetes. A second had diabetes without eye damage. A third had no diabetes at all. Groups matched exactly on age, sex, and race. Outcomes covered dementia, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis. Models adjusted for other illnesses and diabetes mediators. The study tests the eye as a window on brain risk.
pmc-12796379:
Anand Pathak and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on a computer model of the brain built to act like real brain tissue. Most models either track fine cell detail or explain thought, but not both at once. Their model aims to join the two levels. It builds small linked groups of cells based on a real brain circuit that links the outer brain to a deep hub.

The model gives off spikes and waves like those seen in live brains, and it can hold facts in mind, choose, and sort items into groups. Its output matched a large set of tests on monkeys, though it had not been trained on that data. It also found a class of cells whose firing foretells a wrong choice soon after, a pattern later seen in the real data.
pmc-12796479:
Ying Mei and co-authors work in 2025 to cut shared mode noise in high power wireless charge systems for electric cars. Shield plates tame the field the coils throw off, yet they add noise of their own. That noise can break the radio clean rules such gear must meet.

The team maps how coil traits split by side and builds a full noise model from stray links. A balance trick in the match web then trims the noise with no new parts. A full size test rig cut noise at low tones by a fair span, and far more at high tones.
pmc-12796879:
Beatrice Palazzolo and co-authors set out a trial protocol for a web-based contraception decision tool in US clinics in a 2025 paper. Choosing a method is personal, and illness adds hard questions about safety and drug interactions.

The tool, My Health My Choice, walks patients through options in light of their conditions, medicines, and priorities. Fourteen primary care and gynecology clinics will be randomized as whole sites, half adding the tool to usual care and half giving usual care alone. Over seven hundred patients with at least one of sixty listed conditions will enroll. Outcomes span decision quality, method choice, and satisfaction, with interviews adding depth. The mixed design tests both effect and experience.
pmc-12800279:
Shreyasvi Natraj and co-authors built a markerless walking analysis in 2025 that grades gait from a single ordinary video. Laboratory gait labs read movement with reflective markers, at high cost and only in clinic. Continuous, real-world checks matter most in conditions like spinal cord injury, where recovery unfolds at home.

The team first benchmarked leading three-dimensional pose estimation models on injured gait, and one, named in the study, performed best. Its pipeline turns one video into joint angle time series automatically. On the largest spinal cord injury gait set gathered to date, 225 participants, it separated distinct walking patterns on its own and flagged markers like reduced hip and knee motion. Readers get rehabilitation measurement that leaves the lab: a phone camera standing in for a motion capture room.
pmc-12802379:
Priya Patel and co-authors propose video as an upgrade to surgical training assessment in a 2025 paper. Trainees are graded on real procedures through forms filled in with senior surgeons. The team doubted those forms capture true skill, and asked trainees whether video of their own operations would help reflection and grading.

A survey of orthopaedic trainees in eastern England drew replies from fifty-five of seventy-three trainees. Sixty percent felt current forms hide their strengths and faults. Most said video access would aid reflection, and seven in ten said it would help complete the forms. Half had not finished forms with their consultant at all. Legal and ethical issues for filming are weighed in full.
pmc-12804179:
Mingyu Jeong and Andrew Choi improve a vision method that tracks a flying drone so a ground vehicle can recover it, in a 2025 paper. Drones that lose control or lack a runway need safe capture, which demands exact position and tilt in real time. Their system reads a single camera view.

Key points on the drone are found from heat maps whose blur width adapts to the drone's distance. That change lifted correct key point rates by up to two and a half points across several backbones. A geometry solver turns the points into full pose. Tests covered varied heights, steep tilts, and motion blur. Sharper points mean safer catches.
pmc-12804679:
Antonio Yuste-Delgado and co-authors present a 2025 method to group wireless sensors so their batteries last. Sensor nets feed internet of things apps, but most nodes run on small batteries. Grouping nodes under heads that relay data can stretch the net's life, if the heads are picked well.

Their central scheme builds two tiers: cluster heads, then super heads above them. A first filter drops nodes with low charge from head duty. A two stage fuzzy system then grades the rest on energy and other traits to pick heads, and grades heads again to pick super heads. The fuzzy logic is coupled in cascade, so stage one feeds stage two. The aim is an even drain across the whole net.
pmc-12804779:
Tianci Zhang and co-authors fold DNA into a delivery device that releases gene-silencing cargo only inside inflamed gut tissue, in a 2025 paper. Ulcerative colitis scars the colon, and small interfering RNAs can mute the genes driving the attack — if they arrive intact and act only where needed.

Their origami device carries two kinds of siRNA at exact doses, locked by a DNA switch that an enzyme abundant in inflamed cells flips open. The device gathered in the intestine on its own and stayed inert in healthy cells. In mice with induced colitis, treatment raised survival and calmed disease. Smart carriers that wake only at the target could make RNA drugs safer across inflammatory diseases.
pmc-12805679:
Phibansuk Lyngdoh and co-authors study malaria in Meghalaya, a state in northeast India where the disease spreads all year and peaks with the rains. People with malaria-like illness at six health sites in three districts gave blood samples between 2018 and 2021. Just over a thousand people took part.

About four in a hundred tested positive, most with the more dangerous parasite kind. Rates varied sharply by district, from under two in a hundred to over twelve. Having had malaria in the past year was the strongest risk mark. Being outdoors before bed or early in the morning also raised the risk. The authors call for local plans shaped to such patterns.
pmc-12805779:
Caroline Larsson and co-authors lay out the plan for a study on whether exercise can wake repair pathways in damaged lungs, in a 2025 protocol paper. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is usually seen as a one-way decline. Hints that training can improve lung function raise a question: what changes inside the tissue? The team will recruit eighty sedentary adults with stable disease at two centers for twelve weeks of guided training.

Sessions mix aerobic work and muscle strengthening, three times a week, tuned to each person. Tests before and after span lung function, walking and standing capacity, breath gas measures, blood and urine samples, and airway sampling by scope. Two newer lung tests get a validation check along the way. The authors hope the results will name biomarkers and drug targets, and challenge the idea that lung damage cannot turn back.
pmc-12809679:
Simin Yu, Yuting Luo, Tianfeng Dang and colleagues analysed tiny vesicles in blood plasma one by one to find a marker for thyroid cancer in 2025. Tumours shed these small extracellular vesicles, but bulk tests blur the differences between them.

Total vesicle counts were higher in patients than in healthy controls in two cohorts. One surface protein, EPCAM, stood out: vesicles carrying it were clearly raised in cancer. After surgery, EPCAM-positive vesicle counts fell in all twenty tracked patients, while the standard marker thyroglobulin fell in only fourteen. Vesicles from patients also made cancer cells grow and spread faster in the lab, hinting at a role beyond marking disease.
pmc-12809979:
Emre Cem Esen and Hayriye Baykan test a phone app that delivers talk therapy for panic, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Panic disorder affects up to five in each hundred people. Therapy works, but shortages of therapists and long waits keep many from getting it.

Twenty volunteers who had past panic attacks but no current illness used the app. They worked through five sessions in Turkish, covering learning about panic, keeping panic diaries, challenging fearful thoughts, and facing body sensations on purpose. The study checked whether people would finish the sessions, how long they spent, and how usable the app felt. The authors frame the app as a workable way to widen access, while noting that many rival apps lack personal fit and expert oversight.
pmc-12810579:
Jacob Farley and co-authors test whether driving with one hand slows braking, in a study published in 2025. The question matters for patients recovering from arm or hand surgery, who often ask when they can drive. The team used a driving simulator so hand position could be varied safely and measured precisely.

Thirty-three healthy volunteers each ran fifteen trials: both hands, dominant hand only, and non-dominant hand only. Each trial sped to sixty miles per hour and then braked to a stop. Reaction times and braking distance did not differ across the three hand setups. The authors say hand position alone did not hurt braking in healthy drivers under these conditions. They also propose simulators as a fair test bed for judging driving fitness after injury.
pmc-12811979:
Murad Emar and Ali Bhatty report a man whose heart artery spasms killed him despite full drug care. This chest pain type, called vasospastic angina, comes from brief artery squeezes that starve the heart. Most cases yield to drugs that relax vessels. The patient, a man in his fifties, had months of chest pain and fainting, with heart traces that spiked and settled back. Scans showed clean arteries and a sound heart build.

Care piled up over his visits, with vessel relaxers raised step by step and a heart rhythm loop placed under his skin. One drug had to stop after it caused a long pause in his heart beat. Days after a last visit with a clean trace, he had a cardiac arrest at home from a wild rhythm. He died in intensive care. The case marks a rare form that shrugs off standard drugs.
pmc-12812679:
A disturbed sense of self is thought to sit at the core of psychosis, and cannabis may interact with it early in the illness. Valerio Ricci and co-authors review studies on self-disturbance, dissociation, and cannabis in first-episode psychosis. The review, published in 2025 per the text head, gathered 22 studies covering 3,847 participants.

Cannabis users, above all daily users of high-potency products, reported far more dissociative experiences than non-users, with score gaps past the clinical threshold. Daily high-potency use came with about three times the odds of significant dissociation and with more severe odd self-experiences. The authors discuss brain mechanisms involving the endocannabinoid system. They call for early screening of self-disorders in young patients who use cannabis.
pmc-12815279:
Hadi Daneshmandi and co-authors measure strain on car mechanics in a 2025 workplace study. Repair work loads the lower back, shoulders, and hands day after day. The team surveyed 157 independent mechanics in workshops in Shiraz, Iran. Four standard tools scored discomfort and the risk of lifting, shoulder work, and hand tasks.

Scores were set against each other with age and body size held steady. Real world measurement matters here, since lab tasks rarely match the awkward postures of a repair pit. The results show where the cumulative load bites hardest. Shop owners and safety officers can use such maps to target lifts, tools, or task rotation where strain peaks.
pmc-12815979:
Some vaccines leave the innate immune system on higher alert for months, an effect called trained immunity. Kunc and six co-authors ask whether the two main mRNA COVID-19 vaccines do this. They followed people given either the Moderna or the Pfizer vaccine in Denmark, testing blood before vaccination and at four points over six months. The tests measured immune cell mixes and the signals the cells released when provoked.

Cell mixes barely differed between the groups, but the signal patterns did. In the Pfizer group, two key alarm signals stayed flat after later provocation. In the Moderna group, those signals rose and stayed higher for up to 180 days, and a cell-recruiting signal rose too while falling in the other group. The authors say the Moderna vaccine leaves marks consistent with trained immunity, which could shape future vaccine design.
pmc-12816179:
Peng Guo, Mengqi Xiang, Jing Chen, and Huachuan Zhang offer a two thousand twenty-five study merging single-cell and bulk gene data to find prognostic genes in lung cancer. Lung cancer still kills more people than any other cancer. Single-cell maps reveal tumour neighbourhoods, but linking cell states to survival needs bulk cohorts.

Tumours and normal lung yielded tens of thousands of cells across a dozen populations. Malignant programs were projected into large patient cohorts to build a risk model. Validation used two external datasets. One gene, FAM189A2, stood out; lab tests confirmed its functional role in lung cancer cells, nominating it for prognostic use.
pmc-12816279:
Rachel Kowert, Suraj Lakhani, and Constance Steinkuehler open a research topic on extremism in games in a 2026 editorial. Hate groups now use game worlds and their side spaces to spread their word, lure new blood, plan harm, raise funds, and build a base. What was once a fringe fear is now a core care for labs, states, and firms. The topic set gathers fresh field proof on that use.

Four themes sort the set. First, how much hate content sits in game spaces and in what forms. A big survey in the set found over half of players had seen or faced hate speech in games. Next come rule and watch gaps on the platforms. Then come ways to harden player groups, and last, youth risk. The editors frame the set as a base for sound acts by states and firms.
pmc-12816379:
Huang and colleagues published a pig vaccine study against an atypical porcine pestivirus. The virus causes congenital tremor in newborn piglets. Outbreaks have cost the pig industry heavily around the world. The team built the viral E2 protein in common lab bacteria. They mixed that protein with three different adjuvants, which are helpers that boost immune response. Piglets then received the vaccines and later faced a virus challenge.

Vaccinated piglets made clear antibody responses to the virus. Two adjuvant mixes gave much higher antibody levels than the third. The best mix also protected pigs against infection after challenge. Organs of vaccinated pigs looked normal under the microscope. Controls showed marked damage instead. The authors present the vaccine as a strong candidate for further work.
pmc-12816979:
Cancer care has turned, in two short decades, from doubt that guard cells could fight growths to drugs that free them to do so. Mohanraj Sadasivam, Nethaji Muniraj, and Chellappagounder Thangavel open a set of works on that turn in a 2026 piece. Yet many patients still gain no long win, they grant, since growths shift, hide, and hush the guard host.

The works in the set chase two front lines: aim at two marks at once, and shape the growth's own ground. One work treats a drug that blocks both blood feed and a guard brake in one build. Cell gifts, germ foes, and made shots join the ranks. The three frame the set as a map of where the fight turns next.
pmc-12819379:
Yura Moon and co-authors probed this 2025 route by which food bacteria may spread drug resistance. A Staphylococcus strain from salty fermented food carries plasmids with a lincomycin resistance gene and transfer machinery. Earlier work showed it passes that gene to kin when the drug is present. The team asked which genes switch on during that stress.

RNA sequencing after drug exposure found more changed genes at two hours than at four. Transport and metabolism categories dominated the response. Stress regulators and iron-handling genes switched on strongly. The genome also held a competence system and a DNA-moving enzyme that could ferry genes between cells. Short-term checks with a second method filled in fast dynamics. The study names suspect transporters for follow-up tests.
pmc-12820079:
Yihan He and co-authors build a coin-flipping computer in 2025 that docks drug molecules in hardware. Docking searches how a drug might grip its target, a space too vast for easy brute force, while quantum machines still strain at scale. Their machine computes with chance itself, using memory chips whose resistance wobbles by design.

The chips pair with in-memory computing so answers form where data sits, easing the traffic jam of older chance machines, they report. A bell-curve random source built into the design sets each bit's lean, with couplings written into the chip grid. The prototype solved a forty-two-node docking puzzle for an antibiotic target in germ-proof bacteria. Chance, harnessed, becomes a search engine.
pmc-12820179:
Xiaofeng Liao and co-authors fuse design, scanning, and immersive tools into one coordination system for building projects in this 2025 paper. Construction teams juggle drawings, models, and site scans that rarely agree. That isolation breeds clashes found late, when fixes cost most.

Their framework links CAD drawings and building information models directly. A fast scanning method rebuilds the real site as a splatted 3D scene. Immersive views let teams walk the merged model together. An international standard governs how the shared data are managed. A hospital project, dense with structure and services, served as the test case. Whole-life coordination is the goal, from first sketch to handover.
pmc-12820379:
Johann Roske and co-authors report, in a 2025 structural biology study, how the machinery that copies genes can link to the machinery that starts building proteins in bacteria. In many bacteria these two steps are physically coupled, which affects how fast genes are read. The team captured that link using cryo-electron imaging.

They show a paused copying machine, still near the gene's start, joined to the small ribosome part that starts protein building. The message strand sits inside this early complex yet can still be reached by small guide strands and cut by a cleanup crew. The finding suggests cells can tag and shut down a message very early, before full protein building begins.
pmc-12821879:
Hui Xie, Jianfang Zhang, Qing Li, and Tao Tan build, in 2025 work, a no-cut way to call a breast tumour's growth mark from sound scans. That mark steers care, yet is now read from cut tissue. Their path maps the tumour, splits it into zones by like traits, and mines each zone for signs.

Five hundred forty-one patients from two centres fed the build. Zone, whole-tumour, lab, and deep-net signs were winnowed and cast into one model. On held-out cases it scored best of all forms tried, with sound calipers and clear clinic worth. Zone traits — how a tumour's parts differ — carried real weight. The team backs scans as a care guide.
pmc-12822079:
Dongchu Wang, Aixiang Wang, Xiangwu Ding, and Rong Zhou ran a trial in two thousand twenty-five on a gentler way to do colonoscopy without sedation. Pushing a scope to the start of the colon can be slow and painful. They joined two aids: water exchange in the left colon and a small cap on the scope tip, and compared the pair with cap help alone.

Two hundred patients took part at a centre in Wuhan, China. The paired method cut the median insertion time from seven minutes to five. Left colon pain was lower, and more patients said they would repeat the test. Polyp finding and bowel cleaning scores were about the same in both groups.
pmc-12822279:
Zoia Sharif and seven colleagues published a 2025 study of anxiety and depression among breast cancer patients in Pakistan. A cancer diagnosis and its treatment can be profoundly traumatic, and psychological suffering is often greatest where resources are limited. The study was conducted in Abbottabad.

Ninety-six women receiving breast cancer treatment between October 2023 and May 2024 were assessed at a diagnostic center clinic and a teaching hospital. The researchers measured how common anxiety and depression were in this group. They also identified predictors, the social and clinical factors associated with worse mental health. Such evidence from low- and middle-income countries is scarce and can guide the design of affordable psychological support within cancer care.
pmc-12822879:
Sonia Angilletta and five co-authors present a 2025 study of gym teachers in Italian middle and high schools. Teachers who feel well and sure of their skills tend to run better lessons. Pupils also rate such teachers more highly and join in more.

The team surveyed 267 physical education teachers online, 193 women and 74 men. They asked about mental well being, weekly activity levels, and how much the teachers value their subject. The study then compared the answers between middle school and high school staff. The aim was to see whether the two groups differ in health, habits, and views of the worth of gym class.
pmc-12823579:
Rossella La Grotta and co-authors study three circulating microRNAs as markers of aging in work from 2025. The small molecules are linked to inflammation, tissue remodeling, and metabolic trouble.

In adults aged sixty-five to over one hundred, all three rose with age. Two were higher in frail people, and one linked to weaker grip strength. Others tied to kidney markers, daily function, and illness burden. Computer analysis pointed to shared pathways in inflammation and scarring. The authors propose the trio as blood markers that reflect the biology of aging and decline.
pmc-12825279:
Zhongfu Guo and co-authors follow the growth and brain development of very preterm babies to six months of corrected age, in a study from 2025. Babies born before thirty-two weeks face high risks on both fronts. The team reviewed 116 such infants from one hospital in Tianjin. Movement checks came at one month, with fuller checks at three and six months.

Odd movement patterns were common at one month but rare by three. The share of babies with low development scores fell from about seventy percent at three months to about forty-three at six. Earlier birth and twin status raised the risk of low scores. Bleeding in the brain and a lack of early therapy also mattered. The authors urge tight follow-up and early help for these babies. Both steps can cut later harm.
pmc-12827079:
Sofya Ilmer and Parissa Salemi tell of a child's heart block that eased with vitamin D in a 2025 paper, per its head. The boy had Graves disease, an overactive thyroid state. A mild heart block grew to a full block a month before his thyroid name was set.

Thyroid drugs fixed his hormone levels, yet the full block stayed. His heart team urged a pacemaker, but the family chose watchful waits. Daily vitamin D began on his mother's own reading of past work. Night slow beats cleared in three months, and tests showed the block eased to mild. The lone case hints, but does not prove, a vitamin link.
pmc-12827179:
Roberta Grasso and co-authors test in 2025 remote follow-up care for headache patients at a clinic in Foggia, Italy. Remote care is growing in brain medicine, yet its fit for headache follow-up was little studied. Satisfaction, ease of use, and felt benefit all need proof before wider rollout.

Forty five patients with primary headache each held two video visits, four to eight weeks apart. All finished both visits, and satisfaction scored above nine of ten each time. Ease of use rose from the first visit to the second. More than eighty five percent told of time and cost savings, and will to repeat ran high.
pmc-12827279:
Naďa Majerníková and co-authors link a form of cell death to Parkinson's disease in a 2025 study. The death process, ferroptosis, runs on iron and damages cell fats, and blocking it has been floated as a way to protect neurons.

The team checked six ferroptosis-related markers in brain tissue from ten Parkinson's patients and eleven matched controls. Even in healthy brains, the markers varied across parts of the substantia nigra, the region Parkinson's strikes. Where alpha-synuclein clumps grew, iron storage and export proteins fell, a sign of iron handling gone wrong. Cell tests then showed that blocking ferroptosis saves neurons from alpha-synuclein harm, backing it as a treatment target.
pmc-12827479:
Zhuoqing Xu and co-authors study white blood cells in bowel cancer spread in a 2025 paper. Spread to the liver is a main cause of death in colorectal cancer. Neutrophils, the most common white cells, split into subgroups that can push or block that spread.

Signals that switch these cells on steer which subgroup forms, the title reports. Mapping those signals may explain why some tumors seed the liver fast while others stall. The work points to drug targets in the switch paths themselves. Tuning the signal, rather than wiping out the cells, could tilt the balance against spread.
pmc-12828979:
Sanayaa Bhonsle and co-authors measured this 2025 shortfall of vitamin D in children in western India. The deficiency is common in Indian children despite plentiful sunshine. Diet, habits, and little skin exposure all play a part. The team enrolled children aged nine months to twelve years at a hospital clinic in Jamnagar, most of them healthy visitors or siblings.

Blood tests on 277 children found about thirty-five percent deficient and forty-three percent more below the ideal range. Only about twenty-two percent had enough. Surprisingly, vitamin status did not track with age group. The study, run from 2023 to 2025, also recorded sun habits, sunscreen use, and foods like milk and eggs. The authors press for stronger prevention in a sunny country where the gap persists.
pmc-12830579:
Jinghui Ma and co-authors rebuild, in a 2025 study, a missing stretch of ground-level ozone records for central and eastern China. Ozone harms lungs and ecosystems, yet records before 2013 are scarce in that region. The team filled the gap from 1980 to 2012.

A machine learning model trained on many data sources produced daily peak ozone values on a fine grid. Checks against later real observations showed strong agreement across most grids. The rebuilt record shows a regional mean with a clear north-south gradient. Long records like this let scientists judge whether recent clean-air gains reverse older trends. They also support health studies that need exposure history, not just today's air.
pmc-12830779:
Meltem Karahan and four co-authors test tooth space holders made with digital tools. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such holders keep a gap open for a child's later tooth. They ask how the choice of stuff and glue affects tooth drift and stress, using a computer method that splits a model into tiny parts.

They build many models from five band-and-loop materials and three glues, then push down with a set force. One hard ceramic moves least and loads the tooth least. A soft plastic moves most. Among glues, the one with the lowest stiffness lets the tooth drift most. Long-term clinic tests are still needed, they note.
pmc-12831279:
Harry Dawson and co-authors verified how alike the pig, mouse, and human genomes truly are in a 2025 study. Pigs are a major model for human biology, but their genome build is unfinished, and gaps can mislead research. The team hand-assembled clean libraries of pig RNA and protein sequences, each free of duplicates.

With those libraries, they assessed the current pig genome assembly and compared gene sets across the three species. Manual care pays here: automated builds can merge or split genes wrongly. The verified comparisons show where the pig matches humans better than the mouse does, and where it does not. Biomedical teams choosing animal models get a firmer genetic basis for that choice.
pmc-12834179:
Malak Chahid and co-authors report a hard case of jaw cancer treated with radiation after reconstruction with a custom titanium implant. Such implants, printed in three dimensions, restore shape and function well. But metal in the scan can distort images and change how radiation dose spreads.

Their older patient had advanced cancer of the jaw and received the implant, then planned radiation. The team used an arc-based delivery method and hand-corrected the artifacts in the planning system to protect nearby healthy tissue. Surgeons, imaging staff, and radiation specialists worked together throughout. The authors stress tailored planning and more research on protocols for implants in radiation care.
pmc-12834879:
Jinlin Cai and co-authors review the immune landscape of osteosarcoma, a bone cancer of the young, in a 2025 paper. Surgery and chemotherapy have improved care, yet patients whose cancer spreads still face poor odds. The tissue around the tumor, packed with immune and support cells, shapes how the cancer grows and resists treatment. Suppressive cells dominate that space, while killer T cells often wear out.

New single-cell and spatial studies map that landscape in fine detail. The maps link cell layout to prognosis and to treatment response. Standard immune therapies, such as checkpoint drugs and engineered T cells, have so far worked weakly here. The review weighs why, then surveys fresh tactics to break immune resistance. The authors aim the synthesis at translational teams designing the next trials.
pmc-12834979:
Chen-Ping Liu and co-authors stack models twice to forecast building costs in a 2025 paper. Construction cost prediction steers bids, budgets, and loans, yet projects defy simple formulas. Dozens of factors interact in nonlinear ways that shift as work proceeds.

Their DSCostPred method first sorts variables by function to stop cross-talk. Different algorithms then learn each variable group's role separately. A second stacking layer blends the model outputs into one forecast. Variable stacking plus model stacking gives the method its double name. Sharper early estimates could cut the overruns that plague building projects.
pmc-12835179:
Junbo Jung and co-authors build a fast light meter to watch cooling films switch in real time, in a 2025 study. Films that cool by radiating heat can now flip their clarity when wetted, yet slow bench tools miss the flip as it happens. Their system reads light passage in a third of a second.

Checks against a standard bench meter showed errors under three percent. Repeat runs stayed tight as well. With the meter, the team varied solvent thickness and match to find what sets flip speed. A vacuum step that pulls fluid in lifted the wet state clarity past eighty-five percent within five minutes. The tool aids design of smart cooling skins.
pmc-12837079:
Kai Tang and co-authors describe a rare spine infection caused by bacteria that shun oxygen. Among 373 cases of pyogenic spondylodiscitis at their hospital over six years, only 23 came from anaerobic germs. All 23 patients had back pain lasting over a month. Few had fever. The lower spine bore most cases.

Standard cultures found the culprit in under half the patients. Gene sequencing found it in 19 of 20 tested. One coccus and one bacillus led the list. Antibiotics alone cured as often as surgery did. One patient relapsed after a short drug course. The authors warn this infection hides well and urge wider use of sequencing when cultures stay silent.
pmc-12837179:
Tzu-Ying Lee and co-authors published this eye surgery study in 2025. An epiretinal membrane is a thin film that wrinkles the retina and blurs vision. Surgery peels it away, but results vary, and patients who carry a lens implant form a distinct group. The team reviewed sixty-one such eyes treated with vitrectomy and double peeling. Retina scans before and after surgery supplied a checklist of features to test as predictors.

Vision and central retinal thickness improved significantly over six months of follow-up. Two scan features, a cotton ball sign and disorganized inner layers, cleared after surgery. The predictors of disappointment stood out. Eyes starting with a split, sponge-like fovea or with tiny cystic swelling gained less vision. Eyes with better vision before surgery gained the most, favoring earlier intervention. The authors give surgeons a short list of scan signs for counseling patients.
pmc-12838479:
William Banks and co-authors compare three tracer agents for measuring leaks in the blood brain barrier in a 2025 study. Human scans use one agent, animal work uses others, and the field seldom checked them against each other. The team tested all three in human cell layers and in mice with calm or inflamed barriers.

In cell layers, two agents crossed at near the same rate, while the protein agent crossed ten to twenty times more slowly. In mice the order held: a sugar tracer crossed most, then the scan agent, then the protein. Under mild swelling, the sugar tracer showed leaks most readily. The authors map how to translate between studies.
pmc-12838679:
Cyprus had no validated quick test for language loss after stroke, so Marina Charalambous and co-authors built one and put it through its paces in a 2025 study. Their ten-part screen was given to ninety-nine people: stroke survivors with aphasia, stroke survivors without it, and healthy volunteers. Scores repeated almost identically across days and raters.

The screen agreed strongly with a standard Greek aphasia battery, and a cutoff score separated the groups with high accuracy. It needs little equipment and scores easily at the bedside. The authors offer it as the island's first standardized tool for Greek-speaking patients.
pmc-12839179:
Jania Williams and co-authors tune a passive ankle exoskeleton in simulation to find the spring stiffness and timing that save the most walking energy, in a case study from 2025. The device stores and returns energy at the ankle with a spring clutch. The team built it into the OpenSim body model, using motion data from one healthy man walking in his own shoes.

They ran every pairing of 25 stiffness values and ten trigger timings. The biggest saving, a 2.67 percent cut in energy cost, came at about 15 percent of stance with the softest spring, near 5.5 kilonewtons per meter. Energy cost curved smoothly with stiffness, and the soft end won. The authors say the model predicts good settings well enough to personalize such devices.
pmc-12839979: Harsanyi and four co-authors wrote a short comment from twenty twenty-five on a bladder cancer study by Hasan and colleagues. The original study compared three tissue markers, p16, p53, and Ki-67, between bladder cancers that invade muscle and those that do not. The comment engages with those clinical and pathology findings. Such letters let other specialists question methods or add context after publication, a normal part of how medical evidence is refined.
pmc-12842679:
Mihai Grigore and co-authors review how diabetes breeds atrial fibrillation, and how sugar drugs bend that risk. Their 2025 narrative review pools studies on shared paths and outcome trials of the main drug families. Diabetes scars the atria through fibrosis, faulty conduction, nerve imbalance, swelling, sugar swings, oxygen stress, and fat growth around the heart. That soil lets the chaotic rhythm start and stick.

Drug effects split by family. Two older and newer staples leaned kind or neutral for rhythm risk. Incretin drugs brought heart gains with mixed rhythm reads. The authors call for rhythm-aware drug picks in diabetes care.
pmc-12844179:
Xiaokang Dai and co-authors show that a helpful bacterium both fights root rot in a Chinese fir and repairs the soil community around its roots, in a 2025 study. Root rot from the fungus Fusarium solani devastates this timber tree, partly by unbalancing the microbes near its roots. The team treated trees with the bacterium Bacillus mojavensis, strain dxk33, and tracked disease, growth, and soil life.

Treatment cut the disease index by about 72 percent and boosted plant growth. Soil nutrients rose, and so did the activity of enzymes that cycle carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus. Gene surveys showed the bacterium partly reversed the microbe imbalance the fungus caused. Helpful groups such as Pseudomonas grew, while harmful fungi shrank. The authors describe a layered defense: direct attack plus community repair.
pmc-12845179:
Weronika Goraj and five co-authors published a review in twenty twenty-five on resistance to fosfomycin, an older antibiotic now precious because it still works when others fail. Farming's role in spreading that resistance is the focus. The review gathers how use in food animals seeds the environment with resistant microbes and their genes.

Resistance runs through gene families named fosA, fosB, and fosC, with new determinants still appearing. Resistant bacteria have been found in pigs, chickens, pigeons, cattle, and even vegetables. Manure spreading, soil nitrogen, microplastics, metals, and pesticides all shape how the genes persist in fields. Warming climate may widen the spread. The authors call the evidence base still thin and urgent to grow.
pmc-12847879:
George Ioannou and co-authors measure how well updated COVID-19 vaccines worked over time in a 2025 study. The shots targeted the KP.2 variant for the 2024-2025 season. Fresh long-term estimates help officials shape vaccine advice for the next round.

The study matched over half a million vaccinated veterans with similar unvaccinated peers. Follow-up averaged about six months into spring 2025. Protection against simple infection was low, and protection against emergency visits and hospital stays was modest. Protection against death was much higher, above sixty percent. Protection faded as months passed. The target trial design mimics a randomized study using routine health system records.
pmc-12847979:
Akkshita Trivedi, Sandeep Khanna, Santanu Chaudhury, and Gaurav Harit teach a model to grasp the logic links inside documents. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Current tools cope poorly with complex layouts and miss deep links among text, figures, and tables on a page.

Their frame, D-REEL, first picks candidate parts from each article, then turns each into a dense vector. By comparing vectors, it scores how strongly two fields connect, no matter where they sit on the page. It blends layout facts with domain rules for firm extraction. A new score, SSC, gauges such links without fixed spots. On public sets, gains show in both link accuracy and extraction.
pmc-12848079:
Klaudia Strucinska and a large team study a protein called Fis1 and its role in how nerve cells branch. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Mitochondria, the cell's power units, take unlike shapes in the two arms of a nerve cell. A known factor keeps them small in one arm, but the other arm was a puzzle.

They lower Fis1 in lab and live nerve cells. To their surprise, power units in the dendrite arm shrink, while those in the axon arm stay the same. The units also move and change more. Their power charge and calcium uptake fall. At rest, calcium in the cell rises, and the dendrite tree grows more branches but fewer spines.
pmc-12849179:
YuanLin He and co-authors test a blood protein in 2025 as a clue to lung nodule nature. Finding whether a lung spot is cancer or harmless usually needs surgery or biopsy. The team reviews 540 patients who had nodules removed or sampled over nine years, comparing protein levels between groups.

The protein, cystatin C, runs higher in the 443 cancer patients than in the 97 with benign nodules, though levels do not separate cancer subtypes. A cutoff value rules out benign nodules with moderate sensitivity and specificity, both in the mid-sixties percent. The authors suggest the cheap blood test may help triage nodules before invasive steps.
pmc-12849279:
Fen-Ying Lu and thirteen colleagues built a new screening system for stomach cancer that combines a risk score with blood markers. The existing New Gastric Cancer Screening Score is widely used but imperfect. The twenty twenty-five prospective study enrolled 106 stomach cancer patients and 143 patients with non-cancer stomach conditions. Participants were split into discovery and validation sets. Everyone received the standard score plus testing for eight serum markers.

Three traditional tumor markers were combined with five newer ones linked to gastric cancer. Cancer and non-cancer patients showed distinct score patterns in the discovery set. The combined system was then checked in the validation set for robustness. Better screening matters because early stomach cancer is far more treatable. A blood-and-score test could help clinics decide who needs endoscopy first.
pmc-12849379:
Hongyu Liu and co-authors compare the microbes in gum fluid from people with gum disease, implant disease, and healthy mouths, in a 2025 study. Both diseases inflame the tissues holding teeth or implants, but whether their microbial mixes differ was unclear. Fluid samples from nine participants were profiled by gene sequencing.

The two disease groups carried richer microbe mixes than healthy controls, and the implant group's mix looked closer to the gum disease group than to health. Certain genera stood out in the implant group, and its microbes were predicted to focus on energy and building-block chemistry. The authors name candidate markers for implant disease, while noting that bigger studies must confirm them.
pmc-12849579:
Osval Montesinos-López and co-authors build a selection index that picks top breeding candidates without letting them be close kin. Their 2025 paper works in plant genomic selection, where many traits count at once. Picking only on merit drains diversity, which breeding cannot afford to lose.

Their method poses the pick as a binary quadratic program. Trait scores, weighted by value, compete against pairwise relatedness from the genome matrix. Five real datasets tested the approach against a linear rival. The gain-per-relatedness score improved by at least half in every set. The authors offer the tool for durable multi-trait breeding programmes.
pmc-12849679:
Nai Wu and co-authors review a dozen cases of a misplaced developmental cyst found in the belly, in a 2025 paper. Bronchogenic cysts normally form near the airways; in the abdomen they are rare and often mistaken for something else, since they cause vague symptoms or none. The team gathered twelve confirmed cases from their hospital over nine years and compared them with reports in the literature.

Most patients were middle-aged, two thirds had symptoms, and belly pain near the stomach was the most common. Nearly all cysts sat in the upper back part of the abdomen, and almost every case was misdiagnosed before surgery. Nine patients had keyhole removal and three open surgery. Tissue checks confirmed every case, and one cyst regrew after a lesser procedure.
pmc-12852779:
Yang Yang and co-authors design a neural network that traces the fine blood vessels of the retina, in this 2025 paper. Outlining those vessels aids eye diagnosis, but thin branches, lesions, and wide scale swings trip up older models. Their gated U-Net adds three parts: a hub that links features across layers, a gated block that sharpens focus in dim or damaged areas, and an attention module for fine detail.

On three public eye-image datasets, the model set new marks, with top scores on two of them. It held up especially well in low-contrast regions and tangled vessel beds.
pmc-12853579:
Sulaiman Mouselli, Lilas Allahham, and Sanaa Al Ahdab grade the quality of health insurance services in Syria through their customers' eyes, in work from 2025. Syria rebuilt insurance schemes after a devastating war, hoping to cut state health spending and widen access. Whether the service actually satisfies users was unmeasured.

An online survey reached two hundred eighty-four residents who had used health insurance. The SERVQUAL frame scored five sides of service: attitude, safety, efficiency, reliability with trust, and responsiveness. Gaps between what users expect and what they get mark where reform should start. The study gives insurers a customer based baseline in a hard setting.
pmc-12853979:
Youssef Lahmouz and co-authors report a case where a subarachnoid hemorrhage mimicked acute coronary syndrome in an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Their 2025 case report calls this a diagnostic challenge with catastrophic results.

A 42-year-old woman with no cardiovascular risk factors had a sudden cardiac arrest during exercise. Her ECG and troponin levels pointed to a heart attack, but coronary angiography was normal. A head CT then revealed a massive subarachnoid hemorrhage. Despite supportive care, she died on the fifth day from cerebral edema. Bleeding in the brain can cause ECG changes and biomarker rises that send care down the wrong path.
pmc-12855879:
Liujing Chen and co-authors find that lymph vessels talk to tendon stem cells and drive tendon repair, in work from twenty twenty-five. Tendons heal slowly because they get little blood flow. The role of lymph vessels in that repair had been largely missed. Gene checks in young and adult mice flag lymph vessels as key niche parts. Clear-tissue imaging in tagged mice shows lymph signals switch on after injury.

Mice that lack Reelin, in whole or in lymph cells only, heal tendons poorly. A slow-release Reelin carrier built from porous silica beads lifts repair. Gains show in both mice and rabbits in the tests. The work points to lymph signals as a lever for tissue repair.
pmc-12859879:
Chen Guo and co-authors report a 2025 real-world study of heart attack patients. All patients took a class of sugar-lowering drugs called SGLT2 inhibitors. Whether outcomes differ by sex for this drug after heart attack was unclear. The study held 310 patients, 244 men and 66 women. Heart strain markers and pumping strength were the main outcomes. Events such as repeat heart or brain harm were tracked as well.

Lab measures covered blood fats, sugar control, and kidney function. Men and women began with distinct clinical profiles, so raw gaps need care. The title states the headline finding: outcomes were consistent across sexes. Heart teams get real-world support for using the drug in both women and men after heart attack. pmc-12859979:

India Elliott, Shailesh Dalvi, King Leong, and Stephanie Wong report a man whose underactive parathyroid glands calcified his brain and strained his heart, in a 2025 case report. pmc-12861679:

pmc-12864979:

pmc-12865479:

pmc-12865979:

pmc-12866479:

pmc-12876879:

pmc-12882479:
Alyona Mazhnaya, Anna Meteliuk, Sergiy Bogdanov, and Emma McGinty study mental health care in wartime Ukraine in this 2025 paper. pmc-12883779:

pmc-12885179:
Nader Pazyar and colleagues compared two add-on treatments for dark circles under the eyes. Their 2025 trial joins microneedling with either tranexamic acid or vitamin C. pmc-12895479:
Melaku Tadege Engidaw and co-authors measure how many toddlers across South and Southeast Asia eat iron-rich foods, and what predicts those who do. Older toddlers and exclusively breastfed infants fared better, along with children of more educated or wealthier mothers. The multilevel results show where feeding programs and family support could close a stubborn nutrition gap.
pmc-12904479:
Cintia Mussi Milani and four co-authors published a 2025 case report of jaw bone death in a patient with a rare bone disorder. The authors stress taking a full drug history before any mouth surgery in such patients.
pmc-12910479:
Sarah Turner and co-authors studied breastfeeding, family income, and child behavior in work published in 2025. Children in low-income homes are more likely to develop behavior problems. Breastfeeding has been linked to better mental health through childhood, so it might soften that link.

The two factors also interacted: breastfeeding changed how strongly low status tracked with behavior scores.
pmc-12913379:
Richard Giadone and eight co-authors built a screening platform to study spinal muscular atrophy in lab-grown nerve cells, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. The disease kills motor neurons, and today's drugs help most when given very early. Gene readings from each dose built more than four thousand profiles, showing which drugs push the sick cells' gene patterns toward or away from health. The data set is open for other labs to search. The authors say the method could speed drug hunts for this disease and for other nerve diseases where patient genes differ widely.
pmc-12913579:
Huijie Gao and five co-authors swap rats' drinking water for cola for eight weeks and read the fall-out. Their paper is dated two thousand twenty-six in the pack, while its text head says the year before. Sugared drinks are a known health load, but what full swap does to the gut and body was not known. pmc-12929479:
Ahmad Yusuf Abubakar and co-authors characterize in this 2025 study a fungus that spots sugarcane leaves only through wounds. Nigrospora oryzae turns up in cane fields more often, yet its habits and drug weaknesses were unclear. pmc-12935979:
Huiping Guo and co-authors improve a fast image model to spot diseases on grape leaves, in work dated 2026 in the journal record. Growers need quick, light tools that can name several leaf diseases, not just one. Large models are hard to run in the field.

pmc-12950879:
Ivo Julião and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a lean program helping two African hospitals start their own cancer units instead of sending every patient to the capital. Cancer is rising fastest where care is weakest and most centralized. In Lubango, Angola, the team helped launch an oncology unit and a research group. In Mindelo, Cape Verde, it backed a service restructure and a breast cancer working group. pmc-12952379:

Gut medication use was tallied by drug and condition. Diagnostic and treatment procedures were counted as well. The multisystem view shows how wide gut burden runs. pmc-12979179:
Jian Feng and co-authors study how a Chinese fir tree copes with drought based on where its seed came from. Their 2025 paper uses satellite data to grade past drought in three source regions. pmc-13082479:
Shashwat Vyas and Hemant Sharma report a young woman whose swallowed hair caused a rare telescoping of her own intestine. Their 2026 case concerns Rapunzel syndrome, in which a hairball in the stomach trails a tail into the small bowel. Fewer than ten reported cases worldwide add bowel intussusception on top of that rarity.

Surgery removed the bezoar through the stomach, and the folded bowel righted itself. She went home on day seven, with psychiatric review to follow for the hair-eating root.
pmc-13086579:
Artificial intelligence is sold as a climate savior, and Sharon Stein argues in a 2026 comment that the sales pitch repeats the thinking that caused the crisis. It is a short intervention with a long demand: change the relations, not just the models.
pmc-13091979:

pmc-13117379:

For a single patient, though, the spread runs forty points wide in both directions, and the cuff overreads low pressures while underreading high ones. The authors judge it fine for group studies, not yet for steering one patient's care.
pmc-13125879:

Kidney function, tissue damage, gut microbes, and gene activity were all measured.

pmc-13126579:
Sebukoto, Urio, and Ngasala study malaria knowledge and net use in Tanzanian school children, in work from twenty twenty-five. School children face high malaria risk but are often missed by control programs, which focus on pregnant women and children under five.

pmc-13129379:
Yu-Lei Wang and eight co-authors fed farm chickens plant leftovers in a 2026 trial. The leftovers came from distilling the fruit of a Sichuan pepper kin plant with hot water, in a zero waste process. pmc-13132979:

pmc-13134979:

pmc-13139279:

pmc-13141679:

pmc-13141779:

pmc-13142779:

pmc-13144479:

pmc-13144879:

pmc-13144979:

pmc-13145079:

pmc-13145179:

pmc-13145379:

pmc-13145479:

pmc-13145579:

pmc-13145679:

pmc-13145779:

pmc-13145979:

pmc-13146179:

pmc-13146379:

pmc-13146579:

pmc-13146679:

pmc-13147779:

pmc-13151879:

pmc-13152879:

pmc-13152979:

pmc-13155879:

pmc-13156079:

pmc-13156979:

pmc-13157079:

pmc-13157179:

pmc-13157479:

pmc-13157779:

pmc-13159179:

pmc-13159579:

pmc-13163279:

pmc-13164379:

pmc-13181079:

pmc-13184079:

pmc-13187579:

pmc-13189079:

pmc-13189979:

pmc-13191079:

pmc-13191179:

pmc-13193579:

pmc-13193779:

pmc-13194279:
Jip van Elst and seven co-authors checked in two thousand twenty-six whether taste and smell problems linger years after immune therapy for cancer. pmc-13194579:
Wenjing Jiang and co-authors model what drives hand hygiene among hospital staff in China, in work from 2026. Hospital infections threaten patients worldwide, and hand hygiene is the first defense. Staff often know the rules yet skip the act, a stubborn know-do gap.

Theory-based design beats generic reminders, the authors argue.
pmc-13195479:

pmc-13195779:

pmc-13196479:

pmc-13196579:
Depression that first appears late in life may be an early sign of silent brain vessel disease rather than a stand-alone illness. Calypso Mitkani and co-authors test that idea in patients who suffered a first small deep stroke, in a 2026 study.

pmc-13196779:

pmc-13196979:

pmc-13197379:

pmc-13197479:

pmc-13198179:

pmc-13198479:

pmc-13199179:
Mohammad Al-Wardat and colleagues surveyed rehab specialists on remote therapy in Jordan in a 2026 study. pmc-13199579:

pmc-13199779:

pmc-13199879:

pmc-13200279:

pmc-13201279:

pmc-13201379:

pmc-13202279:

pmc-13202679:

pmc-13202979:

pmc-13203879:

pmc-13203979:

pmc-13204579:

pmc-13205179:

pmc-13205579:

pmc-13205779:

pmc-13205979:

pmc-13206279:

pmc-13207279:

pmc-13207379:

pmc-13207579:

pmc-13208179:

pmc-13208479:

pmc-13209179:

pmc-13209479:

pmc-13209979:

pmc-13210079:
