The review argues that gut microbes are the missing middle step. Microbes convert polyphenols into smaller compounds that enter the blood more easily. Those products then block the alarm system at several points at once. Evidence from cell, animal, and human studies supports the chain. The authors frame the three parts as one self-balancing network linking diet to inflammation.
pmc-13210179:
Concentrated pills in Chinese medicine often dissolve too slowly, which can blunt their effect. Xiaojun Wang and co-authors, in 2026, studied how the drying step shapes that slow release. They used a classic pill formula as their test case and compared plain hot-air drying with a mixed method that adds microwaves.

The mixed method left more and larger pores inside the pills, and water soaked in faster as a result, so the pills broke down sooner. Checks on the active compounds showed no real change between the two methods. The team measured water movement and inner structure with several lab tools to back the claim. Their point is practical: tuning the drying step can fix slow pills without changing the medicine itself.
pmc-13210579:
Linzhi Zuo, Kaixiong Xing, Kai Wu and colleagues traced how rainfall shapes nutrient cycling in Casuarina forests on Hainan Island in 2026. These coastal shelterbelt trees sit on poor soils, and soil microbes run the carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles that feed them.

Microbial diversity peaked at middle rainfall levels and was richer in topsoil than below. Three bacterial groups, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria and Acidobacteria, carried most of the key cycling genes. Communities adjusted to rainfall by switching on rain-sensitive genes, and available phosphorus was the main driver of the response. The study shows rainfall steers the cycles both directly, through soil water, and indirectly, by reshaping the microbial workforce.
pmc-13210679:
Cars talk over a shared bus wire, and an attacker who slips in fake frames can fool safety systems. Mohammad Khalaf Khreasat and Gabriel Villarrubia González test which data traits catch such attacks in a 2026 study. They build a light detector from counts, shift patterns, and graph shapes in the traffic stream.

Plain count traits failed when the attack type changed. Traits based on how message codes follow each other held up across attacks on one car type, with near-perfect scores. Graph traits swung with the attack tested. A blend of all traits gave the best working package. Moves to a new data set worked only when attacks broke the stream's rhythm.
pmc-13210979:
Xiaoyu Zhang and co-authors study a defense regulator gene in peanut in a 2026 paper. Peanut crops face steady disease pressure, and strong built-in defenses cut future costs. NPR proteins help switch on plant immunity. The team characterize the peanut NPR4B member and its partners.

The protein sits in the cell nucleus. Plants of a model species that overproduce it resist a major fungal pathogen better. They also tolerate cold better, per measured tests. A partner protein of the PR2-like class binds it, shaping the response. The gene pair looks like a breeding target for tougher peanuts that shrug off both disease and chill.
pmc-13211079:
Soisungwan Satarug asked how well safety guides guard people from cadmium in a 2026 review. Cadmium is a heavy metal with no role in the body, found in nearly all foods, from potatoes and grains to shellfish and organ meats. It harms many organs through cell stress and lasting swelling, and it links to cancer, heart disease, diabetes, weak bones, and kidney disease.

Guides for safe daily intake through food span a wide range, set by kidney and bone harm marks. Satarug weighs whether those marks use the best proof and guard the most at risk. The review presses for guides that match how harm truly builds at low doses.
pmc-13212879:
Mousavi-Kohnesari, Kavousi, and Doosti present a new test kit for tuberculosis, in work from twenty twenty-six. Other mycobacteria cause symptoms like TB but need distinct care. False TB calls can lead to wrong treatment, so exact tests matter.

Their kit uses real time PCR, a gene copying test, aimed at a DNA region unique to the TB germ. Primers and probes were designed and checked on computer databases. A built in control was cloned into a carrier to guard against false negatives. Standards set the lowest amount the kit can detect. Tests on known positive samples checked accuracy and repeat performance.
pmc-13213079:
Paula Condé Lamparelli Elias and colleagues describe in 2026 a young man who never felt thirst despite dangerously high blood sodium, a puzzle they probed with a hormone-related marker called copeptin. He had earlier had a brain tumour removed, which can damage the brain's thirst and water-balance controls.

At presentation his sodium sat well above the normal range, yet he reported no thirst and produced normal urine volumes. Drinking water on a schedule corrected the sodium. During a salt infusion test, his thirst stayed flat and copeptin stayed oddly low for his blood concentration. The pattern points to a partial failure of hormone release, while his kidneys still responded normally.
pmc-13213679:
A septic native joint that cannot be saved needs the joint removed and replaced, and the classic route takes two staged operations with a spacer between. Matthias Wittauer and six co-authors report a shorter route in a 2026 study: the 1.5-stage arthroplasty, tried for hip and knee infections between 2015 and 2024.

The study followed 45 patients for a year after surgery. The revision rate at one year was 26.7 percent, though only two revisions, 6.7 percent, were for surgical complications. About a quarter of patients moved on to a planned second stage within the year, mostly to improve function rather than to fix failure. The middle hospital stay was 13.5 days. The authors weigh the approach against the longer staged route, noting fewer operations as the draw.
pmc-13213779:
Lowanika Victor Tibane, David Mamba, and Zakhele Handsome Nkosi shared a joined data set in 2026 on an iron-rich rock band in South Africa. The band sits in an old greenstone belt on the edge of a vast ancient landmass. Such bands hold clues to early seas and to iron wealth. The team took twenty samples, half from open rock and half from drill cores that reached deep below ground.

Thin slices were read under light microscopes, and X-ray and laser tools gave the mineral and element mix. Two minerals, magnetite and quartz, made up most of the rock. Iron and silica led the element lists. Trace patterns held a few odd notes the team logs in full. The set can ground work on how such bands form.
pmc-13214179:
Inge Knippenberg and seven co-authors build and test two inventories of mood-lifting actions in nursing homes, in a study from 2026. Residents and caregivers do many small things that lift mood without counting as formal depression care. The team wrote item lists for both groups, checked their content with residents and staff in Dutch and Belgian homes, then tested repeat and shared ratings.

Both lists covered the topic well and gave moderate to very good agreement when filled in twice. Ratings shared between caregivers were weaker, above all for residents with severe cognitive decline. Using the lists raised awareness of mood-lifting habits, staff reported.
pmc-13215179:
Juan Diego Toscano and colleagues present in 2026 a method that turns ordinary contrast MRI scans into maps of fluid flow across the whole living brain. Slow fluid circulation clears metabolic waste, and its failure is tied to Alzheimer's disease and stroke, yet deep-brain flow had never been measured directly.

Their physics-informed artificial intelligence rebuilds three-dimensional velocity fields while also estimating tissue permeability and pressure, quantities no other method reaches. The maps separate creeping diffusion-driven drift from much faster channelled flow along vessels. Distinguishing those regimes opens fresh study of brain cleaning in health and disease. The same mathematics could serve other porous systems, from rock to engineered tissue.
pmc-13215379:
Polina Shilo writes a letter in 2026 about a study of thyroid harm during cancer drug therapy. The study under review asked whether thyroid trouble on PD-1 drugs also hints at a better outlook in advanced throat cancer. Shilo praises the work for mapping how often the harm strikes and when.

Her worry is timing. Thyroid trouble grows during treatment, so patients must stay on the drug long enough to develop it. Counting survival from the first dose can then flatter the group with thyroid harm. She also notes the proof is strong for time without growth but weak for overall survival. A time-aware model, she says, would settle the claim.
pmc-13215879:
Imanishi, Toyooka and their co-authors link lung perfusion defects to airway problems after living-donor lobar lung transplant, in work listed for 2026. Airway problems can be fatal after transplant, and bronchial healing depends on blood flow to the graft.

Records covered transplants at one center over a long span of years. Airway problems arose in a small share of transplanted lungs. Perfusion defects on scans were far more common in lungs that later had airway trouble. Those grafts also had higher grades of the fissure between lobes at donor surgery. Survival did not differ by airway status, the authors report.
pmc-13216279:
Galal Elsamak and co-authors present a 2026 experimental study on rescuing weakened reinforced concrete columns, a common problem where rust eats away the internal steel. Their recipe combines bars set into grooves near the surface with a high-performance outer jacket.

Columns were strengthened with steel or glass-fibre bars plus jackets of engineered cementitious composite or ultra-high-performance concrete reinforced with fibre mesh. The ultra-high-performance jacket confined the column best. Pairing grooved glass-fibre bars with that jacket raised load capacity by 49 percent and greatly increased energy absorption. Computer models matched the experiments well and were used to probe how bar diameter changes the benefit, which shrank as bars grew larger.
pmc-13217479:
Lanlan Hu and co-authors gelled apple pectin without sugar, calcium, or heat, in a 2026 study. Pectin is a plant fiber used to thicken foods, and it usually needs one of those triggers to set. The team used a natural plant acid, coumaric acid, at sour conditions instead. The question was how much acid a stable gel needs and what the gel can do.

Gels formed from a clear threshold dose upward and held their shape over time. Stiffness rose steeply with more acid, and the gels thinned under pressure so they could be syringed. They held water well and survived freezing and thawing. The gels also fought oxidation and both broad classes of bacteria, while staying friendly to a helpful gut bacterium. Food, medical, and packaging uses are proposed.
pmc-13217779:
Nini Cheng, Weitao Huang, and Mei Sun survey Chinese college students about AI copies of dead people, built from their photos, voice, and chats. Their 2026 study asks what makes young people accept or reject such digital resurrection. The topic raises hard questions about consent and grief.

Nearly a thousand students answered the online survey. Students who used AI more and who felt its harms were easier to foresee tended to accept the idea. Fear of AI cut both ways, depending on the scene described. Students who had lost a loved one, and medical students, were more open. About half said the wishes of both the dead person and the family should count before any copy is made.
pmc-13217879:
Pin Zuo and co-authors report successful treatment of a tuberculous wound with maggot debridement therapy. Their 2026 case report deals with tuberculosis of bone and soft tissue, where diagnosis and treatment are complex.

Maggot debridement therapy, in which sterile larvae clean dead tissue from wounds, has drawn growing attention as a wound treatment. Its use on tuberculous wounds had not been thoroughly studied. Their case gives preliminary clinical data suggesting the therapy is effective and safe for such a wound. The authors call for further research to test the method more widely and to improve outcomes for patients with these hard-to-heal wounds.
pmc-13217979:
Sarah Persson and colleagues present a 2026 qualitative study of how registered dietitians reason about video consultations. Dietitians often serve wide geographic areas and rarely need to examine patients physically, which makes remote care attractive. The study examines how these clinicians decide when a video visit serves a patient well.

The researchers interviewed nine dietitians and analyzed the transcripts using reflexive thematic analysis, guided by a patient-centered framework on access to care. Three themes emerged, covering good and accessible care, control over one's own working situation, and keeping the whole care process in mind. Participants said video visits improved flexibility and access, yet they preferred meeting in person when a physical assessment was needed or when patients lacked digital skills. The authors call for more work on how clinicians involve patients in choosing the consultation format.
pmc-13218179:
Bakary Kinteh and colleagues survey community awareness of climate change and its health effects in The Gambia's North Bank Region, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The Gambia is highly exposed to climate harm, yet little research has asked ordinary households what they know about the health side of a changing climate. The survey ran across thirty-five communities in seven districts.

Structured questionnaires in local languages were answered by 868 adults in early 2024. About 86 percent had heard of climate change, with radio the main source for over half. Awareness was strong for excessive heat and shifting rainfall but weaker for flooding, while crop failure was the most recognized consequence. Roughly seventy-seven percent said they had felt climate effects in their community within five years. Older age and tertiary education independently predicted awareness. The authors call this the region's first climate-health assessment and note sizeable gaps between population groups.
pmc-13218479:
Catherine G. Sutcliffe and colleagues describe the acute and lingering symptoms of COVID-19 in rural Zambia in a 2026 cohort study. Most knowledge about how SARS-CoV-2 illness unfolds comes from wealthier regions, and sub-Saharan Africa remains underrepresented. The team enrolled people of all ages with infection between December 2020 and March 2022 and followed them for a year.

The cohort included 132 people with COVID-19 and, for comparison, 56 with influenza. Nearly all adults and most children were sick at enrollment, with cough, headache, fever, and body aches the leading complaints. Yet few adults and no children were hospitalized, and almost none had been vaccinated. Most symptoms cleared within thirty days, though between roughly one in nine and one in five participants still reported symptoms at later visits, cough and headache among them. Influenza patients reported lingering symptoms more often. The study documents a mild, self-limited course in this rural population.
pmc-13219879:
Antonio Al Hazzouri and colleagues describe a storm of complications after an ERCP procedure in a 2026 case report. ERCP, the scope procedure used to treat bile duct problems, most often harms patients through pancreatitis. Air leaking into compartments afterward, causing a collapsed lung and air under the skin, is rare, and stranger when no tear in the gut is found.

Six hours after duct stenting and biopsy of a suspected bile duct tumor, a seventy-two-year-old woman developed abdominal pain, respiratory distress, and low oxygen. Scans showed pancreatitis with a collapsed right lung and air in the chest cavity, abdomen, retroperitoneum, and tissues under the skin, yet no perforation. Managed in intensive care with bowel rest, fluids, antibiotics, and oxygen, she improved and imaging showed the air collections shrinking. The authors use the case to argue for recognition and individualized conservative care in stable patients with the picture.
pmc-13220479:
Zhiguo Mao and colleagues test an oil from Curcuma against pulmonary fibrosis in a 2026 study. Pulmonary fibrosis scars the lungs stiff, and the immune cells, macrophages, drive the scarring as they polarize into inflammatory and repair states. The oil, abbreviated RCEO, had eased a lung condition, sarcoidosis, by steering macrophage behavior, which made fibrosis the natural next test.

Network computing first predicted the oil's targets, pointing at two signaling pathways, one running through Tlr4 and one through Pi3k and beta-catenin, both tied to macrophage fate. Chemical analysis identified the oil's main components and which of them reached lung tissue after inhalation. In mice given bleomycin to induce fibrosis, the oil reduced tissue damage and collagen buildup and improved lung function. Cell experiments also tracked macrophage polarization and death. They frame the oil as a candidate to develop, with the two pathways as its proposed mechanism.
pmc-13220579:
Anna Karafová and colleagues measure how temperature responds to ice water in a 2026 study. Cold water immersion and winter swimming are pastimes with claimed health benefits, but the body's reaction depends on the person and dose, and details are thin. Ninety practitioners were divided by what they did: swimming two hundred or four hundred fifty meters, or immersing for five or nine minutes.

Tympanic temperature was measured around each exposure and body mass index calculated for everyone. Temperature shifted after exposure in nearly every subgroup, with the exception of the five-minute immersion in water below one degree, which produced no significant response. Among winter swimmers, leaner participants cooled more: body mass index correlated negatively with the temperature change in women and men. The largest swings appeared in people with three years of practice. The results suggest short dips barely register thermally, while body composition buffers heat loss.
pmc-13221979:
Thenmalarchelvi Rathinavelan and Sruthi Sundaresan map every way a four-stranded DNA fold could be built in this 2026 paper. These quadruplex structures sit in gene-control regions and matter for health, yet only 33 basic motifs were known from lab-made strands. The authors ask what the full landscape looks like.

By reasoning about how strands connect and point, they derive 156 possible motifs covering simple and complex folds. The extra shapes may include fleeting forms that appear while a quadruplex folds. They also release a web tool that builds energy-settled models of all these folds, with options for overhangs and nonstandard quartets in DNA or RNA. The catalog deepens the structural picture considerably.
pmc-13223679:
Yanfeng Tang and co-authors study whether a second round of immunotherapy helps metastatic kidney cancers of non-clear cell type, in a 2026 cohort study of thirty-nine patients. First-line immune treatment had stopped working. The team measured response and survival after rechallenge, and profiled tumors with sequencing and multiplex imaging to hunt predictive markers.

Median time without progression reached nearly twelve months, with about fourteen percent of tumors shrinking and seventy percent controlled. One rare subtype seemed likelier to benefit. Tumors rich in mature lymphoid structures, little immune organs inside the cancer, responded far better, with response in half of high-scoring patients. Treatment was generally well tolerated, though the marker needs validation.
pmc-13223979:
Zheng-Hui Zhao, Wenze Tian, and Xiaoyu Wang study later childbearing and frailty in old age across three national cohorts, in a 2026 paper. Having a first child at thirty five or later is more common now, and its long term link to frailty was unclear. The cohorts from China, Korea, and the United States held over twenty one thousand women.

Later childbearing tracked with higher frailty risk in the Chinese and Korean cohorts after adjustment. The United States cohort showed the same direction at a forty year threshold. Life satisfaction carried part of the link in all three settings, most strongly in the United States data. The authors name life satisfaction a changeable path worth targeting. They suggest support for older mothers may ease later frailty.
pmc-13224479:
Miao Wang and co-authors explore a 2026 genomics study of Priestia megaterium, a bacterium valued in farming and industry. Viruses that infect bacteria, called phages, sometimes lodge inside the genome and reshape it over time. The team compared genomes and chemical DNA marks across strains to see how bacterial defences and resident viruses interact.

Defensive restriction-modification systems formed a strong, widespread barrier against viruses settling in. Successful resident viruses disproportionately carried counter-defence genes, including their own DNA-marking enzymes. Virus-derived genes were also enriched among the strain-specific parts of the genome, and virus content predicted family relationships well. Defence, counter-attack, and gene pickup together appear to drive this species' diversity.
pmc-13225579:
Mohammad Safargar, Abbas Basiri, and Hamed Kord-Varkaneh check whether folate, a B vitamin, links to kidney stones in United States adults. Folate feeds a core chemical cycle in the body that touches paths tied to stone growth. Past findings on the link were thin and mixed.

The team used a national health survey with more than nine thousand adults, tracking folate from food recalls and from four blood measures. About one in eleven adults reported stones. Early checks hinted at a link, but once age, habits, and health were taken into account, no measure of folate tied to stones at all. The authors conclude folate is likely not a main driver of stone growth.
pmc-13226579:
Jiang and colleagues trace how gut microbes pass from mother to baby in the first months of life. The team used structural variations, large changes in microbe genomes, as fine markers of exact strains. Data came from a long study of 98 mother and baby pairs, plus a second group of 25 pairs sampled at several body sites.

They profiled which marked strains appeared in both mother and child, and how delivery mode, feeding, and the mother's body sites shaped that sharing. Strain-level proof matters because species names alone cannot show true transfer. The work sharpens the picture of how a baby's gut is seeded, and by whom.
pmc-13226879:
Maire and co-authors compare older and younger women in a French metastatic breast cancer cohort. The cancer type is triple-negative, a hard-to-treat form. The ESME cohort held 4,246 women treated from 2008 to 2021. Older women numbered 987, at age 70 and above. Younger women numbered 3,259 in the comparison.

Older women had less aggressive tumors at spread diagnosis. They got chemotherapy and targeted drugs less often. Median survival was 13.7 months for older women. Younger women reached 15.8 months, with no firm gap. Spread site count and organ spread drove survival in both groups.
pmc-13229579:
Runjia Shen and co-authors watch two kinds of vessel cells race across lab surfaces, a contest that decides whether implants heal well. Their 2026 paper studies how the two cell types migrate when grown together, as they are in the body.

Mixed culture slowed both cell types down, likely because the unlike neighbors interact more and spread over more area. Mixing also shifted which type migrates faster. The team then grew the cells on nano-patterned surfaces dotted with a sticky peptide at spacings from 29 to 121 nanometers. The spacing alone could reverse which cell type won the race. The findings hand device designers a dial: surface patterning at the nanoscale can bias healing toward the lining cells they want.
pmc-13230279:
Lucas Jansen and colleagues test in 2026 how well zirconia crowns seal when a deep filling edge has been raised first. Forty pulled molars were split into five groups using two glue systems and two filling materials under the crowns. Teeth then endured long water storage plus repeated heating, cooling, and chewing pressure in a machine.

After loading, dye soak tests showed leakage mainly at the raised filling edges, not at the crown edges. The dual-cure filling material leaked much less than the self-cure material. The simpler one-bottle glue also performed better than the two-bottle version in this setup. Raising deep edges this way could spare patients gum surgery or tooth pulling forces, if lab results hold in clinics.
pmc-13231979:
Jing Wang, Shuwen Wang, Yanzheng Wang, Ting Zhang, and Xu Zhang review bacterial extracellular vesicles in a 2026 paper, as agents in human disease and as a base for new therapy. Gram-negative bacteria shed tiny sacs from their outer membrane. Those sacs carry poisons, immune signals, and nucleic acids through the body.

The sacs form when the membrane's balance slips, its wall is reshaped, or the cell is stressed. They cross barriers and reach far sites, so they play a part in many diseases. Their traits also suit them as a platform for vaccines and cancer immune work.
pmc-13232479:
Hairong Xiao and co-authors show that removing a gene brake lets ear stem cells form new hearing cells in mice, in work from 2026. Newborn ear stem cells can briefly rebuild hearing cells, but the power fades fast. Finding what shuts it down is key to restoring hearing.

Gene scans across place, injury, and lineage pointed to a Wnt-blocking gene as a suspect. Deleting that gene in newborn stem cells boosted sphere growth in dishes. In live mice, deletion drove stem cells to become hearing cells. Checks covered cell shape, sound response, and nerve links. Single-cell reads mapped the shift in detail. The brake is a clear drug target for hearing repair.
pmc-13233479:
Tianxiang Lan and others put out a real-world study in 2026. They tested a stroke shot used in China. Anisodine hydrobromide was given in routine hospital care. Over four thousand acute stroke patients took part. About half received the drug plus standard care. The rest got best medical treatment alone. Function after three months was the main outcome. Weighting evened the groups for fairness. Bleeding problems and deaths were also tracked with care.

Poor results were less common with the drug. Adjusted checks backed the gap, which stayed real. Stroke severity scores also got better by more there. The design watched routine care; it was not a trial by lot. Hidden gaps between groups cannot be ruled out fully. Still, the large many-center data support further testing. Safety signals looked fine in routine use.
pmc-13233779:
Miaomiao Yu and nine co-authors tackle a data problem in brain-computer interfaces in this 2026 paper. These systems learn from EEG signals, the small waves picked up from the scalp. Each person's signals differ, and noise from movement limits how much clean data can be gathered, so training sets stay small.

The team borrows an idea from metacognition, the way people watch and steer their own thinking. They built a module with three rules that guide a model as it creates extra EEG data. The rules track how signals change over time and how fine the detail is. On two data sets, the added module made fake signals look more real and helped models work better.
pmc-13233979:
Weiping Huang and colleagues published a 2026 microbiology study on antimicrobial peptides that jam the bacterial ribosome. These proline-rich peptides slide into the tunnel where new proteins exit the ribosome. One family binds facing the same way as the growing protein and freezes ribosomes at stop signals. The other faces backward and blocks translation at start signals.

Mining genome databases, the team found many relatives of a known stop-signal peptide that unexpectedly behaved like the backward-facing family. Structural work confirmed they bind in the flipped orientation. Tiny changes to a peptide's sequence were enough to reverse which way it sits and which signal it blocks. The authors note that hosts could exploit such flips, retuning one defensive peptide against newly emerging pathogens with only a few mutations.
pmc-13234079:
Yun-Tzu Lin and colleagues published a 2026 real-world study of gilteritinib, a targeted drug for acute myeloid leukemia carrying FLT3 mutations, used around stem cell transplantation. Patients whose leukemia had relapsed or resisted treatment took the drug before transplant, then resumed it as maintenance once the graft settled, between days thirty and ninety. Evidence for this salvage-then-maintenance path had been thin, especially in Asian patients.

Three quarters of the cohort reached complete response before transplant. Over a median follow-up of about forty-six months, patients on maintenance relapsed less in the first year and lived longer without relapse than comparison experience suggested. The drug was generally well tolerated, with no rise in virus complications or graft-versus-host problems. Subgroup hints favored patients with no measurable residual disease, though the authors flag the small sample.
pmc-13235279:
Tanya Saxena and colleagues tested in 2026 tiny engineered protein clusters as a treatment for liver scarring and liver cancer in mice. Long-term liver injury drives scarring, called fibrosis, and can progress to a cancer with poor survival. A signalling pathway driven by a growth factor pushes both processes forward. The clusters were designed to block a helper protein that many harmful proteins depend on.

In a chemically induced fibrosis model, treatment lowered markers of scarring and helped break down collagen fibres in the liver. In a chronic cancer model, the clusters reduced proteins that drive tumour growth and spread. Tumour burden fell as a result in the reported experiments. The protein scaffold used is modular and easy to produce, according to the authors. They present the platform as a candidate therapy with low expected immune reaction, pending further testing.
pmc-13235379:
Elena Ellmeier and colleagues examined in 2026 an energy enzyme as a possible drug target for calming harmful T cells in multiple sclerosis. The enzyme, called PKM2, also performs side jobs beyond energy production in immune cells. Blood T cells from patients and healthy controls were compared for enzyme amount and form. Laboratory treatment tested whether blocking the enzyme changed inflammatory output.

Effector and memory T cells carried more of the enzyme than naive T cells in both groups. Levels in those subsets tracked with age and disease duration in patients. The cell types known for driving inflammation showed the highest enzyme levels of all. Blocking the enzyme preferentially cut several inflammatory messengers from patient T cells. Patient immune cells also held more of the enzyme in its single-unit form, which supports its side activities. The authors propose PKM2 as a target worth testing.
pmc-13235579: A. Perrucci and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their article checking cleaning methods for trucks that carry live pigs. The notice is a correction only, fixing source numbers that had been set wrongly from source sixty-one onward in one section. Several sections are printed again with their proper source numbers so readers can match claims to the right sources. The fixed text covers hardy bacteria on trucks, cleaner choice, and biofilm staying power. No methods, data, or findings of the first hygiene study are changed.
pmc-13235979:
Praveen Kumar and a large team hunted in 2026 for self-harm events hidden in United States veterans' health records without diagnostic codes.
