Records for more than a million veterans, sampled from the national veterans system, covered two decades. A specialized learning method designed for data with only confirmed positive labels drove the search.

Only a small share of veterans carried a coded self-harm diagnosis in the raw records. The model suggested the true share was several times higher before calibration. Four expert reviewers checked a sample of charts across the model's probability range to anchor its estimates. About forty of ninety-seven reviewed uncoded patients had documented self-harm in their notes. After calibration, combined prevalence settled lower than the first model estimate. The authors offer the method for fairer prevalence counts and risk finding.
pmc-13236879:
Olga Malas and co-authors checked in 2026 whether a scale for phubbing, meaning snubbing people in favor of a phone, works the same way for men and women in Nigeria. Questionnaires went to 396 university students aged 18 to 25, most of them women. The team tested three versions of the scale and compared scores with measures of technology addiction and digital balance.

A shortened eight-item version with two factors fit the data best, and it met strict standards for measuring the same trait in both sexes. Yet some items behaved weakly in men, and the two factors barely related in the male group. The authors advise using the short scale while treating sex differences with care in comparisons and interventions.
pmc-13238579:
Hao Zheng and eleven co-authors built a prognosis signature for liver cancer and tested a plant compound against it in a 2026 paper. Liver cancer is aggressive and short on reliable markers. Combining network analysis, machine learning, single-cell and spatial data, and docking, the team hunted genes tied to blood vessel growth.

One gene, SCAF1, stood out: raised in tumors, tied to advanced features and worse survival, and concentrated in vessel and immune parts of the tumor scene. Silencing it in cells curbed migration, invasion, and vessel-growth signals. Docking flagged the soy compound genistein as a binder, and lab tests showed it lowered SCAF1 and slowed the cancer cells. The authors propose SCAF1 as both marker and target.
pmc-13238779:
Doueiri, Ratnapreya, and Frankenberger present a gentler way to fix front teeth marked by weak enamel. Molar incisor hypomineralization leaves enamel soft and discoloured, and it can strike the visible front teeth as well as molars. Their patient, a girl of fourteen, had cloudy patches on her upper central incisors, exactly where a smile shows them.

Standard fixes range from resin sealing to sanding the surface or building it up with composite. The team's approach removes the damaged enamel selectively, keeping sound tissue. For teenagers, appearance is not vanity but confidence. A case showing strong cosmetic results with less drilling gives dentists a kinder option to offer.
pmc-13239079:
Erneus Ernest, Devis Simbila, and Poorani Gurumallesh Prabu reported in 2026 an eleven-year-old boy whose excessive urination, constant thirst, salt craving, and weight loss eventually pointed to Gitelman syndrome. The syndrome is a rare inherited kidney salt-wasting disorder. He was first worked up for diabetes, hormone problems, tuberculosis, and malnutrition without an answer. Recurrent bouts of severe potassium and magnesium loss marked his course.

During the key admission he developed worsening muscle weakness, and his chemistry fit renal salt wasting so well that the team diagnosed the syndrome without genetic testing, which their resource-limited setting lacked. Fluids, electrolyte supplements, liberal salt, and nutritional support stabilized him, with follow-up showing marked improvement. The authors urge clinicians to suspect this tubulopathy when children show this symptom cluster with unexplained electrolyte trouble.
pmc-13239379:
Hani Rukh-E-Qamar and co-authors report a 2026 qualitative study of point-of-care technology, devices that give test results where patients are seen. Developers and stakeholders met to discuss what helps or hinders building such tools, especially for cancer, nutrition, and infection testing.

Twenty-four participants from a specialist network joined focus groups at Cornell Tech in New York in May 2024. Discussion exposed weak stakeholder engagement, thin preparation for regulation, and limited market analysis. Scaling production and adapting devices for poorer countries also proved difficult. Participants urged user-centred design, early regulatory planning, and partnerships formed well before a product reaches clinics.
pmc-13239879:
Pathum Weerawarna and co-authors assemble a toolkit of drug-like probes for Alzheimer's research in a 2026 paper. Two kinases, PYK2 and FAK, are tied to the disease, but their role in microglia, the brain's immune cells, is murky. Clean, selective blockers are needed to ask sharp questions.

The team gathered known blockers from papers and patents, made or bought samples, and profiled them in kinase assays. Most showed strong, selective blocking and friendly body-handling traits. Assay choice shifted apparent selectivity, a caution they flag. In human and mouse microglia models, the PYK2-selective tools strongly boosted the cells' debris-eating work. The set is offered as a vetted kit for preclinical studies.
pmc-13239979:
Hamidou Soumana Diaouga and co-authors report the first known case in Niger of an extremely rare birth defect in a 2026 paper. The agnathia-otocephaly complex involves a missing or tiny lower jaw, ears displaced toward the middle, and a very small or absent mouth, arising from faulty development of the first branchial arch.

The condition was discovered only after a premature baby was delivered, since antenatal scanning had not picked it up during an unmonitored pregnancy. Severe forms are usually fatal, although milder isolated variants have survived. The team shares their department's experience to argue for effective pregnancy monitoring and prenatal diagnosis in their region.
pmc-13240379:
Giulia Di Donato and colleagues present a newborn later diagnosed with a rare mosaic chromosome disorder in a 2026 case report. Pallister-Killian syndrome arises when some cells carry an extra copy of part of chromosome twelve, producing a recognisable pattern of features that varies widely between children.

Typical signs include a coarse face, wide-set eyes, sparse hair at the temples, and patchy skin colouring that mirrors the patchwork genetics. Seizures, heart defects, and developmental delay may accompany the pattern. Because the share of affected cells does not predict severity, the authors stress careful physical examination to trigger testing early. A blood-based chromosome array test proved a sensitive way to confirm the diagnosis.
pmc-13240479:
Meng Huang and Jie Wu reported a teen rectal case in 2026 that looked like cancer but was not. A 17-year-old boy had two years of rectal bleeding. A scope at his local hospital showed a cauliflower-like rectal growth, and scans showed wall thickening, raising fear of a tumor. Tests also suggested ulcerative proctitis, and standard drugs for that condition failed to help.

A repeat scope showed many bumpy polyps coated with mucus. Tissue study showed healing-type tissue with distorted glands, and a team review settled on cap polyposis, a rare benign condition. Scope-based surgery removed the lesions and ended his symptoms. Checks at 4, 9, and 16 months showed healed tissue with no return.
pmc-13240779:
Fulya Topuz presents a 2026 case report on saving an arm after a severe workplace crush injury in a 21-year-old man. Scans showed a long blocked segment of the main arm artery with no blood flow beyond it. Direct repair was impossible because the tissue damage was too extensive.

Surgeons harvested a long vein from the leg and tunneled it between muscle layers for protection. They connected it from the brachial artery above the injury to the radial artery in the forearm. Flow returned at once, confirmed by ultrasound and a palpable pulse. Hand circulation held in the short term, though nerve damage still needed broader care. The case shows distal bypass as a salvage option.
pmc-13240979:
Xie's team at Peking spoke with China's data managers about taking up the CDISC submission standards. Thirty-eight leaders from 38 groups spoke between April and August 2022. China's regulator has pushed the global standard since 2020. Talks probed knowledge, views, daily practice, and obstacles.

Nearly all experts called the CDISC requirement key, and most had filed compliant submissions. Cost, scarce trained staff, weak local fit, and sheer complexity topped the barrier list. Proposed fixes include cheaper tooling, more training, and folding Chinese medicine terms into the standard. Clearer guidance was another common request.
pmc-13241479:
Tsuchiya and colleagues at Chiba University hunted for missing links in how cells dispose of stray proteins outside their borders. Clusterin was the only known carrier ferrying misfolded proteins to lysosomes. Screening plasma factors that bind an amyloid-forming blood protein surfaced a second candidate. The enzyme GPLD1 emerged from the search.

GPLD1 binds the amyloid protein directly and escorts it to lysosomal destruction. Its famous cutting activity against membrane anchors proved unnecessary for the job. Cell-surface heparan sulfate serves as the docking receptor instead. Tsuchiya presents GPLD1 as a scavenger carrier with tastes distinct from clusterin's.
pmc-13242679:
Prabhavathi Maddineni and co-authors study glaucoma damage in a 2026 paper on eye nerve cells. Glaucoma slowly kills the retinal ganglion cells that carry sight signals to the brain. High pressure in the eye is the main known risk, yet some patients keep losing sight even when pressure is controlled.

The team focused on autophagy, the cell's system for clearing damaged parts, including worn-out mitochondria. In two mouse models of glaucoma, they tracked markers of that system and of cell damage over time. They also tested mice lacking a key autophagy gene in these cells, and a drug, Torin 2, that boosts the clearing system. Human retina tissue was tested outside the body as well, to see whether boosting cleanup can protect the cells.
pmc-13242779:
Petra Sohlman offers a 2026 register-based tool for predicting which Finnish public sector employees will apply for a disability pension. Early exit from work carries heavy costs for individuals and the pension system. The model uses an unusually rich dataset that includes even short sickness absences, which registers usually miss.

Age, occupation, and accumulated sickness days all raised application risk. Many short spells mattered too, not only long absences. Approaching retirement age and higher earnings lowered risk. The model sorted employee groups accurately and transparently. Public employers in Finland already use its profiles to target early support. Sohlman presents pension application, not approval, as the outcome, since applications themselves signal failing work ability.
pmc-13242979:
Laura Benestan and co-authors asked whether male and female European spiny lobsters wander differently, using genetics across six Mediterranean marine reserves. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. Dispersal shapes how a vulnerable, heavily fished species should be protected, yet it had never been tested between the sexes in a marine invertebrate like this. The team genotyped 180 lobsters at thousands of markers and compared population structure by sex.

Both sexes mixed freely across the study area, with no strong genetic structure overall. Females showed a slight tendency toward more structure, but the difference was not significant. The hunt produced a bonus: seventy-two markers cleanly separated the sexes, letting the team sex sixty-one lobsters of unknown sex. Those markers give the first evidence that this species uses a ZZ/ZW sex determination system. They also hand managers a tool for fisheries where rules differ by sex.
pmc-13243179:
Utshob Sutradhar and co-authors built a phone app that prescreens skin disease from photos in real time. Their feasibility study appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. Skin disease is common where dermatologists are scarce, so a light on-device model could flag who needs care first. Their Android app, SkinLearn, runs a trimmed YOLO11 network directly on the phone with no internet needed, trained on a public seven-class set of skin images.

On its home dataset the model named the right disease almost every time. On a second, different skin cancer dataset its accuracy fell sharply, though it still beat the older model used for comparison. That drop exposes how much image sets differ in lighting, skin tones, and class mix. The authors claim technical feasibility for real-time, offline prescreening on cheap hardware. They insist on more validation before any clinical use.
pmc-13243579:
Zhenshuan Zhao, Xiaoguang Yu, Feng Zhao, and Jun Li trace how a protein switch protects cartilage in osteoarthritis, in a 2026 study. They first mined a public gene data set from arthritic tissue and found inflammation and self-cleaning pathways out of tune. Then they harmed cartilage in animals and cells with an inflammatory signal, IL-1 beta, and watched what the switch, SHP2, did to the damage.

Stained tissue showed SHP2 eased the breakdown of the cartilage matrix. Under the microscope, it also cut damage to the cells' power plants. Protein tests showed it lowered a reader protein, BRD4, plus fire-alarm proteins tied to a bursting form of cell death. At the same time it raised markers of the cell's self-cleaning system. The authors describe a protective chain worth testing as a drug target.
pmc-13243779:
Janine Murr and colleagues found a drug target in the most stubborn form of pancreatic cancer by blocking a master regulatory enzyme. Their study appeared in MedComm in 2026. The mesenchymal subtype of pancreatic cancer shrugs off chemotherapy, so the team hunted its specific weaknesses with genetic screens. The screens fingered PPP2CA, the catalytic heart of protein phosphatase 2A, and the inhibitor LB100 indeed hit those cells selectively.

Treating those cells rewired their metabolism and triggered stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, tipping them toward death. Genome-wide screens mapped which genes tune sensitivity to the drug, pointing at gene reading, RNA processing, and protein building. A surprise mechanism surfaced: the drug speeds up gene transcription, especially of short genes, through the kinase CDK9. Phosphatase and kinase appear to hold each other in check. The authors propose exploiting this activation paradox, and PP2A-based drug combinations, against this subtype.
pmc-13244079:
Zuzana Kubincová and colleagues turned routine moth counts from Czech reserves into a test of what shapes moth communities. Their study appeared in Ecology and Evolution in 2026. They gathered lists from 292 reserves covering 941 moth species, accepting that methods and effort varied by site. The question was whether consistent ecological patterns would still show through the uneven data.

They did. Reserves spanning more elevations, and those holding steppe and moist grassland, carried the most species. Height reshaped the whole mix: lowland reserves favored larger moths with several broods a year that feed on herbs, while mountain reserves favored shrub and tree feeders with fewer broods. Regional history mattered too, with Carpathian-Pannonian reserves hosting big-winged specialists. The authors argue that messy real-world data, read carefully, can guide conservation as well as polished surveys.
pmc-13245079:
Nina Karia and colleagues tested how well standard ultrasound measures spot the mildest form of pulmonary hypertension under its new definition. Their study appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Since 2022 the threshold sits lower, at artery pressures just above twenty, catching a mild group earlier rules missed. Using a British database of nearly two thousand patients, the team graded three echo metrics.

The metrics (jet velocity, estimated artery pressure, and their ratio against heart contraction) separated clear disease well, scoring around eight-tenths accuracy for pressures above the old and new cut-offs. For the mild band specifically, accuracy sagged noticeably. Yet mild disease was far from harmless: within it, a fast jet or a weak contraction-to-pressure ratio flagged patients who died sooner. Echo finds clear disease but under-reads the mild zone, exactly where early risk now hides. Mild, in their data, is worth catching properly.
pmc-13245279:
El-Shalakany, Samir, and Mubarak built a hybrid membrane that cleans several pollutants from water at once, in this 2026 RSC Advances study. Their material layers coconut-shell activated carbon and chitosan, a natural polymer, with graphene oxide nanosheets, forming a sheet riddled with pores at several size scales. Such hierarchy helps dissolved contaminants reach binding sites quickly.

Spectroscopy and microscopy confirmed the three ingredients bonded into a semi-crystalline, porous network with very fine surface pores. The membrane was designed to adsorb both ciprofloxacin, a widely used antibiotic that pollutes waterways, and hazardous heavy metals simultaneously, a harder task than single-pollutant filters. The authors present the hybrid as a multifunctional platform for treating complex polluted water, where medicines and metals arrive mixed together.
pmc-13245879:
Anna Gonsalves, Sarah Baker, Prachi Singh, and Jacqueline Limberg wrote a 2026 review on a hormone-like signal and the harm done by repeated drops in oxygen. Such drops happen in sleep apnea, where breathing stops again and again. They raise blood pressure and strain the heart and metabolism. The signal in question, endothelin-1, makes blood vessels tighten.

The review sums up the group's experiments in healthy young men. Brief low-oxygen sessions raised levels of the signal, nerve activity to muscles, and blood pressure. A drug that blocks the signal's receptors softened the blood pressure rise during low oxygen. Blocking it did not change the nerve or pressure response to repeated drops, though. It did blunt the rise in adrenaline and in fatty acids freed from body fat. The authors argue the signal helps hold resting blood pressure, and may be a drug target for apnea-linked harm.
pmc-13246479:
Eun Hae Oh and colleagues present an automated test that names four major Aspergillus molds in a 2026 study. These molds can invade the lungs of people with weak immunity, and slow diagnosis costs lives. Current lab routes are slow, fussy, or miss cases.

Their platform runs from raw lung wash sample to answer with little hands-on work. It matched a standard lab method on most of 21 cultured isolates from patients. In 22 patient lung samples, it caught most proven infections and named the species correctly each time. It even found proof in some cases where cultures stayed negative. Speed plus species names can sharpen drug choice.
pmc-13246779:
Li, Liu, Wan, and co-authors present an artificial intelligence framework for designing crystals in this 2026 Nature Communications paper. Predicting which crystal structures a material can adopt, and how those forms behave, usually takes separate tools. Their system, PolymorphGen-MLPKD, organizes the search around landscapes combining entropy and symmetry to generate candidate structures and model their properties together.

The framework reproduced phase behavior across crystal families, generated partly disordered structures, and traced the pathway between graphite and diamond. Its distilled simulation potentials ran about a million times faster than the calculations they learned from, while staying accurate enough to compare how metals deform by twinning or dislocations, and to resolve stress-driven phase changes in brittle iridium. The authors also report scaling laws for training such models efficiently.
pmc-13247179:
Valeria Pruzzo and co-authors test whether a brief drug soak helps fat grafts grow blood vessels in skin substitutes in a 2026 study. Skin substitutes fail when vessels arrive too slowly. Seeding them with nanofat, a fine fat preparation, helps, and a drug that mimics low oxygen might prime the fat further.

Fat from glowing donor mice was soaked for an hour in the drug or a plain solution, then seeded onto substitutes placed in skinfold chambers of normal mice. Over two weeks, drug-treated implants built denser working vessel networks at edge and center. Most new vessels came from the treated fat itself. Inflammation around the implant also eased, with fewer white cells sticking and entering. The authors see a cheap priming step for grafting.
pmc-13247279:
Margaret Dimova and co-authors sum up proof that diabetes goes with slower growth of a swollen belly aorta. Their paper from 2026 calls the link a paradox, since diabetes harms vessels in most other ways. A swollen aorta can burst, so growth rate sets how close the watch must be.

Across six long run cohorts, patients with diabetes had slower swelling growth than those without, by about half to one and a half millimeters a year. In three cohorts, the diabetes drug metformin went with a further cut in growth. The authors read body chemistry control as a promising path for tailored watch plans and for future care trials in this disease.
pmc-13247679:
Constantin and co-authors report an urgent inpatient case in this 2026 Case Reports in Psychiatry article. A man in his twenties with bipolar disorder, ADHD, anxiety, and an intellectual developmental disorder was hospitalized with severe intrusive sexual thoughts causing distress and safety concerns. His presentation straddled two diagnoses: obsessive-compulsive style sexual obsessions he found alien, and gratification-driven urges resembling an early compulsive sexual behavior syndrome that formal criteria, requiring six months of symptoms, could not yet confirm.

Standard medication adjustments failed to contain the risk. After doctors started naltrexone, a drug that blunts reward and is used against addictions, his improvement was marked within five days and the intrusive thoughts had resolved by hospital day sixteen. Because other medicines changed too, the authors cannot credit naltrexone alone, but they argue the speed justifies studying reward-targeted treatment for such ambiguous emergencies.
pmc-13247879:
Ruike Xia and co-authors test which scan measure best grades liver health in early to mid-stage disease in a 2026 study. A contrast scan can both find liver spots and grade how well the organ works. The yardstick was a blood score built from two common lab values, known to beat an older score for fairness.

Ninety-nine high-risk patients with liver cancer from hepatitis B had the scan. Eight scan measures were checked against the blood grade. The ratio of liver glow to vein glow split the best grade from the worse ones most sharply. The team calls it the lead scan marker for this use.
pmc-13248779: The Journal of Healthcare Engineering retracted this 2022 meta-analysis in 2026, and this notice is the formal record of that withdrawal. The paper had pooled studies on two anesthesia depth monitors, Narcotrend and the bispectral index, asking which better predicted thinking problems after tumor surgery in elderly patients. The retraction was agreed between the journal's editor, David Hewson, and the publisher, John Wiley and Sons. Readers should not rely on the paper's pooled conclusions, and the notice links to the original article so its record stays traceable.
pmc-13248979:
Skonieczna and a Polish team repackaged a classic chemotherapy drug, in a 2026 nanomedicine study. They tucked 5-fluorouracil inside cholesterol-modified cyclodextrin, a ring-shaped carrier, at three drug ratios. The goal was stronger killing of colorectal cancer cells with less harm elsewhere, a standing problem for this old but harsh drug.

The richest mixture, three drug parts per carrier part, proved most potent. It cut cancer cell metabolism and survival by more than sixty percent and switched on both major cell-suicide pathways. Healthy fibroblasts and heart muscle cells suffered only moderate effects. The authors nominate that ratio for further development toward colorectal cancer therapy.
pmc-13249179:
Rezende reviewed two immune messengers as outlook markers in liver cancer, in a 2026 narrative review. Hepatocellular carcinoma usually grows in a scarred, cirrhotic liver, where chronic inflammation feeds the tumor. Searching literature from 2010 to 2025, the author weighed studies of interleukin-6, which drives inflammation, and interleukin-10, which calms it, in patients' blood.

Raised interleukin-6 consistently accompanied bigger tumor burden and poorer survival after both drug and local therapies. Interleukin-10 also ran high in many patients, but its meaning shifted with disease stage and tumor surroundings. The author calls for standard test methods and shared cut-off values before either marker guides everyday decisions.
pmc-13249679:
Dey systematically reviewed a DNA repair enzyme's role in autoimmune rheumatic disease, in a 2026 paper. The enzyme, PARP1, also helps regulate transcription and immune responses, and hints linked it to lupus and related conditions. Searching two databases, the author sifted more than thirty-five hundred records and kept forty-one studies covering patients and animal models.

Blocking or removing PARP1 often calmed inflammation and tissue damage in experiments. Yet in lupus and systemic sclerosis, patients showed reduced PARP1 activity and weaker DNA repair, a more complicated picture. Genetic findings were mixed, while antibody and activity measures showed diagnostic promise, especially in lupus. The author calls PARP1 a plausible future target needing sharper human evidence.
pmc-13249879:
Elrashedy and colleagues designed a universal foot-and-mouth vaccine on the computer, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. The livestock virus mutates fast and comes in many types, while current vaccines are whole killed virus with weak cross-protection and safety baggage. Focusing on the types common in Egypt, the team stitched conserved pieces of five viral proteins into artificial chimeric proteins.

Modeling rated their second construct as stable and strongly visible to the immune system, rich in sites that killer T cells, helper T cells, and antibodies can recognize. Simulated docking showed the vaccine designs gripping cattle immune sensors firmly over long virtual runs. The authors call for laboratory expression and animal trials to test the blueprint.
pmc-13250179:
Wang and colleagues report a gentle endoscopic treatment for children with repeated belly pain and hardened deposits in the appendix. Their 2026 World Journal of Pediatric Surgery paper reviews cases treated between 2021 and 2023. Each child had ultrasound evidence of appendiceal fecaliths, small stone-like masses, plus swollen gut lymph nodes nearby.

Doctors washed out the appendix through an endoscope guided by ultrasound, a method called retrograde appendiceal irrigation. The procedure succeeded in all seventy-three children, and pain stopped almost at once in nearly every child followed afterward. Minor bleeding or discomfort affected a small share of patients, with no perforations or major harm. Pain returned in about one fifth over the following months, while lymph node swelling dropped sharply.
pmc-13250879:
Wang and Zhang argue that henipaviruses sit on a threshold, dangerous yet not quite able to sustain spread. Their 2026 Emerging Microbes and Infections commentary covers a virus family known for repeated spillovers from animals, severe disease, and limited person-to-person transmission. Nipah and Hendra are its best-known members.

Growing viral diversity and widening contact between wildlife, livestock, and people keep producing episodic outbreaks. The authors say outbreak counting alone misleads preparedness for such irregular, high-consequence pathogens. They urge combined human, animal, and environment surveillance under a One Health approach. They also want adaptive trial designs and ready-to-test countermeasures, so vaccines and drugs can be judged quickly when the next spillover comes.
pmc-13250979:
Ziyue Huang and five co-authors probe how metal frames wake oxygen in a 2026 study. A class of enzymes uses iron and a helper acid to split oxygen for hard chemical work. A metal-organic frame that mimics that enzyme was built of late, but how it wakes oxygen stayed unclear.

Math models of the frame's heart compared iron with two swaps, manganese and cobalt. All three wake oxygen by the enzyme's broad path, yet each lands at a distinct end state. Iron and cobalt form high-spin metal-oxygen units, while manganese stops one step short. The map guides mimics by metal pick.
pmc-13251279:
Bin Wei and co-authors profile blood chemistry in patients with myasthenia gravis, in a 2026 study. Myasthenia gravis weakens muscles when the immune system attacks nerve signals. It comes in an ocular form, limited to the eyes, and a generalized form. The metabolic shifts behind those forms are poorly understood.

The team ran untargeted metabolomic profiling on fasting blood samples. Groups included generalized cases, ocular cases, and healthy controls. Advanced statistics separated the chemical patterns of each group. Distinct metabolite signatures marked the disease subtypes. Such signatures could aid diagnosis or track progression. They may also reveal pathways that new treatments could target. The study opens a metabolic window on a classic autoimmune disease.
pmc-13251479:
Swarnali Akter and a large team link farm hygiene practices with mastitis bacteria on smallholder dairy farms in Bangladesh in a 2026 study. Mastitis, an infection of the udder, is among the costliest diseases of dairy cows, cutting milk yield and quality. The team focused on Gram-negative bacteria, especially Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, and on how resistant those bacteria are to drugs.

Survey and lab results showed Klebsiella in 27.7 percent of cases and E. coli in 20.9 percent across the farms studied. A large share of isolates resisted several drugs at once, with the strongest resistance against common drugs such as ampicillin and tetracycline. Farms scoring well on knowledge, hygiene, and safety surveys did not reliably show fewer of these bacteria. The authors say good scores on paper are not enough and call for checking what farms actually do day to day.
pmc-13252979:
Supriya Peshin and a large team examine ERRFI1 mutations as a treatment clue in biliary tract cancers in a 2026 retrospective study. These cancers of the bile ducts and gallbladder respond poorly to standard therapy. ERRFI1 makes a protein that normally brakes the EGFR growth signal, so losing it might leave tumors unusually dependent on that signal and sensitive to drugs that block it.

The multicenter records search found fourteen patients whose tumors carried ERRFI1 alterations, all cancers of the ducts inside the liver. Eight received EGFR-blocking tablets after standard chemotherapy. Three of the eight achieved partial tumor shrinkage, two of them lasting beyond twenty months, and four more kept their disease stable. Median time before progression was seven months, and side effects were mild, mostly rash and diarrhea. The authors recommend adding ERRFI1 to routine tumor profiling so this opportunity is not missed.
pmc-13253179:
Miwa Kuroyanagi and co-authors give a standard protocol for measuring sperm motility in Japanese medaka fish in a 2026 paper. Changes in sperm movement can flag reproductive harm from chemicals in the environment or from gene changes. Yet motility is very sensitive to salt balance, timing, and other outer factors, so readings often vary between labs.

Their protocol details sperm collection, activation, and computer aided measurement with a named analysis system. It focuses on how the share of moving sperm changes after activation and on effects of freezing. Movement and speed fell over time, and freezing sped the fall. Early measurement after activation is urged for fair comparisons.
pmc-13253779:
L Mansilla Alvarez and co-authors present a 2026 method for tailoring blood flow models to one patient. One-dimensional models can predict flow and pressure in arteries, but patient data are often scarce while model settings are many. The team used a simplified map of the body's artery network and a search method called CMA-ES.

First, a global check ranked which settings shape the model's output most. Then the search method tuned those settings to match a small set of flow and pressure measures. Results showed accurate patient-specific models are feasible even with little data, and the authors map how each setting affects wave shapes and health markers.
pmc-13253979:
Abdolrasoul Safaeeian, Roghayyeh Armand, and Hossein Matlabi survey older adults in Miandoab, Iran, in a 2026 study. They asked 450 older people about their use of traditional medicine and why they choose it. Data came from a structured questionnaire, with participants picked by cluster sampling.

A large majority, 81.6 percent, reported using traditional remedies. Mint, cinnamon, and ginger were the most used herbs, and many would see a bonesetter for fractures. Word of mouth from older generations was the top influence, at 51.4 percent, followed by low cost and fewer felt side effects. Women and less-schooled adults leaned most to these treatments.
pmc-13254979:
Ruixin Liang and colleagues report a 2026 molecular study of how germ cells switch from ordinary cell division into meiosis, the division that makes eggs and sperm. Three proteins, MEIOC, RBM46, and YTHDC2, work together in that switch, destroying selected messages inside the cell. How the trio picks its targets was largely unknown.

Working in cultured cells, the team showed the complex binds certain message ends and marks those messages for destruction. One partner shields MEIOC from being broken down itself, while the target message helps hold the complex together. MEIOC also brings in XRN2, an enzyme that likely chews up the chosen messages. The findings sketch a working model for a step that fertility depends on.
pmc-13255379:
Mahmoud Ezzat and colleagues present a 2026 study of epidemic forecasting that blends graph neural networks with transformer models. Case counts spread across connected cities, so the network side tracks geography and movement while the transformer side tracks time patterns. The team built two versions, one attending only to nearby time windows and one to the full sequence.

They benchmarked the designs on COVID-era data from Spain and Brazil against three established baselines. A simpler linear variant posted the best error and direction scores on the Spain data. On a forty-city Brazil subset, the local-attention version matched or beat the baselines. The authors conclude that simple models can rival transformers on tidy data, while attention helps on noisier sets.
pmc-13255679:
Eight authors, led by Jieun Lee, compared the genomes of harmless-looking lung growths and the cancers beside them in this 2026 paper. Some lung cancers grow next to precursor patches that look benign under the microscope. Whether those patches are true ancestors of the cancer, or unrelated neighbors, was unclear.

The team sequenced the full gene set of thirty-three samples from eleven patients, each with a precursor and its paired cancer. Careful filtering removed artifacts from the preserved tissue. The overlap was small: only about a tenth of cancer-linked variants appeared in both lesions. Half sat in the cancer alone, and two fifths only in the precursor. Benign looks, it turns out, can hide a genome already marching its own way, a caution for how doctors read early lung lesions.
pmc-13256179:
Laura Stanciulescu and Maria Dorobantu developed two prediction scores in a 2026 study of patients who had catheter ablation for scar-related ventricular tachycardia, a dangerous heart rhythm arising from damaged heart muscle. Existing scores focus on the procedure itself and miss how much arrhythmia a patient carries. The pair built their models from a single-center group of treated patients.

From over a thousand candidate models for each outcome, they selected two compact scores covering twenty-four months after ablation. The mortality score, using pumping strength, heart failure class, rhythm variety, and defibrillator shocks, discriminated strongly. The recurrence score performed moderately, leaning on electrical storm history and shocks. The authors conclude that death tracks heart failure severity while recurrence tracks electrical instability, and they call for outside validation.
pmc-13257379:
Ichda Arini Dinana, Yukihiko Kubota, and Masahiro Ito published a 2026 study on the floppy parts of ABC transporters. These proteins ferry substances across cell membranes and form one of the largest protein families. Their neat folded domains are well studied, but the loose regions between domains are not.

The team checked 1,581 transporter sequences from bacteria to complex life. They split the proteins into five build types. Linker and edge regions proved far more disordered than the core domains in every type. They also mapped signs of selection pressure and likely chemical tag sites. Loose regions may tune how each transporter works, and their record across lineages hints at hidden roles.
pmc-13258679:
Dominika Lech and colleagues review flap choices in child jaw reconstruction during a 2026 single center study. Seventy five patients aged one to eighteen had jaw rebuilding with living bone flaps between twenty eleven and twenty twenty five. Donor bone came from the leg, hip, or knee region.

Leg bone was used most often, followed closely by hip bone. Defect shape predicted donor choice far better than patient age did. Apparent age patterns faded once defect class was taken into account. Overall flap survival stayed above ninety percent. Surgeons planning child jaw repair get support for planning around the defect first and age second.
pmc-13258879:
Kun Zhao and colleagues inspect aging housing conditions from photos with a mixture of experts vision model in a 2026 study. A new labeled image dataset supports graded checks of building problems in older communities. Their model routes image regions to specialist subnetworks using a similarity based rule.

A graph method converted pretrained weights into coherent expert starting points. Special losses handled both broad categories and rare fine grained problems. Accuracy rose over a small standard vision baseline and over prior expert models. Computing costs fell at the same time. City renewal teams gain a faster screening aid for large housing inspection workloads.
pmc-13259979:
Kaibo Zhu and colleagues studied in 2026 how mung bean plants cope with salty, alkaline soil. Mung bean is a major grain legume, and such soil cuts its growth and yield badly. The team compared a tolerant line with a sensitive one under mixed salt-alkali stress, sampling tissue at several time points.

Gene activity differed widely between the lines, with thousands of genes switching on or off after stress. The tolerant line showed stronger responses among 42 stress-linked regulator genes. Chemical profiling found thousands of metabolites, and arginine and proline pathways stood out in every comparison. Both data types pointed to the pathway that fixes carbon during photosynthesis as a shared hub. The authors offer the flagged genes as resources for breeding hardier mung bean lines.
pmc-13262079:
Anne Marie Wells and co-authors study a gene called Tbx1 in a 2026 mouse study of brain wiring. The gene sits in a stretch of DNA tied to a known deletion syndrome. Mice with only one working copy of the gene show changed nerve fibers and changed acts. But which cells drive those shifts was unclear. The team cut the gene's dose only in cells that make myelin, the fatty coat on nerve fibers.

Young mice with the change showed a shift in fiber mix in a brain band called the fimbria. One maze effect showed at one month of age and faded by two months. Other tests, from pup calls to social acts, showed no clear change. Lab work also showed the gene acts in both young and mature myelin cells.
pmc-13262279:
Julian Heidecke and co-authors grade a climate model of West Nile virus against thirteen years of European case records. Laboratory-derived thermal curves promise to predict when mosquitoes spread the virus best. Their 2026 study checks that promise against monthly reports of severe human disease from twenty ten onward.

The model's reproduction number nailed the seasonal rhythm and the temperatures where risk peaks. It ranked risky places and months slightly better than temperature alone. But year-to-year outbreak swings and the virus's patchy map escaped it. Finer temperature data helped only at the hot end. Biology alone, they conclude, cannot carry forecasting.
pmc-13262779:
Georgios Petridis and colleagues test whether home device data can flag mental health risk in older cancer survivors in a 2026 journal article. Survivors face higher rates of depression and anxiety, but clinic checks are infrequent and rely on memory. The team used tracker, scale, and smart plug data collected over 12 weeks in daily life.

The study followed 41 survivors with a mean age of 72.3 years, and used a four-question survey to define risk. Machine learning models sorted risk best when smart plug and smart scale data were combined, with strong standard scores. TV use patterns from the smart plug alone also performed fairly, beating tracker-only models. The authors call passive home monitoring a low-burden option needing larger checks.
pmc-13262979:
Jean Zeuikena and co-authors isolate new plant compounds from a traditional medicine tree in a 2026 journal article. The tree, Zanha golungensis, is used as herbal medicine for various ailments. The team extracted flavonoids, a family of plant chemicals, and worked out their structures with mass and magnetic resonance methods. Two of the compounds were new to science.

Alongside three known compounds, the new ones blocked two inflammation enzymes, COX-1 and COX-2, strongly in lab tests at a set dose. The most active compound beat the standard comparison compound on both enzymes. Computer calculations of electron patterns and docking into the COX-2 site supported stable binding. The authors suggest the compounds as leads for anti-inflammatory drug design.
pmc-13263879:
Yuanjing Tian and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the double life of macrophages inside lung tumors, where the same cell family can fight or feed the cancer. Their narrative review searched three databases into early 2026 and screened references by hand. Two independent readers handled study selection.

One macrophage state attacks tumors while another, common inside cancers, shelters them. The review traces how tumor cells coach macrophages toward the sheltering state through vesicles, cytokines, and shared signaling pathways. Three pathways recur in that coaching, alongside gene-level controls. Dense sheltering macrophages track with growth, spread, new blood vessels, and treatment resistance, plus worse patient outlook. Flipping macrophages back toward attack mode emerges as the therapeutic prize. The authors map targets along the polarization machinery for drug developers to test.
pmc-13263979:
Koshiro Fukuda, Tsuyoshi Hamada and Tsuyoshi Takeda review herbal and drug treatments for cancer-related fatigue in a 2026 article. Fatigue linked to cancer differs from ordinary tiredness because rest does not relieve it and daily function suffers. The condition affects most patients receiving treatment for advanced cancer and is tied to lower activity, muscle loss, distress and poorer tolerance of therapy.

The authors survey causes that include inflammation, anemia, hormone changes and treatment side effects. They then consider pharmacological options and herbal approaches used to ease the symptom. For clinicians and patients, the review organizes a complex supportive-care problem and points to where careful assessment matters before any treatment is chosen.
pmc-13264079:
C Falzone and co-authors present a 2026 reproducible workflow in R for cleaning indoor air data from school field studies. Wearable sensors worn by cleaning staff recorded temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide, fine particles and volatile chemicals. Tablet logs noted where each person was, what task was done and which product was used, but timing errors and noisy signals are common in real workplaces.

The pipeline sorts files by campaign, school and device, aligns timestamps across daylight saving changes and merges readings with activity context. Outputs include charts and summaries that separate cleaning periods from storage periods and compare exposure across rooms. Other teams can reuse the steps for occupational exposure work where context matters as much as the sensor numbers.
pmc-13264179:
Rudney da Silva Maia Júnior and colleagues link blood measures before slaughter to final meat pH in beef cattle in a 2026 study. Dark, firm and dry beef is a costly defect tied to stress that drains muscle energy stores before slaughter. Nellore cattle, common in Brazil, react strongly to handling, which raises concern. The team compared blood glucose readings, enzyme activity and age estimates with the pH reached after slaughter.

Activity of the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase tracked with final pH, and age judged from teeth also correlated. Glucose from a portable meter did not match laboratory values or predict pH. Patterns differed between castrated and intact males. Practical screening before slaughter may need laboratory-grade measures rather than quick meter readings.
pmc-13264279:
Marutpong Panya and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on sugars from two farmed mushrooms, Lentinus polychrous and Lentinus squarrosulus. Mushroom sugars can act as prebiotics, foods that feed gut germs. The team tested whether crude extracts change the mix of bacteria from human stool in a lab model.

After fake digestion in the lab, much of both extracts stayed intact, which suggests they could reach the colon. In the test jars, the extracts raised helpful groups such as Bacteroides and Parabacteroides. They also lowered pH and two ratios used to sum up gut balance. One group, Fusobacterium, rose too, and the authors say its role needs more study before claims are made.
pmc-13264579:
Damla Atay and Ozlem Ozmen wrote a 2026 study of budgerigars, small pet parrots, struck by a fungal gut disease. The fungus mainly attacks the proventriculus, a part of the bird stomach. Little was known about local immune signals in birds that catch the disease in the wild, so the team examined stored tissues.

They studied gut tissues from 25 infected birds and 5 healthy controls. Damage centered on the proventriculus, with surface erosion, ulcers, worn cells, and clusters of immune cells near many fungal growths. A signal protein called TNF-alpha showed up in surface and immune cells in the damaged areas. Healthy tissues showed little or none. The authors say this gives a baseline for later work on immune pathways in this disease.
pmc-13264879:
Jennifer M Gurney wrote a 2026 review on using whole blood to revive trauma patients who are bleeding heavily. Bleeding is the top cause of death from injuries that could be survived, in both war and civilian care. Modern blood banks split blood into parts for storage ease, yet whole blood matches the body's needs more closely, she argues.

The review sums up military and civilian proof for whole blood, including fresh blood gathered from walking donors at the scene and stored low-titer group O blood used in civilian centers. It traces how practice swung from whole blood to parts and back. Gurney backs a layered approach and more prehospital use. She notes no direct trials yet compare fresh and stored whole blood, and that fresher blood strains blood bank logistics.
pmc-13264979:
Yue Ma and colleagues published a 2026 study sorting Chinese children with ADHD into subgroups to guide tailored nursing care. ADHD varies widely between children, so one-size care fits poorly. The team grouped 403 newly diagnosed, untreated children by behavior, emotion, and social function, then checked the groups with an objective attention test.

Three types emerged. A functionally balanced type made up 25.8 percent, an impulsivity-led type 55.6 percent, and an emotion and cognition dysregulation type 18.6 percent. On the attention test, the impulsivity-led group made the most errors of acting too soon. The dysregulation group showed the most variable response times. The authors say pairing parent-rated grouping with test proof gives a base for precision nursing paths.
pmc-13265079:
Anurag Mantri and co-authors published this case report in 2026. A woman of sixty-eight had shingles, the painful rash from the chickenpox virus waking up, along two nerve bands of the neck. After the rash, the same zone swelled, hurt, and lost function. Those signs, judged by the Budapest rules, fit complex regional pain syndrome, a rare sequel of shingles that doctors often miss.

The far more common sequel is lasting nerve pain, and this syndrome can hide behind it. Care mixed nerve pain drugs, physical therapy, and support, and her state eased step by step. The authors stress that the syndrome is under-known in poorer lands, where shingles care may stop at the rash. They urge doctors to recheck patients whose pain shifts into swelling and stiffness after shingles.
pmc-13265179:
Chenguang Zhang and colleagues compare two cancers of the maxillary sinus using a United States registry, in a 2026 study. Adenoid cystic carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma behave differently in this rare site. Direct survival comparisons have been limited. Cases diagnosed from 2004 to 2019 were analysed.

Survival was clearly better for adenoid cystic carcinoma at three and five years. Older age, advanced tumour stage, and lack of surgery predicted worse outcomes. Radiotherapy linked to improved survival. A model built from these factors discriminated well between patients. The results can help clinicians counsel patients and plan treatment for each subtype.
pmc-13265679:
Niyaz Mostafa, Esther Hong, and Thomas Stewart review isotretinoin's effects on thyroid blood tests, in a 2026 meta-analysis. The acne drug is highly effective, while thyroid findings have conflicted. Studies from 1980 to 2025 were searched across four databases. Studies reporting thyroid measures before and during treatment qualified.

Fifteen studies were included. Pooled results showed a tiny rise in thyroid-stimulating hormone after treatment. Two thyroid hormones fell modestly. Variation between studies was substantial for some measures. Evidence on thyroid antibodies was limited and inconsistent. The authors note statistical changes whose clinical importance remains uncertain, given observational designs.
pmc-13265879:
Yan Cui and co-authors searched for the best feed mix for a Chinese breed of laying hen during its peak laying period. Three feed factors were varied: energy, protein, and lysine, an amino acid hens must get from food. Too little of any factor cuts egg output, while too much wastes money and burdens the birds.

The trial used 450 hens, twenty weeks old, split into fifteen groups under a statistical design that maps how factors interact. Each mix ran for twelve weeks, with egg output and egg quality recorded. Mapping the surface of responses shows which blend gives strong laying without waste. The results give feed makers for this breed a tested target instead of trial and error.
pmc-13266179:
Youness Touissi and Eric Vallender scanned human brain gene switches in two thousand twenty-six. Human brain change likely ran through shifts in gene control. Such changes alter how genes work, not proteins themselves. The team used hundreds of primate genomes. They tested brain-active switches for signs of selection found only in humans. Thousands of switches showed positive selection signals.

Genes near those switches were not the same in activity versus macaques. Gaps showed in fetal and adult stages. Always-on switches held more psychiatric risk variants. Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder links stood out. Evolution may have traded brain power for weakness. The work connects those roots to modern mental illness.
pmc-13266879:
Ting Cheng and colleagues test in 2026 whether automated CT measurements can track pneumonia outbreaks in a population. Software measured the volume of infected lung tissue in scans from 209 pneumonia patients and 221 healthy controls. The infected share of lung volume separated the groups almost perfectly, giving clear cutoff values for calling a scan positive.

The team then applied the method to tens of thousands of emergency and outpatient scans collected across a year that included the late 2022 COVID wave in China. Weekly counts of positive scans moved closely with other surveillance signals, and estimated case volume led regional pneumonia deaths by about a week. Scan-based tracking could give health systems an early, objective outbreak signal.
pmc-13267079:
Mark A Iron examines in 2026 a mathematical shortcut that quantum chemists use to estimate results for an infinitely large basis set, the ideal limit of their calculations. Real calculations must use finite sets of functions, which leaves a known kind of error. Extrapolation from two finite calculations is a standard fix inside high-accuracy schemes for chemical energies.

Iron shows that three popular extrapolation formulas all reduce to the same simpler correction, so their differences are mathematically meaningless. A factor from any one scheme can be converted into the factors of the others. He also reports ready-to-use factors for coupled-cluster methods and for selected double-hybrid density functionals, and finds that borrowing factors across methods costs little accuracy on test sets.
pmc-13267979: Juan Antonio Álvaro de la Parra and colleagues' study of Holter reading software in three Spanish hospitals is the subject of a 2026 correction. The 2025 paper reported wide benefits from the software. The correction changes no results. It restores two university affiliations that were left out: one doctoral school affiliation for the first author, and one doctoral program affiliation for Cristina Caramés, both at the Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. The affiliations are now added and the rest renumbered.
pmc-13268079:
H A Z Boktor and colleagues present a 2026 letter describing drug-resistant TB in a refugee family with an inherited immune weakness. The family lived in a Syrian refugee camp in Jordan. The letter's first case is a girl born in 2015 who developed a swollen lymph node in her armpit months after the BCG vaccine, a TB shot given to newborns.

Her node illness returned again and again over the years despite several treatment courses. Tests later found rifampicin-resistant TB germs in a node sample, and the node was removed. By age seven she had fluid in her belly, swollen inner nodes, and a blocked portal vein, and she began a modern drug-resistant TB regimen. The letter links her course to a genetic susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, social vulnerability, and limited program capacity in emergency settings.
pmc-13269179:
Keevan Singh and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a young woman found, just before gynecologic surgery, to have cold urticaria. In this rare condition, cold triggers hives and can even close the airway. Operating rooms hold many cold triggers, from fluids to skin cleaners.

Her history showed repeated cold-linked symptoms, including one past episode that hinted at airway trouble. A cold test later confirmed the diagnosis. The team limited cold contact and gave allergy and steroid drugs before surgery. Cold cleaner on her belly still raised local hives during the operation, but she stayed stable and recovered well. The authors stress asking patients about cold symptoms.
pmc-13269479:
Dhruba Pariyar Damay and Angela Peace published a mathematics paper in 2026 modeling plant disease together with soil nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus. Plants need these nutrients to grow, and disease can change how nutrients cycle back. Their model links plant growth, infection, and nutrient supply in a forest setting.

The five-part model lets infection spread faster or slower depending on nutrient levels. Analysis and computer runs showed that nutrient-rich conditions lowered the bar for disease to persist. Enrichment also brought on repeating boom-and-bust cycles sooner, with larger swings. Higher spread rates likewise lowered the nutrient level needed for persistence. The authors say ignoring nutrient feedback gives a misleading picture of outbreak risk.
pmc-13269979:
Saudah Dibaji and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on critical care nurses at King Fahad Hospital in Jazan, Saudi Arabia, and how emotional intelligence relates to patient safety. Emotional intelligence means reading and managing feelings at work. A survey of 132 nurses was run in August and September 2024.

Average emotional intelligence was high, at 3.91 on a five-point scale, and safety practice scores averaged 3.73. The two measures moved together strongly, with a correlation of 0.68. Links held across the background variables tested. The authors conclude that emotionally intelligent nurses deliver safer care in high-stress units. They present emotional skills as a real determinant of safety, not a soft extra.
pmc-13270079:
Praveen Thumbikat and co-authors trace chronic prostate pain to epigenetic marks that muffle the immune system's own brakes. Chronic prostatitis and pelvic pain syndrome is common and disabling, with no clear cause. Their 2026 study examines immune cells from patients' urine and blood, profiling both cell behavior and DNA methylation, the chemical tags that silence genes.

Patient samples showed more activated helper T cell signals and altered methylation at several immune control genes, including the gene for IL-10, a calming cytokine. Patient cells secreted too little IL-10 when provoked, and a demethylating drug restored the response. In a mouse model of the disease, giving IL-10 alone failed to ease pelvic pain, but the demethylating drug cut pain sensitivity. The authors propose that the marks, not missing signals, are the fault, and that erasing them is a plausible therapy.
pmc-13270879:
Alshahwan, Aljohany, Alkandari, and Alsaedi reported in twenty twenty-six a grave eye infection after a drain implant for eye press ill in a man aged seventy-seven. Such implants help when drugs and plain cuts fail, but rare germ ills can follow. Twelve days after a smooth surgery he came in with eye pain, lid swell, and sight cut to light sense.

Scans showed thick eye coats, cloud in the gel, and swell of the eye socket. Germ drugs in the eye and by mouth, plus a gel cut, were all used in his care. No germ grew from his samples in the lab. His sight rose to a fair line by the last check.
pmc-13271879:
Makoto Tokunaga is lead author of a 2026 journal article on predicting stroke patients' independence at discharge. Independence is measured by the motor part of the Functional Independence Measure. That is a standard score of how much help a person needs with daily movement tasks. The question was whether updating the prediction one month into rehabilitation sharpens it.

The study included 849 stroke patients in a recovery rehabilitation ward. Four statistical models were compared: predicting the discharge score directly or via predicted improvement, each with or without first-month progress data. Average prediction error fell from 9.3 points for the basic direct model to 6.3 for the updated improvement model. Predicting improvement and converting it back beat direct prediction, and updating at one month helped both routes.
pmc-13272079:
Xuan Zhang and coauthors profile in 2026 male hormone patterns in adolescent girls with polycystic ovary syndrome. Excess androgens drive many features of the condition, but whether they come mainly from the ovaries or adrenal glands in teenagers was unclear. Precise hormone measurement combined with a suppression test can separate the sources.

Thirty-seven patients and twenty-two healthy peers gave samples for full steroid profiling, and twenty-four patients took the suppression test. Many androgens ran high in patients while a binding protein that lowers free hormone ran low. A calculated free androgen index separated the groups best, serving as a strong diagnostic marker.
pmc-13272179:
Mayank Maan and coauthors review in 2026 how skin is built, how wounds heal, and why some wounds stall. Skin is a barrier, immune organ, and sense organ at once, so repair must coordinate many cell types. Acute wounds usually heal in orderly phases, while chronic wounds freeze in inflammation.

Foot ulcers in diabetes, vein-related leg ulcers, and pressure injuries share enzyme imbalance, aged cells, poor blood vessel growth, and bacterial films. The review sets acute and chronic healing side by side, tracing immune signals and matrix remodeling in each. Less common wounds from radiation or autoimmune disease are also covered, along with treatment strategies that target the stall.
pmc-13272479:
Gong-Han Tu and coauthors forecast in 2026 how climate and land use change will move the habitat of an endangered Himalayan medicinal plant, Sinopodophyllum hexandrum. The plant's current stronghold hugs the eastern edge of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, mostly in Sichuan, Tibet, and Gansu at high altitude. Conservation planning needs to know where suitable ground will remain.

Using 268 location records and a tuned distribution model, the team mapped current suitable area at over a million square kilometers. Warming scenarios pushed suitable ground northwest and uphill, expanding total area by the 2090s under the strongest warming path. Altitude and the coldest month's minimum temperature drove the pattern most.
pmc-13272579:
Thuan Ha and co-authors produced a cropland mask dataset for the Canadian Prairies in a 2026 data article. Knowing which land stays in crops year after year supports farm monitoring, yield models, and land use studies. Their mask covers Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba at fine detail.

They built the data from Google satellite embedding imagery, using Canada's annual crop inventory to teach a random forest classifier. Yearly maps from 2017 to 2024 were made at ten meter resolution across the whole region. Years were then combined, and land cropped for more than two straight years was marked as stable cropland. The result is shared as map files ready for soil, climate, and machine learning work.
pmc-13272679:
Yixin Chen and Helmut Grubmuller present a 2026 model of F1-ATPase, the spinning enzyme part that makes ATP, the cell's main energy carrier. Their aim was the smallest model that still matches how the enzyme links chemistry, binding, and rotation, and stays consistent with energy rules. They tested many variants to find it.

After checking over 14,000 model variants, they found that four distinct shapes of one subunit are needed for a working model. The model settles a long debate by showing two reaction paths can both occur, depending on ATP levels. It also suggests a ratchet-like motion that can explain rotations larger than the usual step.
pmc-13272779:
Mohammod Hafizur Rahman leads a 2026 study of biochar made from the plant Lantana camara for removing a black dye, Acid Black 172, from wastewater. Dye waste from textile work is toxic and resists natural breakdown. The team described the biochar's surface and pores, then tested dye uptake under varied acidity, time, dose, and heat.

Removal was best at pH 3 and reached balance within 90 minutes, with a top capacity of 303.03 milligrams per gram. The process was spontaneous and took in heat, following a pattern tied to chemical binding. After five reuse cycles the biochar still removed over 91 percent of dye, supporting its use as a low-cost, reusable cleaner.
pmc-13272879:
Sudip Phuyal leads a 2026 review of dynamic consent for reuse of health data under European law. Dynamic consent lets people adjust, in detail and over time, how their data may be reused, including taking consent back. Static or broad consent fits poorly in complex digital systems, the authors argue.

European privacy law supports specific and revocable consent, but national differences and weak cross-border withdrawal tools are barriers. A new European health data space law, phasing in from 2029, shifts many uses toward approval by access bodies. The authors propose a three-stage system for consent administration, decisions, and enforcement, while warning about cost, consent fatigue, and digital divides.
pmc-13273179:
Ziying Wang leads a 2026 study of a stretchable skin electrode inspired by kirigami, the art of paper cutting, for recording heart signals during daily life. Electrodes must stick closely to skin while a person moves and sweats, or signals become noisy. The device layers a cut copper electrode between adhesive and protective films.

The design is soft, fills a high area, keeps stable contact while moving, and sticks reliably, the authors report. It collected electrocardiogram signals in real time during daily activities, with strong resistance to sweat and motion artifacts. They position it for dynamic human-machine interfaces, where stable skin contact during exercise has limited earlier static designs.
pmc-13273379:
Parmar and six co-authors screened schoolchildren in Ahmedabad, India, in twenty twenty-six for two enamel defects that weaken young teeth. In these conditions the enamel forms soft and chalky, so teeth chip and ache, and early spotting lets dentists protect them.

The team examined one thousand eight hundred sixty children aged seven to eleven across five zones of the city, using European diagnostic rules. About two percent had the defect in their first permanent molars and front teeth. The baby-tooth version appeared in only a handful of children, about a quarter of one percent. Most cases were mild. Neither defect favored boys or girls, and rates did not shift across the age range. The authors say the low rates should not breed complacency, since damaged enamel can decay fast. They urge routine checks in school dental programs.
pmc-13273479:
Canyu Chen and co-authors reviewed ways to revive muscle stem cells in age related sarcopenia in a 2026 article. Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. Satellite cells, the stem cells that repair muscle, dwindle and weaken over time, which feeds the decline.

The review covers how satellite cells change with age and what current treatments offer. Electrical stimulation of nerves and muscle can wake these cells, partly through calcium signals inside them. Calcium also steers their growth and specialization directly. The authors therefore propose pairing stimulation with calcium signaling modulation so the two reinforce each other. They present the combined plan as a promising direction that still needs direct testing in older muscle.
pmc-13273879:
Berginström and colleagues examine brain links tied to pain and fatigue in chronic pain patients. Their 2026 journal article uses resting state fMRI scans. Participants also performed a twenty-minute attention task designed to tire them.

The study included 24 women with chronic pain. It also included 22 healthy controls of similar age. Patients reported more fatigue and pain than controls. Before the task, the groups differed in several brain networks. The default mode network showed the clearest gaps. After the task, most group gaps could no longer be seen. Only links between the basal ganglia and frontal areas remained distinct. Pain-linked gaps showed up mainly before the task. Fatigue-linked gaps showed up after the task. The authors suggest fatigue can crowd out pain in brain activity.
pmc-13274879:
Hala Sanad and a large team present a 2026 journal article on poor sleep among kidney dialysis patients in Bahrain. Dialysis keeps people with failed kidneys alive but strains daily life, and sleep often suffers. The team surveyed 174 patients at one of the country's main dialysis centers using a standard sleep quality questionnaire.

A striking ninety-one percent of patients scored as poor sleepers. Several factors clustered with worse sleep: older age, poorer self-rated health, anemia, large weight gains between sessions, pain after dialysis, and taking sleep medication. The authors argue the problem is multifactorial and urge clinics to build sleep checks, mental health screening, and support education into routine kidney care.
pmc-13274979:
David Kalmbach and co-authors test two talking therapies for insomnia in pregnancy in a trial published in 2026. Poor sleep in pregnancy often pairs with bad sleep habits and troubled mood. Two treatments are known to ease the insomnia itself, but their wider benefits were unclear.

Sixty-four pregnant women with clinical insomnia were assigned to cognitive-behavioral therapy, a mindfulness-based program, or basic sleep hygiene teaching. Both therapies cut bedtime procrastination sharply and lifted positive mood. In women with anxiety symptoms, both also eased anxiety strongly. The mindfulness program, unlike the other therapy, reduced rumination focused on insomnia. Neither changed negative mood or mindfulness scores. Patients praised the sleep strategies, meditation, and respect for pregnancy in the programs.
pmc-13275679:
Wuliji Batu and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of formononetin, a plant compound, in acute lung injury. The injury is a sudden inflammatory lung condition with few treatment options. The team asked whether the compound protects the lungs by acting through the gut-lung axis.

Mice with chemically induced lung injury received the compound, and lung plus gut tissues were examined closely. Treatment reduced tissue damage and lowered inflammatory signals in both organs. Gut microbe analysis linked the benefit with shifts in Parabacteroides, a bacterial genus. Chemical profiling pointed to bile acid handling and ABC transporter pathways, which the authors flag for follow-up work.
pmc-13276279:
Soledad Perez Santangelo and Richard Macknight present a 2026 journal article on the genes that tell a legume when to flower. Flowering time decides yield and fit to local seasons. Their plant, Medicago truncatula, is a small forage legume used as a research model for crops like alfalfa and peas.

The plant carries six copies of a flowering gene family called FT. Using gene editing, the team knocked out one or two of the copies. Plants missing one copy flowered normally. Plants missing both were late only under long days, while still responding to a cold spell as usual. Gene activity scans showed the pair switches on other flowering genes under long days. The authors say the two genes back each other up, a finding that may guide forage breeding.
pmc-13276779:
Hind Moukham and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a yeast energy sensor that controls its own location in the cell. The sensor, called SNF1 in yeast and AMPK in animals, orchestrates responses when glucose runs out. It is switched on by partner kinases, chief among them Sak1, which itself carries many marks from the sensor.

Live imaging of single cells showed the sensor rushing into the nucleus right after glucose vanished, then drifting out again. That entry depended on Sak1. In a mutant whose Sak1 cannot receive the sensor's marks, the sensor entered the nucleus more and stayed more active there. Those cells also adapted better to glucose scarcity. A nuclear activity reporter confirmed stronger signaling. The authors conclude the sensor fine-tunes itself by marking its own activator, a feedback loop for metabolic stress.
pmc-13277079:
Robert S Krauss wrote a 2026 profile marking Elizabeth Chen's election to the United States National Academy of Sciences on April 28, 2026. Chen, an editorial board member of the journal Skeletal Muscle, was honored for her work on how cells fuse with each other. Her path ran from Jilin, China, to graduate study in the United States.

Working first on fruit flies, Chen found genes needed for muscle cells to merge and form fibers. Her group helped show that actin, a cell skeleton protein, must gather at fusion sites for merging to occur. She later led labs at Johns Hopkins and then in Texas. The profile traces how a basic question in fly development grew into a broad account of cell fusion.
pmc-13277779:
Ross E MacKenzie and colleagues probe the reducing power of divalent rare-earth metal complexes in a 2026 chemistry study. These complexes can donate electrons strongly enough to create bonding patterns found nowhere else. Tuning that power requires knowing what truly drives their reactions.

Seven metals, from yttrium to lutetium, were compared in identical frames. Measured potentials suggested none should reduce the nitrogen ring compounds tested. Yet four complexes did react, joining the rings into dimers and forming radical species. The mismatch implies that binding to the metal switches on the reduction, rather than raw potential alone. Spectra confirmed the radical products, and the work sharpens how chemists design such reactions.
pmc-13278679:
Jean-Philippe R Krieg leads a 2026 study of muscle loss and disease progression in pancreatic cancer, using CT scans over time. Sarcopenia, loss of muscle mass and strength, predicts worse outcomes in cancer. The team studied 62 patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma who had at least three scans over a year, measuring a hip muscle index and extracting image texture features.

Muscle-based sarcopenia affected about forty-five percent of patients by standard cutoffs. The muscle index fell from baseline to three months, then held steady, with women consistently lower. Machine learning models predicted sarcopenia fairly and predicted progression status at twelve months with good accuracy from baseline image features. Muscle and image measures may add prognostic value beyond tumor readings alone.
pmc-13278779:
Mohannad N AbuHaweeleh and Salvatore Rabito present a 2026 case report of a rare benign tumor beside the testicle in a 49-year-old motocross athlete. Such tumors, called paratesticular leiomyomas, grow from smooth muscle near the testicle and are usually slow and painless. He arrived with progressive scrotal enlargement causing discomfort, and exam found a large encapsulated mass pushing the testes aside.

Scans showed a large mixed lesion with new blood vessel growth. Surgeons removed the mass and reshaped the scrotum, sparing the testicle. Tissue tests showed benign spindle cells, a low growth marker, and stains supporting smooth muscle origin. Recognition of this tumor type supports testis-sparing surgery and strong outcomes without long surveillance, the authors say.
pmc-13278879:
Lamiaa Hamad Al-Jamea and a large team study leptin gene variants and blood measures in obese Saudi adults, in a 2026 paper. Saudi Arabia carries one of the region's heaviest obesity burdens. Leptin is a hormone made by fat tissue that helps regulate appetite and weight.

Two hundred two adults took part, split between obese and non-obese groups, with full blood profiling for both. Obese participants showed higher white cell and platelet counts, with lower red cell measures that deepened across obesity classes. Sequencing found two leptin gene variants of interest. One variant roughly doubled obesity risk odds and tracked with higher white cell counts. The other appeared only in obese participants, in a small share.
pmc-13279079:
Alireza Azizpour and colleagues published a 2026 study of social camouflaging in teens with social communication disorder, a condition that makes conversation rules and implied meaning hard to handle. Camouflaging means hiding those difficulties by copying others, rehearsing replies, or forcing oneself to fit in. The study compared 60 teens with the disorder against 60 matched peers aged 14 to 18 in Iran's Fars province, using a standard questionnaire.

Teens with the disorder reported far more of this hiding than peers across all three measured strategies: compensation, masking, and assimilation. Boys reported more than girls, a pattern the authors note runs against much of the autism literature. Since such hiding has been tied to anxiety, depression, and exhaustion in related groups, the authors urge clinicians to ask about its emotional cost. Recognizing the hidden effort behind fitting in could shape kinder assessment and support.
pmc-13279279:
Zhonghua Ma and colleagues report a 2026 study of high pressure in the skull in patients who are not obese. The illness, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, means high fluid pressure with no clear cause. Most cases link to obesity, so the lean form is less well known. Records came from one centre for the years 2015 to 2023.

The team compared eighty two non obese patients with ninety six obese patients from two hundred fifty two cases in all. The non obese group was older on average. They showed fewer scan signs of high pressure, yet worse sight loss. The split shows lean patients form a distinct group that needs care in its own right. Risk facts for the lean form still need more work.
pmc-13279379:

One model beat doctors on pre cancer cases, while doctors led on hard cases with unclear tissue results. The pilot hints at help, not replacement, in cervix care.
pmc-13280279:
Deepa Malhotra and co-authors weigh how harsh each Omicron strain of the COVID virus has been, in a global review from 2026. New strains keep coming, and teams need fresh proof on how sick each one makes people. The review set hospital stays, intensive care, and death as its core marks.

pmc-13280579:
Tarek Zieneldien offers a 2026 poem, Kaleidoscopes in the ICU, set in an intensive care unit. A patient explains that her world has fractured in a chapel window, with colours and faces multiplied like saints. Her chart names the chief complaint as kaleidoscope vision. The poem frames it not as hallucination, but excess truth: too many angles of the same fear. Her spoken history names a deeper complaint, not having enough time to watch her granddaughter grow up.

pmc-13280779:
Jimenez and colleagues surveyed Helicobacter bacteria in captive baboons and tested a treatment. pmc-13280979:

pmc-13281379:

pmc-13281879:

pmc-13282179:

pmc-13282279:

Campylobacter bacteria are a leading cause of food-linked diarrhoea, often passed through undercooked poultry. pmc-13282379:

pmc-13282479:

This solid-state method grows fungi on moist solids rather than in liquid.

It tracked overall intensity and sweet, baked, and grassy notes well. Fungal notes such as fruity and earthy were predicted more weakly. pmc-13282879:

Gene tests in the two bacteria checked genes for biofilm growth and cell talk. Such oils may one day help weak drugs work better.
pmc-13282979:
Yuting Wu and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on lens power formulas for cataract surgery in keratoconus. The letter responds to a review and network analysis by Aljahdali and colleagues. Keratoconus warps the cornea, so lens choice before surgery is hard to get right.
