Automated RAPID software, available in nine of those fifteen, flagged alterations in five patients missed by qualitative reading, with all showing Tmax above four seconds. Male sex and aphasic aura were associated with perfusion alterations, and migraine with aura accounted for about 1% of stroke code activations. The authors conclude that automated analysis may sharpen acute diagnosis.
pmc-13327079:
Arbaaz Gill and team tracked United States public web interest in myopia-control glasses for kids around a key approval. Their 2026 study pulled weekly Google Trends search scores for 2025. It weighed parent-worded and brand terms before and after the Food and Drug Administration cleared Essilor Stellest on September 25, 2025. MiSight searches served as a same-time yardstick. A combined interest score averaged the chosen terms.

Mean combined interest rose from 9.39 before approval to 18.6 after approval, a rise of about 98%. The mean ratio to baseline rose from 0.353 at the start to 0.694 at the end over the same span. MiSight-linked searches stayed flat, which points to a Stellest-only response, not a broad trend. Scaling the scores points to growth past seasonal swings. The team warns web interest does not map straight to awareness, clinic use, or prescribing, but it may help doctors brace for more parent questions.
pmc-13328279:
Wenwen Liu and co-authors create new membrane-attacking antibacterials in a 2026 study. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off many standard drugs, so the team built a family of phthalazine-based quaternary ammonium salts, compounds 2a through 2v, whose chain length could be tuned. Lab tests weighed killing power, safety, and how the best compound works.

Compound 2n led the family, stopping S. aureus, its resistant form, and two other species at 2 μg/mL in the minimum inhibitory tests reported, while sparing red blood cells up to far higher levels. It killed fast, resisted breakdown, and slowed biofilms, and probes showed torn membranes leaking cell contents, with DNA binding as a possible second hit.
pmc-13329979:
Alison Carroll and colleagues show light-driven storage of hydrogen in propane in a 2026 study. Storing hydrogen in chemical bonds avoids high pressure tanks. Propane is cheap and widely available, so the team tested turning propylene into propane at room temperature and pressure with a light-powered catalyst.

The catalyst pairs aluminium light catchers with titanium oxide and single platinum atoms. Light at 450 and 800 nm both drove strong propane output in the reported tests. Theory showed that light-made carriers at either colour hold enough energy for both reaction steps, splitting hydrogen and adding it across the carbon bond. Paired with earlier light-driven release, the cycle could store and free hydrogen under mild conditions.
pmc-13330479:
Pengyu Zhao and Shuai Geng pool studies on pharmacist care in China amid a shift from dispensing to patient care in a 2026 meta-analysis. Searches ran across eight databases to April 2026 for trials and comparison studies of pharmacist work such as prescription review and counselling. Bias was checked with standard tools.

In total, 32 studies entered the pool, with only 5 randomised trials among them. Pharmacist input linked to more single-drug antibiotic use and more sound prescriptions, and to fewer irrational prescriptions in the reported odds values. Spread between studies was wide, which limits exactness. The authors call the gains promising but early, and urge strong trials with patient-centred outcomes.
pmc-13330579:
Yi Zhang and colleagues trace the family history of STAYGREEN genes in tobacco plants in a 2026 study. Those genes steer chlorophyll breakdown, which drives leaf yellowing, maturity, and crop quality. The team compared gene copies across flowering plants, with focus on Nicotiana, whose doubled genome history may have expanded the family.

Family trees placed tobacco copies inside a conserved flowering plant lineage, with extra copies matching the doubled genome past in the reported analysis. Gene activity differed across tissues. Core catalytic parts stayed tightly conserved, while end regions varied by lineage. Most copies kept signals that send the protein to chloroplasts, though strength varied. The work frames how leaf ageing stays stable yet flexible.
pmc-13332579:
Danny R Vesevick and colleagues test 2026 whether the experimental drug RNS60 protects upper motor neurons in a mouse model of ALS with TDP-43 pathology. TDP-43 pathology appears widely in the cortex of people with ALS. RNS60 had previously improved mitochondrial growth and function in other preclinical models. The team treated TDP-43 mice and control mice, both with upper motor neurons marked by green fluorescent protein, with RNS60 or placebo every other day from day 30 to day 90.

Brain and spinal cord inflammation, mitochondrial structure, mitochondrial function, and neuromuscular junction health were measured. RNS60 cut the share of defective mitochondria in upper motor neurons sharply, from about half in untreated diseased mice to about one fifth in treated mice. Junctions in leg and diaphragm muscles were also assessed. The work supports RNS60 as a mitochondrial-protective candidate in TDP-43 ALS, while stressing that mouse results must still pass human trials.
pmc-13333179:
Christopher Tom and colleagues report a 2026 case linking diffuse large B-cell lymphoma to Agent Orange exposure in a Vietnam veteran. Agent Orange is a toxic herbicide mixture containing dioxin, used widely during Vietnam fighting in the 1960s and 1970s. The patient was an older veteran who came in with a right neck mass that kept growing after heavy combat exposure to Agent Orange. He was diagnosed with stage I diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with locally advanced, bulky disease.

He was judged at higher risk for systemic disease given skin breakthrough at presentation. Additional labs showed prior hepatitis B infection with immunity, a virus also linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk and worse outcomes in large studies. He began six cycles of R-CHOP therapy: rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. The case adds to the exposure history clinicians should take when lymphoma appears in Vietnam veterans.
pmc-13333279:
Jean Pierre Díaz-Paz and co-authors present a labeled dataset in 2026 for cleaning speckle noise from Sentinel-1 radar images. Radar pictures are grainy by nature, and training smart filters requires matched noisy and clean examples, which are hard to build honestly.

The dataset holds 512 by 512 pixel radar tiles in both VV and VH polarizations, gathered worldwide through an automated Python and Google Earth Engine workflow with random sampling and quality filtering. For each spot, cleaner reference images were made by averaging stacks of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 passes, letting users study how averaging depth affects speckle removal. Land cover maps from ESA WorldCover v200 and a metadata file ride along, and benchmark scores including ENL, MSE, SSIM, and PSNR are supplied for sample tiles. The set is hosted on Mendeley Data as a reproducible training resource.
pmc-13333679:
Thomas Buttgereit and a large international team report on the first two years of the Chronic Angioedema Registry, known as CARE. Launched in October 2023, the registry gathers clinical and patient-reported data on recurrent angioedema of any type during routine care.

By December 2025, 550 patients had enrolled at 23 centers spread across 18 countries, meeting its early milestones on time. Hereditary angioedema and mast cell related forms were among the diagnoses tracked. A survey of physicians in the specialist center network explored why centers join or hold back, and how communication could improve. The report shows a global registry for a rare swelling condition can grow steadily, while naming practical barriers that slow wider participation.
pmc-13333779:
Jin Han and co-authors looked at ligustilide, a natural compound from Angelica sinensis and Ligusticum chuanxiong, for central nervous system disorders in a 2026 article. Ligustilide draws interest for calming inflammation, fighting oxidation, and protecting nerves.

Three sources were searched for studies through October 2025, and 55 original studies were left after screening. Evidence links the compound to help in ischemic stroke, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, traumatic brain injury, and anxiety disorders. Its effects run through pathways including PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-kB, and Nrf2/ARE, lowering oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and mitochondrial failure. The review also covers how the body absorbs and clears ligustilide and what safety data exist, sketching what stands between the compound and clinical use.
pmc-13333879:
Luqing Zhao and co-authors study how hairline cracks in loess soil reshape its inner pore network, in a 2026 paper. Shallow loess collapses threaten roads and railways in loess regions, and millimeter cracks steer the earliest damage. Samples with cracks of varied depth, tilt, and combination were squeezed in a press while CT scans watched the pores.

Machine learning rebuilt the pore networks in 3D for measurement. Cracked samples reached the first damage stage at far lower stress, with cuts of roughly 68 to 83 percent depending on crack layout. Small pores multiplied while large ones shrank, and pores near the horizontal and vertical took heavy damage. The maps link crack patterns to the strength and seepage of loess ground.
pmc-13333979:
Removing a bone tumor that has crept into a joint can go wrong if the capsule tears and tumor-laced joint fluid spills. Yuki Funauchi and co-authors review in 2026 thirty-six osteosarcoma patients who had such extra-articular resections, calling the leaky ones inadequate. Nine of thirty-six, a quarter, leaked.

Five-year local control ran 95.5 percent after clean surgery but only seventy-five percent after a leak. Leaks clustered in patients whose tumors had answered chemotherapy poorly, and their margins tended to run thinner. The authors warn that weak chemotherapy response predicts surgical trouble and costs local control, urging extra care in those cases.
pmc-13334079:
Jeong-Ah Yoon and co-authors tested a candidate probiotic strain, Pediococcus acidilactici MBEL10321, in a 2026 study pairing lab tests with genome sequencing. The strain came from Nuruk, a classic Korean fermentation starter.

In culture the strain survived acid and bile salts well and held back several pathogens, beating two control strains, among them Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus cereus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Staphylococcus aureus. It showed no blood-cell-breaking activity. Its genome spans 2,044,106 base pairs with 1,980 protein-coding genes, and screens found no virulence factors, no drug resistance genes, and no transferable plasmid replicons. The paired safety and function evidence backs the strain as a probiotic candidate for food or supplement use.
pmc-13334879:
Nerve pain after injury is hard to treat, and most research blames neurons. Qiao and seven co-authors look instead at oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap nerves in myelin. In mice with a nerve injury mimicking this pain, myelin broke down and a protein called PDK1 fell in the central nervous system. Mice engineered to lack PDK1 only in these wrapping cells developed the same pain signs: soreness to touch and heat.

Gene readings showed PDK1 loss harms myelination through a chain involving c-Myc and SOX10. Boosting remyelination with a drug, or quieting c-Myc with a gene tool, repaired the nerve wrapping and eased the pain in those mice. The authors name PDK1 upkeep in oligodendrocytes as a key guard against nerve pain. They propose tuning c-Myc as a fresh treatment strategy.
pmc-13334979:
Chenhui He and co-authors built an ultrasound-driven sticky hydrogel for infected wounds in a 2026 materials study. Long-term infected wounds resist treatment because bacteria persist, tissue states vary, and antibiotics lose ground.

Their hydrogel, PA-ZA, embeds tiny composites of ZIF-8 studded with nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots in a polyacrylamide-alginate base. Set ultrasound, first at kilohertz then megahertz speeds, triggers tissue sticking, pushes nanoparticles through skin, and switches on sound-driven production of reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria. The gel proved body-safe and sped cell migration and blood vessel growth in vitro. In infected full-thickness wounds in animals, switching it on lowered bacterial burden, sped the end of inflammation, and hastened repair, with similar benefit in a deeper infection model.
pmc-13335479:
Patricia C Hernandez and co-authors showed how small molecules selectively block the DNA-chewing enzyme TREX1 in a 2026 structural biology study. TREX1 clears stray cytoplasmic DNA; losing it causes autoimmune disease, while blocking it in cancer cells can wake anti-tumor immunity.

X-ray crystallography revealed the inhibitors sitting in the active site, competing with the end of the DNA substrate and hydrogen-bonding to a conserved glutamate. Binding also locks a tyrosine, Tyr129, into an alternative pose that cannot grip DNA and opens a deep hydrophobic pocket that cradles part of the drug. That pocket explains why the compounds spare the close relative TREX2 and viral cousins. The structures give medicinal chemists a blueprint for selective TREX1 blockers.
pmc-13336379:
Jianya Luo and co-authors found a compound that resensitizes a dangerous hospital pathogen to an old antibiotic in a 2026 microbiology study. Acinetobacter baumannii shrugs off most drugs, and colistin, a last-resort option, is losing ground too.

A structure-based virtual screen against the bacterium's lipopolysaccharide transport system produced a somatostatin-like peptide, C4. Alone it barely kills, but with colistin the synergy is strong. Lipid and gene analyses showed C4 remodels the membrane, selectively building up phosphatidylglycerol and raising expression of mlaC, a phospholipid transport gene. Deleting mlaC erased both the lipid change and the synergy, while extra copies strengthened it. The work reveals membrane lipid management as a lever for rescuing colistin therapy.
pmc-13336779:
Zhaoqiang Jiang and a large team connect night shift work to higher blood pressure in a 2026 study of people and mice. Shift work scrambles the body clock, and the authors point to failing mitochondria, the cell's power units, as the main link. Mice on simulated night shifts developed higher pressure and disturbed clock genes such as PER1 and BMAL1.

The shifted mice also showed power-unit damage and oxidative stress. Human night workers showed the same pattern: longer shift exposure tracked with higher systolic and diastolic pressure and with disturbed clock and mitochondrial markers. The shared pathway helps explain the heart risks of night work and may guide ways to blunt them.
pmc-13336979:
Yiming Fu and colleagues study why windows for imaging the living mouse brain cloud over in a 2026 methods review and study. Thinned skull and clearing methods let multiphoton microscopes watch brain cells over time, yet image quality fades fast. Systematic tests with adaptive optics compared window types for lifespan, sharpness, and distortion.

Progressive skull regrowth emerged as the core limit across all types, steadily blurring signal and resolution. A local glucocorticoid delivery method stretched good performance to one month. Sealing the window with a drug-loaded hydrogel suppressed regrowth while keeping optics clear. The findings give labs a practical route to month-long, high-fidelity brain imaging and explain what ends it.
pmc-13338379:
Flor Hernandez and co-authors read whole genomes to test whether the endangered Hawaiian duck began as a hybrid, in work dated 2026. Mixing between species is now seen as a common force in evolution. The Hawaiian duck was long suspected to be a recent hybrid of the Laysan duck and the mallard.

The full genomes of all three ducks were compared. The Hawaiian duck's genome proved a mosaic of both parents, with more coming from the Laysan duck. Some regions carry alleles found only in the Hawaiian duck itself. The authors also deliver the first reference genomes for both island ducks, tools for their protection.
pmc-13339179:
Dawei Lin and colleagues studied mitral valve leakage in 2026 among patients receiving transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic regurgitation. Some patients also have functional mitral regurgitation, yet whether aortic valve replacement improves it and what predicts improvement was unknown. Patients treated at Zhongshan Hospital from June 2020 to June 2024 were enrolled.

Groups were split by whether mitral leakage improved one month after the procedure, and baseline, imaging, and follow up data were compared. Finding predictors helps heart teams counsel patients and plan extra mitral treatment when needed. The work refines expectations for combined valve disease treated by catheter.
pmc-13339779:
Chia-Heng Lin and colleagues compare victim choices among sexual offenders with and without severe mental illness in a 2026 forensic study. Court-referred evaluations in Taiwan from 2009 to 2022 supplied the records. Understanding pattern differences may sharpen risk assessment.

Among 86 men, 21 had psychotic or bipolar disorders and 65 did not as reported. Offenders with severe illness more often had adult and stranger victims in the reported comparisons, with odds near fourfold for each in adjusted models. Substance disorders were more common without severe illness. Small subgroup size urges caution, but distinct patterns suggest assessment should weigh diagnosis alongside victim history.
pmc-13341179:
How nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blockers protect the kidney from inside is reviewed by Eun Sil Koh and colleagues in 2026. Drugs such as finerenone cut albuminuria and improve outcomes in chronic kidney disease, but the exact vessel-level mechanics remain partly unclear.

The review gathers clinical and lab evidence on sodium handling and pressure inside the glomerulus. These drugs mildly increase sodium excretion, ease aldosterone-driven tightening of outgoing vessels, and restore feedback signals that guard against overfiltration. Whether they beat older steroidal blockers at fixing hyperfiltration is unproven. Their edge may instead be safety and tolerability that let patients stay on treatment.
pmc-13341479:
A gene that pushes colon cancer cells toward iron-driven death is studied by Haiying Sun and co-investigators in a 2026 analysis. RBMS3 had unclear significance, so the team mined pan-cancer and colon adenocarcinoma datasets, then validated findings in lab cultures.

Tumors expressed less RBMS3 than normal tissue, and low levels meant worse survival, supporting a tumor-suppressor role. Expression tracked with tumor stage, and adding it to staging improved a prognostic nomogram. Cell work showed M2 macrophages suppress RBMS3 through STAT3 signaling, weakening ferroptosis. The pathway names both a biomarker and a possible lever for treatment.
pmc-13341779:
Hudabia Murtaza, Ahmed Ibrahim, Quratul Ain and colleagues computed how squeezing a lutetium perovskite oxide changes its behaviour in 2026. Using the Wien2k code, they applied pressures from zero to 32 gigapascals in steps and tracked structure, elasticity and electronic properties.

The oxide stayed stable and ductile across the range, and it grew more mechanically uniform as pressure rose. Its electronic bandgap shrank from 5.02 to 2.69 electron volts, dragging its light absorption from the ultraviolet into visible light. That shift could suit the material to solar cells, photocatalysis, visible-light detectors and light-emitting diodes. The study is purely computational, so experiments would need to confirm the predicted tuning.
pmc-13342079:
Marta Neila-Montero and co-authors ask where brown bear sperm comes from to predict how well it survives freezing, a tool for banking the genes of wild species. Their 2026 study compares three sources: sperm taken from the epididymis, sperm caught before ejaculation, and full ejaculate. Freezing tolerance varies widely in wild animals, for reasons still unclear.

Before and after thawing, the team ran working checks, from motility to cell death and stress chemistry, plus a protein census. Epididymal sperm swam best at first but fell hardest after thawing. Ejaculated sperm started mid-pack yet kept the best quality after the freeze. The middle source declined more gently. Stress readings hinted why: the epididymal stock carried the highest baseline strain.
pmc-13342579:
Musalula Sinkala and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six genome-wide study comparing cardiovascular trait genetics across African and European ancestries in UK Biobank data. Genetic maps built mostly on Europeans transfer poorly to other populations. Blood pressure traits offered a test case at scale.

Hundreds of thousands of European-ancestry and several thousand African-ancestry participants were analyzed jointly across four traits. Hundreds of new variants appeared in Europeans and dozens in Africans. Crucially, the shared genetic control of the two blood pressure measures, dense in Europeans, was absent in Africans. Risk models clearly cannot simply cross populations.
pmc-13342679:
Dongheon Kang, Seon-Deok Eun, and Jiyoung Park pilot a community exercise program for stroke survivors in South Korea. Their 2026 trial targets lasting weakness in strength, balance, mobility, and fitness after hospital discharge. Such limits raise the risk of falls and injury during daily life at home.

Twenty adults with chronic stroke were assigned at random to an exercise group or a usual-activity control group. Seventeen finished the study. The exercise group trained twice a week for eight weeks in a supervised circuit program. Adherence was high and no adverse events occurred. Exploratory results pointed to gains across several function domains for the exercise group. Some gains lost statistical strength after adjustment, as expected in a small pilot.
pmc-13343979:
Shumin Fan and colleagues screened tag stripping enzymes in 2026 for regulators of IRF7, the master switch for immune signal output, above all in myeloid cells. Virus infection swiftly triggers immune signal output that boosts antiviral responses in infected and nearby cells. Tagging of IRF7 with ubiquitin is key to its activation, yet molecular routes stayed poorly mapped.

A gene screen with an siRNA library of human tag stripping enzymes named USP2 as a positive switch and OTUD5 as a negative switch for IRF7 activity. OTUD5 bound IRF7 and blocked its K63 linked ubiquitin tagging. The switches offer new levers for tuning immune signal responses in viral infection and autoimmunity.
pmc-13344079:
Sojiro Amamoto and colleagues told of a retrograde recanalisation case in 2026 in a 90 year old woman on haemodialysis with a blocked dialysis graft. Chronic total occlusion at the venous join of an arteriovenous graft resists endovascular treatment, above all when antegrade approach through the graft fails. The patient grew progressive access failure from occlusion reaching to the downstream basilic vein.

Antegrade recanalisation had failed and surgical revision seemed less desirable given advanced age, frailty, and fragile skin. Preprocedural ultrasound found a downstream basilic segment fit for retrograde puncture, and ultrasound guided retrograde treatment restored access. The case offers a swap route when standard graft routes fail in frail patients.
pmc-13346079:
Joyce Jebet and co-authors systematically review tools for screening mothers' mental health across Africa in 2026. Pregnancy and new motherhood carry heavy mental burdens that clinics rarely test for. The team gathered African studies from 2014 to 2024 to see which questionnaires actually get used and how they perform.

The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale dominated the shelf, with the PHQ-9 common in Ethiopia and the SRQ-20 favored in West Africa. Studies clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, with samples from 37 to 3,311 women. Disorders stay common yet under-detected, and the authors push for screening folded into routine mother-and-child visits, better staff training, and tools fitted to local culture.
pmc-13346679:
Alita Mrema and co-authors studied in 2026 factors linked to low mood in Tanzanian women living with both HIV and cervical cancer. Cervical cancer is the top cause of cancer death in women in sub-Saharan Africa. It hits women with HIV hardest. Yet the mental health load of both diagnoses is poorly charted in Tanzania.

The team surveyed 160 women at least three months after cervical cancer treatment from January to June 2024. They measured low mood, social support, HIV stigma, and coping, plus clinical and life details. Pinpointing which factors track with low mood can guide screening and support in clinics that already manage two hard illnesses. Mental health care need not stay an afterthought.
pmc-13346779:
Gabrielly Cristina Galvão Xavier and four co-authors tested a safer way in two thousand twenty-six to preserve anatomy specimens for teaching. Formaldehyde, the classic fixative, carries health risks. Their method, plastination, replaces fluids in tissue with a polymer, giving dry, odourless specimens that last. They tried polyvinyl acetate, a cheap and non-toxic polymer.

Bovine heart and kidney served as test specimens. A blend of the polymer with glycerol and acetic acid worked best. Specimens kept their shape and cell structure, with slightly darker colour and better heat stability than formalin-fixed samples. The team backs this polymer as a safe, low-cost swap.
pmc-13346879:
Kristína Burdová and thirteen co-authors ask whether blocked airways in sleep deepen brain shrinkage in early Parkinson's disease. Sleep apnea is known to raise the risk of mental decline on its own. The study scanned people with brand-new, untreated Parkinson's, some with moderate to severe apnea and some without, plus healthy controls. Fine-grained scans measured the volume of deep brain structures and of subfields inside the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub.

Patients with apnea showed a clear bilateral shrink of the hippocampus, concentrated in three named subregions. Controls with apnea showed no such pattern, so the effect tied to the combination of diseases rather than apnea alone. The authors suggest the pairing may drive early brain change in Parkinson's. They urge timely diagnosis and treatment of apnea to possibly slow mental decline.
pmc-13346979:
Lulu Guo, Reed Holyoak, and Udaya DeSilva give the first map of the viruses that live in a mammal's uterus, drawn from healthy mares. The uterus was long thought sterile, yet recent work shows a resident microbial community there. The viruses in that community had not been characterized in any mammal. Their 2026 study took samples from healthy mares and sequenced all viral genomes in them.

The haul held 513 non-redundant viral genomes above a size floor, a sparse but diverse set. Three in four represented novel species not in any database. The kinds spanned bacterial viruses, called phages, and a few viruses that live in animal cells. Antibiotic resistance genes sat in the mix, a hint that genes transfer between bacteria and viruses there. Predicted bacterial hosts for the phages matched past uterine microbiome work. The map opens a new field for horse and human health.
pmc-13347079:
Juan Huang and colleagues test whether walking patterns can flag thinking decline in Parkinson disease, in a diagnostic study published in 2026. Patients classed as normal, subjectively declining, or mildly impaired did timed up-and-go walks, both plain and with a second task. While a wearable system recorded 209 motion measures for each trial.

Extra measures captured how much the added mental task cost each walker. Several learning models were trained to sort the three groups, checked with cross-validation and a held-out set. Importance tools were used to show which gait features drove each call. The aim is a low-burden clinic test that spots early decline without long paper testing.
pmc-13347379:
Aarti Gupta and colleagues characterise a doped bismuth ferrite powder for cleaning toxic chromium from water with sunlight, in a study published in 2026. Praseodymium and cobalt were added into the crystal without forming second phases, shrinking grain size. A combined heat-based instrument read thermal flow, energy gap, and charge lifetime in one pass.

Moderate doping improved heat flow and charge separation, while heavy doping added trap sites that sped charge loss and slowed heat spread in the reported measures. Under plain sunlight the best powder cut the harmful chromium form by about 96 percent within 120 minutes, turning it toward a safer form. Linked structure and heat data guide tuning of such cleaners.
pmc-13347979:
Ayenew Genet and co-authors review emergency care for HIV-positive adults at a major hospital in Addis Ababa in a 2026 study. HIV care has improved worldwide, yet many patients in Ethiopia still arrive at emergency departments with advanced disease and severe infections. The team read electronic records for patients seen in the first half of 2025.

Just over one hundred patients were included, with women in the majority. Vomiting, diarrhea, and fatigue were the leading complaints. About one in seven died in the emergency department, and most stayed at least a day. Advanced disease stage, high white cell counts, and low hemoglobin each predicted death on their own. The authors urge that patients with these signs be triaged first for urgent, aggressive care.
pmc-13348579:
Yadav, Lashkari, and Deshpande compare two relaxation methods for recovery after cesarean birth. Both methods add to standard physical therapy exercise. The study tracks pain, bladder leaks, sleep quality, and daily tasks after lower segment surgery.

Forty-six women who had a cesarean will take part, split into two groups by chance. One group uses Benson's relaxation and the other uses Mitchell's relaxation. Both groups also get the standard exercise plan. Scores are taken before and after the program, with blinded data checks. The team expects gains across all four outcome areas.
pmc-13348679:
Bereket Sisay Gebremichael and three co-authors look for predictors of metabolic syndrome in people with type 2 diabetes in Ethiopia in this 2026 paper. The syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor blood fats and sugar control. In diabetic patients it raises the risk of heart disease and stroke.

The study compared one hundred thirty-two patients who had the syndrome with two hundred sixty-eight who did not, all at public hospitals in the Sidama Region. Older age, female sex, and city living each raised the odds. Higher income, a family history of high blood pressure, longer time with diabetes, and poor sugar control also raised them. The authors call for focused screening and lifestyle programs for diabetic patients in the region.
pmc-13348979:
Shuxin Zheng and co-authors study whether a slanted sacrum after spine surgery relates to uneven shoulders in teenagers with scoliosis, in a 2026 paper. The operation aims to straighten the spine and level the shoulders, yet uneven shoulders afterward disappoint many patients. The team followed 231 teenagers with double-curve patterns for at least two years after fusion surgery.

Patients left with uneven shoulders had, on average, a larger sacral slant than balanced patients. Among slant subgroups, those slanted to the right recovered shoulder balance best, alongside an adaptive change in a lower spine angle. Curve correction itself did not differ between groups. The authors caution that the link is an association, not proof of cause.
pmc-13349779:
Chao Gong and colleagues reported a cohort study in 2026 on whether HDL cholesterol levels predict outcomes in non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. They followed 297 patients who had cardiac magnetic resonance scans between 2017 and 2024.

Over a median 35 months of follow-up, 41 patients reached the main endpoint of death or heart transplant, and 97 reached a wider endpoint adding heart failure readmission. Lower HDL cholesterol was linked to higher risk in adjusted models, and patients with higher levels stayed event-free longer. Adjusting for estimated pulmonary artery pressure weakened the link somewhat. The authors propose HDL cholesterol as a cheap, routine marker for sorting risk in these patients.
pmc-13349979:
Jiahuan Tang and colleagues fine-tuned a multimodal GPT-4o model in 2026 to write diagnostic impressions for a tricky breast MRI finding. The finding is called non-mass enhancement. Earlier work showed public language models handled breast lesion grading poorly. This lesion type had never been singled out.

Records from 229 patients supplied scan images, reports, and clinical histories. Six model versions were built. Some were untuned. Others trained on text alone, or on images plus text. Their impressions were compared with three radiologists of differing experience. Other experts then graded the outputs. The study tests whether targeted training lifts AI reporting to a clinically useful level.
pmc-13350179:
Jiale Huang and colleagues used combined gene and chemistry profiling in 2026 to explain why blueberries fail after years in the same soil in Dalian, China. Soil was sampled around roots and away from them after zero, two, four, and six years of continuous cropping.

Microbial diversity fell steadily with cropping years, especially near roots, and communities separated clearly by period. Helpful microbe groups thinned while stress-tolerant ones grew, and soil chemistry showed accumulating compounds harmful to the plants themselves. The picture blames a sickened soil community plus self-poisoning as twin drivers of the decline, pointing growers toward soil restoration rather than more fertiliser.
pmc-13350279:
Gupta and four co-authors grade bite force and speech cross false-teeth types in this twenty twenty-six study. Tooth loss cuts chew force and can blur speech for years. Each teeth build should give back a set share of both lost acts.

Inside, five bands of ten folks bit a force pad and read a set text. Born teeth topped both bite and speech grades by wide spans. Fixed post teeth came next, well past all lift-out builds. Full lift-out teeth gave a mere tenth of born bite force. Speech grades tracked the same rank, with fixed builds on top.
pmc-13350379:
Chun-Ka Wong and a multicentre team reported Asia-Pacific experience in 2026 with cutting heart valve leaflets during catheter valve replacement to stop the new valve blocking a coronary artery. The registry covered consecutive patients at seven centres from 2019 to 2026 treated with two techniques, one slicing the leaflet and one burning through it with a radiofrequency needle.

Success meant completing the cut and implant with no coronary blockage, emergency surgery, stroke, or death. Most published proof comes from North America and Europe. Real-world results from this region tell local teams whether the demanding trick works in their own patients and systems.
pmc-13350479:
Ningbo Yin and colleagues pooled ultrasound strain measurements of the heart's right side in a 2026 meta-analysis, aiming to set normal values. Speckle tracking follows tiny heart muscle patterns to measure how the right atrium and ventricle deform, but healthy ranges were never standardised.

Studies of healthy adults published up to July 2025 were gathered from three databases. Pooled values covered ventricle strain and strain rates plus three phases of atrial strain, and subgroup checks probed race, sex, age, and the software and machine used. Reference numbers that account for equipment differences let clinicians tell true right-heart weakness from measurement noise.
pmc-13350679:
Yuhan Fan and co-authors used deep learning in 2026 to regenerate radiotherapy positioning images that clinics normally throw away. Cone-beam projections for head and neck cancer patients are bulky, so they are discarded after building the three-dimensional scan, yet later checks may need them.

Working from 50 patients, they first computed synthetic X-ray views from the stored scans, then trained networks to convert those into realistic projections. Three network designs were compared, with tests on scatter correction, scan sharpness, and training size. Regenerating discarded images from kept data could rescue old treatment records for review and research.
pmc-13351079:
Qu and co-authors trace how H7 bird flu viruses spread around the world and which hosts move them. These viruses threaten both birds and people, with real pandemic risk. The team joined family-tree methods with maps of where strains appeared. Data showed epidemic waves in Asia in 2013-2014 and 2016-2017, and in Africa in 2023. The Eurasian virus line spread at a median of about 661 km per year.

Wild birds and waterfowl moved the Eurasian line faster and farther than chickens and farm birds. Their spread neared 654 and 587 km per year. Greater geographic distance slowed viral spread. The study sorts which hosts and settings drive global reach.
pmc-13351679:
Chenjia Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report on emergency non-heart surgery in a child with Eisenmenger syndrome. The condition marks late, untreated congenital heart disease with fixed high lung pressure, reversed blood flow, and low oxygen. An 11-year-old girl needed urgent surgery under general anaesthesia for a twisted right ovary.

Her lung artery pressure was 105/49 mmHg, and anaesthesia used etomidate, midazolam, vecuronium, and sufentanil, then propofol, remifentanil, and sevoflurane. Readings stayed stable during surgery, but a lung pressure crisis followed with fast heart rhythm, low blood pressure, and low oxygen. Amiodarone, treprostinil, bicarbonate, and oxygen restored normal rhythm, and she went home on day 11.
pmc-13351879:
Sen Lin and colleagues report a 2026 surgical technique for easing pressure on nerves at two neighbouring lower back levels through a single small cut. Endoscopic decompression is a key low-impact option for narrowed spinal canals. Reaching two levels often needs several cuts, so the team set out to do both through one opening.

Working over the top to the far side, they trimmed bone and removed thickened ligament at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels. Surgery took 115 minutes through a 0.7-cm cut with six brief X-ray checks. Pain scores fell from 8 to 0 by follow-up at 2 and 6 months, and the patient walked within 24 hours. The case shows the one-cut route is workable.
pmc-13352479:
Feiyang Liu leads a 2026 project building a scale for the healthy mental effects of exercise in Chinese college students. Existing tools capture only general or narrow mental outcomes after exercise. Scale items were drafted from theory, prior work, interviews, and open surveys, then tested in staged samples.

An early sample of 612 students shaped the item set, and a formal sample of 945 students checked reliability and validity. The final scale holds 55 items in five parts: emotional feelings, self-cognition, frustration coping, control and social efficacy, and social interaction. Variance explained per part ranged from 62.546 to 73.711 percent. A retest group of 597 students after 1 month supported stability over time.
pmc-13352879:
Yanan Zhou and co-authors map, in twenty twenty-six, brain structure and cognition in methamphetamine use disorder. Methamphetamine is a widely misused drug. How it harms the brain and thought was unclear. The team studied forty-five people with the disorder and forty-three healthy controls. All took a standard cognitive battery of ten subtests across seven domains. All also had structural brain scans on a 3T MRI scanner, which maps gray matter volume and cortical thickness.

The disorder group had reduced gray matter in several regions, including the insula and frontal areas. Cortical thickness was also lower across many frontal and related regions. Two regions showed an interaction: the link between thickness and a coding test score differed by group.
pmc-13352979:
Zhiyong He and co-authors build test samples that labs can use to check how well they read DNA marks in blood. Their 2026 paper deals with loose DNA in blood, which can carry marks that hint at cancer. Two sets of samples were made with known shares of marked DNA. One set came from a US standards lab and one from a UK firm.

Six labs then ran their own tests on the samples, each with its own method. All labs found shares close to the true values, and each method gave steady results on repeat runs. Small gaps between methods showed why shared test samples matter for trust in blood tests for cancer.
pmc-13353379:
Xiaoyu Ma leads a 2026 review of oxidative enzymes that break down plant biomass. Plant walls are mostly lignocellulose, a tough mix that resists biological dismantling. The review maps how microbes, mainly filamentous fungi, attack with redox enzymes, including newly found AA families.

Laccases and lignin-active peroxidases lead lignin attack, while lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases and their redox partners cut sugar chains. Hydrogen peroxide acts as a shared middleman whose supply and use are tightly timed and placed. Non-enzyme radical systems join the synergy. Structural computing sharpens the picture, and the authors argue the knowledge can speed next-generation biorefineries for a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13354279:
Sascha Gerd Decker and others matched virtual reality training with standard teaching for scoring psoriasis severity, in 2026. Care decisions depend on the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, yet accurate and reproducible scoring needs practice. A virtual reality program might train doctors more effectively than a lecture alone.

In a random forward trial, one group received a classical lecture and the other trained with the VR-PASI program, and scoring was checked afterward. pmc-13354579:

Film analysis showed the parts mixed compatibly, blocked more light, and let through more water vapor than the plain film. The full strength spray killed four test microbes, including E. coli and Listeria. Sprayed berries decayed less, lost less weight, and kept firmness statistically unchanged.
pmc-13417479:
Yuanyi Wang and co-authors review records of heavily pretreated metastatic breast cancer patients given vessel blocking therapy plus chemotherapy, in a 2026 multicentre study. Options run thin after many prior treatments. Records for 348 patients were matched into 174 pairs comparing combined treatment with chemotherapy alone.

Matched patients on combined treatment went a median 122 days without progression, versus 90 days on chemotherapy alone. Side effect rates were similar, and most events were mild or moderate. Results varied by which vessel blocking drug and chemotherapy base were used. Dose comparisons were descriptive only, the authors caution, and cannot prove lower doses work as well.
pmc-13418479:
Mathis Neuhaus and colleagues compare belly fat and under skin fat from patients with obesity, in a 2026 study. Paired samples came from 22 patients during weight loss surgery. Fat cell size, gene activity, glucose uptake, and fat release were measured in whole tissue and isolated cells to see how the two depots differ in expandability.

Under skin fat cells were larger and released fat faster at rest, with more flexible scaffolding proteins. Belly fat cells responded more strongly to stimulation for both fat release and glucose uptake. One skin fat gene tracked with insulin resistance across a public dataset. Depot specific biology may shape metabolic risk.
pmc-13418879:
Francesca Lessi and colleagues study tumor cells found in the blood of people with glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor. Such tumors almost never spread outside the skull, yet loose tumor cells show up in the blood again and again. That puzzle raises the hope of a blood test that tracks the disease without brain surgery.

The team examined blood-borne tumor cells from 27 patients, both in bulk groups and one cell at a time. The grouped cells shared many gene changes with the matched brain tumors. Single cells varied widely, and some carried no clear gene copy changes at all. The mix suggests that blood cells sample many parts of the tumor, a useful trait for watching the disease over time.
pmc-13419179:
Valério and colleagues present a 2026 computational study of lunar calendars across East Polynesia, including Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island. Communities kept lists of about thirty named moon nights. The team compared 48 such lists from every major island group, measuring how their words and structures differed, and built a family tree of the calendars.

The tree splits into two main branches. One joins the Marquesas with Mangareva and Rapa Nui; the other joins the Cook Islands, New Zealand, Hawai'i, Tahiti, the Tuamotu group, and the Austral Islands. That split matches a recent grouping of East Polynesian languages into Distal and Proximal branches. Since calendars and languages both pass down within communities, the match suggests the calendars divided early, mirroring the first voyages and language splits that settled the region.
pmc-13419879:
Baramett Somtha and colleagues profile the bacteria riding on dialysis catheters of patients with chronic kidney disease, using gene sequencing instead of culture alone. Kidney failure patients face high infection risk, and catheter lines raise the danger of deadly blood infection further. Slow or missed germ naming can leave treatment off target.

Sequencing of a ribosomal gene named the microbes present and ranked their shares in each sample. Known troublemakers appeared in the list, including Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Acinetobacter baumannii, among other named species. A full census of catheter life shows which germs to expect before culture results land. That foresight can shape first antibiotic choices and line-care practice in dialysis units.
pmc-13420479:
Kaushal Patel and colleagues report two patients with a stubborn bladder pain condition, marked by ulcers inside the bladder wall, who improved under an Ayurvedic oil treatment given through the urethra. Standard care for interstitial cystitis often brings only short relief and can scar the bladder over time. Both patients were tracked with pain scales and quality-of-life questionnaires for two years.

Each patient showed major clinical improvement, and quality-of-life scores pointed to near-complete settling of symptoms in the report. The gains held stable across the full two-year follow-up, an unusually long window for a case series. Two patients cannot prove a therapy, yet durable relief in a condition known for relapse earns attention. The authors present the method as a candidate for formal trials beside standard care.
pmc-13421079:
Le Gao and colleagues test whether a pre-trained model can guess where a person is looking during a film, using brain scan data alone. Eye tracking is often missing in older and shared scan sets, yet gaze shapes what the brain is doing during natural viewing. The model was applied cold, with no retraining, across three independent data sets.

Predicted gaze matched the true gaze modestly, with correlations between 0.24 and 0.37 across the sets in the reported range, and the brain maps it produced hugged the visual cortex. Age effects on the predictions wobbled between sets. The authors judge the cold model too weak for person-level claims without local training. The work still maps what can be salvaged from legacy scans that never recorded the eyes.
pmc-13421279:
Titherington and colleagues present a 2026 review of high-volume blood filtration for children in septic shock, a life-threatening infection state. The treatment runs blood through a filter at high flow to clear inflammatory signals, alongside standard kidney support. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign gave it a conditional backing, despite low-certainty evidence. The review tests that stance against the data.

The targeted signals are small enough, in theory, for high-flow membranes to clear. But pediatric studies are small, single-center, and use mixed dose definitions, so their estimates are fragile. The largest observational data sets in children show no consistent benefit, and adult evidence is also weak.  The idea is sound, the proof is not, and routine use should wait for stronger trials.
pmc-13421379:
Lukas C Bal and six colleagues map, in a 2026 study, how the brain's outer layer rewires its gene activity during daily torpor in the Djungarian hamster. Torpor lets warm-blooded animals slash their metabolic rate for hours to survive harsh conditions, and the cortex's response had not been charted at single-cell resolution.

Sequencing RNA from individual cell nuclei in hamster cortex across seasons and metabolic states, the team found a division of labour. Non-neuronal cells adjusted mainly with the seasons, through clock genes, while neurons changed during torpor itself, favouring RNA breakdown programmes. The cortical pattern diverged from the hypothalamus during metabolic depression. The authors frame torpor as a coordinated, cell-type-specific programme rather than a uniform shutdown.
pmc-13421479:
Jiawei Wu and colleagues built VUS.Life in 2026 to judge whether uncertain genetic variants cause disease, a bottleneck in genomic medicine where millions of variants lack clear meaning. The tool turns Variant Effect Predictor annotations into plain-language text, embeds them with language models, and scores new variants by closeness to known harmful ones.

Across more than 10000 variants in eight major disease genes, the method reached Matthews scores from 0.895 to 0.989 with F1 scores at or above 0.94, and its protein-level embeddings separated distinct harm mechanisms in one gene. Geneticists gain a fast, annotation-aware aid for resolving variants of uncertain significance.
pmc-13422879:
Aylı and colleagues add up the environmental bill of dialysis in this 2026 national modeling study of Türkiye, where in-center hemodialysis keeps thousands alive at heavy resource cost. They combined international per-session parameters with measurements from two Turkish centers running 4,000 sessions a month, then scaled to the country's 9.27 million sessions in 2023.

The literature-based estimate lands at 4.57 million cubic meters of water a year, up to 181.8 gigawatt-hours of electricity, and greenhouse emissions between 45.3 and 171.1 thousand tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually. Turkish measurements came in kinder on water, about 390 liters per session against the international 493, a 21 percent saving, while electricity use sat mid-range. Electricity dominated emissions at up to 72 percent of the total, making grid decarbonization and waste segregation the biggest levers.
pmc-13423079:
Grace Van Winkle and six colleagues describe the CHAMP trial, a pragmatic randomised study at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. The trial compares two ways to monitor intravenous heparin, a widely used blood thinner whose effects vary sharply between patients. One protocol adjusts the dose by the aPTT clotting test; the other uses an anti-Xa assay. The two have never been tested head to head in a prospective trial.

Running inside the hospital's learning health system from June 2024, the trial randomises inpatients who need heparin infusions to one monitoring protocol or the other. Outcomes will show which approach keeps levels in range more reliably. The authors designed the study to answer a daily dosing question with ordinary ward data.
pmc-13423479:
Fan, Wei, and Yan introduce in 2026 a special issue on nanozymes, engineered nanomaterials that act like enzymes. After nearly two decades of growth, the field now stretches across chemistry, physics, biology, and medicine.

The issue gathers 40 papers from research groups worldwide. Themes include sharpening catalytic performance, sensing, environmental cleanup, and therapies that fight oxidation, infection, or immune imbalance. The editors highlight several directions. One is tuning the small molecules attached to carbon dot iron nanozymes to control two enzyme-like activities at once. Another is a cerium nanozyme built on renewable lignin that stayed stable when heated and broke up bacterial biofilms. A third is an iron framework grown directly on a 3D-printed metal support to make a reusable glucose sensor. Together, the collection shows design shifting from discovering activity to engineering it deliberately.
pmc-13425579:
Thyago de Moraes and coauthors compared peritoneal dialysis modalities in a 2026 analysis of the PDOPPS cohort covering 9,463 patients in six countries or regions. Automated dialysis dominates in many high-income settings and is spreading elsewhere, yet survival differences against continuous ambulatory dialysis remain unclear. Patients entered the analysis within three months of starting peritoneal dialysis.

Cox models with intent-to-treat handling examined survival, permanent transfer to hemodialysis, and time to first peritonitis, adjusting for patient and facility factors. Clinicians and policymakers gain large-scale comparative evidence for a modality choice often driven by habit and resources. The scale of the data set lets small gaps show up that a single site could not hope to spot on its own at all. The pool is vast, with men and women from six lands and all walks of life in the mix of those who took part.
pmc-13425779:
Bennet Rohan Fernando Devasahayam and coauthors used nanopore sequencing to study barley roots and their microbes together in a 2026 multi-omics project. Wild, landrace, and modern barley types host different rhizosphere communities, a legacy of domestication, yet two-way influence between root and microbe stayed unclear. Long-read metagenomics was combined with root gene expression and plant genome data across genotypes and seasons.

Microbe communities shifted with genotype, while core functions such as amino acid metabolism and energy production stayed shared. Genotype-dependent differences in carbohydrate handling point to breeding targets for crops that recruit helpful root microbes. Roots and germs trade food and cues both ways, so a change on one side soon shows up on the other side as well.
pmc-13425879:
Dan Ziegler and colleagues critically appraise two modern diabetes drug classes for diabetic neuropathy in a 2026 review. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors transformed type 2 diabetes care through heart and kidney benefits shown in outcome trials. Animal and early human work hints they might also ease nerve damage and neuropathic pain.

Human evidence so far rests on small, short phase II trials of mixed design and quality, without clear gains in clinical or nerve conduction outcomes. Real-world responses also vary widely, so the authors caution against assuming nerve protection from glucose or organ benefits alone.
pmc-13426379:
Lyra C. Ceblano, Benilda C. Sanchez-Gan, and Patricia C. Orduña studied caregiver burden and well-being at Philippine General Hospital in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Their participants were 95 primary caregivers of children with neurological conditions admitted to the pediatric neurology ward between December 2024 and January 2025, chosen by purposive sampling. Long hospital stays push caregiving demands well beyond ordinary parenting and can damage caregiver health.

Structured questionnaires gathered social, demographic, and clinical details alongside a modified caregiver burden measure and well-being ratings. Linking burden scores with well-being shows where hospital support for families should focus. Moms and dads who stay at the bed side for weeks feel strain in body, mood, and purse, and the poll takes all three in view.
pmc-13427079:
Zaman and colleagues built and field-tested in 2026 HerCare, a women's health chatbot. It answers from two sources at once, expert medical knowledge and peer stories, and shows the source of each answer. Health chatbots tend to be either dry and clinical or warm but unreliable. Showing where an answer comes from is meant to let users judge trust for themselves.

In a single-session online study, 243 women completed the test. Usability scores ran high, and seven in ten users said they would recommend it. Text analysis found the bot's tone stayed warmly positive even when users wrote in distress. It followed a validate-then-guide pattern: first naming the feeling, then steering to advice.
pmc-13427479:
Abdishakur Mohamed Abdi and colleagues report a newborn whose neck tumor critically squeezed his airway in a 2026 case study. The boy was delivered at 38 weeks by planned cesarean because prenatal scans showed a large neck mass with excess amniotic fluid. He developed severe breathing distress soon after birth and required a breathing tube. CT measured a heterogeneous mass of 10 by 12 by 13.5 centimeters spanning mouth, jaw, neck, and upper chest, mixing cystic and solid parts, fat, and calcium.

The mass compressed and displaced the trachea without reaching inside the skull, and the tumor marker alpha-fetoprotein was markedly elevated before surgery. Complete surgical removal of such cervical teratomas is the goal despite their usually benign tissue type.
pmc-13427779:
Vieira and colleagues reported in 2026 on pain catastrophizing, a pattern of expecting the worst from pain, in people with knee osteoarthritis. They asked how this pattern relates to anxiety and low mood, and whether brain-wave patterns add any signal. The team studied 62 patients from a rehab cohort, recording resting brain activity and scoring mood, catastrophizing, and clinical details with standard scales.

Vieira found that catastrophizing was linked on its own to both higher anxiety and higher low-mood scores, across both standard statistics and machine learning checks. Low mood also tied to stronger slow brain waves over the back of the head, lower education, and higher body weight. Brain-wave data alone were weak predictors, but they added a small amount when combined with clinical details. Most patients had mild symptoms, so the findings describe gradual links, not diagnosed illness.
pmc-13428079:
Lampertico and eleven co-authors measure the daily burden of chronic hepatitis D in a 2026 study. This liver infection rides along with hepatitis B and is among the harshest viral liver diseases, yet little was known about how patients feel day to day. The team surveyed two hundred eleven patients in Germany, Italy, Spain, and the United States.

Patients were grouped by disease stage, from no scarring through stiff, failing livers to liver cancer. Quality of life scores fell steadily as the disease advanced, and nearly every part of a hepatitis-specific questionnaire worsened with stage and symptom load. Fatigue scores climbed along the same path. The authors argue that treatments slowing the disease could ease a heavy and growing burden, and they call such treatments an urgent need.
pmc-13428179:
Dakota Van Parys, Sarah Williams, and Catherine Haase studied how bat groups changed at a military base after a deadly fungal disease reached North America. White-nose syndrome, caused by a fungus, has killed millions of hibernating bats since 2006.

The team used 30 years of netting records from Fort Campbell, on the Tennessee and Kentucky border, covering four bat species the disease spares. Some spared species rose after the disease arrived, but the pattern varied by species and by scale of analysis. Forest cover and how broken up the forest was explained capture rates better than the loss of rival species did. The authors say habitat and disease act together, so bat conservation must plan for both at once.
pmc-13429279:
Adam and colleagues measure how many women in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have heard of cervical cancer, a preventable disease that kills widely where screening is rare. Their 2026 study analyzes the Demographic and Health Survey of 2023 to 2024, covering 27,583 women aged 15 to 49. The team weighs which traits, from schooling to media habits, separate women who know the disease from women who do not.

Only about one woman in five had heard of cervical cancer. Awareness rose with age, city living, schooling, paid work, radio listening, internet use, and recent contact with health facilities. The strongest link was a past breast cancer exam, which came with nearly five times the odds of awareness, a hint that any cancer contact teaches. Facility based childbirth and Christian affiliation also tracked with knowledge. Campaigns should aim hardest at young, rural, unschooled women, the authors conclude.
pmc-13429579:
Saeed Mohammadpour and colleagues forecast groundwater levels in a shallow aquifer in northern Iran, where patchy recharge, heavy pumping, and weather swings defeat standard models. Their test ground is the Astaneh-Kuchesfahan alluvial aquifer, a thin store that swings with irrigation demand and evaporation.

Two hybrid models pair neural networks with nature-inspired optimisers, honey badger and pelican methods, to tune network weights in scarce, shifting data. Hydraulic conductivity there ranges from 10 to 35 metres per day across the ground. Water managers get models built for thin aquifers where deep learning alone overfits and stalls.
pmc-13430179:
Qiong Wu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a low-cost gene test panel tailored to a protected Chinese chicken breed. Hetian chickens are prized for richly flavored meat and hold national protection status, yet breeders lacked a dedicated genetic tool. The team sequenced 50 birds deeply and found over 16 million variable spots in their DNA. Strict filters for reliability, frequency, and even spacing across the genome shrank that list to 5,781 chosen markers.

Those markers form a liquid chip panel using targeted sequencing, a cheaper route than full genome reads. Validation on 307 birds returned a call rate of 99.9 percent, near perfection. The panel also sorted birds into families accurately and estimated relatedness well, the two jobs conservation breeding needs most. Indigenous breed programs elsewhere can copy the recipe for their own protected stock.
pmc-13430479:
Thomas and co-authors describe the career bottleneck facing early-stage investigators in diabetes translational research. That is the work of turning laboratory findings into real prevention and treatment. The bottleneck hits as they try to reach mid-career independence. Input came from 34 early investigators and 19 senior faculty at 23 United States institutions. All attended the inaugural national enrichment conference of the diabetes translational research centers.

The group catalogued challenges, opportunities, and needs across the transition. The backdrop is a nation where diabetes affects over 38 million Americans. It costs more than 327 billion dollars yearly. Only around half of patients have met glycemic targets over the past two decades, despite strong care guidance. That underscores why the field needs these researchers to persist. The authors aim to keep multidisciplinary early investigators engaged. They offer guidance for strengthening and sustaining their careers within the center network.
pmc-13431879:
Huynh and colleagues reported in 2026 a gentle way to purify boron nitride nanotubes, thread-like tubes prized for heat and strength uses, using slow spinning rather than harsh acids or fast centrifuges. Raw batches carry compact impurities, and standard cleaning can damage the tubes. Their method rests on settling physics: dense lumps sink fast, while long thin tubes drift down slowly.

By spinning slowly in water with common stabilizers, the team let impurities settle out while the tubes stayed suspended. The cleaned batches reached an estimated purity near 95 percent, with a good share recovered and no visible damage. The purified tubes still formed aligned structures when filtered, a trait needed for heat-spreading films. The authors offer slow spinning as a green cleaning route for thin nanomaterials.
pmc-13436079:
Zijin Zhou and Yutong Shao wrote a 2026 letter questioning the numbers in a trial of needle-knife treatment for tennis elbow. The trial, by Zhang and colleagues, compared treatment aimed at deep versus shallow tissue layers under ultrasound guidance.

Zhou and Shao show that the trial's reported ratios mix up two different measures, which changes how strong the benefit looks. They also note that the pain threshold used to judge real benefit came from shoulder research, not elbow research. The letter flags clashing claims about whether all 70 patients finished treatment, plus missing detail on how gaps in the data were filled. The authors ask for corrected figures and clearer reporting before the trial's claims are trusted.
pmc-13436279:
Feng Jiang and a large team grade five coronavirus variants descended from the JN lineage for entry skill and immune escape in 2026. Cell tests weigh infection rates, receptor grip, and membrane fusion for each variant. Blood serum from prior cases tests how well antibodies still block them.

Two of the variants infect cells far better than their kin. One grips the ACE2 receptor tightest, while the other fuses membranes best in key cells. All five dodge antibodies better than the parent strain. All still enter cells bearing animal versions of the receptor. Vaccine updates should track this fast moving family.
pmc-13436679:
Kyunyeon Kim and coauthors ablate a faulty heart pathway in a 57 year old man whose heart sits shifted right in 2026. The man survived a ventricular fibrillation arrest tied to early excited atrial rhythm. Scans confirmed the heart is displaced, not mirrored, which keeps vessel layout normal.

Shifted landmarks made the extra pathway hard to map with X ray views alone. Three dimensional mapping plus ultrasound from inside the heart guided the burn. The pathway was cut without harm to the normal conduction node. Rare anatomy need not bar standard cure when imaging stacks up. Case lessons aid teams facing displaced hearts.
pmc-13437979:
Caris Bogdanov and colleagues used brain wave recordings to test whether ear rehabilitation truly changes the brains of adults with cochlear implants. The implants bypass damaged ears, and structured practice can sharpen what users make of the signal. Their 2026 study enrolled adults with one implant and late-onset deafness into a ten-week guided listening program.

Speech scores told one story and brain waves another. After training, the program group recognized sounds and words better than controls, in the implanted ear alone and both ears together. Yet the cortical response peaks the team recorded, a standard sign of sound reaching the brain, did not shift at all. The gains were real but modest, arriving without a measurable change in that brain signal. The authors draw a careful lesson: absence on the trace does not cancel progress. Clinics should weigh behavior and brain measures side by side .
pmc-13438179:
Boustani and colleagues, writing for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, update the evidence behind Medicare's coverage rules for amyloid-targeting Alzheimer's drugs in this 2026 paper. Since 2022, Medicare has covered these drugs only under coverage with evidence development. That policy requires further proof. A 2024 review addressed the regulator's stated questions. The extension studies show the treatment benefit continuing to build over time, with no new safety signals appearing during the longer follow-up periods covered. Safety analyses identified baseline traits that raise the risk of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, the brain swelling or bleeding side effects of these drugs. A slower dose-escalation schedule for donanemab lowered the risk of the swelling type, and the authors argue the evidence now justifies reconsidering the coverage policy.
pmc-13438379:
Chunyu Chen and colleagues trained machine learning models to flag which scrub typhus patients will turn severe. The mite-borne fever is common across Asia-Pacific and can crash into organ failure. Their 2026 study reviewed 492 patients in Jiangmen, 2013 to 2025. Standard statistics first picked candidate risk factors, then seven learning models were built and checked on held-out patients, .

Needing a breathing machine topped the list, a sign lung failure sits at the core of severe disease. High bilirubin, slow blood clotting, and low platelet counts followed as close markers. The strongest model, a boosted tree method, separated severe from mild cases with high accuracy in both its training and check groups. The authors argue such models could sort patients early at hospitals where the disease is common, steering intensive care toward those heading downhill. They note the models grew from one city's records and need outside testing.
pmc-13438579:
Roghayeh Babaei's team made silver-zinc oxide nanoparticles in 2026 with black seed extract to fight herpes simplex virus type 1. Cold sore virus is widespread, recurs, and can resist standard antivirals, which also carry side effects. Green-made composites, plain zinc oxide, silver alone, and heat-treated composites were compared on size, charge, toxicity, and viral inhibition in cell tests.

The green composite blocked ninety-five percent of virus after infection at a dose with no toxicity in the tested range, close to zinc oxide and better than silver alone. Virologists get a plant-made antiviral lead with a favorable lab safety window. Animal and human proof must follow before any clinical claim.
pmc-13439479:
Xin Wang's team set shaking check standards in 2026 for RV40E units, fine gears used in robots where factory shaking testing lacked shared rules. Fault types in failing units could then be identified from shaking alone.

Small-scale factory validation reached about ninety-seven percent fault identification accuracy under complex settings, well ahead of old methods. Makers get a practical quality standard that also guides repair. Wider factory adoption will test whether the standard holds across reducer models.
pmc-13440979:
Pereira and colleagues presented in 2026 a shortened version of the MBGR protocol, a structured exam of the mouth, face, and swallowing structures used by speech-language pathologists. The full protocol is thorough but long, which limits its use in busy clinics. The team set out to cut it down while proving the short form still measures well.

A draft of 36 items went through two rounds of expert review, and 17 items were dropped. Expert agreement on the kept items reached a strong level. Eleven trained clinicians then applied the short form to 11 patients and judged it clear and workable, with most calling the original too long for routine care. The authors conclude the short protocol keeps validity with a shorter testing time.
pmc-13441879:
Rahul Gupta's team traced age-related mitochondrial DNA mutations in 2026 using whole genomes from about seven hundred fifty thousand people. Mitochondrial sequence, abundance, and heteroplasmy were called in blood, with genome-wide association for mutation burden.
