Aging teams get a unifying mechanism and a sensitive blood marker of somatic mosaicism.
pmc-13442479:
Young Son and co-authors test a workout hormone on lab grown muscle in a 2026 paper. Muscle waste from steroids or cancer speeds decline and death. Workout fights waste in life, in part through a hormone called irisin.

Grown muscle strips give a clean test bed, sans whole body noise. Irisin eased steroid driven waste in the strips, with growth marks restored. It fired a key growth path and curbed the waste tag path. Heart harm from the same states is in the test frame as well. The bed may screen waste drugs fast and cheap.
pmc-13444279:
Yngve Forslin and colleagues report a routine drain swap that turned life-threatening in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case paper. He had lost his left kidney to surgery and grown a deep abscess that needed a drain. During a planned swap to a larger drain tube, the tube nicked the stump of his renal artery and massive bleeding followed.

An emergency vessel team raced in to stop the flow. A stent graft alone could not seal the bleed, given the stump's tight shape. Coil plugs added through the graft path sealed the stump at last, while the graft kept coils from drifting. The authors stress that routine swaps in post-surgery bellies need full plans and rescue gear at hand, even in expert hands.
pmc-13444479:
Rishav Kumar and colleagues compare two broiler stunning methods by the chemistry they leave in breast meat in a 2026 research note. Gas stunning and electric stunning both precede slaughter, yet their early meat chemistry had scant head-to-head data. Breast fillets came from Ross 708 birds under pilot plant terms, six per method.

Fillets were drawn about 30 minutes after death, with sourness read at 15 minutes and color logged before deep freeze. Gas-stunned meat ran more sour than electric-stunned meat, at p below 0.001 in their tests, while color marks matched. Wide chemical scans found 508 compounds, with five split by method at raw p below 0.05 in the screen. The authors share the split as a lead for meat quality work.
pmc-13445379:
Pharis B. Sasa and colleagues report a small case series on a weight-loss artery procedure done in an office lab, with patients going home the same day, published in 2026. The procedure blocks select stomach arteries to curb hunger signals, and past reports kept patients in hospital overnight. The team asked whether that stay is truly needed for safety.

Six patients with at least class II obesity had the procedure at one accredited office lab between December 2024 and August 2025. Flow to the target stomach arteries stopped in every case, and all six went home the same day with no unplanned hospital stay. No side effects of any grade appeared over a median follow-up of nine months. The authors urge a larger planned trial.
pmc-13445879:
Md Tahidur Rahman and coauthors map a 2026 analysis of poor feeding drivers among children under five in Bangladesh, using the 2022 population and Health Survey. The team applied multi-factor variance and math models to height, weight, and wasting scores across ages and home factors.

Children aged 12 to 23 months scored lower by a wide margin than infants on all three growth scores. Mothers who were too thin dragged scores down, while mother's schooling and home wealth lifted them. The authors urge states and NGOs to put first mother's schooling and feeding, income earning for poor homes, and birth spacing.
pmc-13446179:
James Williamson and colleagues weigh a new computing workflow that aims to make base editing, a precise gene tweaking method, easier for labs to plan, in a 2026 commentary. Base editors swap single DNA letters without cutting both strands, which trims stray damage. Yet many labs still default to older CRISPR cutting, in part for want of friendly design tools.

The workflow under review, from Eaton and co-workers, joins existing design tools with a fresh analysis platform for knockout experiments with adenine base editors. It walks users through editor choice, guide design, delivery, and proof checks, with immune targets as the worked case. The commentary sets the tool in context and asks how far such pipelines can widen careful use of base editing.
pmc-13447079:
Xiaoying Li and colleagues review how the tumor's neighborhood rebuilds itself under treatment and breeds drug resistance, in a 2026 paper. Resistance was once blamed on tumor cells alone, yet the stroma, immune cells, vessels, and matrix around them shift under fire and carve safe niches. Those niches block drug entry, hide tumors from immunity, and shelter stem-like cells.

The review sorts the machinery: stiffening matrix signals, low-oxygen switches, gene mark changes, fuel rewiring, and bubble messages between cells. Counter-plans follow the same map, from softening stroma and retraining macrophages to fixing vessels and loading drugs in nanoparticles. The authors tie hope to place-aware gene reads and organ-like lab models that sort patients for paired attacks.
pmc-13447179:
Farah Yasmin and co-authors compare rural and city hospital care in a 2026 United States study of patients who had both heart failure and liver cirrhosis. Together the two conditions raise the risk of kidney injury, infection and long stays. Whether place of care widens those risks on a national scale was the question.

Hospital records from 2016 to 2022 yielded close to half a million stays meeting the study rules. About fifteen percent occurred in non-city hospitals. Death during the stay was slightly higher in rural settings, while city stays ran a little longer and cost more after price adjustment. Matched comparisons gave the same picture. The authors call for better regional access and support for complex care outside large cities.
pmc-13447279:
Mao and colleagues studied in 2026 why subtropical broadleaf trees release very different scent chemicals.  The team measured seven tree species from distinct lineages using cut branches in controlled settings. They combined gas analysis with measures of photosynthesis, meaning how leaves turn light into food, and with leaf traits.

Trees fell into two camps based on which chemical dominated their emissions. Trees rich in isoprene showed higher photosynthesis rates and stronger electron transport, the flow that powers food making. Trees rich in monoterpenes had heavier leaves and relied more on stored chemicals released for defence. Emission profiles tracked leaf weight and photosynthetic capacity closely across species. The authors suggest future emission models should include leaf weight and electron transport as inputs. That change would sharpen forecasts of forest emissions under climate change.
pmc-13447379:
Yun-Hee Kim, Seyoung Shin and Jinuk Kim review brain rewiring after stroke and what it means for rehabilitation in 2026. Stroke often leaves lasting movement loss, while recovery leans on neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to remodel connections and reroute signals. Two forms anchor the account, one strengthening active links through use and one keeping overall network balance.

Intensive, task-focused practice taps the use-driven form, and repeated goal-directed training improves movement in animal and human studies. Robots, sensor feedback, brain stimulation, drugs and stem cells aim to boost the same processes with high, personalised doses. Results across those add-ons stay uneven, the authors note. They urge matching treatment to lesion features, brain markers and recovery stage, with combined approaches and precise tools as the way forward.
pmc-13447479:
Seyedeh Ala Mokhtabad Amrei and colleagues test a behaviour scale for executive problems in a fragile X related tremor disorder in 2026 work. The disorder stems from a moderate repeat expansion in a gene and erodes planning, control and thinking with age. A scale based on observed behaviour is widely used for executive function, yet its tie to brain scan markers in this condition was unexamined.

Fifty-six carriers with and without the disorder completed the scale, a brief mental test and computerised executive tasks, alongside brain scans. Worse scan scores tracked with worse scale scores in a strong pattern that survived adjustment for age, sex and repeat length. Computerised executive tasks rose with scan burden in a smaller complete sample, while the brief mental test moved the other way. The scale earns a supporting role beside other measures.
pmc-13448079:
Filip Milisav and co-authors test how nested modular structure shapes computation in brain-like networks in a 2026 modelling study. Brains organise into specialised subnetworks nested inside larger ones, yet what that layered layout buys computationally was unclear. A simple generator for multi-level modular networks let the team build artificial reservoirs, networks whose internal dynamics do the computing, with controlled structure.

Layered modular reservoirs remembered more, handled several tasks at once and produced richer timing patterns than strictly modular or random rivals. Recurring loop motifs enriched in the layered design explained much of the advantage. Human brain wiring data showed the same benefits when its natural layered layout was used, including brain-like timescales of activity. Hierarchy itself, not just modularity, emerges as a functional asset.
pmc-13448279:
Battalapalli and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract DSAI-09, a head-to-head test of an interpretable imaging signature against two black-box artificial intelligence models. The puzzle is classic: telling recurrent tumor from radiation necrosis, dead tissue from earlier radiosurgery, on MRI scans of treated brain metastases.

The team assembled 233 scans from three institutions, most with pathology confirmation, and computed 944 texture and spatial features per lesion for their SMART-Risk signature. On the held-out Wisconsin test set it reached an accuracy in the high seventies. It clearly beat a standard deep network and a fine-tuned medical imaging foundation model, which managed only the low-to-mid sixties. Importance analysis showed recurrent tumors display greater spatial complexity than necrotic tissue, giving clinicians an explanation, not a bare score. The authors argue such transparency could cut unnecessary surgery for what is only treatment damage.
pmc-13448579:
Sidiki Kaba and Alexandre Avdeev trace movements between contraceptive states among women in Guinea in a 2026 analysis of survey calendar data. Understanding when women start, switch or stop methods matters more than a single snapshot of use. Monthly calendars from the 2018 national survey let the team rebuild five years of contraceptive and pregnancy histories for women aged fifteen to forty-nine.

A recurrent-event survival model handled repeated transitions per woman across non-use, traditional methods, modern methods and pregnancy states. Monthly movement chances were low during contraceptive states, rose during pregnancy and jumped after pregnancy outcomes. Age, education and wealth shifted the chances only slightly, while media exposure and residence showed no clear link. Reproductive events, not social background, drive switching in this setting, so support around pregnancy and delivery moments is emphasised.
pmc-13448679:
Anmol Mathur and co-authors present in 2026 an electrochemical system that pulls carbon dioxide straight from the air. Instead of treating a bulk liquid, the device makes hydroxide right at the air-facing electrode, where capture happens. A porous layer spreads that reactive surface through a three-dimensional volume.

Captured carbon dioxide is later released in pure form through a mediator that moves protons and electrons together, keeping regeneration energy low. With a tuned porous layer and pulsed current, the system ran steadily for over 50 hours at current densities about ten times higher than earlier devices of this kind. Modeling and cost analysis in the paper sketch how the design might scale.
pmc-13448879:
Sean Wharton and colleagues pool in 2026 the liver safety data from seven phase 3 trials of orforglipron, a once-daily GLP-1 pill for obesity and type 2 diabetes. The analysis covered 11,220 participants, 6,920 on the drug and 4,300 on placebo or active comparators, followed for up to 104 weeks. Liver enzymes were tracked over time, and cases were screened against the standard pattern for serious drug-induced liver injury.

On average, liver enzyme levels fell during orforglipron treatment, a pattern consistent with the metabolic gains of weight loss. Marked enzyme elevations occurred at equal low rates in both arms, six participants each, and every orforglipron case had another explanation, so none met the injury criteria. Liver-related side effects were likewise balanced. Results held for participants whose enzymes started normal or elevated, easing a key safety question for the drug class.
pmc-13449479:
Wenhao Bao and colleagues show in 2026 that a routine stained tissue slide can reveal a pancreatic cancer's stromal stiffness program, a trait normally invisible without molecular testing. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma wraps itself in dense, cross-linked scar tissue that squeezes vessels and blocks drugs, one reason survival barely improves. The team trained foundation models, large pretrained image networks, on standard hematoxylin and eosin slides to predict that remodeling program from appearance alone.

External validation on an independent national cohort, CPTAC, confirmed the transcriptomic predictions. Spatial gene mapping then checked where the model looked: its attention landed on tissue zones expressing COL12A1, LOX, and LOXL2, the very genes that build and cross-link the matrix. The authors offer the result as a histology-derived biomarker candidate, a way to read stromal biology from slides every pathology lab already produces.
pmc-13449679:
Dol Raj Thanet and colleagues used Nepal's 2020 lockdown as a natural experiment in 2026 to study how human pressure shifts mammal activity times. Wildlife often changes when it is active to avoid people, but species responses across gradients of protection were poorly mapped. The lockdown cut human movement sharply, offering a rare comparison.

Camera traps ran in matched thirty-day windows in 2019 and 2020 across Bardia National Park, its buffer zone, and human-dominated land outside it. Activity patterns were compared by overlap, peak-time shifts, and night activity share, with the park in 2020 as baseline. Species responded in their own ways across zones and years. Conservation planners gain evidence that protection level, not just human presence alone, shapes when animals dare to move.
pmc-13449779:
Mohammed Said Bouya, Hamza Najout, and Najib Bouhabba propose in 2026 a new way to think about patients who cannot come off a ventilator after surgery. Hospitals usually record liberation failure as a single late yes-or-no event, yet the authors argue vulnerability accumulates quietly through anesthesia, the ventilator itself, paralysis drugs, pain control, fluids, and surgical stress. Their conceptual review builds a framework from four interacting dimensions of that vulnerability.

The four are weak respiratory muscle contraction, diaphragm injury from effort, suppressed central breathing drive, and a cardiovascular system that cannot bear the load. Mapped across readiness checks, the stress of a spontaneous breathing trial, and life after the tube comes out, these dimensions form stage-specific risk trajectories. The authors are explicit that the model is a testable architecture, not a validated bedside score, meant to define patient phenotypes and aim future trials at mechanisms.
pmc-13450479:
Jinyu He and colleagues modeled how personality shapes quality of life in older adults with chronic disease in 2026, testing two mediators: self-efficacy and medication adherence. Quality of life is a central goal of chronic care, yet the pathways from traits to wellbeing were not unified in one model. The team drew on a 2021 survey of Chinese residents.

The final sample included 1,037 patients aged forty-five and older with chronic disease who were on medication, across 120 cities. Standard scales measured Big Five traits, self-efficacy, adherence, and quality of life, and structural equation modeling tested the links. The model clarifies whether traits act directly or through confidence and pill-taking habits. Clinicians gain a map for interventions that target confidence and adherence rather than traits themselves.
pmc-13451779:
Ewan Flintham and Charles Mullon wrote this 2026 study of why sex chromosomes stop swapping DNA. In many species, the X and Y, or Z and W, chromosomes cease to recombine over most of their length. Two camps explain the arrest: capture of genes that help one sex and hurt the other, or neutral drift with no sex-specific push.

The authors model how fast a full recombination blocker, such as an inversion, spreads under each story. Even very weak sex-antagonistic selection sped the spread by orders of magnitude over neutrality. The result held up when harmful genes elsewhere on the chromosome were added. Breeding systems mattered: where males vary hugely in mating success, the pattern flipped between XY and ZW systems. The paper sharpens a classic evolution debate.
pmc-13452279:
Yaroslav Chushak, Teresa Sterner, and Rebecca Clewell build in 2026 learning models that guess whether a chemical can cross the brain's gate wall. Lab tests can flag brain-active chemicals, yet only those that cross the blood-brain barrier act the same in a body. The team trained varied models on molecular traits and checked them with split tests that guard against easy wins.

A merged consensus model proved steadiest, with balanced accuracy near the top range on the hard split. One trait, the polar surface share of the molecule, mattered most, and nitrogen rings showed often in crossers. Run over 6,000 brain-receptor blockers from lab assays, the model warned that over a quarter likely never cross, triage news for testers.
pmc-13452379:
Ahmed and colleagues measured fat hormones and trace elements in 2026 in the blood of patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, before and after treatment. The hormones leptin and adiponectin link body fat to cancer biology, and several minerals shift in illness. The team asked whether these blood patterns could help diagnose the cancer or follow it after care.

Fifty new patients and fifty healthy volunteers were compared. Before treatment, patients carried higher leptin and lower adiponectin than both treated patients and controls. Zinc, selenium, and magnesium ran low, while manganese, copper, and iodine ran high. Levels largely settled after treatment. A ratio of the two hormones separated patients from healthy people with excellent accuracy, and the authors suggest it as a cheap marker for diagnosis and follow-up.
pmc-13452479:
Mateusz Wróbel and six co-authors measure how well ultra thin layers built from ring shaped carbon compounds block electric current. These single molecule layers, made from a class called N heterocyclic carbenes, could serve as insulation in organic electronic parts. Their 2026 study tests a matched set of such layers and checks their strength as blockers.

Every layer in the set blocked current strongly, even one just 3.3 angstroms thick, a span far below a nanometre. That thinnest layer blocked current about 100,000 times better than a standard layer of the same length built from chain like molecules. Math checks ruled out one quantum effect that some blamed for low flow in ring compounds. The result points to a simple route to very thin, strong insulation for gate parts in future devices.
pmc-13453479:
Liu and colleagues tackle in 2026 a weak point of lithium batteries: the solid electrolyte interphase. This thin film forms on an electrode and controls how long the battery survives repeated charging. Uneven films cause uneven lithium deposits and early failure.

Instead of adding more film-forming chemical, the team applied 45 kilohertz ultrasound during a narrow voltage window of the very first discharge. The film then grew as a two-layer structure with a compact mineral-rich inner layer. Graphite cells treated this way kept about four fifths of their capacity after 500 charge cycles at a fast rate. Cells made without ultrasound began a rapid capacity decline after roughly 250 cycles.
pmc-13453579:
Megumi Takahashi and others checked a Japanese kin survey for intensive care in 2026, to see if it taps the same ideas as the first version. Kin views on care, on news given, and on choice-making matter in intensive care, but a Japanese form needs proof it works the same. The team ran the FS-ICU form in many sites.

Factor checks showed a fair fit, so the Japanese data kept the first form's shape. Scores held firm within each part, high for care and news, fair for choice-making. Care scores fell as worry and low mood rose, which backs the form's truth. Intensive care wards in Japan gain a trusted form to hear kin and lift care.
pmc-13454079:
Li and collaborators compared blood levels of chemerin in 160 Chinese breast cancer patients and 160 matched controls. Chemerin is a fat-derived signaling protein. They tested whether the adipokine tracks cancer risk, and whether blood lipids carry part of any effect. Risk factor questionnaires accompanied the blood measurements in this one-to-one matched case-control study.

Patients had higher chemerin than controls overall and within both menopausal subgroups examined separately in the analysis. Women above the control median for chemerin had 2.217 times the odds of breast cancer, rising to 4.713 among premenopausal women and 2.103 after menopause in the stratified results. The dose-response relationship was linear across the measured range rather than threshold-like in spline modeling. Triglycerides statistically mediated part of the link, accounting for about 15.0 percent of the total association between chemerin and breast cancer odds.
pmc-13454279:
Jeffery A. Jones and John F. Houde wrote the 2026 editorial that opens the third volume of a series on how sensory feedback guides speech. Earlier volumes dealt first with hearing and then with touch and body sense. The new volume asks how the brain weighs errors from each sense and how that balance shifts in speech disorders.

Contributions summarized here report that speakers correct sound shifts more strongly when the shift moves a vowel toward a nearby natural category. One study found that pitch adaptation faded fast with repetition, dropping by about two thirds after a second exposure. The editors use such findings to argue that error size alone does not drive correction.
pmc-13454579:
Shuyuan Zhang and Alexei A. Lapkin propose, in a 2026 methods study, a transformer model that reads molecules through two graphs at once. Predicting a molecule's properties drives work in chemistry, materials, and drug hunting. Standard models lean on atom maps alone, which can miss what the bonds themselves carry.

Their dual graph transformer fuses atom features, bond features, overall shape, and three-dimensional geometry inside one attention system. Benchmarks across standard datasets showed clear gains over the best current models. Follow-up tests credited the dual view, the position and structure codes, and the geometry input for the lift. The model also highlights which parts of a molecule drive a prediction, aiding interpretation. The authors aim the tool at faster, more transparent screening of candidate compounds.
pmc-13455379:
Zeng and colleagues trained a deep learning network to clean up PET scans taken faster or with half the usual radioactive tracer dose. The aim was to cut patient radiation exposure and scanner time without losing detail. They studied 322 patients, faking half-dose imaging and scan times from 30 to 90 seconds per position.

A residual U-Net rebuilt the noisy images, lifting reader quality scores in the half-dose group from 3.45 at baseline to 4.33 after processing, on the five-point scale used. Numeric similarity climbed too, with structural similarity rising from 0.75 at the low end to 0.87 at the high end and peak signal-to-noise from 37.65 decibels before to 41.37 decibels after in half-dose reconstructions. Even the fastest 30-second protocol recovered strongly after processing in the reported metrics. Detection of small lesions improved by up to 16.3 percent in shortened scans, judged by two nuclear medicine physicians, supporting efficient AI-enhanced protocols.
pmc-13456379:
Hongmei Yang and seven colleagues write, in a 2026 letter, about estimating a key lung severity ratio without repeated blood draws for ventilated patients at high altitude. The ratio of arterial oxygen to inhaled oxygen guides care in acute respiratory distress syndrome, a lethal lung failure. Drawing arterial blood often is painful, costly, and hard where staff and equipment are thin.

A fingertip saturation ratio has been proposed as a stand-in, with formulas built mostly on sea-level patients. Thin air changes how saturation maps to blood oxygen, so those formulas may mislead in the mountains. The team's earlier work in non-ventilated patients showed promising agreement. Their letter sets out a systematic check in the sickest group: patients on invasive ventilators at a hospital in Lijiang. The goal is a validated, needle-free severity read for high-altitude intensive care.
pmc-13457079:
Courtney Bartel leads a sixteen-author study, from 2026, hunting blood clues that show whether a child's Crohn disease has truly healed inside the gut. Healing seen by scope, not just calm symptoms, predicts fewer setbacks. Eighty-seven patients aged one to twenty-two, all on anti-TNF biologics for over six months, had drug measures and scope checks at several centers.

About 55 percent had healed. Three members of a marker family called CD64 ran lower in the healed group, each with a usable cutoff. Standard drug trough levels did not differ, but children clearing infliximab faster healed less. A combined model using clearance, platelet count, and albumin sorted healing with an accuracy score of 0.90. The authors say the split matters: slow drug clearance calls for dose changes, while a drug that is present yet failing calls for a switch.
pmc-13457279:
Matthew J. Schweickle and colleagues issue a 2026 position statement for Exercise and Sports Science Australia on helping athletes when the pressure peaks. Pressure can sharpen performance or ruin it, and the statement speaks to sport scientists and high-performance managers supporting athletes in those moments. The authors drew on systematic reviews and data-based studies on where pressure comes from, how athletes respond, and which strategies hold up.

Training design comes first: practice that builds implicit learning and rehearses pressure on purpose can prepare athletes before the big moment. On the day, four families of psychological strategy have evidence behind them: pre-performance routines, attentional strategies that run implicitly, psychological skills training, and mindfulness-based approaches. The statement advises matching the tool to the sport and setting, treating support as a whole-team job rather than the psychologist's alone. Eight closing steps assign actions to organizations, staff, and researchers.
pmc-13457379:
Aliaa Khalili and five colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 73-year-old man with high-risk antiphospholipid syndrome, an immune disorder that promotes clotting. He developed fast-spreading leg ulcers with active MRSA and Pseudomonas infection, alongside severe thrombocytopenia, a shortage of platelets. Steroids risked feeding the infection, and blood thinners risked bleeding, so standard options were blocked.

The team used intravenous immunoglobulin, a pooled antibody treatment, as a bridge: it calms immune attack without broad suppression, and it also raises platelet counts. He received a dose every three weeks with targeted antimicrobials, while blood thinners were paused and another immune drug stopped. Once platelets recovered past the safety threshold, anticoagulation resumed. Over five months the ulcers steadily resurfaced with skin and closed completely. The authors present the sequence as a workable template for similarly trapped cases.
pmc-13458579:
Mateusz Marcinek and colleagues review surgery for varicocele, the tangled scrotal veins that form the most common fixable cause of male infertility. Their 2026 narrative review searched PubMed and Embase for trials from 2010 to April 2026 and drew on 24 core studies reporting semen measures, pregnancy rates, or harms after repair.

Surgery improved the standard semen measures and reduced sperm DNA fragmentation, the DNA damage marker the review adds to older reviews. Technique mattered throughout: microsurgical repair beat laparoscopic and open approaches on both natural pregnancy rates and complication counts, locking its place as the method of choice. Fog remains around the edges: whether a silent varicocele on the other side deserves surgery too, where cohorts disagree. Reporting of long-term outcomes varied enough to frustrate comparison. The authors ask future trials to share endpoints and group men by baseline traits so selection for surgery can sharpen.
pmc-13458779:
Nazareno Scaccia and colleagues build a fast loop test for a fosfomycin resistance gene in a 2026 study. The drug has returned as a first-line drug for simple bladder bugs from resistant germs, yet spotting drug resistance is hard. Primers for the fosA gene were designed and tested on 63 previously sequenced strains, 34 Klebsiella pneumoniae and 29 Escherichia coli, all drug resistant, with visual colour change and gel checks.

Positive reactions turned yellow at 65 degrees Celsius in 40 minutes, with products visible by 20 minutes, and the spotting limit reached 8 trillionths of a gram per tiny drop. Overall catch rate was 90.5 percent and correct-clear rate 90.9 percent, with 100 percent catch rate in Klebsiella but only 43 percent in E. coli, where correct-clear rate held at 90.9 percent. The first fosA LAMP test thus suits on-site use in poor places, pending E. coli improvements.
pmc-13460179:
Wei Gan and colleagues report in 2026 early experience with EndoFusion, a system that overlays a patient's three-dimensional scan model onto the live camera view during keyhole lung surgery. Finding small, faint nodules inside the lung is notoriously hard, and the usual needle localization is invasive. Fifteen patients carrying nineteen peripheral nodules, most of them pure ground-glass shadows with a median size of eight millimeters, underwent assisted resection at one center.

Every nodule was removed without converting to open surgery, through wedge cuts or segment removal. Registration of the model took a median of just over two minutes, blood loss was minimal, and no complications occurred during surgery. Two patients had minor problems afterward, and the median stay was four days.
pmc-13460479:
Cali Loblundo and co-authors measured how often voice box problems follow a COVID-19 infection, in a 2026 study. Using a global electronic health record network of over one hundred and eighty million patients, the team matched adults who had COVID with similar uninfected controls, none with prior laryngeal trouble. They tracked chronic cough, swallowing difficulty, voice disorders, vocal fold paralysis, and laryngeal spasm for up to five years.

Every outcome was significantly more common after COVID. Odds peaked at about sevenfold for chronic cough and roughly threefold for swallowing problems and voice disorders, though absolute risk differences stayed small. Most outcomes peaked one to two years after infection, spasm later. Hospitalization and ventilator use raised several risks sharply. The authors conclude that new laryngeal dysfunction is a real, delayed part of long COVID that clinicians should watch for.
pmc-13461179:
Fabiana Pereyra-Goday and co-authors weighed the trade offs of Uruguayan farms that rotate crops and cattle pasture together, judging them on profit, environment, and food security at once. Integrated crop and livestock systems promise greener intensification, but single score claims hide real tensions. In their 2026 evaluation drawing on long term experiments, the team scored rotations for productivity, gross margins, soil erosion, emissions, and nitrogen gains. It also scored the protein produced for human food.

The long rotation, alternating pasture and crops over more years, emerged as the most eco efficient system, emitting 9.6 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per dollar of gross margin in the indicator reported. Legumes in the pasture phase fixed nitrogen biologically, lifting how well nitrogen was used, and erosion stayed well below the regulatory tolerance limit of seven tonnes per hectare yearly. Combining pastures with crops can raise productivity while improving environmental performance.
pmc-13461279:
Tara Khoeini, Gholam Ali Shahidi, and Mohammad Rohani describe three patients whose neck dystonia eased without any touch, in a 2026 letter. Cervical dystonia twists the neck into abnormal postures. Many patients find relief from a light touch trick, called a sensory trick. These cases worked through attention or imagined touch alone, with no contact at all.

One man's twisted neck straightened when he pictured a ruler held beside his head, or mimed it in the air. A woman improved by holding her hand near her nose without touching, and by imagining the move. The effect repeated on demand and was caught on video. The authors call it an overlooked variant with treatment promise.
pmc-13461579:
Qing Zhang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how to get the best results from teduglutide for children with short bowel syndrome. In that condition much of the gut is missing or fails, so children cannot absorb enough food and depend on nutrition given into a vein. Teduglutide copies a natural gut hormone and helps the remaining bowel adapt. New trials and clinic reports update older advice on timing and dose.

Recent work finds that up to 30 percent of treated children reached full feeding by mouth or tube, well above an earlier figure of 16 percent. Children who started with lower volumes of vein feeding and fewer infusions each week tended to gain the most. The authors argue against one fixed start rule, urging plans fitted to each child. They also advise giving the drug for at least a year before judging whether it works, since gains build slowly.
pmc-13461679:
Christian Zambach, Sofia Gerward, Steven van Zanten and colleagues checked whether blood pressure reactions to standing stay stable over a year in 2026. They re-examined 142 generally healthy middle-aged adults from a Swedish population study eleven to thirteen months after their first test.

The same protocol was used both times: pressure after five minutes lying down compared with pressure after three minutes standing. Long-term repeatability data like this are scarce, since most earlier work repeated tests within hours or days. Knowing how much these readings wander in healthy people matters because a drop on standing can signal autonomic problems, and single measurements guide real clinical decisions.
pmc-13462079: Neil Bowley and colleagues issued a 2026 correction notice in the journal Eye for their article on the environmental cost of a higher-dose eye drug. The notice is a correction only and carries no new findings. One printed measurement for the larger-dose syringe packet was wrong: the middle dimension should read 165 millimeters, not 135 millimeters as first printed. With that size fixed, the claim stands that many more units fit on one shipping pallet, cutting transport emissions by about one third. The journal states the original article has been updated.
pmc-13462679:
Yuyu Hua and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a risk model for neck lymph node spread in patients who have both Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune thyroid inflammation, and papillary thyroid cancer. Judging node spread is hard because the inflamed gland distorts ultrasound pictures of nodes. The team reviewed 261 patients whose diagnosis was confirmed after thyroid surgery at a hospital in Guizhou between 2018 and 2023.

Seven traits stood as independent risk factors: age, a blood enzyme, calcium spots and blood flow in the main tumor, and shape, brightness, and calcium spots in the nodes. Four models were built from feature mixes: tumor ultrasound alone, node ultrasound alone, both together, and a full model adding clinical data. The full model sorted patients best, with accuracy in internal checks and risk estimates matching real rates. The authors offer the model as an aid for surgery and follow-up in this patient group.
pmc-13463079:
Cong Wang and colleagues built a rock model in 2026 for deep tunnels and mines, where high ground stress bends the rules that shallow models assume. Older particle models fix contact stiffness, which flattens the early squeezing stage and misses how stiffness grows with pressure. The team tied stiffness to stress in real time, using triaxial tests on granite, slate, and sandstone.

An exponential link between early-stage stiffness and mean stress anchors the model, with a three-state rule that updates stiffness as contacts change and a calibration scheme across several pressures. Tests on carbon-rich slate matched full stress-strain curves well, catching shorter squeezing stages, stronger peaks, and a brittle-to-ductile shift. The tool should help engineers forecast rock failure before digging deep.
pmc-13463379:
Yagmur Unsal leads a 2026 case report of, the authors say, the first known patient whose CD70 deficiency appeared as severe type 1 diabetes. CD70 is an immune signaling protein; lacking it brings immune dysregulation, runaway inflammatory episodes, abnormal lymph cell growth, and cancer risk. The child arrived with severe diabetic ketoacidosis, failure of several organs, and later puzzles: repeated ketoacidosis, skin lesions, and celiac disease.

Gene testing confirmed a double-copy missense variant in CD70, and family studies backed the finding. A stem cell transplant from a donor treated the immune defect. After transplant, sugar control improved, with the median long-term sugar marker falling and daily insulin needs dropping. The authors argue the case shows an intact CD27 and CD70 signaling pair guards against immune attack on the pancreas's insulin-making cells. They point to that pathway as a candidate target for immune therapies against type 1 diabetes.
pmc-13463479:
Fu and co-authors described in 2026 a faster way to multiply a rare medicinal orchid, Anoectochilus roxburghii. The plant is highly valued, endangered in the wild, and slow to reproduce on its own. Starting from stem segments with nodes, they built a lab culture system. The system grows protocorm-like bodies directly from buds. These are small cell clusters that behave like orchid seeds, and no messy callus stage intervenes.

On the best hormone mixture, each starting piece produced more than 30 new bodies. The authors call that multiplication rate rare for this species. The full cycle ran about 110 days to prepare sterile material and 160 days of body induction. Rooting took 90 days, and hardening off took 60 more. Every plantlet rooted on the strongest rooting medium. More than 95 in 100 survived the move to normal conditions. Chromosome checks showed no genetic drift at any stage.
pmc-13463579:
Alba Díaz González and four co-authors study death risk in dogs with acute pancreatitis, a sudden swelling of the pancreas. Some dogs heal in days, while others grow gravely ill. The team followed 134 owned dogs seen at a hospital and compared them with healthy dogs.

Two scores built from routine blood tests, both tied to creatinine, stood out at intake. One score pairs creatinine with albumin, and the other pairs white cell counts with creatinine. Dogs with higher scores died in hospital more often, and the scores beat single blood values at sorting risk. Since the tests are already routine, vets can flag fragile dogs early at no extra cost.
pmc-13463979:
Karel Huard and six co-authors review how to judge venous congestion, backed-up blood in the veins, in critically ill patients. Congestion can injure many organs and can shift within hours. No single test captures it well, so the authors join three ultrasound methods at the bedside.

Heart ultrasound grades how stiffly the heart fills, vein ultrasound scores excess flow in organs, and lung ultrasound spots fluid in the lungs. Worked examples and flow charts show how the three views correct each other's blind spots. A stiff heart with quiet veins tells a different story than swollen veins with dry lungs. Intensive care teams gain a fuller, faster read on fluid overload and organ risk.
pmc-13464079:
Luping Wang leads a team that targets SIRT6, a gene-tuning enzyme, to calm blood cancers with runaway neutrophil growth. A screen of gene-tuning compounds flagged a SIRT6 activator, MDL-800, as a strong brake on the excess growth. Zebrafish bred with a faulty sirt6 gene developed a like disease on their own.

Sirt6 trims a chemical mark at the switch of c-myb, a growth gene for early blood cells. Without Sirt6, young blood cells and neutrophils multiplied out of bounds, while extra Sirt6 calmed them. The activator boosted the standard drug imatinib in fish and mouse leukemia models. It even restored drug response in resistant mouse tumors, which marks a fresh pairing for hard cases.
pmc-13464179:
Veronica Jimenez and colleagues tested a gene therapy in 2026 that raises the hormone FGF21 in aged mice, aiming to stretch healthy life rather than just lifespan. No approved drug yet sustains healthspan, though lifestyle steps help only while kept up. Old and very old mice of both sexes received a muscle-targeted viral vector carrying the FGF21 gene.

Treated mice normalised weight and fat, handled sugar better, kept liver detox power, resisted kidney ageing, and showed stronger hearts, muscles, and memory. Tissue studies pointed to better energy handling, cleaner protein control, and less inflammation, scarring, and amyloid build-up, with AMPK signalling switched on. The results mark FGF21 gene therapy as a candidate geroprotector, though human dosing and safety remain far off.
pmc-13464279:
Aguiar and Mioto wrote this 2026 editorial about a heart tumor that was misdiagnosed as benign. They discuss the case of a woman 31 weeks pregnant. She developed acute heart failure from two large left atrial masses. Three years earlier, surgery had removed a tumor labeled a myxoma. Re-examination of both the original and the new tissue showed cardiac myxofibrosarcoma, a rare cancer that mimics myxoma.

Fewer than five percent of primary cardiac sarcomas are this type, yet it tends to grow invasively and recur, so the label matters greatly for outcome. The authors explain that scans, however advanced, cannot reliably separate the two tumors, which both appear gelatinous and mobile in the left atrium. Only microscopic and immunostaining examination settles the diagnosis, and they argue the case was most likely a misclassification from the start, not a cancerous transformation.
pmc-13464879:
Xu and co-authors examined tumor tissue from 25 patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma in 2026. They tracked how immune cells inside the tumor change after chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy given before surgery. pmc-13468479:

pmc-13469679:

pmc-13469779:

pmc-13471679:

pmc-13472079:

Mamode and colleagues present a 2026 commentary on the collapse of kidney care in Gaza during the war that began in October 2023, arguing that not to act is itself an act. pmc-13478479:

pmc-13483479:

pmc-13483579:

The authors argue that late repair should still proceed, since careful preparation and aftercare can bring outcomes closer to global norms.
pmc-13484879:
Jake Grange and co-workers review if forms filled in by patients steer care choices in joint diseases marked by swelling. Their 2026 review searches four databases to February 2025. It covers three diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and axial spondyloarthritis. From near seventeen thousand records, 29 studies made the cut, most on the first disease.

The forms helped care in three ways. Most often, they guided drug changes in treat-to-target plans. They also aided talk in clinic visits and checks done at home. Staff followed form-based plans less well for complex patients. Home checks matched standard care results, though thin services cut their worth. Scores also built trust between patients and staff. Wide gaps in how forms are used waste much of what patients report.
pmc-13486679:
Simegn and a large team charted how blood sugar control evolves in Ethiopian patients who carry both type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, a pairing that multiplies complication risk. Their 2026 study pulled records for 600 such patients followed at Debre Markos hospital between 2014 and 2023. A flexible statistical model traced each patient's glycated hemoglobin, the three-month average sugar marker, over years of visits.

Average glycated hemoglobin ran high compared with the target range of the American Diabetes Association cited by the authors. Seven factors predicted worse trajectories, including injected medication use, obesity, kidney damage, heavier weight, and family history of diabetes. Uncontrolled blood pressure and more than six years of treatment also tracked poorer control over time. Simegn recommends tighter combined management of sugar and pressure rather than treating the two conditions in separate silos.
pmc-13487679:
Tiffany Tu and Alejandro Ochoa warn that pooling genome studies can quietly break when the studies share relatives. Published in 2026, the theory and simulation work starts from a live proposal to fix participation bias with sex-stratified pooling, which ignores that men and women from one population are heavily related. Between-study relatedness correlates test statistics and inflates false positives.

Simulations across family and population structures show ordinary pooling inflating badly whenever family links cross study borders, with inflation growing as samples grow. Genomic control patches the symptom yet costs real power in high-signal settings. The authors' correlated meta-analysis method, shipped as the metalcor package, models the correlation directly and restores calibration. Real data confirm severe inflation inside family studies and negligible effects in population studies up to ten thousand people.
pmc-13487979:
Li-Pang Chen and Wan-Yi Chang present a software package for gene network work in this 2026 paper. Gene activity data often hold many linked measures at once. A key task is to map the network among genes, which can reveal pathways broken in disease and guide new therapies.

Extra known facts about samples can sharpen that mapping, but picking the useful ones is hard. Gene data also carry measurement error from tool limits or human slips, which can distort the network. Their package, called PAGE, fixes measurement error, picks useful extra facts, and estimates the network under both straight and curved models. A yeast cell cycle data set is used to show the tool at work.
pmc-13488279:
Shuyuan Zhang and co-authors build an artificial intelligence tool to spot cardiac amyloidosis in a 2026 multicenter study from China. The disease thickens the heart wall as abnormal protein deposits build up, and it is often mistaken for other causes of thickening. Heart tracings and ultrasound measures came from a Beijing hospital cohort, with patients from ten other hospitals held back for outside testing, and a learning system combined eleven model types.

Seven features carried the diagnosis, mixing tracing measures, wall thickness, blood pressure, and pumping indices. The combined model separated amyloidosis from its mimics with very high accuracy, and performance held up in the outside hospitals in the reported tests. A simplified score built from the same features also performed well for bedside use.
pmc-13488579:
Shala Cunningham and colleagues evaluate stroke rehabilitation training for physiotherapists in Myanmar in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Conflict and disruption have cut access to rehabilitation, although stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Seventeen professionals took blended training mixing online coursework, live mentoring, and hands-on clinical sessions, with surveys before training, after each stage, and at six months, judged against a four-level training evaluation model.

Self-rated knowledge and skill rose significantly, strongest for methods needing little equipment in the reported comparisons. Follow-up surveys showed evidence-based assessment and treatment entering routine practice for many participants. Seven therapists joined focus groups at six months to explain how changes held under local constraints. The authors present the tailored design as a model for fragile settings.
pmc-13490379:
Sun and co-authors sped up the scheduling mathematics for neighborhoods that share electricity and heat with each other. Community energy systems juggle power, heating, and cooling, and sharing between communities raises efficiency, but central scheduling is slow and exposes private data. Their 2026 study built a day-ahead stochastic model, which plans under green-power uncertainty, with dynamic prices set by an operator. They solved it with a new distributed algorithm that splits the problem apart.

Case simulations showed the sharing model and pricing scheme cut operating costs and carbon emissions for individual communities and the whole system. The new algorithm converged faster than the standard distributed approach it improves on, according to the comparisons reported. Privacy survives because each community solves its own sub-problem and exchanges only limited signals. Sun presents the scheme as ready for multi-community energy markets.
pmc-13491579:
Hai Wang and four co-authors examine a 2026 multicenter records study on blood pressure medicines during acute kidney injury. Drugs called ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers protect the heart and kidneys long term, yet doctors disagree about stopping them when kidneys fail suddenly. The authors sorted patients by whether these medicines were stopped, continued, or newly started.

The records covered 1,285 patients across several hospitals. People who stayed on the medicines had lower odds of kidney injury worsening within fourteen days than people who stopped them. A survival advantage seen before adjustment faded once other factors were counted, and starting the drugs looked no different from stopping them. The authors call for prospective trials because deaths were few and estimates were unstable.
pmc-13491679:
Eglė Šidlauskaitė and four colleagues set out in 2026 to derive bonding radii, the standard sizes chemists assign to atoms when deciding which atoms in a crystal are bonded. X-ray crystallography gives atom positions but rarely shows bonds directly, so distance rules do the everyday work. Existing radius sets lean on a commercial database or on hand-adjusted values, which limits open checking.

Their unsupervised workflow learns radii from crystal structures in the free Crystallography Open Database instead. Two atoms count as bonded when their distance is no more than the sum of their radii plus a small tolerance. Published sets can disagree by more than an angstrom for some elements, so an openly derived set matters. The paper lays out the method and the resulting radii for reuse by other researchers.
pmc-13492279:
Leonardo Bernal and eight colleagues combine chemistry software with machine learning in 2026 to hunt for old drugs that might fight aggressive prostate cancer. Advanced, treatment-resistant disease still kills many men, and repurposed medicines arrive with known safety records. Their workflow filtered candidates by chemical similarity and used applicability checks to weed out false leads before laboratory testing.

Screening the DrugBank library produced five candidates that slowed cancer cell growth in both flat cultures and three-dimensional models. An antifungal medicine, chlormidazole, performed best, acting mainly by pausing cell division rather than killing cells outright, and sparing non-cancer cells comparatively. It raised a cell-cycle brake protein and pushed cells into arrest. Chlormidazole also boosted the chemotherapy drug docetaxel, matching its effect at much lower docetaxel doses.
pmc-13493779:
Lavecchia and colleagues map how stress is arranged inside the rocks of peninsular Italy, work that feeds directly into earthquake hazard estimates. Their 2026 study rests on roughly 8,200 measurements of fault slip, the scratches and offsets left where rock masses slid past each other, gathered at outcrops across the country. From these they rebuilt the directions and relative sizes of underground stresses over roughly the last three and a half million years.

The team outline a belt of stretching crust about 1,000 kilometres long running through the Apennines, where the ground is being pulled apart. Stress directions form nested arcs at several scales, from single faults up to the whole crust, and they bend in line with the deep boundary beneath the crust. Modern earthquake records and satellite measures of ground movement point the same way, suggesting the old pattern still drives today's deformation.
pmc-13493879:
Joerg F Hipp leads a nine-author team probing in 2026 a brainwave signature of Dup15q syndrome, a rare genetic condition causing developmental delay, autism features, and epilepsy. Extra copies of a chromosome segment overload certain calming receptors, and children's brain recordings show unusually strong beta rhythms as a result. The team isolated that rhythm cleanly from background noise in fifty-two affected children and fourteen typically developing peers.

The beta excess was large, nearly two standard effect sizes above typical children. Among children without epilepsy, stronger excess meant lower cognitive scores and weaker everyday adaptive skills, both correlations solidly significant. That dose relationship supports the idea that overactive calming receptors drive real functional loss, not just a pretty signal. A measurable brainwave that tracks severity could help future trials judge whether treatments actually help.
pmc-13494079:
Shunming Zhang and co-authors ask, in a 2026 cohort study, whether people whose lab results clash with their body mass index face a different risk of heart failure. Body mass index, or BMI, gauges weight for height but says little about inner health. The team used UK Biobank data on 394,198 adults. They grouped people by how far markers such as blood sugar, blood fats, and C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, sat from what their BMI would predict.

Over a median follow-up past twelve years, groups whose inflammation or blood sugar ran worse than BMI suggested developed heart failure more often, in both men and women. Some other groups, such as women with higher than expected blood pressure, showed lower risk. Liver enzyme groups showed no clear link. The authors argue that sorting people by these marker patterns could sharpen efforts to prevent heart failure.
pmc-13495279:
Sufen Wang and colleagues run, in a 2026 randomized study, a teaching trial that blends problem-based learning with medical humanities in a pathology lab course. The course went to anesthesiology undergraduates at a Chinese medical university. Four classes were assigned by lot: two got the blended model and two got standard lecture-based teaching, with 115 students in all.

Both groups improved on theory exams, and final theory scores did not split clearly between them. A microscope image test leaned toward the blended group without quite reaching the bar for proof. Blended students did score higher on drive to learn, self-directed study skill, and communication, and they rated the teaching better overall. Ethics awareness and social responsibility scores did not differ. The authors offer the blend as a reference for reforming lab teaching, with gains in engagement rather than raw exam points.
pmc-13499879:
Zwirner and colleagues explore whether squeezing the spleen can tell forensic doctors how long someone has been dead. Temperature-based methods fail once a body equilibrates with its surroundings, leaving a gap at longer intervals. Their 2026 study collected spleen samples from 53 adult cadavers, spanning roughly two days to three weeks after death. The team measured the tissue's squishiness with an instrument that wiggles samples and records how they store and lose energy.

One measure, the loss modulus, which captures how much energy the tissue dissipates, fell significantly as time since death grew, while the storage measures showed no useful pattern. A threshold value on that measure gave strong evidence for death within about 200 hours, performing well on the authors' diagnostic accuracy analysis. The team presents spleen mechanics as a promising addition to the time-of-death toolkit, pending larger studies.
pmc-13500079:
Austin Erickson, Jennifer Griffith, and Trushar Patel chart in 2026 when and where urology conferences gather across the United States, using public listings from 2022 to 2025. Conferences anchor education, networking, and research sharing in the specialty, yet their calendars had never been mapped. Working from a Florida medical school, the team collected events from organiser sites and calendars, recording dates, frequency, and location for each meeting.

Eighty-five organisations held 293 events across the four years. Texas and California hosted the most, and the Western regional section led the sections, followed by the Southeast and South Central. Meetings lengthened slightly on average, and autumn dominated the calendar, with October the busiest month and July the quietest by a wide margin. The authors suggest spreading events more evenly across months and regions to ease scheduling clashes and improve access.
pmc-13500379:
Miku Goto and co-authors profile in 2026 the liver enzymes that break down drugs in squirrels, a group frequently treated with veterinary medicines despite almost no baseline data on their metabolism. The team combined gene sequencing, gene expression measurement, and functional tests on liver microsomes, tiny cell fragments carrying the enzymes, focusing on two enzyme families central to foreign chemical handling. Three squirrel species were compared with mouse and rat laboratory rodents, using the flea treatment fipronil as a test substance.

No clear squirrel-specific loss or major divergence appeared in the two focal enzyme families, and fipronil breakdown efficiency did not differ significantly among the species examined in the reported analysis. Wider expression profiling did show distinct patterns, with one enzyme family making up under one percent of major expression in the Eurasian red squirrel, below rodent levels. The work supplies baseline data for comparative wildlife drug metabolism studies.
pmc-13501779:
Mario Giuseppe Zotti leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 diagnostic study linking electrical nerve tests to muscle wasting seen on MRI in chronic lower back problems. The cohort took 100 consecutive eligible patients with chronic lumbar symptoms, drawn from 119 who underwent electrodiagnostic testing. Needle electromyography sorted them into confirmed chronic lumbar radiculopathy, a pinched or damaged nerve root condition, versus a symptomatic control group with normal electrical findings. Two independent observers graded multifidus muscle atrophy on MRI using a modified Goutallier scale and fat measurements.

Atrophy appeared in 98 percent of the confirmed radiculopathy group but also in 64 percent of the symptomatic controls, a significant gap with an odds ratio of 27.2 on that comparison. Grading showed most confirmed cases at mild to moderate levels, with 11 percent at the severe grade 3, which never appeared among controls. The authors propose the wasting pattern as a supporting biomarker, not proof on its own.
pmc-13504779:
Xiangyang Li and three colleagues ask how few muscle sensors a rehab glove system needs to read hand gestures, in a 2026 study. Wearable muscle-signal gear often uses eight or more channels, which adds bulk, power draw, and discomfort. Fewer channels would ease daily use if accuracy holds.

Their check plan rests on clean signal capture, a full search of all channel subsets from six sites, and stress tests with degraded signals. Data came from 24 healthy adults, judged by leaving one person out in turn. Three channels passed a 90 percent accuracy bar on average but failed badly for some users. Four channels scored higher and left no user stranded. The winning four sites sit on forearm muscles that drive the wrist.
pmc-13504979:
Timms and colleagues ran a feasibility study for a bigger question: can painting silver diamine fluoride on children's rotten baby teeth beat usual NHS dental care? The fluoride compound arrests decay without drilling, a prize for treating small children, but a trial inside British practices faces recruitment and retention hurdles. Their 2026 study randomised children aged one to eight with decay across eight practices, following them for a year and interviewing families and dentists.

Eight sites recruited 54 children, and nearly every eligible family approached agreed to join, an encouraging sign for willingness. The obstacles lay elsewhere: recruitment ran slower than the team planned, and keeping the randomised allocation intact inside busy practices proved tricky. The standard decay-scoring system also looked weak as the main outcome measure. Their verdict is a conditional yes: a definitive trial is feasible, with slower timelines, stronger randomisation support, and a better primary outcome.
pmc-13505079:
Sarah Hainer and six co-authors marked twenty years of induced pluripotent stem cells in a 2026 essay. In 2006, a Kyoto team showed that four factors could rewind adult mouse skin cells into embryo-like cells able to become many cell types. The result overturned the old picture of development as a one-way roll downhill. A journal collection now gathers where the field heads next.

Cell identity questions sit at the core of developmental biology and now support regenerative medicine, disease modeling, and cell therapies. Earlier work had shown a mature cell's nucleus could still build a whole animal when placed in an egg. The 2006 breakthrough proved the embryo state can be switched back on inside ordinary cells.
pmc-13507279:
Alexander Wood and colleagues show that intensive care patients with COVID-19 and patients with trauma go through immune changes that look much the same. Critical illness sets off immune dysregulation tied to morbidity and death, but a direct comparison across causes is still needed. The prospective cohort study matched innate immune cell function and plasma proteins over five days of intensive care.

The study took in twenty-six COVID-19 patients, twenty trauma patients, and eighteen controls. Both groups shared deep changes: neutrophilia, and fewer non-classical monocytes and dendritic cells. They also had a neutrophil state that was hyper-phagocytic and rich in reactive oxygen species. Their classical monocytes failed to upregulate key activation markers when stimulated. A dendritic cell group with poor phagocytosis grew from day one.
pmc-13508279:
Zhengqing Bao, Jiaqi An, Guizhong Li, and Jianwei Wang pool studies on whether a simple blood ratio forecasts survival in urinary tract cancers, in 2026 work. The ratio compares fibrinogen, a clotting protein tied to inflammation, with albumin, a nutrition-linked protein. Earlier pooling had covered bladder and kidney cancers only thinly. The team searched three databases through March 2026 and found six studies with 1,603 patients in all. They combined risk figures for overall, cancer-specific, and disease-free survival.

Patients with a high ratio before surgery fared worse on every survival measure. The combined risk of death was more than double that of patients with lower ratios. The pattern held when kidney cancer and bladder cancer were judged apart. Disease-free survival also suffered in the high-ratio group. The authors argue this ratio offers a cheap warning sign for planning follow-up after surgery.
pmc-13508979:
Su Shan and five co-authors probe how adrenomedullin helps yak fat cells cope with thin air. Yaks live at high altitude, where low oxygen strains metabolism, and subcutaneous fat helps them face cold and hypoxic stress. Yak preadipocytes were grown under normal oxygen, mild hypoxia, and stronger hypoxia. The team tracked growth, cell death, energy output, and lipid markers, with transcriptome sequencing on top.

Adrenomedullin acted both ways by dose. Low doses eased hypoxia damage and restored energy and lipid building. High doses plus hypoxia switched on many metabolic pathways and rerouted energy supply. Cells stressed defense first under hard hypoxia and tuned metabolism under mild hypoxia.
pmc-13510279:
Yuyang Wei, Weijie Fei, Jiarong Wang, and Luzheng Bi present Mechanics-AI, an open-source system that pairs physics simulation with machine learning for engineering design, in 2026 work. Direct simulation gives clear physical answers yet runs slowly and ignores real-world context, while machine learning runs fast yet needs much data and hides its reasoning. The design copies living bodies, where sensors read physical signals and the brain places them in context.

A first learning layer stands in for costly simulations, producing readable measures such as stress, strain, and heat or moisture fields. A second layer blends those measures with outside data to predict outcomes and suggest designs. The system tests eight methods, keeps the best for each task, and shows which physical factors drove each answer. Trials spanned brain injury prediction, a tissue-growth device, and low-carbon building design with recycled concrete.
pmc-13512379:
Wanting Li and seven co-authors study sugars shed by a probiotic bacterium as allergy fighters, in this 2026 paper. The bacterium, a new strain of Lacticaseibacillus casei, coats itself in exopolysaccharides, long sugar chains with many reported health effects. The team screened four high-yield strains and picked the one whose sugars scored best across early tests.

Two pure sugar fractions came out of the winning strain's coat. One is a neutral chain of four sugars; the other is a larger acidic chain of six. In a standard allergy cell model, the coat sugars and both fractions calmed the allergic response. Cells released less histamine and fewer alarm signals. A key immune balance also shifted back toward normal. The authors propose these sugars as natural anti-allergy ingredients for foods and supplements, pending animal and human checks.
pmc-13512579:
James Barton, Clayborn Barton, and Ronald Acton wrote a 2026 paper mapping one gene variant across Europe. The variant sits in a gene that controls iron in the body, and it is tied to European ancestry. No full map of it existed. The team gathered published gene counts from across the continent.

They found forty-four study groups from twenty-four countries, covering about two hundred thirty-three thousand people. About one person in fifty-four carried one copy of the variant, and roughly one in six thousand carried two. Its frequency varied by region, reaching about three and a half percent in the highest areas. Maps like this help doctors judge how useful gene screening would be in each country.
pmc-13512979:
D'Amato and colleagues tested two things in hospitalized heart failure patients. First, whether a staging system called HLM, which grades heart, lung, and multiorgan involvement, predicts outcomes. Second, whether starting an SGLT2 inhibitor drug during the hospital stay helps at every stage. Their 2026 prospective multicenter study enrolled 711 consecutive patients admitted between late 2022 and mid 2025 and followed them for six months.

D'Amato found the combined endpoint of cardiovascular death or heart failure readmission in 82 patients, rising clearly with each HLM stage. Each stage step carried roughly forty percent higher risk regardless of drug status. Starting the SGLT2 inhibitor during the index admission was independently linked to about forty percent lower endpoint risk. The drug class also protects kidneys and metabolism, and benefit showed no weakening in advanced stages. The authors support combining whole-body staging with early drug initiation in routine heart failure care.
pmc-13515479:
Md Imran Hossain, Sitansu Sekhar Nanda, and Dong Kee Yi review, in a 2026 article, surface-engineered magnetic nanoparticles for rebuilding skeletal muscle. Lost or damaged muscle needs scaffolds that copy its aligned fibres, softness, and high energy use, and ordinary cell culture falls short. Tiny magnetic particles, tuned by their coatings, answer outside magnets without contact, which opens several tricks at once.

The review covers coating choices, both organic and inorganic, and the weaving of particles into scaffolds that respond to magnets. Aligned fields can line muscle cells up, guide stem cells and drugs to a target, and stiffen or move a construct on cue. Magnetic resonance imaging can then watch the implant without cutting. Hossain's team weighs the safety record and the body's handling of the particles. Regulation and long-term fate remain the gates between this platform and patients.
pmc-13515879:
Xu and co-authors screen a probiotic strain, Lactiplantibacillus plantarum CLPX21, using gene and lab tests. Ten lactic acid bacteria were tried, and this strain stood out for killing germs and handling stress. It resisted acid and bile salts, key tests for gut survival.

The strain clumped strongly and stuck to pig gut cells in lab tests. It fought common food germs such as E. coli, Salmonella, and Staphylococcus aureus. It also blocked E. coli biofilm growth and calmed immune cell swelling. It showed no red-cell harm, and its gene map backed up the lab findings.
pmc-13516679:
Biondi and colleagues profiled oxidative stress and inflammation in horses naturally infected with Theileria equi, a tick-borne parasite that lives inside red blood cells and causes equine piroplasmosis. Their 2026 study enrolled thirty-five infected horses and twenty healthy controls, confirming infection by antibody testing and gene amplification. Measuring inflammatory signals plus markers of cell damage and antioxidant reserves in blood.

Biondi found infected horses had lower platelet counts and higher liver enzyme activity than controls. Two inflammatory messengers were clearly raised, showing persistent immune activation, while a damage marker from fat oxidation rose and the key antioxidant glutathione fell, consistent with worn-down defenses. The damage marker tracked with clinical severity scores and lower red cell counts, and antioxidant levels fell as white cell counts rose. The authors conclude chronic infection couples oxidative stress with sustained inflammation, and combined markers could help monitor disease and treatment.
pmc-13517579:
Hari Iyer and co-authors use camera vision to measure how much factory workers move, with no gear on the body. Their 2026 paper notes that worker output hinges on motion, yet stock tools fall short. Wearable sensors need tuning and cramp movement, while marker studios cost much and fit the field poorly. Their framework reads joint spots from pose software in live video and tracks upper and lower limb motion with a statistical gauge.

Warnings fire when motion passes set limits. Warning counts tracked well with a known workload survey score. A learned model trained on the motion data flagged odd motion patterns with high accuracy on the home data set, though scores varied on outside sets.
pmc-13518479:
Xuan Xuan Song and four colleagues open the mail of a parasitic tapeworm larva in a 2026 study. Spirometra mansoni larvae burrow through human tissue, causing blindness or paralysis, and biopsy diagnosis is hard. Like many parasites, the larvae shed extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane parcels. The team cultured larvae, harvested the vesicles, and profiled their proteins and small RNAs.

The parcels measured eighty to one hundred fifty nanometres and carried the classic vesicle markers. Their protein cargo ran to twenty-seven hundred entries, rich in transport, secretion, and signalling roles. The RNA haul held thirty-seven known and one hundred eighteen new microRNAs, with targets touching cell death, cholesterol handling, and host interplay. Rabbit serum against the vesicles stirred a mixed but mainly Th1-style immune answer. Song's team offers the catalogue as a base for diagnostics and for decoding how the larva talks to its host.
pmc-13518879:
Chengming Ma and six colleagues build a mechanics-based method in 2026 for choosing how fast to flow back fracturing fluid from coalbed methane wells. Crews today pick rates by experience, which transfers poorly between wells. Flowing too fast drags out proppant sand and coal fines, damaging the fractures that carry gas.

Their model balances forces on particles before and after fracture closure, using measurable inputs such as particle size, fluid thickness, and pressure difference. Calculations for two wells gave critical proppant velocities spanning wide ranges depending on closure stage. Particle size, density, and pressure difference dominated the results. Ma and co-authors offer the workflow as a screening tool, openly noting no new lab validation.
pmc-13518979:
Barbara Szymanik, Sam Ang Keo, Franck Brachelet, and Didier Defer refine in 2026 a harmless way to find steel rebar hidden inside concrete. Crews must locate rebar and judge its state without harming buildings. Their method heats the concrete with microwaves and watches the surface with an infrared camera, since steel warms at another rate than concrete.

The study pairs fine computer models of a microwave source, broadband antenna, and steel-laced concrete block with matching bench tests. How the source fired and how the antenna sat against the sample both shaped the heat patterns on the surface. Matching mock and real heat maps, the team works toward settings that make rebar spotting precise and repeatable.
pmc-13520079:
Zhang Jing and co-authors report a prostate infection from a meningitis germ in a 2026 case paper. Neisseria meningitidis rarely infects the urinary tract, and chronic prostatitis from it is rarer still. Its symptoms mimic gonorrhea closely enough to mislead first treatment.

A man of thirty-four had recurring burning urination and discharge after oral sex. Standard therapy for gonorrhea helped only partly, hinting at a wrong label. Cultures of urine and prostate fluid, confirmed by mass spectrometry and gene sequencing, named meningococcus. Targeted antibiotics then cleared both symptoms and germ. Recurring urethritis deserves a true name before more medicine.
pmc-13520179:
Valerio Zaccaria and co-authors argue, in a 2026 comment, that coaches and trainers stand in a prime spot to catch eating disorders early, because exercise itself can turn pathological. Compulsive training tied to weight control is a core feature of these illnesses. Most cases surface only after body or mind is badly harmed.

Sport professionals see at-risk young people weekly, in settings where warning signs show. The authors propose a practical framework to equip them for early detection. It grew from a European sport project on friendship and fitness culture. Training the observers who are already present could move detection months earlier, when treatment works best.
pmc-13520379:
Sylvester R Groen and colleagues compare in 2026 three questionnaires for adults living with faecal incontinence, asking whether a broader well-being measure adds anything beyond symptom and quality-of-life scales. Patients often value independence and stability, not only fewer accidents.

Data came from 72 trial participants, mostly women, with an average age near 67 years. The capability measure scored higher on its scale than the generic health measure and showed good agreement with related scores. Each tool separated known groups somewhat differently, with no single winner across all checks. Clinicians gain guidance on matching questionnaire choice to the question asked.
pmc-13520779: Daigo Imasato and co-authors report an asthma-like airway disease case in a 2026 paper. A 59-year-old man came in with sore throat and cough, and scans plus a camera inspection showed his windpipe narrowed by widespread inflammation. Four standard criteria supported relapsing polychondritis, a rare disorder where cartilage turns inflamed again and again. Strong steroid treatment joined with an immune-suppressing drug eased his symptoms and the airway lesions. The authors stress early recognition and repeated airway checks, since a swollen windpipe can close without warning.
pmc-13521779:
Mucheng Zhang, Yueyang Shao, and Jian Liu trace how homework type reaches math scores through interest, in this 2026 paper. China's Double Reduction policy reshaped homework, and eighth graders' routines vary widely. Over eighteen thousand students answered a mixed online and paper survey.

Practice homework served as the comparison base. Mixes with test-preparation homework lifted scores directly. Mixes adding applied or project work lifted scores by first raising interest. Interest in homework fed interest in learning, which fed performance, a chain the analysis confirms. The findings tell schools which mixes buy points and which buy motivation.
pmc-13522479:
Nawab John Dar, David Soriano-Castell, and Pamela Maher describe a long-lasting stress state in nerve cells exposed to excess iron in a 2026 laboratory study. Iron builds up in brain areas harmed by Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, yet the effect of prolonged exposure was unclear. Cultured neuronal cells received either a brief exposure of hours or a chronic exposure lasting nine days.

Brief exposure caused little change and did not make cells more fragile. Chronic exposure raised iron-storage protein, damaged fat molecules, depleted a key protective chemical, and lowered a protective enzyme, while cells stayed alive. Those chronically stressed cells then died more easily when faced with further oxidative challenges. The authors name the state chronoferroptosis and present it as an early vulnerability stage.
pmc-13522879:
Juan Pablo Frias wrote a practical guide for doctors on spotting and treating hypercortisolism, a state of excess cortisol, the body's stress hormone. The guide aims at hard cases hiding inside stubborn type 2 diabetes, resistant high blood pressure, and adrenal growths.

A simple overnight drug test, where a steroid pill should switch cortisol off, forms the guide's main case-finding tool. Confirmed excess appears in under 4 percent of broad diabetes groups, but about one in four patients in selected high-risk groups fail the test. Mild cortisol excess without classic Cushing signs still raises blood pressure, diabetes, belly fat, and death risk. Surgery cures best when the source can be cut out, and Frias details drug options when it cannot.
pmc-13523279:
