Chen Xu and colleagues describe a modified technique for placing an iliac branch device through the same-side leg artery in a 2026 two-center study. Branch devices preserve blood flow to the internal iliac artery during aneurysm repair, yet standard access routes can fail in patients with short or difficult anatomy. Twenty-three patients treated between 2023 and 2024, in whom the opposite leg route was judged unsuitable, received the balloon-anchored approach.

Deployment succeeded in every case, with the branch artery open and no major leaks on early imaging. At one year, the main device was open in all patients and the bridging stent in nearly all. No related reoperations were needed over a median sixteen months. Two minor complications occurred, supporting the technique as feasible for selected difficult anatomies.
pmc-13523379:
Jolanta Guz and colleagues follow chemical changes in DNA during chemotherapy for breast cancer in a 2026 study. Seventy-one patients received standard drug treatment before surgery, with blood and urine collected at four points and tumor tissue taken at operation. Levels of methylcytosine and its oxidized derivatives were measured by advanced chromatography, and activity of the genes that drive this demethylation pathway was assessed.

During treatment, several derivative levels in white blood cell DNA rose, while expression of the pathway genes fell. Patients whose pre-treatment levels of one derivative were lower in blood and urine, and whose tumors showed a particular post-treatment pattern, fared better over six years of follow-up. The authors link the pathway's behavior during therapy to disease-free and overall survival, suggesting prognostic value.
pmc-13523479:
Daryna Maruniak and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study, risk factors for massive bleeding after heart transplantation. The operation remains the standard for end-stage heart failure, yet heavy bleeding afterward raises illness and transfusion needs. Predictors, especially from bedside clot testing, were poorly described.

The single-center study included 75 adults transplanted between 2019 and 2025 who had preoperative ClotPro viscoelastic testing. Massive bleeding, defined by a standard bleeding scale, occurred in 31 patients, about four in ten. Transfusion use was high, and about one in six patients needed reoperation for bleeding. Many factors linked with bleeding in simple analyses, but only a clot firmness measure from the EX test stayed independent in adjusted analysis. The authors propose it for early risk flagging.
pmc-13524079:
Basu and colleagues showed in 2026 that two plant regulators best known for nitrate sensing also hold back sulfate uptake, linking two nutrient pathways in thale cress. Nitrogen and sulfur work together in crops, but the wiring between their control systems was largely unknown. The regulators, transcription factors TGA1 and TGA4, sit in the nitrate response cascade and also play roles in immunity.

Adding nitrate quickly raised sulfate uptake and use, then a delayed brake cut activity of the main sulfate transporter, and that brake required TGA1 and TGA4. Both factors bind the transporter's control region and dampen it directly. Plants missing both factors took up more sulfate, built more of the amino acid cysteine, and fared better under long sulfur shortage, while sulfur defense compounds also shifted. The authors say the pair keeps nutrient intake in balance and may help breed crops that use fertilizer better.
pmc-13524279:
Parasitic worms leave DNA traces in water, sludge, and food long before anyone falls sick. Juan Zuluaga and co-authors built a surveillance method around those traces. They sequenced a ribosomal gene region from environmental samples in Colombia's Andean region and placed the matches on family trees to name the species.

Twenty samples from treatment plants, farm bio-inputs, and food yielded twenty-five distinct sequence types across six worm taxa. The finds included human whipworm, pinworm, and hookworm, plus a rat lungworm that infects people who eat snails. The authors argue the method scales better than microscope identification. It offers health programs a replicable early-warning net for parasitic disease.
pmc-13525079:
Yuan Ji and Bajin Wei review how small chemical edits to proteins help drive ulcerative colitis. The disease is a chronic, relapsing inflammation of the colon whose causes mix genes, immune faults, a leaky gut barrier, and disturbed microbes. Their 2026 paper focuses on post-translational modifications, the tags cells attach to proteins after building them, which can switch a protein's activity, stability, and partners.

The review walks through the main kinds of tag, from phosphate and sugar groups to ubiquitin, and traces what each does in the inflamed colon. Again and again the tags land on immune signaling, on the junctions that seal the gut lining, and on the pathways that keep inflammation burning. Mapping them, the authors argue, could reveal drug targets that current therapies miss, since a tag can be added or removed by enzymes that medicines know how to reach.
pmc-13525379:
Edoardo Loru, Marco Delmastro, Francesco Gesualdo, and Matteo Cinelli model the COVID-19 infodemic across 30 countries. An infodemic is the flood of information, true and false, that rides along with an outbreak. The team joined WHO case and death data, vaccination records, WHO EARS social listening data, and Google Trends. Regression models tested which epidemic traits drove the volume of public conversation.

New deaths proved the strongest predictor of document production. Disease burden in neighboring countries mattered more than conditions at home. The authors build a data-driven grouping of countries by how their infodemic tracked the epidemic, and they trace how that link changed over time.
pmc-13525779:
Simon Vieth reviews how vitamin D supplements change blood levels of the vitamin in infants and children, published in 2026. Deficiency stays common in the young, above all at northern latitudes and in babies fed only breast milk. Supplements are widely advised, yet the rise in blood levels varies across groups.

The narrative review collected clinical studies that used one standard formulation and reported levels before and after. Seven studies from four countries, covering a few thousand children, met the rules. Doses ran from a modest daily amount to a large weekly one, over one to twelve months. The synthesis asks how large and how steady the response is across settings, a practical question for dosing guidance and for designing future trials in children.
pmc-13526179:
A virus best known for sickening dogs can also strike other mammals, sometimes in ways vets rarely see. Jennifer Black and co-authors report, in a 2026 case report, a four-year-old two-toed sloth in a private collection that fell ill while pregnant. The animal showed lung and gut illness, lost its unborn young, and then died.

Examination found severe inflammation of the placenta, with clots and virus marks inside vessel cells. The mother also had pneumonia, liver damage, and a secondary fungal infection. Lab tests found the distemper virus in her womb, lung, and placenta, and its gene code matched a virus seen earlier in a raccoon. The case shows the virus can attack pregnancy in species far from dogs.
pmc-13526479:
Fernandez Placencia and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of eosinophilic cellulitis, or Wells syndrome, a rare skin inflammation that mimics bacterial infection. Their patient, a 72-year-old woman with lupus and other autoimmune conditions, first received antibiotics for red, swollen legs and seemed to improve. Three days after finishing the course she returned with itchy red plaques across arms and legs, swelling, and pain, and antihistamines did not help.

Blood tests showed a raised count of eosinophils, a white cell type tied to allergy and inflammation, and a high sedimentation rate, a general inflammation marker. A skin punch biopsy found eosinophil-rich inflammation around and between vessels, matching Wells syndrome, and steroid treatment brought improvement. The authors stress that recurrent cellulitis-like eruptions that answer antibiotics only briefly deserve an early biopsy, since clinic and lab correlation is what separates this mimic from true infection.
pmc-13526879:
Mumtaz Y Balkhi and colleagues showed that the SchistoShield vaccine triggers lasting immune memory in people on two continents. Published in 2026, the study examined blood cells from United States and African trial volunteers who had received the Sm-p80 plus GLA-SE vaccine. It targets schistosomiasis, a worm disease infecting about 250 million people. Recall tests re-exposed immune cells to the vaccine antigen in the lab.

Vaccinated volunteers produced strong effector and memory T-cell responses, releasing a broad mix of signaling proteins and killer molecules. Antibody-secreting cells specific to the antigen also appeared in volunteers followed over time. The authors read these hallmarks as signs of a potentially effective vaccine, building on earlier safety trials in the United States, Madagascar, and Burkina Faso. Readers get immunological backing for a vaccine aimed at a major neglected disease.
pmc-13527479:
Liyang Duan and Xianjie Wu describe, in a 2026 case report, treating a child's severe contact dermatitis from lacquer tree exposure with abrocitinib, a targeted immune drug. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell reaction, and standard care relies on avoidance, topical steroids, calamine, and antihistamines, which can fall short in children with widespread disease.

An eight-year-old boy developed intensely itchy red papules and plaques over trunk and limbs for ten days after exposure to Toxicodendron vernicifluum. Three days of topical steroid, emollients, and an antihistamine failed as the rash spread to his face, with a severity score in the severe range. His parents declined systemic steroids over growth concerns, so after counseling the team started daily oral abrocitinib plus nightly cetirizine. Photographs chart facial clearing by day three and near resolution by day eleven.
pmc-13527679: A 2026 digest in a global health bulletin sums up the articles in that month's issue on one short page. Items cover health funding pressure in Kenya, antibiotic use in livestock in Bangladesh, and a child illness prevention study in Madagascar. Other items review counting maternal deaths in Tanzania and the market for a key drug in South-East Asia. Short notes also cover disease coding updates, lab tools for drug resistance, heat risks for workers, and a long study of healthy life paths.
pmc-13527979:
Emma J. Steel and seven colleagues report a 2026 qualitative evaluation of software that flags chest X-rays for priority reading in a Scottish NHS board. The qXR program from Qure.ai aims to speed lung cancer detection. Staff and patients were asked how acceptable they found it. Sixteen staff took part in interviews before and after rollout. Eight service users joined focus groups.

Staff saw the tool as a helpful adjunct that could shorten the path to scans and treatment. Patients also welcomed faster answers. They preferred brief anxiety with prompt action over long uncertainty. Radiology staff worried about accuracy, over-trust, and biased decisions. The authors say adoption will hold only if the tool fits existing systems and keeps proving itself.
pmc-13528079:
Nicholas C. Nicolaides, James Bradford Kline, and Luigi Grasso develop a blocker drug against a cancer shield protein in a 2026 study. Many tumors release CA125, a protein that coats treatment antibodies. Coated antibodies cannot trigger immune killing well. The team engineered fusion proteins to grab CA125 tightly. Their lead design, NAV-005, bound it with high strength.

In cell tests NAV-005 kept CA125 off treatment antibodies. Immune cells then killed targets at full strength again. A second killing route, driven by complement proteins, also recovered. Antibody-drug conjugates slipped past the shield too. They entered cancer cells and killed as intended. The authors say such blockers could rescue many existing antibody drugs. Clinical testing is the next step they propose.
pmc-13528179:
Brieuc Leger, Stephane Perrey, and co-authors test a fake move feel trick in young, older, and stroke groups, in work from 2026. A buzz on a tendon can make the brain sense a move that did not occur. Stroke often dulls this sense and harms arm control.

Brain blood flow was tracked while the buzz ran, with and without sight of the arm. Older adults showed broad brain use, more than young adults. Stroke cases showed near no task linked brain use at all. Their brain thrift score still matched the older group. Saved coping paths may thus aid early rehab work.
pmc-13528379:
Zheng-Bin Liao and Ye-Ran Wang replied in 2026 to two letters about their study of omega-3 supplements and mental decline. Critics had pressed them on whether the link they found could be read as cause and effect. The authors stress that they never claimed the supplements cause decline. Their backward-looking design, rough exposure data, and possible hidden factors all demand caution.

They explain that exposure came from self-reported medication records over time, not one baseline question. Dose, stopping, and steady use went unrecorded, so some misclassification is likely. Blood levels of omega-3 were higher in users, which supports the grouping but not dose claims. They call the pattern a signal for caution, not proof of harm.
pmc-13528579:
Nishant Kumar, Matthias Blatnik, and Jan Čechal watch a rust mineral skin heal back after it has been stripped down, in a study from 2026. The skin matters for clean up work, catalysis, and plant use, and its return hinges on heat and oxygen levels.

With a live electron scope, the team tracked a new honeycomb skin phase as it formed and spread. Heat sped the birth of new patches yet slowed their spread at set oxygen push. Below a low oxygen floor, spread stalled. The work shows oxygen supply, not heat drive alone, sets the pace of skin recovery.
pmc-13528679:
Ian Richard Hambleton and co-authors analyze injury burden across the Americas in a 2026 study. Injuries kill and disable many people, but the load is not shared evenly by place or by sex. The team used World Health Organization estimates for thirty-five countries, covering the years from 2000 to 2021, and compared death and disability rates by cause and subregion.

In 2021 injuries caused more than six hundred sixty thousand deaths in the Americas, with men bearing nearly three quarters of the loss. Rates fell in most areas, yet wide gaps stayed. Violence between people was the top cause, then road injuries, with young men hit hardest. Self-harm rose in both sexes, and falls rose as populations aged. The authors call for fair, joint action on prevention.
pmc-13528779:
Yuto Sato and co-authors map studies on family history in developmental stuttering. A relative who stutters is a known risk factor, yet reported rates swing wildly between studies. The team screened three databases and kept 19 studies that reported family history for people who stutter.

Positive family history ranged from 20 to 91 percent across studies. The spread traced to method choices: which relatives counted, how stuttering in the family was defined, and how data were gathered. The authors call for shared definitions and cleaner reporting so genetics and clinic work can build on the numbers.
pmc-13529879:
Joao Pedro Rueda Furlan and co-authors track drug-proof bacteria in sewage in Brazil, focusing on microbes that resist carbapenems, a last-line drug class. Wastewater plants can act as pools where such germs and their genes gather and trade. The team reads the full genomes of strains pulled from raw plant inflow.

Drug tests showed wide resistance, spanning carbapenems and polymyxins, in Klebsiella and Enterobacter strains. Genome reads found two key resistance genes, KPC-2 and GES-16, meeting in the same strains, with GES-5 also present. The KPC-2 gene sat inside jumping DNA segments that help it spread. Some strains matched high-risk clones known from hospitals. The findings warn that sewage can merge rare resistance traits into harder-to-treat forms.
pmc-13530179:
H Elhendawi and co-authors blend two natural polymers with an ionic liquid to make an eco-friendly light-absorbing film. Their study appeared in 2026. The base mixes polyvinyl alcohol with chitosan, a shell-derived polymer, cast into films with rising shares of the liquid additive. X-ray and infrared checks showed the additive knits into the blend through strong molecular interactions, and the films grow less crystalline as its share rises, from about 56 percent down to 30.

The optical gap narrowed too, signaling better light handling for electronics. Absorption tests confirmed the films catch light well. The authors pitch the composite for energy storage and optoelectronic devices where green materials are wanted. They note the recipe is simple casting, easy to scale.
pmc-13531079:
Jeffrey Yim and colleagues report in 2026 the catheter retrieval of a leg vein stent that migrated into the heart and straddled a valve. The 38-year-old patient felt palpitations and breathlessness one day after vein treatment. Imaging showed the stent crossing the tricuspid valve, causing severe leakage and brief dangerous rhythm bursts.

Two snares, one from each leg vein, gripped both stent ends under ultrasound guidance from within the food pipe, with surgeons standing by. Removal left only mild leakage and no fluid around the heart. The patient recovered smoothly, avoiding open surgery.
pmc-13532579:
Junlei Zhang and colleagues built a single-atom cobalt catalyst that cleans polluted water with unusual selectivity. Published in 2026, the study made a cobalt-on-carbon-nitride catalyst whose metal sites shift on activation by peroxymonosulfate, a common oxidant, from Co-N2O1 toward Co-N1O2. How metal coordination and spin states steer oxidation remains poorly mapped in such water-treatment systems.

The shifted site favored singlet oxygen while still producing sulfate radicals in parallel, speeding oxytetracycline breakdown more than fivefold over the bare support and beating over thirty rival catalysts. Activity held across diverse antibiotics and dyes, in complex water matrices, and under continuous flow. The authors link reaction-induced site change to spin-aware oxygen transfer, offering design rules for selective, durable treatment catalysts. Readers get a mechanism-led advance for water cleanup.
pmc-13533579:
Ya Ling Shih and co-authors present a 2026 randomized trial of a web platform that teaches women about phthalates, chemicals in plastics and cosmetics that disturb hormones. Daily products expose women often, yet standard health talks rarely allow repeat, personal, interactive learning. The platform, called Phthalates Free, was built to fill that gap.

Women were assigned at random to the platform or to usual education. The trial measured overall and topic-by-topic health literacy about these chemicals before and after. It also tracked how platform use related to what women learned. The results test whether tailored e-learning can turn awareness into habits that cut exposure at home.
pmc-13533779:
Hajer Alturki and co-authors test iron catalysts that split methane into hydrogen and carbon, in a 2026 study. This route makes hydrogen without releasing carbon oxides, and the solid carbon left behind has value as nanostructures. The team placed iron on several base materials called supports. Some supports were alumina reshaped with added metal oxides.

A battery of lab tools mapped each catalyst's structure and behavior. Plain alumina gave the best start among the single supports. Adding a zirconium oxide layer to alumina did even better, reaching the highest methane conversion and hydrogen yield. That catalyst also survived repeat regeneration cycles well. Strong bonds between iron and support seem to keep the iron particles stable and active.
pmc-13533879:
Most plant genes have no proven link to a trait, so picking which to test first is a costly guess. Nikee Shrestha and co-authors build a sorter for that guess in a 2026 study. Their tool reads gene sequence and family history traits that need no lab work to compute.

Trained only on maize genes, the sorter still flagged the right genes in rice and in a model weed. Its high picks were rich in genes with proven trait links. Many high picks sit in gene families no one has studied yet. Scores from the tool can rank genes for any crop with a mapped genome. That ranking cuts wasted effort in trait hunts.
pmc-13534179:
Lei Luo and colleagues review in 2026 a long non-coding RNA called HIF1A-AS2 and its role across many human cancers. The RNA does not build proteins, yet raised levels appear in many tumour types and link to poor outlook. Lab studies tie it to cell growth, spread, drug resistance, and cell death control.

The RNA can sponge up smaller RNAs or bind proteins directly, lifting cancer traits through several paths. The review compares patterns across 12 cancer types and weighs barriers to clinical use. Readers see why this RNA draws interest as a diagnostic mark and drug target.
pmc-13534579:
Junwon Lee and co-authors present a system for checking coolant levels in air conditioners in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Low coolant hurts energy use and stable running, yet models trained on one unit type often fail on another. Users also need clear reasons for a warning, not just a score.

Their system aligns sensor data across six kinds of home air conditioner so one model can serve them all. A large language model, tuned on many expert-checked cases, then explains each call in plain words tied to the sensor pattern. Tests on six data sets beat older deep learning and domain methods. The authors say the system can support real repair and upkeep work.
pmc-13534679:
Zhi-Ming Zeng and colleagues mapped how tau pathology spreads across Alzheimer stages in ordered layers. Published in 2026, the study integrated amyloid and tau PET scans, diffusion and resting-state MRI, and gene-expression maps across disease stages. Tau defines Alzheimer disease yet spreads unevenly, and the roles of amyloid, brain wiring, and intrinsic weakness were unclear.

Tau followed a hierarchical gradient that stratified by amyloid load and clinical stage. Amyloid patterns plus structural and functional links predicted tau patterns and explained much spatial variation. A leftover tau pattern tracked gene programs for signaling, synapses, energy, and RNA control, shifting by stage. Tau geometry also mediated links between network organization and symptoms. Readers get a joint marker tying amyloid, wiring, and weakness to decline.
pmc-13534779:
Wen-Ling Li and seven colleagues published a nanomedicine study in two thousand twenty-six on stopping inflammation at its source. Damaged cell power plants leak oxidised fragments of their DNA, which trigger fierce inflammation. Most treatments mop up after the fact; the leak keeps flowing.

The team designed a small inhibitor that blocks the enzyme cutting those fragments loose. A targeted carrier, built on a sugar polymer and selenium particles, ferried it to inflamed cells. The selenium also neutralised harmful oxygen species and helped clear escaped DNA. In a severe lung injury model, the combined treatment calmed the inflammatory cascade and eased tissue damage. The authors pitch source control for many such diseases.
pmc-13534979:
Hee Ju Kim and co-authors test a citrus peel extract for brain health in a 2026 study. The Korean citrus is rich in plant compounds that fight oxygen damage, a driver of nerve cell death. Memory loss and weak signaling follow that damage in many brain diseases.

In cell tests, the extract shielded mouse brain cells from a toxic hit, cutting stress waste and cell death. It tuned two signal paths tied to defense and growth in the cells. In mice given a memory blocking drug, daily extract doses lifted scores on behavior tests. Brain tissue showed less cell damage and restored growth signals after dosing. Blood checks also showed shifts in fuel and fat pathways tied to cell defense.
pmc-13535379:
Caroline Dahlberg and co-authors delete one enzyme from human cells and watch the whole protein economy reorganize under stress. Ube2j2 helps the endoplasmic reticulum destroy misfolded proteins, part of the unfolded protein response. Mass spectrometry profiled cultured bone tumor cells, with and without the enzyme, as a drug flooded their reticulum with bad proteins.

The abundance patterns fell into twelve modules, each summarized by its most typical member and its biological annotations. Familiar pathways tied to the enzyme lit up, protein quality control above all. So did functions nobody had connected to it: RNA metabolism, transport between reticulum and Golgi, and cell-cycle progression. The authors deposit the data publicly and offer the map as a set of leads for what this enzyme quietly does all day.
pmc-13535679:
Seyyed Hosseini, Mohammad Motamedifar, and Shabnam Ajami test germ-fighting coatings for clear dental aligners. Their twenty twenty-six study coats aligners with chitosan, cellulose nanocrystals, or both. Aligners are seen as clean, yet they link to more white spot lesions on teeth.

Five groups of aligner samples were compared in the lab. Some discs fed germ tests, while cubes fed hardness and bending tests. Surface shape was also scanned for change. The aim is a coating that kills germs without weakening the plastic or clouding its look. Results guide whether such coats are ready for clinic trials in orthodontic care.
pmc-13535879:
Isbilir and four co-authors describe the tongue of the Anatolian wild boar, in work from twenty twenty-six. Detailed anatomy of wild animal tongues aids veterinary care, wildlife studies, and understanding of feeding adaptation. This subspecies had not been fully characterized.

Tongue samples from two adult wild boars found dead in nature were examined soon after death. Gross anatomy was recorded first. Tissue then went through standard histology, special stains, and scanning electron microscopy for surface detail of the papillae. The three scales of observation give a complete reference for future comparative anatomy work.
pmc-13536579:
Yunho Jeong and colleagues describe in 2026 a rare skin B-cell lymphoma in a 12-year-old spayed female Shih Tzu dog. Skin B-cell lymphoma is extremely rare in dogs, so single cases still shape what vets know. The dog showed many nodules under the skin across the body.

Stains and flow tests confirmed B-cell type with clonal gene changes, while liver and spleen sampling found no spread. Standard four-drug chemotherapy brought only a brief partial response before fast progression. The case warns that this rare form can behave aggressively and resist usual treatment.
pmc-13536679:
Megha Anand leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two hands-on approaches for tight hamstrings in desk-based computer workers. Thirty information technology professionals were split evenly between static stretching and myofascial release, a pressure-based soft tissue technique. Each group trained five times a week for three weeks. Knee extension range and a self-rated leg function scale were measured at the start and on three later days.

Both groups gained range and function over the three weeks, with no harmful events reported. Stretching produced slightly larger gains in knee extension by the second and third checks. The authors note those gaps were smaller than the smallest change the knee test can reliably detect, so the practical edge remains unclear. Function gains were also close between groups, and the short follow-up without a control group limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13536979:
Angela Higgins and co-authors track how technology use and confidence changed for older adults in British retirement villages, in work from twenty twenty-six. Assistive tech can protect independence, but confidence gaps limit uptake. Lockdowns forced a natural experiment in digital adoption rates. Surveys bracket the pandemic in twenty twenty and twenty twenty-three. Interviews with trial participants add lived detail to the numbers.

Adoption and confidence rose clearly between the two survey waves. Device ownership and internet use climbed across activities measured. Family and friends became the dominant route for learning tech. Age gaps in confidence visible earlier had vanished by the later wave. Men still reported higher confidence than women in both waves. Providers learn where support still matters for older residents.
pmc-13537579:
Brooke Hawkes and co-authors compare antibody responses to COVID-19 shots and infection in children and adults, using an Arizona cohort of essential workers. Age shapes COVID risk and how bad the illness gets, but its effect on antibody levels was not clear. The cohort was followed from September 2020 to April 2023 and included health, emergency, and other frontline staff.

Two groups were built. One had two doses of the first mRNA vaccine and no prior infection. The other was unvaccinated people after a first infection. Antibody response was summed over time for two viral targets, the receptor-binding domain and the S2 part of spike. Children under 18 were compared with adults, with finer age bands too. The models took account of chronic illness, drugs, days since the shot or illness, and social factors. The design keeps vaccine-made and infection-made immunity apart.
pmc-13538079:
Hayat Jirde Ali and three co-authors follow patients with chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy for at least five years, in a study published in 2026. Patients had earlier been in a randomized trial, treated between 2016 and 2018 with either bipolar radiofrequency microtenotomy or physical therapy. Questionnaires in 2025 measured pain and foot and ankle outcomes.

Twenty-five of the original 38 patients were included in the follow-up. Both groups improved a great deal on pain and outcome scores compared with before treatment. The surgery group reported better pain and quality of life scores at follow-up. The authors warn that loss to follow-up left the study underpowered, so results need care.
pmc-13538279:
Gaia Fattorini and a large team test a cell-image method as a sign of a rare gene disease that stiffens the legs. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, centers on the most common form of that disease.

The disease group kills the long nerves of the spine in a slow way, and its main mark is a stiff gait. The form at stake stems from a gene that makes spastin, a protein that trims cell rails and shapes fat drops. No cure is there yet, but ways to bring spastin back are on the rise. A test that tracks the disease is thus in need. The team checks whether cell images can serve as that sign.
pmc-13538379:
Rajesh Kannan Megalingam and Naveen Prasaad Selvarajan present a hybrid network for predicting pedestrian crossing intent on Indian roads in a 2026 study. Crowded, unstructured streets with frequent blocking views and rule-bending walkers challenge models trained abroad. The design mixes image and graph networks with a gate that shifts weight between visual and motion clues by scene, plus a pose tool tuned for distant or partly hidden walkers. A new local road collection supports testing.

Accuracy reached moderate levels on both a standard foreign collection and the new Indian collection, with the fastest response times among compared methods. Extra tests covered blocked views, walker sizes, and cross-collection transfer, plus a run on a small onboard computer showing near real-time speed. The authors argue the trade-off suits driverless use in messy traffic.
pmc-13538479:
Hyun-Jeong Yang and colleagues test a metabolic nutrient for myelin repair after teen social isolation in mice in a 2026 study. Isolation after weaning thins myelin in a social brain hub and dulls sociability. The nutrient, acetyl-L-carnitine, links energy and fat handling. Dish tests traced uptake and conversion in myelin-making cells, while feeding tests in isolated mice checked behavior, myelin protein, and fat profiles in a major white matter tract.

In dishes, the nutrient widened myelin sheaths without boosting early cell growth, switched on growth signals, and raised breathing power in mature cells. Feeding restored social preference and myelin protein in isolated mice, while a myelin poison erased those gains. Fat chain patterns in the tract also normalized. The authors frame the nutrient as a metabolic lever for myelin disorders.
pmc-13538579:
Hyunhee Choo and co-authors present a retrospective orthodontics study, published in 2026, on correcting deep bites with clear aligners. Twenty-seven adults whose upper teeth overlapped the lower ones too deeply were treated with Invisalign fitted with precision bite ramps. The team compared head X-rays before and after treatment, using the tooth's center point to separate true vertical movement from mere tipping.

The lower front teeth sank by a small but clearly significant amount, and the overbite shrank by about two millimeters. The bite plane angle opened slightly, while jaw angles and molar height barely moved, pointing to tooth level change rather than skeletal change. The authors conclude the aligner system can intrude lower incisors in adult deep bite cases.
pmc-13539779:
Dandan Ling and colleagues test a back nerve block for pain after breast reconstruction, in a randomized trial from 2026. Implant based reconstruction after mastectomy causes sharp early pain for many patients. The trial asks whether one erector spinae plane block at chest level five lowers that pain.

One hundred adults at a cancer centre in China were split evenly between block and no block care. Both groups had standard anaesthesia and patient controlled pain pumps after surgery. Resting pain at six hours did not differ clearly at the median value. Pain scores were lower at later checks, and opioid use fell at one and two days. Early recovery scores rose, but the authors say larger trials must confirm real benefit.
pmc-13539879:
Heidi Kruit, Mika Gissler, and Leena Rahkonen analyse, in a 2026 cohort study, how the reason for starting labour artificially relates to how the birth turns out. Inductions keep rising as mothers get older and heavier, so clinicians need reason-specific evidence.

Hospital records from Helsinki covered 16,377 induced births at term between 2017 and 2021. Going past the due date and waters breaking early were the commonest reasons. Caesarean rates peaked when induction followed blood pressure disorders, while poor newborn outcomes clustered in inductions done for fetal concerns. First-time motherhood, an unready cervix, older age, shorter height, and higher body weight each raised caesarean risk.
pmc-13540279:
Annagowni and colleagues review nanotechnology platforms that combine ultrasound and photoacoustic imaging with treatment, an approach called theranostics, in 2026 medical research. Photoacoustic imaging fires light pulses into tissue and listens to the faint sound waves produced, marrying light's sensitivity with sound's depth. Natural tissue components such as hemoglobin, lipids, and melanin already absorb light and give signals, but engineered nanoparticles sharpen targeting and signal strength for diseased tissue.

The review explains the physics of the combined ultrasound and photoacoustic method, lists contrast agents both natural and manufactured, and surveys uses across diseases. Designed nanomaterials can also carry drugs, so the same particle that lights up a tumor on the scan can deliver therapy to it under image guidance. Remaining difficulties include weak signals from deep tissue and proving safety of new particles. Annagowni presents the pairing as a pillar of precision nanomedicine still maturing toward routine care.
pmc-13540879:
Kristine Mørch leads a 2026 prospective study of giardiasis that refuses to clear with standard nitroimidazole drugs, an intestinal parasite infection increasingly seen in travellers. Four centres in Norway and England enrolled 120 adults between 2009 and 2024, fifty-nine of them with resistant disease.

A treatment ladder gave a repeat nitroimidazole course first, which cured only about a quarter of those who tried it. Pairing the drug with albendazole cured roughly three quarters, and quinacrine, an older medicine, worked in every case where it was used. Infection caught in India and a more recent diagnosis year predicted standard treatment failure. Parasite strain patterns varied by travel region.
pmc-13541179:
Daniel Opinile Mark Igga and co-authors study vaccine dropout in South Sudan in this 2026 study. Many infants start their vaccine schedule but never finish it, a gap that weakens protection. In Maridi County, the team followed fourteen health facilities for three months in late 2023, half in areas with an active community health program and half without.

Three facilities had no monitoring chart at all, and over a quarter recorded dropout above ten percent. Facilities with current charts were far less likely to show high dropout. Community health workers, who rally families and trace those who miss visits, were present in most low-dropout facility months and few high-dropout ones. Over the study, the share of high-dropout facilities fell. The authors back both chart discipline and community tracing.
pmc-13541779:
Roland Cormier, Manon Mallet, and Gabriel Goguen show how sampling plans can check whether site safeguards for water quality really work. Building sites must control erosion and sediment so soil does not wash into streams. Inspecting every control is too costly, so the team adapts acceptance sampling, a method that judges a batch from a sample. Their 2026 paper works through an erosion and sediment control case from start to finish.

The plan weighs two risks: passing bad work, which harms the environment, and failing good work, which burdens the builder. Sample size decides how sharp that judgment can be. The authors lay out the math for the pass number for any sample size. They argue the method gives regulators a fair, clear check during active work.
pmc-13542079:
Vijay Kumar and seven colleagues run, in a 2026 engine study, a single-cylinder diesel engine on blends of Karanja biodiesel while tracking vibration alongside performance and exhaust. Biodiesel from this non-edible seed oil may cut emissions, yet shaking behaviour affects engine life and comfort.

Blends of twenty and thirty percent biodiesel were tested across loads, compression ratios, and recirculated exhaust settings. Vibration rose with load, fell with higher compression, and dipped then climbed as exhaust recirculation grew. Both blends vibrated less than plain diesel, and the stronger blend cut hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, and smoke noticeably. Fuel efficiency dropped and nitrogen oxides rose, marking the trade-off.
pmc-13542179:
Nimra Gillani and co-authors measure the stigma carried by breast cancer survivors in Muzaffarabad, and which women carry the most of it. Stigma corrodes friendships, mental health, finances, and even the will to keep treatment appointments. In conservative settings it can be heavier than the disease itself.

One hundred twenty-four women treated for stage one to three breast cancer at a tertiary hospital were surveyed with an adapted stigma questionnaire; one hundred one complete responses were analyzed. The team linked stigma scores to social and clinical characteristics. Naming who suffers most, younger or older, richer or poorer, married or not, tells support services where to aim first.
pmc-13542279:
Sieb Chanchamnan, Weiyi Wang, Se Rim Jang, and Il Won Suh borrow a beetle shell joint to make stretchy systems tougher. Their 2026 paper copies the interlocked suture of the diabolical ironclad beetle, famous for surviving crushing force. Stretchable electronics need shapes that spread stress instead of gathering it at weak points.

Long oval motifs slot together in the new design. Simulations show strain spreading more evenly and peak stress dropping versus classic curve layouts, above all in flat runs. Pull tests confirm the beetle design stretches further before failure. Sensor interconnect models show lower peak stress near stiff islands. The authors pitch the geometry for flexible devices that must endure repeated bending and stretching without tearing apart.
pmc-13543279:
Dewi Ummah and co-authors study how ready young children and their caregivers feel, in mind, for a volcano eruption, in a 2026 study from Ternate Island, Indonesia. Small volcanic islands face high risk, and early schooling there rarely covers the mental side of readiness. The team survey 127 teachers, parents, and community members, then hold six group talks.

Readiness scores came out moderate to high across all three groups, with personal coping ranked highest. Group talks showed strong cultural resources: faith, shared coping, and trust in one's own strength. Gaps sat elsewhere: thin knowledge of eruptions, weak calm-down skills, and uneven talk between families, schools, and officials. The team urge the three sides of a child's world to plan together, so strong personal coping gains matching support around the child.
pmc-13543479:
Fen Liu and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of early-onset dyslipidemia, abnormal blood fats arising in younger adults, using health check-up data from more than 3.5 million people in northwest China during 2019. The region lacked high-quality figures of its own. Everyone received questionnaires, physical examination, and laboratory tests including a full lipid profile, allowing the team to count each abnormality type and test which traits travelled with them.

One in four participants, 25.7 percent, had dyslipidemia. Low protective cholesterol was the commonest single fault at 14.5 percent, followed by high triglycerides at 10.6 percent, while most affected people had only one abnormal measure. Male sex, older age within the adult range, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, drinking, and excess weight all raised the odds independently. Screening should focus on those combined risks, the authors conclude, even though regional prevalence sits below the national level.
pmc-13543679:
Toby Freeman, Connie Musolino, and Fran Baum test a group method in 2026 for finding shared fixes to health unfairness in Australia. Health gaps grow from housing, work, schooling, and town design, so no single sector owns the cure. Their method, the World Cafe, runs relaxed rounds of small-group talk to draw out joint ideas.

Eight sessions, one per state or territory, drew 162 people from universities, government, and civic groups. Fields ranged from health and housing to jobs and town planning, with voices for Indigenous peoples, disabled people, and youth among them. Groups from unlike sectors found common ground with ease, the team reports, and built shared policy ideas. The test case supports cafes as a tool for cross-sector work.
pmc-13543879:
Qiaoli Zhao and co-authors published this study in 2026. It builds a food gel meant to carry quercetin, a healthy plant compound. Quercetin dissolves poorly in water, breaks down fast, and absorbs badly in the gut. The gel base is tilapia fish protein. The team treated the protein with ultrasound, then paired it with lambda-carrageenan, a seaweed thickener, at three levels.

Ultrasound partly unfolded the protein, which helped it bind the thickener into a denser, more ordered gel. The richest mix gave the smallest droplets and the stiffest gel. It kept more quercetin after light and heat than the plain protein gel. In digestion tests, the share the body could reach more than doubled. The authors offer the system as a carrier for fragile, fat-loving nutrients.
pmc-13543979:
Shang-Ming Huang and co-authors tested whether plant compounds from common vegetables can cut harmful compounds that form when pork is grilled over charcoal, in work published in 2026. Those compounds, which arise in browned meat, are a health concern.

The team screened twelve vegetables and profiled their plant compounds. Three stood out: sweet potato leaves, water spinach, and coriander. In grilling tests, the cuts in harmful compounds ranged widely, from about forty-three to about ninety-three percent, depending on whether the extract was used alone or in a sauce. Coriander did best as a plain marinade. Computer modeling suggests two compounds may bind to a meat protein near a key site.
pmc-13544079:
Steven Lâm and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of OHRECA, a six-year One Health centre. It worked across several African countries from 2020 to 2025 to build capacity against diseases jumping between animals, people, and environments. Africa carries the world's heaviest load of such threats, yet how capacity programmes achieve lasting results is poorly documented. The evaluators used a realist mixed-methods design, asking not just what changed but how and why.

The centre contributed to scientific output and workforce growth in its target countries. Two mechanisms did the work: learning by doing, and genuine partnership, both sustained by long time horizons and institutions that stayed the course. With no baseline or comparison group for many outcomes, the authors present the findings as an explanatory case study rather than proof of effectiveness. They offer design lessons for similar programmes in lower-income settings.
pmc-13545079:
Vikas Vohra and co-authors test genomic selection in Sahiwal cattle in India in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Genome-based breeding values can speed genetic gain and cut reliance on long field trials. Little work has tested the method in this breed, especially where few animals are genotyped.

The team predicted breeding values for milk yield over a standard lactation using a single-step genomic method. Its mean accuracy edged past the pedigree-only method, and cross-checks favored it more clearly. The genomic values also agreed with the expected progeny differences already used for culling on the farm. The authors recommend the method for routine evaluation, noting it can even catch pedigree errors.
pmc-13545779:
Ryosuke Miura and co-authors test a special stem cell type for lung injury in newborn rats, in a 2026 paper. The injury mimics a chronic lung disease of premature infants, caused in part by high oxygen. Trials in infants using these stress enduring cells, called Muse cells, have begun.

Rat pups breathed high oxygen for fifteen days, and cells were given on day five through a vein or the windpipe. The two routes gave similar gains in lung function and tissue findings. The windpipe route, though, worsened weight gain and survival. Vein delivery of Muse cells eased tissue injury and inflammation more than control cells. The authors favor vein delivery for later work.
pmc-13545979:
John Phamnguyen, Elaine Kuan, Puneet Dheer, Viktor Vegh, and David Reutens study brain links in people whose seizures spread to both sides of the brain, in a research paper from 2026. These severe seizures carry a high risk of harm and sudden death. The cerebellum, at the back of the brain, may help control how often they strike.

The team scanned thirty patients with temporal lobe epilepsy and twenty healthy controls. Patients with recent spreading seizures showed weaker links between two cerebellar areas than controls. Links between the cerebellum and deeper brain areas were also lower. The authors say this supports a role for the cerebellum in seizure control.
pmc-13546379:
Shyun Ping Tiong and co-authors audit outbreak response in care homes in a 2026 study. Flu-like infections spread fast in care homes, where residents are frail. Fast public health action and early antiviral drugs can limit harm. The team reviewed how responses played out across South East England during the 2024 to 2025 flu season.

In that season, 340 incidents were reported from 2,737 care homes. The team examined 103 homes in detail. The median gap from first symptoms to notifying public health was four days. Once notified, assessment came fast, with a median of one day from the latest symptom report. The study weighs where delay creeps in and how prescribing matched guidance, to sharpen future outbreak playbooks.
pmc-13546679:
Christine Olwedo Adoch and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on hearing loss in children with sickle cell disease in eastern Uganda. The disease's blocked blood flow and chronic anemia can damage the inner ear. Yet hearing in these children is rarely checked in the region, even though the Mbale area carries one of Uganda's heaviest sickle cell loads.

The team tested two hundred twenty-five children and teens, aged five to eighteen, at a hospital clinic while they were in a steady state. A specialist ran tone tests, and impairment was set by the world standard threshold. They also looked for traits that travel with hearing loss. Numbers like these can push clinics to add hearing checks to routine sickle cell care.
pmc-13546779:
Li, Malakooti, and Jhaveri make a financial case for giving infectious disease doctors protected time for quality improvement work. Such work is usually local to one hospital, which makes outside funding hard to win. Yet its local payoff can be strong. Their 2026 piece draws on experience at a freestanding children's hospital.

Reviews already show the money value these specialists bring through antibiotic stewardship and infection control. Their training also suits them to lead diagnostic stewardship, trimming costly tests that rarely change care. Local projects cut use of two broad, pricey tests safely, the authors report. They argue hospitals should treat protected time as a sound business choice, not a favor.
pmc-13547579:
Max Blücher and co-authors test in 2026 whether quantitative brain wave measures can detect delirium types after stroke and link them to inflammation markers. Stroke delirium is common but often missed, and binary labels hide its severity range. They assessed eighty-seven stroke patients within two days, recording sixty-four-channel brain waves and blood markers in a subgroup.

Delirium occurred in about a third of patients. It showed slowed rhythms and altered network coupling. A combined brain wave model separated delirium with strong accuracy overall, though it caught only about sixty-three percent of true cases. Some network measures correlated with inflammatory markers, hinting at mechanism.
pmc-13547679:
Eye scans may hold clues to heart risk. Dongjin Nam and co-authors tested a learning tool that reads such scans for people with high blood pressure or diabetes, in work from twenty twenty-six. The group held near eight thousand Korean patients with no past heart disease. Scans dated back across near two decades.

The tool's score tracked deaths from artery disease over ten years, even after standard risk facts were weighed in. Adding the score to a clinic model sharpened its sorting of who is at risk and moved many people to the right risk tier. A five-year check backed the pattern. The authors pitch eye scans as a painless add-on for heart risk checks.
pmc-13548179:
Mercedes Serrano and three colleagues report the first treatment results for a new enzyme-replacement drug in three adults with PMM2-CDG, a rare inherited glycosylation disorder. The disease cripples a sugar-handling step and produces a prominent balance disorder, ataxia, scored on a standard rating scale. The drug delivers the missing middle molecule in liposomes.

Weekly infusions for twenty-four weeks were well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Ataxia scores improved clearly by week twelve and further by week twenty-four, across all scale subdomains, and both patients and clinicians reported global gains. With only three patients the authors urge caution, but the signal supports continued trials.
pmc-13548279:
Female genital cutting is near-universal in Somalia, and its deepest form is blamed for a lifetime of urinary trouble. Umut Erkok and nine co-authors tested that link in a 2026 study of 122 women who came to care with urinary symptoms. They compared women cut in the milder types I and II with those who had type III, the sewn-shut form.

The type III group showed more positive urine cultures, more past infections, more antibiotic use, and more abdominal pain. A standard long questionnaire scored each woman's symptom burden and bother. The authors argue the anatomy left by type III cutting traps urine and invites infection, so symptom patterns in clinic should prompt questions about cutting history. Their data give clinics a sharper picture of which patients carry the heaviest urinary load.
pmc-13548579:
Vincenzo Quagliariello and colleagues review whether a class of diabetes drugs could protect the hearts and metabolism of breast cancer survivors, in a 2026 narrative review. Hormone-driven breast cancer is common, and hormone-blocking treatment saves lives while raising fat around the organs, disturbing lipids, and inflaming blood vessels. Heart disease has become a leading non-cancer killer in this group, prompting interest in sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors.

These drugs, first made to lower blood sugar, also guard the heart and kidneys. The review gathers laboratory, animal, and observational evidence that they calm insulin signaling, fat tissue inflammation, liver fat, and vessel dysfunction, and may even counter hormone therapy resistance. Matched patient studies in cancer populations are summarized with caution. The authors frame the drugs as a targeted candidate strategy needing direct trials in survivors on hormone therapy.
pmc-13548779:
Moro and a large team describe pancreas injury caused by immune cancer drugs in twenty twenty-six. Five rare cases with tissue samples were charted in depth. All but one patient were women, and all got paired immune drugs. Injury struck months after therapy began.

Scans mimicked autoimmune pancreatitis in four cases. Steroids cleared the flare in three patients. Two patients lost pancreas function or tissue over time. Two had surgery on a false cancer scare. Their tissue matched one autoimmune type closely, with duct centered inflammation. Pathologists should know the overlap, the authors stress.
pmc-13549179:
Eva Santi Hutasoit and co-authors identify the core parts of a stunting prevention model for teens in a 2026 study. Stunting, or stunted growth in children, traces back through the life cycle to teen health, anemia, early marriage, and poor access to care. Prevention aimed at teens before pregnancy is still rare, and the team asked what such a model needs.

They ran group talks and deep interviews with 27 people, including teens, parents, school leaders, health workers, and policymakers. The talks produced eight main themes, from teen and family factors to service quality, access, governance, and the local environment. The authors argue that joining all eight parts gives a full teen-centered approach that can also lift quality of life.
pmc-13549579:
Dian Zhang and Meifang Pan report a rare vein variant found by chance in a healthy 37-year-old man. Their 2026 case report concerns a persistent left superior vena cava with no right counterpart, a birth variant of the great vein that drains the upper body. Most carriers feel nothing, so the variant is often missed until a scan or procedure stumbles on it.

A routine exam flagged a widened coronary sinus on an ultrasound of the heart. A CT scan then confirmed the missing right vein and showed the right neck vein joining the left one. The man had no breath trouble, chest pain, or family history of heart disease. He stayed well on follow-up. The authors advise regular checks and heart rhythm monitoring, since the variant can complicate lines, surgery, and pacemaker work.
pmc-13549679:
Chen and Wang present a skin case as a diagnostic puzzle. A fifty-two-year-old woman had rings and arcs of red rash return for thirty years. The marks spread across her trunk, arms, and legs without body-wide symptoms. Readers are given her history, photos, and lab results, then asked for the diagnosis.

Her workup held surprises: a lung nodule proved to be an early lung cancer. Skin samples showed dense clusters of a white blood cell type called neutrophils, with no vessel damage. The answer given is neutrophilic figurate erythema, a rare rash pattern. The discussion weighs how the team separated it from similar ring-shaped rashes. Cases like this train doctors to read pattern, history, and microscope together.
pmc-13549779:
Hee-Jin Yang wrote a short editors' pick piece for a Korean brain surgery journal in 2026. From sixteen papers in the September issue, the board chose two to lift up for readers. Yang sums up each pick and why the board found it worth close attention.

One pick reports that stem cells coaxed toward nerve-like traits helped rats heal after spinal cord injury. The cells calmed a harmful reaction from support cells in the cord. That reaction, long seen as a pure block to repair, may also guard the cord in some ways. The note gives busy readers a quick guide to the issue's strongest work.
pmc-13550479:
Liang Zhao tests a video intelligence system that watches volleyball practice and turns what it sees into tailored drills, in a 2026 study. The pipeline detects players with a standard object detector and tracks their trajectories with a sorting algorithm. A neural network then reads body keypoints. From those it judges jump mechanics, approach angles, and arm-swing and block timing. Fifty-six competitive athletes trained for six weeks, half with the system's real-time feedback and half with standard coaching.

The supported group improved more across transition speed, serve-receive accuracy, rotation speed, defensive coverage, jump height, and timing consistency. Match-like indicators such as side-out rate and attack efficiency also rose further, and several gains survived one to two weeks later. Zhao concludes that fused trajectory and keypoint data can sharpen coaching decisions, pending tests in other venues and competitions.
pmc-13550579:
Liang Liang, with four colleagues, published a 2026 atlas of how male and female mouse brains respond differently to repeated stress. Depression is more common in women, so the team exposed mice to sub-chronic variable stress and then sequenced single nuclei from the hippocampus, a brain region tied to mood. Behavior was checked with tests for loss of pleasure.

Females showed stronger loss of pleasure and a drop in blood serotonin, while males changed little. Sequencing 31,256 cells revealed about three times as many altered genes in females, with little overlap between sexes. Female changes centered on support cells called oligodendrocytes, their energy-producing genes, and weakened oxytocin signaling, which the authors offer as leads for sex-specific depression treatments.
pmc-13550679:
Body weight alone may hide how fat affects male fertility, so a Danish team measures fat percentage directly. They study 1,058 young men from a national birth cohort in a 2026 report. Each man gave semen and blood samples, measured his own testicular volume, and had his body fat read by an electrical impedance device. The team compares fat percentage with the more common measures of body mass index and waist-to-height ratio.

Higher fat percentage went with poorer semen traits and disturbed reproductive hormone levels. Testicular volume showed no link. The pattern held even among men whose body mass index counted as normal. The authors argue that fat percentage tells the fertility story more sharply than weight-based measures.
pmc-13550879:
Ahmed Hageen and co-authors pool trial data to compare two diabetes drugs, tirzepatide and dulaglutide, across doses. Their 2026 network meta-analysis addresses a gap: few trials test the drugs head to head. Yet doctors must choose doses for blood sugar control, weight loss, and safety. The patients in view have type 2 diabetes, with or without heart disease.

Four trials with 14,348 patients form a seven-node network, though one large trial supplies most patients. The highest tirzepatide dose gave the largest weight loss by week sixteen. Low doses of either drug lost less weight. The authors also rank the options for heart events, deaths, and side effects. Rankings place each dose against the rest.
pmc-13550979:
Tae-Young Kim and seven co-authors track upper arm fractures in Korea in a 2026 study. Weak bones make such breaks a growing public health burden. The humerus is the third most common site for these fractures. Trends in repeat breaks and death rates were little studied.

Insurance claims from 2006 to 2022 supplied the data. Nearly two hundred thousand fracture cases were counted. Case numbers rose steeply in the first years, then leveled off. Women outnumbered men about two and a half to one throughout. One year death rates in women fell across the study span. Rates in men stayed about twice as high as in women. Age was the strongest single predictor of death after fracture.
pmc-13551679:
Andrea Pieroni and co-authors argue, in an editorial published in 2026, that village and community scholars should move from the edges to the center of ethnobiology. The field studies how people know and use their living surroundings, and it was born in rural and Indigenous communities. Yet credit and authority still sit in city universities.

The authors, many raised in villages or migrant communities, call local knowledge a science in its own right, with its own logic and rigor. They ask for community scholars to lead at every stage, from framing questions to sharing results. Mere inclusion in outside projects is not enough. Without the shift, they warn, the field stays detached from the realities it studies.
pmc-13551779:
Shen Chen and eight colleagues reported in 2026 on how mixing two nitrogen forms affects strawberry growth in protected cultivation. Growers know ammonium plus nitrate usually beats either form alone, yet the mechanism was unclear. Using the cultivar Benihoppe at a fixed total nitrogen level, the team varied the ammonium-to-nitrate ratio and measured growth, hormones, and gene activity.

A ratio of seven to three ammonium to nitrate promoted height and stalk growth and raised fruit yield without changing fruit size in the reported results. At the green fruit stage that mix raised auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels, and gene analysis highlighted hormone signaling pathways. The authors propose the ratio coordinates nitrogen uptake with hormone signals, offering a basis for precise fertilizer management.
pmc-13551879:
Prachi Mishra and co-authors study how a high-fat diet early in life affects adult fruit flies, in work from two thousand twenty-six. Flies fed fat as larvae kept clear changes as adults. The team read genes in head and fat tissue, measured small body chemicals, and checked gut microbes.

The fat tissue showed the strongest changes, with key energy genes turned down. Energy units in cells worked less well, and harmful oxygen by-products built up. Gut microbe mixes also stayed changed. Three adult treatments, among them helpful bacteria, eased the harm and lengthened life. The state seems partly open to reversal.
pmc-13551979:
José Manuel García-Heredia, Sara M Ortega-Campos, and Amancio Carnero published a 2026 study of gene splicing in tumors. The gene is called NUMB. It makes four protein versions through alternative splicing, the reshuffling of gene parts. NUMB has been cast as both tumor blocker and tumor helper. The team mined public databases for version levels in tumors and healthy tissue. They grouped samples by which versions ran high.

Two versions rose in tumors, while two others ruled healthy tissue. The two clusters tied to distinct activity in four key signaling paths. A score built on version balance split breast cancer cell lines by biology and drug response. High scores linked to worse patient survival. The team proposes version balance as a marker for precision cancer care.
pmc-13552079:
Kenta Inagaki, Yasuchika Aoki, and Seiji Ohtori report three cases of stiff shoulders after joint surgery, in work from twenty twenty-six. Each woman had a reverse shoulder replacement, a swap that lets other muscles lift the arm. Three months on, none could lift her arm well. The team traced the block to a pinched nerve in a tight space at the back of the shoulder.

Doctors freed the nerve by injecting fluid around it, a method called hydrorelease. All three women soon lifted their arms much more, and the gain held at one year. Scores for pain and arm use rose in each case. All three were small women, under five feet, which may have stretched the nerve more.
pmc-13552379:
Yehonatan Herman and nine co-authors published this study in 2026. It reviews children treated for chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis, a rare inflammatory bone disease with no infection behind it, at a Melbourne children's hospital over ten years. The focus is zoledronic acid, a bone drug used off-label when standard anti-inflammatory treatment falls short.

Fifty-seven children were followed for a median of nearly four years; most had disease in several bones. Twenty-two received the drug, averaging under three infusions. Over three-quarters improved markedly in symptoms, and four-fifths of those rescanned showed clear imaging improvement. About half reported brief flu-like aches after infusion; no serious harms occurred. A few children later needed stronger immune drugs. The authors say the drug's twice-yearly dosing makes it a practical option for severe cases, while calling for controlled trials to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13552779:
Qiang Yue and six co-authors build a model that predicts the strength of grouting material made from industrial waste, in a paper from 2026. Such alkali-activated mixes are low in carbon and use waste at scale, but their strength is hard to forecast from few, tangled experiments. The team gathered 179 test records from three studies and held fifteen aside for a final check.

A generative network expanded the training data while keeping its patterns. A tuned gradient-boosting model then predicted strength with high accuracy on held-out tests. Importance analysis ranked cement content, water ratio, curing age, and slag content as the top drivers of strength.
pmc-13553179:
Jessica Wcislo, Andrew Posen, and Jared Davis write this 2026 letter about a patient whose brain lesion cut his sympathetic drive. The man, aged 40, had a brain lymphoma pressing on a brain region that raises blood pressure and heart rate. He arrived cold, with low pressure and a slow pulse. Standard pressor drugs held his pressure but not his heart rate.

After two days on two infusion drugs, the team tried an oral decongestant drug with like action. The infusions were stopped soon after the first doses. Brief slow-pulse spells in the next day led to a dose increase. The letter presents the cheap, widely sold drug as a stopgap for this rare failure of central sympathetic control, while cancer care was restarted.
pmc-13553679:
Jiayi Fu, Yuxin Zhou, Mingliang Yuan, and Ying Cai ask why working memory training helps some untrained tasks but not others. Their 2026 meta-analysis pools 55 studies with 208 effect sizes and 3,492 people. Two rival ideas frame the puzzle: transfer may flow from harder tasks to easier ones, or from broad-ability tasks to narrow ones.

Span tasks and updating tasks give a clean test, since updating is harder while span is broader. Training in updating reliably lifted span scores, with a small effect. Training in span did not lift updating. That one-way street backs the demand-based account. The updating edge also reached beyond working memory tasks and grew stronger at low training doses, in younger samples, and with verbal material. Coaches can use the asymmetry to design smarter training.
pmc-13554079:
Marion Ferreira leads a seven-author team showing that how immune drugs reach the lung changes their safety and power in a 2026 mouse study. Lung cancer drugs that rouse the immune system can work well yet cause harsh side effects. The team gave three such agents through the airway or into a vein in healthy mice. They then tested one antibody given each way in mice with lung tumours.

Airway dosing spared the liver and calmed body-wide inflammation compared with vein dosing. Weight held steadier and blood markers looked calmer under airway care. Airway dosing also drew more immune cells into the lung, in step with dose. In tumour-bearing mice, airway delivery filled lungs with helper and killer cells and gave better tumour control.
pmc-13554279:
Kirsten O'Brien leads a seven-author team testing tiny perfluorocarbon droplets for bone work in a 2026 study. These droplets, smaller than a cell, carry a liquid core in a fatty shell and may deliver gases or drugs. Related bubbles already aid bone repair research, yet droplet effects on bone cells were untested. The team tracked droplet contact with bone-forming cells and bone-eating cells, under normal and low oxygen.

Long exposure over twelve days cut the number of bone-eating cells in both oxygen settings. Short exposure under low oxygen instead boosted their formation. Bone-forming cells from several sources stayed healthy throughout. The authors call the droplets compatible with key bone cells, with effects that depend on timing and oxygen, a base for targeted bone delivery.
pmc-13554379:
Iqra Farzeen leads an eight-author team reviewing chemical modulators of synaptic plasticity as a route to treat Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 paper. Synapses strengthen or weaken with experience, and that flexing underlies learning and memory. The disease creeps in years before symptoms, marked by amyloid plaques and tangles of the tau protein. Failing synapses and shrinking synapse counts track the loss of thinking power.

Damage signals from amyloid are thought to rouse immune cells in the brain, whose chemicals then push tau toward its harmful form. The review surveys compounds that tune synapse strength as candidate medicines. Aiming at plasticity offers a target earlier than late-stage damage. Readers get the biology of memory formation beside the case for such drug strategies.
pmc-13554579:
Małgorzata Starzec-Proserpio and four colleagues review shear wave elastography for pelvic floor muscle assessment. Shear wave elastography is a known, non-invasive, real-time tool for thyroid, liver, and breast disease. It also shows value for skeletal muscle. Yet pelvic floor checks bring their own technical challenges, still poorly addressed. Their 2026 review warns of pitfalls in image capture and analysis.

The method may look straightforward, but it carries real complexity and a real risk of misreading. The review covers image capture, analysis, common artifacts, and other technical points for pelvic floor work. By airing these issues, it aims to promote quality and steady work in future research. It also flags areas needing further study.
pmc-13555279:
Niloufar Nezhadrekabi and seven co-authors linked sleep habits to body measures in adults in Iran, in a 2026 study. Data came from a large regional cohort of people aged thirty-five to seventy. More than ten thousand adults gave data on sleep, lifestyle, and body size. About a third were obese by the standard body index.

Patterns differed sharply by sex. Men who slept seven to nine hours, or more, had lower odds of obesity than short sleepers. Daytime napping raised men's odds of central obesity. For women, later bedtimes raised obesity odds. Waking in the morning window lowered women's central obesity odds. Short sleep was reported by over four in ten adults. The authors urge that sleep checks join obesity prevention and care plans.
pmc-13555379:
A stomach-lining protein has become one of the hottest targets in oncology, and the drugs aimed at it are now meeting resistance. Yutao Xia and co-authors organize that resistance in a 2026 review. The first antibody against the target won approval in 2024, and over a hundred trials of related agents are running.

The review sorts resistance into six biological dimensions, separating tricks specific to this target from generic escape routes. Each mechanism is paired with a countermeasure, graded by the strength of its evidence. The authors argue that target levels erode under treatment pressure, so therapy sequencing matters. For patients starting with high, uniform expression, they favor an intensive induction followed by maintenance over endless combination therapy.
pmc-13555579:
SangPhil Ahn and colleagues built T-cell-receptor-like antibodies that recognise a KRAS G12D cancer fragment displayed on tumour cells, publishing the workflow in 2026. KRAS drives many pancreatic, bowel, and lung cancers, but it sits inside cells where ordinary antibodies cannot reach it. Its broken-down peptide, however, is shown on the cell surface by an immune molecule, offering a target if antibodies can read that display precisely.

The team combined computer docking with a yeast-display library to select antibodies that bound the KRAS fragment on one immune type with high affinity and no detected human off-targets. Reformatted as cell therapies or T-cell engagers, the antibodies killed only target-bearing cells. The pipeline offers a practical route to drugging KRAS G12D cancers that current inhibitors reach poorly.
pmc-13555679:
Christopher Latimer, Robert Thompson Stone, and Elizabeth Troy argue residency assessment should trade checkboxes for stories, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-six. Rating scales produce numbers but little a trainee can act on. Narrative comments change behavior, yet systems underuse them.

Their child neurology program at the University of Colorado rebuilt assessment in two thousand twenty-three. Forms require choosing a competency, then writing about it, mapped to national milestones. The design fits existing software workflows and adapts to clinical context. Feasibility of the reform was the evaluation target. The paper's title states the philosophy: assessment is more than a checkbox. Programs elsewhere can copy the mechanics wholesale.
pmc-13555879:
Tom Caput leads a six-author team pooling studies that compare two fixes for a collapsed lung in a 2026 analysis. Air leaking into the chest space can be drawn out by simple needle aspiration or by a chest tube left to drain. Nineteen studies, trials and comparisons alike, entered the pool. Outcomes covered instant success, side effects, hospital stay, and pain.

Success rates matched between the two approaches overall. Aspiration brought far fewer side effects than tube drainage. Patients treated by aspiration left hospital about two and a half days sooner. They also reported clearly lower pain scores. The authors back aspiration as the first strategy, echoing international guidelines, since equal success comes with a gentler course.
pmc-13556079:
Lulu Li and five colleagues sequenced in 2026 the full genome of an industrial bacterium used to make 2-ketogluconic acid, a building block for a common food antioxidant. The strain, Pseudomonas plecoglossicida JUIM01, produces the acid through fermentation, and knowing its genes should help engineers improve it. The team read the whole chromosome and annotated what each predicted gene likely does.

The genome is a single circular chromosome carrying more than four and a half thousand predicted proteins. Annotation revealed a control network of 75 core regulators grouped into six cooperating modules that seem to manage metabolism and stress responses. Pathways for glucose use, fat metabolism, and energy generation tied to acid production were mapped in detail. The authors offer the sequence as a resource for building hardier, higher-yielding production strains.
pmc-13556379:
P-C Wu and four co-authors used machine learning in two thousand twenty-six to forecast who will respond to ketamine for stubborn depression. Ketamine acts fast, but responses vary widely, so a pre-treatment marker would help doctors choose. They drew data from two separate randomized trials, training on one and testing on the other.

Features joined resting brain connectivity, network graph measures, and brain structure. A nearest-neighbour classifier, tuned with careful feature picking and noise-based data boosting, hit about eighty-one percent accuracy on the unseen trial. It was especially good at spotting non-responders. Selected features centred on networks linking the thalamus, vision, and salience.
pmc-13556479:
Khoo and four colleagues asked people in the UK with insomnia what they value in a sleep medicine. Many drug options now exist, so patient taste matters for shared decisions. The study grew out of earlier work with trial patients on a drug called daridorexant. This round reached people in everyday life instead.

One hundred fifty people took part through an online panel. Each person chose between pairs of made-up treatments that differed in seven features. Most took at least half an hour to fall asleep, and most slept five hours or less a night. People leaned toward treatment over no treatment. The results rank which drug features patients care about most. That ranking can help doctors match a medicine to the person in front of them.
pmc-13556579:
W Yimeng and co-authors combine brain scans and thinking tests to sort psychosis risk in 2026. Groups included clinical high-risk youth, first-episode schizophrenia patients, and healthy controls. Early sorting matters because early care improves outcomes.

Structural MRI measured cortical and deep brain features. Thinking scores were gathered with standard tests. Machine learning models joined the two data types. The team asked whether the mix sorted groups better than either alone. Each group was compared with the other two in turn. Readers see how combined markers might flag who needs close watch or early treatment, and where single measures fall short.
pmc-13556679:
Subramaniam and co-authors review the burden of prolonged seizures in the Asia-Oceanic region in a 2026 conference abstract. Status epilepticus, a seizure that will not stop, is the second most common nerve emergency after stroke. A five-year literature sweep found eleven fitting papers. Death within a month strikes about one adult in six worldwide, more in poorer lands.

Early, well-dosed calming drugs in the field set how long seizures run and how much harm follows. The review names gaps: medics barred or untrained in giving the drugs, under-dosing, scarce new medicines, and doctors straying from guidelines. The authors press for timely care as the main lever against death and disability.
pmc-13556779:
Konara Mudiyanselage and co-authors presented this 2026 conference study on loneliness and social thinking in bipolar disorder. People with the disorder often struggle socially even between mood episodes. Those whose illness includes psychotic features tend to fare worse still. Social support might soften loneliness's harm, but the chain of links was untested across patient groups.

The study covered 239 people: 59 with psychotic features, 94 without, and 86 healthy comparisons. Standard scales measured loneliness and support, and tasks tested theory of mind, the skill of reading others' thoughts.
