The team compared the three groups and checked whether support carries loneliness's effect on social thinking. The work targets a fixable factor, support, in a group where isolation runs deep.
pmc-13556979:
Khola Noreen and five colleagues listened to parents, girls, teachers, health workers, and religious scholars across Punjab ahead of Pakistan's first national HPV vaccine drive. The vaccine guards against cervical cancer, but uptake turns on trust as much as supply. Fieldwork ran from February to August twenty twenty-five in north and south Punjab districts. Talks were grouped under a world health framework for vaccine choices.

Blocks included fear of side effects, doubt about the vaccine, false claims spread on social media, and religious unease. Thin funds and a fragile health system added strain. The same talks surfaced helpers too, voices and channels that carry weight in each village and school. Knowing both sides before the launch lets planners craft messages that answer real fears. The twenty twenty-six study is a field map for the rollout, not a guess from the capital.
pmc-13557079:
Liaoliao Gao and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a spatial atlas of the immune clusters that form inside a lethal bile duct cancer. These clusters, called tertiary lymphoid structures, are pockets where immune cells gather, and their shape and placement vary widely. Whether that variety shapes patient outcomes in this cancer was unclear. The team mapped the clusters across tumor samples with several imaging and protein methods.

Protein profiles from 214 cases, checked against 155 more, sorted tumors into four classes by their cluster patterns. Clusters sitting inside the tumor itself stood out as an independent sign of better prognosis. Detailed imaging showed that tumors rich in these inner clusters held orderly immune neighborhoods, with distinct cell types arranged around them. The authors also trained a classifier that predicts the classes from protein data, and offer the map as a guide for prognosis and treatment choices.
pmc-13557279:
Chandler Catanzaro and six co-authors present a 2026 surgical study on shoulders that slip out of place in more than one direction. The patients included people with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a condition that makes joints loose. The operation studied tightens the shoulder capsule through small incisions with a camera, a method called arthroscopic capsular plication.

The team reviewed cases from 2015 to 2023 with at least two years of follow-up. After surgery, patients gained clear gains in shoulder function scores and reported less pain. Failure, meaning the shoulder slipped again or needed new surgery, occurred in only a small share of patients. Gains passed the level patients can feel for the main score in every case. The results support this operation for a hard-to-treat joint problem.
pmc-13557879:
Hyo Kyen Park and co-authors test whether smoking history predicts survival differently in the two lung cancer kinds, in a 2026 study. Smoking worsens results after surgery for non-small cell lung cancer, but the two types, glandular and squamous, may not share the effect. The team reviewed over eight thousand patients operated on with curative intent over a decade, and modelled survival with smoking-by-histology interaction.

In the glandular group, smoking history raised the death risk, by about a quarter to a third depending on the model. In the squamous group, the estimate sat near no effect, with wide uncertainty. The interaction test did not reach significance. The authors read the squamous result: almost everyone there had smoked, so a yes-no history can barely separate patients there. They advise judging smoking risk inside each histology, not across the disease.
pmc-13558279:
After heart surgery, children often develop lung problems that need quick spotting. Nehad Bakry and five co-authors compared two bedside checks in a 2026 pilot study of 30 children under four at one hospital. Each child got both a chest X-ray and a lung ultrasound at three set times after surgery, and the team compared what each method found.

The two methods agreed on lung congestion, but ultrasound found far more fluid around the lungs and somewhat more collapsed or solid patches. Five children failed to come off the breathing machine, which tied to longer intensive care. The authors call ultrasound a strong bedside tool worth wider testing.
pmc-13558579:
Tzu-Shun Lin and seven colleagues build HUMID-Atlanta, a fine-scale weather dataset for the Atlanta metro region. City weather data at fine scale is needed for questions in health and environmental science. Their 2026 paper models Atlanta at 1-kilometer grid spacing for 2010 to 2023 with a coupled city weather system. It then corrects temperature and moisture with machine learning that learns shared dependencies.

Bias correction validated well for air temperature but transferred less well across space for dew point. The team also computes heat exposure indices, including heat index, Humidex, wet bulb globe temperature, universal thermal climate index, and apparent temperature. The dataset supports estimates of population heat exposure and heat-health links for health research, risk assessment, and economic evaluation.
pmc-13558879:
Yohanes Windi and three co-authors survey bystander readiness for cardiac arrest in Indonesia in a study from two thousand twenty-six. When a heart stops in public, a bystander's first minutes decide survival. Five hundred residents at four community health centers answered a structured questionnaire.

Few recognized sudden cardiac arrest as its own emergency; heart attack was the familiar term. Most would call for help rather than act, and hands-on help was rare. Fear of blame, low knowledge, and feeling unskilled topped the barriers. Those willing to help leaned toward waking the victim or familiar local practices; CPR was seldom named. The authors urge community training in hands-only CPR and clearer, culturally tuned guidance.
pmc-13559079:
Ye and colleagues build the first chemical atlas of histone marks in this 2026 study of fetal Down syndrome brains, hunting epigenetic changes beyond the extra chromosome 21 itself. Using advanced mass spectrometry on fetal cortex tissue, they catalogued the modifications decorating all four core histones, then zoomed in on the mark that moved most.

Healthy fetal cortex carried 172 distinct histone modifications against 168 in Down syndrome samples. Of the quantifiable marks, one acetylation, H3K79ac, fell furthest, down 34 percent in syndrome tissue in the comparison. Genome mapping placed the depleted mark at three neurodevelopmental genes, and its loss paired with abnormal activity in each: one gene silenced, two overexpressed. The authors nominate this single depleted mark as a candidate driver of the syndrome's brain development differences and a possible drug target.
pmc-13560079:
Siika and colleagues report in 2026 on how strongly the width of the lower aorta runs in families, using Sweden's Stockholm screening program. The program ultrasound-scans men for abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the body's main artery. The question was whether siblings share not just aneurysms but subtler width patterns.

Linking screening records for over sixteen thousand 65-year-old men to the national multigeneration registry yielded nearly nine thousand sibling pairs. Aortic width correlated modestly between full siblings, weakly between half siblings, and strongly between twins, in line with shared genetics. If one sibling had an aneurysm-width aorta, the estimated chance that a brother's aorta was at least borderline wide ran about five percent for full siblings. For twins it ran twenty-one percent. Heritability estimates came out around four tenths for width itself and six tenths for aneurysm-range categories.
pmc-13560179:
Lihua Wang and three co-authors report a 2026 study on twin pregnancy and a stitch used to keep the cervix closed. When that stitch fails, twins can be born far too soon. The team asked whether simple blood markers of swelling in the body can flag which cases are at risk.

They looked back at 111 twin cases where the stitch was placed for a short or open cervix. Blood was drawn before the procedure, and four marker scores were worked out for each woman. Birth before 28 weeks took place in 13 cases. The paper tests how well each score foresaw that outcome.
pmc-13560279:
Alhassan Sibdow Abukari, Shelley Schmollgruber, and Emmanuel Kwame Korsah develop an instrument to measure family-centered care in neonatal intensive care units in low-resource settings. Their 2026 three-phase study begins with a scoping review, interviews, and focus groups that drafted forty candidate items. Surveys of 346 family members and one hundred clinicians then fed factor analysis for item reduction.

The final tool holds twenty items across four domains: family acceptance, education, environmental design, and sufficient resources. Psychometric checks came out strong, with reliability coefficients above 0.94 across the reported indices. A two-round expert Delphi panel confirmed content validity for every item. The authors note that no validated measure previously existed for family-centered care in resource-limited newborn units. They offer the FEES instrument to guide nursing adjustments and future research design in neonatal care.
pmc-13560879:
Nakarin Subjalearndee and co-authors spin battery fibers out of spent graphite, in a 2026 paper. Electric vehicle growth leaves mountains of used lithium batteries. Recycling chases the pricey cathode metals while anode graphite, cheap and plentiful, is mostly discarded. The team asked whether that waste could live a second life in zinc-ion batteries.

They took industrial spent graphite, oxidized it into graphene oxide, and wet-spun it into fibers. After reduction, the fibers were coated with manganese oxide and carbon black to form a fiber cathode, paired with a zinc wire in a gel electrolyte. The work sketches a cheap, flexible battery format built from another battery's leftovers, easing both waste and metal demand.
pmc-13560979:
Kwabena Oppong Amoako and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on what shapes the quality of sickle cell care at a major hospital in Ghana. Sickle cell disease burdens health systems across sub-Saharan Africa. Access to high-quality, patient-centered care remains limited. The team asked patients themselves how good their care felt, and which steps in the care process drove that judgment.

The survey covered 424 patients at a tertiary facility in Accra, gathered in late 2023. Ages ran from 15 to 66, with a median of 32. Most patients were female, carried the SS genotype, and took hydroxyurea, a standard drug for the disease. First-time visitors and emergency cases were excluded. The study links perceived quality to process factors, giving managers concrete levers for improvement.
pmc-13561079:
Zhou, Schitter, and Csencsics published a study in twenty twenty-six on how the pollen-bearing parts of a flower shake during buzz pollination. Some bees grab a flower and vibrate it so pollen sprays out of tiny pores, and the flower's own shaking behavior decides how well that works.

The team studied the strongly curved stamens of Medinilla magnifica, a tropical plant. They built a small shaker and a laser sensor to track the motion in fine detail. The measurements showed three natural shaking frequencies, and the middle one fell inside the range of real bee buzzes. Computer models matched the measured motion and showed how the curved shape creates the complex pattern. The approach gives plant scientists a precise way to compare how different flowers handle a bee's buzz.
pmc-13561679:
Takeshi Yamada and a large surgical team ask whether keyhole surgery lowers a serious complication after bowel cancer operations, in a study published in 2026. Small bowel obstruction, often caused by internal scar tissue, is a major late risk of colorectal surgery. The team analyzed 5,458 patients treated at thirty-two Japanese hospitals between 2012 and 2014 and followed their five-year obstruction risk.

Overall, 5.2 percent developed an obstruction. Rectal surgery carried the highest risk. Laparoscopic surgery was linked to 42 percent lower odds of obstruction, with clear gains in operations on the ascending and sigmoid colon. Adhesion prevention materials and stoma creation were also examined. The findings support the minimally invasive approach as one practical way to cut this complication.
pmc-13561879:
Abdul Mateen Qadri and co-authors improve heart procedure guidance in a 2026 study. Computer twins of a patient's heart can point doctors to the spots to treat for a dangerous fast rhythm. Two barriers block clinic use: the models run slowly, and their maps rest on scans whose reading carries doubt.

Their frame gives near real time guidance while folding that doubt into the math from the start. Scar shape, the key input, is treated as a range of options rather than one fixed map. Tests showed close match with slower standard results. A guide that admits its own doubt may earn more trust at the table.
pmc-13562079:
Víctor Juan Vera-Ponce estimates how many adults across dozens of countries would qualify for evaluation for weight-loss surgery under old versus new criteria. Updated guidance from surgical societies in recent years lowered thresholds, potentially expanding the pool a great deal. The scope of that expansion across settings was unclear.

Using global risk-factor surveys covering many settings and well over a hundred thousand people, the study projects figures to a future year. The new criteria flag nearly three times as many adults as the old ones, mostly people in a lower obesity band who also have metabolic disease. Rates run higher in women and older adults and vary by setting. The author stresses these are people needing evaluation, not automatic candidates.
pmc-13562379:
Jessica Campisi and three colleagues present two patients with adventitial cystic disease, a rare condition where jelly-filled cysts grow in an artery wall and squeeze the vessel shut. The disorder usually strikes the artery behind the knee in healthy middle-aged men, causing leg pain when walking. Open removal of the cyst has been the classic fix. Their 2026 report sets a catheter-based repair against open surgery, one patient each.

A young, healthy patient received a stent placed through a catheter for disease in the thigh artery. An older patient with other illnesses received a vein bypass around the blocked knee artery. Both were free of symptoms one year later. The authors argue that the choice should follow the lesion site and the patient's overall health. Stenting may serve selected cases, while open repair stays vital where a stent cannot go.
pmc-13562579:
Yangyang Gao and Shuxian Liu design a detector that finds tiny objects in drone photographs, where people and vehicles shrink to a few pixels. High-altitude views pack small targets densely against cluttered ground, and deep networks often wash their outlines away. Their 2026 network, EDC-Net, adds three parts. An edge-aware module feeds contour cues back into learning, a context module gathers wide scene information cheaply, and a detection head uses flexible convolution that follows bent, irregular shapes.

Tested on the VisDrone2019 benchmark, the network beat its YOLO11s baseline by 4.5 points on the looser accuracy measure and 3.0 points on the stricter one. It did so with 29.8 percent fewer parameters. A second test on the TinyPerson dataset, built around very small people, confirmed the skill transferred. The authors aim the design at traffic watching, power-line inspection, farming, and fire patrol from the air.
pmc-13562679:
Moustafa and co-authors swap nickel into a ferrite and watch its character change in a 2026 study. Ferrites are magnetic ceramics used across electronics, and their traits can be tuned by replacing one metal with another. The team worked on a copper-magnesium ferrite, also holding iron and chromium, and raised the nickel share step by step across six recipes.

Standard tools mapped the changes. X-ray diffraction showed better lattice order as nickel entered and shuffled the metal ions between sites. Light measures shifted in step: the optical band gap widened from 3.2 to 3.7 electron volts while the refractive index fell. The material stayed a soft ferromagnet, though its peak magnetization eased down. Tracking charge hopping explains the linked electrical changes. The work is a recipe card for dialing one material to several jobs.
pmc-13563579:
Vural Akın and five co-authors studied whether Bell's palsy cases follow seasonal patterns in this 2026 paper. Bell's palsy is the most common cause of sudden one-sided facial weakness, and its trigger is still unknown. Some past work blamed weather or season, but findings conflict, so the team tested the idea with ten years of clinic data.

The records covered 352 patients seen from 2015 to 2024. Cases peaked in October and dipped in February, yet the gaps by month, season, and year were too small to count as real. A trend-splitting method hinted at mild swings in spring, and severity stayed flat across all periods. The authors stress that without direct weather data, their results describe timing patterns only, not causes.
pmc-13563679:
Aura Cruz Heredia and six co-authors wrote this 2026 study on whether language and music share one mental workshop. Sentences and chord runs both build long links between far parts. The team had people read sentences while music played, then judge both, with no broken rules in either stream to muddy the test.

Both streams were varied in how tangled their structures were and how far their links reached. The two domains did sway each other, but unevenly: language pushed music harder than music pushed language. The push traced mostly to structural tangle, not to the reach of the links. Cross-talk peaked when key words and chords landed at the same moment. The authors read this as fresh proof for shared mental tools.
pmc-13563779:
Li Wang and four colleagues test a teamwork model for the hardest COPD admissions: flare-ups in patients juggling heart failure, diabetes, and more. Clashing treatments for clashing diseases sink outcomes under routine care. The 2026 study, at a Chinese tertiary hospital, compared routine care with a doctor-nurse integrated model built on joint rounds, one shared plan covering lungs and companions, and discharge planning done together. Records ran from 2022 to 2025, and statistical matching produced 52 pairs.

The integrated group fared better on the combined measure of death or cardiopulmonary readmission within a year, with a hazard ratio of 0.58. Stays shortened from about eleven days to about eight on average. Symptom scores improved more, and in-hospital complications fell from 29 to 12 percent, led by fewer sugar crises and heart failure episodes. The authors argue that managing the whole patient jointly, rather than each disease in turn, is what moves the needle.
pmc-13563879:
Erdal Meriç published this education management study in 2026. Mushroom management describes bosses who keep staff in the dark, sharing little information and excluding them from decisions, as mushrooms are grown. Quiet quitting describes employees who do only their required duties and no more. Meriç asked whether the first predicts the second among public school teachers. The survey covered 460 teachers across seven regions of Türkiye, using two standardized scales.

Teachers reported generally low levels of mushroom management, though information sharing scored only moderately. Quiet quitting was very low overall. Even so, the two measures moved together: the link was moderate, positive, and statistically significant. In regression, mushroom management significantly predicted quiet quitting behavior. Two theories frame the result: social exchange and the psychological contract, both of which say people repay how they are treated. Meriç draws practical implications for school leadership and suggests directions for further research.
pmc-13563979:
Dai Mengting and colleagues track, in a 2026 retrospective study, how gut microbes change as chronic liver disease worsens toward liver failure. Samples from 947 patients covered early disease, two stages of cirrhosis, and acute-on-chronic liver failure, with ten common gut bacteria measured by a targeted genetic test.

Four patterns of change emerged, and a ratio favoring harmful over helpful bacteria rose more than fivefold across the stages. Computer models predicted each stage change well, best for the step into liver failure. A simple ratio of two bacteria also separated stages. The results suggest stool testing might one day warn clinicians that a patient's liver disease is about to turn dangerous.
pmc-13564079:
Mohammad Adeel Zafar and co-authors trace how the amino acid glutamine feeds runaway immune cells in autoimmune disease, in work from 2026. When the tolerance gene Foxp3 fails, T and B cells attack the body, and they burn extra glutamine doing it.

The question was whether glutamine serves as fuel or as building material. In mouse models of Foxp3 deficiency and colitis, the building pathways mattered. In T cells, glutamine routes kept a brake molecule, inosine, from piling up and calming the cells. In B cells, glutamine supplied asparagine needed to make autoantibodies. Blocking that asparagine supply emerged as a possible therapy for antibody-driven disease.
pmc-13564879:
Minna Sivonen and co-authors show in 2026 that virus shaped silica particles, coated with cell membrane, can switch on natural killer cells through talks with monocytes. Many cancer immune therapies lean on T cells and stall against mixed tumors. Killer cells of the innate arm offer a backup that needs no antigen match. The team tuned spike length, surface treatment, and coating on the particles.

Inside mixed blood immune cells, the best build raised activation marks and a key signal protein on killer cells. Removing monocytes blunted the effect, proving the cross talk route. On purified killer cells, the coated particles sparked early activation and supported growth without feeder cells. Design rules for innate immune particles follow.
pmc-13564979:
Tao Jiang, Shubing Lin, Xiubao Chen, and Junren Xue test whether the eggs of an anchovy-like fish reveal where the mother lived. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Two forms of the fish share spawning grounds in Poyang Lake, China: one migrates from the sea, the other stays in fresh water for life.

The team gathered one hundred and two fish and picked twenty mature females with intact egg masses. Ear stones, which record water history, told the two forms apart. Chemical ratios in the eggs of sea migrants were clearly higher than in those of lifelong lake fish. That split matches the migrants' richer feeding during travel. The egg test could help tell the forms apart without cutting into the ear stone, aiding study of this valued fish.
pmc-13565079: Yok-Fong Paat writes on mental health care for marginalized communities in a 2026 article that frames mental health as a core human right. Mental health, in this view, covers emotional, psychological, and social well-being, not just the absence of mental disorders. The piece addresses the disparities that keep marginalized groups from fair access to care, and argues for breaking the barriers behind those gaps.
pmc-13565379:
Hsiao-Yen Wu, Pey-Ling Shieh, and Yen-Chun Liu study how a mother's low mood links to her toddler's sleep in Taiwan, in a 2026 paper. Toddler sleep is firmer than baby sleep and may show lasting patterns. Proof tying a mother's state of mind to that sleep had stayed thin.

The team surveyed 126 mothers of children aged one to three online. A third of the mothers showed signs of low mood. Most toddlers slept less than 12 hours at night, and half took long to fall asleep. Higher low-mood scores tracked with worse toddler sleep and longer time to drift off. Sharing a bed made that link stronger, while steady bedtime routines did not change it.
pmc-13565679:
Qichao Wu and co-authors built a scoring model in 2026 to catch lung cancer spread to the membranes around the brain, a diagnosis that scans and first fluid tests often miss. Their records covered 533 patients whose lung adenocarcinoma had reached the central nervous system. About two-thirds truly had the membrane spread.

An eight-item model, using clinic facts and spinal fluid measures, sorted patients with very strong accuracy in repeated internal tests. It flagged over nine in ten of the cases that brain scans alone had missed, and a similar share of those missed by the first fluid check. The authors are careful that scans and fluid tests helped define the truth, so the contest was not fully fair. They offer the model as a prompt for deeper checks, pending outside proof.
pmc-13565779:
Jiaxiang Liang and co-authors mine public data in 2026 to build a forecast model for stomach cancer. The goal is twofold: find tumor markers fit for an mRNA vaccine, and predict patient outcomes. From multi-omics data they screen candidate antigen genes, then test over a hundred model setups built by ten learning methods.

A survival forest model with seven genes wins. Those genes tie closely to how tumors present antigens to the immune system, at both gene and protein levels. The team also probes how tumors dodge immunity, designs vaccine templates on a public platform, and screens small drug compounds against the seven genes, checking their binding stability in simulations.
pmc-13566379:
After a stroke, families want to know how much arm and leg movement will return months later. Yoo Jin Choo, Min Cheol Chang, and Ji-Yeon Shin built prediction tools for that question in this 2026 study. They used records from 353 patients whose stroke came from a blocked brain vessel. The tools had to forecast movement at six months.

One tool used only the early checks done soon after the stroke. A second tool added a fresh set of checks at one month. Three learning methods were tried, from a simple statistical model to a deep network. The team graded the tools by how well they sorted outcomes and by their value in real care choices. Their title states the point: one-month data adds real value. A better early forecast can shape rehab plans and honest talks with families.
pmc-13566979:
Josephine Dudzik and co-authors review evidence on whether plant pigments in food link to better sleep, in a paper from 2026. The pigments, called carotenoids, give red, yellow, and orange fruits and vegetables their color. They fight oxidation and inflammation, two processes tied to sleep health.

The team searched two databases for studies in adults and in live animals. Of more than a thousand papers screened, twenty-nine fit the rules. Survey studies mostly linked higher intake or blood levels of the pigments to better sleep quality and length. Most supplement trials reported gains in at least one sleep measure, though gains over a dummy pill were not always clear. Animal studies gave early support. Mixed definitions of sleep made cross-study checks hard.
pmc-13567379:
Zeping Liu and nine co-authors published a spectroscopy study in twenty twenty-six on measuring how much worthless rock hides in coal, using terahertz waves and physics-informed machine learning. Knowing gangue content guides coal use and automated sorting. Terahertz scans captured time and frequency signals plus optical constants from mixtures of known composition.

Five algorithms competed under cross-validation. A neural network constrained by effective medium theory, forced to respect the physics of mixtures, won clearly. Its predictions explained most variance with errors of a few percentage points, beating random forests, support vector, Gaussian process, and plain neural rivals. The authors present the hybrid as fast, interpretable quality control for an industry that still samples by hand.
pmc-13567579:
Adriana Verdezoto Alvarado and co-authors study diet quality in Mexican born immigrant women in this 2026 paper. Food security and the local food environment may shape how well these women eat. The study was exploratory and small. It compared women with high and low food security.

The sample held 57 women. Diet was scored with a healthy eating index from a food frequency questionnaire. Food security was classed with a six item federal scale. Perceived access to healthy food nearby was also reported. Tests compared diet scores, fast food use, and intake of fruit, vegetables, snacks, and sugar by security status. A further analysis asked whether nearby food access changed the link between security and diet quality.
pmc-13568079:
Kasem Khalil presented in 2026 a hardware guard for the way smart devices announce themselves on a network. The plug-and-play discovery method is light and center-free, but it leaks fixed identities that attackers can spoof, replay, or track. Software fixes rely on stored secrets and do not hide the discovery itself.

Khalil built a new physical unclonable function, a circuit whose tiny build quirks act as an uncopyable fingerprint. The design layers recursive delays and fresh randomness to resist learning attacks. Paired with a hardware accelerator, it keeps discovery private and proves each device is genuine.
pmc-13568179:
Dental fillings fail most often when bacteria colonize the seam and carve new decay beneath. Chuan-Chi Chen and co-authors review in this 2026 paper how to build germ-fighting power into the filling material itself, judging designs by their polymer structure rather than by the agent alone.

Fillings that leak their killer work fast but run dry and weaken with water uptake. Agents locked into the network keep working at the surface for longer. Mineral and metal particles add their own effects, from ion release to light-driven attack. The authors stress that lasting protection must survive chewing, aging, and safety checks, not just lab tests.
pmc-13568279:
Minh Long Hoang compares seven versions of a classic learning method for spotting human activities from wearable sensors. His 2026 study covers support vector machines, widely used in health care, smart homes, and mobile apps to tell walking, sitting, and other motions apart. Most past work used a single kernel, the part that shapes how the method compares data points.

All seven variants were tested in one shared setup, with the same data cleaning and the same tuning search. Kernel based versions beat plain and shortcut models. A version that blends several kernels scored highest, just above the standard radial kernel version, by drawing on more than one view of the data. The study gives builders a fair ranking of the options.
pmc-13568379:
Allan Roberto Amorim da Silva and co-authors present a 2026 study on software shells that let factories swap product variants fast. In mass-customized production, new variants arrive faster than certified machine models can be rebuilt. Their design splits each digital shell into a reactive layer and separate decision services that can be deployed on their own.

On the buyer side, process steps name the skill each step needs. On the maker side, offered skills map to the skills that perform them. Tests ran on a university robot that drives screws, not a live line. Of 104 calls for bids, 102 drew a reply, with a middle wait of four seconds.
pmc-13569879:

pmc-13570679:

pmc-13570879:

pmc-13572079:
Van Hattem and three co-authors review a bedside score used in heart surgery care in a 2026 paper. pmc-13572379:

pmc-13572479:

pmc-13572579:

pmc-13572779:

pmc-13573479:

pmc-13573679:
Meng Yuan and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, machine learning models that predict thirty-day death after cardiac arrest complicated by kidney injury. Both events together strain intensive care, and early risk estimates guide hard decisions.

pmc-13573779:

pmc-13574379:
Tufan Gumus and four co-authors study lasting pain after liver donation surgery in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Living donors give part of their liver to save another person. pmc-13574779:

pmc-13574879:

pmc-13575179:

pmc-13575379:

pmc-13576779:

pmc-13576879:

pmc-13577179:

pmc-13577279:

pmc-13577479:

pmc-13577779:

pmc-13578179:

pmc-13578279:

pmc-13579379:

pmc-13579879:

pmc-13580379:

pmc-13582379:

pmc-13582579:

pmc-13582879:

pmc-13583179:

pmc-13583579:

pmc-13583679:

pmc-13583779:

pmc-13583979:

pmc-13584379:
Maoyao Ling and colleagues probe how a breathing machine can injure the lungs it is meant to save, using mice in this 2026 study. Strong air pressure can trigger fierce inflammation in lung tissue, a problem called ventilator-induced lung injury. The team focused on two pathways: a cell-stress pathway named PERK and an immune sensor named NOD1, each feeding a master inflammation switch.

Mice breathed at high volume for four hours and came out with damaged, leaky lungs and high levels of inflammatory signals. Mice bred without the NOD1 sensor fared better, and a drug that blocks the PERK pathway also eased the harm. Using both blocks at once protected the lungs most of all, which hints that care may need to hit more than one pathway.
pmc-13584779:
Jintao An and co-authors simulate how drilling fluid escapes into shallow formations under deep water, a costly hazard of offshore wells. Such formations are loose, porous, and easily cracked, leaving a narrow band of safe pressure. Their 2026 study builds a coupled model that mixes finite and discrete elements. It tracks fluid through the rock matrix and through opening fractures at once, and checks the results against a South China Sea field case.

Slow seepage through the rock stayed limited and pressure-driven. Once pressure hit the cracking point, fresh fractures opened express lanes and losses jumped sharply. Repeated pressure swings weakened the rock near the well and narrowed the safe band further. Porosity, permeability, fluid thickness, and pressure history all steered the loss size. The authors say the work clarifies how mild breathing of a formation can tip into severe loss, guiding pressure management at the rig.
pmc-13585079:
Lomada Lakshmidevi and five co-authors compared two single-file rotary systems in two thousand twenty-six for root canal care in children's molars. Hand filing with steel tools is slow and has drawbacks. Nickel-titanium rotary files are faster, and single-file versions simplify the job further. Two such systems, Kedo-S and XP-Endo Shaper, went head to head.

Fifty molars in children aged four to nine were split evenly between the systems. Timing was clocked, and fill quality was graded from X-rays by standard criteria. The XP-Endo Shaper was significantly quicker, with more optimal fills and fewer voids, though fill quality overall did not differ significantly between groups.
pmc-13585179:
Ran Sun and co-authors use first-principles calculations to map which phase of a cobalt-tungsten catalyst is active during carbon nanotube growth, published in 2026. These catalysts are among the most promising for growing nanotubes with a set chirality, or twist. Which phase does the work, and how it changes during growth, has been debated.

The team built phase diagrams for the cobalt, tungsten, and carbon system. The diagrams vary with temperature, carbon supply, and the ratio of the two metals. At low carbon supply, one intermetallic phase is favored. At higher supply, carbide phases form in sequence. The picture unifies phases reported before into one framework, and suggests carbon supply itself steers the catalyst phase.
pmc-13585479:
Xiang Yao and co-authors review how artificial intelligence could tailor bone-protecting drugs to each patient, in a 2026 paper. Bisphosphonates are the standard treatment for osteoporosis, but diagnosis lags, responses vary, and rare harms like jaw bone death worry doctors. The team searched three major databases across twenty years of work at the meeting point of these drugs and computing.

They map four uses. Learning systems can scan routine CT images to catch silent spine fractures and grade bone quality. They can forecast who will gain bone density and who should switch drugs. They can flag patients at risk of the rare harms before they strike. And modeling can design carriers that deliver the drug to bone with less spill. Gaps in openness and validation remain.
pmc-13585579:
Ting Liu and co-authors review trials of traditional Chinese medicine added to standard stroke care, in this 2026 paper. Ischemic stroke is a top cause of death and disability, and these formulas are widely used beside standard care in East Asia. The reviewers judged each formula on its own rather than lumping them together.

Nine randomized trials with more than twelve thousand patients covered eight formulas across three phases of care. Because the trials measured outcomes differently, the results were not pooled. Two formulas improved function scores after acute stroke in their trials. Two others showed no clear difference from standard care. The review grades the strength of evidence behind each claim.
pmc-13585679:
Jun-young Seo, Jiseon Kang, Do Hoon Kim, and Namkug Kim test whether a deep learning model can help doctors spot stomach infection from camera images taken during endoscopy. The infection, caused by a common bacterium, is a major driver of stomach disease. Finding it from images alone would spare patients invasive tests.

The team built the model on cases from a large medical center in Seoul, confirmed by lab tests. Fourteen readers of varied experience then read images twice, once on their own and once with the model's help. Scores covered accuracy at both the single-image and whole-patient levels. The reader study asks whether the tool lifts real clinical judgment, not just machine scores.
pmc-13585779:
Rafael Quirino Moreira and colleagues sampled animals where wildlife meets livestock in Brazil in 2026, hunting for leptospirosis bacteria. The disease spreads worldwide among domestic and wild animals, thriving in warm, wet conditions. The study site sat where two major Brazilian ecosystems meet, and blood samples were tested to trace which animals carry the pathogen at that shared edge.

Results pointed to small mammals sharing ground with livestock as important hosts, with signs of further unstudied reservoirs in the farm ecosystem. The authors call for work on how long the bacteria survive in soil and water, genetic typing of local strains, and wider host surveys to clarify how infection moves between species.
pmc-13585979:
Elena Moreno-Charco and seven co-authors pool studies from 2026 on mental health and seizures in a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis type 1. Past estimates of how common these problems are varied widely. The team searched three databases and merged fifty studies, also splitting out a subgroup whose gene fault is a larger deletion.

About one in three patients had attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and about one in nine had autism or seizures. Learning disability was far more common in the deletion subgroup than in the group as a whole. Depression and anxiety each affected roughly one in eight. Screening for these problems is urged.
pmc-13586479: Hongbo Gao and Wencai Weng sound a caution about a blood-based score in rectal cancer care, in a 2026 letter. The score, called the pan-immune-inflammation value, is built from four blood cell counts. It has been used to judge how patients fare on immune therapy. The authors warn that in one small subgroup of sixteen patients, the effects of chemoradiotherapy cannot be separated from the effects of the immune drug itself. Other unadjusted factors cloud the reading further, so the score needs careful handling in such studies.
pmc-13586579:
Xin Li and co-authors build a smart wound dressing from liquid metal and spider silk protein, in a research paper from 2026. The dressing takes the form of striped microneedles that can bend and coil on command. Such active dressings aim to watch a wound and adjust care in real time.

Droplets of gallium-based liquid metal sit inside a matrix of lab-made spider silk protein, cast into uneven needle stripes. Near-infrared light triggers the bending, while tiny channels steer wound fluid along set paths with no pump. The metal core doubles as a soft electrode and energy harvester that senses its own motion. Bandages loaded with a growth factor wrapped skin wounds snugly and sped closure in animal tests, with no clear toxicity.
pmc-13586879:
Li Hao and four co-authors model how acid eats into sandstone over time, weakening it from the grains up. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Acid mine drainage attacks rock around mines, and the damage couples chemistry with mechanics.

Sandstone samples soaked in dilute sulfuric acid for up to twenty days. Mineral scans, microscope images, and solution chemistry tracked the decay, while compression tests at three pressures measured strength. Carbonate dissolved steadily and cement degraded; peak strength fell by roughly a quarter to a third. A time-based damage model reproduced the stress curves across all conditions. The framework links what acid does to minerals with what engineers measure as failure.
pmc-13586979:
Anna Lagerdahl and Vanessa Butorova survey cancer support services in a 2026 paper. Distress is a common and serious response to cancer. Specialist psycho-oncology teams help patients carry that load, yet provision varies widely across the UK and national data on staffing and access were missing.

An eighteen item survey went to services through professional networks. Twenty five NHS services led by psychologists replied, all in England and Scotland. They reported staffing, referrals, wait times, and activity for 2022 and 2023, scaled by full time staff. The snapshot shows where patients wait longest and where teams run thinnest.
pmc-13587379:
Yibin Cai and colleagues test a blood inflammation score as a forecast tool in esophageal cancer. The cancer, of the squamous type in the food pipe, is often found at a locally advanced stage, where chemo plus radiation is the main hope of cure. Outcomes still scatter widely, so the team asked whether the pan-immune inflammation value, a score built from routine blood counts, could sort patients before treatment began.

Their 2026 study covered 696 patients who received that combined treatment. Higher scores traveled with bigger tumors and, in both simple and adjusted models, with shorter overall and cancer-free survival. The link bent rather than running straight, and it held in nearly every subgroup. Blending the score with standard staging split patients into three risk bands more sharply than staging alone. The authors offer the pairing as a cheap guide for tailoring care.
pmc-13587479:
Ida Höijer and co-authors report a 2026 study on how to read the results of gene editing more fully. When the CRISPR tool cuts DNA, cells can end up with a mix of edits, called mosaicism. Rare large changes are hard to spot with standard reads.

The team used long, highly exact reads from PacBio machines, with no copying step before reading. They tested edited zebrafish and their young across thirty samples. Coverage was deep, and each read came from a single DNA strand. Long copying by PCR gave a less even picture by contrast. The method helps labs check both intended cuts and stray cuts with more trust.
pmc-13588779:
Song, Yuan and their co-authors track brain dynamics over time in people with methamphetamine use disorder, in work listed for 2026. Brain function and structure can recover during abstinence, but large network changes after long abstinence were unclear.

Using resting scans and an energy landscape method, the team compared patients and healthy controls at baseline and after long abstinence. Patients showed rigid brain dynamics tied to poor network coordination and behavior. After abstinence, flexibility partly improved. Baseline dynamic measures also predicted how much craving would change later. The authors propose these measures as markers for craving change.
pmc-13588879:
Dawid Plutecki and co-authors pool anatomy studies in a 2026 paper on arm nerves. The nerve web of the upper arm holds many cross links between its cords, each with its own name and pattern. Surgeons and nerve testers need to know how common each link is and how it varies.

Nine major databases were searched for studies of six named cross links, from the Martin-Gruber link in the forearm to links in the hand. Rates, sizes, and types were pooled across studies. A current, complete map of these variants helps clinicians read odd test results and plan surgery around the links a patient may hold.
pmc-13589079:
Antonis Armoundas, Constantine Tarabanis, and Joseph Loscalzo sort out the two ways artificial intelligence enters medical trials. Their 2026 paper draws a line that shapes the whole review. In one role the tool is itself the treatment under test; in the other it props up the trial, from design and sign-up to checks and reports.

That split matters, the authors argue, because the proof each role needs is not the same. A tool that steers care needs trials planned in advance with tight oversight. A tool that runs back-office steps is judged more on speed, accuracy, and safe use in real wards. The paper walks through each phase of a trial, weighs the proof at hand, and marks the gaps that still block sound use.
pmc-13589479:
Federica Tavaglione and Rohit Loomba review a fast-growing drug family for a serious liver disease called MASH. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. In MASH, fat and scarring build up in the liver, and the first approved drugs have only just arrived.

The drugs covered here copy a gut hormone called GLP-1, alone or paired with one or two partner hormones. They act on sugar and fat handling across many organs, and they also help the heart and kidneys. The review walks through how each type works and what phase two and phase three trials found on liver scarring. Open questions remain about how long treatment should last, how well patients tolerate the drugs, and why responses vary.
pmc-13589579:
Mohadese Panaei and co-authors load an old drug on tiny coal dots that free it when a cell guard runs high. The study appeared in 2026. The drug is an old anti-drink pill with fresh cancer hopes. Set free at the wrong place, it wastes its force.

The dots bear sulfur tags that let the drug hang by a split link. Load yield hit near three in four. In plain baths the shells held near shut for a day, an off state. With the guard high and sour bath, near four in five freed in a day, the on state. Breast tumor cells took the test in glass runs.
pmc-13589979:
Anna Mingazzini and four co-authors reviewed extra drug therapy after curative treatment for liver cancer in a 2026 paper. Even after surgery or ablation, this cancer often returns, from hidden remnants or fresh growth. No added therapy is standard today, and older drug classes failed in this role.

Interest has shifted to immune drugs that free T cells to attack tumors, above all one antibody given after surgery. A large trial of that drug against placebo found no gain in time without return. The authors read this as proof that immune blocking alone, without picking patients by leftover disease, is not enough. Giving such drugs before or around surgery remains little explored and may work better while the tumor is still present.
pmc-13590079:
Kosuke Horita and seven co-authors made a spin method run on its own to clean gene therapy virus stock, sorting full capsids from empty ones. Their 2026 set-up links zonal-rotor cesium chloride ultracentrifugation with an ÄKTA chromatography platform. It loads, watches, and takes off each slice by itself. Plain column work often fails to split the intermediate capsids.

Bench runs mapped the density band, then the plan scaled up to a one point six five liter rotor. Of two virus products, one full slice was ninety-five point five percent full, with empty capsids at zero point four percent. The other was ninety-one point eight percent full, with no empty capsids found. Recoveries rose as high as ninety-three point four percent. The slice in between held some DNA signal but showed weak expression in cells. They pitch it as a scalable polishing step for virus making.
pmc-13590279:
Jianhua Mu and co-authors build a machine learning model that flags the risk of a bone cancer spreading to the lungs, in a study from 2026. Spread to the lungs is a top cause of death in this cancer, called osteosarcoma. Standard checks often catch the spread late. The team mined medical records from 522 patients for early warning signs.

They narrowed the clues to twelve factors, from blood clotting times to tumor size. Eleven models were built and compared. A gradient boosting model won, with strong scores in training and fair scores on fresh cases. A tool that ranks each factor's push showed tumor size mattered most. Blood and immune clues also counted. The authors say the open, explained model could guide closer watch on high-risk patients.
pmc-13591279:
Florine de Haes and co-authors present a 2026 study of reusable cloth in operating rooms. Hospitals pollute a lot, and surgery suites drive a large share through throwaway packs. The team compared full disposable trays with hybrid trays that swap in washable drapes and gowns. Three surgery types fed the test, from womb scopes to limb work and cesarean births.

A full life cycle audit covered 18 harm types under set global norms. Hybrid trays scored lower on nearly every type. On climate harm, the cut ran from 40 to 51 percent. In throwaway trays, the drapes and gowns drove much of the load. The results make a strong case for bringing washable cloth back to the suite.
pmc-13591479:
Rachel Cianciolo and co-authors review evidence that a growth factor drives kidney scarring in dogs and cats, in this 2026 paper. The factor is well tied to kidney fibrosis in rodents and humans. Small-animal proof has grown through blood and urine markers, tissue gene reads, and cell culture work.

Strong signs come from natural kidney disease in cats and a genetic model in dogs. Yet lab proof has snags: stains for the active factor in pet tissue are weak and cross-react with its stored form. How the factor wakes scar cells in pets stays open. The authors map agreement and gaps for future work.
pmc-13591979:
Roee Admon and a large team of co-authors set out in 2026 the design of a long-term study of survivors of the Nova music festival attack. The October 2023 assault killed hundreds at the festival, and survivors endured hours of life threat in a tight window, many while under the influence of substances taken for the party.

That grim uniformity makes the group scientifically precious for learning how trauma settles into body and mind. The protocol layers brain scans, biology, and psychology over years. The aim is prediction: spotting early who will recover and who will need the most help.
pmc-13592779:
Orleane Souza de Brito and three co-authors hunted asbestos fibers in water near a dead mine in Brazil. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with Bom Jesus da Serra in Bahia. A mine there dug chrysotile for near three decades and was left with no clean up. Brazil banned the fiber in twenty seventeen, but old sites still leak. The team took surface water and silt in late twenty twenty-two.

They read the samples for the fiber's presence in kind. The aim was to show if the banned carcinogen still rides the town's streams. Readers in health and land care get ground truth for a site whose risk was long just feared, not read.
pmc-13592879:
Fran Espinoza-Carhuancho and five co-authors map in 2026 world research on bisphenol and other hormone-disrupting chemicals in heart disease. Output on the topic grows fast, yet its shape and leaders were uncharted. A scientometric map can show who works with whom and where themes drift.

The study covers 2019 to 2024 in the Scopus database, keeping papers with bisphenol in title or abstract. In all, 640 documents in 402 sources qualify, with a yearly growth rate of 6.1 percent. More than 3500 authors take part, and about eighteen percent of papers cross borders. Citation and network tools chart the field's hubs. The map guides new teams toward gaps and partners.
pmc-13593079:
Tian Zou and co-authors tested enzyme links to gut organ diseases in two thousand twenty-six. Cathepsins are protein-cutting enzymes inside cell compartments. They stir inflammation and tissue remodeling. Gallbladder, bile duct, and pancreas diseases share those traits. Simple observation cannot prove the enzymes cause disease. The team used Mendelian randomization for causal leverage.

Gene variants tied to enzyme levels in blood served as tools. Outcome data covered six related diseases. Gallstones and gallbladder inflammation were included. Two chronic bile duct diseases were also tested. Acute and chronic pancreas inflammation completed the set. Genetic evidence can separate cause from consequence. Findings point to which enzymes merit drug attention.
pmc-13593579:
Martyniuk and McNeil appraise in 2026 OpenEvidence, a web-based artificial intelligence tool that answers clinicians' questions at the point of care. The product presents itself as an AI copilot for doctors facing high-stakes decisions.

The review describes how the tool works. A clinician types a question in natural language, even a long one carrying full patient case details. The answer is a synthesized summary of the research with a linked reference list, plus suggested follow-up questions. Its maker stresses that sources accompany every answer and calls the product a search engine rather than an answer engine. Access is free for verified health professionals and students in Canada and the United States, with occupational proof required. The appraisal walks through the registered and public versions and the audience the product targets.
pmc-13593679:
Xiaoxiao Li and a sizable team examined whether chrysophanol, a natural compound from the anthraquinone family, can protect the kidneys during sepsis, the body's overwhelming response to infection. Their 2026 work paired cell experiments on human kidney cells with a mouse model in which a bacterial toxin triggers septic kidney injury.

In the cell tests, pretreatment with chrysophanol kept more cells alive. It lowered the output of inflammatory signals such as IL-6 and TNF-α, raised the calming signal IL-10, and cut levels of damaging reactive oxygen. In the mice it reduced tissue damage, cell death, and scarring in the kidneys, and standard blood measures of kidney function improved. The authors present the compound as a promising protective candidate, while noting that exactly how it works at the molecular level remains to be pinned down.
pmc-13593879:
Rongchang Liu and co-authors build a fast lab test for a virus that kills young geese, in a paper from 2026. The virus, goose adenovirus type 4, causes liver damage in goslings. Death rates can reach eighty percent in bad outbreaks. It was first found in China in 2022 and has spread through the main goose-raising regions since then.

Their test copies and counts the virus's DNA in real time, aimed at a key shell gene. It proved sharp, steady, and free of false hits from like viruses. The team then ran it on 582 samples from farms and clinics. It found more true cases than the older standard test, and extra hits were confirmed by sequencing. The authors say the test gives farms a solid tool for tracking and control. That can help limit losses in the goose trade.
pmc-13594479:
Daisuke Yoshimoto and co-authors describe a simple electrical trick for placing a pacing lead in the Bachmann bundle, the bridge that carries signals to the left atrium. Pacing there may cut the onset and persistence of atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 single-center series covers fifty patients. In each, the approach was attempted during pacemaker or defibrillator implantation.

Operators advanced the lead delivery system from the great vein toward the atrium and fixed the lead just below the spot where the atrial signal abruptly grew stronger. Every patient received a septal lead, and in forty-four the paced tracing met the criteria for true bundle capture, with mapping taking only a couple of minutes. Thresholds improved by the end of the procedure and stayed stable over six months, with no dislodgements, fluid around the heart, or infections.
pmc-13594779:
New vessels in the retina drown sight, and the standard shots block one growth signal while the fire that lit them burns on. Siyu Jiang and nine co-authors aim a spice-born drug at both in 2026. Curcumin fights both fire and vessel growth, but it will not dissolve or travel well in the eye.

Wrapped in a plastic shell a hair over a hundred nanometres wide, it can be shot into the eye. Two mouse stands test it: pups starved of air, and a bred line that grows its own vessels. Cell-level gene reads and chemistry maps trace its path: it damps the alarm hub first, then the vessel cascade below. Retention in the eye is tracked by glow.
pmc-13595079:
Haiyan Hu, Fangfang Deng, and Bo Chen study recovery after hip fracture in older adults in a 2026 paper. Hip fractures often trigger lasting loss of daily function. Frailty, a state of low physical reserve, might make that loss worse in two ways. It could deepen the drop caused by the fracture itself, or simply mark a worse outlook. The team used a Chinese aging survey covering 2011 to 2020 to separate the two roles.

Each fracture case was matched with up to four peers without fracture. Fracture clearly added difficulty in daily tasks, beyond normal change. That added drop did not clearly grow with frailty scores. But among fracture patients, the chance of staying alive with function intact fell steeply as frailty rose. The authors say frailty predicts a poorer outlook after fracture, rather than clearly amplifying the fracture's own effect.
pmc-13595179:
Sooyeon Song and three colleagues studied how often older veterans get orthopedic care that brings little or no benefit. Such low-value care wastes money and is a target of federal policy. The team asked whether use of these services varies by region, and whether regions high in one service are high in others.

The study used Medicare claims for veterans aged sixty-five and older who saw an orthopedic surgeon. It tracked five low-value services across hospital referral regions. Looking at services together matters for policy. If high use clusters in some regions, broad local fixes may work best. If each service varies on its own, fixes must target one service at a time.
pmc-13595579:
Kyle Stokes and a large team of co-authors report a way to freeze human brain organoids, in two thousand twenty-six. Organoids are small lab-grown clusters that mimic parts of the cortex. A fast-freeze method that limits ice crystals is used for eggs and early embryos, and the team adapted it here.

After thawing, the frozen organoids matched fresh ones in cell growth, cell death, and cell types. Electrical tests also showed like activity in both groups. Early signs suggest the clusters can be stored for over a year and shipped far with little harm. The method could help labs bank and share these models.
pmc-13597179:
Jintao He leads a large team in charting a drug-proof germ behind hospital lung infections across China. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, shrugs off carbapenem drugs in most cases and drives high death rates. Large nationwide data on the pneumonia form were scarce.

They read the genomes of over eight hundred samples from dozens of hospitals for two years. Four in five prove drug-proof, and deaths run far higher in those cases than in tame ones. One strain type rules, and one gene drives most of the drug proof. Some drugs still work. Strain families split by region, and one clone packs more harm genes than the rest.
pmc-13597279:
Dediu, Zielinski, Preoteasa, and Bulzan reappraised treatment order for early triple-negative breast cancer in twenty twenty-six. For stage I tumors of this aggressive subtype, guidelines favor chemotherapy before surgery, a plan borrowed from trials in larger tumors.

The authors reviewed registry studies and meta-analyses comparing chemo-first with surgery-first care in stage I disease. The retrospective data linked surgery first, then chemotherapy, to better survival. Adding platinum drugs before surgery raised tumor disappearance rates but gave inconsistent survival gains. Capecitabine given after surgery, by contrast, showed a robust long-term benefit. The authors propose a stage-specific plan: operate first, then give chemotherapy built on standard drug families plus capecitabine, avoiding possible undertreatment from the chemo-first route in small tumors.
pmc-13597679:
Cexiong Fu and four co-authors build, in a 2026 study, machine learning models that predict liver cancer from routine hospital data. Early detection improves the odds in this cancer, yet models built on ward data were thin. The team drew files on over nine thousand patients at a hospital in Hainan, China, from 2020 to 2023.

Seventy-four variables per patient fed six model kinds, after a selection step kept the strongest terms. One boosted tree model won, with top scores in training and sound scores in held-out validation. Its predictions also gave the best net benefit across decision thresholds in a clinical utility test. A tool that splits credit among inputs named the top predictors: a blood sugar acid, a liver enzyme ratio, and a bile enzyme led the list. The authors call for checks in outpatients and high-risk groups before wide use.
pmc-13597779:
Mohamed Habib and co-authors published this animal study in 2026. Chemotherapy patients often suffer chemobrain: foggy thinking that lingers after treatment. The drug doxorubicin is a known trigger, disturbing brain chemistry and the glutamate balance that neurons depend on. The team tested whether lurasidone, a psychiatric drug with pro-cognitive effects, could protect the brain. Forty-eight male rats were split into control, drug-only, chemo-only, and combined groups.

Chemo-only rats performed badly on memory and maze tests. Their brain tissue showed oxidative stress, inflammation, neuron loss, and weakened growth signaling in memory regions. Glutamate ran high while its calming counterpart GABA fell. Rats given both drugs fared far better on behavior. Signaling recovered, the chemical balance normalized, and tissue damage eased. The authors call this the first evidence that lurasidone can blunt doxorubicin chemobrain. They propose it as a candidate therapy worth further study.
pmc-13597879:
Nitin Bansode and co-authors review fresh ways to make circular RNA, a ring-shaped cousin of the messenger RNAs in vaccines. Their 2026 review notes the ring form shrugs off chewing enzymes, lasts longer in cells, and still builds protein without a cap. Those traits suit vaccines, cancer drugs, and gene fixes.

Classic builds stitch rings with enzymes or self-cutting RNA. Newer chemical and mixed routes close rings faster, scale better, and allow custom edits along the chain. Delivery trucks and deep data checks add strength to the field. Hurdles in yield and purity stay on the table. The review weighs each route's gains and limits for makers.
pmc-13598179:
Jingna Xun and co-authors report a small trial of a plant medicine in people with HIV. Their 2026 paper tests Euphorbia kansui, used in traditional Chinese medicine. The aim was to wake latent virus hiding in cells while patients stayed on standard therapy. That wake-up step is part of a shock and kill plan for a cure.

Nine men took part at a Shanghai center, in three dose plans over one or two weeks. Signs of waking virus showed mostly in the first week. Four people had at least a twofold rise in one viral marker. Two had brief rises in blood virus levels. Stored viral DNA did not fall for good. No serious side effects were seen, and the authors call for more study.
pmc-13598879:
Edson Marchiori, Bruno Hochhegger, and Gláucia Zanetti present an imaging case of a rare, harmless cause of chest pain, in this 2026 report. Their patient was a thirty-five-year-old man with a week of discomfort low in the right chest, worsening over three days. He had no injury and no other illness, and his blood tests, chest X-ray, and heart tracing were all normal. Doctors first suspected a blood clot in the lung.

A CT scan with contrast showed the true culprit: an oval pocket of fat beside the heart, ringed by a soft-tissue rim. The picture fits mediastinal fat necrosis, a brief, self-limited death of a small fat deposit. No procedure was needed; common anti-inflammatory painkillers eased his pain. The case teaches a useful lesson: a classic scan pattern can spare a patient clot treatment and further invasive tests.
pmc-13599579:
Michael E. Cloesmeijer and colleagues ask in 2026 why people with milder hemophilia A respond so differently to one drug. Hemophilia A is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by low levels of clotting factor VIII. Desmopressin can raise those levels, but the size of the rise varies by person, and the gene variant each patient carries plays a large part. Doctors now test each person before relying on the drug.

The team applied machine learning to a population model built from 1,441 patients carrying 55 different variants in the F8 gene. Ten variants shifted the response in a clear way. Three blunted the rise, one cutting it by more than half. Seven boosted it, the strongest reaching over three times the typical level. Delivery route mattered too: nose and skin routes peaked lower than a vein drip. Adding patient factors cut unexplained variation nearly in half, toward predicting response without a test dose.
pmc-13599679:
Anna-Kay West and six colleagues test new probe designs for studying how carrier proteins pass building blocks along enzyme assembly lines. Such lines make polyketides, fatty acids, and peptides. The team built light-reactive copies of pantetheine, the arm that carries growing chains.

Their probes use a diazirine group that can link to nearby proteins when lit. The team loaded the probes onto a carrier protein from Escherichia coli and tested linking with a second enzyme. The results expose design limits for these crypto-acyl carrier protein probes. That lesson should help chemists build better tools for catching brief protein contacts.
pmc-13600379:
Xia Gan and a large team test whether body makeup read from scans predicts cancer outcomes, in this 2026 paper. Their patients had nasopharyngeal cancer that had come back or spread, treated first with chemo plus immune therapy. Doctors lack good markers to sort these patients or to check early whether treatment works.

The team studied 199 patients, and 99 of them also had scans after two treatment rounds. Patients who began with more skeletal muscle lived longer without the disease growing, survived longer overall, and responded better. Keeping muscle steady or gaining a little in the early rounds also tracked with better survival. A deeper fall in belly fat density helped too. The authors suggest routine scans, already taken for care, can double as a cheap outlook marker.
pmc-13600579:
Michael G Ross, writing alone, examines how weak science enters obstetric malpractice cases about brain injury in newborns. Claims that a baby's brain damage was caused during pregnancy or delivery must rest on sound proof of cause, he argues. Yet cerebral palsy cases are among the costliest in medicine, and they attract theories built on shaky ground. Judges decide which expert claims count as science under standards such as Daubert and Frye.

Ross walks through popular theories blaming newborn brain injury on events around birth, critiquing each against basic physiology. pmc-13646379:

Guidelines set flag levels for both fasting and non-fasting samples, plus a severe range that demands checks for pancreas risk. The authors find that reporting still varies widely between labs. That spread can hide related metabolic disease and delay treatment. Their review pushes for standard wording and thresholds across the country.
pmc-13647279:

pmc-13647379:
Kei-Fong Ng and nine colleagues mine the roots of Aconitum coreanum, a monkshood plant, for new alkaloid chemicals and test them against a cancer immune shield. All the new finds share a classic skeleton for this plant family, with varied oxidation patterns, and four carry a rare sulfonate group never seen in this class.

Microscope staining confirmed the effect for the strongest few. The authors claim a first: this alkaloid family can modulate PD-L1. pmc-13647579:

Complications that bend recovery, such as spasticity, frailty, and seizures after stroke, get dedicated attention.

The authors keep quality of life and return to social life in view as the true endpoints, not test scores alone. Evidence-based, patient-centered care is their stated standard throughout. The closing sections chart future directions for stroke survivors and frail older people, the groups with the most to gain from rehabilitation that adapts to the person.
pmc-13648179:
Neo, Fa, and Zhou build in 2026 a cross cultural framework for existential distress in palliative care, called the Personhood Pentadigm. pmc-13649279:

In pulmonary arterial hypertension, high pressure in lung vessels drives muscle cells in the walls to multiply, narrowing the vessel. Current drugs widen vessels but leave some patients with poor outlooks.

pmc-13649379:
Ioannis Theocharis and Björn Bohnenkamp set out a workshop tool that uses futures literacy to probe how homes might revalue stored stuff. Cutting demand is a leg of climate action, and clear-outs are one door in. Most clear-out aids stay solo and stuck in the now, though.

Blocking it did the reverse. The protein paired with a partner that steers waste sacs to disposal, and the pair grew closer under fat stress. The authors see this as a new shield for vessel health.
pmc-13649679:

pmc-13650679:

Inside the tissue, overactivated immune cells, a fired-up inflammatory sensor complex, faltering support cells, and a disrupted blood-brain barrier amplify neuronal and synaptic damage, while viral evasion tricks prolong the assault. pmc-13651579:
Zakaria Yahya Khawaji and co-authors describe a 62-year-old woman whose yellowed skin traced back to an overactive thyroid, not her gallstone. Further tests showed heart failure and a congested liver, while a scope cleared the bile ducts of obstruction. pmc-13651879:
César Feniou and five colleagues present a new algorithm for doing chemistry calculations on fault-tolerant quantum computers. pmc-13652379:
Abdulaziz and co-authors report the removal of a giant, rare liver cancer from a 32-year-old man. The tumor weighed twelve kilograms and stretched thirty-four units across. Fewer than thirty cases of this cancer variant have ever been reported, and it tends to strike young adults.

Drug treatment first was ruled out by his weakness and hunger state. Surgeons removed the left half of the liver with the tumor. A stapling mishap in the warped anatomy forced them to rebuild the liver's blood inflow and bile path on the spot. The case shows the strain of late, huge tumors.
pmc-13652479:
Roberta Boffo and co-authors report a breast reconstruction that avoided implants entirely. Her recovery was smooth, and the rebuilt breast kept good volume and symmetry. Doing the fat grafting at once may spare patients later touch-up operations, and the flank harvesting adds a contouring bonus. pmc-13652679:
Gene sequencing of spinal fluid for brain infection in newborns is assessed in a Chinese-language paper led by Li. Sequencing results helped shape care decisions in twenty-three infants, guiding treatment changes or allowing antibiotics to be reduced or stopped. Li and colleagues conclude that spinal-fluid sequencing can support diagnosis and decisions in newborn brain infection.
pmc-13652779:

pmc-13654179:

Long after, a coil worked its way into the colon, an unusual late event the title flags. The case walks through the signs, the scans, and the treatment choices. It warns teams that gut bleeding after such a repair may trace back to the coils themselves.
pmc-13655879:

The models are meant to support doctors, not replace lab proof. A fast, fair guess early in care can steer the first choice of drugs. The study checks whether the tools stay accurate outside their home hospital, a step many such models fail.
pmc-13655979:
Katelyn Battista and co-authors check whether the COVID-19 pandemic changed self-poisoning rates among Swedish youth, in a 2026 study. The authors urge readiness for the side effects of future health crises.
pmc-13657579:

Later pain and blood-stained vomit marked the moment the sac burst into the gut and emptied itself. He recovered fully with watchful care alone. pmc-13657679:

pmc-13657779:

pmc-13657879:

pmc-13660179:

pmc-13662279:

pmc-13662879:

pmc-13664079:

pmc-13669479:

The authors report the technique is workable in the office, and that patients bore it well.
pmc-13671479:

pmc-13671679:

pmc-13672079:

pmc-13672179:

pmc-13672279:

pmc-13672779:

pmc-13672979:

pmc-13673279:

pmc-13674479:

pmc-13675479:

pmc-13675579:

pmc-13677779:

pmc-13677979:

pmc-13678079:

pmc-13678279:
